alkali, and intersected by clumps of the dwarfish chaparral bushes.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Dr. Watson, a recently returned army surgeon whose health was ruined in Afghanistan, meets young Stamford in London while seeking inexpensive lodgings. Stamford introduces him to Sherlock Holmes, a chemically skilled and eccentric researcher working in a hospital laboratory. Holmes demonstrates a new test that detects hæmoglobin and identifies blood stains, then agrees to share a suite of rooms with Watson in Baker Street. Holmes also infers that Watson has been in Afghanistan, though he does not explain how.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Dr. Watson returns to England after serving as an army surgeon in Afghanistan, wounded at Maiwand and weakened by enteric fever. In London, he seeks cheaper lodgings and meets Sherlock Holmes through young Stamford, agreeing to inspect rooms with him in Baker Street.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is introduced as an eccentric, highly knowledgeable investigator of chemistry and anatomy who works intermittently in a hospital laboratory. He discovers a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin, demonstrates its use in detecting blood stains, and agrees to share lodgings with Dr. Watson. Holmes correctly infers that Watson has been in Afghanistan without explaining his method.

records.l: young Stamford, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Young Stamford, formerly a dresser under Dr. Watson at Barts, meets Watson in London and takes him to the hospital laboratory. He describes Sherlock Holmes’s scientific interests and peculiar habits, introduces the two men, and warns Watson that Holmes may be difficult to understand.

records.l: London, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: London is where Dr. Watson stays after returning from India and where his finances deteriorate while he lives in a private hotel in the Strand. He meets young Stamford at the Criterion Bar and begins looking for more economical lodgings.

records.l: chemical laboratory, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The chemical laboratory is located in a wing of the hospital and is filled with bottles, tables, retorts, test-tubes, and Bunsen lamps. Sherlock Holmes works there on a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin.

records.l: Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Baker Street is the location of a suite of rooms that Sherlock Holmes has found and believes will suit him and Dr. Watson. Holmes and Watson plan to inspect and settle the arrangements there.

records.l: suite of rooms, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has his eye on a suite of rooms in Baker Street that can be shared with Dr. Watson. The two men agree to see the rooms and determine the arrangements together.

records.l: hæmoglobin, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes discovers a reagent that is precipitated by hæmoglobin and by nothing else. He dilutes a drop of blood in water and demonstrates the resulting reaction to Dr. Watson.

records.l: blood stains, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Blood stains can be difficult to distinguish from mud, rust, or fruit stains when found on clothing months after a suspected crime. Sherlock Holmes’s discovery is presented as a means of identifying them reliably, whether they are old or new.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes’ test, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes’ test uses a reagent that produces a mahogany colour and brownish precipitate when hæmoglobin is present. Holmes claims that it will provide a reliable medico-legal test for blood stains and could have affected numerous past criminal cases.

records.l: Afghanistan, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Afghanistan is where Dr. Watson served during the second Afghan war and was wounded at the battle of Maiwand. Holmes recognizes that Watson has been there, and Watson later reflects that he has experienced enough noise and excitement in Afghanistan to last him a lifetime.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Dr. John Watson moves into 221B, Baker Street, with Sherlock Holmes, and observes Holmes’s unusual habits, appearance, knowledge, and abilities. Watson learns that Holmes works as a consulting detective, applying observation, deduction, chemistry, anatomy, knowledge of crime, and other specialized skills to cases brought by official and private investigators. Holmes explains how he deduced that Watson had come from Afghanistan and correctly identifies a visitor as a retired sergeant of Marines. The chapter establishes Holmes’s confidence in the Science of Deduction and Analysis and his disdain for fictional detectives such as Dupin and Lecoq.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes moves into 221B, Baker Street, with Dr. John Watson and settles into a quiet, highly regular life. He reveals that he is a consulting detective who advises official and private investigators, and he demonstrates his powers of observation and deduction by identifying Watson’s past and a visitor’s former occupation.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Dr. John Watson moves his belongings from the hotel into 221B, Baker Street, and begins living with Sherlock Holmes. He becomes increasingly curious about Holmes, records Holmes’s areas of knowledge and ignorance, initially dismisses Holmes’s theories of deduction, and witnesses Holmes’s accurate deductions.

records.l: 221B Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: 221B, Baker Street consists of two comfortable bedrooms and a large, airy sitting-room with two broad windows. It becomes the shared residence of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson and serves as Holmes’s place of business, where clients and investigators come to consult him.

records.l: the Science of Deduction and Analysis, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Science of Deduction and Analysis is described as a discipline based on long and patient study of observation and reasoning. Sherlock Holmes applies it professionally, using small physical details to infer a person’s history, occupation, and circumstances.

records.l: consulting detective work, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Consulting detective work is Sherlock Holmes’s occupation. Government detectives and private investigators bring him evidence or cases when they are at fault, and he studies the details, draws on his knowledge of crime, and directs them toward the correct solution.

records.l: observation and deduction, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes treats observation and deduction as practical skills essential to his livelihood. He explains that his reasoning about Dr. John Watson’s military and medical appearance, injuries, complexion, and recent hardships led him to conclude that Watson had come from Afghanistan.

records.l: The Book of Life, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Book of Life is an article in a magazine that argues that an observant person can infer a man’s history and profession from details such as his fingernails, clothing, boots, callosities, expression, and shirt cuffs. Dr. John Watson considers its reasoning exaggerated and impractical, while Sherlock Holmes reveals that he wrote it and relies on its principles.

records.l: Dr. Watson's move into 221B, Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Dr. Watson concludes the arrangement for the rooms at 221B, Baker Street and moves his belongings from the hotel there that evening. He and Sherlock Holmes spend the next days unpacking and arranging their possessions before settling into their new surroundings.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has profound knowledge of chemistry, accurate but unsystematic knowledge of anatomy, practical knowledge of geology and British law, extensive knowledge of sensational literature, and skill with the violin, singlestick, boxing, and swordsmanship. His knowledge of literature, philosophy, and astronomy is described as nil, his knowledge of politics as feeble, and his botany as variable, while his ability to distinguish poisons is strong.

records.l: Afghanistan, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Afghanistan is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the place from which Dr. John Watson had recently come. Holmes reaches this conclusion by combining observations about Watson’s medical and military appearance, tropical complexion, illness, hardship, and injured left arm.

records.l: the retired sergeant of Marines, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The retired sergeant of Marines approaches 221B, Baker Street carrying a large blue envelope and looking for the correct number. Sherlock Holmes identifies him as a retired sergeant of Marines, and the man confirms that he was a sergeant in the Royal Marine Light Infantry before explaining that he is currently a commissionaire.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and the Doctor travel to 3, Lauriston Gardens after Tobias Gregson’s letter reports the body of Enoch J. Drebber in an empty house. Holmes examines the scene, the body, the blood, the footprints, and the objects found in Drebber’s pockets, concluding that Drebber was murdered by poison. Lestrade discovers the blood-red inscription “RACHE,” while Holmes argues that it means “revenge” in German rather than referring to a woman named Rachel. Holmes deduces that the murderer was a tall man who arrived with Drebber in a four-wheeled cab and smoked a Trichinopoly cigar, then leaves with the Doctor to question John Rance.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Tobias Gregson’s report and goes with the Doctor to 3, Lauriston Gardens. He examines the grounds, the body, the room, the blood, and the objects found in Enoch J. Drebber’s pockets, concluding that Drebber was murdered by poison. Holmes deduces that the murderer was a man over six feet tall, in the prime of life, with small feet, coarse square-toed boots, a florid face, long fingernails on his right hand, and a Trichinopoly cigar; he also infers that the man arrived with Drebber in a four-wheeled cab.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Doctor accompanies Sherlock Holmes to 3, Lauriston Gardens and observes the investigation and the body of Enoch J. Drebber. He reads Tobias Gregson’s letter aloud and records Holmes’s deductions about the crime.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber is identified by cards found in the pockets of the dead man at 3, Lauriston Gardens. He was from Cleveland, Ohio, and appears to have been preparing to return to New York.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson’s name is found on the fly-leaf of a pocket edition of Boccaccio’s Decameron in Enoch J. Drebber’s possession. A letter addressed to Stangerson is also found among Drebber’s belongings, and Tobias Gregson has sent inquiries about him.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Tobias Gregson writes to Sherlock Holmes about the body found at 3, Lauriston Gardens and meets Holmes and the Doctor at the house. He has preserved the interior but allowed the pathway to become crowded with footprints, and he reports the objects found in Enoch J. Drebber’s pockets and the inquiries sent about Joseph Stangerson.

records.l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Lestrade participates in the investigation at 3, Lauriston Gardens. He discovers the blood-red inscription “RACHE” on the wall and interprets it as the beginning of the female name Rachel, but Holmes says it is the German word for “revenge.”

records.l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes states that the murderer was a man over six feet tall and in the prime of life, with small feet, coarse square-toed boots, probably a florid face, and unusually long fingernails on his right hand. Holmes says the man smoked a Trichinopoly cigar and came to 3, Lauriston Gardens with Enoch J. Drebber in a four-wheeled cab drawn by a horse with three old shoes and one new shoe on its off fore leg.

records.l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: 3, Lauriston Gardens is an empty house off the Brixton Road where Enoch J. Drebber’s body is found. The house has a bare, dusty dining-room with a dirty window, a red wax candle, and a blood-red inscription on a section of exposed plaster.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The murder of Enoch J. Drebber occurs during the night at 3, Lauriston Gardens. There is no wound on Drebber, but blood is scattered around the room, a woman’s wedding-ring is found beneath the body, and Sherlock Holmes concludes that poison was used.

records.l: Enoch Drebber's death, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber’s death is discovered after a constable notices a light in the empty house at about two in the morning. His body shows an expression of horror and hatred, but no visible wound; Sherlock Holmes concludes that he died from poison.

records.l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The investigation at Lauriston Gardens is conducted by Tobias Gregson and Lestrade, with Sherlock Holmes and the Doctor observing and assisting. Holmes studies the grounds and room in detail, collects grey dust, examines the inscription, and asks for the address of John Rance, the constable who found the body.

records.l: poisoning, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies poison as the means by which Enoch J. Drebber was killed. The text gives no further details about the poison.

records.l: the letter for Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The letter from Tobias Gregson informs Sherlock Holmes that a well-dressed man has been found dead at 3, Lauriston Gardens. It identifies the man through cards bearing the name Enoch J. Drebber, reports blood in the room but no wound or apparent cause of death, and asks Holmes to come and give his opinion.

records.l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: A plain gold wedding-ring rolls out when Enoch J. Drebber’s body is lifted. Lestrade identifies it as a woman’s wedding-ring, which Tobias Gregson says complicates the case.

records.l: RACHE inscription, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The blood-red inscription consists of the single word “RACHE,” written on exposed plaster where the wallpaper has peeled away. Lestrade believes it is the unfinished name Rachel, while Sherlock Holmes says that “Rache” is German for “revenge.”

records.l: the body of Enoch J. Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The body of Enoch J. Drebber is found lying on the bare floor of the dining-room at 3, Lauriston Gardens. Drebber is middle-aged, broad-shouldered, dressed in respectable clothing, and has clenched hands, interlocked legs, and a face marked by horror and hatred; no wound is found on him.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson leave No. 3, Lauriston Gardens and visit constable John Rance to obtain firsthand evidence about the murder. Holmes explains his deductions about the two suspects, identifying Patent-leathers as shorter and Square-toes as a tall, agitated man who likely returned for the ring. Rance reports finding a tall, red-faced, drunken man in a brown overcoat near the house, whom Holmes believes was the second suspect. Holmes concludes that the writing “RACHE” was a deliberate false clue and continues pursuing the mystery.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains that the cab tracks, footprints, stride lengths, writing height, fingernail marks, and cigar ash led him to deductions about the suspects. He interviews John Rance and identifies the tall, red-faced drunken man as the second suspect, believing that the man returned for the ring. Holmes plans to use the ring as bait if necessary and describes the murder as a scarlet thread to be unraveled.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Doctor Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes from No. 3, Lauriston Gardens to question John Rance. He remains puzzled by several aspects of the case but recognizes that Rance’s description matches Holmes’s idea of the second suspect.

records.l: John Rance, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: John Rance tells Holmes and Watson that he found a light and a body inside the apparently empty house in Lauriston Gardens during his night beat. He also reports encountering a tall, red-faced, extremely drunken man in a brown overcoat near the gate, whom he and Murcher had to support.

records.l: the first suspect (Patent-leathers), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Patent-leathers is identified through marks in the dust as one of the two people who arrived at the house by cab. He walked around a puddle rather than across it and apparently stood still while Square-toes paced and became increasingly agitated.

records.l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Square-toes is identified as the taller man, whose stride measured about four and a half feet and whose writing was placed just over six feet high. He crossed a puddle by hopping over it, paced excitedly while talking, and is believed to be the tall, red-faced drunken man seen by John Rance; Holmes thinks he returned for the ring.

records.l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson leave No. 3, Lauriston Gardens after examining the scene of the murder. Holmes bases several deductions about the suspects and their movements on evidence found there.

records.l: Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The two houses in Lauriston Gardens were empty because their owner would not have the drains inspected, and the last tenant of one had died of typhoid fever. John Rance became suspicious when he saw a light in one of the houses during the night.

records.l: cab, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: A cab left two deep wheel ruts and distinctive hoof marks near the curb at No. 3, Lauriston Gardens. Holmes concludes that it arrived during the night and brought Patent-leathers and Square-toes to the house; Rance later reports hearing no cab after the drunken man was found.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The murder occurred inside the empty house in Lauriston Gardens after the two suspects entered together. Holmes says that the evidence indicates Square-toes became increasingly agitated while speaking before the tragedy occurred.

records.l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Holmes says his mind is made up about the main facts of the case, though some details remain obscure. He believes the evidence provides a working basis for continuing the investigation.

records.l: the Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Holmes says the tall, red-faced man found by John Rance holds the clue to the mystery. He intends to capture him, using the ring as bait if necessary.

records.l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The woman’s ring was found at the scene and is one of the unexplained facts troubling Doctor Watson. Holmes believes the second suspect returned to the house to recover it and may use it to catch him.

records.l: RACHE inscription, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Holmes says that “RACHE” was a false clue intended to divert the police toward Socialism, secret societies, or a German suspect. He argues that the lettering was made by a clumsy imitator rather than a real German.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Dr. Watson and Sherlock Holmes use an advertisement about a gold wedding ring found near Brixton Road to lure the suspected murderer in the brown coat to 221B Baker Street. Instead, Mrs. Sawyer arrives claiming the ring belongs to her daughter Sally, but Holmes suspects that the old woman is a disguised accomplice. Holmes follows her to Duncan Street, where she escapes from the cab and leaves no trace. Holmes concludes that the visitor was actually a young, agile man and that the murderer has allies willing to help him.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Dr. Watson rests at 221B Baker Street after the Brixton Road murder but is unable to sleep because of the case. He speaks with Sherlock Holmes, prepares his service revolver, receives Mrs. Sawyer, and later waits anxiously for Holmes to return from following her.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes hypothesizes that the murderer lost the wedding ring while bending over Enoch J. Drebber’s body and places an advertisement in Dr. Watson’s name to recover it. He expects the murderer in the brown coat to respond, but instead follows the disguised visitor to Duncan Street and realizes that the apparent old woman was an agile young man.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber’s distorted face continues to trouble Dr. Watson, who regards him as deeply vicious despite believing that justice must be done. Holmes thinks the murderer dropped a wedding ring while stooping over Drebber’s body.

records.l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The murderer in the brown coat is suspected by Sherlock Holmes of having lost the wedding ring at the murder scene and of returning to the house after discovering it was missing. Holmes expects him to answer the advertisement, but the person who appears is a disguised accomplice.

records.l: Mrs. Sawyer, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Mrs. Sawyer appears at 221B Baker Street claiming that the advertised wedding ring belongs to her daughter Sally. She gives an address in Duncan Street and leaves with the ring, but Sherlock Holmes concludes that she was actually a young man in disguise and that the stated identity was false.

records.l: Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Baker Street is where Dr. Watson and Sherlock Holmes discuss the Brixton Road murder and wait for someone to answer the ring advertisement.

records.l: 221B Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: 221B Baker Street is given in the advertisement as the place where the wedding ring may be claimed. Mrs. Sawyer visits the address, and Sherlock Holmes follows her after she leaves.

records.l: Brixton Road, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Brixton Road is the location of the murder and the roadway where the gold wedding ring was supposedly found between the White Hart Tavern and Holland Grove.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Brixton Road murder remains unsolved in this unit, though Sherlock Holmes develops a theory involving poison, a dropped wedding ring, and a murderer who returned to the scene. The case prompts Holmes to use a newspaper advertisement as a trap.

records.l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The wedding ring was found near Brixton Road after Enoch J. Drebber’s murder, and Sherlock Holmes believes the murderer dropped it while leaning over the body. Holmes uses a facsimile ring to support the advertisement trap and gives it to the disguised visitor.

records.l: advertisement for the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The advertisement appears in the evening paper’s “Found” column under Dr. Watson’s name, announcing that a plain gold wedding ring was found in Brixton Road and could be claimed at 221B Baker Street. It attracts Mrs. Sawyer, whom Sherlock Holmes believes is an accomplice in disguise.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Newspapers report on the Brixton Mystery, offering speculative political explanations and praising the police investigation. Tobias Gregson traces Enoch J. Drebber through his hat to Madame Charpentier’s boarding house, questions the family, and arrests Arthur Charpentier for Drebber’s murder. Gregson believes Arthur followed Drebber to Brixton Road and killed him with a heavy stick, while Sherlock Holmes listens skeptically. G. Lestrade then arrives and reveals that Joseph Stangerson has been murdered at Halliday’s Private Hotel.

records.l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The newspapers describe the Brixton Mystery as an unusually strange crime and speculate that political refugees or revolutionists were responsible. Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson discuss the reports, while Tobias Gregson and G. Lestrade investigate the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reads the newspaper reports with amusement and observes that Gregson and Lestrade will claim credit whether the case succeeds or fails. He employs a group of street Arabs to gather information and listens as Gregson explains his arrest of Arthur Charpentier.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Doctor Watson reads the newspaper reports with Sherlock Holmes and hears Tobias Gregson’s account of the investigation. He confirms details about the hat found beside Enoch J. Drebber’s body.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Tobias Gregson traces Enoch J. Drebber through a hat made by John Underwood and Sons to Madame Charpentier’s boarding establishment. After questioning Madame Charpentier, he arrests her son Arthur Charpentier and theorizes that Arthur followed Drebber to Brixton Road and killed him with a heavy stick.

records.l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: G. Lestrade is pursuing Joseph Stangerson while Tobias Gregson is pursuing Arthur Charpentier. He arrives at Sherlock Holmes’s rooms troubled and reports that Stangerson was murdered at Halliday’s Private Hotel.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber is identified in the newspapers as the American found dead in an empty house in Brixton Road. Madame Charpentier describes him as frequently drunk, coarse, and offensive toward her daughter Alice; Gregson believes Arthur Charpentier killed him after following him from the boarding house.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson is described as Enoch J. Drebber’s private secretary and travel companion. G. Lestrade reports that Stangerson was murdered at Halliday’s Private Hotel about six o’clock in the morning.

records.l: Arthur Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Arthur Charpentier, a sub-lieutenant in Her Majesty’s navy, intervenes when Enoch J. Drebber attempts to take Alice Charpentier away. He follows Drebber with a stick, is later arrested by Tobias Gregson, and acknowledges that he is being arrested for involvement in Drebber’s death.

records.l: Madame Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Madame Charpentier runs the boarding establishment where Enoch J. Drebber and Joseph Stangerson stayed. She tells Tobias Gregson that Drebber behaved offensively toward her daughter and that Arthur followed Drebber after a confrontation, but she cannot say when Arthur returned home.

records.l: Halliday’s Private Hotel, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Halliday’s Private Hotel is the place where Joseph Stangerson was murdered at about six o’clock in the morning.

records.l: Brixton Road, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Brixton Road is where Enoch J. Drebber’s body is discovered in an empty house. Tobias Gregson believes Arthur Charpentier followed Drebber there and killed him.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Brixton murder concerns the death of Enoch J. Drebber in an empty house on Brixton Road. Tobias Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier for the crime, while G. Lestrade’s investigation leads to the separate discovery that Joseph Stangerson has also been murdered.

records.l: the murder of Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The murder of Joseph Stangerson is reported by G. Lestrade, who states that Stangerson was killed at Halliday’s Private Hotel about six o’clock in the morning.

records.l: arrest of Arthur Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Tobias Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier after learning from Madame Charpentier that Arthur followed Enoch J. Drebber with a heavy stick. Arthur’s reference to Drebber’s death before the officers had mentioned it appears suspicious to Gregson.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Inspector Lestrade reports that Joseph Stangerson has been murdered in his hotel room, with the word “RACHE” written in blood above him. Sherlock Holmes connects Stangerson’s death to the murder of Enoch Drebber through the discovery of two pills, one harmless and one poisonous, and confirms the poison by testing them on a dying terrier. Holmes identifies the murderer as Jefferson Hope and captures him after luring him into the room disguised as a cabman. Holmes, Dr. John Watson, Lestrade, and Gregson then secure Hope for transport to Scotland Yard.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies the connection between the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson through the pills found in Stangerson’s room. He tests the pills on a terrier, discovering that one is deadly poison and the other harmless. Holmes then lures Jefferson Hope into the room, places handcuffs on him, identifies him as the murderer, and helps subdue him.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Dr. John Watson listens to Lestrade’s account, assists Holmes by examining the pills, and fetches the dying terrier for Holmes’s test. He helps restrain Jefferson Hope after Hope tries to escape through the window.

records.l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Inspector Lestrade traces Joseph Stangerson to Halliday’s Private Hotel and discovers his murdered body. He reports the blood-written word “RACHE,” the witness’s description of the escaping man, and the clues found in the room. Lestrade helps capture and restrain Jefferson Hope.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Inspector Gregson hears Lestrade’s report and acknowledges that his own earlier theory was wrong. He presses Sherlock Holmes to name the murderer and helps overpower Jefferson Hope when Hope attempts to escape.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Enoch Drebber’s purse is found in Joseph Stangerson’s possession, apparently because Stangerson usually handled the paying. Sherlock Holmes identifies Jefferson Hope as the murderer of Drebber.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson is found dead in his locked hotel room, wearing his nightdress, with a deep stab wound in his left side. The word “RACHE” is written in blood above him, and his room contains Drebber’s purse, a telegram, a novel, a pipe, a glass of water, and two pills.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Jefferson Hope is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the murderer of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. Disguised as a cabman, he is lured into Holmes’s room, handcuffed, and captured after violently trying to escape through a window.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The murder of Enoch Drebber is linked to the murder of Joseph Stangerson by the discovery of the two pills in Stangerson’s room. Sherlock Holmes concludes that Jefferson Hope committed the murder.

records.l: the murder of Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The murder of Joseph Stangerson occurs in his room at Halliday’s Private Hotel. He is stabbed through the heart, while the murderer leaves “RACHE” written in blood and escapes through the window after washing his hands and wiping his knife.

records.l: the investigation, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The investigation shifts from Inspector Lestrade’s suspicion of Stangerson to the search for an unknown murderer. Sherlock Holmes uses the pills, the blood-written word, the witness’s description, and other details to complete his deductions and identify Jefferson Hope.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's arrest, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The arrest of Jefferson Hope is carried out by Sherlock Holmes after Hope arrives disguised as a cabman. Holmes secretly fastens handcuffs on him, and Holmes, Dr. John Watson, Inspector Lestrade, and Inspector Gregson restrain him after he tries to flee.

records.l: the poison pills, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The pills are small, pearly grey, nearly transparent, and soluble in water. Sherlock Holmes tests them on a dying terrier and discovers that one is harmless while the other contains deadly poison, confirming their importance to the case.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: John Ferrier and the five-year-old Lucy Ferrier are stranded on the Great Alkali Plain after their twenty-one-person immigrant party loses its way and suffers fatal hunger and thirst. A large Mormon caravan discovers and rescues them, taking them toward Zion under the leadership of the Mormons. Ferrier agrees to join the Mormons on the condition that he and Lucy accept their creed. The caravan continues westward after providing them with food, drink, and shelter.

records.l: great Alkali Plain, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The great Alkali Plain is portrayed as a vast, barren desert between the Sierra Nevada and Nebraska, extending from the Yellowstone River to the Colorado. Its saline dust, lack of water, and scattered bones make it a deadly barrier to westward travel.

records.l: Sierra Blanco, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Sierra Blanco overlooks the great Alkali Plain. John Ferrier reaches its northern slope and a rocky elevation, hoping to find signs of water, but sees only the desolate plain and distant mountains.

records.l: Nauvoo, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: Nauvoo, in Illinois, is identified as the place where the Mormons had founded their temple before leaving in search of refuge from persecution.

records.l: Zion, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: Zion is the destination invoked by the Mormon caravan as it continues westward. The Mormons cry, "On, on to Zion!" as their wagons resume their journey.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: John Ferrier is a gaunt, starving traveler who has crossed the desert with Lucy Ferrier after the rest of their party died. He protects Lucy, claims her as his child because he saved her, and agrees to join the Mormons and accept their conditions when they rescue him.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier is a five-year-old girl who survives the desert journey with John Ferrier after her mother dies. She remains cheerful and trusting, comforts herself with the thought of rejoining her mother, and is rescued and taken into the Mormon caravan with Ferrier.

records.l: Mormons, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Mormons are a persecuted religious people traveling west in search of refuge under the leadership of their Prophet. They require John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier to become believers in their creed before admitting them to the group.

records.l: Mormon caravan, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Mormon caravan is an enormous westbound migration containing wagons, carts, armed horsemen, women, and children. It discovers John Ferrier and Lucy on the Sierra Blanco, rescues them, and provides them with food, drink, and a wagon.

records.l: twenty-one-person immigrant party, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The twenty-one-person immigrant party becomes lost after expecting to find another river. Its water supply runs out, and only John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier remain alive when the Mormon caravan finds them.

records.l: desert, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The desert is an arid and hostile region of alkali plains, mountains, ravines, and scarce water. It is marked by the bones of people and oxen who have died along the long caravan route.

records.l: Mormon creed, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Mormon creed is presented as a sacred belief based on writings in Egyptian letters on plates of beaten gold that were handed to Joseph Smith at Palmyra. The Mormons insist that Ferrier and Lucy accept this creed if they are to travel with them.

records.l: Mormon migration to Utah, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Mormon migration west is driven by persecution and the search for a new refuge, even in the heart of the desert. The migrants leave Nauvoo and travel in a vast organized caravan toward an unknown destination identified as Zion.

records.l: rescue of John Ferrier and Lucy, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: A group of young Mormon scouts climbs the bluff after seeing Lucy's pink clothing and discovers her sleeping beside John Ferrier. The Mormons carry Lucy and support Ferrier to the wagons, where both receive food, drink, and shelter.

records.l: deaths from hunger and thirst, A Study in Scarlet, PART II. / CHAPTER I.
records.s: The immigrant party suffers repeated deaths after its expected river fails to appear and its water runs out. Mr. Bender, Indian Pete, Mrs. McGregor, Johnny Hones, Lucy's mother, and the other members of the party die, leaving only John Ferrier and Lucy.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Mormons establish a prosperous settlement in Utah, with Brigham Young organizing the city, farms, trades, and construction of a great temple. John Ferrier becomes a wealthy and respected farmer, while his adopted daughter Lucy grows into a skilled and admired young woman. Lucy meets Jefferson Hope when he rescues her from a frightened horse trapped among cattle, and they quickly fall in love. Hope leaves to develop silver lodes in the Nevada Mountains after securing Lucy’s promise to marry him when he returns.

records.l: Mormons, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Mormons complete their migration to the valley of Utah after enduring severe hardships. They establish farms, trades, streets, and squares, and construct a great temple in the centre of their city.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: John Ferrier travels with the Mormons as a useful guide and indefatigable hunter and receives a large, fertile tract of land. He builds a substantial home, becomes one of the wealthiest men in Salt Lake City, and remains strictly celibate while otherwise conforming to the religion.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier is adopted by John Ferrier and travels with the Mormons in Elder Stangerson’s waggon. She grows into a skilled rider and admired young woman, falls in love with Jefferson Hope, and promises to be ready to leave with him when he returns.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Jefferson Hope is a tall, capable hunter who has worked as a pioneer, scout, trapper, silver explorer, and ranchman. He rescues Lucy Ferrier from a frightened horse among a drove of cattle, falls deeply in love with her, and leaves to work silver lodes after securing her promise to marry him.

records.l: Utah, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Utah is the promised land where the immigrant Mormons settle after their westward journey. Its valley becomes a prosperous agricultural region, and Lucy Ferrier is described as the fairest specimen of American girlhood in the whole Pacific slope.

records.l: Salt Lake City, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Salt Lake City develops as the centre of the Mormon settlement, with streets, squares, farms, and a great temple. John Ferrier becomes one of the city’s richest men.

records.l: Mormon settlement, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Mormon settlement prospers rapidly through organized farming, trade, craftsmanship, and construction. It lies along the Overland Route and receives travelers, livestock, and traffic connected with the gold fever in California.

records.l: the farm (John Ferrier's farm), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: John Ferrier’s farm grows from a log-house and tract of fertile land into a prosperous property with a roomy villa. Lucy Ferrier lives there and assists her adopted father in his work, and Jefferson Hope repeatedly visits the farm.

records.l: the old Nevada mines, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Jefferson Hope and his companions discover silver lodes in the Nevada Mountains while prospecting. Hope leaves Salt Lake City to raise enough capital to work the lodes and expects to return within two months.

records.l: Mormon migration to Utah, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Mormon migration to Utah follows a difficult journey from the shores of the Mississippi across the plains and toward the Rocky Mountains. The migrants overcome hunger, thirst, fatigue, disease, hostile people, and wild animals before reaching their promised land.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope's first meeting, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope first meet when her horse becomes trapped and frightened among long-horned cattle near Salt Lake City. Hope seizes the horse’s bridle and leads it out, after which Lucy invites him to visit her and her father.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope's engagement, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope become attached after his visits to the Ferrier farm. John Ferrier gives his consent provided Hope’s mining venture succeeds, and Hope and Lucy agree that she will marry him when he returns.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Three weeks after Jefferson Hope left Salt Lake City, Brigham Young visits John Ferrier and warns him that Lucy must marry a Mormon, preferably Stangerson's or Drebber's son. Young gives Lucy one month to choose and threatens Ferrier and his daughter if they resist the orders of the Sacred Council of Four. Ferrier and Lucy fear the consequences, but Ferrier plans to send word to Jefferson and escape Utah before the month ends. That night, Ferrier secures the house and loads his shotgun despite reassuring Lucy that they are not in danger.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: John Ferrier is warned by Brigham Young that Lucy must marry a Mormon. He intends to send Jefferson Hope a message, sell or abandon the farm, and leave Utah if necessary; he also prepares his house and shotgun for danger.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Lucy learns that Brigham Young expects her to choose between Stangerson's son and Drebber's son. She remains devoted to Jefferson Hope and fears what may happen to her and her father if they oppose the Prophet.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Jefferson Hope has been away from Salt Lake City for three weeks with his comrades. John Ferrier plans to send him a message about the danger, believing he will return quickly and advise them.

records.l: Brigham Young, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Brigham Young visits the Ferrier farm and reproaches John Ferrier for failing to marry and for allowing Lucy to be associated with a Gentile. He demands that Lucy marry a faithful Mormon, gives her a month to choose, and threatens Ferrier and Lucy if they resist.

records.l: Mormons, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Mormons rescued John Ferrier from starvation, brought him to the Chosen Valley, gave him land, and protected him. Their society is described as enforcing religious conformity through fear and secret violence.

records.l: the Church, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Mormon Church is portrayed as having authority over personal conduct and marriage in Utah. Its members are expected to follow its usages, and opposition to its leaders is presented as dangerous.

records.l: the Elders, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Elders are described as powerful Mormon leaders with harems and children to provide for. Brigham Young says that Stangerson's and Drebber's sons are suitable prospective husbands for Lucy.

records.l: the Sacred Council of Four, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Sacred Council of Four has decided that Lucy's faith will be tested through her marriage. Brigham Young presents its orders as commands that John Ferrier cannot safely resist.

records.l: the avenging angels, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Danite Band, also called the Avenging Angels, is identified as a secret and sinister organization associated with murders, violence, disappearances, and the persecution of opponents of the Mormon authorities.

records.l: Salt Lake City, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Salt Lake City is where Jefferson Hope and his comrades departed from three weeks before Brigham Young's visit. It is part of the Utah society described as dominated by fear of religious authorities.

records.l: Utah, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Utah is depicted as a place where religious dissent is dangerous and secret powers punish resistance. John Ferrier proposes leaving Utah with Lucy before the order concerning her marriage is enforced.

records.l: polygamy, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Polygamy is described as dependent on an adequate supply of women, which had become scarce. The shortage is linked to rumors of murdered immigrants and women appearing unwillingly in the harems of the Elders.

records.l: Mormon creed, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Mormon faith requires, according to Brigham Young, that a maiden marry one of the elect rather than a Gentile. John Ferrier claims to have followed many of its public requirements but has not married or arranged Lucy's marriage to a Mormon.

records.l: persecution, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Persecution has turned former victims into persecutors in the society described. People who oppose or question the Mormon authorities may disappear, while others remain silent because they fear secret retaliation.

records.l: Brigham Young's visit to the Ferrier farm, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: During Brigham Young's visit to the Ferrier farm, he confronts John Ferrier about his conduct and Lucy's proposed relationship with a Gentile. He leaves after giving Lucy one month to choose a Mormon husband and threatening the family.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier's proposed marriage, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier is ordered to choose between Stangerson's son and Drebber's son, both described as young, rich, and faithful Mormons. The proposed marriage conflicts with her attachment to Jefferson Hope.

records.l: the planned escape from Utah, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
records.s: John Ferrier plans to raise as much money as possible from the farm and leave Utah with Lucy after Jefferson Hope returns. He believes they have a month before they must escape, although Lucy warns that they may not be allowed to leave.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: John Ferrier refuses to let either Joseph Stangerson or young Drebber marry his daughter Lucy, defying the Mormon authorities and provoking threats against them. Young’s promised punishment begins with mysterious warnings and a daily countdown, while the watched roads and hidden agents leave Ferrier and Lucy nearly trapped. Jefferson Hope returns from the Nevada Mountains, helps them escape the farm at night, and leads them through guarded country toward Carson City. They evade the sentinels and pass into the mountain route with horses and supplies.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: John Ferrier rejects the marriage proposals of Joseph Stangerson and young Drebber and declares that he would rather see Lucy dead than married to either of them. After receiving mysterious threats and daily countdown warnings, he prepares to flee with Lucy and Jefferson Hope, carrying their money and riding one of the horses through the mountains.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Lucy supports her father’s refusal of the two young Mormons and trusts that Jefferson Hope will return. She leaves the farm with John Ferrier and Jefferson Hope at night, riding a mule during their escape toward the mountains.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Jefferson Hope returns from the Nevada Mountains after receiving Ferrier’s message and secretly reaches the watched farm by crawling across the ground. He brings horses, a mule, money, provisions, and water, then leads John Ferrier and Lucy through the fields and mountain pass toward Carson City.

records.l: Brigham Young, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Young had promised John Ferrier a month to amend his conduct. After Ferrier refuses the marriage proposals, the twenty-nine-day warning indicates that Young’s threat is being carried out.

records.l: Mormons, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson and young Drebber, identified as young Mormons, visit John Ferrier to solicit Lucy’s hand in marriage. When Ferrier orders them out, they threaten him with punishment from the Prophet and the Council of Four.

records.l: the Elders, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Elders are the authorities whose power John Ferrier has defied by refusing the proposed marriages. Their authority is feared throughout the settlement, and Ferrier believes that even wealth and position cannot protect him from them.

records.l: the Sacred Council of Four, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Council of Four is invoked by Stangerson as an authority Ferrier has defied. The roads around the settlement are watched and guarded, and passage requires an order from the Council.

records.l: the Chosen People, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Saints’ jurisdiction extends into the mountain pass, where a solitary armed sentinel challenges the fugitives. Jefferson Hope gives the correct countersign, allowing them to pass.

records.l: Nevada Mountains, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Jefferson Hope is contacted through an acquaintance traveling toward the Nevada Mountains. He returns from that direction to help Ferrier and Lucy escape.

records.l: Utah, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Jefferson Hope says that before harm comes to Lucy there will be one less member of the Hope family in Utah. The fugitives attempt to leave the settlement and travel through the surrounding mountains.

records.l: Carson City, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Jefferson Hope plans to take John Ferrier and Lucy through the mountains to Carson City. Their nighttime flight begins along that route.

records.l: Eagle Ravine, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Jefferson Hope has a mule and two horses waiting in Eagle Ravine for the escape. The fugitives travel from the farm toward the ravine after crossing the fields.

records.l: Eagle Cañon, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Eagle Cañon is the narrow mountain defile where Jefferson Hope’s horses are waiting. He guides the fugitives through its rocky path, after which they encounter an armed sentinel.

records.l: the farm (John Ferrier's farm), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: John Ferrier’s farm is watched on every side after he rejects the marriage proposals and defies the authorities. Ferrier, Lucy, and Jefferson Hope escape from it through a side window and cross the fields under cover of darkness.

records.l: the flight for life, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The flight for life begins when Jefferson Hope secretly joins John Ferrier and Lucy and urges them to leave immediately. They evade watchers, reach the waiting animals, and proceed through the mountains toward freedom.

records.l: the threatened punishment of John Ferrier and Lucy, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Stangerson and young Drebber threaten John Ferrier after he rejects them, invoking the Prophet, the Council of Four, and the Lord. Ferrier understands that he and Lucy may be killed or otherwise punished, and he chooses escape rather than submit to Lucy’s dishonour.

records.l: the twenty-nine-day warning, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: A paper pinned to John Ferrier’s bed announces that twenty-nine days are given for amendment, followed by an unfinished threat. Ferrier recognizes it as the remaining portion of the month promised by Young.

records.l: the countdown, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: After the twenty-nine-day warning, the numbers 28, 27, and successive lower numbers appear mysteriously around the farm each morning. The countdown reaches 2 before Jefferson Hope arrives, making the next day the last of the allotted time.

records.l: the sentinels, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Hidden watchers and armed sentinels guard the roads, fields, and mountain routes around the settlement. Jefferson Hope detects two men near the farm, and later gives a countersign to a mountain sentinel, who allows the fugitives to pass.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Jefferson Hope flees through the mountains with Lucy Ferrier and her father, John Ferrier, but returns from hunting to find John dead and Lucy captured by their pursuers. Lucy is forced to marry Drebber and dies within a month, after which Hope devotes his life to revenge against Drebber and Stangerson. He follows them from Salt Lake City through the United States and Europe, eventually tracking them to London.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Jefferson Hope leads Lucy Ferrier and John Ferrier through the mountains toward safety, but returns from hunting to find John dead and Lucy taken by their pursuers. He spends years pursuing revenge against Drebber and Stangerson, following them from Utah through the United States and Europe until he reaches London.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier flees with her father and Jefferson Hope, but she is captured when their pursuers overtake the camp. She is forced to marry Drebber, pines away, and dies within a month; Jefferson Hope removes her wedding ring before her burial.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: John Ferrier escapes with Lucy and Jefferson Hope but is captured by the pursuing party while Hope is away hunting. Stangerson shoots him, and he is buried at the mountain camp with a brief inscription identifying him as formerly of Salt Lake City.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Drebber is chosen over Stangerson to marry Lucy Ferrier after their dispute is decided by the Prophet and Drebber's party proves stronger. He later leaves Utah with his property, travels through the United States and Europe, and is pursued by Jefferson Hope.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Stangerson is part of the party that pursues the Ferriers and shoots John Ferrier. He loses Lucy to Drebber in the marriage decision, later becomes Drebber's private secretary, and is pursued with him by Jefferson Hope.

records.l: the fugitives, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The fugitives are Jefferson Hope, Lucy Ferrier, and John Ferrier as they flee through the mountains. A large mounted party overtakes them; John is killed, Lucy is carried back, and Jefferson Hope escapes their pursuers.

records.l: Salt Lake City, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Salt Lake City is the destination from which the pursuers come and to which their tracks return after John Ferrier is killed and Lucy is captured. It is also where Lucy is forced to marry Drebber and where Jefferson Hope later searches for Drebber and Stangerson.

records.l: the avenging angels, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The avenging angels are the pursuers whose track Jefferson Hope follows back toward Salt Lake City after discovering John Ferrier's grave and Lucy's capture. Their pursuit separates the fugitives and leads to John's death and Lucy's forced return.

records.l: the pursuit of the fugitives, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The pursuit follows Jefferson Hope, Lucy Ferrier, and John Ferrier through the mountain defiles. The pursuers eventually overtake the camp while Hope is away, kill John Ferrier, and take Lucy back to Salt Lake City.

records.l: John Ferrier's murder, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: John Ferrier's murder occurs at the fugitives' mountain camp while Jefferson Hope is hunting for food. Stangerson shoots him, and the pursuers bury him in a newly dug grave before returning toward Salt Lake City.

records.l: the forced marriage of Lucy Ferrier and Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: After John Ferrier is killed and Lucy is carried back, a council gives her to Drebber rather than Stangerson. She is married to Drebber in Salt Lake City despite her unwillingness and visibly declining condition.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier's death, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier dies within a month of her father's death and her forced marriage to Drebber. Her other husband's wives mourn her, and Jefferson Hope takes her wedding ring from her body before the burial.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's pursuit and vengeance, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Jefferson Hope resolves to devote his life to revenge after finding John Ferrier dead and learning that Lucy has been taken. He stalks Drebber and Stangerson, attempts to kill them in the mountains, searches for them across the United States, and finally tracks them through Europe to London.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope explains to John Watson, M.D., Sherlock Holmes, and the police that he pursued Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson because they were responsible for the deaths of John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier. He describes finding the men in London, killing Drebber with one of two poison pills, and later killing Stangerson. Hope says that he used Lucy Ferrier's marriage ring and the word "RACHE" to connect Drebber's death with his vengeance, and he confesses that his own aortic aneurism may soon kill him.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: John Watson, M.D., accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Gregson, Lestrade, and Jefferson Hope to the police-station. He examines Hope's chest, recognizes an aortic aneurism, and later records that Hope's statement was accurate by consulting Lestrade's note-book.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes helps restrain Jefferson Hope, takes him to the police-station, and invites John Watson, M.D., and the detectives to accompany them. Hope praises Holmes for persistently following his trail.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope confesses that he pursued and killed Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson in vengeance for the deaths of John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier. He says that he followed them from Salt Lake City across two continents and that his work is complete, although he expects his aortic aneurism to kill him soon.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Enoch Drebber is identified by Jefferson Hope as the man who forced Lucy Ferrier into marriage and helped cause her death. Hope lures Drebber to the house in the Brixton Road, makes him choose between two pills, and watches him die after taking the poisoned one.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson travels with Enoch Drebber and is described as Drebber's secretary and paid servant. Jefferson Hope says that Stangerson also perished by Hope's hand, though this unit gives no detailed account of that killing.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Lucy Ferrier was engaged to marry Jefferson Hope but was forced to marry Enoch Drebber, and Hope says that she died with a broken heart. Hope repeatedly sees her memory during his vengeance and carries her marriage ring as a reminder of her.

records.l: London, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope follows Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson through London after finding them living at a boarding-house in Camberwell. He works as a cab driver while learning his way through the city's confusing streets.

records.l: Salt Lake City, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope says he followed Enoch Drebber from Salt Lake City to St. Petersburg and across two continents. He also attributes the worsening of his aortic aneurism to exposure and under-feeding in the Salt Lake Mountains.

records.l: Brixton Road, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Brixton Road contains the house that Jefferson Hope uses as a secluded place for his confrontation with Enoch Drebber. Hope drives Drebber there late at night during a storm.

records.l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope has a duplicate key to the house in the Brixton Road and brings Enoch Drebber inside while he is drunk. There, Hope reveals his identity, forces Drebber to choose a pill, and leaves him dead on the floor.

records.l: aortic aneurism, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: John Watson, M.D., identifies Jefferson Hope's condition as an aortic aneurism after feeling the powerful throbbing in his chest. Hope says it has worsened for years and that a doctor told him it is bound to burst within days.

records.l: the cab, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope uses his cab to follow Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson around London and to transport Drebber to the house in the Brixton Road. After Drebber's death, Hope returns to the house in the cab's vicinity after realizing that he has lost Lucy Ferrier's marriage ring.

records.l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope takes Lucy Ferrier's marriage ring from her dead finger and carries it while pursuing Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. He holds it before Drebber's eyes as Drebber dies, but later discovers that it is missing and returns to the house to search for it.

records.l: poison alkaloid, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope obtains a powerful poison alkaloid extracted from a South American arrow poison while working at York College. He says that even a small grain causes instant death.

records.l: the poison pills, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope makes two small pills for each intended victim: one containing poison alkaloid and one harmless. He forces Enoch Drebber to choose one pill and swallows the other, leaving chance to determine which of them will live.

records.l: the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope admits responsibility for the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson, saying that both men had forfeited their lives for the deaths of John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier. He describes Drebber's poisoning in detail and states that Stangerson also perished by his hand.

records.l: the forced marriage of Lucy Ferrier and Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope says that Lucy Ferrier was forced into marrying Enoch Drebber and that the marriage broke her heart. He regards Drebber's role in the marriage as part of the crime for which Drebber deserved punishment.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's pursuit and vengeance, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope follows Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson across two continents, eventually locating them in London and tracking them through the city. He plans a personal judgment and execution because he believes the legal system can no longer convict them.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's confession, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jefferson Hope gives his confession at the police-station after John Watson, M.D., confirms that his aortic aneurism creates an immediate danger of death. He explains his motives, pursuit, use of poison pills, killing of Enoch Drebber, and responsibility for Joseph Stangerson's death.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope recounts how he killed Stangerson after giving him the same choice of poisoned pills he had offered Enoch Drebber. He says Stangerson attacked him, so he stabbed him in self-defence, and then continued working as a cabman while planning to return to America. Hope is arrested after being summoned to 221B, Baker Street, and he claims that he acted as an officer of justice. Sherlock Holmes asks about Hope’s accomplice, but Hope refuses to identify him.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope tells how he tracked Stangerson to Halliday’s Private Hotel and entered his bedroom through a window. He says he killed Stangerson in self-defence after Stangerson attacked him, then continued cabbing until he was arrested.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope says that Enoch Drebber’s death led him to pursue Stangerson in order to pay off John Ferrier’s debt.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Stangerson stayed indoors at Halliday’s Private Hotel after Enoch Drebber disappeared, apparently suspecting danger. When Jefferson Hope confronted him and offered him poisoned pills, Stangerson attacked Hope and was stabbed to the heart.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope says that killing Enoch Drebber and Stangerson was intended to pay off John Ferrier’s debt.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Sherlock Holmes listens to Jefferson Hope’s account and asks who collected the ring advertised by Holmes. He praises the unnamed accomplice for acting smartly.

records.l: Enoch Drebber's death, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope describes Enoch Drebber’s death to Stangerson and says that it was followed by his effort to kill Stangerson as well.

records.l: Stangerson's death, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Stangerson’s death occurs when he attacks Jefferson Hope after being offered a choice of poisoned pills. Hope says he stabbed Stangerson to the heart in self-defence.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's arrest, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope is lured to 221B, Baker Street, after a ragged youngster tells him that his cab is wanted there. The young man places bracelets on Hope’s wrists, and Hope is later led away by warders.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's confession, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope confesses to killing Enoch Drebber and Stangerson and explains how he carried out both confrontations. He refuses to reveal the identity of his accomplice, saying that he does not get other people into trouble.

records.l: justice and revenge, A Study in Scarlet, “That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was
records.s: Jefferson Hope presents his killings as acts of justice for the life taken by Enoch Drebber and Stangerson and as payment of John Ferrier’s debt. He says he considers himself as much an officer of justice as the officers questioning him.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Jefferson Hope dies in custody after his aneurism bursts, preventing the magistrates from hearing testimony about the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. Sherlock Holmes explains to Doctor Watson how he reasoned backward from physical evidence, including footprints, a cab track, poison, a ring, and information from Cleveland, to identify Hope as the murderer and cabdriver. Holmes’s Street Arab detective corps located Hope among London’s cab proprietors, leading to his capture. The Echo wrongly credits Inspectors Gregson and Lestrade with the arrest and describes the crimes as the result of an old romantic feud involving love and Mormonism.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Doctor Watson how ordinary deductions and analytical reasoning led him from the crime-scene evidence to Jefferson Hope. He identifies Hope as the murderer and former cabdriver, organizes a Street Arab detective corps to find him, and complains that the Echo credits Gregson and Lestrade instead of him.

records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Doctor Watson discusses Hope’s death with Sherlock Holmes and listens as Holmes reconstructs the investigation. He records the facts in his journal and intends to make the public aware of Holmes’s role.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Jefferson Hope is identified as the man who killed Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson in revenge connected with an old romantic feud. He is captured in Sherlock Holmes’s rooms and dies in his cell when an aneurism bursts before he can appear before the magistrates.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Inspector Gregson failed to inquire in his telegram to Cleveland about Enoch Drebber’s former career. The Echo nevertheless credits Gregson and Inspector Lestrade entirely with Hope’s capture and suggests that they deserve a testimonial.

records.l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Inspector Lestrade is named with Inspector Gregson as one of the Scotland Yard officials whom the Echo credits with Jefferson Hope’s capture. Sherlock Holmes expects them to be angry because Hope’s death prevents their anticipated public advertisement.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Enoch Drebber was poisoned after Jefferson Hope forced poison upon him. Holmes learns from Cleveland that Drebber had sought legal protection against Hope, an old rival in love, and uses a ring found at the scene to infer the personal motive.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Joseph Stangerson is murdered by Jefferson Hope in an unexpected incident during the investigation. His death enables Holmes to obtain the pills whose existence he had already surmised.

records.l: the Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The investigation is presented by Holmes as a chain of logical sequences based on cab tracks, footprints, poison, a ring, a cigar, nail marks, blood, and information from Cleveland. Holmes traces the crimes to Jefferson Hope, while the public account wrongly gives the principal credit to Gregson and Lestrade.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The murder of Enoch Drebber was carried out deliberately by poison, which was forced upon him. Holmes concludes that the crime was a private revenge connected with a woman rather than robbery or politics.

records.l: the murder of Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The murder of Joseph Stangerson occurs after the Drebber investigation has begun and is described as an incident that Holmes could hardly have prevented. It gives Holmes possession of the pills connected with the case.

records.l: Hope's death, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Hope’s aneurism bursts on the night after his capture, and he is found dead on the floor of his cell with a placid smile. His death prevents the scheduled testimony and leaves the full details of the case unlikely to become known publicly.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's Street Arab detective corps, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes organizes a Street Arab detective corps and sends its members systematically to every cab proprietor in London. The corps successfully finds Jefferson Hope among the city’s cabdrivers.

records.l: Scotland Yard, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Scotland Yard is represented in the newspaper report by Inspectors Lestrade and Gregson, who are credited with Hope’s capture. Holmes regards that credit as undeserved.

records.l: the Echo, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Echo publishes a report about Hope’s death and the Drebber–Stangerson case. It credits Lestrade and Gregson with the capture, calls Holmes an amateur, and predicts that the two officials will receive a testimonial.

records.l: the newspaper report about the case, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The newspaper report says that the public has lost a sensational treat because of Hope’s sudden death and that the complete details may never be known. It attributes the crimes to an old romantic feud involving love and Mormonism and gives Scotland Yard officials the credit for the capture.

records.l: the cab, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Holmes finds marks showing that a cab was at the house during the night and determines from the narrow wheel gauge that it was a cab rather than a private carriage. The horse’s wandering indicates that its driver was inside the house, leading Holmes to conclude that the murderer had used the cab to follow Drebber.

records.l: the testimonial, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The newspaper report predicts that a testimonial will be presented to Inspectors Lestrade and Gregson in recognition of their supposed services. Holmes jokes that the result of the investigation is to get them a testimonial.

records.l: analytical reasoning, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes describes analytical reasoning as reasoning backward from a known result to the events that produced it. He says that few people can do this and uses it to reconstruct the steps leading from the crime-scene evidence to Jefferson Hope.

records.l: the romantic feud, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The romantic feud is identified as the motive behind the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. The Echo describes it as an old-standing feud involving love and Mormonism, while Holmes connects it specifically with Drebber’s conflict with Hope over a woman.

records.l: A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The document follows Dr. John Watson, an army surgeon returned from Afghanistan with damaged health, as he meets Sherlock Holmes in London and becomes his roommate at 221B Baker Street. Holmes, an eccentric chemist and consulting detective, impresses Watson with his powers of observation and deduction, including his inference that Watson has been in Afghanistan. Their first major case begins when Enoch J. Drebber is found dead in an empty house at Lauriston Gardens. Holmes studies blood, footprints, a cab track, a ring, cigar ash, and the blood-written word “RACHE,” concluding that Drebber was poisoned by a tall man who had arrived with him in a cab. While police inspectors Tobias Gregson and Lestrade pursue incorrect or incomplete theories, Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier, Holmes follows clues through constable John Rance, a failed advertisement for the ring, and the murder of Drebber’s companion, Joseph Stangerson. Stangerson’s room contains the same word, “RACHE,” and two pills, one poisonous and one harmless. Holmes proves the poison and captures the killer, cabman Jefferson Hope, at Baker Street. Hope’s confession supplies the earlier history. John Ferrier and his adopted daughter Lucy, dying on the Great Alkali Plain, were rescued by a Mormon caravan and taken to Utah. Ferrier became prosperous, and Lucy fell in love with Hope. After Hope left to seek silver, Brigham Young ordered Lucy to marry either Stangerson’s or Drebber’s son. Ferrier resisted, and he, Lucy, and Hope fled, but Ferrier was killed and Lucy was captured. Forced to marry Drebber, Lucy died within a month. Hope devoted himself to pursuing Drebber and Stangerson across the United States and Europe to London. He made Drebber choose between two pills, killed Stangerson after Stangerson attacked him, and used Lucy’s ring and “RACHE” to mark his revenge. Hope dies in custody when his aneurism bursts, refusing to name an accomplice. Holmes later explains that he identified Hope through the physical evidence and his Street Arab detective corps, though public credit goes to Gregson and Lestrade.
