records.l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Doctor Watson is a doctor of medicine and army doctor who served as an Assistant Surgeon with the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers and with the Berkshires during the Afghan campaign. Wounded in the shoulder by a Jezail bullet at Maiwand, rescued from Ghazis by Murray, and later afflicted with enteric fever at Peshawar, he returns to England with his health irretrievably ruined, weak and convalescent. With only eleven shillings and sixpence a day, no relatives in England, and a desire to avoid rows because of shaken nerves, he seeks economical rooms while staying at a private hotel in the Strand. Through young Stamford, a former dresser under him at Barts, Watson meets Sherlock Holmes in a chemical laboratory and agrees to share rooms at 221B Baker Street. He moves in, keeps his old service revolver and a bull pup, and becomes Holmes’s companion and narrator. Initially curious about Holmes’s uneven knowledge and doubtful of his deductions, Watson witnesses their accuracy and records them. During the Lauriston Gardens and Brixton Road investigation, he accompanies Holmes, observes Enoch J. Drebber’s body, reads Gregson’s letter, questions John Rance with Holmes, follows newspaper reports and police accounts, and anxiously awaits Holmes’s return from pursuing Mrs. Sawyer. He assists with examining pills and testing them with a dying terrier, helps restrain Jefferson Hope, examines Hope’s chest and recognizes an aortic aneurism, and verifies Hope’s statement through Lestrade’s notebook. At the end, Watson records the case in his journal and intends to make Holmes’s role public.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is a man of eccentric scientific studies, especially chemistry, anatomy, poisons, and postmortem subjects, whose passion is definite and exact knowledge. He works intermittently at a chemical laboratory, discovers a hæmoglobin-based blood-stain test, smokes strong tobacco, plays the violin remarkably and eccentrically, and can be silent or in the dumps. He shares rooms at 221B, Baker Street with Dr. John Watson. Holmes’s trade is consulting detective work. He serves official detectives, private inquiry agencies, and people in trouble through observation, deduction, special knowledge, and analytical reasoning. He is highly trained in such matters as footstep tracing and cigar ashes, and he demonstrates his method early by inferring Watson’s connection with Afghanistan and identifying a visitor’s former occupation. He regards Gregson and Lestrade as inferior in detective work and expects them to seek credit for a solved case. The central action follows Holmes’s investigation of the deaths of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. At Lauriston Gardens, he studies tracks, footprints, the body, blood, writing, fingernail marks, and cigar ash. He concludes that Drebber was poisoned and reconstructs the murderer as a tall, florid, red-faced man with particular boots, a long right-hand fingernail, and a Trichinopoly cigar, who arrived in a four-wheeled cab. A lost wedding ring becomes bait: Holmes advertises for it, detects a disguised response, interviews John Rance, and pursues the connection. As the investigation expands, Holmes uses street Arabs, telegraphs Cleveland, and tests pills from Stangerson’s room on a terrier, proving that one is poisonous and one harmless. He identifies the cab and its driver, Jefferson Hope, before the arrest, lures Hope into Baker Street, handcuffs him, and helps take him to the police station. Holmes then hears Hope’s account, asks about the person who collected the advertised ring, and explains to Watson how ordinary deductions led to the solution within three days, despite public credit going to Gregson and Lestrade.

records.l: young Stamford, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Young Stamford, formerly a dresser under Dr. Watson at Barts, meets Watson in London, leads him to the laboratory, describes Sherlock Holmes’s scientific interests and habits, introduces them as prospective lodgers, and warns Watson that Holmes may be difficult to understand.

records.l: London, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: London is the city where Dr. Watson, back from India, faces dwindling finances in a Strand hotel and seeks cheaper lodgings after meeting Stamford. It also contains Camberwell and Brixton Road, many detectives and inquiry agencies, and its confusing streets are learned by cab driver Jefferson Hope while he follows Drebber and Stangerson.

records.l: chemical laboratory, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a laboratory [in a hospital wing] The chemical laboratory is located in a wing of the hospital and is filled with bottles, tables, retorts, test-tubes, and Bunsen lamps. Sherlock Holmes works there on a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin.

records.l: Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Baker Street contains 221B, a suite Holmes finds suitable for himself and Watson; they plan to inspect it, then later discuss the Brixton Road murder and await a ring advertisement response there.

records.l: suite of rooms, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has his eye on a suite of rooms in Baker Street that can be shared with Dr. Watson. The two men agree to see the rooms and determine the arrangements together.

records.l: hæmoglobin, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: reacts_with Sherlock Holmes’ test [the reagent is precipitated by it] Sherlock Holmes discovers a reagent that is precipitated by hæmoglobin and by nothing else. He dilutes a drop of blood in water and demonstrates the resulting reaction to Dr. Watson.

records.l: blood stains, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: are_detectable_by Sherlock Holmes’ test [even when old] Blood stains can be difficult to distinguish from mud, rust, or fruit stains when found on clothing months after a suspected crime. Sherlock Holmes’s discovery is presented as a means of identifying them reliably, whether they are old or new.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes’ test, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes’ test is a reagent-based medico-legal blood-stain test: hæmoglobin yields mahogany colour and brownish precipitate, reliably detecting old or new stains and, Holmes says, surpassing Guiacum and microscopy.

records.l: Afghanistan, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Afghanistan is where Dr. Watson served during the second Afghan war and was wounded at the battle of Maiwand. Holmes recognizes that Watson has been there, and Watson later reflects that he has experienced enough noise and excitement in Afghanistan to last him a lifetime. Afghanistan is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the place from which Dr. John Watson had recently come. Holmes reaches this conclusion by combining observations about Watson’s medical and military appearance, tropical complexion, illness, hardship, and injured left arm.

records.l: 221B Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: 221B, Baker Street consists of two comfortable bedrooms and a large, airy sitting-room with two broad windows. It becomes the shared residence of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson and serves as Holmes’s place of business, where clients and investigators come to consult him. 221B Baker Street is given in the advertisement as the place where the wedding ring may be claimed. Mrs. Sawyer visits the address, and Sherlock Holmes follows her after she leaves.

records.l: the Science of Deduction and Analysis, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a science [acquired through long and patient study] The Science of Deduction and Analysis is described as a discipline based on long and patient study of observation and reasoning. Sherlock Holmes applies it professionally, using small physical details to infer a person’s history, occupation, and circumstances.

records.l: consulting detective work, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Consulting detective work is Sherlock Holmes’s occupation. Government detectives and private investigators bring him evidence or cases when they are at fault, and he studies the details, draws on his knowledge of crime, and directs them toward the correct solution.

records.l: observation and deduction, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes treats observation and deduction as practical skills essential to his livelihood. He explains that his reasoning about Dr. John Watson’s military and medical appearance, injuries, complexion, and recent hardships led him to conclude that Watson had come from Afghanistan.

records.l: The Book of Life, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: An article by Sherlock Holmes argues that observation and deduction reveal a man’s history and profession from physical details; Watson doubts it until Holmes identifies himself as its author and practitioner.

records.l: Dr. Watson's move into 221B, Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: occurs 221B, Baker Street [after leaving the hotel] Dr. Watson concludes the arrangement for the rooms at 221B, Baker Street and moves his belongings from the hotel there that evening. He and Sherlock Holmes spend the next days unpacking and arranging their possessions before settling into their new surroundings.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has profound chemistry, practical geology and British law, extensive sensational literature, and strong poison recognition; anatomy is accurate but unsystematic. He plays violin and practices fighting skills, while literature, philosophy, and astronomy are nil, politics feeble, and botany variable.

records.l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Lestrade is a quick, energetic Scotland Yard inspector and detective. At 3, Lauriston Gardens, he joins the investigation and finds the blood-red word “RACHE,” mistakenly reading it as the start of “Rachel” rather than “revenge.” While Gregson follows another suspect, Lestrade pursues Joseph Stangerson, traces him to Halliday’s Private Hotel, and discovers his murder. He gathers Stangerson’s pills, Drebber’s purse, a telegram, and other clues, recording an account in shorthand. He reports the escapee’s description and helps capture and restrain Jefferson Hope. Newspapers credit Lestrade and Gregson with the capture, though Holmes says that credit is incorrect.

records.l: the letter for Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The letter from Tobias Gregson informs Sherlock Holmes that a well-dressed man has been found dead at 3, Lauriston Gardens. It identifies the man through cards bearing the name Enoch J. Drebber, reports blood in the room but no wound or apparent cause of death, and asks Holmes to come and give his opinion.

records.l: the retired sergeant of Marines, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A retired Royal Marine Light Infantry sergeant, now a commissionaire, comes to 221B Baker Street with a large blue envelope for Sherlock Holmes. Holmes identifies his former service; he confirms it and explains his civilian employment before delivering the letter.

records.l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber is an American gentleman from Cleveland, Ohio, a former member of the Latter Day Saints, and the murder victim found in an empty house at 3, Lauriston Gardens. Identified by cards in his pockets, he had a gold watch and was apparently preparing to sail from Liverpool to New York. Before his death, he and his private secretary, Joseph Stangerson, had boarded at Charpentier’s establishment for nearly three weeks. Madame Charpentier describes Drebber as often drunk, coarse, and offensive toward her daughter Alice; his distorted, baboon-like face strikes Watson as vicious. In his younger days, Drebber was selected to marry Lucy Ferrier when the Prophet settled a dispute in favor of Drebber’s stronger party. The marriage was forced, and Drebber acquired much of John Ferrier’s property through it, later becoming wealthy and leaving Utah to travel through the United States and Europe. Jefferson Hope regards him as guilty for forcing Lucy into marriage and helping cause her death, and pursues him as an old rival in love. In Brixton, Hope lures Drebber to the empty house, compels him to choose between two pills, and kills him when he takes the poisoned one. Drebber’s death leads Hope to pursue Stangerson as well. Although others initially suspect Arthur Charpentier, Holmes identifies Hope as Drebber’s murderer and connects the crime to its personal motive.

records.l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Joseph Stangerson is a young Mormon, son of an Elder, formerly of the Chosen People and associated with the Latter Day Saints. He has four wives and is described as cunning, guarded, and quietly reserved. In the pursuit of the Ferriers, he shoots John Ferrier; Lucy is ultimately assigned to Enoch J. Drebber rather than him. Stangerson later becomes Drebber’s private secretary, paid servant, and travel companion, boards with him at Charpentier’s establishment, and is linked to him through a letter, a book bearing his name, and Drebber’s purse. After Drebber’s death, Stangerson’s whereabouts are initially unknown, but he remains indoors at Halliday’s Private Hotel, apparently fearing danger. Jefferson Hope confronts him there and offers poisoned pills. Stangerson attacks Hope and is stabbed to the heart in self-defence. He is found dead in his locked room in nightdress, with a deep wound, “RACHE” written in blood, and the purse, telegram, novel, pipe, water, and pills nearby. His death provides the pills sought in the investigation.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Inspector Gregson is a Scotland Yard inspector and detective, described as quick, energetic, conventional, and among the smartest Yarders. He begins the Lauriston Gardens investigation by writing to Sherlock Holmes, preserving the room but allowing footprints outside to be disturbed, and reporting Drebber’s possessions and inquiries about Stangerson. Using Drebber’s hat, he traces him to Madame Charpentier’s establishment, arrests Arthur Charpentier, and wrongly concludes Arthur killed Drebber. After Lestrade’s report disproves that theory, Gregson asks Holmes to identify the murderer and helps subdue Jefferson Hope during his escape attempt. Although the newspaper credits Gregson and Lestrade with Hope’s capture, Holmes says this credit is incorrect.

records.l: John Rance, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: John Rance is a police constable living at 46 Audley Court, Kennington Park Gate, who patrols Brixton Road. During a night beat, he finds a light and a body in an apparently empty Lauriston Gardens house and encounters a drunken man near its gate.

records.l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Square-toes is the second suspect in the Lauriston Gardens murder: a tall man, over six feet, in the prime of life, with small feet in coarse square-toed boots, a florid or red face, and remarkably long right-hand fingernails. He smokes Trichinopoly cigars, wears a brown overcoat, and is described as desperate, with an accomplice and friends willing to risk something for him. He came with Enoch J. Drebber in a four-wheeled cab, paced and hopped across a puddle, and was likely the tall red-faced man seen by John Rance. Holmes believes he lost a wedding ring at the scene and returned for it; when an advertisement is placed, a disguised accomplice appears instead of him.

records.l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens is an empty house off the Brixton Road, its owner refusing drain repairs. In its bare, dusty front dining-room, Enoch J. Drebber’s body is found beside a red wax candle and a blood-red inscription. Holmes and Watson examine the murder scene and draw deductions from its evidence. Earlier, Jefferson Hope entered with a duplicate key, brought in the drunk Drebber, forced him to choose a pill, and left him dead.

records.l: Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: contains No. 3, Lauriston Gardens The two houses in Lauriston Gardens were empty because their owner would not have the drains inspected, and the last tenant of one had died of typhoid fever. John Rance became suspicious when he saw a light in one of the houses during the night.

records.l: Brixton Road, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Brixton Road is a roadway containing the White Hart Tavern, Holland Grove, and an empty house. A gold wedding ring is supposedly found there. Late in a storm, Jefferson Hope brings Enoch Drebber to the house for a confrontation; Drebber’s body is discovered there, and Tobias Gregson suspects Arthur Charpentier.

records.l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The murder of Enoch J. Drebber takes place during the night in an empty house at 3, Lauriston Gardens on Brixton Road. Drebber has no wound, but blood is scattered in the room; a woman’s wedding ring lies beneath his body, and an inscription, candle, and ring are present at the scene. Holmes concludes that poison was forcibly administered and that the killing was deliberate, motivated by a romantic feud and private revenge rather than robbery or politics. Evidence suggests Drebber entered with Square-toes, who grew agitated before the death. The case initially remains unsolved: Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier, while Lestrade discovers that Joseph Stangerson has also been murdered. Holmes investigates the dropped ring and uses a newspaper advertisement to draw back the murderer. The two pills found in Stangerson’s room link the killings, leading Holmes to conclude that Jefferson Hope killed Drebber.

records.l: Enoch Drebber's death, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Enoch J. Drebber’s death is a poisoning discovered around two in the morning in an empty house after a constable sees a light. His unwounded body bears horror and hatred; Holmes identifies poison, and Jefferson Hope later says he caused Drebber’s end before pursuing Stangerson.

records.l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Brixton Mystery is a murder investigation at Lauriston Gardens, conducted by Tobias Gregson and Lestrade while Sherlock Holmes unofficially observes and assists. Holmes closely examines the grounds, room, grey dust, and inscription, and seeks constable John Rance's address. He soon believes the main facts are clear enough to continue, despite obscure details. Newspapers widely cover the strange crime and speculate about political refugees or revolutionists.

records.l: poisoning, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: causes Enoch J. Drebber's death [according to Sherlock Holmes] Sherlock Holmes identifies poison as the means by which Enoch J. Drebber was killed. The text gives no further details about the poison.

records.l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A plain gold woman’s wedding-ring is taken by Jefferson Hope from Lucy Ferrier’s dead finger and carried as he pursues Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. Hope uses it to remind Drebber of Lucy as Drebber dies, but drops it while leaning over the body and later returns to recover it. Found in the roadway near Brixton Road, it becomes an unexplained clue. Holmes uses a facsimile in an advertisement trap; the ring is claimed by Sally Dennis in Mrs. Sawyer’s story.

records.l: RACHE inscription, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: “RACHE” is a blood-red, single-word inscription on exposed wall plaster, written with Jefferson Hope’s blood after Enoch Drebber’s death. Though Lestrade reads it as an unfinished “Rachel,” it means “revenge” in German. Its non-German-style lettering and false German appearance make it a blind, inspired by a German New York murder case, to divert police toward Socialism, secret societies, or a German suspect.

records.l: the body of Enoch J. Drebber, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The body of Enoch J. Drebber is found lying on the bare floor of the dining-room at 3, Lauriston Gardens. Drebber is middle-aged, broad-shouldered, dressed in respectable clothing, and has clenched hands, interlocked legs, and a face marked by horror and hatred; no wound is found on him.

records.l: the first suspect (Patent-leathers), A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Patent-leathers is identified by dust marks after arriving by cab with Square-toes, walking around a puddle and standing still as Square-toes paces, increasingly agitated.

records.l: Jefferson Hope, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope is a hunter, scout, trapper, silver explorer, ranchman, and later London cabman who becomes the confessed killer of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. Tall, powerfully built, sunburned, and marked by determination and sustained vindictiveness, he begins as a Washoe hunter from the Nevada Mountains. After rescuing Lucy Ferrier from a frightened horse, he falls in love with her and becomes engaged to her with John Ferrier’s consent. While working silver lodes, he receives Ferrier’s warning that Lucy and John are endangered in Salt Lake City. He returns secretly with horses, a mule, money, provisions, water, and firearms, and leads them toward Carson City. The escape fails when he returns from hunting to find John dead and Lucy carried off by pursuers. Lucy’s death and John’s fate turn Hope’s life into a pursuit of revenge. He returns to the Nevada mines to restore his health and gather money, then follows Drebber and Stangerson from Utah across the United States, Europe, and two continents. In London he works as a cabdriver, using his cab both for employment and for pursuing them. He kills Drebber by making him choose between poisoned pills, and later enters Stangerson’s hotel room through a window; he says he stabs Stangerson in self-defence after being attacked. He regards these killings as justice and revenge, including a debt owed to John Ferrier, rather than mere murder. Sherlock Holmes identifies Hope, lures the disguised cabman to his rooms, and captures him after he tries violently to escape through a window. Arrested at 221B Baker Street and held as a prisoner, Hope gives a confession to the investigators. He says his work is complete, but has a life-threatening aortic aneurism expected to burst soon. It does burst the night after his capture, and he dies in his cell before appearing before the magistrates.

records.l: cab, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A cab left two deep wheel ruts and distinctive hoof marks near the curb at No. 3, Lauriston Gardens. Holmes concludes that it arrived during the night and brought Patent-leathers and Square-toes to the house; Rance later reports hearing no cab after the drunken man was found.

records.l: the Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation is Holmes’s logical reconstruction of clues, cab tracks, footprints, poison, a ring, cigar, nail marks, blood, and Cleveland information, to identify Jefferson Hope. Holmes focuses on a tall red-faced man seen by John Rance, plans to use the ring as bait, and solves the crimes despite public credit going to Gregson and Lestrade.
records.t: The Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation is Holmes’s logical reconstruction of clues—cab tracks, footprints, poison, a ring, cigar, nail marks, blood, and Cleveland information—to identify Jefferson Hope. Holmes focuses on a tall red-faced man seen by John Rance, plans to use the ring as bait, and solves the crimes despite public credit going to Gregson and Lestrade.

records.l: the investigation, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_concluded_by the arrest of Jefferson Hope The investigation shifts from Inspector Lestrade’s suspicion of Stangerson to the search for an unknown murderer. Sherlock Holmes uses the pills, the blood-written word, the witness’s description, and other details to complete his deductions and identify Jefferson Hope.

records.l: Mrs. Sawyer, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Mrs. Sawyer appears at 221B Baker Street claiming an advertised wedding ring for her daughter Sally, gives 13 Duncan Street, Houndsditch, and leaves with it; Sherlock Holmes concludes she was a young man in disguise.

records.l: Scotland Yard, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Police organization represented by Lestrade and Gregson, publicly credited with Hope’s capture, though Holmes mocks their failed pursuit and disputes the credit.

records.l: advertisement for the ring, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A Found-column advertisement in the evening paper, placed under Dr. Watson’s name to conceal Holmes, announces a plain gold wedding ring found in Brixton Road and directs claimants to 221B Baker Street, drawing Mrs. Sawyer, believed to be an accomplice in disguise.

records.l: the cab, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The cab is a growler driven by Jefferson Hope in his pursuit and vengeance against Enoch Drebber. Hope uses it to follow Drebber and Joseph Stangerson around London, transport Drebber to the Brixton Road house, and return after losing Lucy Ferrier’s marriage ring. Its narrow wheel marks and the wandering horse help Holmes infer that the murderer drove it and entered the house.

records.l: Arthur Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Arthur Charpentier, Madame Charpentier’s son and Alice Charpentier’s brother, is a naval sub-lieutenant who confronts Drebber over Alice, pursues him with a heavy stick, and is arrested in connection with Drebber’s death.

records.l: Madame Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Madame Charpentier, a widowed boarding-house proprietor and mother of Arthur and Alice, reports Drebber’s offensive behavior toward Alice and Arthur’s pursuit of Drebber after confronting him.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's Street Arab detective corps, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Sherlock Holmes organizes an informal, mobile information-gathering corps, which systematically searches London’s cab proprietors and finds Jefferson Hope among cabdrivers.

records.l: Halliday’s Private Hotel, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_site_of murder of Joseph Stangerson [about six o’clock in the morning] Halliday’s Private Hotel is the place where Joseph Stangerson was murdered at about six o’clock in the morning.

records.l: the murder of Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The murder of Joseph Stangerson, unexpectedly linked to the Drebber investigation, is reported by G. Lestrade after Stangerson is killed in his room at Halliday’s Private Hotel about six in the morning. He is stabbed through the heart; the murderer writes “RACHE” in blood, washes, wipes the knife, and escapes through a window. It is not robbery-motivated and gives Sherlock Holmes the poison pills.

records.l: arrest of Arthur Charpentier, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_based_on suspicion of Brixton murder [according to Gregson’s theory] Tobias Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier after learning from Madame Charpentier that Arthur followed Enoch J. Drebber with a heavy stick. Arthur’s reference to Drebber’s death before the officers had mentioned it appears suspicious to Gregson.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's arrest, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope’s arrest occurs at 221B Baker Street after a young messenger lures the disguised cabman there by saying his cab is wanted. Sherlock Holmes, assisted by Watson and Inspectors Lestrade and Gregson, secretly handcuffs Hope; when he tries to flee, they restrain him and he is led away by warders.

records.l: the poison pills, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope makes two small pills for each intended victim, Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson: one with poison alkaloid and one harmless. He forces Drebber to choose while taking the other himself. After Stangerson’s death, pills found in his room are tested by Sherlock Holmes, who confirms one is deadly and one harmless.

records.l: poison alkaloid, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A powerful alkaloid extracted from South American arrow poison, obtained by Jefferson Hope at York College; a grain in a pill causes instant, fatal death.

records.l: great Alkali Plain, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Great Alkali Plain is a vast, barren, inhospitable desert between the Sierra Nevada and Nebraska, from the Yellowstone River to the Colorado. Snow-capped mountains and gloomy valleys lie within it, but it has no inhabitants. Saline dust, little water, bones, and a marked caravan route make it a deadly barrier to westward travel.

records.l: Sierra Blanco, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: overlooks great Alkali Plain [from its northern slope] The Sierra Blanco overlooks the great Alkali Plain. John Ferrier reaches its northern slope and a rocky elevation, hoping to find signs of water, but sees only the desolate plain and distant mountains.

records.l: Nauvoo, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a place [in Illinois where the Mormons founded their temple] Nauvoo, in Illinois, is identified as the place where the Mormons had founded their temple before leaving in search of refuge from persecution.

records.l: Zion, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Zion is the destination invoked by the Mormon caravan as it continues westward. The Mormons cry, "On, on to Zion!" as their wagons resume their journey.

records.l: John Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: John Ferrier is a solitary, starving traveller on the great Alkali Plain who survives after his companions die and protects Lucy Ferrier, carrying her in a grey shawl and claiming her as his daughter. Rescued by Mormons, he accepts their religious terms to live, adopts Lucy, and becomes a useful guide and indefatigable hunter during their migration. Granted fertile land, he builds Ferrier farm into a large, prosperous holding and becomes a rich, practical farmer of Salt Lake City. Though he otherwise conforms to the Mormon religion, he remains unmarried and strictly celibate. When the Elders demand that Lucy marry, Ferrier refuses the authority of Brigham Young and rejects Joseph Stangerson and young Drebber, preferring Lucy dead to either marriage. Threatened by daily warnings, he prepares his loaded shotgun, gathers two thousand dollars in gold, and plans flight with Lucy and Jefferson Hope. They escape into the mountains, but Ferrier is captured while Hope hunts. Stangerson shoots and kills him; he is buried as a former resident of Salt Lake City. Hope later says that killing Drebber and Stangerson repaid Ferrier’s debt.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Lucy Ferrier is John Ferrier’s adopted daughter, a child rescued with him after her mother dies during a desert journey and brought into a Mormon caravan. Cheerful and trusting at five, she grows into a skilled rider and an admired young woman, regarded by Brigham Young as “the flower of Utah.” She loves Jefferson Hope, becomes engaged to him with John Ferrier’s conditional consent, and waits for his return. Brigham Young requires her to choose between Stangerson’s son and Drebber’s son, but Lucy and her father refuse, fearing punishment while remaining devoted to Hope. She escapes the farm at night with John Ferrier and Hope, but pursuers overtake their camp and capture her. Mormon authorities force her to marry Drebber. She pines away and dies within a month, said by Hope to have died of a broken heart. Hope removes and keeps her wedding ring, and her memory remains central to his vengeance.

records.l: Brigham Young, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Brigham Young is portrayed as a Mormon leader, Prophet, skilful administrator, and resolute chief. He visits John Ferrier’s farm to enforce Mormon marriage requirements, reproaching Ferrier over marriage and Lucy’s association with a Gentile. Young orders Lucy to marry a faithful Mormon, grants a month of grace, and, after Ferrier refuses, carries out his threat through a twenty-nine-day warning.

records.l: Mormons, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Mormons are an immigrant religious community, described as persecuted while traveling west under Brigham Young, their leader, Prophet, and religious head. Admission requires belief in the Mormon creed. After a difficult pilgrimage, they migrate to Utah, establish a settlement with farms, trades, streets, squares, and a central temple, and control Utah through religious and coercive authority. They rescue John Ferrier, give him land and protection, but require conformity, subject members to the Elders, practice polygamy, and are portrayed as using fear and secret violence. Their authority culminates when Stangerson and Drebber seek Lucy Ferrier’s marriage and threaten punishment from the Prophet and Council of Four after Ferrier refuses.

records.l: Mormon caravan, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: An enormous westbound caravan of about ten thousand Mormons crosses the desert with wagons, carts, armed horsemen, women, and children, rescuing John Ferrier and Lucy on the Sierra Blanco.

records.l: twenty-one-person immigrant party, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The twenty-one-person immigrant party becomes lost after expecting to find another river. Its water supply runs out, and only John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier remain alive when the Mormon caravan finds them.

records.l: desert, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The desert is an arid and hostile region of alkali plains, mountains, ravines, and scarce water. It is marked by the bones of people and oxen who have died along the long caravan route.

records.l: Mormon creed, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Mormon creed is a sacred belief based on Egyptian-lettered writings on plates of beaten gold handed to Joseph Smith at Palmyra. Mormons demand that Ferrier and Lucy accept it to travel with them. Its requirements culminate in Brigham Young’s rule that each maiden marry one of the elect, which Ferrier has not arranged for Lucy.

records.l: Mormon migration to Utah, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Mormon migration west is driven by persecution and the search for a new refuge, even in the heart of the desert. The migrants leave Nauvoo and travel in a vast organized caravan toward an unknown destination identified as Zion. The Mormon migration to Utah follows a difficult journey from the shores of the Mississippi across the plains and toward the Rocky Mountains. The migrants overcome hunger, thirst, fatigue, disease, hostile people, and wild animals before reaching their promised land.

records.l: rescue of John Ferrier and Lucy, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_carried_out_by Mormons [after the pair are found on the Sierra Blanco] A group of young Mormon scouts climbs the bluff after seeing Lucy's pink clothing and discovers her sleeping beside John Ferrier. The Mormons carry Lucy and support Ferrier to the wagons, where both receive food, drink, and shelter.

records.l: deaths from hunger and thirst, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: causes_death_of twenty-one-person immigrant party [most members died during the journey] The immigrant party suffers repeated deaths after its expected river fails to appear and its water runs out. Mr. Bender, Indian Pete, Mrs. McGregor, Johnny Hones, Lucy's mother, and the other members of the party die, leaving only John Ferrier and Lucy.

records.l: Utah, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Utah, also called the Land of the Saints, is a broad-valley Mormon settlement and promised destination after a westward journey. Its valley prospers agriculturally and includes Lucy Ferrier, praised across the Pacific slope. Later, religious dissent becomes dangerous; resistance is secretly punished, prompting John Ferrier, Lucy, and fugitives to attempt escape through surrounding mountains.

records.l: Salt Lake City, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Salt Lake City is a city in Utah and a Mormon city called the home of the saints. It develops as the centre of Mormon settlement, with streets, squares, farms, and a great temple, while John Ferrier becomes one of its richest men. Its society is dominated by fear of religious authorities. After Ferrier is killed and Lucy captured, pursuers return there; Lucy is forced to marry Drebber, and Jefferson Hope searches for Drebber and Stangerson before following Drebber abroad.

records.l: Nevada Mountains, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope is contacted through an acquaintance traveling toward the Nevada Mountains. He returns from that direction to help Ferrier and Lucy escape.

records.l: Mormon settlement, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A strange Mormon settlement with a central great temple prospers through organized work, Overland Route traffic, and California gold-fever travelers.

records.l: the farm (John Ferrier's farm), A Study in Scarlet
records.s: John Ferrier’s farm, owned and improved by John Ferrier, grows from a log-house and fertile tract into a prosperous property with a roomy villa. Lucy assists Ferrier and Jefferson Hope visits. After Ferrier defies the authorities, sentinels watch it; the three escape through a side window across the fields.

records.l: the old Nevada mines, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: are_discovered Jefferson Hope's companions [during prospecting in the mountains] Jefferson Hope and his companions discover silver lodes in the Nevada Mountains while prospecting. Hope leaves Salt Lake City to raise enough capital to work the lodes and expects to return within two months.

records.l: the Sacred Council of Four, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Sacred Council of Four, an authority whose commands Brigham Young conveys, tests Lucy Ferrier's faith by ordering her marriage to an eligible Mormon; after John Ferrier defies it, it controls guarded roads and travel orders.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope's first meeting, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: occurs_in Salt Lake City [when Lucy is riding into the city] Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope first meet when her horse becomes trapped and frightened among long-horned cattle near Salt Lake City. Hope seizes the horse’s bridle and leads it out, after which Lucy invites him to visit her and her father.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope's engagement, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: depends_on silver mines in the Nevada Mountains [John Ferrier’s consent is conditional on successful operation] Lucy Ferrier and Jefferson Hope become attached after his visits to the Ferrier farm. John Ferrier gives his consent provided Hope’s mining venture succeeds, and Hope and Lucy agree that she will marry him when he returns.

records.l: polygamy, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a Mormon doctrine [dependent on a sufficient female population] Polygamy is described as dependent on an adequate supply of women, which had become scarce. The shortage is linked to rumors of murdered immigrants and women appearing unwillingly in the harems of the Elders.

records.l: the Church, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Mormon Church governs personal conduct and marriage in Utah, demands adherence to its usages, and punishes dissent through dangerous opposition and confiscation of wealthy dissenters’ goods.

records.l: the Elders, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Elders are a polygamous Mormon leadership group wielding religious and political authority over the settlement. Powerful and feared, they maintain harems and families, endorse Stangerson's and Drebber's sons for Lucy, and confront John Ferrier after he refuses the proposed marriages.

records.l: the avenging angels, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Avenging Angels are a secret, sinister organization linked to Mormon authorities, feared for violence, murders, disappearances, and persecuting dissenters under religion. They pursue Jefferson Hope, John Ferrier, and Lucy, separating the fugitives; John dies, Lucy is forced back to Salt Lake City, and Hope follows their trail.

records.l: persecution, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a coercive religious repression [practiced in Utah] Persecution has turned former victims into persecutors in the society described. People who oppose or question the Mormon authorities may disappear, while others remain silent because they fear secret retaliation.

records.l: Brigham Young's visit to the Ferrier farm, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: concerns Lucy Ferrier's proposed marriage [enforcing a Mormon marriage requirement] During Brigham Young's visit to the Ferrier farm, he confronts John Ferrier about his conduct and Lucy's proposed relationship with a Gentile. He leaves after giving Lucy one month to choose a Mormon husband and threatening the family.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier's proposed marriage, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Lucy Ferrier is ordered to choose Stangerson's or Drebber's son, though she loves Jefferson Hope.

records.l: the planned escape from Utah, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: John Ferrier plans to raise farm money and escape Utah with Lucy after Jefferson Hope returns; with only a month, the plan depends on Hope's help amid fears they may be stopped.

records.l: the Chosen People, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: control Eagle Cañon [through an outlying sentinel post] The Saints’ jurisdiction extends into the mountain pass, where a solitary armed sentinel challenges the fugitives. Jefferson Hope gives the correct countersign, allowing them to pass.

records.l: Carson City, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope plans to take John Ferrier and Lucy through the mountains to Carson City. Their nighttime flight begins along that route.

records.l: Eagle Ravine, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope has a mule and two horses waiting in Eagle Ravine for the escape. The fugitives travel from the farm toward the ravine after crossing the fields.

records.l: Eagle Cañon, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The Eagle Cañon is the narrow mountain defile where Jefferson Hope’s horses are waiting. He guides the fugitives through its rocky path, after which they encounter an armed sentinel.

records.l: the flight for life, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The flight for life begins as Jefferson Hope leads John Ferrier and Lucy from Utah, evading Mormon authority and watchers while traveling through the mountains toward Carson City.

records.l: the threatened punishment of John Ferrier and Lucy, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Stangerson and young Drebber threaten John Ferrier after he rejects them, invoking the Prophet, the Council of Four, and the Lord. Ferrier understands that he and Lucy may be killed or otherwise punished, and he chooses escape rather than submit to Lucy’s dishonour.

records.l: the twenty-nine-day warning, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: threatens John Ferrier [with punishment after the period expires] A paper pinned to John Ferrier’s bed announces that twenty-nine days are given for amendment, followed by an unfinished threat. Ferrier recognizes it as the remaining portion of the month promised by Young.

records.l: the countdown, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: marks_remaining_days the month of grace [through daily numbers from twenty-nine downward] After the twenty-nine-day warning, the numbers 28, 27, and successive lower numbers appear mysteriously around the farm each morning. The countdown reaches 2 before Jefferson Hope arrives, making the next day the last of the allotted time.

records.l: the sentinels, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: guard the roads [to prevent unauthorized escape] Hidden watchers and armed sentinels guard the roads, fields, and mountain routes around the settlement. Jefferson Hope detects two men near the farm, and later gives a countersign to a mountain sentinel, who allows the fugitives to pass.

records.l: the fugitives, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: The fugitives, Jefferson Hope, Lucy Ferrier, and John Ferrier, flee Salt Lake City through the mountains until mounted pursuers kill John, take Lucy back, and Jefferson escapes.
records.t: The fugitives—Jefferson Hope, Lucy Ferrier, and John Ferrier—flee Salt Lake City through the mountains until mounted pursuers kill John, take Lucy back, and Jefferson escapes.

records.l: the pursuit of the fugitives, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_conducted_by the avenging angels [through the mountains] The pursuit follows Jefferson Hope, Lucy Ferrier, and John Ferrier through the mountain defiles. The pursuers eventually overtake the camp while Hope is away, kill John Ferrier, and take Lucy back to Salt Lake City.

records.l: John Ferrier's murder, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_committed_by Stangerson [during the pursuit of the fugitives] John Ferrier's murder occurs at the fugitives' mountain camp while Jefferson Hope is hunting for food. Stangerson shoots him, and the pursuers bury him in a newly dug grave before returning toward Salt Lake City.

records.l: the forced marriage of Lucy Ferrier and Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: After John Ferrier is killed, a council gives Lucy Ferrier to Enoch Drebber rather than Stangerson. Despite her unwillingness and declining condition, she is married to Drebber in Salt Lake City; the forced marriage breaks her heart.

records.l: Lucy Ferrier's death, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: occurs_in Salt Lake City [within a month of her forced marriage] Lucy Ferrier dies within a month of her father's death and her forced marriage to Drebber. Her other husband's wives mourn her, and Jefferson Hope takes her wedding ring from her body before the burial.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's pursuit and vengeance, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope's lifelong pursuit and vengeance begins after Lucy Ferrier is forced to marry Enoch Drebber and John Ferrier is found dead. Seeking punishment for Drebber and accomplice Joseph Stangerson, Hope stalks them, attempts to kill them in the mountains, searches across the United States, follows them through Europe, and finally tracks them in London to impose his own judgment.

records.l: aortic aneurism, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: has_cause over-exposure and under-feeding among the Salt Lake Mountains [according to Jefferson Hope] John Watson, M.D., identifies Jefferson Hope's condition as an aortic aneurism after feeling the powerful throbbing in his chest. Hope says it has worsened for years and that a doctor told him it is bound to burst within days.

records.l: the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope confesses to murdering Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson, claiming they forfeited their lives for John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier's deaths; he poisons Drebber and kills Stangerson.

records.l: Jefferson Hope's confession, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope’s police-station confession, made while an aortic aneurism threatens his life, explains his pursuit of justice and revenge. He recounts using poison pills to kill Enoch Drebber, describes his responsibility for Joseph Stangerson’s death, and refuses to identify his accomplice so as not to implicate another person.

records.l: Stangerson's death, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a death [caused by a stab wound to the heart] Stangerson’s death occurs when he attacks Jefferson Hope after being offered a choice of poisoned pills. Hope says he stabbed Stangerson to the heart in self-defence.

records.l: justice and revenge, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope presents his killings as acts of justice for the life taken by Enoch Drebber and Stangerson and as payment of John Ferrier’s debt. He says he considers himself as much an officer of justice as the officers questioning him.

records.l: Hope's death, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: Jefferson Hope dies when an aneurism bursts the night after his capture; found smiling in his cell, his death prevents testimony and keeps the case’s full details from becoming public.

records.l: the Echo, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: publishes the newspaper report about the case [reporting on Jefferson Hope's death and the murders] The Echo publishes a report about Hope’s death and the Drebber–Stangerson case. It credits Lestrade and Gregson with the capture, calls Holmes an amateur, and predicts that the two officials will receive a testimonial.

records.l: the newspaper report about the case, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: A newspaper report says Hope’s sudden death deprived the public of a sensational account whose full details may remain unknown; it attributes the crimes to a romantic feud involving love and Mormonism and credits Scotland Yard officials with the capture.

records.l: the testimonial, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_intended_for Inspector Gregson [and Inspector Lestrade, as public recognition of their supposed services] The newspaper report predicts that a testimonial will be presented to Inspectors Lestrade and Gregson in recognition of their supposed services. Holmes jokes that the result of the investigation is to get them a testimonial.

records.l: analytical reasoning, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: is_a reasoning backwards Sherlock Holmes describes analytical reasoning as reasoning backward from a known result to the events that produced it. He says that few people can do this and uses it to reconstruct the steps leading from the crime-scene evidence to Jefferson Hope.

records.l: the romantic feud, A Study in Scarlet
records.s: involves Mormonism [according to the newspaper report] The romantic feud is identified as the motive behind the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. The Echo describes it as an old-standing feud involving love and Mormonism, while Holmes connects it specifically with Drebber’s conflict with Hope over a woman.
