records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Sherlock Holmes uses cocaine in Baker Street and explains his belief that mental work is necessary to prevent stagnation. Dr. John Watson challenges Holmes to analyze a watch, and Holmes correctly infers that it belonged to Watson’s elder brother, who was careless, sometimes poor, and died from drinking. Holmes demonstrates how observation and deduction lead from small physical details to broader conclusions. The visit of Miss Mary Morstan is announced at the end of the chapter.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Sherlock Holmes takes cocaine and describes himself as the only unofficial consulting detective, working as an expert of last resort for cases that challenge Gregson, Lestrade, and Athelney Jones. He explains his methods through analyses of tobacco ashes, footsteps, hands, Watson’s movements, and Watson’s watch. He agrees to meet Miss Mary Morstan when she arrives at Baker Street.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Dr. John Watson objects to Sherlock Holmes’s cocaine use and explains the medical dangers he believes it poses. He tests Holmes by giving him a watch and is astonished when Holmes accurately reconstructs the history of its former owner. Watson has a wounded leg from a Jezail bullet and identifies himself as the author of A Study in Scarlet.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Miss Mary Morstan is introduced when Mrs. Hudson announces her arrival at Baker Street. Sherlock Holmes does not remember her name and asks that she be shown upstairs.

records.l: Watson’s elder brother, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Watson’s elder brother was the former owner of Watson’s watch. Holmes infers that he was careless, had good prospects that he wasted, experienced poverty and occasional prosperity, pawned the watch repeatedly, and eventually died from drinking.

records.l: Wigmore Street Post-Office, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: The Wigmore Street Post-Office is identified by Holmes as the place Watson visited earlier that day. Holmes notices reddish earth on Watson’s instep and connects it with pavement work outside the post-office, then deduces that Watson went there to send a telegram.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: The Sign of the Four is the title of the work containing this unit. Its contents list this chapter as Chapter I, “The Science of Deduction.”

records.l: Holmes’s consulting-detective profession, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Holmes’s consulting-detective profession involves examining difficult cases referred by official detectives and giving specialist opinions. Holmes says that he created the profession, claims no newspaper credit, and regards the work and the exercise of his powers as their own reward.

records.l: observation and deduction, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Holmes distinguishes observation from deduction: observation reveals details such as reddish earth on Watson’s instep, while deduction connects those details to conclusions such as a visit to the Wigmore Street Post-Office and the sending of a telegram. He says that the ideal detective needs observation, deduction, and knowledge.

records.l: cocaine, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Cocaine is used by Holmes as a seven-per-cent solution injected with a hypodermic syringe. Holmes considers it mentally stimulating and clarifying, although Watson warns that it may damage the body and produce a severe reaction.

records.l: Watson’s watch, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: Watson’s watch has recently been cleaned, but Holmes examines its case and mechanism with a lens and still draws conclusions about its former owner. Dents, scratches, pawnbrokers’ numbers, and marks around the key-hole lead Holmes to infer carelessness, financial difficulties, intermittent prosperity, and drunkenness.

records.l: the cocaine habit, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: The cocaine habit is described through Holmes’s repeated injections, which Watson has witnessed three times a day for many months. Watson is increasingly distressed by it, while Holmes says he turns to cocaine when he lacks intellectual work and cannot tolerate mental stagnation.

records.l: the science of deduction, The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four / Chapter I
records.s: The science of deduction is presented by Holmes as an exact, unemotional discipline based on analyzing effects and tracing them to causes. Holmes illustrates it by explaining how physical evidence from Watson’s clothing, desk, and watch supports broader conclusions.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Miss Mary Morstan asks Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson to investigate her father Captain Morstan’s disappearance from London in 1878. She explains that an anonymous person has sent her a valuable pearl every year since 1882 and has now summoned her to the Lyceum Theatre, promising justice. Holmes identifies the anonymous letter and the pearl-box addresses as being written by the same person and agrees to accompany Mary with Watson. Watson becomes personally interested in Mary, while Holmes insists that emotional impressions must not influence his reasoning.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Miss Mary Morstan visits Sherlock Holmes to seek help concerning her father’s disappearance and the mysterious pearls sent to her. She agrees to meet an unknown correspondent at the Lyceum Theatre and asks Holmes and Dr. John Watson to accompany her.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Miss Mary Morstan about her father, the pearls, and the anonymous correspondence. He determines that the handwriting on the letter and the pearl-box addresses belongs to the same person, agrees to attend the Lyceum Theatre meeting, and plans to make further inquiries.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Dr. John Watson remains in the room at Miss Mary Morstan’s request and agrees to accompany her and Sherlock Holmes to the Lyceum Theatre. He is strongly attracted to Mary and reflects on her age, circumstances, and his own limited prospects.

records.l: Captain Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Captain Morstan was an officer in an Indian regiment and the senior captain of his regiment in 1878. He returned to England on leave, sent for his daughter, and disappeared after leaving the Langham Hotel.

records.l: London, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: London is where Captain Morstan arrived in 1878, where he disappeared, and where Mary later received the anonymous newspaper advertisement and letter.

records.l: Langham Hotel, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The Langham Hotel was Captain Morstan’s stated address after he returned to London. Mary went there and learned that he had gone out the previous night and had not returned; his luggage remained at the hotel.

records.l: the Lyceum Theatre, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The Lyceum Theatre is the location where the anonymous correspondent instructs Miss Mary Morstan to meet at seven o’clock, at the third pillar from the left.

records.l: the case, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The case concerns Captain Morstan’s unexplained disappearance, the annual delivery of valuable pearls to Mary, and an anonymous promise that a wronged woman will receive justice. Sherlock Holmes considers it a particularly strange mystery.

records.l: Captain Morstan's disappearance, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Captain Morstan disappeared on 3 December 1878 after arriving in London and going out from the Langham Hotel. Police inquiries and newspaper advertisements produced no result, and no word of him was heard afterward.

records.l: the 1878 newspaper advertisement, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: After Captain Morstan disappeared, inquiries led to advertisements in the papers, but they produced no result.

records.l: the pearl deliveries, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Beginning about six years before this meeting, a similar box containing a pearl arrived for Miss Mary Morstan every year on the same date. No writing or clue identifying the sender accompanied the deliveries.

records.l: pearls sent to Mary Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The pearls sent to Mary Morstan are described as very large, lustrous, and handsome. An expert pronounced them to be of a rare variety and considerable value.

records.l: pearl boxes sent to Mary Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The pearl boxes were small cardboard boxes addressed to Miss Mary Morstan. Each contained a pearl, and Holmes examines the writing on their addresses for comparison with the anonymous letter.

records.l: the anonymous letter, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The anonymous letter tells Mary to be at the third pillar outside the Lyceum Theatre at seven o’clock and promises justice to a wronged woman. It warns her not to bring the police and says that she may bring two friends if she is distrustful.

records.l: the anonymous correspondent, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The anonymous correspondent sends Mary annual pearls and writes the letter arranging the Lyceum Theatre meeting. The correspondent’s identity is unknown, but Holmes concludes that the same person wrote the letter and the pearl-box addresses.

records.l: the handwriting, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Holmes finds that the handwriting on the pearl-box addresses is disguised but matches the handwriting of the anonymous letter. He notes an irrepressible Greek e and a recurring twirl in the final s as evidence of common authorship.

records.l: the meeting at the Lyceum Theatre, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: The meeting at the Lyceum Theatre is arranged for seven o’clock at the third pillar from the left. Miss Mary Morstan will attend with Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson, and the correspondent warns that police must not be brought.

records.l: the investigation, The Sign of the Four, Chapter II
records.s: Sherlock Holmes begins the investigation by recording details of Captain Morstan’s disappearance and examining the correspondence. He intends to consult references before the Lyceum Theatre meeting and asks to keep the handwriting samples.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Sherlock Holmes connects Captain Morstan’s disappearance with Major Sholto’s death and the yearly presents sent to Miss Morstan, though he acknowledges unresolved difficulties. Miss Morstan brings a mysterious paper from her father’s pocket-book, bearing a building plan, a red cross, the note “3.37 from left,” and the names associated with the sign of the four. Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Miss Morstan travel by four-wheeler through foggy London to the Lyceum Theatre, where a coachman takes them to an unknown destination. They arrive at an unoccupied suburban house, where a Hindoo servant announces that the Sahib awaits them.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Sherlock Holmes finds that Major Sholto died on April 28, 1882, and reasons that Sholto’s heir may have sent yearly presents to Captain Morstan’s daughter as compensation for knowledge of her father’s fate. He examines the mysterious paper with a double lens, recognizes it as Indian-manufactured paper containing a building plan and unusual writing, and admits that the case is deeper than he first supposed. He carries a revolver and studies London’s streets during the night’s expedition.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Miss Morstan on the night’s expedition. He carries a heavy stick, observes Holmes’s investigation and the ominous atmosphere, and tries to entertain Miss Morstan with reminiscences of his adventures in Afghanistan during the journey.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Miss Morstan accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson on the night’s expedition while maintaining a composed and resolute manner despite her uneasiness. She explains that Major Sholto was a close friend of her father and brings Holmes a mysterious paper found in Captain Morstan’s pocket-book. She gives her word that neither of her companions is a police-officer before the coachman takes them away.

records.l: Captain Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Captain Morstan disappeared after coming to London, and Major Sholto was the only person there whom he could have visited. A curious paper found in his pocket-book contains a building plan, a red cross, a distance note, and references to the sign of the four.

records.l: Major Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Major Sholto, of Upper Norwood and formerly of the 34th Bombay Infantry, was a particular friend of Captain Morstan and had served with him at the Andaman Islands. He denied having heard that Captain Morstan was in London and died on April 28, 1882.

records.l: London, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: London is covered by a dense, drizzly fog during the evening expedition. Holmes identifies streets and districts as the four-wheeler travels through the city, eventually crossing the Thames and reaching a questionable suburban neighbourhood.

records.l: the Lyceum Theatre, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The Lyceum Theatre is the rendezvous where Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Miss Morstan meet a small, dark coachman. The coachman questions Miss Morstan there before arranging their departure in a four-wheeler.

records.l: the mystery, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The mystery initially appears to Holmes to have one explanation connecting Captain Morstan’s disappearance, Major Sholto’s death, and the presents sent to Miss Morstan. The mysterious paper introduces further complications, causing Holmes to reconsider his ideas.

records.l: the night’s expedition, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The night’s expedition is undertaken by Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Miss Morstan to resolve the mystery. They travel in secrecy through foggy London to an unknown destination and arrive at a dark, newly built suburban house.

records.l: Captain Morstan's disappearance, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Captain Morstan’s disappearance is linked by Holmes to Major Sholto because Sholto was the only person in London whom Morstan could have visited. Holmes suspects that Sholto’s heir knows something about what happened and has tried to compensate Morstan’s daughter.

records.l: Major Sholto’s death, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: Major Sholto’s death occurred on April 28, 1882. Holmes notes that within a week of it, Captain Morstan’s daughter began receiving valuable presents that continued yearly.

records.l: the anonymous letter, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The letter sent to Captain Morstan’s daughter describes her as a wronged woman and promises justice. Holmes connects it with the presents she has received since shortly after Major Sholto’s death, although the reason for its timing remains uncertain.

records.l: the mysterious paper, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The mysterious paper was found in Captain Morstan’s pocket-book and is made of native Indian paper that had apparently been pinned to a board. It contains a plan of part of a large building, a red cross, the note “3.37 from left,” and a reference to the sign of the four; Holmes considers it important and tells Miss Morstan to preserve it.

records.l: the sign of the four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: The sign of the four appears on the mysterious paper as a hieroglyphic resembling four touching crosses. It is accompanied by the names Jonathan Small, Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan, and Dost Akbar.

records.l: the four-wheeler, The Sign of the Four, Chapter III
records.s: A four-wheeler brings Miss Morstan to the Lyceum Theatre and later carries her, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. Watson through the foggy streets. A coachman drives it at a furious pace to an unknown destination, eventually stopping at a new suburban terrace.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto brings Miss Morstan, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. Watson to his richly furnished rooms and tells them about the Agra treasure and Captain Arthur Morstan’s death. He explains that his father, Major John Sholto, concealed Morstan’s death and kept Morstan’s share of the treasure, later confessing the matter to his sons before dying. A mysterious bearded intruder appeared at Major Sholto’s death, and a torn paper bearing “The sign of the four” was found afterward. Thaddeus says Bartholomew Sholto has discovered the treasure at Pondicherry Lodge, so they travel to Norwood to pursue Miss Morstan’s inheritance claim.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Miss Morstan meets Thaddeus Sholto to learn what he wishes to tell her about her father and the treasure. She learns that her father died during a quarrel with Major John Sholto and that she is entitled to at least half of the Agra treasure; the news makes her pale, but she continues with the others to Pondicherry Lodge.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Sherlock Holmes accompanies Miss Morstan and Dr. Watson to meet Thaddeus Sholto and agrees that the information will go no further. He listens closely to Sholto’s account and says that they may be able to throw light on the remaining mystery before urging the party to leave for Norwood.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Miss Morstan and Sherlock Holmes and examines Thaddeus Sholto’s heart at Sholto’s request, finding it normal apart from his evident fear. He listens to the account of Captain Morstan’s death and observes Miss Morstan’s distress; on learning of her possible fortune, he privately realizes that selfishness has affected his feelings.

records.l: Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto invites Miss Morstan, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. Watson to his rooms and tells them about Major John Sholto, Captain Arthur Morstan, and the Agra treasure. He says he sent Miss Morstan pearls at intervals, argues that she should receive her share, and asks her and her companions to accompany him to Norwood to claim it from Bartholomew Sholto.

records.l: Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Bartholomew Sholto is Thaddeus Sholto’s twin brother and is described as clever but angry with Thaddeus over his decision to contact Miss Morstan. He discovered the hidden treasure by calculating that four feet of the house’s height were unaccounted for and locating a sealed garret above the highest room.

records.l: Major Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Major John Sholto was a former Indian army officer who lived at Pondicherry Lodge with his sons after returning from India with wealth and valuable curiosities. He concealed Captain Arthur Morstan’s death and kept Morstan’s share of the treasure, then confessed the matter to his sons before dying.

records.l: Captain Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Captain Arthur Morstan had been Major John Sholto’s friend and came to Pondicherry Lodge to claim his share of a treasure acquired in India. During a quarrel, he suffered a fatal attack connected with his weak heart, fell backward, and struck his head against the treasure-chest.

records.l: Pondicherry Lodge, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Pondicherry Lodge was Major John Sholto’s home in Upper Norwood, where he lived in luxury with his sons and native servants. Captain Morstan died there, and Bartholomew later discovered the hidden treasure in a sealed garret above the highest room.

records.l: Norwood, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Norwood is where Pondicherry Lodge is located. Thaddeus Sholto says that the party must travel there to meet Bartholomew Sholto and demand Miss Morstan’s share of the treasure.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: The Agra treasure was a considerable treasure that Captain Arthur Morstan and Major John Sholto acquired in India and that Major Sholto brought to England. Bartholomew Sholto discovered it hidden in a sealed garret at Pondicherry Lodge, and its jewels are estimated to be worth at least half a million pounds.

records.l: Morstan’s share of the treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Morstan’s share of the treasure was owed to Miss Morstan, but Major John Sholto concealed it along with the body and kept it despite making no use of it. Thaddeus Sholto says that he and Bartholomew must make restitution, and he travels with Miss Morstan to pursue the claim.

records.l: the torn paper bearing The sign of the four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: After Major Sholto’s death, his room was found disturbed and a torn piece of paper bearing the words “The sign of the four” was fixed to his chest. The meaning of the phrase and the identity of the visitor connected with it remained unknown to Thaddeus and Bartholomew.

records.l: Captain Morstan's disappearance, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Captain Morstan’s death occurred at Pondicherry Lodge after he and Major John Sholto argued over the division of the treasure. Morstan, who had a weak heart, suddenly collapsed and struck his head on the treasure-chest; Major Sholto and Lal Chowdar concealed the body rather than report the death.

records.l: Major Sholto’s death, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Before his death, Major Sholto confessed to his sons that he had concealed Captain Morstan’s death and retained Morstan’s share of the treasure. While he was revealing the treasure’s hiding place, a bearded face appeared at the window, after which Major Sholto cried out and died.

records.l: the discovery of the treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: Bartholomew Sholto discovered the treasure by measuring the house and finding four feet of height unaccounted for. He opened the ceiling of the highest room and found a sealed garret containing the treasure-chest.

records.l: the inheritance claim, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IV
records.s: The inheritance claim concerns Miss Morstan’s right to at least half of the Agra treasure, which Major John Sholto had withheld. Thaddeus Sholto intends to accompany her to Pondicherry Lodge and demand her share from Bartholomew Sholto.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Watson, Sherlock Holmes, Miss Morstan, and Thaddeus Sholto arrive at Pondicherry Lodge and discover that Bartholomew Sholto has been murdered. Bartholomew is found dead in his locked chemical laboratory, with a strange grin, a poisoned thorn near his ear, and a note bearing “The sign of the four.” Thaddeus reports that the treasure is gone through an opening in the ceiling and fears that he will be suspected. Holmes advises Thaddeus to report the matter to the police while he, Watson, and Miss Morstan remain at the lodge.

records.l: Pondicherry Lodge, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Pondicherry Lodge stands within grounds surrounded by a high stone wall topped with broken glass, with a single guarded entrance. The house is huge, gloomy, and silent, and its grounds are covered with heaps and excavations made by treasure-seekers.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Sherlock Holmes gains entrance to Pondicherry Lodge by reminding the porter McMurdo of their former boxing match. He examines marks on the stairs and the locked chamber, identifies the death as murder, and recognizes the thorn as poisoned. Holmes tells Thaddeus Sholto to report the matter to the police.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Watson accompanies Holmes, Miss Morstan, and Thaddeus Sholto to Pondicherry Lodge. He comforts Miss Morstan and helps Thaddeus ascend the stairs, then examines Bartholomew Sholto’s body and the note reading “The sign of the four.”

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Miss Morstan accompanies the others to Pondicherry Lodge and instinctively takes Watson’s hand during the frightening wait outside. She comforts the distressed housekeeper, Mrs. Bernstone, whose fear is eased by Miss Morstan’s presence.

records.l: Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto brings Holmes, Watson, and Miss Morstan to Pondicherry Lodge, but becomes terrified when Bartholomew does not answer. He says that he helped Bartholomew lower the treasure through an opening in the ceiling, fears being suspected of the murder, and follows Holmes’s advice to report the death to the police.

records.l: Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: Bartholomew Sholto is found dead in his locked chemical laboratory, seated in a chair with his head on his shoulder and a ghastly fixed smile on his face. His limbs appear twisted, and a poisoned thorn has been stuck into the skin above his ear.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: The treasure that Bartholomew Sholto and Thaddeus had lowered through an opening in the ceiling is missing when the chamber is entered. Thaddeus declares that the treasure has been stolen.

records.l: the murder of Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: The death of Bartholomew Sholto is identified by Sherlock Holmes as murder. The locked room contains a poisoned thorn, a peculiar hammer-like instrument, a torn note, and an opening in the ceiling, while the treasure is gone.

records.l: the sign of the four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: The words “The sign of the four” are scrawled on a torn sheet of note-paper beside Bartholomew Sholto’s body. Holmes treats the message as significant evidence in the murder.

records.l: the poisoned thorn, The Sign of the Four, Chapter V
records.s: A long, dark thorn is found embedded in the skin just above Bartholomew Sholto’s ear. Holmes warns that it is poisoned, and Watson removes it, leaving only a tiny speck of blood.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the locked room where Bartholomew Sholto died and deduces that Jonathan Small entered through the window with a rope, while a mysterious ally entered through the roof trap-door. Holmes finds small naked footprints, traces of creosote, and evidence that Bartholomew was killed by a poisoned thorn that caused extreme muscular contraction. Athelney Jones arrests Thaddeus Sholto, but Holmes rejects Jones’s theory and identifies Jonathan Small from the physical evidence. Holmes sends Dr. Watson to bring back Toby so the scent of creosote can be tracked.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the locked room, window, rope, footprints, creosote, and poisoned thorn, reconstructing how the intruders entered and escaped. He identifies Jonathan Small from the evidence, promises to clear Thaddeus Sholto, and sends Dr. Watson to fetch Toby while he continues investigating.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Dr. Watson follows Holmes through the lower room and secret room, observes the evidence, and agrees that Bartholomew Sholto died from a powerful vegetable alkaloid. Holmes asks him to escort Miss Morstan home and then fetch Toby from Sherman in Lambeth.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Jonathan Small is identified as one of the two people in the room. Holmes describes him as a poorly educated, small, active, sunburned, middle-aged former convict with his right leg missing, a worn wooden stump, a distinctive left boot, and skin missing from his palm.

records.l: the Islander, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The mysterious ally helps Jonathan Small enter and leave the room by lowering and drawing up the rope, securing it to the wall hook, and closing the window from inside. Holmes believes this ally entered through the roof trap-door and considers him an unusual figure in the history of crime.

records.l: Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto is found in a distressed state after his brother’s death and is suspected by Athelney Jones because he had quarreled with Bartholomew and was with him beforehand. Jones arrests him for being concerned in his brother’s death, but Holmes says he can clear him.

records.l: Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Bartholomew Sholto is found dead in the locked room with severely contracted muscles and a distorted face. Holmes concludes that a poisoned thorn was driven or shot into his scalp through the hole in the ceiling.

records.l: Athelney Jones, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Athelney Jones arrives with an inspector and develops a theory that Thaddeus Sholto killed his brother and took the treasure. He arrests Thaddeus despite the evidence of an outside intruder, while Holmes dismisses his conclusions as flawed.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Miss Morstan is to be escorted home from the stricken house by Dr. Watson. She lives with Mrs. Cecil Forrester in Lower Camberwell.

records.l: Toby, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Toby is a queer mongrel owned or kept by Sherman, the bird-stuffer in Pinchin Lane. Holmes regards Toby’s extraordinary sense of smell as more useful than the entire London detective force for following the creosote trail.

records.l: Pondicherry Lodge, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The house contains the locked room where Bartholomew Sholto died, an inaccessible window, a garret, and a roof trap-door. Police and investigators enter it during the murder investigation.

records.l: the chemical laboratory at Pondicherry Lodge, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The secret room is the upper chamber where the treasure was found. It has a dusty rafter floor, no furniture, and a trap-door leading to the roof; its floor is covered with small naked footprints.

records.l: the murder of Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The death of Bartholomew Sholto is attributed by Holmes to a powerful vegetable alkaloid delivered through a poisoned thorn. The body’s extreme contraction and risus sardonicus indicate a strychnine-like poison producing tetanus.

records.l: the arrest of Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Athelney Jones arrests Thaddeus Sholto in the Queen’s name for being concerned in the death of his brother. Holmes immediately tells Thaddeus not to worry and says he expects to clear him.

records.l: the theft of the treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The treasure is missing from the locked house after Jonathan Small and his ally enter and leave by unusual routes. Holmes links the theft to the two intruders rather than to Thaddeus Sholto.

records.l: the case, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The murder investigation focuses on the locked room, the route used by the intruders, the missing jewels, and the poison that killed Bartholomew Sholto. Holmes and Athelney Jones pursue competing explanations, with Holmes relying on physical traces and Jones accusing Thaddeus.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The treasure was found in the secret room and is later missing. Athelney Jones treats its disappearance as evidence against Thaddeus Sholto, while Holmes connects it to the intruders.

records.l: the rajah's treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The jewels, described by Athelney Jones as worth half a million, are missing from the house. Their disappearance forms a central part of Jones’s accusation against Thaddeus Sholto.

records.l: the rope, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The rope is secured to a wall hook and is used by Jonathan Small to climb up to and descend from the window with help from his ally. Blood marks on it show that Small slipped while descending and injured the skin of his hand.

records.l: the narrator's wooden leg, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The wooden stump leaves circular muddy impressions on the sill, floor, and near the table. Holmes uses these marks to establish that a wooden-legged man entered through the window.

records.l: creosote, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: Creosote has leaked from a cracked carboy in the room. Jonathan Small or one of the intruders steps in it, leaving a small footprint, and Holmes plans to have Toby follow the powerful scent.

records.l: the poisoned thorn, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The poisoned thorn is found in Bartholomew Sholto’s scalp, apparently driven or shot through the ceiling opening. It is long, sharp, black, and coated near the point with a dried gummy substance; Holmes believes it caused the fatal poisoning.

records.l: the trap-door in the roof, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The trap-door connects the secret room’s garret with the roof. Holmes concludes that Jonathan Small’s ally entered through it, and Athelney Jones treats it as evidence supporting his own mistaken theory about the escape.

records.l: the footprints, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: A heavy boot print and a circular wooden-stump mark appear near the window, while the secret room contains many clear prints from a naked foot about half the size of an ordinary man’s. Holmes interprets these traces as evidence of the intruders’ movements.

records.l: the poison, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VI
records.s: The poison produces extreme muscular contraction, a distorted face, and risus sardonicus. Dr. Watson and Holmes identify it as a powerful vegetable alkaloid resembling strychnine and causing tetanus.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Dr. John Watson escorts Miss Mary Morstan home, then retrieves Toby from Mr. Sherman and returns to Pondicherry Lodge. Sherlock Holmes examines the footprints, creasote scent, and a pouch of poison spines before using Toby to track the escaping perpetrators. Holmes concludes that the wooden-legged man is Jonathan Small and that an unnamed associate entered Bartholomew Sholto’s room, killed him with poison, and fled with the Agra treasure. Watson and Holmes follow Toby’s trail through the London suburbs toward the fugitives.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Dr. John Watson escorts Miss Mary Morstan home and then obtains Toby from Mr. Sherman. He returns to Pondicherry Lodge, helps Sherlock Holmes examine the crime scene, and follows Toby and Holmes in pursuit of Jonathan Small and his associate.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Miss Mary Morstan remains calm while supporting the frightened housekeeper but faints and weeps in the cab after the night’s events. Dr. John Watson restrains his declaration of love because she is distressed and may become an heiress through the Agra treasure.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the footprints, identifies the distinctive separation of the toes, and uses the creasote scent to direct Toby’s pursuit. He deduces that the wooden-legged man is Jonathan Small and that an unnamed associate committed the murder, then follows the trail with Dr. John Watson.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The Agra treasure is rediscovered and immediately followed by the murder of Bartholomew Sholto. Sherlock Holmes believes Jonathan Small came to England to regain what he regarded as his rights and that the treasure-box was lowered from the garret and carried away.

records.l: Major Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Major Sholto possessed the Agra treasure and kept its hiding place secret except from one faithful servant who later died. After receiving a frightening letter from India, he guarded himself against a wooden-legged man, whom Sherlock Holmes identifies as Jonathan Small.

records.l: Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Bartholomew Sholto was murdered in the garret after discovering the Agra treasure. Sherlock Holmes believes the unnamed associate of Jonathan Small entered the room and killed him with poison.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Jonathan Small is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the middle-aged, bearded, sunburned, wooden-legged white man connected with Captain Morstan’s chart. Holmes believes he sought revenge on Major Sholto, watched the search for the treasure, helped remove the treasure-box, and left the scene with his associate.

records.l: Jonathan Small’s associates, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Jonathan Small’s associates were convicts who could not obtain the treasure when Captain Morstan’s chart was made. The chart identifies Jonathan Small and his associates as the four connected with the treasure.

records.l: the Islander, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The unnamed associate of Jonathan Small could reach the lofty garret that Jonathan Small could not reach because of his wooden leg. He entered Bartholomew Sholto’s room, killed him with poison, and left a trail marked by a naked foot dipped in creasote.

records.l: Toby, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Toby is an ugly, long-haired, brown-and-white dog obtained from Mr. Sherman. After smelling the creasote handkerchief, Toby follows the scent from Pondicherry Lodge through the grounds and London streets toward the fugitives.

records.l: Pondicherry Lodge, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Pondicherry Lodge remains guarded by constables after the murder. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson return there, examine the garret and roof, and begin the pursuit from the grounds.

records.l: the Agra treasure mystery, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The Agra treasure mystery leads from Captain Morstan’s death and the pearls to the chart, Major Sholto’s death, the treasure’s rediscovery, and Bartholomew Sholto’s murder. Sherlock Holmes develops a reconstruction involving Jonathan Small and his unnamed associate.

records.l: the murder of Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The murder of Bartholomew Sholto is associated with footprints, unusual weapons, a card bearing words corresponding to Captain Morstan’s chart, and poison. Sherlock Holmes concludes that Jonathan Small’s unnamed associate committed the killing while Jonathan Small removed the treasure-box.

records.l: the pursuit of Jonathan Small and his associate, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The pursuit of Jonathan Small and his associate begins when Toby follows the creasote scent from Pondicherry Lodge. Toby tracks them across the grounds and through Streatham, Brixton, Camberwell, and Kennington toward the continuing trail.

records.l: Captain Morstan’s chart, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: Captain Morstan’s chart bears the name Jonathan Small and the sign of the four. Sherlock Holmes uses it to connect Jonathan Small with the convict group and the buried treasure.

records.l: the sign of the four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The Sign of the Four is the name Jonathan Small gave to the mark representing himself and his associates on Captain Morstan’s chart.

records.l: the poison spines, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The poison spines are dark wooden, sharply pointed objects found in a small woven pouch dropped during the escape. Sherlock Holmes identifies them as like the weapon that struck Bartholomew Sholto and warns Dr. John Watson not to prick himself.

records.l: the creasote trail, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VII
records.s: The creasote trail was left when the unnamed associate placed a bare foot in creasote while escaping through the garret window. Sherlock Holmes uses the scent on a handkerchief to direct Toby, whose nose follows it despite the traffic on the London road.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and the narrator follow Toby through Nine Elms to Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard. Toby races through the yard and identifies a large barrel on a hand-trolley as the end of the trail. The barrel and trolley are smeared with a dark liquid, and the air smells strongly of creosote, causing Holmes and the narrator to laugh.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: Sherlock Holmes follows Toby to Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard. He appears to think they are nearing the end of their journey, then laughs uncontrollably with the narrator when Toby stops at the barrel.

records.l: Toby, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: Toby becomes frantic with excitement and leads Sherlock Holmes and the narrator into Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard. He races through the sawdust, shavings, alleys, passages, and wood-piles before springing onto a large barrel and looking for appreciation.

records.l: Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard lies just past the White Eagle tavern on Nine Elms. Toby enters it through a side-gate and runs through the working yard to a barrel on a hand-trolley.

records.l: the creasote barrel, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: The barrel stands on the hand-trolley on which it was brought, and Toby springs onto it with a triumphant yelp. Its staves are smeared with a dark liquid, and the air around it smells of creosote.

records.l: creosote, The Sign of the Four, leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in
records.s: Creosote is identified by its strong smell in the air around the barrel and trolley.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson recover Toby’s trail to the river, where they learn that Mordecai Smith’s steam launch, the Aurora, has been taken downstream by Smith and a wooden-legged man. Holmes questions Mrs. Smith and concludes that the fugitives have carefully covered their tracks, so he recruits Wiggins and the Baker Street Irregulars to search both banks of the river. A newspaper reports that Athelney Jones has arrested Thaddeus Sholto and several servants for Bartholomew Sholto’s murder, while Holmes privately investigates the stolen gems and the criminals’ escape. Holmes also identifies the second fugitive as probably an Andaman islander based on his small bare footprints, blow-pipe darts, and stone-headed weapon.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Holmes follows Toby’s recovered scent to a wharf and learns from Mrs. Smith that the Aurora was taken away during the night by Mordecai Smith and a wooden-legged man. He recruits Wiggins and the Baker Street Irregulars to search for the launch, studies the clues concerning the second fugitive, and identifies him as probably an Andaman islander.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Watson accompanies Holmes during the search for the fugitives and helps question the evidence concerning the Aurora. He is exhausted after the night’s events, reads the newspaper account of the case, and falls asleep while Holmes plays the violin.

records.l: Toby, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Toby initially follows a false creasote trail but is not blamed because two trails had crossed. After being returned to the point of confusion, he picks up the true trail toward the river and is retained by Holmes as a possible future aid.

records.l: Mordecai Smith, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Smith owns the Aurora and hires out boats at his landing-stage. According to his wife, he left in the steam launch after being roused during the night by a wooden-legged man, and she is worried because he has not returned.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Holmes associates Small with the Andaman Islands and reasons that this may explain his having an Andaman islander as a companion. Holmes suggests that Small might regret employing such a dangerous companion.

records.l: the wooden-legged man, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The wooden-legged man visited Mrs. Smith’s house during the night, calling for Smith and departing with him in the Aurora. He is described as brown-faced, monkey-faced, thick-voiced, and capable of moving with a wooden leg.

records.l: the Islander, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Holmes infers that the fugitives’ second companion is an Andaman islander from his diminutive bare footprints, stone-headed wooden mace, and poisoned blow-pipe darts. Holmes describes the Andaman islanders as fierce and dangerous, with a reputation for attacking shipwrecked crews.

records.l: Wiggins, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Wiggins receives Holmes’s telegraph and brings the Baker Street Irregulars to Baker Street. Holmes places him in charge of their reports during the search for the Aurora.

records.l: the Baker Street Irregulars, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The Baker Street Irregulars arrive at Holmes’s rooms after receiving his message. Holmes pays them to search both banks of the river, watch Mordecai Smith’s landing-stage, and report immediately if they find the Aurora, offering a guinea to the boy who locates it.

records.l: the Aurora, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The Aurora is Mordecai Smith’s steam launch, described as black with two red streaks and a black funnel with a white band. Smith and the wooden-legged man take it down the river, and Holmes sends the Irregulars to locate it.

records.l: the Thames, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Toby’s trail leads Holmes and Watson to the river’s edge at a small wharf. Holmes believes the fugitives boarded a boat there and notes that the many landing-places below the bridge would make a systematic search difficult.

records.l: the Andaman Islands, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: Holmes consults a gazetteer and learns that the Andaman Islands lie north of Sumatra in the Bay of Bengal. The book describes their aborigines as exceptionally small, fierce people with remarkably small feet who use stone-headed clubs and poisoned arrows.

records.l: the steam launch chase, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The chase leads Holmes and Watson from the recovered scent to Mordecai Smith’s landing-stage and the missing Aurora. Rather than search every wharf themselves or alert the police and fugitives, Holmes employs the Baker Street Irregulars to watch both banks and await news.

records.l: the murder of Bartholomew Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The newspaper reports that Bartholomew Sholto was found dead at Pondicherry Lodge under circumstances suggesting foul play. Athelney Jones has arrested Thaddeus Sholto, Mrs. Bernstone, Lal Rao, and McMurdo, and the report falsely credits Jones with proving that the criminals entered through the roof.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The newspaper states that a valuable collection of Indian gems inherited by Bartholomew Sholto was carried off. Watson regards recovering the treasure as especially important because it belongs rightfully, at least in part, to Miss Morstan.

records.l: the case, The Sign of the Four, Chapter VIII
records.s: The case concerns Bartholomew Sholto’s murder, the theft of the Indian gems, and the escape of the suspected criminals by the Aurora. Holmes continues investigating independently while using the Irregulars to find the launch and studying the unusual evidence identifying the fugitives’ companions.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Sherlock Holmes becomes frustrated when the search for Mordecai Smith’s missing steam launch produces no results, then disguises himself as an aged sailor to investigate further. After Holmes leaves, Dr. Watson learns from the newspaper that Thaddeus Sholto and Mrs. Bernstone have been released because Sholto’s alibi clears him of involvement in the Upper Norwood tragedy. Athelney Jones arrives seeking Holmes’s help, and Holmes returns in disguise with a plan to capture the fugitives and recover the treasure. Holmes arranges for a police steam launch and officers to meet at Westminster Stairs, while Dr. Watson is to deliver the treasure to Miss Morstan first.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is troubled and restless because the search for the fugitives and the steam launch has stalled. He places an advertisement, travels down the river in disguise, and returns disguised as an old sailor after learning enough to arrange a police pursuit. He requires Athelney Jones to follow his orders and plans to capture the men, recover the treasure, and question Jonathan Small.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Dr. Watson visits Miss Morstan and Mrs. Forrester, reports the investigation’s progress, and remains at Baker Street as Holmes’s representative. He receives Holmes’s telegram, meets Athelney Jones, and helps detain Holmes while Holmes is disguised as an old sailor. Holmes suggests that Watson take the recovered treasure to Miss Morstan first.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Miss Morstan is weary after the night’s adventures but eager to hear the news. She says that her main concern is clearing Thaddeus Sholto of the unfounded charge because he has behaved kindly and honourably. Holmes intends for her to be the first to open the recovered treasure.

records.l: Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto is released after proving an unshakable alibi showing that he was continually seen after leaving his brother’s room. The newspaper reports that it is impossible for him to have taken part in the Upper Norwood tragedy.

records.l: Athelney Jones, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Athelney Jones admits that his theory against Thaddeus Sholto has failed and asks for Sherlock Holmes’s assistance. He agrees to place himself under Holmes’s direction, provide a police steam launch and officers, and allow Holmes an unofficial interview with Jonathan Small if Small is captured.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Jonathan Small is identified by Holmes as one of the men being pursued. Holmes wants to obtain detailed information about the case directly from him after he is captured.

records.l: Mordecai Smith, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Mordecai Smith is the boatman who left Smith’s Wharf with his son Jim in the steam launch Aurora. His whereabouts remain unknown, and Holmes’s advertisement seeks information about him, his son, and the launch.

records.l: the Sholto gang, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Holmes’s telegram states that he is close on the track of the Sholto gang. He plans to give Athelney Jones two new prisoners in place of the released suspects.

records.l: Baker Street, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Baker Street is Holmes’s address and the location where Dr. Watson waits for news. Holmes places it in the advertisement as a contact address, and his telegram directs Athelney Jones to go there.

records.l: Mordecai Smith's boats and landing-stage, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Smith’s Wharf is the place from which Mordecai Smith and his son Jim departed in the Aurora. The advertisement directs anyone with information to contact Mrs. Smith there.

records.l: Westminster Stairs, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Westminster Stairs is the meeting point where Holmes requires a fast police steam launch to be at seven o’clock.

records.l: Upper Norwood, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Upper Norwood is associated with the tragedy involving the Sholtos. The newspaper reports that new evidence cleared Thaddeus Sholto of involvement.

records.l: the Thames, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The river is searched on both sides for the missing launch, without success. Holmes goes down the river in disguise after considering that the launch may have gone upstream.

records.l: the Aurora, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The steam launch Aurora is described as black with two red stripes and a black funnel with a white band. It left Smith’s Wharf at about three o’clock on Tuesday morning with Mordecai Smith and his son Jim, and its whereabouts remain unknown.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The treasure is believed to be in the possession of the fugitives. Holmes expects it to be recovered when the men are captured and proposes that Dr. Watson take the box first to Miss Morstan, who is entitled to half of it.

records.l: the advertisement, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The advertisement offers five pounds for information about Mordecai Smith, his son Jim, and the Aurora. It is placed at Mrs. Smith’s address and at Baker Street so the fugitives might read it as an ordinary message from a worried wife.

records.l: Holmes's telegram, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Holmes’s telegram, sent from Poplar, tells Athelney Jones to go to Baker Street and wait if Holmes has not returned. It says that Holmes is close on the track of the Sholto gang and invites Jones to join the pursuit that night.

records.l: Holmes's disguise, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: Holmes uses a simple disguise because members of the criminal classes are beginning to recognize him. He works all day in the disguise while pursuing information about the missing launch and the fugitives.

records.l: the old sailor disguise, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The old sailor disguise consists of a wig, white whiskers and eyebrows, a pea-jacket, a coloured scarf, a cudgel, and an affected aged and asthmatic manner. Holmes uses it to enter Baker Street as an apparently impoverished master mariner carrying information, then reveals himself.

records.l: the Upper Norwood tragedy, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The Upper Norwood tragedy is reported in the newspapers, which had initially treated Thaddeus Sholto as a suspect. Fresh evidence establishes that Sholto could not have been involved, and he is released.

records.l: the search for the fugitives, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The search for the fugitives is delayed because no trace of the Aurora or the missing men can be found. Holmes uses other agencies, an advertisement, river searches, and a disguise before arranging a police-boat pursuit.

records.l: the missing-launch investigation, The Sign of the Four, Chapter IX
records.s: The missing-launch investigation concerns Mordecai Smith, his son Jim, and the Aurora, which disappeared after leaving Smith’s Wharf. Despite searches along the river and inquiries with Mrs. Smith, no immediate news is obtained until Holmes develops a new lead.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Athelney Jones pursue Jonathan Small and his companions down the Thames in a fast police launch. Holmes identifies Jacobson's Yard as the place where Mordecai Smith has concealed the Aurora, and the pursuers catch the launch after a prolonged chase. Small is captured after the Aurora runs aground, while the Islander is shot and falls into the river. The Sholtos' iron treasure-chest is recovered, but the Islander's body is not found.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Sherlock Holmes deduces that Jonathan Small concealed the Aurora at Jacobson's Yard and organizes an ambush there. He leads the pursuit down the Thames, orders the crew to increase speed, and fires at the Islander when he raises a weapon. Afterward, he identifies the recovered iron chest as the one that contained the Sholtos' treasure and finds one of the Islander's darts embedded in the hatchway.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Athelney Jones on the launch, carrying his old service-revolver. He takes part in the pursuit of the Aurora and fires at the Islander, later feeling sick when he realizes how narrowly the dart passed them.

records.l: Athelney Jones, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Athelney Jones joins Holmes and Watson in the launch and helps direct the pursuit of the Aurora. He doubts at first that their faster launch can catch it, but they eventually come alongside and capture the fugitives.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Jonathan Small has Mordecai Smith conceal the Aurora at Jacobson's Yard while he prepares to escape with the treasure. He pilots or directs the launch during the chase, runs it onto the southern bank, and becomes stuck in the mud by his wooden leg before being hauled aboard and captured.

records.l: Mordecai Smith, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Mordecai Smith is found by Holmes at Jacobson's Yard and announces that he wants the Aurora at eight o'clock for two gentlemen. During the chase, he shovels coal aboard the Aurora, and afterward he and his son sit sullenly in the launch before meekly coming aboard when ordered.

records.l: the Islander, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Islander is the small, distorted companion of Jonathan Small, wrapped in a dark ulster or blanket. He threatens the pursuers with a short wooden weapon and falls into the Thames after Holmes and Watson fire at him.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's launch, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The launch carrying Holmes, Watson, Jones, and several police workers is a fast craft with its green police lamp removed. It pursues the Aurora down the Thames, catches it near the marshes, hauls it off the bank, and tows it upstream.

records.l: the Aurora, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Aurora is handed over to Jacobson's Yard by a wooden-legged man for a trivial alteration to its rudder. It leaves the yard at high speed with Jonathan Small, the Islander, and the Smiths aboard, but eventually runs aground and is captured by Holmes's party.

records.l: Jacobson's Yard, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: Jacobson's Yard conceals the Aurora after Jonathan Small arranges for a minor change to its rudder. Holmes discovers the launch there and places a boy nearby to signal when it departs.

records.l: the Thames, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Thames is the setting for the pursuit of the Aurora, which travels rapidly downstream past bridges, docks, and marshes. The Islander falls into the river, and his bones are said to lie somewhere in the dark ooze at its bottom.

records.l: the Sholtos, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Sholtos are connected to the iron chest recovered from the Aurora, which Holmes identifies as the chest that contained their ill-omened treasure.

records.l: the Sholtos' treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Sholtos' treasure is found in a solid iron chest of Indian workmanship aboard the Aurora. The chest has no key but is heavy, so the pursuers transfer it carefully to their cabin.

records.l: the pursuit and capture of Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The pursuit begins when the Aurora leaves Jacobson's Yard and races down the Thames. Holmes's launch follows through heavy river traffic, gradually gains on it, and finally catches it after the Aurora runs onto a muddy bank.

records.l: the Islander's death, The Sign of the Four, Chapter X
records.s: The Islander is shot after he draws a short wooden weapon and raises it to his lips. He falls into the Thames, and although the pursuers search with their light, they find no sign of him; the text states that his bones lie at the bottom of the river.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Jonathan Small, captured after the chase on the Thames, tells Sherlock Holmes that Tonga killed Thaddeus Sholto with a poisoned dart and that he himself did not attack Sholto. Small explains that he pursued the Agra treasure, which he believes would have made him nearly half a million pounds richer, but which has brought him imprisonment and misfortune instead. Dr. Watson takes the iron treasure box to Mary Morstan, only to find it completely empty. Believing the treasure lost, Watson declares his love for Mary, and she accepts him.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Jonathan Small is held captive after being captured during the pursuit on the Thames. He insists that he did not raise a hand against Thaddeus Sholto and says that Tonga killed Sholto with a poisoned dart; he describes the Agra treasure as having brought him slavery and misfortune.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Jonathan Small and offers him a cigar and a drink. Holmes says he believes the poison acted so quickly that Thaddeus Sholto was dead before Small reached the room, and he arranged for Dr. Watson to take the treasure box to Mary Morstan.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies the captured Jonathan Small and brings the iron treasure box to Mary Morstan. He breaks open the box, discovers that it is empty, and then declares his love for Mary.

records.l: Athelney Jones, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Athelney Jones takes charge of Jonathan Small and joins Holmes and Dr. Watson after the capture. He arranges for Dr. Watson to land at Vauxhall with the treasure box and assigns an inspector to accompany him.

records.l: Tonga, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Tonga shoots Thaddeus Sholto with one of his poisoned darts, according to Jonathan Small. Tonga leaves behind his club and some darts while escaping, which helps place Holmes on his track.

records.l: Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Thaddeus Sholto is killed by a poisoned dart fired by Tonga. Jonathan Small says that Sholto was already dead when he climbed through the window, and Holmes believes the poison acted before Small reached the room.

records.l: Miss Morstan, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Mary Morstan is at Mrs. Cecil Forrester's house when Dr. Watson brings her the iron treasure box. She learns that it is empty, and she accepts Watson's declaration of love.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The Agra treasure is believed by Jonathan Small to be worth nearly half a million pounds and is to be divided between Mary Morstan and Thaddeus Sholto. The treasure is ultimately found to be missing from the box, and Small says it has brought murder, fear, guilt, and slavery to those connected with it.

records.l: the Sholtos' treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The iron treasure box is brought by Dr. Watson to Mary Morstan and is forced open because its key is at the bottom of the Thames. It is massively constructed with ironwork two-thirds of an inch thick, but it contains no treasure.

records.l: the Aurora, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The Aurora is a fast launch used by Jonathan Small and Tonga because Small had heard that it was a flier. Its speed makes the pursuit difficult, although Holmes and the police eventually overhaul it.

records.l: the Thames, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The Thames is the river down which the Aurora is pursued. Jonathan Small says that he threw the key to the iron treasure box into the Thames.

records.l: the pursuit and capture of Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Athelney Jones, and their companions pursue the Aurora down the Thames and capture Jonathan Small. Jones says that they barely overhauled the fast launch, while Small reveals that he had intended to reach the Esmeralda at Gravesend.

records.l: the murder of Thaddeus Sholto, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The murder of Thaddeus Sholto is attributed by Jonathan Small to Tonga, who fired a poisoned dart. Small denies committing the killing, and Holmes believes Sholto died before Small entered the room.

records.l: the treasure's loss, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: The treasure's loss is discovered when Dr. Watson and Mary Morstan open the iron box and find it completely empty. The loss removes what Watson sees as a barrier between him and Mary, allowing him to confess his love.

records.l: Watson and Mary Morstan's love, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XI
records.s: When the treasure is found to be gone, Dr. Watson tells Mary Morstan that he loves her and that the riches had sealed his lips. Mary does not withdraw her hand and whispers that she also says, "Thank God," as they come together.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: Inspector Jones learns that the box believed to contain the Agra treasure is empty, and Athelney Jones is dismayed because the reward may be lost. Jonathan Small admits that he disposed of the treasure when the pursuing launch was about to overtake him, saying he acted for the three imprisoned men and himself. He argues that the treasure belongs to them because of the suffering he endured while imprisoned in the Andaman Islands. Holmes says that they cannot judge whether justice was originally on Small’s side until they hear his story, which Small agrees to tell.

records.l: Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: Jonathan Small has hidden or discarded the Agra treasure so that neither the authorities nor the Sholto and Morstan families can recover it. He insists that he acted for the three men imprisoned in the Andaman convict-barracks as well as himself, and he describes the twenty years of hardship he endured there as the price by which he earned the treasure. He agrees to tell Holmes and the others his story.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: Holmes sits with Jonathan Small after the pursuit and responds calmly to Small’s claims. He observes that they cannot know whether justice was originally on Small’s side until they have heard his story.

records.l: Athelney Jones, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: Athelney Jones is angered and dismayed when he sees that the box is empty. He accuses Small of thwarting justice and warns that this may damage Small’s chances at trial.

records.l: the Agra treasure, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: The Agra treasure is not found in the recovered box. Jonathan Small says he put it in a safe place, possibly scattering it over several miles, so that the authorities would have difficulty recovering it.

records.l: the empty box, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: The empty box is shown to the inspector and then to Athelney Jones after the pursuit. Its emptiness reveals that Jonathan Small removed the treasure before the authorities could capture him.

records.l: the pursuit and capture of Jonathan Small, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: The pursuit ends with Jonathan Small captured and taken to Baker Street, while the launch nearly catches him before he can dispose of the treasure. Small says that the approaching launch caused him to hide or discard the loot.

records.l: justice, The Sign of the Four, Chapter XII
records.s: Athelney Jones claims that Small has thwarted justice by withholding the treasure. Small rejects this idea, arguing that it is unjust for people who did not earn the treasure to enjoy it, while Holmes says justice cannot be assessed until Small’s account is heard.

records.l: The Sign of the Four, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The narrator recounts how he lost his right leg in India, became an indigo-plantation overseer for Abel White, and survived the Indian Mutiny by reaching Agra. At the Agra Fort, he joined a volunteer corps and was assigned to guard an isolated postern gate with the Sikh soldiers Mahomet Singh and Abdullah Khan. Abdullah and Mahomet threatened him into joining a conspiracy to murder Achmet, a merchant carrying the rajah’s jewels, and divide the treasure. When Achmet arrived with Dost Akbar, the narrator ordered the Sikhs to take him to the main guard instead of allowing them to kill him.

records.l: the unnamed narrator, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The narrator says he was born near Pershore in Worcestershire and joined the 3rd Buffs after getting into trouble over a girl. A crocodile took his right leg in the Ganges, after which he became an indigo-plantation overseer, survived the Mutiny, and joined the volunteer corps at Agra. He initially agreed to help Mahomet Singh and Abdullah Khan rob and kill Achmet, but ultimately sent Achmet to the main guard.

records.l: India, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: India is where the narrator served in the army, lost his leg in the Ganges, worked on an indigo plantation, and experienced the Mutiny. He describes the country as being engulfed by fighting, burning, murder, and disorder.

records.l: Abel White, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Abel White was an indigo-planter who employed the narrator as an overseer of his coolies. He remained at his bungalow during the early stages of the Mutiny, but rebels attacked and burned it while the narrator was away.

records.l: the Indian Mutiny, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The Indian Mutiny suddenly spread across the country after a period of apparent peace. It left Europeans fleeing toward places such as Agra and brought widespread fighting, torture, murder, and outrage.

records.l: Agra, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Agra was the nearest place of refuge for many Europeans fleeing the disturbances around Muttra. Its city was filled with fanatics and fierce groups, while the British defenders eventually concentrated in the old fort.

records.l: the British, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The British in the region were reduced to small groups holding only the ground commanded by their guns. At Agra, soldiers, volunteers, women, children, and stores were gathered inside the fort.

records.l: the rebel army, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The rebel army was made up of forces opposing the British during the Mutiny. Abdullah Khan planned to pass over to the rebels if the conspiracy at the gate failed.

records.l: the Sepoys, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The Sepoys were described as the British-trained troops who had turned against them, using British weapons and bugle-calls. Four Sepoys were found dead near Dawson, and many others were among the rebels surrounding Abel White’s bungalow.

records.l: the Sikh friends, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Sikh troops formed part of the forces defending Agra and included the two Sikh troopers assigned to the narrator. The two men under his command were Mahomet Singh and Abdullah Khan, both experienced fighters.

records.l: the Agra Fort, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The Agra Fort contained a modern occupied section and a much larger deserted quarter filled with halls, passages, and corridors. Its many gates were guarded by small detachments because the defenders lacked enough men for stronger posts.

records.l: Mahomet Singh, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Mahomet Singh was a tall Sikh trooper and an old fighting-man who had fought against the British at Chilian-wallah. He helped Abdullah Khan threaten the narrator and was ordered to watch for the arrival of Dost Akbar and Achmet.

records.l: Abdullah Khan, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Abdullah Khan was a fierce Sikh trooper who held a knife to the narrator’s throat and demanded that he join the conspiracy. He explained the plan to seize Achmet and divide the rajah’s jewels, then helped escort Achmet through the gate.

records.l: Dost Akbar, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Dost Akbar was Abdullah Khan’s foster-brother and the person who knew Achmet’s secret. He was supposed to lead Achmet to the isolated gate and share in the planned treasure.

records.l: Achmet, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: Achmet was a frightened merchant traveling with an iron box containing valuable family possessions. He sought protection inside the Agra Fort, and the narrator ordered that he be taken to the main guard rather than killed by the Sikhs.

records.l: the rajah, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The rajah of the northern provinces possessed substantial wealth and had divided it between gold and silver kept in his palace and jewels sent secretly to Agra. He supported the Sepoys after believing that the British were being defeated, causing his property to be treated by the conspirators as loot.

records.l: the rajah's treasure, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The rajah’s treasure included precious stones and choice pearls placed in an iron box and sent to Agra for safekeeping. Abdullah Khan proposed that it be divided equally among himself, Mahomet Singh, Dost Akbar, and the narrator.

records.l: the Sholtos' treasure, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The iron box was carried by Achmet in a bundle wrapped in a shawl. Achmet said it contained family matters of little value to others, but the conspirators believed it held the rajah’s jewels.

records.l: the postern gate, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The postern gate was a small isolated door on the southwest side of the Agra Fort. The narrator guarded it with Mahomet Singh and Abdullah Khan, and Dost Akbar chose it as the entry point for Achmet.

records.l: the conspiracy to rob Achmet, The Sign of the Four, “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you
records.s: The conspiracy involved allowing Achmet into the fort, killing him, concealing his disappearance, and taking the rajah’s jewels for the conspirators. Abdullah Khan forced the narrator to swear that he would not interfere, but the narrator finally directed that Achmet be taken to the main guard.

The narrator trips the fat man with his firelock because of the treasure, causing him to fall. The Sikh catches him and stabs him twice in the side with a knife, after which the man lies motionless. The narrator says he is recounting the events exactly, whether they favor him or not.

records.s: The firelock catches the fat man's legs, causing him to roll twice over like a shot rabbit. He may have broken his neck in the fall.

records.s: Small recounts how he, Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan, and Dost Akbar murdered Achmet the merchant during the Indian mutiny and hid Achmet’s jewels in the Agra fort. After the four conspirators were arrested and imprisoned, Small persuaded Major Sholto and Captain Morstan to help them escape in exchange for knowledge of the treasure, but Sholto recovered the treasure and betrayed them. Small later escaped the Andamans with Tonga, killing a hostile convict-guard before they sailed away in Tonga’s canoe and were rescued by a trader.

records.s: Small describes his role in Achmet’s murder, the concealment and later loss of the Agra treasure, and his imprisonment with the three Sikh conspirators. He bargains with Major Sholto and Captain Morstan for the conspirators’ freedom, then escapes the Andamans with Tonga after killing a convict-guard.

records.s: Mahomet Singh helps Small, Abdullah Khan, and Dost Akbar carry Achmet’s body into the fort and initially guards the door. He joins the other conspirators in hiding the treasure, taking oaths, preparing charts, and negotiating with Major Sholto and Captain Morstan.

records.l: Abdullah Khan, The Sign of the Four, He stopped, and held out his manacled hands for the whiskey-and-water
records.s: Abdullah Khan helps carry Achmet’s body into the Agra fort and participates in concealing the treasure. He is one of the four conspirators who swear to remain united and later negotiates with Major Sholto and Captain Morstan.

records.s: Dost Akbar helps Small and the other conspirators carry Achmet’s body into the fort. He joins their oath to act together and takes part in the later bargain with Major Sholto and Captain Morstan.

records.s: Achmet the merchant is carried into the Agra fort after being attacked and is buried beneath loose bricks in a natural grave. His murder is discovered after a spy reports that Achmet entered the fort but cannot be found.
