He learns that Adler frequently sees the lawyer Godfrey Norton and follows them to the Church of St. Monica, where he unexpectedly serves as witness to their marriage. Holmes then recruits Dr. John Watson to assist with a planned operation at Briony Lodge, involving a staged disturbance, a smoke-rocket, and a cry of fire. He disguises himself as a Nonconformist clergyman before setting out for the operation.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes spends the morning investigating Irene Adler and Briony Lodge while disguised as an unemployed groom. He gathers information from local horsemen, follows Adler and Godfrey Norton to the Church of St. Monica, unexpectedly witnesses their marriage, and later plans an operation at Briony Lodge with Dr. John Watson's assistance.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Dr. John Watson waits at Baker Street for Sherlock Holmes and listens to Holmes's account of the morning's events. He agrees to assist in the planned operation, remaining near the sitting-room window, throwing in the smoke-rocket at Holmes's signal, and shouting that there is a fire.

records.l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Irene Adler lives at Briony Lodge, sings at concerts, drives out daily, and is regarded by local men as exceptionally attractive. She travels to the Church of St. Monica and marries Godfrey Norton, then plans to return to her house after driving in the park.

records.l: Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Godfrey Norton is a dark, handsome, dashing lawyer of the Inner Temple who visits Irene Adler once or twice a day. He hurries to the Church of St. Monica, where he marries Adler with Sherlock Holmes serving as the required witness.

records.l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Briony Lodge is Irene Adler's two-story villa, built close to the road with a garden behind it. Holmes examines its Chubb-locked door, sitting-room windows, passage window, and coach-house, and later selects it as the scene of his planned operation.

records.l: Church of St. Monica, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The Church of St. Monica is where Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton go to be married. A clergyman requires a witness because of an informality in their license, and Sherlock Holmes unexpectedly fills that role.

records.l: the investigation into Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The investigation concerns Irene Adler and the location or protection of a photograph. Holmes examines Briony Lodge, investigates Adler's routine and relationships, and focuses particularly on Godfrey Norton as a possible factor in determining where the photograph may be kept.

records.l: the compromising photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The photograph is the object Holmes is trying to locate or recover in the investigation into Irene Adler. Holmes considers whether Adler may have transferred it to Godfrey Norton's keeping, but this unit does not establish where it is.

records.l: the marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton takes place unexpectedly at the Church of St. Monica. Sherlock Holmes is drawn into serving as their witness, and Adler gives him a sovereign afterward.

records.l: Holmes's disguise as a groom, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Holmes uses the disguise of a drunken-looking, ill-kempt groom to investigate Briony Lodge and learn about Irene Adler from local horsemen and cabmen. In this role, he examines the house and discovers details about Adler's routine and her association with Godfrey Norton.

records.l: Holmes's disguise as a Nonconformist clergyman, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Holmes changes into the disguise of an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman before leaving for the planned operation. His costume, expression, manner, and apparent character are all altered.

records.l: the planned break-in at Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: Holmes plans an operation at Briony Lodge for the time Irene Adler returns from her drive. He tells Watson that a disturbance will result in Holmes being taken into the house, after which Watson must watch the sitting-room window and act on Holmes's signal.

records.l: the fire diversion, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The fire diversion is designed to draw attention and create confusion during Holmes's operation at Briony Lodge. At Holmes's signal, Watson is to throw an object into the sitting room and shout that there is a fire, prompting others to repeat the cry before Watson leaves the street.

records.l: the ordinary plumber’s smoke-rocket, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
records.s: The ordinary plumber's smoke-rocket is a cigar-shaped device with self-lighting caps at both ends. Holmes gives it to Watson to throw into the sitting room when Holmes raises his hand during the planned operation.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and the doctor wait in Serpentine Avenue for Irene Adler to return to Briony Lodge so they can locate a compromising photograph. Holmes and his accomplices stage a street quarrel, fake an injury, and use a false fire alarm to make Adler reveal where she has hidden the photograph. Holmes discovers it is behind a sliding panel above the right bell-pull in the sitting-room, but he postpones taking it until the next morning. As Holmes and the doctor reach Baker Street, an unidentified slim youth addresses Holmes, suggesting that someone may have recognized him.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Sherlock Holmes directs the doctor to carry out a staged street disturbance and a false fire alarm designed to make Irene Adler reveal the photograph's hiding place. He pretends to be injured, is carried into Briony Lodge's sitting-room, and sees Adler reach behind a sliding panel above the right bell-pull. He plans to return with the King at eight the next morning, but postpones taking the photograph because the coachman is watching him.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The doctor waits with Sherlock Holmes in Serpentine Avenue and follows Holmes's instructions during the staged quarrel and false fire alarm. He throws the smoke-rocket into Briony Lodge and later learns how Holmes discovered the photograph's location. He feels ashamed of conspiring against Irene Adler but continues because he believes withdrawing would betray Holmes.

records.l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Irene Adler arrives at Briony Lodge in her carriage and is caught amid a staged fight outside her house. She permits the apparently injured Holmes to be carried into her sitting-room and responds to the fire alarm by rushing to the photograph's hiding place. She briefly draws the photograph from behind a sliding panel, replaces it after Holmes announces the alarm is false, and then leaves the room.

records.l: the King of Bohemia, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The King is seeking to recover the photograph and has previously had Irene Adler waylaid and searched. Sherlock Holmes plans to return with him to Briony Lodge the next morning so that he may potentially regain the photograph with his own hands.

records.l: Serpentine Avenue, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Serpentine Avenue is where the doctor and Sherlock Holmes wait outside Briony Lodge for Irene Adler. Although it is in a quiet neighbourhood, the street is unusually animated with several people who are revealed to be accomplices in Holmes's operation.

records.l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Briony Lodge is Irene Adler's house and the location where the photograph is hidden. Holmes is carried into its sitting-room after pretending to be injured, and the doctor observes the events through an uncurtained window. Holmes intends to return there with the King the following morning.

records.l: the compromising photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The photograph is a cabinet-sized object that Irene Adler is unlikely to carry and that both Adler and the client wish to keep from another person's eyes. It is hidden in a recess behind a sliding panel just above the right bell-pull in the sitting-room at Briony Lodge. Holmes locates it but does not take it during the ruse.

records.l: marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: Irene Adler's marriage to Mr. Godfrey Norton simplifies the situation because she may be as reluctant to let him see the photograph as the original client is to let the King's princess see it. Sherlock Holmes also believes the marriage may soon change Adler's life and habits.

records.l: staged street quarrel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The staged street quarrel is carried out by accomplices posing as loafers, guardsmen, and other bystanders near Briony Lodge. The fight gives Sherlock Holmes an opportunity to pretend to be struck and injured while the doctor and the other participants make the disturbance appear genuine.

records.l: the fire diversion, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The doctor throws a smoke-rocket into the sitting-room while shouting "Fire!" after Holmes signals him. The smoke and shouting prompt Irene Adler to rush to the photograph's hiding place, allowing Holmes to see where it is concealed before he declares the alarm false.

records.l: the quest for the photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
records.s: The quest for the photograph is practically finished when Sherlock Holmes identifies its hiding place in Briony Lodge. He plans to return with the King and the doctor at eight the next morning, when Adler is expected to be asleep and the house may offer a clear opportunity to recover it.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and the King of Bohemia return to Briony Lodge, where they learn that Irene Adler has married an English lawyer named Norton and left England with him. Holmes finds a photograph of Irene and a letter explaining that she recognized his deception, discovered the King’s intended plan, and fled with her husband. Irene leaves the photograph for the King but promises not to interfere with his plans, while Holmes asks to keep her photograph. The King considers the matter successfully resolved, and Watson concludes that Irene’s wit defeated Holmes’s investigation and prevented a scandal from affecting Bohemia.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes returns to Briony Lodge with the King of Bohemia and learns that Irene Adler has left England. He finds her photograph and letter, realizes that she has outmaneuvered him, and asks the King to give him the photograph as his reward.

records.l: the King of Bohemia, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: The King of Bohemia accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Briony Lodge in search of the photograph. He is relieved when Irene Adler leaves the photograph behind, declares himself immensely indebted to Holmes, and gives Holmes permission to keep it.

records.l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Irene Norton, née Adler, explains in a letter that she recognized Sherlock Holmes’s disguise and discovered the purpose of his investigation. She flees with her husband, keeps the incriminating photograph as protection, and leaves another photograph for the King.

records.l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Briony Lodge is found with its door open after Irene Adler’s departure. Its furniture, shelves, and drawers are scattered as though Irene searched the house before fleeing, and Holmes finds her photograph and letter hidden behind a sliding shutter.

records.l: Irene Adler's photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Irene Adler’s photograph is found by Sherlock Holmes at Briony Lodge. Irene leaves it for the King, and Holmes asks to receive it instead; the King agrees.

records.l: the marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells the King of Bohemia that Irene Adler married an English lawyer named Norton the previous day. Irene’s letter identifies her as Irene Norton, née Adler, and says that she loves and is loved by her husband.

records.l: Irene Adler and Norton's flight to the Continent, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Irene Adler and Norton leave England on the 5:15 train from Charing Cross for the Continent. In her letter, Irene says that they chose flight because they were being pursued by so formidable an antagonist as Sherlock Holmes.

records.l: the King of Bohemia case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: The threatened scandal involving the kingdom of Bohemia is prevented when Irene Adler leaves the photograph behind and promises not to interfere with the King’s plans. The King believes that her word is inviolate and that the photograph is as safe as if it were destroyed.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes’s investigation is intended to recover the photograph that could trouble the King of Bohemia. Although Holmes gains access to Briony Lodge by disguising himself and staging an alarm of fire, Irene recognizes the deception, searches for information about him, and escapes before he can obtain the photograph.

records.l: Irene Adler's wit, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
records.s: Irene Adler’s wit enables her to recognize Sherlock Holmes’s disguise, determine that he is investigating her, and arrange her escape with Norton. Her cleverness defeats Holmes’s plans, leading Watson to refer to her as the woman.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes asks Jabez Wilson to recount how he obtained and lost an unusual position with the Red-Headed League, while Dr. John Watson observes and records the case. Wilson explains that his assistant, Vincent Spaulding, directed him to an advertisement offering a well-paid vacancy to qualified red-headed men. Duncan Ross selected Wilson, who spent eight weeks copying the Encyclopædia Britannica at Pope's Court for £4 a week. The employment abruptly ended when Wilson found a notice stating that the Red-Headed League had been dissolved.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Jabez Wilson about the Red-Headed League and asks him to repeat his story in detail for Dr. John Watson. He identifies facts about Wilson's background from his appearance, including manual labor, snuff-taking, Freemasonry, time in China, and recent writing.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Dr. John Watson visits Sherlock Holmes and listens to Jabez Wilson's account. He examines Wilson's appearance, records the newspaper and date, and reads the Red-Headed League advertisement.

records.l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Jabez Wilson is a red-headed pawnbroker who is recruited into the Red-Headed League after applying for its advertised vacancy. He copies the Encyclopædia Britannica at Pope's Court for eight weeks, earning £4 per week, until he finds a notice announcing that the League has been dissolved.

records.l: Vincent Spaulding, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Vincent Spaulding works as Jabez Wilson's assistant for half wages and brings the Red-Headed League advertisement to Wilson's attention. He encourages Wilson to apply, helps him get through the crowd at Pope's Court, and says he can look after the pawnbroker's business while Wilson performs the League's duties.

records.l: Duncan Ross, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Duncan Ross interviews Jabez Wilson, verifies that his hair is genuine, and awards him the Red-Headed League vacancy. He tells Wilson to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica from ten o'clock until two and initially supervises his work before appearing less frequently.

records.l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Red-Headed League is presented as a fund established from the bequest of Ezekiah Hopkins to provide well-paid, nominal positions for eligible red-headed men. It employs Jabez Wilson for eight weeks before being abruptly dissolved.

records.l: red-headed men, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Red-headed men over twenty-one who are sound in body and mind are described as eligible for the Red-Headed League. Many red-headed men gather in Fleet Street and Pope's Court to compete for the advertised vacancy.

records.l: Jabez Wilson's pawnbroker's business, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Jabez Wilson's pawnbroker's business is a small concern at Coburg Square that has declined to the point where Wilson keeps only one assistant. Wilson leaves it during the mornings while he works for the Red-Headed League, relying on Vincent Spaulding to look after it.

records.l: the Red-Headed League advertisement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Red-Headed League advertisement announces a vacancy paying £4 a week for purely nominal services. It requires eligible red-headed men to apply in person to Duncan Ross at 7 Pope's Court, Fleet Street.

records.l: the Red-Headed League vacancy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Red-Headed League vacancy attracts numerous red-headed applicants, but Duncan Ross selects Jabez Wilson because his hair meets the required vivid color and he satisfies the other stated conditions. The position requires attendance in the League's office or building from ten to two without leaving.

records.l: the Red-Headed League employment, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Red-Headed League employment requires Jabez Wilson to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica using his own ink, pens, and paper. He attends daily for eight weeks and receives four golden sovereigns each Saturday.

records.l: the Red-Headed League dissolution, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Red-Headed League dissolution ends Jabez Wilson's employment suddenly after eight weeks. Wilson learns of it when he finds the office locked on October 9, 1890.

records.l: the Encyclopædia Britannica, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The Encyclopædia Britannica is the text Jabez Wilson is instructed to copy as part of his Red-Headed League employment. During eight weeks, he copies material from the letter A, including entries such as Abbots, Archery, Armour, Architecture, and Attica.

records.l: Pope's Court, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: Pope's Court in Fleet Street is the address where red-headed applicants gather and where the Red-Headed League maintains its office. Jabez Wilson works there from ten o'clock until two each day.

records.l: the dissolution notice, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
records.s: The dissolution notice is a piece of cardboard fastened to the locked office door. It states, "THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890."

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Mr. Jabez Wilson tells Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson that the Red-headed League vanished after costing him a four-pound-a-week position, and Holmes begins investigating. Holmes suspects that Wilson’s assistant, Vincent Spaulding, is central to the mystery after learning about his appearance and examining his trouser knees. Holmes inspects Saxe-Coburg Square and the surrounding businesses, then attends a concert at St. James’s Hall while reasoning about the case. He concludes that a considerable crime is being contemplated and asks Watson to join him at ten o’clock with his revolver.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. Jabez Wilson about the Red-headed League, its advertisement, and Vincent Spaulding. He inspects Saxe-Coburg Square, examines Spaulding’s trouser knees, and identifies Spaulding as a highly capable and daring man. Holmes believes a considerable crime is in contemplation and asks Dr. John Watson to help stop it that night.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes while Holmes investigates Mr. Jabez Wilson’s story. He admits that he cannot understand the mystery, attends the concert at St. James’s Hall with Holmes, and agrees to meet him at ten o’clock with his army revolver.

records.l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Mr. Jabez Wilson explains that the Red-headed League disappeared after he lost a position paying four pounds a week. He says that inquiries led him to discover that the supposed Duncan Ross was actually associated with a man named William Morris, whose stated new address was false. Wilson asks Sherlock Holmes to identify the League and determine why it played the prank on him.

records.l: Vincent Spaulding, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Vincent Spaulding is Mr. Jabez Wilson’s assistant, hired about a month earlier at half wages because he was handy and cheap. He is described as small, stout-built, quick, clean-shaven, over thirty, marked by a white splash of acid on his forehead, and having pierced ears. Sherlock Holmes recognizes him as a remarkably smart and daring man and examines his trouser knees.

records.l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: The Red-headed League is the organization that gave Mr. Jabez Wilson work copying the Encyclopaedia and then vanished without explanation. Its supposed officials and addresses proved false, and Wilson lost a position that had paid him four pounds a week.

records.l: Saxe-Coburg Square, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Saxe-Coburg Square is the shabby location of Mr. Jabez Wilson’s pawnbroking business. Sherlock Holmes studies the square and its surrounding buildings, including the nearby bank, restaurant, shops, and carriage-building depot, because he believes a serious crime may be connected with it.

records.l: St. James’s Hall, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: St. James’s Hall is where Sarasate performs an afternoon concert. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson attend the concert, and Holmes spends the afternoon absorbed in the music while continuing to think about the investigation.

records.l: the Red-Headed League advertisement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: The advertisement first drew Vincent Spaulding’s attention and led Mr. Jabez Wilson to the Red-headed League opportunity. After the League disappeared, a card or announcement was left on Wilson’s door stating that it had been dissolved.

records.l: the Red-headed League scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: The Red-headed League scheme gave Mr. Jabez Wilson a temporary position copying the Encyclopaedia and cost him the opportunity to earn four pounds a week when it ended. Wilson regards it as a possible prank costing its perpetrators two and thirty pounds, while Sherlock Holmes suspects that it concealed a more serious purpose.

records.l: the contemplated crime, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
records.s: Sherlock Holmes says that a considerable crime is being planned in connection with the case. He believes there is still time to stop it, but the fact that it is Saturday complicates matters, so he asks Dr. John Watson to assist him at night and bring his revolver.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather hide in the City and Suburban Bank’s cellar to stop John Clay and his accomplice from robbing French gold. Clay and his red-haired accomplice emerge through a tunnel from Jabez Wilson’s cellar, but Holmes and Jones capture Clay while officers wait for the accomplice. Holmes later explains how the Red-headed League scheme kept Wilson away from his shop while the tunnel was dug. The attempted bank robbery is defeated, and Holmes receives repayment for his expenses and satisfaction from solving the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Sherlock Holmes organizes the ambush in the bank cellar and captures John Clay when he emerges from the tunnel. He explains that the Red-headed League scheme was designed to keep Jabez Wilson away from his shop so Clay’s accomplice could dig toward the bank. He concludes that the tunnel was complete and predicts the robbery attempt for Saturday night.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather to the bank cellar and hides there during the ambush. He keeps his revolver ready and witnesses the capture of John Clay. Holmes later explains the case to him at Baker Street.

records.l: Peter Jones, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Peter Jones joins Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson in the expedition and brings an inspector and two officers to guard the bank’s front door. During the arrest, he grabs at John Clay’s accomplice and later places handcuffs on Clay.

records.l: Mr. Merryweather, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Mr. Merryweather, a bank director and chairman of the bank directors, leads the group into the bank cellar. He explains that the cellar contains 30,000 napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and helps Holmes guard the bullion.

records.l: John Clay, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: John Clay emerges from the tunnel with his accomplice and is seized by Sherlock Holmes. He remains cool and sarcastic while being arrested, insists that he has royal blood, and is taken to the police station by Peter Jones.

records.l: John Clay’s accomplice, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: John Clay’s accomplice, a small, lithe man with a pale face and very red hair, follows Clay through the tunnel carrying or seeking the chisel and bags. He dives back into the hole when Holmes appears, but officers are waiting at the front door.

records.l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Jabez Wilson is described as a not-over-bright pawnbroker whose presence at his shop is removed for several hours each day. The Red-headed League scheme lures him away so that John Clay’s accomplice can work in the cellar.

records.l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The Red-headed League is presented as a false organization created to occupy Jabez Wilson while the bank robbery was prepared. Its offices close after the tunnel is completed, signaling to Holmes that the criminals are ready to act.

records.l: the City and Suburban Bank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The City and Suburban Bank is the bank whose cellar adjoins Jabez Wilson’s premises. Its unusually large reserve of French gold becomes the target of John Clay’s planned robbery.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: Baker Street is where Dr. Watson meets Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather before the expedition. Holmes and Watson return there after the arrest, where Holmes explains how he solved the case.

records.l: the bank cellar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The bank cellar is a heavily secured vault containing crates and massive boxes, including the French gold. Holmes, Dr. Watson, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather hide there and capture John Clay when he breaks through the floor.

records.l: the tunnel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The tunnel is dug from Jabez Wilson’s cellar toward the adjoining City and Suburban Bank. Holmes infers its existence from the accomplice’s work in the cellar and uses the evidence to anticipate the attempted robbery.

records.l: French gold, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The French gold consists of 30,000 napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and stored in the City and Suburban Bank’s cellar. Its presence motivates John Clay and his accomplice to dig the tunnel and attempt the robbery.

records.l: bank robbery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The bank robbery is an attempt by John Clay and his accomplice to reach the City and Suburban Bank’s French gold through a tunnel. Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, Dr. Watson, and Mr. Merryweather stop it before the criminals can take the bullion.

records.l: the Red-headed League scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The Red-headed League scheme uses an advertisement, a temporary office, and a £4-a-week position to draw Jabez Wilson away from his shop. This gives John Clay’s accomplice time to dig the tunnel from the cellar to the bank.

records.l: the robbery preparations, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
records.s: The robbery preparations include keeping Jabez Wilson away from his cellar, digging a tunnel, and arranging bags and a chisel for the theft. Once the Red-headed League offices close, Holmes realizes the preparations are complete and arranges the ambush.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Mary Sutherland about the disappearance of her fiancé, Mr. Hosmer Angel, who vanished from a cab on their wedding day. Mary explains that Hosmer was a shy cashier who courted her secretly while her stepfather, Mr. Windibank, was away. She believes that an unforeseen catastrophe prevented Hosmer from reaching the church, while Holmes advises her to forget him and agrees to investigate. Mary leaves Holmes four letters from Hosmer, an advertisement, and details about herself and her family.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Mary Sutherland as a client and infers details about her short sight and typewriting. He listens to her account of Mr. Hosmer Angel's disappearance, advises her to let the matter become a sealed book, and takes her letters and other papers to investigate.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Dr. Watson is present with Sherlock Holmes during Mary Sutherland's interview. Mary is told that she may speak freely in his presence.

records.l: Mary Sutherland, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Mary Sutherland consults Sherlock Holmes because Mr. Windibank refuses to involve the police or investigate Mr. Hosmer Angel's disappearance. She describes her engagement and planned wedding to Hosmer, gives Holmes four of his letters and an advertisement, and insists that she will remain true to him.

records.l: Mr. Hosmer Angel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Mr. Hosmer Angel is described as a shy, well-dressed cashier with weak eyes, tinted glasses, and a hesitant, whispering voice. He courted Mary Sutherland, became engaged to her, and disappeared from a four-wheeler outside the church on the day they were to marry.

records.l: James Windibank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Mr. Windibank is Mary Sutherland's stepfather and a traveller for Westhouse & Marbank. He dislikes Mary attending social events and visitors, is away in France during her first meetings with Hosmer, and declines to go to the police after Hosmer disappears.

records.l: A Case of Identity, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: A Case of Identity concerns Sherlock Holmes's investigation of Mary Sutherland's account of her missing fiancé, Mr. Hosmer Angel. The unit introduces the case through Mary's interview and the unexplained disappearance on her wedding day.

records.l: the Hosmer Angel disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: The Hosmer Angel disappearance occurs when Hosmer fails to emerge from the four-wheeler that follows Mary and her mother to the church. No one has heard from him since the previous Friday, and Mary believes that an unforeseen catastrophe separated them.

records.l: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel's engagement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel become engaged after their first walk together. Hosmer makes Mary swear that she will remain true to him, and they plan to marry quickly while Mr. Windibank is away.

records.l: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel's wedding, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
records.s: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel's wedding is arranged for a quiet ceremony at St. Saviour's near King's Cross, followed by breakfast at the St. Pancras Hotel. Mary and her mother reach the church in one cab, but Hosmer disappears from the other cab before entering the church.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Sherlock Holmes concludes that Hosmer Angel was James Windibank in disguise, created to prevent Windibank's stepdaughter, Miss Mary Sutherland, from marrying and causing the loss of her income. Holmes identifies Windibank through the typewritten letters, the matching typewriter defects, the disguised man's suspicious conduct, and confirmation from Windibank's employer. Windibank admits the deception was initially intended as a joke but flees when Holmes threatens him with a hunting crop. Holmes tells Dr. John Watson that the law cannot punish Windibank, though his conduct deserves punishment.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines Miss Mary Sutherland's clothing and physical details, including her sleeves, gloves, boots, and pince-nez marks, to infer that she is a typewriter user who left home in haste. He compares the typewritten letters from Hosmer Angel with James Windibank's writing, identifies matching defects in the typewriter, confronts Windibank, and explains how Windibank carried out the deception.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Dr. John Watson describes the woman and initially misses the significance of her clothing and other details. He is away attending a professional case, returns to Baker Street for the confrontation with Windibank, and listens as Holmes explains the solution.

records.l: Mary Sutherland, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Miss Mary Sutherland is a warm-hearted young woman whose stepfather seeks to prevent her from marrying because her marriage would cost the household her income. She is deceived by Windibank's disguise as Hosmer Angel and is left believing that the bridegroom has mysteriously disappeared.

records.l: James Windibank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: James Windibank is Mary Sutherland's stepfather and the man who benefits financially from preventing her marriage. Holmes reveals that Windibank disguised himself as Hosmer Angel, used typewritten correspondence, abandoned Mary at the church door, and then fled Baker Street after being exposed.

records.l: Mr. Hosmer Angel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Hosmer Angel is presented as a missing bridegroom, but Holmes establishes that he was James Windibank in disguise. The disguise included tinted glasses, a moustache, bushy whiskers, and an altered voice, and the apparent disappearance was staged to keep Mary attached to him and discourage other suitors.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Sherlock Holmes's Baker Street residence is where Holmes works on the case, receives Dr. John Watson, and confronts James Windibank. Holmes briefly locks Windibank inside during the confrontation, then opens the door as Windibank escapes.

records.l: the typewriter, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: The typewriter is treated by Holmes as having identifying characteristics comparable to a person's handwriting. The machine used by Windibank's office produces a slurred 'e,' a defective tail on the 'r,' and fourteen other distinctive features that match the letters attributed to Hosmer Angel.

records.l: the typewritten letters, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: The typewritten letters attributed to Hosmer Angel contain no clear clue to his identity apart from a quotation from Balzac, but their typewritten signatures are significant. Their distinctive defects match the typewritten letter sent by James Windibank and help prove that Windibank produced them.

records.l: the missing-bridegroom mystery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: The missing-bridegroom mystery concerns the disappearance of Hosmer Angel after he accompanied Mary Sutherland to the church door. Holmes determines that it was a deliberate deception by Windibank rather than a genuine disappearance, although he concludes that the law likely cannot punish Windibank.

records.l: Windibank's impersonation of Hosmer Angel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Windibank's impersonation of Hosmer Angel was designed to keep Mary Sutherland from attracting another suitor and to preserve the income she contributed to the household. He disguised his appearance and voice, courted Mary, became engaged to her, and then vanished in a way intended to leave her faithful to his invented identity.

records.l: Mary Sutherland's disappearance of Hosmer Angel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still
records.s: Mary Sutherland's disappearance of Hosmer Angel is revealed to be the staged abandonment of her supposed bridegroom at the church door. The apparent disappearance was engineered by James Windibank so that Mary would remain emotionally bound to Hosmer Angel and avoid marrying anyone else.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Dr. John Watson joins Sherlock Holmes on a journey to investigate the Boscombe Valley tragedy, in which Charles McCarthy was found dead beside Boscombe Pool. Evidence presented at the inquest strongly implicates Charles’s son, James McCarthy, who was arrested after being found near the body with blood on his hand and sleeve. Holmes considers the circumstantial case serious but believes James’s unusual statements, including references to a rat and a vanishing grey cloth, may support his innocence. Holmes plans to test James’s account personally at the scene.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Dr. John Watson receives Sherlock Holmes’s request and travels with him to Boscombe Valley. He reads James McCarthy’s testimony and initially considers the evidence against James extremely damaging.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is asked to investigate the Boscombe Valley tragedy after Inspector Lestrade becomes puzzled. He reviews the reported facts, questions the apparent strength of the case against James McCarthy, and intends to investigate personally while initially assuming that James’s account is true.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Inspector Lestrade is retained to work on James McCarthy’s behalf but becomes puzzled by the case. He refers the investigation to Sherlock Holmes.

records.l: John Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: John Turner is the largest landed proprietor in the Boscombe Valley area. He made his money in Australia, returned to England, owned Hatherley Farm, and had an only daughter.

records.l: Charles McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Charles McCarthy was an ex-Australian who rented Hatherley Farm from John Turner. He went to Boscombe Pool on June 3rd for an appointment, was later found dead with repeated blows to his head, and reportedly had a violent quarrel with his son, James.

records.l: James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: James McCarthy, Charles McCarthy’s eighteen-year-old son, was seen following his father toward Boscombe Pool with a gun. He was found near his injured father with blood on his right hand and sleeve, arrested, and charged after the inquest, but he maintained that he was innocent and had left Charles shortly before the fatal attack.

records.l: William Crowder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: William Crowder, a game-keeper employed by John Turner, saw Charles McCarthy walking toward Boscombe Pool and James following several minutes later with a gun under his arm. He believed that Charles was in sight of James at the time.

records.l: Patience Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Patience Moran, the fourteen-year-old daughter of the lodge-keeper, was picking flowers near Boscombe Pool. She saw Charles and James apparently quarrelling, heard Charles use strong language, and saw James raise his hand as if to strike his father.

records.l: the coroner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The coroner questioned James McCarthy at the inquest about the quarrel, the signal “Cooee!”, Charles’s dying words, and the grey object near the body. In concluding remarks, the coroner emphasized discrepancies and omissions that appeared to prejudice James’s case.

records.l: the coroner's jury, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The coroner's jury returned a verdict of “wilful murder” after considering the evidence against James McCarthy. James’s remark that his arrest was no more than his deserts helped remove remaining doubt in the jury’s minds.

records.l: Boscombe Valley, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Boscombe Valley is a country district near Ross in Herefordshire. The tragedy connected with it concerns the death of Charles McCarthy near Boscombe Pool.

records.l: Hatherley Farm, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Hatherley Farm is a farm held by John Turner and rented by Charles McCarthy. Charles left it on June 3rd to walk toward Boscombe Pool, and James later returned there before being informed that he was under arrest.

records.l: Boscombe Pool, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Boscombe Pool is a small lake formed by the spreading stream in Boscombe Valley. Charles McCarthy was found dead beside it after being seen there with James during an apparent quarrel.

records.l: Boscombe Valley tragedy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The Boscombe Valley tragedy is the reported killing of Charles McCarthy near Boscombe Pool. James McCarthy was arrested and referred for trial after witnesses and physical circumstances appeared to implicate him.

records.l: the murder of McCarthy senior, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Charles McCarthy's murder was apparently committed with repeated blows from a heavy, blunt weapon. The injuries could have been inflicted by the butt-end of James McCarthy’s gun, which was found near the body.

records.l: the inquest, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: At the inquest, witnesses described Charles and James going toward Boscombe Pool, their quarrel, James’s bloodstained hand and sleeve, and the gun near the body. James testified that he had left Charles alive and returned after hearing a later outcry.

records.l: James McCarthy's arrest, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: James McCarthy was arrested after returning to Hatherley Farm and being informed by the inspector of constabulary that he was a prisoner. He said he was not surprised and that the arrest was no more than his deserts, but he also protested his innocence.

records.l: the investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The investigation is undertaken by Sherlock Holmes after Inspector Lestrade refers the case to him. Holmes intends to examine the scene and determine whether James McCarthy’s account can be supported.

records.l: circumstantial evidence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: Circumstantial evidence appears to point strongly toward James McCarthy through his presence near the body, his bloodstained hand and sleeve, the quarrel, and the nearby gun. Holmes warns that such evidence may point differently when viewed from another perspective.

records.l: the quarrel between James McCarthy and Mr. McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The quarrel between Charles and James McCarthy occurred beside Boscombe Pool and was described as violent. James refused to disclose its subject, though he insisted that it had nothing to do with the subsequent tragedy.

records.l: James McCarthy's testimony, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: In James McCarthy's testimony, he said that Charles summoned him with “Cooee!”, that they argued, and that he left before hearing a hideous outcry. He returned to find Charles fatally injured, noticed a vague grey object near the scene, and could not explain the reference to a rat or why Charles had used the signal before seeing him.

records.l: James McCarthy's gun, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: James McCarthy's gun was found on the grass within a few paces of Charles McCarthy’s body. Its butt-end could have caused the repeated blows to Charles’s head.

records.l: the grey cloth, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The grey cloth was a vague object James McCarthy recalled seeing on the ground about a dozen yards from the body and roughly the same distance from the wood. He said it had disappeared while he was kneeling beside Charles or before he went for help.

records.l: the dying reference to a rat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The rat was mentioned in Charles McCarthy’s final, indistinct words, according to James. James said that the reference conveyed no meaning to him and believed Charles was delirious.

records.l: the signal “Cooee!”, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
records.s: The signal “Cooee!” was a usual signal between Charles and James McCarthy. James said that he heard Charles use it before seeing him, although Charles apparently did not know that James had returned from Bristol, creating a discrepancy in the testimony.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to Ross with Lestrade to investigate the crime involving Mr. McCarthy and the charge against James McCarthy. Miss Turner asks Holmes to clear James, insisting that he is innocent, and reveals that Mr. McCarthy had wanted her to marry James despite opposition from both James and Mr. Turner. Holmes learns that James secretly married a barmaid at a registry office and was in Bristol when his father was killed. After visiting James in prison, Holmes identifies Mr. McCarthy's appointment at the pool and his cry of “Cooee!” as crucial points in the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes travels to Ross with Dr. Watson and Lestrade, initially preferring to remain at the hotel because of the high barometric pressure and good weather. After speaking with Miss Turner and visiting James McCarthy in prison, he becomes confident that James can be cleared and focuses on Mr. McCarthy's appointment at the pool and his cry of “Cooee!”

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Ross but remains at the hotel while Holmes and Lestrade travel to Hereford to see James McCarthy. He studies the inquest report, noting that Mr. McCarthy was struck from behind and considering the significance of the reference to a rat and the grey cloth.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Lestrade meets Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson at Ross and believes the case against James McCarthy is straightforward. He objects that Holmes is raising Miss Turner's hopes, although he accompanies Holmes to visit James in prison.

records.l: Alice Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Miss Turner asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate James McCarthy's case because she knows James is innocent. She explains that Mr. McCarthy wanted her to marry James, that James and his father had quarrelled about the matter, and that her father opposed the proposed marriage. She also tells Holmes that her father is seriously ill.

records.l: James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: James McCarthy is accused of killing his father, Mr. McCarthy, but Miss Turner insists that he is too tender-hearted to commit the crime. Holmes visits him in prison and concludes that James is as puzzled as everyone else, although he may know nothing about the identity of the killer.

records.l: Charles McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Mr. McCarthy is the murdered man and had been anxious for a marriage between James McCarthy and Miss Turner. He had known Mr. Turner in Victoria and had an appointment with someone at the pool before his death.

records.l: John Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Mr. Turner opposed the proposed marriage between James McCarthy and Miss Turner. He had known Mr. McCarthy at the gold-mines in Victoria, and his illness prevents Miss Turner from allowing Holmes to see him immediately.

records.l: Ross, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Ross is the pretty country town where Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Lestrade arrive. They stay at the Hereford Arms, and Miss Turner comes there by carriage to speak with Holmes.

records.l: the crime, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: The crime concerns the fatal attack on Mr. McCarthy and the accusation against James McCarthy. The circumstances include a blow from behind, a dying reference to a rat, a grey cloth seen by James, and Mr. McCarthy's appointment and call of “Cooee!” at the pool.

records.l: Mr. McCarthy's murder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Mr. McCarthy's murder was caused by a heavy blow that shattered the posterior third of the left parietal bone and the left half of the occipital bone. The injury indicates that the blow came from behind, and Mr. McCarthy had apparently arranged to meet someone at the pool.

records.l: the quarrel between James McCarthy and Mr. McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: The quarrel between James McCarthy and Mr. McCarthy concerned Mr. McCarthy's wish that James marry Miss Turner. James did not want to marry her because he was already secretly married, while Mr. McCarthy was unaware of that marriage.

records.l: the proposed marriage between James McCarthy and Miss Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Mr. McCarthy wanted James McCarthy and Miss Turner to marry, but both James and Mr. Turner opposed the proposal. James and Miss Turner had loved each other since childhood, though Miss Turner describes their relationship as being like that of brother and sister.

records.l: James McCarthy's registry-office marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: James McCarthy secretly married a barmaid at a registry office in Bristol when he was young. He had spent the three days before the crime with her, and she later wrote to him that she had a husband already in the Bermuda Dockyard, leaving no tie between them.

records.l: Mr. McCarthy's appointment at the pool, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Mr. McCarthy had an appointment with someone at the pool before he was killed. Sherlock Holmes considers this important because James McCarthy was away and Mr. McCarthy did not know when James would return.

records.l: the evidence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: The evidence includes James McCarthy's reported quarrel with his father, the injury to Mr. McCarthy's skull, the reference to a rat, the grey cloth seen by James, and Mr. McCarthy's cry of “Cooee!” The evidence appears less conclusive to Sherlock Holmes than to Lestrade.

records.l: James McCarthy's innocence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: Miss Turner is certain of James McCarthy's innocence, and Sherlock Holmes tells her that it is very probable. After seeing James in prison, Holmes says that he thinks he can clear him.

records.l: the charge against James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the
records.s: The charge against James McCarthy is that he murdered his father, Mr. McCarthy. Lestrade considers the charge well supported, but Sherlock Holmes sees important facts that may undermine it.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade investigate the murder of McCarthy senior at Boscombe Pool near Hatherley Farm. Holmes examines footprints, tobacco traces, and other evidence, concluding that the murder was committed by a tall, left-handed, lame man wearing a grey cloak and using a stone. By interpreting McCarthy senior’s dying reference to “Ballarat” and the Australian cry “Cooee!”, Holmes identifies the criminal as John Turner. The evidence clears McCarthy junior of the murder for which he had been accused.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the boots, tracks, ground, trees, tobacco ash, and a stone near Boscombe Pool. He deduces the murderer’s physical characteristics and concludes that the criminal is John Turner.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Holmes and Inspector Lestrade to Hatherley Farm and Boscombe Pool, observes Holmes’s investigation, and listens as Holmes explains how he solved the case.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Inspector Lestrade believes that McCarthy junior killed McCarthy senior and dismisses Holmes’s theories. He accompanies Holmes to the crime scene but remains skeptical of Holmes’s deductions.

records.l: John Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: John Turner is identified by Holmes as the criminal. Holmes connects him with the Australian reference to Ballarat, the grey cloak, and the physical and material traces found at Boscombe Pool.

records.l: Charles McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: McCarthy senior was murdered at Boscombe Pool. Before dying, he cried “Cooee!” and apparently tried to say “Ballarat,” which Holmes interprets as a reference to his murderer.

records.l: James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: McCarthy junior was accused by Inspector Lestrade of killing his father. Holmes accepts his account as true, including that he ran when he found his father on the ground, and concludes that he is innocent.

records.l: Hatherley Farm, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Hatherley Farm is where McCarthy senior and McCarthy junior lived or stayed, and it borders Boscombe Pool. Holmes begins his examination there by measuring the boots belonging to the father and son.

records.l: Boscombe Pool, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Boscombe Pool is the site where McCarthy senior’s body was found. Holmes examines the surrounding wet ground and woods, finding tracks and other evidence that lead him to the murderer.

records.l: Australia, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Australia is associated with the cry “Cooee!”, which Holmes recognizes as a distinctly Australian call used between Australians. This suggests that McCarthy senior expected to meet someone who had been in Australia.

records.l: Ballarat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Ballarat is a place in the Australian colony of Victoria. Holmes interprets McCarthy senior’s dying reference to “Ballarat” as part of the name or identification of his murderer.

records.l: the investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: The investigation moves from Hatherley Farm to Boscombe Pool and relies on physical traces, McCarthy junior’s narrative, and McCarthy senior’s final words. Holmes declares the mystery solved after identifying John Turner as the criminal.

records.l: the murder of McCarthy senior, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: The murder occurred at Boscombe Pool and was caused by a blow from a stone. Holmes concludes that the attack was delivered from behind by a left-handed man.

records.l: the charge against James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: McCarthy junior is accused by Inspector Lestrade of killing McCarthy senior. Holmes’s examination and interpretation of the evidence undermine that accusation and point instead to John Turner.

records.l: the criminal's identity, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Holmes identifies the criminal as John Turner. He reaches this conclusion from the references to “Cooee!” and “Ballarat,” the grey cloak, and the physical and material evidence at the scene.

records.l: the murder weapon stone, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Holmes finds a jagged stone in the woods and determines that it was used to kill McCarthy senior. The grass growing beneath it shows that it had lain there for only a few days, and its shape corresponds with the injuries.

records.l: the grey cloth, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: The murderer wore a grey cloak. Holmes treats the cloak as a certain detail if McCarthy junior’s statement is correct and uses it to narrow the search.

records.l: the murderer's footprints, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: The murderer’s footprints lead from the woods toward the crime scene and return, including tiptoe tracks made by unusual square boots. Holmes finds that the right-foot impression is less distinct, indicating that the murderer put less weight on that foot.

records.l: the physical description of the murderer, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Holmes describes the murderer as tall, left-handed, lame in the right leg, and wearing thick-soled shooting-boots and a grey cloak. He also says that the man smokes Indian cigars, uses a cigar-holder, and carries a blunt pen-knife.

records.l: Holmes's method of deduction, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright
records.s: Holmes bases his deductions on observation of trifles, including stride length, boot impressions, the direction of the fatal blow, tobacco ash, a cigar stump, and the cut end of a cigar. He also uses McCarthy senior’s words and the map of the Colony of Victoria to interpret “Ballarat.”

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes meets old Turner, who confesses to killing McCarthy after years of blackmail and threats against his daughter, Alice. Turner explains that he was once the highway robber known as Black Jack of Ballarat and that McCarthy had discovered his past and exploited it. Holmes records and witnesses Turner's confession, intending to use it only if necessary to save James McCarthy. James McCarthy is acquitted at the Assizes, while old Turner dies seven months after the interview and Alice remains unaware of the secret.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes summons old Turner privately, records his confession, and has Turner sign it with Watson as witness. He prepares objections for the defense, helping secure James McCarthy's acquittal, and keeps Turner's confession secret because it is no longer needed.

records.l: John Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Old Turner confesses to killing McCarthy, whom he says had blackmailed him for twenty years after recognizing him as Black Jack of Ballarat. He says he acted to protect Alice from McCarthy's threats and from being forced to marry McCarthy's son. He lives for seven months after the interview and then dies.

records.l: James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: James McCarthy is accused of killing his father, McCarthy, but is acquitted at the Assizes after objections prepared by Sherlock Holmes are submitted to the defending counsel.

records.l: Alice Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Alice Turner is old Turner's daughter. Her father says he killed McCarthy to prevent her from being controlled by McCarthy and his son, and she remains unaware of the criminal secret in her family's past.

records.l: the Assizes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: The Assizes are the court proceedings at which James McCarthy faces condemnation for McCarthy's killing. James McCarthy is acquitted there after objections prepared by Sherlock Holmes are used by the defense.

records.l: James McCarthy's acquittal, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: James McCarthy's acquittal is secured at the Assizes through a number of objections drawn up by Sherlock Holmes and submitted to the defending counsel. Because McCarthy is not condemned, Holmes does not need to reveal Turner's confession.

records.l: Turner's confession, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Turner's confession states that he was formerly the highway robber Black Jack of Ballarat and that he killed McCarthy, who had blackmailed him for years and threatened his daughter Alice. Turner signs the statement, and Sherlock Holmes agrees to keep it secret unless it becomes necessary to save James McCarthy.

records.l: Turner's criminal past, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,
records.s: Turner's criminal past began in the early 1860s, when he joined the Ballarat Gang and participated in highway robberies and a gold-convoy attack. He later settled in England, bought an estate, and tried to live respectably, but McCarthy recognized him and used the past to extort money, land, and houses from him.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: John Openshaw visits Sherlock Holmes in London during a violent storm to seek help against a hereditary threat affecting his family. He recounts how his uncle Elias Openshaw received a warning letter from Pondicherry containing five orange pips and marked K. K. K., then died seven weeks later; John’s father, Joseph Openshaw, later received a similar warning from Dundee and died in an apparent accident. John has now received the same warning from London and fears he will be killed. He gives Holmes a blue-tinted diary page suggesting that Elias had destroyed papers connected with earlier warnings and named men in Florida.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives John Openshaw at Baker Street and listens to his account of the threats against the Openshaw family. He urges John to act immediately, criticizes the police for treating the warnings as practical jokes, and examines the surviving blue-tinted diary page.

records.l: John Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: John Openshaw tells Sherlock Holmes that his uncle Elias and father Joseph died after receiving warnings marked K. K. K. and accompanied by five orange pips. He has now received the same kind of warning from London instructing him to put the papers on the sundial, and he seeks Holmes’s help.

records.l: Colonel Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Elias Openshaw, John’s uncle, was a former Confederate colonel who lived near Horsham after making a fortune in America. He received five orange pips from Pondicherry with the mark K. K. K., burned papers from a brass box, made a will, and died seven weeks later in a pool; his death was judged a suicide.

records.l: Joseph Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Joseph Openshaw, John’s father, inherited Elias Openshaw’s estate and money. He received five orange pips from Dundee with a warning to put the papers on the sundial, ignored it, and died after falling into an unfenced chalk-pit; his death was judged accidental.

records.l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: London is where Sherlock Holmes lives at Baker Street and where John Openshaw comes for help. John’s latest warning letter bears a London eastern-division postmark.

records.l: Horsham, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Horsham is the town near Elias Openshaw’s Sussex estate, where Elias lived and where John and his father later lived. John’s father’s estate and the family’s surviving papers were located there.

records.l: Pondicherry, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Pondicherry is the postmark on the letter Elias Openshaw received in March 1883. The letter contained five orange pips and the mark K. K. K.

records.l: Dundee, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Dundee is the postmark on the warning letter Joseph Openshaw received in January 1885. That letter contained five orange pips and instructed him to put the papers on the sundial.

records.l: five orange pips, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Five orange pips are sent with each of the warnings described in this unit. They appear first in Elias Openshaw’s letter from Pondicherry, then in Joseph Openshaw’s letter from Dundee, and finally in John Openshaw’s letter from London.

records.l: the Ku Klux Klan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: K. K. K. appears on the warning letters sent to Elias Openshaw, Joseph Openshaw, and John Openshaw. Elias also saw the initials on the brass box and reacted with terror when he received them.

records.l: the warning letters, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: The warning letters received by the Openshaws contain five orange pips and the initials K. K. K. Elias’s letter came from Pondicherry, Joseph’s from Dundee, and John’s from London; the latter two also state, “Put the papers on the sundial.”

records.l: the brass box, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Elias Openshaw took an old rusty key and a small brass box from the attic after receiving his warning. The box contained papers that he burned, and its lid bore the initials K. K. K.; it was later found empty.

records.l: the Openshaw papers, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: The destroyed papers were kept in Elias Openshaw’s brass box and were burned after he received the warning from Pondicherry. A surviving fragment suggests they may have included letters, memoranda, receipts, and a register, while the later warnings instruct the recipients to put the papers on the sundial.

records.l: the sundial, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: The sundial is the place named in the warnings received by Joseph Openshaw and John Openshaw. Both letters instruct the recipient to put the papers on the sundial.

records.l: the blue-tinted diary page, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: The blue-tinted diary page is a torn sheet John Openshaw found after Elias burned the papers. Written in Elias’s hand and headed “March, 1869,” it records Hudson’s visit, the setting of pips on McCauley, Paramore, and John Swain of St. Augustine, and later notes that McCauley and John Swain were cleared while Paramore was visited.

records.l: the Openshaw family curse, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: The Openshaw family curse is John Openshaw’s description of the recurring threat that has followed Elias, Joseph, and now John. John believes it is connected with an incident in Elias’s American life and fears that it has not ended with the previous generation.

records.l: the deaths of the Openshaws, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
records.s: Elias Openshaw died in a shallow, green-scummed pool after receiving a warning, and his death was recorded as suicide. Joseph Openshaw died after falling into an unfenced chalk-pit after receiving a similar warning, and his death was recorded as accidental; John believes both deaths were connected to the warnings.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes advises John Openshaw to place his remaining paper and a note in the brass box and put it on the sundial, but John is killed near Waterloo Bridge before he can do so. Holmes deduces that the warning letters came from members of the Ku Klux Klan, who are pursuing the Openshaw family to recover papers taken from America. He traces the perpetrators to the barque Lone Star, sends Captain James Calhoun five orange pips as a warning, and alerts the police, but the Lone Star sinks in the Atlantic before its crew can be arrested.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes advises John Openshaw to put the remaining paper and a note in the brass box and place it on the sundial. After learning of John's death, Holmes investigates the case, traces the perpetrators to the Lone Star, and sends Captain James Calhoun five orange pips as a warning. He is deeply distressed that his advice sent John into danger and resolves to pursue the gang.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Dr. Watson listens as Holmes analyzes the Openshaw case and helps identify the Ku Klux Klan from the American Encyclopaedia. He discovers the newspaper report of John Openshaw's death and records Holmes's subsequent investigation.

records.l: John Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: John Openshaw is instructed to return home, place the remaining paper and a note in the brass box, and put it on the sundial. He leaves Holmes's rooms armed, but is found dead in the water near Waterloo Bridge that night.

records.l: Colonel Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Colonel Openshaw is believed to have left America because he feared someone or something. Holmes connects his disappearance with the sudden collapse of the Ku Klux Klan and believes Colonel Openshaw took papers that implicated important men in the South.

records.l: the Openshaw family, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Openshaw family is subjected to relentless persecution by members of the Ku Klux Klan because of papers carried away from America. Holmes believes the family is being pursued by implacable Klan members seeking to recover those papers.

records.l: Captain James Calhoun, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
