records.s: Captain James Calhoun is identified by Holmes as the leader of the gang pursuing the Openshaws. Holmes addresses him aboard the Lone Star and sends him five orange pips as a precursor of his fate, while arranging for the Savannah police to be informed that he is wanted for murder.

records.l: the Ku Klux Klan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Ku Klux Klan is described as a secret society formed by ex-Confederate soldiers in the Southern states after the Civil War. Its members used warnings before murdering or driving away their targets, and Holmes concludes that the Klan is responsible for persecuting the Openshaws.

records.l: the Lone Star, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Lone Star is a barque that was reported at Pondicherry and Dundee and later arrived in London before sailing for Savannah. Holmes identifies it as carrying Captain Calhoun and two other American members of the gang, but it later disappears in severe gales.

records.l: the brass box, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The brass box is the container John Openshaw is told to place on the sundial. Holmes instructs him to put the remaining paper and a note claiming that all the other papers were burned by his uncle inside it.

records.l: the Openshaw papers, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Openshaw papers are considered vital by the people pursuing the family. Holmes believes they include a register and diary capable of implicating prominent men in the South and that their disappearance from America helped cause the Klan's collapse.

records.l: the warning letters, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The warning letters were sent to Colonel Openshaw and his successors from Pondicherry, Dundee, and East London. Holmes concludes that their senders were traveling by sailing ship and that the letters preceded the attacks by roughly the time needed for the ship to arrive.

records.l: five orange pips, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Orange pips were one of the recognized warning tokens used by the Ku Klux Klan. Holmes places five orange pips in an envelope for Captain James Calhoun, but the envelope never reaches him.

records.l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: London is the location where Holmes says the secret lies and where he begins his investigation. The third warning letter came from East London, and the Lone Star is found in the port of London before departing.

records.l: Waterloo, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Waterloo Station is the station from which John Openshaw planned to return home by train. Holmes notes that John was likely hurrying to catch the last train when he was killed.

records.l: Waterloo Bridge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Waterloo Bridge is near the place where Police-Constable Cook heard a cry and a splash. John's body is recovered from the water there, and Holmes believes the bridge area may have been used to decoy him.

records.l: Pondicherry, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Pondicherry is the source of the first warning letter. Holmes examines shipping records for vessels that visited Pondicherry in January and February of 1883 and finds the Lone Star among them.

records.l: Dundee, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Dundee is the source of the second warning letter. Holmes finds that the Lone Star was there in January 1885, strengthening his conclusion that its crew was connected with the persecution.

records.l: Savannah, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Savannah, Georgia, is the destination of the Lone Star. Holmes addresses his warning to Captain Calhoun aboard the barque there and arranges for the Savannah police to be notified.

records.l: America, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: America is where Colonel Openshaw lived before leaving for England, and where the Ku Klux Klan operated after the Civil War. The papers taken from America are believed to explain the Klan's pursuit of the Openshaw family.

records.l: John Openshaw's murder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: John Openshaw's murder is disguised in the newspaper as an accidental fall from a riverside landing place. Holmes concludes that the Klan arranged his death and later works to identify those responsible.

records.l: John Openshaw's death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: John Openshaw's death occurs near Waterloo Bridge after he leaves Holmes's rooms. His body is recovered from the water, with no visible traces of violence, and Holmes is shaken by having sent him away without preventing the danger.

records.l: the sinking of the Lone Star, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Lone Star is apparently lost in severe equinoctial gales while sailing toward Savannah. Only a shattered stern-post marked with the letters “L. S.” is later found, and the fate of Captain Calhoun and the other perpetrators remains unknown.

records.l: the Klan's persecution of the Openshaws, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: The Klan's persecution of the Openshaws involves warning letters, deadly attacks, and an effort to recover papers taken from America. Holmes connects the attacks on Colonel Openshaw, his successor, and John Openshaw with the Klan's organized methods.

records.l: Holmes's investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our
records.s: Holmes's investigation begins with the warning letters, their seaport postmarks, and the timing of the attacks. He consults Lloyd's registers and old newspapers, traces the perpetrators to the Lone Star, identifies Captain James Calhoun as their leader, and alerts the police, though the ship is lost before arrests can be made.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Kate Whitney comes to Watson and his wife for help because Isa Whitney has been missing for two days and is believed to be at the Bar of Gold opium den in Upper Swandam Lane. Watson finds Isa there, pays his bill, and sends him home in a cab. At the den, Watson discovers that Sherlock Holmes is disguised as an old opium smoker while investigating the disappearance of Neville St. Clair. Holmes takes Watson to The Cedars near Lee, where he begins explaining the case.

records.l: Isa Whitney, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Isa Whitney is addicted to opium and has been missing from home for two days. Watson finds him at the opium den in a weak and confused condition, and sends him home in a cab.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Watson is asked by Kate Whitney to find Isa and goes to the Bar of Gold in Upper Swandam Lane. He finds Isa, then discovers Sherlock Holmes in disguise and joins him in investigating Neville St. Clair's disappearance.

records.l: Watson's wife, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Watson's wife comforts Kate Whitney when she arrives distressed at their home. She is told by Watson that he has joined Holmes and will not return immediately.

records.l: Kate Whitney, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Kate Whitney comes to Watson and his wife because Isa has not returned home for two days. She believes he is at the Bar of Gold and asks Watson to bring him back.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is disguised as a decrepit old man in the opium den, where he is listening for clues while investigating Neville St. Clair's disappearance. He reveals himself to Watson, sends Isa home, and takes Watson to The Cedars to discuss the case.

records.l: Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Neville St. Clair is the subject of Sherlock Holmes's investigation. Holmes fears that he entered the opium den and never left it.

records.l: Bar of Gold, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: The Bar of Gold is the place where Kate believes Isa Whitney is staying during an opium binge. Watson finds Isa there, and Holmes says the establishment is connected to his investigation.

records.l: Upper Swandam Lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Upper Swandam Lane is a vile alley behind the wharves east of London Bridge. The Bar of Gold opium den is located there.

records.l: The Cedars, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: The Cedars is Mr. St. Clair's house near Lee, in Kent. Sherlock Holmes is staying there while conducting his investigation.

records.l: the opium den, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: The opium den in Upper Swandam Lane is a smoky, dangerous place where people lie in wooden berths and smoke opium. Holmes describes it as a murder-trap and says a trap-door near the back may reveal what happened there.

records.l: opium addiction, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Opium addiction has enslaved Isa Whitney for many years after he began using laudanum to imitate De Quincey's described sensations. His addiction causes repeated binges, during which he disappears into opium dens and returns physically and mentally distressed.

records.l: Isa Whitney's disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Isa Whitney has been absent from home for two days during an opium binge. Kate Whitney believes he is at the Bar of Gold, and Watson locates and brings him home.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Neville St. Clair's disappearance is being investigated by Sherlock Holmes. Holmes fears that St. Clair entered the opium den and may have been killed there.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes's investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
records.s: Sherlock Holmes's investigation concerns the disappearance of Neville St. Clair. He searches for clues among the opium users, suspects the Bar of Gold and its trap-door may be involved, and conducts the inquiry from The Cedars.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Neville St. Clair, a prosperous and respected resident of Lee, disappeared after being seen by his wife at an upstairs window of an opium den in Swandam Lane. Mrs. St. Clair saw him agitated and without a collar or necktie, but he vanished before she could reach him. Police found his clothing, a box of children's bricks, and blood traces near a bedroom window overlooking a tidal strip, but no sign of Neville. Suspicion fell on the Lascar manager and Hugh Boone, a crippled professional beggar lodging at the opium den.

records.l: Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Neville St. Clair is described as a thirty-seven-year-old man of temperate habits, a good husband, an affectionate father, and a popular local resident with sufficient money. He was seen by Mrs. St. Clair at an upstairs window of the opium den, appearing terribly agitated and beckoning frantically, after which he vanished; his clothes, apart from his coat, were later found in the building.

records.l: Mrs. St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Mrs. St. Clair went into the City to collect a valuable parcel and passed through Swandam Lane at about 4:35. She saw Neville St. Clair at a second-floor window, rushed into the opium den when he disappeared, was forced back by the Lascar and a Dane, and later brought an inspector and constables to the premises.

records.l: Hugh Boone, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Hugh Boone is a crippled but apparently powerful man who lodged at the opium den and was the last person whose eyes were believed to have rested on Neville St. Clair. He is a professional beggar who pretends to trade in wax vestas, and he was found in the building after Neville disappeared; he denied that anyone else had been in the front room.

records.l: the Lascar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: The Lascar manager, described as a man of vile antecedents, resisted Mrs. St. Clair and helped push her out of the opium den with the assistance of a Dane. He denied knowing what Hugh Boone had done and could not explain the presence of Neville St. Clair's clothes.

records.l: Inspector Barton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: The inspector met Mrs. St. Clair in Fresno Street and accompanied her and two constables back to the opium den. He initially became doubtful because the Lascar and Hugh Boone denied that anyone else had been present, but the discovery of the box of children's bricks led him to treat the matter as serious and investigate the rooms.

records.l: Fresno Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Fresno Street contains the offices of the Aberdeen Shipping Company and branches out of Upper Swandam Lane. Mrs. St. Clair met the inspector and constables there after leaving the opium den.

records.l: Swandam Lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Swandam Lane is described as an unpleasant area branching from Fresno Street. Mrs. St. Clair was walking through it toward the station when she saw Neville St. Clair at the opium den's window.

records.l: the opium den, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: The opium den in Swandam Lane was the place where Mrs. St. Clair saw Neville St. Clair and where he subsequently disappeared. Its rooms included a furnished front room, a small bedroom overlooking a wharf, and lodgings occupied by Hugh Boone; the Lascar manager resisted the search.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Neville St. Clair's disappearance occurred after Mrs. St. Clair saw him frantically beckoning from an open second-floor window. He vanished so suddenly that she thought he had been pulled backward, and no trace of him was found despite an examination of the opium den; investigators believed he had apparently gone through the bedroom window.

records.l: police investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: The police investigation began when Mrs. St. Clair brought an inspector and two constables back to the opium den. They searched the rooms, questioned the Lascar and Hugh Boone, examined the window and floor for evidence, and concluded that the circumstances pointed to an abominable crime.

records.l: box of children's bricks, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: The box of children's bricks was found on a table in the front room of the opium den. Mrs. St. Clair identified it as the toy Neville St. Clair had promised to bring home for their little boy, and its discovery, together with Hugh Boone's confusion, convinced the inspector that the matter was serious.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's other clothes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Neville St. Clair's boots, socks, hat, and watch were found hidden behind a curtain in the front room, along with the rest of his clothes except for his coat. None of the garments showed signs of violence, and their presence offered no explanation for his disappearance.

records.l: blood traces, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Some years ago—to be definite, in May, 1884—there came to Lee a
records.s: Blood traces were found on the sill of the bedroom window and in several scattered drops on the wooden floor. Because the window overlooked a strip covered by deep water at high tide, the traces appeared to make escape by swimming unlikely.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Inspector Barton and the police search the premises after Mrs. St. Clair reports seeing Neville St. Clair at the window of an opium den, but they find no decisive clue. Hugh Boone is arrested, and Neville St. Clair's coat is recovered from the mud-bank, weighted with 421 pennies and 270 half-pennies, while his body remains missing. Sherlock Holmes discusses the disappearance with Dr. Watson and Mrs. St. Clair, who produces a letter apparently written by Neville and posted from Gravesend. Holmes remains uncertain whether Neville is alive, dead, or the victim of a forgery, while Mrs. St. Clair insists that the handwriting is genuine.

records.l: Mrs. St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Mrs. St. Clair is escorted home by the police after fainting at the sight of blood upon the window. She tells Sherlock Holmes that she believes Neville is alive and identifies the handwriting in the letter as one of his forms of writing. She answers Holmes's questions about seeing Neville at the window in Swandam Lane and maintains that she would have sensed his death.

records.l: Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Neville St. Clair remains missing after Mrs. St. Clair apparently sees him at the window in Swandam Lane. His coat is found in the river mud, but his body is not recovered. A letter apparently written by him says that a huge error is being rectified and asks Mrs. St. Clair to wait patiently.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates Neville St. Clair's disappearance with Dr. Watson and questions Mrs. St. Clair at The Cedars. He examines the letter, infers details about its envelope and posting, and considers both Neville's survival and the possibility of a forgery. He plans further inquiries for the following day.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to The Cedars and is introduced to Mrs. St. Clair as Holmes's friend and colleague. He listens as Holmes explains the evidence and questions Mrs. St. Clair.

records.l: Hugh Boone, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Hugh Boone is arrested after being found at the premises and is searched without any incriminating object being discovered. Blood-stains on his right shirt-sleeve are explained by a cut near his ring-finger. He denies knowing Neville St. Clair and says that the clothes found in his room are as mysterious to him as to the police.

records.l: Bow Street police force, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The police escort Mrs. St. Clair home, arrest and search Hugh Boone, and investigate the premises. Inspector Barton remains at the site hoping that the ebbing tide will reveal a clue, and the police recover Neville St. Clair's coat from the mud-bank.

records.l: The Cedars, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The Cedars is the villa near Lee where Mrs. St. Clair lives. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel there, and Mrs. St. Clair provides Holmes with two rooms for his investigation.

records.l: Swandam Lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Swandam Lane is the location of the opium den where Mrs. St. Clair unexpectedly sees Neville at a window. Neville had never spoken to her about the place, and Holmes questions her closely about what she saw there.

records.l: the St. Clair disappearance case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The case concerns Neville St. Clair's unexplained disappearance after he is apparently seen at a window in Swandam Lane. The main unresolved questions are what Neville was doing in the opium den, what happened to him, where he is, and what Hugh Boone had to do with his disappearance.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's possible death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes initially believes that Neville St. Clair probably died on Monday, though he does not state that Neville was murdered. The recovery of a letter apparently written by Neville weakens that conclusion, but Holmes notes that it could have been written earlier or forged.

records.l: the disappearance investigation's false murder charge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The working hypothesis is that Hugh Boone thrust Neville St. Clair through the window, removed his clothes, and weighted Neville's coat with coins so it would sink. The hypothesis suggests that the body was then carried away by the river while Boone had no time to dispose of the other garments.

records.l: the opium den, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The opium den is the place where Neville St. Clair is apparently seen by Mrs. St. Clair at a window. Holmes asks whether Neville had ever shown signs of taking opium, and Mrs. St. Clair says that he had not.

records.l: St. Clair residence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The Cedars villa is a large house within its own grounds near Lee. Holmes and Dr. Watson arrive there after midnight, where Mrs. St. Clair welcomes them and serves a cold supper.

records.l: the window at Swandam Lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The window at Swandam Lane is where Mrs. St. Clair says she saw Neville St. Clair, apparently without a collar or tie. Blood was found upon it, and Holmes considers whether Neville may have called for help, expressed surprise, or leaped back rather than being pulled away.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's coat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Neville St. Clair's coat is found uncovered on the mud-bank as the tide recedes. It contains a large quantity of coins, leading the investigators to think that it may have been deliberately weighted to sink while Neville's stripped body was carried away.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's other clothes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Neville St. Clair's other clothes are found in the room at the opium den. Their presence creates a difficulty for the theory that Neville was thrown from the window, though the working hypothesis proposes that Hugh Boone had no time to dispose of them.

records.l: the coins in Neville St. Clair's coat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The pockets of Neville St. Clair's coat contain 421 pennies and 270 half-pennies. Their weight explains why the coat was not swept away by the tide and supports the theory that it was deliberately weighted.

records.l: the letter from Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The letter from Neville St. Clair is delivered to Mrs. St. Clair on the day Holmes visits, bearing a Gravesend postmark and the date of that day or the previous day. Its coarse envelope appears to have been addressed by someone unfamiliar with the address, and Holmes observes signs that the writer or sender had a dirty thumb and used chewing tobacco.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's signet-ring, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: Neville St. Clair's signet-ring is enclosed with the letter. Holmes says that the ring proves nothing because it might have been taken from Neville, while Mrs. St. Clair insists that the accompanying handwriting is genuine.

records.l: the message in Neville St. Clair's handwriting, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,
records.s: The message reads: "Dearest do not be frightened. All will come well. There is a huge error which it may take some little time to rectify. Wait in patience., NEVILLE." It is written in pencil on the fly-leaf of an octavo book, and Mrs. St. Clair identifies it as Neville's hurried handwriting.
records.t: The message reads: "Dearest do not be frightened. All will come well. There is a huge error which it may take some little time to rectify. Wait in patience.—NEVILLE." It is written in pencil on the fly-leaf of an octavo book, and Mrs. St. Clair identifies it as Neville's hurried handwriting.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes concludes that Hugh Boone, the beggar arrested in connection with the disappearance of Neville St. Clair, is actually Neville St. Clair in disguise. At Bow Street, Holmes uses a bath-sponge to remove Boone's makeup and reveals St. Clair, who explains that he became a professional beggar after first disguising himself for a newspaper article. St. Clair says his wife discovered him at the opium den, leading him to throw his ordinary clothes and money into the Thames and preserve his disguise. Inspector Bradstreet agrees that the matter may be kept out of court if St. Clair abandons begging, while Holmes credits his solution to sitting on pillows and smoking an ounce of shag.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes spends the night analyzing the case, then takes Watson to Bow Street to test his theory. He reveals that Hugh Boone is Neville St. Clair by removing Boone's disguise, and explains that he solved the matter through prolonged thought and observation.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes from their lodgings to Bow Street and witnesses the exposure of Hugh Boone's disguise and Neville St. Clair's confession.

records.l: Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair is revealed to be the prisoner known as Hugh Boone. He explains that he left reporting to make a living as a disguised beggar, hid this occupation from his family, and preserved his disguise after his wife saw him at the opium den.

records.l: Hugh Boone, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Hugh Boone is held in a Bow Street cell as a dirty, scarred, red-haired beggar accused in connection with Neville St. Clair's disappearance. Holmes removes his makeup and wig, revealing that Boone is St. Clair.

records.l: Inspector Bradstreet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Inspector Bradstreet allows Holmes and Watson to visit Hugh Boone in the cells. After Boone is revealed as Neville St. Clair, Bradstreet agrees that the matter may not go to court if St. Clair stops presenting himself as Hugh Boone.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's wife, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair's wife sees him at the opium den while he is dressed as himself, causing him to conceal his identity again. She spends a week fearing for him until the note he sent through the Lascar reaches her.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's children, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair says he maintained his disguise because he could not bear for his children to be ashamed of their father.

records.l: the Lascar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: The Lascar keeps rooms in Swandam Lane where Neville St. Clair changes between his beggar and ordinary identities. St. Clair entrusts him with his ring and a note for his wife, and Inspector Bradstreet says the Lascar probably gave the note to a sailor, delaying its delivery.

records.l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Holmes and Watson drive through London before dawn, passing the Waterloo Bridge Road, crossing the river, and reaching Bow Street.

records.l: Lee, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Lee is identified as Neville St. Clair's place of residence in the charge and police inquiry concerning his disappearance.

records.l: Swandam Lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Swandam Lane contains the low den where the Lascar lodges Neville St. Clair and helps him change into and out of his beggar disguise.

records.l: Bow Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Holmes and Watson go to Bow Street, where Inspector Bradstreet is on duty and Hugh Boone is confined in the cells.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: After resolving the matter, Sherlock Holmes suggests that he and Watson drive back to Baker Street in time for breakfast.

records.l: the opium den, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair dresses and changes his appearance in a room above the opium den. His wife sees him there, prompting him to resume his beggar disguise and discard his ordinary clothes.

records.l: the disappearance of Neville St. Clair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: The apparent disappearance of Neville St. Clair is explained when Hugh Boone is exposed as St. Clair himself. St. Clair had not been murdered or abducted; he had been maintaining his identity as a beggar.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's arrest, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair is arrested as Hugh Boone's supposed murderer after he throws his ordinary clothes from the opium den window and keeps his disguise. He says he was relieved that the police arrested him as a murderer rather than identifying him as St. Clair.

records.l: the St. Clair disappearance case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: The investigation leads Holmes to suspect that the beggar Hugh Boone is Neville St. Clair. Holmes confirms this by washing away Boone's makeup, after which St. Clair gives a full account of his double life.

records.l: professional begging, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair discovers that begging can earn him far more than reporting, taking about £2 on a bad day and averaging less than £700 a year. He is prosecuted many times but treats the fines as insignificant until Inspector Bradstreet orders him to stop.

records.l: Hugh Boone's disguise, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Hugh Boone's disguise consists of painted grime, a false scar, a flesh-coloured plaster that twists one side of the lip, a red wig, and beggar's clothing. Holmes removes the disguise with a wet bath-sponge, exposing Neville St. Clair.

records.l: the secret of Hugh Boone's identity, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: The secret is that Hugh Boone is Neville St. Clair, a respectable married man who secretly works as a professional beggar. St. Clair fears public exposure because he does not want his children to be ashamed of him.

records.l: the Gladstone bag, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes brings a Gladstone bag to Bow Street, initially claiming that it contains the key to the case taken from the bathroom. He uses it to carry the large bath-sponge used to remove Hugh Boone's disguise.

records.l: the bath-sponge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Holmes takes a very large bath-sponge from the Gladstone bag, wets it, and rubs it across Hugh Boone's face. The sponge removes the false complexion and scar, helping reveal Neville St. Clair.

records.l: the message in Neville St. Clair's handwriting, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair writes his wife a hurried note saying that she has no cause to fear and gives it to the Lascar along with his ring. The note reaches her only after a delay, probably because a sailor carried it from the Lascar.

records.l: the disappearance investigation's false murder charge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: The supposed murder charge results from Neville St. Clair's decision to remain disguised as Hugh Boone after his wife saw him. Once Holmes reveals his identity, Inspector Bradstreet recognizes that no murder has occurred.

records.l: Neville St. Clair's begging career, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our
records.s: Neville St. Clair begins begging as research for newspaper articles, then abandons reporting after discovering that the disguise allows him to earn much more money. He maintains the career secretly for years, becoming a recognized beggar in the City while living as a respectable married man.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines a battered black felt hat found with a Christmas goose after Henry Baker fled a confrontation on Tottenham Court Road. Peterson discovers the blue carbuncle, stolen from the Countess of Morcar's jewel-case at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, in the goose's crop. Holmes advertises for Henry Baker, intending to determine whether he is connected to the theft, while John Horner remains accused of stealing the gem. Dr. John Watson observes Holmes's deductions and plans to return to Baker Street that evening.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the battered black felt hat and deduces details about its unknown owner, including his intellect, former prosperity, declining circumstances, age, habits, and domestic situation. After Peterson finds the blue carbuncle in the Christmas goose, Holmes connects it to the Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery and advertises for Henry Baker so he can investigate further.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Dr. John Watson visits Sherlock Holmes after Christmas, listens to Holmes's deductions about the hat, and admits that he cannot follow all of Holmes's reasoning. He learns about the blue carbuncle and says he will return to Baker Street that evening to see the case's solution.

records.l: Peterson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Peterson, a commissionaire, finds the battered black felt hat and Christmas goose after Henry Baker flees on Tottenham Court Road. He brings them to Sherlock Holmes, later discovers the blue carbuncle in the goose's crop, and is sent to place an advertisement for Henry Baker in the evening papers.

records.l: Henry Baker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Henry Baker is identified as the owner of the battered black felt hat and the Christmas goose marked for Mrs. Henry Baker. He drops the goose and flees after a window is broken during a confrontation on Tottenham Court Road; Sherlock Holmes considers him likely to be innocent but seeks to question him.

records.l: the Countess of Morcar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The Countess of Morcar owns the blue carbuncle, which was stolen from her jewel-case at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. She has offered a reward of £1000 for its recovery and is said to have sentimental reasons for wanting it back.

records.l: Horace Harker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: John Horner, a plumber, is accused of taking the blue carbuncle from the Countess of Morcar's jewel-case. He protests his innocence, struggles during his arrest, and is referred to the Assizes after evidence of a previous robbery conviction is presented.

records.l: James Ryder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: James Ryder, an upper-attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, testifies that he showed John Horner to the Countess of Morcar's dressing-room to repair a grate. He says that after leaving Horner briefly, he returned to find the jewel-case forced open and the blue carbuncle missing.

records.l: the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The blue carbuncle is a unique, brilliantly sparkling blue precious stone belonging to the Countess of Morcar. It was stolen from her jewel-case, passed into the Christmas goose, and is recovered by Peterson from the goose's crop; Holmes keeps it in his strong box.

records.l: the battered black felt hat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The battered black felt hat bears the initials H. B. and is old, cracked, dusty, stained, and missing its elastic hat-securer. Sherlock Holmes uses its size, lining, hair-ends, odors, dust, moisture marks, and tallow stains to infer characteristics of its owner, Henry Baker.

records.l: Henry Baker's original goose, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The Christmas goose is carried by Henry Baker and marked with a card reading “For Mrs. Henry Baker.” Peterson takes it to Sherlock Holmes after Baker abandons it, and its crop is found to contain the blue carbuncle before the goose is eaten.

records.l: the Countess of Morcar's jewel-case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The Countess of Morcar's jewel-case is kept in her dressing-room at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. It is forced open, and the small morocco casket inside is found empty after John Horner leaves the room.

records.l: the Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery concerns the disappearance of the blue carbuncle from the Countess of Morcar's jewel-case on December 22nd. John Horner is arrested and accused, but the stone is not found on him or in his rooms before it later appears in the Christmas goose.

records.l: the blue carbuncle theft, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The blue carbuncle theft is attributed by the police-court evidence to John Horner, who was working in the Countess of Morcar's dressing-room when the jewel disappeared. The recovery of the stone in a goose leads Sherlock Holmes to investigate the sequence connecting the theft to Henry Baker.

records.l: the adventure of the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The adventure of the blue carbuncle begins as Sherlock Holmes investigates an apparently ordinary lost hat and goose. Peterson's discovery of the stolen gem transforms the matter into an investigation involving the Countess of Morcar, John Horner, Henry Baker, and the Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery.

records.l: Tottenham Court Road, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Tottenham Court Road is where Peterson sees Henry Baker carrying the Christmas goose on Christmas morning. A confrontation occurs near Goodge Street, after which Baker breaks a shop window, abandons the goose and hat, and flees.

records.l: Goodge Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Goodge Street is the corner where Henry Baker is confronted by roughs while carrying the Christmas goose. After a shop window is broken, Baker abandons the goose and battered black felt hat nearby.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: Baker Street is the location of Sherlock Holmes's rooms at 221B, where he keeps the hat and investigates the blue carbuncle. Holmes's advertisement instructs Henry Baker to apply there at 6:30 that evening.

records.l: the Hotel Cosmopolitan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
records.s: The Hotel Cosmopolitan is the site of the Countess of Morcar's jewel robbery. John Horner is alleged to have stolen the blue carbuncle from the Countess's dressing-room there.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Watson arrives at Baker Street with Henry Baker, who has come to recover his hat and goose. Sherlock Holmes explains that Baker's original goose was eaten but offers him a fresh replacement. Baker accepts the replacement goose and retrieves his hat. He explains that he received the original goose through a Christmas goose club at the Alpha Inn.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Sherlock Holmes greets Henry Baker and returns his hat and a replacement goose. He explains that Baker's original goose was eaten and asks where it came from.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Watson arrives at Baker Street just as Henry Baker is being shown into Sherlock Holmes' room and observes their meeting.

records.l: Henry Baker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Henry Baker comes to Sherlock Holmes' rooms to recover his hat and goose, believing that roughs who assaulted him had taken them. He accepts the replacement goose after learning that his original was eaten and says that he received it through a goose club at the Alpha Inn.

records.l: the Alpha Inn, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: The Alpha Inn, near the Museum, is frequented by Henry Baker and others. Its host, Windigate, instituted a goose club there.

records.l: the goose club, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: The goose club was instituted by Windigate at the Alpha Inn. Members paid a few pence each week and were to receive a goose at Christmas.

records.l: Henry Baker's original goose, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Henry Baker's original goose was recovered by Sherlock Holmes but was eaten because it would otherwise have been of no use. Its feathers, legs, crop, and other remains were retained.

records.l: replacement goose, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Sherlock Holmes offers Henry Baker a fresh goose of about the same weight as his original. Henry Baker accepts it and carries it away under his arm.

records.l: the battered black felt hat, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six
records.s: Henry Baker's hat was retained with the goose and returned to him by Sherlock Holmes. Baker says that a Scotch bonnet is unsuitable for his age and gravity.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson trace Henry Baker’s goose through the Alpha Inn and Mr. Breckinridge to Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business. They discover that James Ryder, a head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, stole the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle and hid it inside a goose. Ryder mistakenly took the wrong barred-tail goose, allowing the stone to reach the market and eventually Holmes. Holmes frightens Ryder into confessing but releases him, believing this may save him from becoming a habitual criminal and will cause the prosecution of Horner to collapse.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Sherlock Holmes follows the goose supply chain from the Alpha Inn to Covent Garden Market and uses a wager to obtain Mr. Breckinridge’s records. He identifies James Ryder, obtains his confession, and releases him rather than sending him to the police, reasoning that this may save Ryder from a life of crime.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes through London, observes the inquiries at the Alpha Inn and Covent Garden Market, and helps Holmes with the fainting James Ryder. He hears Ryder’s confession and Holmes’s decision to release him.

records.l: Henry Baker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Henry Baker is identified as a member of the Alpha Inn’s goose club. Sherlock Holmes concludes that he knows nothing about the theft and traces his goose through the club’s supply chain.

records.l: James Ryder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: James Ryder, initially using the name John Robinson, is revealed to be the head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. He stole the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle, placed it in a goose, mistakenly took another barred-tail goose, and confessed after Holmes confronted him. Holmes releases him after Ryder pleads for mercy.

records.l: the Countess of Morcar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The Countess of Morcar owned the blue carbuncle that was stolen in the jewel robbery.

records.l: Mrs. Oakshott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Mrs. Oakshott, of 117 Brixton Road, supplied twenty-four geese to Mr. Breckinridge on December 22nd. She kept and fattened poultry for the market and had two white geese with barred tails that she could not distinguish.

records.l: Mr. Breckinridge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Mr. Breckinridge sold two dozen geese from his Covent Garden stall to Mr. Windigate of the Alpha Inn. He resists James Ryder’s repeated inquiries about the birds but reveals his supplier and sales records after Holmes tricks him into a wager.

records.l: the police, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The police arrested Horner for the jewel robbery, while Holmes believes their investigation missed the line of inquiry provided by the goose. Ryder feared that the police would search him and discover the blue carbuncle.

records.l: the Alpha Inn, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The Alpha Inn is a small public-house in Bloomsbury whose landlord bought two dozen geese from Mr. Breckinridge. Its goose club included Henry Baker, and its landlord identifies Breckinridge as the supplier.

records.l: the Hotel Cosmopolitan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The Hotel Cosmopolitan employed James Ryder as a head attendant. The blue carbuncle was stolen there from the Countess of Morcar’s jewel-case.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and James Ryder return to discuss the goose and the stolen stone. Holmes displays the blue carbuncle there and obtains Ryder’s confession.

records.l: Covent Garden Market, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Covent Garden Market contains Mr. Breckinridge’s stall, where the geese from Mrs. Oakshott were sold. Holmes uses the stall’s records to trace the birds and encounters James Ryder there.

records.l: Brixton Road, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Brixton Road is the location of Mrs. Oakshott’s house and poultry business. James Ryder went there after the theft and hid the blue carbuncle inside a goose.

records.l: the goose club, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The goose club at the Alpha Inn supplied Henry Baker with a goose. Its birds form the first link in Holmes’s investigation into the stolen blue carbuncle.

records.l: the geese, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The geese passed from Mrs. Oakshott to Mr. Breckinridge, then to the Alpha Inn and its goose club. One of them carried the blue carbuncle after James Ryder mistakenly chose a different barred-tail goose.

records.l: the blue-barred-tail goose, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The white goose with a barred tail was the bird James Ryder selected to carry the blue carbuncle, but he accidentally took another nearly identical bird. The goose containing the stone was sold through Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business and eventually reached the Alpha Inn.

records.l: the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The blue carbuncle was stolen from the Countess of Morcar and hidden by James Ryder inside a goose. The goose carrying it reached Holmes, who keeps the stone in his strong-box and displays it to Ryder.

records.l: Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business fattened geese for the market. It supplied twenty-four geese to Mr. Breckinridge, including the goose that carried the blue carbuncle.

records.l: the jewel robbery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The jewel robbery involved the theft of the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle from the Hotel Cosmopolitan. James Ryder and Catherine Cusack arranged circumstances that caused suspicion to fall on Horner.

records.l: the police-court proceedings against John Horner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Horner was arrested and placed in the dock for a crime of which Holmes says he knew nothing. Holmes concludes that the case must collapse because Ryder will not appear against Horner.

records.l: the blue carbuncle theft, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: Ryder’s theft was the deliberate stealing of the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle after he and Catherine Cusack helped implicate Horner. Ryder hid the stone in a goose but never recovered it because he took the wrong bird.

records.l: the adventure of the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The blue carbuncle investigation follows the stone through Henry Baker’s goose, the Alpha Inn, Mr. Breckinridge, and Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business. Holmes solves the investigation by identifying Ryder and securing his confession.

records.l: the Alpha Inn’s goose supply chain, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
records.s: The Alpha Inn’s goose supply chain runs from Mrs. Oakshott at Brixton Road to Mr. Breckinridge at Covent Garden Market, then to Mr. Windigate of the Alpha Inn and its goose club. Holmes reconstructs this chain to locate the goose that carried the blue carbuncle.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Helen Stoner visits Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street in terror, seeking help regarding the suspicious death of her sister Julia and a recent low whistle heard in Julia's former bedroom. She explains the violent history of her stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and describes Julia's death after she cried out about a “speckled band.” Helen is now engaged to Percy Armitage, but fears that the same danger threatens her after moving into Julia's room. Holmes discovers five-finger bruises on Helen's wrist and decides to travel with Dr. Watson to Stoke Moran to investigate.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Helen Stoner at Baker Street and questions her closely about her sister's death, the whistle, the bedroom, and the circumstances at Stoke Moran. He identifies mud and a return ticket as evidence of Helen's journey, notices five livid finger marks on her wrist, accuses her of screening her stepfather, and agrees to investigate the manor with Dr. Watson.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Dr. Watson is awakened by Sherlock Holmes and accompanies him to hear Helen Stoner's account. He agrees to travel with Holmes to Stoke Moran and inspect the rooms.

records.l: Helen Stoner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Helen Stoner comes to Sherlock Holmes in a state of terror because she has heard the same low whistle that preceded her sister Julia's death after moving into Julia's former room. She describes Dr. Grimesby Roylott's violence, Julia's death, and her own impending marriage, and Holmes finds five livid finger marks on her wrist.

records.l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott is Helen Stoner's stepfather and the last survivor of the Roylotts of Stoke Moran. He is described as immensely strong, violently temperamental, feared by the village, hostile to others, and associated with the unexplained death of Julia, though no cause was established.

records.l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Julia Stoner was Helen's twin sister and was engaged to a half-pay major of marines. She died two years before this account after hearing or encountering something connected with a low whistle, and her final words referred to a “speckled band.”

records.l: the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The Roylotts of Stoke Moran were once among the richest families in England, but four successive dissolute heirs ruined the family fortune. Their remaining estate consists of a few acres and the heavily mortgaged ancestral house.

records.l: Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Stoke Moran is the old ancestral home and estate of the Roylotts, located on the western border of Surrey. Helen and Julia live there with Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and Holmes and Watson plan to visit it.

records.l: Percy Armitage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Percy Armitage, the second son of Mr. Armitage of Crane Water near Reading, is Helen Stoner's friend and intended husband. He has asked Helen to marry him, and their wedding is planned for the spring.

records.l: the Stoke Moran manor-house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The Stoke Moran manor-house is very old, and only one wing is inhabited. Its bedrooms are on the ground floor, while the sitting-rooms are in the central block.

records.l: the three ground-floor bedrooms, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The three ground-floor bedrooms consist of Dr. Roylott's room, Julia's room, and Helen's room, arranged along the same corridor with no communication between them. Their windows open onto the lawn.

records.l: the corridor, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The corridor connects the three ground-floor bedrooms and contains a lamp. Helen entered it after hearing Julia scream and saw Julia emerge from her room.

records.l: the gipsies, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The gipsies are allowed by Dr. Grimesby Roylott to camp on the bramble-covered land at Stoke Moran. Helen initially suggested that they might have caused or explained the low whistle, and Julia's reference to a “speckled band” was possibly connected in Helen's mind with their spotted head handkerchiefs.

records.l: the cheetah, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The cheetah is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to Helen and Julia's practice of locking their bedroom doors at night.

records.l: the baboon, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The baboon is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to the sisters' feeling that they were not safe unless their bedroom doors were locked.

records.l: the low whistle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The low whistle was heard by Julia at about three in the morning during the nights before her death. Helen heard a similar whistle immediately after Julia screamed and again two years later when Helen slept in Julia's former room.

records.l: the metallic sound, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Helen says that after hearing the low whistle on the night of Julia's death, she heard a clanging or metallic sound like a mass of metal falling. Holmes questions whether she is certain of this sound, since the storm and the old house may have confused her.

records.l: the speckled band, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The “speckled band” was Julia Stoner's final intelligible reference as she lay dying. Helen is uncertain whether it referred to a group of people, such as the gipsies, or was merely delirious speech.

records.l: Julia Stoner's death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Julia Stoner's death occurred two years before Helen consulted Holmes, shortly before Julia's wedding. She was found convulsed and unconscious after crying out, and medical aid failed; the coroner found no satisfactory cause, no poison, no violence, and no way for an intruder to have entered her locked room.

records.l: Helen Stoner's impending marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Helen Stoner is engaged to Percy Armitage and expects to marry in the spring. She says her stepfather has offered no opposition, but her move into Julia's former room and the repeated whistle have caused her to fear for her safety.

records.l: the locked bedroom, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The sisters customarily locked their bedroom doors at night because of the cheetah and baboon. On the night of Julia's death, her door was secured from the inside, while the barred windows, solid walls, and blocked chimney appeared to exclude any intruder.

records.l: the five-finger bruises, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: The five-finger bruises are livid marks on Helen Stoner's wrist, showing the impressions of four fingers and a thumb. Sherlock Holmes uses them to establish that Helen has been cruelly handled, although Helen excuses Dr. Roylott by saying he may not know his own strength.

records.l: fear and nervous shock, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
records.s: Helen believes that Julia died from pure fear and nervous shock because no poison, violence, or other cause was found. Her own terror is intensified by hearing the low whistle in Julia's former room, but the text does not establish that this belief is correct.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Watson investigate the suspicious death of Helen Stoner’s sister and the danger facing Helen at Stoke Moran. Dr. Grimesby Roylott confronts Holmes, threatens him, and demonstrates his strength by bending a poker. Holmes examines Stoke Moran mansion, discovers a dummy bell-rope, a useless ventilator, a saucer of milk, and a tied dog lash, and concludes that Roylott has strong financial motives to prevent his stepdaughters’ marriages. Holmes instructs Helen to leave a signal and spend the night in another room while he and Watson investigate the danger.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes considers the nocturnal whistles, the gipsies, Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s financial interest, the dying woman’s words, and the metallic clang as possible clues. He confronts Roylott’s threats calmly, investigates the will of the deceased wife, examines Stoke Moran mansion, and concludes that Helen Stoner’s life may be in danger. He orders Helen to signal him after Roylott retires so that he and Watson can investigate her room during the night.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Stoke Moran mansion, observes Roylott’s confrontation, and assists in examining the rooms and grounds. He carries a revolver at Holmes’s request and joins Holmes in planning to spend the night investigating the danger threatening Helen Stoner.

records.l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott visits Holmes after tracing Helen Stoner to him and demands to know what she has said. He threatens Holmes, bends a steel poker with his hands, and leaves after warning Holmes not to meddle in his affairs. Holmes learns from the will that Roylott has a strong financial motive for preventing his stepdaughters’ marriages.

records.l: Helen Stoner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Helen Stoner meets Holmes and Watson at Stoke Moran after Roylott has gone to town. She confirms details about the rooms, shutters, bell-rope, ventilator, and repairs, and agrees to follow Holmes’s instructions by signaling from her window and sleeping in another room. Holmes warns her that her life may depend on obeying him.

records.l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Julia Stoner is identified as Helen Stoner’s sister, who died mysteriously in the middle bedroom at Stoke Moran. The examination of the room reveals features that Holmes considers connected with her death.

records.l: the gipsies, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The gipsies are connected with Dr. Grimesby Roylott and are on intimate terms with him. Holmes considers their presence, the nocturnal whistles, and the dying woman’s reference to a band as possible elements of the mystery, but he cannot determine what they did.

records.l: Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Stoke Moran is the place where Dr. Grimesby Roylott lives and where Helen Stoner’s sister died. Holmes and Watson travel there to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death and the danger facing Helen.

records.l: the Stoke Moran manor-house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The Stoke Moran mansion is an old, partly ruined grey stone building with a central portion and two wings. Holmes examines its exterior, rooms, windows, shutters, repairs, and internal features while investigating the death and the threat to Helen.

records.l: the will of the deceased wife, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The will of the deceased wife provides each daughter with an income of £250 in case of marriage. Holmes calculates that the reduced agricultural income would leave Roylott with very little money if both daughters married and would seriously reduce his means even if one married.

records.l: the marriage arrangement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The marriage arrangement would give each daughter an income of £250 upon marriage. Holmes determines that the arrangement gives Dr. Grimesby Roylott a strong financial motive to prevent his stepdaughters from marrying.

records.l: Julia Stoner's death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Helen Stoner’s sister’s death occurred in the middle bedroom after she was apparently alone in a room with sound walls and flooring and impassable doors, window, and chimney. Holmes investigates the room and its unusual fixtures because he believes the death had a tangible cause rather than being caused solely by fright.

records.l: the mystery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The mystery concerns Helen Stoner’s sister’s unexplained death, the nocturnal whistles, the dying woman’s words, and the danger now facing Helen. Holmes believes the mystery may be connected with Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s motives and the unusual construction of the bedroom.

records.l: the nocturnal whistles, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The nocturnal whistles were heard in connection with the mysterious death at Stoke Moran. Holmes considers them alongside the gipsies, the dying woman’s words, and the other clues, but their meaning remains unresolved in this unit.

records.l: the dying woman’s words, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The dying woman’s words include an allusion to a band. Holmes treats this allusion, together with the nocturnal whistles and the presence of the gipsies, as a possible clue to the mystery.

records.l: the poker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott seizes the poker and bends it into a curve with his hands before throwing it into the fireplace. After Roylott leaves, Holmes straightens the poker again and remarks that his own grip is not much weaker.

records.l: the dummy bell-rope, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The bell-rope beside the bed in the middle bedroom appears to communicate with the housekeeper’s room, but Holmes discovers that it is a dummy and is not attached to a wire. It is fastened to a hook just above the opening for the ventilator.

records.l: the ventilator, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The ventilator in the middle bedroom opens into Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room rather than to the outside air. Holmes considers this unusual construction, which was installed around the same time as the dummy bell-rope, significant.

records.l: the shutters, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: Holmes examines the shutters of Helen’s room and finds that they cannot be forced open when barred. Their iron hinges are firmly built into the masonry, and there is no opening through which a knife could raise the bar.

records.l: the dog lash, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: A small dog lash hangs in Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room with its end curled and tied into a loop of whipcord. Holmes considers the unusual knot significant and becomes visibly grim after examining it.

records.l: the examination of Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
records.s: The examination of Stoke Moran includes an inspection of the mansion’s exterior, windows, shutters, bedrooms, bell-rope, ventilator, safe, saucer of milk, chair, and dog lash. The findings give Holmes stronger grounds to suspect Dr. Grimesby Roylott and lead him to plan a nighttime investigation.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigate the suspicious bedroom at Stoke Moran Manor House and wait through the night for Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s attempted murder. Holmes identifies the ventilator, dummy bell-rope, and clamped bed as parts of a method for sending a snake into the bed. When Holmes attacks the snake with his cane, it turns on Dr. Grimesby Roylott, who dies from its bite. Holmes and Watson then secure the swamp adder and take Miss Stoner to safety.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Sherlock Holmes deduces that the ventilator, dummy bell-rope, and clamped bed form a route for a snake to reach the bed. During the vigil, he attacks the snake with his cane, causing it to turn on Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and afterward explains how he reconstructed the murder scheme.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Stoke Moran Manor House despite the danger. He keeps watch through the night, carries his revolver, witnesses Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s death, and helps Holmes remove Miss Stoner to safety.

records.l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott uses a snake, the ventilator, and the dummy bell-rope to attack the occupant of the bedroom. After Sherlock Holmes strikes at the snake, it turns upon him, and Dr. Grimesby Roylott dies within ten seconds of being bitten.

records.l: Helen Stoner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Miss Stoner is the intended victim of Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s snake-poison murder scheme. After Roylott’s death, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson convey her by morning train to the care of her good aunt at Harrow.

records.l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Miss Stoner's sister had reported that she could smell Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s cigar, which led Sherlock Holmes to deduce that a communication existed between the two bedrooms. She died after being exposed to the murder method.

records.l: Stoke Moran Manor House, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: Stoke Moran Manor House contains the connected bedrooms, ventilator, dummy bell-rope, clamped bed, and Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson enter its grounds and investigate it during the night.

records.l: the swamp adder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The swamp adder is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the deadly snake used by Dr. Grimesby Roylott. After biting Roylott, it is removed with a dog-whip and locked in the iron safe.

records.l: the ventilator, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The ventilator is a small opening connecting the bedroom to Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room. Roylott uses it to send the snake toward the bed, and Sherlock Holmes attacks the snake when it emerges through it.

records.l: the dummy bell-rope, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The dummy bell-rope hangs beside the bed but is not connected to a bell. Sherlock Holmes concludes that it serves as a bridge for the snake passing from the ventilator to the bed.

records.l: the clamped bed, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The clamped bed is fastened to the floor so that it cannot be moved. Its fixed position keeps it aligned with the ventilator and the dummy bell-rope.

records.l: the iron safe, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The iron safe in Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room contains the snake. After removing the swamp adder from Roylott, Sherlock Holmes places it back inside and closes the safe.

records.l: the speckled band, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The yellow speckled band appears around Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s head after his death. Sherlock Holmes identifies it as the swamp adder rearing from among Roylott’s hair.

records.l: the snake-poison murder scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The snake-poison murder scheme uses the ventilator, dummy bell-rope, clamped bed, whistle, and a trained snake to attack the bedroom occupant. Dr. Grimesby Roylott sends the snake through the ventilator and later recalls it by whistle, while the poison causes rapid death and would be difficult to detect.

records.l: the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
records.s: The death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott occurs when the snake he used against the bedroom occupant turns upon him after Sherlock Holmes strikes at it. The official inquiry concludes that he died while indiscreetly playing with a dangerous pet.
