records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Dr. John Watson introduces the strange case of Victor Hatherley, a hydraulic engineer whose thumb was hacked off during a secret nighttime commission near Eyford. Hatherley comes to Watson after traveling from Paddington, and Watson treats the severe injury before taking him to Sherlock Holmes. Hatherley explains that Colonel Lysander Stark hired him for fifty guineas to inspect a defective hydraulic press at a secluded country property. Stark claimed that the press was being used to process a valuable deposit of fuller’s-earth and demanded absolute secrecy about the visit.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Dr. John Watson receives Victor Hatherley at his home after a Paddington guard brings him there. He treats Hatherley’s missing thumb, recognizes that the injury resulted from a murderous attack, and takes Hatherley to Sherlock Holmes for help.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Watson and Hatherley at his Baker Street rooms, gives Hatherley food, brandy, and a place to rest, and listens as Hatherley begins recounting his strange experience.

records.l: Victor Hatherley, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Victor Hatherley is a young, orphaned, unmarried hydraulic engineer living alone in London. After accepting a highly paid secret commission from Colonel Lysander Stark, he travels to Eyford and returns with his thumb torn or hacked off.

records.l: Colonel Lysander Stark, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Colonel Lysander Stark hires Victor Hatherley for fifty guineas to inspect a hydraulic stamping machine at a secluded property near Eyford. He questions Hatherley closely about secrecy and claims that the machine is connected with processing fuller’s-earth.

records.l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: London is where Victor Hatherley lives and maintains professional chambers in Victoria Street. He travels from London to Eyford by a late train after accepting Colonel Lysander Stark’s commission.

records.l: Eyford, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Eyford is a small place in Berkshire near the Oxfordshire border and within seven miles of Reading. Colonel Lysander Stark directs Hatherley to meet him there at about 11:15, after which they are to travel seven miles by carriage to the country property.

records.l: hydraulic engineering, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Victor Hatherley works as a hydraulic engineer and has seven years of experience gained through an apprenticeship to Venner & Matheson. His professional expertise is the reason Colonel Lysander Stark seeks his opinion about a hydraulic stamping machine.

records.l: fuller’s-earth, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Fuller’s-earth is described as a valuable product found in only one or two places in England. Stark claims to have discovered a deposit on his land near Reading, linked to larger deposits on neighboring properties.

records.l: the hydraulic machine, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: The hydraulic press at Stark’s property is said to have become defective and is the stated subject of Hatherley’s inspection. Stark claims that the press is used to compress fuller’s-earth into bricks for removal.

records.l: the narrator's thumb injury, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Hatherley’s thumb has been hacked or torn out from the root by an instrument like a cleaver. Watson cleans and dresses the wound, which has bled heavily, and Hatherley travels to Holmes with four fingers remaining and a red, spongy surface where the thumb was.

records.l: the murderous attack on Hatherley, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Hatherley states that his injury was not an accident but the result of a very murderous attack. He fainted when the injury occurred and later tied his handkerchief tightly around his wrist and braced it with a twig to control the bleeding.

records.l: Hatherley’s commission at Eyford, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Hatherley accepts Colonel Lysander Stark’s offer of fifty guineas for a nighttime professional opinion about a hydraulic stamping machine. Although he is uneasy about Stark’s manner, the secrecy, and the late hour, he travels to Eyford as agreed.

records.l: the fuller’s-earth mining operation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Stark claims that he and his associates are secretly working a small deposit of fuller’s-earth in order to earn enough money to purchase neighboring fields containing larger deposits. He says they erected a hydraulic press to assist their operations and compress the earth into bricks.

records.l: professional secrecy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB
records.s: Colonel Lysander Stark demands absolute and complete secrecy from Hatherley before, during, and after the commission, including no reference to the matter in speech or writing. He says secrecy is necessary because knowledge of the operation could expose the fuller’s-earth deposits and ruin their chance of buying the neighboring fields.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: The narrator travels from Eyford to a secluded residence where Colonel Lysander Stark and Mr. Ferguson ask him to inspect a powerful hydraulic press. After discovering a leaking cylinder and realizing that the fuller’s-earth explanation is false, the narrator is locked inside the press as Stark activates it. Elise secretly helps him escape, but Stark attacks him with a cleaver and cuts off his thumb as he climbs from a window. The narrator reaches the road near Eyford railway station by morning and reports the adventure to Holmes.

records.l: the narrator, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: The narrator travels by train to Eyford and is taken by carriage to Colonel Lysander Stark’s residence. He examines Stark’s machine, is trapped inside the hydraulic press, escapes with Elise’s help, and returns to the vicinity of Eyford railway station after suffering a severe injury to his thumb.

records.l: Colonel Lysander Stark, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: Colonel Lysander Stark meets the narrator at Eyford railway station and transports him to the Stark residence. He asks the narrator to inspect the hydraulic press, then locks him inside it and activates it after learning that the narrator suspects the fuller’s-earth explanation is false. Stark pursues the narrator with a cleaver and cuts off his thumb as he escapes through a window.

records.l: Elise, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: Elise warns the narrator to leave the Stark residence before it is too late. She opens a concealed panel to save him from the hydraulic press and leads him toward a bedroom and window, then tries to restrain Stark and prevent him from attacking the narrator.

records.l: Eyford, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: The narrator reaches Eyford by train and is told that the Stark residence lies roughly ten miles away. After escaping, he returns to the vicinity of Eyford and takes the morning train to Reading.

records.l: Eyford railway station, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: The narrator arrives at the little, dim-lit Eyford railway station after eleven o’clock and is the only passenger to leave the train. The same porter is on duty when he returns in the morning, but the porter has not heard of Colonel Lysander Stark or seen a carriage waiting for the narrator.

records.l: the Stark residence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “At Reading I had to change not only my carriage but my station.
records.s: The residence is a dark, silent, isolated old house with barred shutters, neglected upper corridors, and concealed passages. records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives a letter from Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon asking for help concerning the painful events surrounding his wedding. Dr. John Watson reviews newspaper reports showing that St. Simon married Miss Hatty Doran, the daughter of the wealthy Aloysius Doran, at a quiet ceremony. Hatty Doran disappeared during the wedding breakfast after a woman identified as Miss Flora Millar caused a disturbance outside the house. Holmes and Watson prepare to investigate the disappearance as Lord St. Simon is expected to arrive.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives a letter from Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon requesting his judgment and discretion concerning the events surrounding the wedding. He reviews newspaper reports with Dr. John Watson and begins preparing to investigate Hatty Doran's disappearance.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Dr. John Watson remains at home with an injured leg and reviews newspaper reports about Lord St. Simon's marriage and the bride's disappearance. He reads the reports aloud to Sherlock Holmes and agrees to remain as a witness during the forthcoming consultation.

records.l: Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon, the second son of the Duke of Balmoral, marries Miss Hatty Doran. After she disappears during the wedding breakfast, he contacts Sherlock Holmes for assistance, while Mr. Lestrade of Scotland Yard is already acting in the matter.

records.l: Miss Hatty Doran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Miss Hatty Doran, the only daughter of Aloysius Doran, marries Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon in a quiet ceremony at St. George's, Hanover Square. At the wedding breakfast she complains of sudden indisposition, goes to her room, takes an ulster and bonnet, and leaves the house without explanation.

records.l: Aloysius Doran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Aloysius Doran, a wealthy man from San Francisco, is the father of Miss Hatty Doran and has taken a furnished house at Lancaster Gate for the wedding party. After learning that his daughter has disappeared, he joins Lord St. Simon in contacting the police.

records.l: Flora Millar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Miss Flora Millar, formerly a danseuse at the Allegro, causes a disturbance by trying to enter the house after the wedding party and claiming to have some claim upon Lord St. Simon. She is arrested because the police suspect that jealousy or another motive may connect her with the bride's disappearance.

records.l: the wedding of Lord St. Simon and Hatty Doran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: The wedding takes place at St. George's, Hanover Square, with only a small group of relatives and friends present. The party then proceeds to Aloysius Doran's house at Lancaster Gate for breakfast, but the occasion is disrupted by Miss Flora Millar and Hatty Doran's subsequent disappearance.

records.l: Lady St. Simon’s disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: Hatty Doran disappears during the wedding breakfast after briefly retiring to her room. She leaves the house wearing an ulster and bonnet, and the police begin energetic inquiries while newspapers report rumors of foul play.

records.l: the wedding breakfast, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR
records.s: The wedding breakfast is held at Aloysius Doran's house after the ceremony. During it, Miss Flora Millar's attempted intrusion has already caused a painful scene, and Hatty Doran leaves after complaining of sudden indisposition.

records.s: Lord Robert St. Simon consults Sherlock Holmes about the disappearance of his bride, Hatty Doran, shortly after their wedding in London. He describes Hatty’s independent, impetuous character, her dowry, her strange agitation after the ceremony, and her departure from the breakfast-room with her maid Alice’s assistance. He also reports that Hatty was later seen walking in Hyde Park with Flora Millar, who had threatened Hatty after the wedding. Holmes concludes that he has solved the case, though he does not yet reveal where Hatty is.

records.s: Lord Robert St. Simon consults Sherlock Holmes about his bride’s disappearance. He describes Hatty Doran as a wealthy American mining heiress with a wild, fearless, impetuous nature, and admits that Flora Millar had previously been on a very friendly footing with him.

records.s: Hatty Doran marries Lord Robert St. Simon but leaves her father’s house shortly afterward. She is described as a wealthy, independent, tomboyish woman who became agitated after dropping her bouquet at the wedding and later departed wearing an ulster and bonnet; she was subsequently seen walking in Hyde Park with Flora Millar.

records.s: Alice is Hatty Doran’s American maid from California. After the wedding, she speaks with Hatty, helps cover Hatty’s bridal dress with a long ulster, and reports that Hatty put on a bonnet and went out.

records.s: Flora Millar had been on a very friendly footing with Lord Robert St. Simon and was devotedly attached to him. She threatened Hatty after learning of the marriage, caused a disturbance at Mr. Doran’s house, was pushed out by police, and was later seen walking with Hatty in Hyde Park; she is taken into custody.

records.s: Lestrade of Scotland Yard considers it serious that Hatty was seen walking with Flora Millar. He appears at Sherlock Holmes’s rooms after Lord Robert St. Simon’s interview.

records.s: The case concerns Hatty Doran’s disappearance immediately after her wedding to Lord Robert St. Simon. Holmes gathers details about her conduct, Alice’s account, Flora Millar’s involvement, and the circumstances at the breakfast-table before declaring that he has solved it.

records.s: The wedding takes place quietly in London because Lord Robert St. Simon fears that Flora Millar may cause a scandal. Hatty appears cheerful before and during the ceremony, but after dropping her bouquet into a pew she becomes abruptly agitated and later leaves the wedding breakfast.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes solves the St. Simon marriage case by identifying Lady St. Simon as an American woman who had previously married Francis Hay Moulton and left the wedding when she saw him alive. Inspector Lestrade mistakes the abandoned wedding clothes and a note for evidence that Flora Millar abducted or killed her, but Holmes uses the note’s initials and a hotel-bill fragment to find the couple at Gordon Square. Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton explains that Francis had been presumed dead after being captured by Apaches, while she had agreed to marry Lord St. Simon. Holmes brings the Moultons and Lord St. Simon together, though Lord St. Simon leaves angrily after learning that the marriage has been abandoned.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: Sherlock Holmes quickly concludes that Lady St. Simon is not dead and eventually reveals that she is a myth under that name. He deduces that she saw an American from her past at the wedding, identifies Francis Hay Moulton through the initials and hotel-bill fragment, finds the couple at 226 Gordon Square, and brings them before Lord St. Simon.

records.s: Dr. Watson witnesses Lestrade’s presentation of the evidence, receives the Moultons with Holmes, and hears Holmes explain the solution. He observes that Lord St. Simon is not gracious after losing both his bride and her fortune.

records.s: Flora Millar is wrongly suspected by Lestrade of decoying Lady St. Simon away and causing her disappearance. The note’s initials appear to support his theory, but the unit provides no evidence that Flora Millar was involved.

records.s: Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton explains that she had married Francis years earlier and believed him dead after an Apache attack. At the St. Simon wedding she saw Francis alive, abandoned the ceremony, followed him from the house, and went with him to Gordon Square.

records.s: Francis Hay Moulton had been engaged to the woman who became Mrs. Moulton, secretly married her, and left to make his fortune. After surviving captivity among the Apaches, he followed her to England, appeared at her second wedding, and took her to lodgings in Gordon Square.

records.s: The Serpentine is searched because Lestrade thinks Lady St. Simon’s body may be near the wedding clothes found floating by its margin. Holmes dismisses this idea and explains that the clothes were discarded to prevent the newly reunited couple from being traced.

records.s: Gordon Square is the location of lodgings taken by Francis Hay Moulton and later the place where Holmes finds the couple. Their letters were to be forwarded to 226 Gordon Square.

records.l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: London is where the St. Simon wedding, the investigation, the hotel stay, and the Moultons’ reunion take place. Holmes traces Francis Hay Moulton through London hotels and locates him at Gordon Square.

records.l: the St. Simon marriage case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: The St. Simon marriage case concerns the bride’s disappearance immediately after her wedding to Lord St. Simon. Holmes resolves it as a case of a woman abandoning the ceremony after discovering that her presumed-dead first husband was alive.

records.l: Lady St. Simon’s disappearance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: Lady St. Simon’s disappearance results from her leaving the wedding breakfast and following Francis Hay Moulton. She is not dead or abducted; she has gone with her earlier husband to Gordon Square.

records.s: At the St. Simon wedding, the bride is willing to marry Lord St. Simon until she sees Francis Hay Moulton in the first pew. She secretly receives his note, leaves the wedding party, and follows him from the house.

records.l: the earlier Moulton marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: The earlier Moulton marriage was secretly arranged and performed in America before Francis Hay Moulton left to seek his fortune. Mrs. Moulton believed Francis had died, but their marriage remains the prior claim that leads her to abandon the St. Simon wedding.

records.l: the wedding clothes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: The wedding clothes consist of a watered-silk dress, white satin shoes, a bride’s wreath and veil, and a new wedding ring. They are found floating near the Serpentine, and Francis explains that he discarded them so that the couple would not be traced.

records.l: the note from Francis Hay Moulton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: The note from Francis Hay Moulton asks the bride to meet him when all is ready and bears the initials F. H. M. Lestrade mistakes it for evidence against Flora Millar, while Holmes recognizes that the initials identify Francis Hay Moulton.

records.l: the hotel bill fragment, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: The hotel bill fragment lists expensive London charges for a room, breakfast, a cocktail, lunch, and sherry. Holmes uses its prices to identify a select hotel and matches its entries to Francis H. Moulton, who had recently left with his letters forwarded to Gordon Square.

records.l: Holmes’s investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which
records.s: Holmes’s investigation begins with the facts that the bride willingly entered the ceremony but changed her mind within minutes. By reasoning that she must have seen an influential American, then connecting the note’s initials and the hotel bill to Francis Hay Moulton, Holmes finds the couple and establishes what happened.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Alexander Holder, senior partner of Holder & Stevenson, comes to Sherlock Holmes in great distress after the Beryl Coronet, left with him as security for a £50,000 advance, is damaged at Holder's house. Holder believes he caught his son Arthur handling and trying to wrench the coronet, with one gold corner and three beryls missing. Arthur denies stealing anything and refuses to explain himself after Holder threatens to call the police. The household includes Holder, Arthur, his niece Mary, several servants, and the absent influence of Arthur's friend Sir George Burnwell.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Alexander Holder at Baker Street and calms him after Holder arrives in extreme distress. He listens to Holder's detailed account of the coronet, the loan, and the events at Holder's house.

records.l: Mr. Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Alexander Holder is the senior partner of Holder & Stevenson and the guardian of the Beryl Coronet after accepting it as security for a £50,000 loan. He takes the coronet from the bank to his house, locks it in his dressing-room bureau, and later sees Arthur holding the damaged coronet. Holder accuses Arthur of theft and threatens to involve the police.

records.l: Arthur Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Arthur Holder is Alexander Holder's only son, whom Alexander describes as wild, financially irresponsible, and heavily influenced by gambling and expensive companions. He asks Alexander for £200, is refused, and is later found beside the coronet holding and apparently wrenching or bending it. Arthur denies that any jewels are missing and refuses to explain further after being called a thief.

records.l: Mary Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Mary Holder is Alexander Holder's niece and adopted daughter, whom he describes as gentle, capable, and his right hand in the household. She has twice refused Arthur's marriage proposals, notices that Lucy Parr has returned through the back door, and checks that the house is secured.

records.l: Sir George Burnwell, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Sir George Burnwell is Arthur Holder's older friend and a man whose influence repeatedly draws Arthur back into dangerous company. Alexander Holder admires Burnwell's charm but distrusts his cynical speech and the look in his eyes.

records.l: Holder & Stevenson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Holder & Stevenson is the banking firm in Threadneedle Street of which Alexander Holder is senior partner. The firm makes loans against valuable property and agrees to advance £50,000 against the Beryl Coronet.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes receives Alexander Holder. Holder reaches it from the Metropolitan Station after traveling by Underground and hurrying through the snow.

records.l: the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: The Beryl Coronet is described as a magnificent and nationally important piece of jewellery containing thirty-nine enormous beryls and valuable gold chasing. It is left with Alexander Holder as security for a loan, carried to his house, and later found with one gold corner and three beryls missing.

records.l: Fairbank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Holder's house at Streatham contains the coronet overnight after Alexander carries it there from the bank. Alexander locks it in his dressing-room bureau, while members of the household and servants remain in or move through the house.

records.l: the coronet loan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: The coronet loan is arranged when a prominent unnamed client leaves the Beryl Coronet with Alexander Holder as security for money. The client promises to repay the advance in four days and collect the coronet personally on Monday morning.

records.l: the damage to the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: The damage consists of one gold corner being torn or removed, along with the three beryls set in it. Alexander Holder sees Arthur holding the coronet and apparently trying to wrench or bend it when the damage is discovered.

records.l: the alleged theft of the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Alexander Holder alleges that Arthur stole three jewels from the coronet after finding him beside it at night. Arthur denies the theft and says that no jewels are missing, but he refuses to provide further information.

records.l: the public scandal, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: Alexander Holder believes that any harm to the Beryl Coronet would cause a great public scandal because it is regarded as a national possession. He fears that the damage will bring public disgrace upon him and affect the noblest people in the land.

records.l: the £50,000 advance, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: An unnamed exalted client asks Holder & Stevenson for a £50,000 advance, promising repayment the following Monday with interest. Alexander Holder orders his cashier to pay the client fifty £1,000 notes against the Beryl Coronet as security.

records.l: the Holder family, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
records.s: The Holder family household consists of the widowed Alexander Holder, his son Arthur, and his niece and adopted daughter Mary, along with several servants. Arthur is financially troubled and influenced by Sir George Burnwell, while Mary manages the household and has rejected Arthur's proposals of marriage.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: The narrator calls the police after Arthur is found with the ruined coronet, and the investigation becomes a public matter because the coronet is national property. Arthur asks to leave, but the narrator refuses and has him arrested after he will not explain what he did with the three missing stones. Searches of Arthur, his room, and the house find no trace of the gems, while Arthur remains silent. The narrator seeks help because he has lost his honour, the gems, and his son.

records.s: The narrator calls the police, places the investigation in their hands, and insists that the law should proceed. He questions and pleads with Arthur to reveal the location of the missing stones, then has him taken into custody when he refuses. The narrator offers a reward of £1000 and seeks help in solving the matter.

records.l: Arthur Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: Arthur stands sullenly with his arms folded and asks whether the narrator intends to charge him with theft. He refuses to explain what he did with the three missing stones and remains silent despite persuasion and threats. He is arrested, searched, and removed to a cell.

records.l: the police, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: The police are called to investigate the ruined coronet and Arthur's alleged theft. They search Arthur, his room, and every part of the house where the gems might have been hidden, but find no trace of them. They later admit that they cannot currently make anything of the case.

records.l: the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: The coronet is found ruined, with three stones missing. The narrator states that it is national property, making the matter public rather than private.

records.l: investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: The investigation is placed in the hands of the police after the narrator calls them. It includes searches of Arthur and the house, but it does not locate the missing gems, and the police cannot presently solve the matter.

records.l: the alleged theft of the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: Arthur is questioned about whether he will be charged with theft. The narrator treats the matter as a public theft because the ruined coronet is national property, and Arthur is taken into custody.

records.l: missing stones (the coronet), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: Three stones are missing from the coronet. The narrator urges Arthur to disclose where the beryls are, but searches reveal nothing and Arthur refuses to speak about them.

records.l: narrator's honour, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in
records.s: The narrator says that his honour is at stake along with the honour of someone far greater than himself. He reports that he has lost his honour, the gems, and his son in one night.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes sits silently for several minutes. His brows are knitted, and his eyes remain fixed upon the fire.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes sat silent for some few minutes, with his brows knitted
records.s: Sherlock Holmes sits silent for some few minutes with his brows knitted. He keeps his eyes fixed upon the fire.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the theft of three gems from Mr. Holder’s coronet and challenges the belief that Arthur Holder stole them. At Fairbank in Streatham, Holmes studies the house, the damaged coronet, the bureau, and the surrounding grounds, then conducts further inquiries in disguise. He recovers the three stolen gems and tells Mr. Holder that Arthur is innocent, while Mary Holder leaves a note saying she is departing forever. Holmes also reveals that Arthur already knows the truth but had refused to explain the incident.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. Holder and Mary Holder, inspects Fairbank and the coronet, and notices that breaking off the missing section would require great force and make a loud noise. He investigates in disguise, recovers the three stolen gems, and tells Mr. Holder that Arthur Holder is innocent.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Mr. Holder to Fairbank, observes the investigation, and remains unaware of Holmes’s conclusions until the matter is explained. He later records Mr. Holder’s visit and Holmes’s recovery of the gems.

records.l: Mr. Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Mr. Holder believes he saw Arthur Holder holding the coronet and initially regards this as proof of Arthur’s guilt. After Sherlock Holmes recovers the three gems, Mr. Holder pays for them, rejoices at being saved, and learns that he owes Arthur an apology.

records.l: Arthur Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Arthur Holder is imprisoned after Mr. Holder sees him holding the coronet, but he remains silent about why he was in the dressing-room. Sherlock Holmes concludes that Arthur did not take the gems, and Arthur later confirms Holmes’s account after Holmes has explained the case to him.

records.l: Mary Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Mary Holder insists that Arthur Holder is innocent and asks Mr. Holder to have him liberated. After Mr. Holder says that Arthur might have been saved if he had married her, Mary leaves Fairbank and writes that she will not be happy under his roof and that he should not search for her.

records.l: Fairbank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Fairbank is Mr. Holder’s modest white-stone residence in Streatham. It has a front carriage-sweep, a tradesmen’s path, a stable lane, a garden, and the dressing-room where the coronet was kept.

records.l: Streatham, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Streatham is the southern suburb where Fairbank is located. Sherlock Holmes travels there with Watson and Mr. Holder to examine the house and its surroundings.

records.l: the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: The coronet is kept in a case inside a bureau in Mr. Holder’s dressing-room. It has thirty-six remaining gems and a cracked edge where a corner holding three gems was torn away; Holmes determines that removing such a corner would normally make a loud noise.

records.l: missing stones (the coronet), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: The gems are part of Mr. Holder’s coronet, and three of them disappear while thirty-six remain in the damaged coronet. Sherlock Holmes recovers the missing three and returns them to Mr. Holder.

records.l: the alleged theft of the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: The stolen coronet gems are the three gems removed with a triangular piece of gold from the coronet. Sherlock Holmes finds them during his investigation and gives them to Mr. Holder in exchange for a £4,000 check.

records.l: the investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: The investigation begins with questions about the household, the noise heard during the night, the locked windows and doors, and possible routes into the house. Sherlock Holmes examines the grounds, the lower windows, the bureau, and the coronet, then continues investigating in disguise before recovering the stolen gems.

records.l: Arthur's imprisonment, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Arthur's imprisonment follows Mr. Holder’s accusation after he sees Arthur holding the coronet. Sherlock Holmes maintains that Arthur is innocent and tells Mr. Holder that Arthur deserves an apology.

records.l: Mary's departure, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Mary's departure occurs after she leaves a note for Mr. Holder saying that she has brought trouble upon him and cannot remain happy under his roof. She asks him not to search for her and says that her future is provided for.

records.l: Arthur's guilt or innocence, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “Do you receive much company?” he asked.
records.s: Arthur's guilt or innocence is disputed because Mr. Holder saw him holding the coronet, while Arthur offers no explanation. Sherlock Holmes concludes that Arthur is innocent, later tells Arthur how he believes the events occurred, and receives Arthur’s confirmation.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Mr. Holder that Mary secretly aided Sir George Burnwell in stealing the coronet, then fled with him. Arthur discovered the theft, pursued Sir George through the snow, recovered most of the coronet, and was wrongly suspected by his father. Holmes reconstructed the events from footprints and other evidence, identified Sir George, recovered the missing gems from a receiver, and prevented a public prosecution. Mr. Holder learns that Mary and Sir George are together and that Arthur acted to protect her.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reconstructs the coronet theft from footprints, blood, window marks, and other evidence. He disguises himself as a loafer, identifies Sir George Burnwell through his valet and cast-off shoes, confronts him, and recovers the missing gems without a prosecution.

records.l: Mr. Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Mr. Holder learns that Mary betrayed him with Sir George Burnwell and that Arthur was innocent of stealing the coronet. He regrets misjudging Arthur and prepares to apologize to him, while grieving over Mary's flight.

records.l: Mary Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Mary secretly meets Sir George Burnwell at the hall window and tells him about the coronet. She brings it to him, faints when the coronet is recovered, and flees with Sir George.

records.l: Arthur Holder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Arthur sees Mary take the coronet from Mr. Holder's dressing-room and pass it through the hall window. He pursues Sir George barefoot, struggles with him, recovers the coronet, and keeps Mary's involvement secret to protect her.

records.l: Sir George Burnwell, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Sir George Burnwell is identified as a ruined gambler and dangerous villain who manipulates Mary into helping steal the coronet. Arthur wounds him during the struggle, and Holmes later forces him to reveal that he sold the three missing stones to a receiver.

records.l: Fairbank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Holder's house contains the dressing-room from which Mary takes the coronet and the hall window through which it is handed outside. Holmes examines the house and its surroundings for evidence of the theft.

records.l: the hall window of Holder's house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The hall window is where Mary hands the coronet to Sir George and where Arthur later exits and re-enters during the pursuit. Holmes finds evidence on its sill and framework that someone passed through it.

records.l: the stable lane, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The stable lane preserves tracks showing that Sir George waited outside the hall window and that Arthur followed him barefoot. Farther down the lane, the snow shows where the two men struggled and where blood fell.

records.l: the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The coronet is taken from Mr. Holder's dressing-room and handed through the hall window to Sir George. Arthur recovers it during the struggle, but it is twisted and missing three gems until Holmes later retrieves them.

records.l: missing stones (the coronet), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The missing gems are retained by Sir George after the struggle and sold by him to a receiver for six hundred pounds each. Holmes buys them back for one thousand pounds apiece.

records.l: Sir George Burnwell's cast-off shoes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Holmes buys Sir George Burnwell's cast-off shoes from his valet for six shillings. He uses them at Streatham and confirms that they exactly fit the boot tracks in the stable lane.

records.l: the snow, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The snow preserves the impressions because no new snow has fallen and a strong frost has hardened it. Its tracks reveal Sir George's movements, Arthur's barefoot pursuit, the struggle, and the blood left by the injured man.

records.l: the alleged theft of the Beryl Coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The coronet theft is carried out by Mary and Sir George Burnwell, with Mary taking the coronet from the dressing-room and handing it to him. Arthur discovers the theft and recovers the coronet, while Holmes establishes the truth and retrieves the missing gems.

records.l: the struggle over the coronet, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Arthur catches Sir George in the stable lane, and they pull against each other from opposite sides of the coronet. Arthur strikes Sir George over the eye, and the coronet is twisted as a piece breaks away.

records.l: Mary and Sir George Burnwell's flight, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Mary and Sir George Burnwell flee together after the theft. Holmes concludes that Mary is wherever Sir George is and says that her sins will soon receive sufficient punishment.

records.l: the investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: The investigation follows physical evidence at the house and in the snow, including footprints, blood, and marks on the hall window. Holmes supplements this work by questioning Sir George's valet, buying the cast-off shoes, confronting Sir George, and locating the receiver.

records.l: the public scandal, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”
records.s: Holmes avoids a prosecution because exposing the theft would create a serious public scandal for Mr. Holder's family. Mr. Holder says that Holmes's actions have saved England from such a scandal.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson meet Violet Hunter at Baker Street after she seeks advice about an unusually well-paid governess position at the Copper Beeches in Hampshire. Jep hro Rucastle and his wife offer Violet Hunter £120 a year, require her to obey unusual instructions, wear an electric-blue dress, and cut her hair short. Holmes cannot determine the reason for the conditions but warns that the household may be dangerous and promises help by telegram. Two weeks later, Violet Hunter sends an urgent telegram asking Holmes and Watson to meet her at the Black Swan Hotel in Winchester.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Violet Hunter at Baker Street and examines her account of the governess position at the Copper Beeches. He considers the high salary and unusual conditions suspicious, warns that the household may be dangerous, and promises to help if she sends a telegram. When her telegram arrives, he postpones his chemical research and plans to travel with Dr. John Watson to Winchester.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Dr. John Watson is with Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street when Violet Hunter seeks advice. He records the interview and agrees to accompany Holmes to Winchester after Violet Hunter sends an urgent telegram.

records.l: Violet Hunter, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Violet Hunter, an unemployed governess, asks Sherlock Holmes whether she should accept a position with Jep hro Rucastle. Although the position requires unusual obedience, an electric-blue dress, and short hair, she accepts it because of the high salary. Two weeks later, she sends an urgent telegram asking Holmes to come to Winchester because she is at her wit's end.

records.l: Mr. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Jep hro Rucastle offers Violet Hunter a governess position at the Copper Beeches with a salary of £120 a year. He describes unusual household requirements, including wearing a particular dress, sitting where indicated, and cutting her hair short, and says that his wife wants these conditions.

records.l: Mrs. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Mrs. Rucastle is described by Jep hro Rucastle as being fond of unusual household requirements. She supposedly wants Violet Hunter to wear an electric-blue dress, sit where directed, and cut her hair short.

records.l: Edward Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Rucastle's son is described as a six-year-old child whose care would be one of Violet Hunter's duties. Jep hro Rucastle says that the child amuses himself by killing cockroaches with a slipper.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson discuss Violet Hunter's case at Baker Street and decide to travel together to Winchester. They plan to take the train arriving at 11:30 and meet Violet at the Black Swan Hotel.

records.l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson sit after breakfast and receive Violet Hunter. Holmes later receives and reads her urgent telegram there.

records.l: Hampshire, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Hampshire is the county where Jep hro Rucastle says he lives. The Copper Beeches is described as being five miles beyond Winchester in Hampshire.

records.l: the Copper Beeches, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: The Copper Beeches is Jep hro Rucastle's country house near Winchester in Hampshire. It is the location of the unusually well-paid governess position offered to Violet Hunter.

records.l: Winchester, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Winchester is the nearest named destination to the Copper Beeches. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson arrange to travel there after receiving Violet Hunter's telegram.

records.l: Black Swan Hotel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: The Black Swan Hotel in Winchester is the meeting place specified in Violet Hunter's urgent telegram. She asks Sherlock Holmes to be there at midday the following day.

records.l: the governess position at the Copper Beeches, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: The governess position at the Copper Beeches offers Violet Hunter £120 a year, far more than the usual salary she describes. Its duties include caring for one child and obeying Mrs. Rucastle's proper commands, including unusual instructions about dress, seating, and hair.

records.l: wire (the telegram to Mr. Holmes), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Violet Hunter's telegram asks Sherlock Holmes to meet her at the Black Swan Hotel in Winchester at midday the next day. She says that she is at her wit's end and urges him to come.

records.l: Violet Hunter's letter from Jep hro Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Violet Hunter's letter from Jep hro Rucastle offers her £30 a quarter and urges her to reconsider the governess position. It explains that she should wear an electric-blue dress indoors, may sit or amuse herself as directed, and is expected to cut her hair short.

records.l: the Adventure of the Copper Beeches, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches concerns Violet Hunter's unusual prospective employment with Jep hro Rucastle and the unexplained conditions attached to it. It begins with Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson discussing the case at Baker Street and preparing to investigate after Violet Hunter's urgent telegram.

records.l: the electric-blue dress, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: The electric-blue dress is a particular shade of clothing that Mrs. Rucastle supposedly wants Violet Hunter to wear indoors in the morning. Jep hro Rucastle says that a dress belonging to his daughter Alice, who is in Philadelphia, should fit her.

records.l: Violet Hunter's hair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES
records.s: Violet Hunter's hair is long, luxuriant, and chestnut-colored, and she initially refuses to cut it for the position. After receiving Jep hro Rucastle's increased offer, she decides to sacrifice it and cut it before starting work.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to Winchester to meet Miss Hunter, who seeks advice about strange events at the Copper Beeches. Miss Hunter describes the Rucastle household, including Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle, their child, the servants Toller and his wife, and the dangerous mastiff Carlo. She explains that after her haircut she is repeatedly dressed in a blue dress and made to sit facing away from the window while Mr. Rucastle entertains her. She also reports finding a duplicate of her hair in a locked drawer and entering a forbidden suite, where a barricaded central room contains an unseen person or thing.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. Watson to Winchester to investigate Miss Hunter's appeal for help. He listens closely to her account and says that he has devised seven possible explanations for the facts known so far.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Dr. Watson travels with Sherlock Holmes to Winchester and records Miss Hunter's account. During the journey, he admires the countryside, while Holmes views its isolated houses as places where crimes might be committed with impunity.

records.l: Violet Hunter, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Miss Hunter meets Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson at The Black Swan to seek advice about the Rucastle household. She describes the strange treatment she has received, the duplicate hair in her locked drawer, and her frightening entry into the forbidden suite.

records.l: Mr. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Mr. Rucastle employs Miss Hunter and drives her from Winchester to the Copper Beeches. He is usually amiable, jovial, and boisterous, but he makes Miss Hunter wear a blue dress, sit facing away from the window, and entertain him; he also becomes angry when she approaches the forbidden suite.

records.l: Mrs. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Mrs. Rucastle is described as a pale, silent woman devoted to her husband and young son, though she often appears sorrowful and has been seen in tears. She helps direct the blue-dress performances, watches Miss Hunter closely, and has the blind drawn when the bearded man is seen outside.

records.l: Toller, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Toller is one of the two servants at the Copper Beeches. He is a rough, frequently drunken man who can control Carlo, works in the deserted suite, and is apparently responsible for leaving its key in the door while drunk.

records.l: Mr. Fowler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The bearded man in the Southampton Road is a small man in a grey suit who stands by the railings and looks earnestly toward Miss Hunter at the Copper Beeches. At Mrs. Rucastle's urging, Miss Hunter motions for him to go away, after which the blind is drawn and he is not seen again.

records.l: Carlo, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Carlo is Mr. Rucastle's mastiff, kept chained in an outhouse near the kitchen. He is fed sparingly, released every night by Toller, and is considered dangerous enough to threaten the life of anyone who crosses the grounds after dark.

records.l: the Copper Beeches, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The Copper Beeches is a large, square, whitewashed house near the Southampton high road, surrounded by grounds and woods. It contains the Rucastle household, a dangerous mastiff, and a deserted suite with a barricaded central room.

records.l: Winchester, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Winchester is the old English capital to which Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to meet Miss Hunter. Holmes says that if Miss Hunter lived in Winchester rather than five miles away in the countryside, he would not fear for her safety.

records.l: Black Swan Hotel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The Black Swan is a reputable inn in Winchester's High Street, near the station. Miss Hunter waits there in a private sitting-room with lunch prepared for Holmes and Watson.

records.l: Southampton Road, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The Southampton Road is an important highway about a hundred yards from the front door of the Copper Beeches. The bearded man stands beside its railings and looks toward the house.

records.l: the Rucastle household, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The Rucastle household includes Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle, their spoiled and cruel young son, the servants Toller and his wife, and Miss Hunter as governess. Miss Hunter finds the household unsettling despite receiving no direct physical ill-treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle.

records.l: the journey to Winchester, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: During the journey to Winchester, Sherlock Holmes initially reads the morning papers and then studies the spring countryside after passing the Hampshire border. Holmes and Dr. Watson discuss how isolated country houses may conceal crimes and learn that Miss Hunter is not personally trapped because she can leave for Winchester.

records.l: Miss Hunter's appeal for help, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Miss Hunter's appeal for help brings Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson to Winchester. She asks for their advice because she cannot understand the Rucastles' conduct and feels unsafe and uneasy at the Copper Beeches.

records.l: the haircut, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Miss Hunter cuts off her hair before or soon after arriving at the Copper Beeches. Mr. Rucastle says that the haircut has not harmed her appearance, and the cut hair later becomes part of the mystery when an identical coil is found in a locked drawer.

records.l: the blue-dress performances, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The blue-dress performances involve Miss Hunter changing into a particular dress, sitting with her back to the central window, and listening to Mr. Rucastle tell amusing stories or reading aloud. The performances occur more than once, and the Rucastles appear unusually eager for her to take part.

records.l: the electric-blue dress, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The electric-blue dress is a well-made but previously worn garment that fits Miss Hunter exactly. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle show exaggerated delight when she wears it during the performances by the window.

records.l: Violet Hunter's hair, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Miss Hunter keeps her cut hair in a coil at the bottom of her trunk. She later finds an identical coil in the locked lower drawer of an old chest, while her own hair remains in her trunk.

records.l: the locked drawer, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The locked lower drawer of an old chest in Miss Hunter's room opens with her first key. It contains a coil of hair identical in tint and thickness to Miss Hunter's own hair, creating an unexplained duplicate.

records.l: the forbidden suite, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The forbidden suite is an apparently uninhabited wing of the Copper Beeches that is normally kept locked. Miss Hunter enters it when Toller leaves the key in the door and finds two empty rooms and a barricaded central room.

records.l: the barricaded central room, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The barricaded central room in the forbidden suite has a locked door secured by an iron bed bar, a padlock, and stout cord. Light comes from beneath the door, and Miss Hunter sees a shadow and hears footsteps moving inside before fleeing in terror.

records.l: the mastiff, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The mastiff at the Copper Beeches is a huge, tawny dog with a black muzzle, hanging jowl, and large bones. It is kept hungry, released at night, and serves as a frightening guard against trespassers.

records.l: house (the Rucastles' house), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: The Rucastle house is a large, damp-stained, whitewashed building with grounds, woods on three sides, and the Southampton high road nearby. It contains the drawing-room where Miss Hunter performs for Mr. Rucastle and a concealed suite with a barricaded room.

records.l: crime in the countryside, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old
records.s: Sherlock Holmes believes that isolated country houses can conceal cruelty and wickedness for years because neighbours and the machinery of justice are farther away. He considers the countryside potentially more dangerous than London's poorest alleys.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The young lady tells Mr. Holmes that she entered the empty wing of the Rucastles' house and was confronted by a man who warned her never to cross its threshold again. She became frightened of the house and everyone in it, including the mastiff, and sent a wire asking Mr. Holmes for help. She returned safely after Toller became insensible from drink and has come to Winchester to seek Mr. Holmes's advice, though she must return before three o’clock to care for the child.

records.l: narrator (young lady), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The young lady explains to Mr. Holmes that she entered the empty wing, became frightened by its loneliness and eerie stillness, and was threatened when she came out. She sent for Mr. Holmes because she feared the house and its occupants, but her curiosity remained almost as strong as her fear.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: Mr. Holmes is the person whom the young lady contacts for help and advice about the household. She comes to Winchester hoping that his assistance will make the situation better.

records.l: house (the Rucastles' house), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The house frightens the young lady, who says that the man, woman, servants, and child in it all seemed horrible to her. She returns to it after sending a wire and must go back before three o’clock to look after the child.

records.l: empty wing (the Rucastles' house), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The young lady enters the empty wing despite not knowing that she should stay out. She finds it lonely, eerie, dim, and dreadfully still, then runs out in fear.

records.l: door (the empty wing's door), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The door is locked to keep out people who have no business in the empty wing. The man warns the young lady that if she crosses its threshold again, he will throw her to the mastiff.

records.l: Carlo, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The mastiff is described as savage and dangerous enough to be used as a threat against the young lady. Toller is the only person in the household said to have influence over it or to dare set it free.

records.l: advice about the household situation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be
records.s: The young lady seeks advice from Mr. Holmes because she feels unable to remain in the household without guidance. She asks him what the events mean and, above all, what she should do.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and John Watson return to the Copper Beeches with Violet Hunter to investigate the locked chamber and rescue its prisoner, whom Holmes identifies as Alice Rucastle. Alice has escaped through the skylight with help from Mr. Fowler and Mrs. Toller, while Mr. Rucastle attacks the investigators and is mauled by his starving dog. Mrs. Toller explains that Mr. Rucastle imprisoned Alice to control her inheritance and used Violet Hunter to impersonate her. Alice and Mr. Fowler marry after their escape, while Mr. Rucastle survives as a permanently broken man.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Sherlock Holmes arranges with Violet Hunter to investigate the Copper Beeches after the Rucastles leave, asking her to lock Mrs. Toller in the cellar. He deduces that Violet was brought there to impersonate Alice Rucastle and that Alice was imprisoned in the chamber. Holmes confronts Mr. Rucastle, helps expose the escape route, and later recognizes that Mrs. Toller’s account explains the remaining mystery.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to the Copper Beeches and helps force open the prisoner’s chamber. He carries his pistol, shoots the dog to save Mr. Rucastle, and treats the badly mauled man.

records.l: Violet Hunter, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Violet Hunter follows Holmes’s instructions by luring Mrs. Toller into the cellar and locking her there before Holmes and Watson arrive. She is present when the empty chamber and escape route are discovered and is frightened when Mr. Rucastle appears. Holmes later escorts her back to Winchester, and she eventually becomes the head of a private school at Walsall.

records.l: Mr. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mr. Rucastle imprisoned his daughter Alice and brought Violet Hunter to the house to impersonate her so that Mr. Fowler would believe Alice was content and no longer wanted his attentions. He returns to confront Holmes and the others, then releases the starving dog, which attacks and horribly mauls him. He survives but remains a broken man, cared for by his devoted wife.

records.l: Mrs. Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mrs. Rucastle is away from the Copper Beeches when Holmes and Watson arrive and later returns with the country surgeon. She remains devoted to Mr. Rucastle and cares for him after the dog’s attack.

records.l: Alice Rucastle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Alice Rucastle was unhappy under her father’s control and had rights to property or money under a will. After she refused to sign away control of her money, Mr. Rucastle’s pressure caused her to suffer brain-fever; afterward he imprisoned her and used Violet Hunter to impersonate her. Alice escapes through the skylight with Mr. Fowler and marries him in Southampton.

records.l: Mr. Fowler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mr. Fowler remained devoted to Alice Rucastle after her illness and persisted in trying to reach her. He blockaded the house, won Mrs. Toller’s assistance through kindness and payment, arranged the ladder, and helped Alice escape. He later married Alice and received a government appointment in Mauritius.

records.l: Toller, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Toller is drunk when Holmes and Watson arrive, and he lies snoring on the kitchen rug. After Mr. Rucastle is attacked, Toller becomes sober enough to help carry him inside and is sent to inform Mrs. Toller.

records.l: Mrs. Toller, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mrs. Toller initially gives the alarm by her presence, so Violet Hunter locks her in the wine-cellar, but Mr. Rucastle later releases her. She reveals that she supported Alice and Mr. Fowler, accepted Mr. Fowler’s help, kept Toller supplied with drink, and assisted the escape plan. Her testimony explains Alice’s imprisonment, Violet’s impersonation, and the ladder at the skylight.

records.l: the Copper Beeches, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: The Copper Beeches is the house where Alice Rucastle is imprisoned and Violet Hunter is made to impersonate her. Holmes and Watson investigate it, discover Alice’s escape, and witness Mr. Rucastle’s attack by the dog there.

records.l: the Rucastles, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: The Rucastles leave the Copper Beeches before Holmes and Watson arrive, though Mr. Rucastle secretly returns. They continue living there with their old servants, who know enough about Mr. Rucastle’s past to make it difficult for him to dismiss them.

records.l: the dog, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: The dog is used to prevent Mr. Fowler from communicating with Alice and is left unfed for two days. Mr. Rucastle releases it against the investigators, but it attacks him instead; John Watson shoots it to stop the attack.

records.l: the barricaded central room, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Holmes, Watson, and Violet Hunter force open the prisoner’s chamber after the keys fail. It contains only a pallet bed, a small table, and a basket of linen, because the prisoner has escaped through the open skylight.

records.l: the skylight, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: The skylight above the prisoner’s chamber is found open. Holmes determines that Alice was removed through it, using a ladder placed against the eaves.

records.l: the ladder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: A long light ladder is found against the eaves beneath the skylight. Mrs. Toller confirms that Mr. Fowler arranged for it to be ready after Mr. Rucastle went out.

records.l: Alice Rucastle’s imprisonment, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mr. Rucastle imprisoned Alice after she refused to sign over control of her money and used Violet Hunter as a substitute for her. Alice’s imprisonment ends when Mr. Fowler helps her escape through the skylight.

records.l: Violet Hunter’s impersonation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Violet Hunter was brought to the Copper Beeches because she resembled Alice in height, figure, and hair color. She wore Alice’s dress and appeared at the window so that Mr. Fowler would think Alice was happy and no longer wanted him.

records.l: Alice Rucastle and Mr. Fowler’s escape, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Alice Rucastle escapes from the prisoner’s chamber through the skylight with the help of Mr. Fowler, who provides a ladder and gains Mrs. Toller’s cooperation. Alice and Mr. Fowler marry by special license in Southampton the following day.

records.l: Mr. Rucastle’s mauling, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mr. Rucastle releases the starving dog after confronting Holmes, Watson, and Violet Hunter. The dog attacks and severely mauls him before Watson shoots it, and Mr. Rucastle survives as a permanently broken man.

records.l: Mr. Fowler’s blockade of the house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My
records.s: Mr. Fowler blockades the Copper Beeches because he is determined to reach Alice Rucastle. He wins Mrs. Toller’s support through kindness and payment, enabling her to keep Toller drunk and prepare the ladder for Alice’s escape.

records.l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: This document is a collection of twelve Sherlock Holmes cases narrated or framed by Dr. John Watson, following Holmes’s investigations from Baker Street through London and the countryside. Holmes’s powers of disguise, observation, deduction, and occasional moral judgment drive each story, while Watson assists, records events, and often provides the human perspective. It begins with the King of Bohemia seeking recovery of a compromising photograph from Irene Adler. Holmes locates it, but Adler recognizes and outwits him, leaves with her husband Godfrey Norton, and becomes the woman whose wit defeats Holmes. In the Red-Headed League, Holmes exposes a fake employment scheme designed to clear Jabez Wilson’s shop while John Clay tunnels toward a bank. He next proves that James Windibank invented the fiancé Hosmer Angel to keep Mary Sutherland’s income in the family. The middle cases range from murder and inherited menace to mistaken identity and theft. Holmes clears James McCarthy by uncovering John Turner’s confession in the Boscombe Valley killing. He tries too late to save John Openshaw from the K. K. K., though he identifies the men pursuing the family papers. He reveals that beggar Hugh Boone is actually Neville St. Clair, hiding a profitable double life. The blue carbuncle is traced through a Christmas goose to James Ryder, whom Holmes releases after his confession. At Stoke Moran, Holmes discovers that Dr. Grimesby Roylott used a snake to kill Julia Stoner and endanger Helen; the snake kills Roylott instead. Later, Holmes investigates Victor Hatherley’s severed thumb and identifies Colonel Lysander Stark’s hydraulic press as part of a counterfeiting operation. He solves Hatty Doran’s apparent wedding disappearance by finding that she has reunited with her presumed-dead husband, Francis Hay Moulton. In the Beryl Coronet affair, Holmes clears Arthur Holder and shows that Mary Holder aided Sir George Burnwell’s theft. Finally, at the Copper Beeches, Holmes and Watson help Violet Hunter uncover Alice Rucastle’s imprisonment by her father, who used Hunter to impersonate her and control her inheritance. Across the collection, apparent scandals, crimes, disappearances, and mysteries are resolved through Holmes’s reconstruction of concealed motives and events, though some wrongdoers escape legal punishment or tragedy cannot be prevented.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is a consulting and professional detective, described by Watson as a reasoning and observing machine and a specialist in crime. From Baker Street, where he has chambers and lodgings and is closely associated with Dr. John Watson, he conducts investigations chiefly for the love of his art rather than wealth. His central methods are disciplined observation, deduction before theorising, examination of physical traces, disguises, and prolonged thought. He is energetic, generally successful, and regarded as a last court of appeal, although his methods may be theoretical and fantastic. He has extraordinary observational and incisive reasoning powers, plays the violin, uses a black clay pipe, keeps newspaper cuttings, and has Bohemian habits; he also habitually uses cocaine, alternating it with ambition. The record unfolds through cases in which Holmes repeatedly converts apparently minor details into solutions. In the Irene Adler matter, he identifies the King of Bohemia, locates the hidden photograph through a staged fire alarm, but finds that Adler has anticipated him; he retains her photograph as his reward. He exposes the Red-Headed League as a diversion for a bank tunnel and captures John Clay. For Mary Sutherland, he proves that James Windibank created the Hosmer Angel deception. In Boscombe Valley, he clears James McCarthy by identifying John Turner and privately preserving Turner’s confession. After John Openshaw’s death, Holmes traces the threatening gang to the Lone Star and seeks to warn its captain. He resolves Neville St. Clair’s supposed disappearance by removing Hugh Boone’s disguise, follows the blue carbuncle through a goose supply chain to James Ryder, and releases Ryder after obtaining his confession. He uncovers Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s snake-based murder scheme at Stoke Moran, identifies a coining gang near Eyford, and explains Hatty Doran’s disappearance by tracing Francis Hay Moulton. He restores the stolen coronet gems and establishes Arthur Holder’s innocence through disguise and physical evidence. Finally, responding to Violet Hunter’s appeal at the Copper Beeches, he deduces that she was meant to impersonate Alice Rucastle, exposes Alice’s imprisonment and escape route, and resolves the remaining mystery through Mrs. Toller’s account. Throughout, Watson is his friend, colleague, assistant, witness, and chronicler.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dr. Watson is a married medical practitioner and physician in civil practice in London, living near Paddington Station after having shared rooms with Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street. A veteran of the Afghan campaign who carries an army revolver and bears a jezail bullet in a limb, he is Holmes’s longtime friend, trusted companion, colleague, medical adviser, and chronicler. His marriage separates him socially from Holmes, but he repeatedly visits or travels with him, records his cases, and narrates their investigations. Across the records, Watson begins by observing Holmes’s deductions and agreeing to assist in the operation at Briony Lodge, where he follows instructions, throws a smoke-rocket, and despite misgivings about Irene Adler remains loyal to Holmes.
