records.s: Tavistock is the Devonshire town where Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, Colonel Ross, and Inspector Gregory arrive. Inspector Gregory searches its stables and outbuildings for Silver Blaze, and the party later prepares to return there.

records.l: King’s Pyland, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: King’s Pyland is the stable from which Silver Blaze disappeared and where John Straker was employed. Holmes reasons that a loose horse would likely return there or go to Mapleton, but establishes that Silver Blaze is not at King’s Pyland.

records.l: Mapleton stables, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: Mapleton stables lie across the moor from King’s Pyland and belong to the competing trainer Silas Brown. Horse tracks lead to the stables, where Holmes determines that Silver Blaze is being concealed.

records.l: Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: Silver Blaze is the missing favorite for the Cup. Sherlock Holmes follows his tracks to Mapleton stables and concludes that Silas Brown is hiding him there.

records.l: the murder of John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The murder of John Straker remains unresolved in this unit. Sherlock Holmes examines the scene and evidence but deliberately sets aside the question of who killed Straker after locating Silver Blaze.

records.l: the disappearance of Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The disappearance of Silver Blaze is traced through horse tracks across Dartmoor to Mapleton stables. Holmes concludes that the horse wandered from the scene and was then taken and concealed by Silas Brown.

records.l: Wessex Plate, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The Cup is the race for which Silver Blaze is the favorite and Desborough is second in the betting. Colonel Ross considers withdrawing Silver Blaze from the entries, but Holmes tells him to leave the horse’s name in the race.

records.l: the criminal investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The criminal investigation examines John Straker’s death and the disappearance of Silver Blaze. Inspector Gregory pursues Fitzroy Simpson, while Sherlock Holmes finds the horse and postpones further work on the murder.

records.l: the circumstantial case against Fitzroy Simpson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The circumstantial case against Fitzroy Simpson includes his suspected motives, alleged poisoning attempt, presence during the storm, heavy stick, and cravat found in Straker’s hand. Sherlock Holmes argues that a clever counsel could undermine the case because key supporting details are missing or unexplained.

records.l: the horse tracks, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: The horse tracks are found in soft ground away from the original crime scene and are matched by Silver Blaze’s horseshoe. They first show the horse moving toward Mapleton, then reveal a man accompanying it and a return route ending at the gates of Mapleton stables.

records.l: Straker’s cataract knife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,
records.s: Straker’s cataract knife is a delicate, inflexible knife marked Weiss & Co., London, with bloodstains on its blade. Holmes notes that it was an unusual weapon for a rough expedition, while Inspector Gregory says Straker had picked it up from his dressing-table and protected its tip with cork.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes leaves with his companions after saying that the horse should start on Tuesday, though he acknowledges serious difficulties in arresting the murderer of John Straker. He obtains a photograph of John Straker and questions a maid before departing for Tavistock. Holmes then learns that three sheep have gone lame and identifies this as potentially important. He also draws Inspector Gregory’s attention to the curious fact that the dog did nothing during the night.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes says that there are grave difficulties in arresting the murderer of John Straker, but he expects the horse to start on Tuesday. He obtains a photograph of John Straker, questions the maid, notices the lameness among the sheep, and points Inspector Gregory toward the dog's inactivity at night.

records.l: Inspector Gregory, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Inspector Gregory is present when Sherlock Holmes discusses the case and gives Holmes a photograph of John Straker. Holmes urges him to investigate the unusual lameness among the sheep, which Gregory recognizes as potentially important.

records.l: Colonel Ross, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Colonel Ross is disappointed with Sherlock Holmes and doubts that Holmes has advanced the investigation. He says that Holmes’s assurance about the horse is less satisfactory than having the horse itself.

records.l: John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: John Straker is identified as the murdered man. Sherlock Holmes asks Inspector Gregory for a photograph of him.

records.l: Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes expresses confidence that the horse will start on Tuesday. Colonel Ross would prefer possession of the horse rather than Holmes’s assurance that it will run.

records.l: sheep, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: A stable-lad says that three sheep in the paddock have gone lame. Sherlock Holmes is extremely pleased by this information and considers it important.

records.l: dog, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes calls attention to the curious incident of the dog in the night-time. The dog did nothing during the night.

records.l: murder of John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes says that there are grave difficulties in the way of arresting the murderer of John Straker. The investigation remains unresolved in this unit.

records.l: epidemic among the sheep, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes describes the three lame sheep as a singular epidemic and recommends that Inspector Gregory investigate it. He considers the condition exceedingly important.

records.l: Wessex Plate, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes expresses hope that the horse will start on Tuesday and asks Colonel Ross to have the jockey ready. Colonel Ross remains skeptical of Holmes’s assurance.

records.l: dog's inactivity at night, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies the dog's failure to do anything during the night as the curious incident. He draws Inspector Gregory’s attention to this fact.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel with Colonel Ross to Winchester for the Wessex Cup, where Silver Blaze unexpectedly runs and wins the Wessex Plate disguised as a bay horse. Holmes reveals that the horse's markings were concealed by a faker and that Silver Blaze killed John Straker in self-defence. He explains that Straker had drugged the stable-boy with powdered opium, intended to lame Silver Blaze with a surgical knife, and was planning a horse-race fraud. Holmes also concludes that Fitzroy Simpson was not involved and that Straker's debts and secret relationship helped motivate the crime.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies the disguised bay horse as Silver Blaze and reveals that John Straker was killed by the horse in self-defence. He reconstructs the crime from the curried mutton, the silent stable dog, Straker's surgical knife, his bills, and the horse's behaviour, and later finds the recovered horse with a neighbour.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Dr. Watson travels with Holmes and Colonel Ross to Winchester and observes Silver Blaze's unexpected race and victory. He listens as Holmes explains how he solved the murder of John Straker.

records.l: Colonel Ross, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Colonel Ross is initially distressed because Silver Blaze is missing and believes the horse running under his colours is not his own. After Holmes reveals the horse's identity and solves Straker's murder, Ross expresses gratitude and acknowledges Holmes's achievement.

records.l: Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Silver Blaze is disguised as a powerful bay horse by having his white markings concealed, but Holmes recognizes him and enters him in the Wessex Plate. He wins the race by six lengths and is revealed to have killed John Straker by kicking him in self-defence.

records.l: John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: John Straker drugged the stable-boy and secretly took Silver Blaze onto the moor to lame the horse by making a delicate cut in its ham tendons. The horse frightened at Straker's light and kicked him in the forehead, while Straker's knife also gashed his thigh; Holmes further learns that Straker had debts connected with an expensive mistress.

records.l: Fitzroy Simpson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Fitzroy Simpson was initially believed by Holmes to be the likely culprit, but the curried mutton and powdered opium show that he could not have arranged the poisoning. Holmes therefore eliminates Simpson from the case.

records.l: Winchester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Winchester is the destination to which Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to see the race for the Wessex Cup.

records.l: King’s Pyland, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The Dartmoor training-stables are the setting of the Monday-night events that Holmes reconstructs. John Straker drugged the stable-boy there, removed Silver Blaze, and attempted to injure the horse.

records.l: Wessex Cup, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The Wessex Cup is the race that Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Colonel Ross travel to Winchester to see.

records.l: Wessex Plate, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The Wessex Plate is a one-mile-and-five-furlong race in which six horses, including Silver Blaze, compete. Silver Blaze wins it by six lengths, with Desborough second and Iris third.

records.l: the murder of John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The murder of John Straker is solved by Holmes as an accidental killing in self-defence. Straker was attempting to lame Silver Blaze when the horse kicked him, and Holmes links the crime to Straker's attempted horse-race fraud.

records.l: curried mutton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Curried mutton was served to the stable-boy and provided a way to disguise the perceptible taste of powdered opium. Holmes reasons that only John Straker or his wife could have chosen and poisoned the portion set aside for the boy.

records.l: powdered opium, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: Powdered opium was mixed into the stable-boy's curried mutton to incapacitate him. Its use helped Holmes conclude that the culprit was someone in the trainer's household rather than Fitzroy Simpson.

records.l: Straker’s cataract knife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The surgical knife found in John Straker's hand was designed for delicate surgical operations rather than ordinary violence. Holmes determines that Straker intended to use it to nick Silver Blaze's tendons beneath the skin and make the horse lame.

records.l: horse-race fraud, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for
records.s: The horse-race fraud involved John Straker's plan to prevent Silver Blaze from winning after bets were placed against the horse. Straker intended to lame Silver Blaze subtly, presumably to secure money through betting agents.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: Watson describes a hot August day in Baker Street when Sherlock Holmes demonstrates how he inferred Watson’s unspoken thoughts from his facial expressions and movements. Holmes explains that Watson’s thoughts progressed from portraits of General Gordon and Henry Ward Beecher to the Civil War and the perceived absurdity of settling disputes through war. Holmes then directs Watson’s attention to a newspaper paragraph about a packet sent to Miss Cushing of Cross Street, Croydon. The packet’s remarkable contents are presented as a new problem that Holmes believes may be more difficult to solve.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reads Watson’s train of thought from his facial expressions, eyes, gestures, and other movements, then explains each deduction. He brings Watson’s attention to a newspaper report about a packet sent to Miss Cushing and identifies it as a potentially difficult problem.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: Watson spends a hot August morning with Sherlock Holmes in Baker Street and is amazed when Holmes accurately reconstructs his unspoken thoughts. He reads aloud, at Holmes’s request, a newspaper paragraph about a packet sent to Miss Cushing.

records.l: thought reading, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: Thought reading is described as the process of inferring another person’s unspoken thoughts from observed actions, facial expressions, and eyes. Sherlock Holmes demonstrates it by tracing Watson’s thoughts from a picture of General Gordon through Henry Ward Beecher and the Civil War to the idea that war is a preposterous way to settle disputes.

records.l: Miss Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: Miss Cushing is identified as the recipient of a packet whose remarkable contents are reported in a newspaper paragraph. She is associated with Cross Street, Croydon.

records.l: the package sent to Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: The posted packet was sent through the post to Miss Cushing of Cross Street, Croydon. Its contents are described in a newspaper paragraph as remarkable.

records.l: the packet’s remarkable contents, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box
records.s: The packet’s remarkable contents are mentioned as the subject of a short newspaper report. The text does not yet reveal what those contents are.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigate a packet containing two freshly severed human ears sent to Miss Susan Cushing at Cross Street, Croydon. Holmes determines that the ears are from a woman and a man and rejects the theory that medical students sent them as a practical joke. His questioning reveals connections among Susan Cushing, her sisters Sarah and Mary, and Mary’s husband, James Browner, a violent alcoholic steward. Holmes visits Sarah, finds her seriously ill, and then gives Inspector Lestrade the name of the suspected criminal after receiving a telegram.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the packet, its tarred twine, wrapper, box, salt, and the two ears. He concludes that the ears came from a woman and a man who were probably murdered, connects the case to Mary Cushing’s husband James Browner, and gives Inspector Lestrade the suspected criminal’s name.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Croydon and observes the examination of the packet and interviews with Miss Susan Cushing. He records Holmes’s deductions and the developments of the investigation.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Inspector Lestrade investigates the packet for Scotland Yard and brings Holmes and Watson to Miss Susan Cushing’s house. He initially favors the medical-student theory, but receives from Holmes the name of the suspected criminal and is told that an arrest cannot be made until the following night at the earliest.

records.l: Miss Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Miss Susan Cushing receives the packet containing two human ears and reports it to the police, insisting that it was probably sent to her by mistake. She tells Holmes about her sisters Sarah and Mary, Mary’s husband James Browner, and her former medical-student lodgers.

records.l: Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Sarah Cushing is Susan Cushing’s sister and formerly lived with Susan in Croydon. She later moved to New Street, Wallington, but is reported to be extremely ill with severe brain symptoms when Holmes visits.

records.l: Mary Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Mary Browner is Susan and Sarah Cushing’s younger sister. She married James Browner, but has stopped writing to Susan, leaving the family uncertain about how she and James are doing.

records.l: James Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: James Browner is Mary Browner’s husband and a steward who worked on ships including the May Day. He resumed drinking after breaking his pledge, became violently irrational when intoxicated, and quarrelled with Susan and Sarah; Holmes identifies the suspected criminal as James Browner.

records.l: Croydon, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Croydon is the town containing Cross Street and the police investigation site. Holmes and Watson travel there from London to examine the packet and question Susan Cushing. The address on the packet is written as “Cross Street, Croydon,” although Holmes observes that “Croydon” was first spelled with an “i” and then corrected to a “y.”

records.l: the package sent to Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: The cardboard packet is wrapped in brown paper and sent by parcel post from Belfast. Its wrapper bears a straggling handwritten address, smells of coffee, and is tied with tarred twine secured by an unusual intact knot.

records.l: the cardboard box, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: The cardboard box is a yellow half-pound honeydew tobacco box filled with coarse salt. It bears two thumb marks and contains the two human ears.

records.l: the two human ears, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: The two human ears are fresh, preserved in coarse salt, and cut off with a blunt instrument. They are not a pair: one is a small woman’s ear pierced for an earring, and the other is a sun-burned man’s ear also pierced for an earring.

records.l: the double murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: Holmes presumes that the two ears are evidence of a double murder committed on Wednesday, Tuesday, or earlier. He believes the sender is the murderer and that the packet was sent to communicate that the deed had been done or to cause pain.

records.l: the sending of the ears, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: The ears are sent by parcel post from Belfast on Thursday morning to Susan Cushing in Croydon. Holmes concludes that the sending is not a medical-student practical joke and must have been motivated by a strong connection between the sender and the recipient.

records.l: the investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the
records.s: The investigation begins with Inspector Lestrade’s inquiry into the packet and the medical-student theory. Holmes examines the physical evidence, questions Susan, investigates Sarah’s address, receives a telegram, and reports that he has uncovered the crime’s details and identified the suspected criminal.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. Watson how he identified Jim Browner as the likely author of the murders involving Mrs. Browner and a seafaring man. A little yellow box containing human ears, addressed to Miss S. Cushing, provided clues linking the crime to sailors and to the Cushing sisters. Holmes concluded that the packet was intended for Miss Sarah and that jealousy was probably the motive. Information from Liverpool indicates that Mrs. Browner’s house has been closed and that Browner sailed aboard the May Day, which is expected in the Thames the following night.

records.l: the investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: The case concerns a packet containing human ears and the murders of Mrs. Browner and a man presumed to be a seafaring man. Holmes considers the essential facts established and suspects Jim Browner as the author of the crime.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reasons backward from the evidence and identifies the sailor-related clues in the little yellow box. He matches one ear in the box to Miss Cushing’s ear, learns about the Cushing sisters and Jim Browner, and concludes that Browner probably committed the murders from jealousy.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Dr. Watson discusses the case with Holmes and asks whether Holmes suspects Jim Browner. Holmes addresses him as a medical man when explaining the distinctive anatomical features of human ears.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Inspector Lestrade is expected to meet Jim Browner when the May Day arrives. Holmes considers him lacking in reason but tenacious and reliable once he understands his task.

records.l: James Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Jim Browner is a steward of a Liverpool boat and the man Holmes suspects of committing the murders. He was married to one of the Cushing sisters, had been involved in a quarrel with Miss Sarah, and sailed aboard the May Day after the suspected crime.

records.l: Mrs. Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Mrs. Browner was Jim Browner’s wife and is believed to have been murdered. Her house had been closed for more than three days, and neighbors thought she had gone south to visit relatives.

records.l: Miss Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Miss Cushing is the oldest sister and the recipient named on the packet addressed to Miss S. Cushing. Holmes observes that her ear corresponds exactly to the female ear in the box, establishing that the victim was probably a close blood relation.

records.l: Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Miss Sarah is one of the Cushing sisters and had formerly lived at the same address as Miss Cushing. She had been intimate with Jim Browner, had moved to Liverpool to be near the Browners, and became estranged from him after a quarrel; Holmes believes the packet was intended for her.

records.l: Liverpool, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: Liverpool was associated with Jim Browner’s boat, his residence with Mrs. Browner, and his former relationship with Miss Sarah. Holmes learned that Browner had departed from Liverpool aboard the May Day.

records.l: May Day, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: The May Day is the steamer aboard which Jim Browner left. Holmes calculates that it will arrive in the Thames the following night, where Lestrade is expected to meet Browner.

records.l: the package sent to Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: The little yellow box contained human ears and was addressed to Miss S. Cushing. Its sailmaker’s string, sailor’s knot, posting from a port, and a pierced male ear led Holmes to connect the crime with seafaring people.

records.l: the double murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: The murders are believed to include Mrs. Browner and a seafaring man. Holmes considers jealousy the likely motive and suspects that Jim Browner committed both killings.

records.l: the investigation into the murders, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars
records.s: The investigation proceeds from physical evidence in the packet to information about the Cushing sisters and the Browners. Holmes sends inquiries through Lestrade and Algar of the Liverpool force, and expects the remaining details to be established when Browner arrives.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Inspector Lestrade's report and James Browner's confession after Browner is arrested aboard the S.S. May Day. Browner admits killing his wife, Mary Browner, and Alec Fairbairn after following them to New Brighton and attacking them in a boat. He blames Sarah Cushing's influence for destroying his marriage but accepts responsibility for the murders. Holmes reflects on the wider problem of suffering, violence, and whether human misery serves any meaningful end.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Inspector Lestrade's report and reads James Browner's statement aloud to Watson. He considers the investigation simple in retrospect but ends by questioning what purpose is served by the cycle of misery, violence, and fear.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Inspector Lestrade investigates James Browner aboard the S.S. May Day, has him arrested, and sends Holmes a report and a typed copy of Browner's statement. He learns that Browner voluntarily confessed at the police station.

records.l: James Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: James Browner is found aboard the S.S. May Day, withdrawn and apparently remorseful, and is taken into custody. He confesses to killing Mary Browner and Alec Fairbairn, sinking their bodies in a boat, and returning to his ship without immediate suspicion.

records.l: Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Sarah Cushing is described as one of three sisters and as a woman who loved James Browner before turning to poisonous hatred. Browner believes that she encouraged suspicion between him and Mary and sent her a packet containing signs of what her meddling had caused.

records.l: Mary Browner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Mary Browner is portrayed by James as a loving and innocent wife whose trust changes into suspicion after Sarah's influence and the appearance of Alec Fairbairn. She is killed by Browner in a boat after he sees her with Fairbairn and attacks them.

records.l: Alec Fairbairn, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Alec Fairbairn is described as a charming, adventurous sailor who becomes closely associated with Mary Browner. James Browner follows him and Mary to New Brighton and kills him with an oak stick before sinking his body.

records.l: James Browner's confession, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: James Browner's confession recounts the breakdown of his marriage, his return to drinking, his jealousy of Alec Fairbairn, and the murders of Mary and Alec. He says that he has been unable to sleep because he continually sees their faces and believes his punishment has already begun.

records.l: the murders of Mary Browner and Alec Fairbairn, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: The murders occur after James Browner follows Mary Browner and Alec Fairbairn to New Brighton and pursues them onto the water in a haze. He strikes Alec with a stick, kills Mary when she embraces Alec, uses his knife, ties the bodies into the boat, and sinks them.

records.l: the investigation into the murders, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Inspector Lestrade's investigation leads to James Browner's arrest aboard the S.S. May Day. The investigation produces little physical evidence, but Browner's voluntary statement provides a full confession, making the case appear straightforward.

records.l: the love triangle involving James Browner, Mary Browner, and Sarah Cushing, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Sarah Cushing loves James Browner, but he remains devoted to Mary Browner and rejects Sarah's advances. Sarah's resentment contributes to suspicion and conflict between James and Mary, helping to create the circumstances that end in Mary's relationship with Alec Fairbairn and her murder by James.

records.l: the problem of suffering and human violence, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two
records.s: Holmes reflects on the chain of jealousy, betrayal, violence, remorse, and fear surrounding the murders. He asks what purpose such a circle of misery serves and suggests that human reason remains unable to answer whether suffering and violence have any meaningful end.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson receive Grant Munro, who seeks advice about a sudden secret between himself and his wife, Effie Munro. Grant says that Effie has begun visiting a newly occupied cottage near their home, including secretly leaving at three in the morning, and that she denies having been there. He also describes seeing a rigid, chalky-white face watching him from the cottage window and meeting a hostile Northern woman who lives there. When Grant finds Effie leaving the cottage, she begs him not to enter and seizes his sleeve with great force.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Grant Munro at Baker Street and agrees to hear his domestic problem. Before Grant explains the case, Holmes examines a pipe left behind by the earlier visitor and deduces that its owner is muscular, left-handed, well-to-do, careless, and has strong teeth.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes on a walk and is present when Grant Munro comes to seek advice. He listens as Grant describes the estrangement from Effie and the mysterious cottage.

records.l: Grant Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Grant Munro is a married hop merchant whose previously happy life has been disrupted by a secret involving his wife, Effie. He reports that Effie obtained one hundred pounds without explaining why, visited the nearby cottage at night, lied about where she had been, and was later seen leaving the cottage. When he threatens to enter, Effie pulls him back with convulsive strength and begs him not to do so.

records.l: Effie Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Effie Munro is Grant Munro's wife, formerly Mrs. Hebron, and a widow from Atlanta whose first husband and child died of yellow fever. She secretly visits the cottage, including at three in the morning, appears frightened and guilty, denies having been there, and begs Grant not to enter it.

records.l: Baker Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson receive Grant Munro after he first visits and waits there impatiently for them.

records.l: Norbury, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Norbury is where Grant Munro and Effie Munro live in a rural area near London. Grant returns there after walking to the Crystal Palace and passes the nearby cottage, where he sees Effie leaving.

records.l: Grant Munro and Effie Munro's villa, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Grant Munro and Effie Munro's villa is an eighty-pound-a-year home in Norbury, surrounded by fields and only a few nearby buildings. The cottage occupied by the mysterious newcomers lies across a field from it.

records.l: the cottage near Grant Munro's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: The cottage near Grant Munro's house had stood empty for eight months before new occupants moved in. Grant sees a strange pale face at an upper window, encounters a tall, hostile Northern woman at the door, and later discovers Effie leaving the cottage.

records.l: the strange domestic affair, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: The strange domestic affair concerns the sudden barrier between Grant Munro and Effie Munro after three years of happiness. Its known features include Effie's unexplained request for money, secret nighttime visits to the nearby cottage, apparent lies, and Grant's sighting of an unnatural face there.

records.l: the yellow face, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: The yellow face is seen by Grant Munro watching from an upper window of the newly occupied cottage. He cannot determine whether it belongs to a man or a woman, but describes it as livid, chalky white, rigid, and shockingly unnatural.

records.l: Effie and Grant Munro's marriage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, III. The Yellow Face
records.s: Grant Munro says that he and Effie Munro had loved each other and lived happily for three years without any disagreement. Their trust is damaged when Effie develops a secret life involving unexplained money, nighttime departures, visits to the cottage, and statements Grant believes are false, although he insists that she still loves him.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: Jack's wife begs him not to enter the cottage, promising that she will explain everything someday and warning that doing so would bring misery. Jack agrees to leave with her on the condition that there will be no more secret nightly visits or hidden actions. As they depart, Jack sees a yellow, livid face watching them from the cottage's upper window. He remains determined to solve the mystery connecting the creature, the cottage, and his wife.

records.l: Grant Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: Jack is persuaded by his wife's desperation not to enter the cottage. He agrees to trust her only if she promises that the mystery will end and that there will be no more secret nightly visits or concealed actions. Although he leaves with her, he knows he will not be at ease until he solves the mystery.

records.l: Effie Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: Jack's wife clings to him and urgently begs him not to enter the cottage, promising to tell him everything someday. She says that the secret is being kept for his sake and warns that entering the cottage would end their relationship. She agrees to Jack's condition that there be no more secret visits or hidden activities.

records.l: the cottage near Grant Munro's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: The cottage is the place Jack's wife has been visiting at night and urges him not to enter. Jack leaves without going inside, but sees a yellow, livid face watching them from its upper window.

records.l: creature (the woman connected to Jack's wife), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: The creature is seen as a yellow, livid face watching Jack and his wife from the cottage's upper window. Jack wonders what connection the creature has to his wife and how it could be related to the coarse, rough woman he saw the previous day, but he does not learn the answer.

records.l: mystery concerning Jack's wife and the cottage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: The mystery involves Jack's wife's secret nightly visits to the cottage and her possible connection with the creature inside it. Jack agrees to stop pressing her for an immediate explanation, but remains intent on solving the mystery.

records.l: secret kept by Jack's wife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘I implore you not to do this, Jack,’ she cried. ‘I swear that I
records.s: Jack's wife says she will tell him everything someday but insists that the secret is being kept for his own sake. She promises that there will be no further actions or visits kept from his knowledge, while retaining the secret for the present.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Grant Munro asks Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson to investigate why his wife, Effie, secretly visits a cottage at Norbury where a strange face appears at the window. Holmes suspects that Effie's first husband or his associates are blackmailing her, but the cottage is inhabited by an old nurse and Effie's daughter, Lucy, whose face has been covered by a mask. Effie reveals that Lucy is her child by her deceased first husband, John Hebron, an African American man, and that she concealed the child because she feared losing Grant. Grant accepts Effie and Lucy, and Holmes later uses “Norbury” as a reminder not to become overconfident.

records.l: Grant Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Grant Munro becomes convinced that his wife is concealing a serious secret in the cottage at Norbury. He forces his way inside with Holmes and Watson, learns that the supposed strange occupant is his wife’s daughter, Lucy, and responds by kissing and carrying the child home while offering Effie his hand.

records.l: Effie Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Effie secretly visits the cottage because she wants to see her daughter Lucy, whom she has kept hidden from Grant. She explains that fear of losing Grant caused her to conceal Lucy, and she asks what will become of herself and her child after the secret is exposed.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the cottage mystery and initially theorizes that Effie’s first husband or his associates are blackmailing her. He discovers that the livid face belongs to a masked child and later admits that the case should remind him not to become overconfident.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Dr. Watson listens to Grant Munro’s account, accompanies Holmes and Grant to the cottage, and witnesses the revelation of Lucy’s identity. He initially finds the strange face horrifying but then laughs when the mask is removed.

records.l: Lucy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Lucy is Effie’s daughter by John Hebron and has been living in the cottage under the care of a former servant. She is a little black girl dressed in a red frock and white gloves, and her face has been covered to conceal her racial identity from the neighbours.

records.l: John Hebron, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: John Hebron was Effie’s first husband in Atlanta and the father of Lucy. Effie describes him as a noble and handsome man of African descent who had died before the events of this unit.

records.l: the cottage near Grant Munro's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: The cottage appears deserted when Grant first enters it, but later it is shown to be occupied by an old woman and Lucy. Its comfortable upper room contains Effie’s photograph and becomes the place where Effie’s hidden child and her secret are revealed.

records.l: Norbury, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Norbury is the location of Grant and Effie’s home and the mysterious cottage. Holmes later tells Watson that the word “Norbury” should be used to remind him of this case if he becomes overconfident.

records.l: mystery concerning Jack's wife and the cottage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: The secret is that Effie has arranged for her daughter Lucy to stay in the cottage under the care of a nurse. Effie has concealed Lucy from Grant because she feared that he would reject her child because of Lucy’s African ancestry.

records.l: blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Holmes initially believes that blackmail explains Effie’s secrecy, the hundred pounds she sent, and her efforts to prevent Grant from entering the cottage. This theory proves mistaken when Effie reveals that the money was sent to Lucy’s nurse.

records.l: Effie and Grant Munro's marriage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Effie’s concealment of Lucy creates the first serious shadow between her and Grant. After the truth is revealed, Grant indicates that he will accept Effie and Lucy and discuss the matter more comfortably at home.

records.l: the revelation of Lucy's identity, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Lucy’s identity is revealed when Holmes removes the mask from the livid face at the window and exposes a little black girl. Effie then explains that Lucy is her daughter, born to her and John Hebron.

records.l: the photograph of Effie, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: A full-length photograph of Effie stands on the mantelpiece in the cottage’s comfortable room. Effie had given the photograph to the nurse as part of the arrangements for Lucy’s stay.

records.l: the yellow face, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: The face at the window appears unnaturally coloured and rigid, vanishing with a jerk whenever Grant approaches. It is later explained as Lucy’s masked face, deliberately covered so that neighbours would not see that she was a black child.

records.l: the mask on Lucy's face, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Lucy wears a mask that makes her face appear livid and expressionless, creating the frightening apparition seen by Grant. Holmes removes it by passing his hand behind her ear, revealing Lucy’s true face.

records.l: racial identity and prejudice, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
records.s: Effie explains that she married John Hebron despite his African descent and that Lucy inherited a much darker appearance from her father. Effie concealed Lucy because she feared Grant would reject her, while Grant’s final acceptance shows that he does not abandon Effie or the child after learning the truth.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Dr. John Watson, now running a medical practice in Paddington, joins Sherlock Holmes on a journey to Birmingham to investigate Hall Pycroft’s strange employment experience. Pycroft describes losing his position at Coxon & Woodhouse before receiving a lucrative job offer from Arthur Pinner to become business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. Arthur sends Pycroft to Birmingham with £100 and a written agreement, where Harry Pinner supposedly confirms the appointment and assigns him work compiling lists from a Paris directory. Pycroft realizes that Arthur and Harry are the same man and asks Holmes to explain why he was sent from London to Birmingham.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Dr. John Watson is visited by Sherlock Holmes shortly after taking over a medical practice in Paddington. He accompanies Holmes and Hall Pycroft to Birmingham and listens as Pycroft recounts the suspicious job offer.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Sherlock Holmes deduces from Watson’s scorched slippers that Watson recently had a severe chill. He takes Watson to Birmingham to investigate Hall Pycroft’s case and recognizes that the two supposed Pinner brothers are the same man because they share the same voice, figure, and identically stuffed tooth.

records.l: Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Hall Pycroft is a former clerk of Coxon & Woodhouse who is offered a position at Mawson & Williams after the collapse of his former firm. He is persuaded by Arthur Pinner to accept a much higher-paying position with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, receives £100, and is sent to Birmingham, where he becomes suspicious after meeting the supposed Harry Pinner.

records.l: Arthur Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Arthur Pinner visits Hall Pycroft in London and praises his financial ability, offering him the position of business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, at a salary of £500 plus commission. He gives Pycroft a £100 advance, obtains a written agreement, and directs him to meet his supposed brother in Birmingham.

records.l: Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Harry Pinner supposedly meets Hall Pycroft at 126B Corporation Street in Birmingham and confirms his engagement with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. He assigns Pycroft the task of marking hardware sellers in a Paris directory and later asks him to list furniture shops; Holmes and Pycroft conclude that Harry is actually Arthur Pinner in disguise.

records.l: Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Mawson & Williams is a wealthy stockbroking firm in Lombard Street that offers Hall Pycroft a clerkship paying £200 a year. Arthur Pinner tries to persuade Pycroft not to resign from the firm.

records.l: the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: The Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, is presented to Hall Pycroft as a company with 134 branches in France, plus one in Brussels and one in San Remo. Its supposed temporary offices in Birmingham are sparsely furnished and have no company name displayed.

records.l: Birmingham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Birmingham is where Hall Pycroft is directed to report for his new employment. He meets the supposed Harry Pinner there at 126B Corporation Street and is given work compiling commercial lists.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: London is where Hall Pycroft receives the offer from Arthur Pinner and where Mawson & Williams is located. Pycroft returns to London by night train to consult Sherlock Holmes after becoming suspicious in Birmingham.

records.l: 126B Corporation Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: 126B Corporation Street in Birmingham is given to Hall Pycroft as the temporary office address of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. The address consists of a passage leading to offices, but no company name appears on the wall.

records.l: Pycroft's £100 advance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: Arthur Pinner gives Hall Pycroft a £100 advance on his supposed salary. Pycroft keeps the money while working on the lists in Birmingham, despite his growing doubts about the company.

records.l: Pycroft's written agreement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: At Arthur Pinner’s request, Hall Pycroft writes that he is perfectly willing to act as business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, at a minimum salary of £500. Arthur puts the written agreement in his pocket.

records.l: Paris directory, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: The supposed Harry Pinner gives Hall Pycroft a large Paris directory and orders him to mark all hardware sellers and their addresses. After Pycroft completes that task, Pinner asks him to compile a list of furniture shops as well.

records.l: Franco-Midland job offer, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: The Franco-Midland job offer promises Hall Pycroft the position of business manager, a starting salary of £500, and one percent commission on business conducted by his agents. The offer leads Pycroft away from the safer position at Mawson & Williams and sends him to Birmingham.

records.l: hardware trade, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
records.s: The supposed company is described as intending to purchase English crockery and distribute it through agents and branches in France. Hall Pycroft is asked to identify hardware sellers and furniture shops in Paris as part of this purported trade.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft visit Arthur Harry Pinner at the temporary offices of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, where Pinner attempts to hang himself after seeing them. Holmes deduces that Pinner and his brother obtained Pycroft’s handwriting so one brother could impersonate him at Mawson & Williams. An Evening Standard report reveals that the impersonator, Beddington, attempted to rob Mawson & Williams, murdered its watchman, and was captured with stolen securities. Pinner’s suicide attempt is explained as his response to learning that his brother’s crime had been exposed.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Arthur Harry Pinner with Dr. John Watson and Hall Pycroft, questions the circumstances, and breaks into the inner room when Pinner begins choking himself. He deduces that Pycroft’s handwriting was obtained for imitation and that one of the criminals impersonated Pycroft at Mawson & Williams; he later recognizes the Evening Standard report as explaining Pinner’s suicide attempt.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Hall Pycroft to the temporary company offices. He helps rescue Arthur Harry Pinner, examines him, treats him with water and artificial movement, and reads aloud the Evening Standard report about the attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams.

records.l: Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Hall Pycroft brings Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson to meet Arthur Harry Pinner and explains the arrangements connected with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. He learns that his handwriting was obtained so that another man could impersonate him at Mawson & Williams, and he is sent to contact the police after the robbery is revealed.

records.l: Arthur Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Arthur Harry Pinner is found in a state of extreme terror at the temporary company offices and asks to be left alone. He enters an inner room and attempts to hang himself with his braces, but Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft rescue him; he later explains that the newspaper report is the reason for his action.

records.l: Beddington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Beddington is identified in the Evening Standard as the criminal who used the false name Hall Pycroft to obtain employment at Mawson & Williams. He obtained mouldings of locks and knowledge of the strong room, murdered the watchman, stole securities, and was captured while leaving with a carpet bag.

records.l: Beddington's brother, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Beddington's brother worked with him in the scheme and impersonated Hall Pycroft at Mawson & Williams. He is identified with Arthur Harry Pinner, who attempts suicide after learning that Beddington has been captured and that the crime has been exposed.

records.l: the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, is presented as the company for which Arthur Harry Pinner claims to be managing director. Its supposed employment arrangements are used to obtain Hall Pycroft’s handwriting, keep him away from London, and support the impersonation scheme.

records.l: Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Mawson & Williams is the financial house where the false Hall Pycroft obtains a clerk’s position. It holds securities worth considerably more than a million pounds, and Beddington uses his position there to prepare an attempted robbery.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: London is where Mawson & Williams is located and where the attempted robbery, murder of the watchman, and capture of Beddington take place. The conspirators keep Hall Pycroft in the Midlands to prevent him from returning to London and discovering the impersonation.

records.l: the temporary company offices, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The temporary company offices are a bare, unfurnished set of rooms on the fifth floor. Arthur Harry Pinner meets Hall Pycroft, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. John Watson there, then attempts to hang himself in an inner room.

records.l: the Evening Standard, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The Evening Standard carries an early report titled “Crime in the City. Murder at Mawson & Williams,” describing the attempted robbery, the murder of the watchman, and the capture of Beddington. Its report explains to Holmes and the others why Arthur Harry Pinner attempted suicide.

records.l: the attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams involves Beddington using a false identity to gain access to the firm, learn about its safes, and steal securities. He is intercepted while leaving with nearly a hundred thousand pounds’ worth of American railway bonds and other scrip.

records.l: the murder of the watchman, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The watchman at Mawson & Williams is murdered by a blow from a poker delivered from behind. His body is hidden inside the largest safe and is discovered after Beddington is stopped.

records.l: Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Arthur Harry Pinner's suicide attempt occurs immediately after he meets Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft at the temporary company offices. He hangs himself with his braces but is found in time and revived by the three men.

records.l: the capture of Beddington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The capture of Beddington occurs after Sergeant Tuson follows him from Mawson & Williams and, with Constable Pollock, overcomes his resistance. Beddington is found carrying stolen securities in a carpet bag.

records.l: handwriting imitation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: Handwriting imitation is central to the scheme because the criminals obtain Hall Pycroft’s written declaration as a specimen. One of them learns to copy his writing so that an impersonator can take Pycroft’s expected position at Mawson & Williams without immediate suspicion.

records.l: the impersonation of Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
records.s: The impersonation of Hall Pycroft allows Beddington to obtain a clerk’s position at Mawson & Williams under Pycroft’s name. The real Pycroft is kept away from London by promises of employment and an advance, while the false Pycroft studies the premises and prepares the robbery.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. Watson about the case of the Gloria Scott, which was the first criminal investigation in which Holmes was involved. As a college student, Holmes visited Donnithorpe and observed that Victor Trevor's father, Mr. Trevor, feared a past connection involving the sailor Hudson and another man named Beddoes. Hudson gained power over Mr. Trevor, and a strange coded message sent from Hampshire caused Mr. Trevor to suffer a fatal stroke. Holmes determines that every third word of the message, beginning with the first, contains a warning that explains Mr. Trevor's terror.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Sherlock Holmes recounts his first criminal case to Dr. Watson. During his visit to Donnithorpe, he deduces details about Mr. Trevor's past from his appearance and later recognizes that the strange message contains a hidden meaning.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Dr. Watson listens as Sherlock Holmes explains the case of the Gloria Scott and examines the papers and coded message Holmes shows him.

records.l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Victor Trevor was Sherlock Holmes's only friend during his two years at college and invited him to Donnithorpe. He later summoned Holmes back when his father was dying and explained how Hudson had gained control over the household.

records.l: Mr. Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Mr. Trevor was Victor Trevor's father, a wealthy landowner, Justice of the Peace, and former traveler and gold-digger. He had a half-effaced tattoo bearing the initials J. A., feared a past connection, and fell under Hudson's power before suffering a fatal stroke after receiving a coded message.

records.l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Hudson was a sailor who had known Mr. Trevor and Mr. Beddoes many years earlier. After returning to Mr. Trevor's house, he obtained employment there, behaved abusively, and appeared to use knowledge of the past to control Mr. Trevor.

records.l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The Gloria Scott is the subject of the extraordinary case documented in the papers Sherlock Holmes shows Dr. Watson.

records.l: the case of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The case of the Gloria Scott was the first case in which Sherlock Holmes was ever engaged. Its documents concern Mr. Trevor's past, Hudson's threats, and the coded message that preceded Mr. Trevor's death.

records.l: the warning message, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The coded message appeared to discuss game, a head-keeper, fly-paper, and a hen-pheasant's life. Sherlock Holmes realizes that reading every third word, beginning with the first, reveals a threatening message capable of explaining Mr. Trevor's terror.

records.l: the secret code, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The secret code hides a second meaning in an apparently trivial and grotesque message. Sherlock Holmes discovers that the message is deciphered by taking every third word, beginning with the first.

records.l: the secret held over the men by Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The guilty secret appears to involve Mr. Trevor, Hudson, and Mr. Beddoes, who had been associated in the past. Holmes believes Hudson may have threatened to expose it or that Beddoes may have warned Mr. Trevor about such an exposure.

records.l: Donnithorpe, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Donnithorpe was the Norfolk home of Mr. Trevor and Victor Trevor, where Sherlock Holmes spent part of the long vacation. Hudson later lived and acted abusively within the household there.

records.l: the papers concerning the Gloria Scott case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The papers concerning the Gloria Scott case were kept in the back drawer of the Japanese cabinet. Victor Trevor retrieved them after his father's death and gave them to Sherlock Holmes.

records.l: Mr. Trevor's death, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Mr. Trevor died shortly after suffering a stroke caused by the coded message. Before his death, he briefly regained consciousness and said that the papers were in the back drawer of the Japanese cabinet.

records.l: Mr. Trevor's stroke, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: Mr. Trevor suffered a stroke immediately after reading a letter bearing the Fordingbridge postmark. The paralysis spread, he did not regain consciousness except briefly before his death, and the letter was later understood to contain a hidden warning.

records.l: the threat and blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
records.s: The text suggests that Hudson used knowledge of the guilty secret to blackmail or otherwise control Mr. Trevor. Victor Trevor also believed Hudson might have intended to blackmail Mr. Beddoes.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: The warning message tells Victor Trevor that Hudson has revealed everything and that he must flee for his life. Holmes explains that the message uses a prearranged cipher and infers from its sporting terms that Beddoes likely sent it. Victor recalls that his father received invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves. Victor then gives Holmes a statement written by his father about the danger posed by Hudson and asks Holmes to read it aloud.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: Holmes explains how the warning message's prearranged cipher works and infers that its sporting vocabulary suggests the sender is an ardent shot or interested in breeding. He asks Victor whether he knows anything about Beddoes and concludes that Beddoes sent the note.

records.l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: Victor is distressed by the warning, believing that its meaning involves disgrace as well as danger. He recalls his father's invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves and gives Holmes his father's statement, asking Holmes to read it because he lacks the strength and courage to do so himself.

records.l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: Hudson is identified in the warning as having told all. He is described as a sailor who held a secret over the heads of two wealthy and respected men, including Victor Trevor's father.

records.l: Beddoes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: Beddoes is identified by Holmes as the likely sender of the warning because of its sporting references. Victor recalls that Beddoes used to invite his father to shoot over his preserves every autumn.

records.l: Victor Trevor's father, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: Victor Trevor's father received autumn invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves. He wrote a statement when the danger from Hudson became imminent, and Victor found it in the Japanese cabinet.

records.l: the warning message, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: The warning says, "The game is up. Hudson has told all. Fly for your life." It uses a prearranged cipher in which the writer fills spaces with two additional words, including the sporting terms "head-keepers" and "hen pheasants."

records.l: the statement drawn up by Victor Trevor's father, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: The statement was written by Victor Trevor's father when Hudson's danger had become imminent. Victor found it in the Japanese cabinet and hands it to Holmes to read aloud.

records.l: the secret held over the men by Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
records.s: The secret is described as something that Hudson held over the heads of two wealthy and respected men. Victor fears that it concerns sin and shame, but its nature is not revealed in this unit.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The unit concerns papers read to Watson, including a letter in which Trevor reveals that his real name is James Armitage. Armitage explains that he was convicted of breaking the law, transported aboard the Gloria Scott, and placed among thirty-eight convicts bound for Australia. He describes meeting Jack Prendergast, who had organized a conspiracy involving prisoners, the crew, the chaplain, two warders, and the second mate to seize the ship. The conspirators secretly obtained weapons and planned a nighttime attack before events forced the plot to begin sooner than expected.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: Watson is present as the papers are read aloud to him. The papers include a letter describing James Armitage's past and the voyage of the Gloria Scott.

records.l: James Armitage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: James Armitage says that he formerly used the name Trevor. He was convicted of breaking the law after using money that was not his own to pay a debt of honour, and he was sentenced to transportation aboard the Gloria Scott.

records.l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: Trevor is revealed to be the name James Armitage used later in life. The letter is addressed by Trevor to his son and explains his former identity and conviction.

records.l: Jack Prendergast, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: Jack Prendergast is a very tall convict and the leader of a plot to gain command of the Gloria Scott. He had obtained large sums of money through fraud, retained money that was not recovered, and used it to recruit the crew and others to the conspiracy.

records.l: Wilson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The chaplain is described as a partner in Prendergast's plan. He is secretly a sham chaplain who comes aboard with correct papers, money, and a black bag, and he has bought the loyalty of the crew, two warders, and the second mate.

records.l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The Gloria Scott is an old five-hundred-ton vessel formerly used in the Chinese tea trade and later used to transport convicts. It carries thirty-eight convicts, twenty-six crew members, eighteen soldiers, officers, a doctor, a chaplain, and four warders.

records.l: Watson's papers, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: Watson's papers are read aloud and are endorsed with particulars of the voyage of the bark Gloria Scott from its departure from Falmouth to its destruction. They contain the letter in which James Armitage recounts his past and the events aboard the ship.

records.l: letter about the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The letter is written by Trevor to his son. It states that Trevor's real name is James Armitage and records his conviction, transportation, and involvement in the events aboard the Gloria Scott.

records.l: the voyage of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The voyage begins with the Gloria Scott leaving Falmouth on October 8, 1855, carrying nearly one hundred people toward Australia. During the voyage, the prisoners receive weapons, organize a conspiracy, and prepare to seize the ship.

records.l: the destruction of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The papers are endorsed as covering the destruction of the Gloria Scott on November 6, in north latitude 15º 20’ and west longitude 25º 14’. This unit has not yet described the destruction itself.

records.l: transportation to Australia, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: James Armitage is sentenced to transportation to Australia after his conviction. He is carried there aboard the Gloria Scott with thirty-seven other convicts.

records.l: James Armitage's conviction, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: James Armitage is convicted of breaking his country's laws after using money entrusted to him to pay a debt of honour. He receives the sentence of transportation and is placed aboard the Gloria Scott on his twenty-third birthday.

records.l: the conspiracy to seize the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The conspiracy is organized before the prisoners come aboard, with Jack Prendergast as its leader and his money as its motive power. Its members obtain pistols, powder, files, and slugs, recruit the crew and others, and plan a sudden nighttime attack.

records.l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The prisoners include thirty-eight convicts transported aboard the Gloria Scott. Nearly all join the conspiracy after receiving weapons, except for one prisoner considered mentally weak and another suffering from jaundice.

records.l: the conspirators, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The conspirators include Prendergast, many of the prisoners, the sham chaplain, two warders, Mercer the second mate, and the crew. They conceal weapons in their cells and prepare to attack the opposing officers, soldiers, warders, and doctor.

records.l: the crew of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: The crew are described as ruffians specially picked for the conspiracy. Prendergast's partner, posing as the chaplain, buys their loyalty before they sign on.

records.l: Australia, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
records.s: Australia is the destination to which James Armitage and the other convicts are being transported aboard the Gloria Scott.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The narrative describes the mutiny aboard the transport ship Gloria Scott, in which the prisoners and some sailors seize the vessel and massacre most of its officers and soldiers. Prendergast leads the surviving mutineers, while Evans and others refuse to participate in the execution of the remaining prisoners and escape in a boat. The Gloria Scott is destroyed when the first mate threatens to ignite a powder barrel and an explosion kills those aboard. Years later, Evans and Beddoes are threatened and blackmailed by Hudson, a sailor who survived the wreck, but all three men ultimately disappear.

records.l: Jack Prendergast, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: Prendergast leads the mutiny after the prisoners break free, killing soldiers and insisting that the remaining warders, mates, and doctor must be silenced. He refuses to spare them, permits Evans and seven others to leave in a boat, and later kills the surgeon before the first mate causes the Gloria Scott to explode.

records.l: Evans, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: Evans participates in the mutiny but refuses, with seven others, to approve the cold-blooded killing of the surviving officers and warders. He escapes in a boat, is picked up by the brig Hotspur, changes his name in Sydney, and later becomes wealthy with Beddoes. He recognizes Hudson as the sailor rescued from the wreck and fears Hudson's threats.

records.l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: Hudson is a young seaman who survives the destruction of the Gloria Scott by clinging to wreckage and is rescued by Evans and the others. Years later, he tracks down Evans and Beddoes and lives upon their fears by threatening to expose their past. He and Beddoes eventually disappear.

records.l: Beddoes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
