records.s: Beddoes is one of the men involved in the mutiny and later changes his name with Evans after reaching Sydney. He becomes wealthy and lives peacefully for more than twenty years before Hudson threatens to reveal their past. A cipher warns that Hudson has told all; Beddoes then disappears, probably after killing Hudson and fleeing with money.

records.l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The prisoners are held aboard the Gloria Scott and help carry out the mutiny after the doctor discovers hidden pistols. Most of them participate in the fighting and subsequent massacre, while Evans and four other convicts refuse to support the killing of the remaining prisoners and leave in a boat.

records.l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The convicts overpower the guards and soldiers, seize weapons, and take control of the Gloria Scott. Some convicts join Prendergast in killing the remaining officers, while five convicts, including Evans, reject the executions and escape. A group of convicts later confronts the first mate beside an open powder barrel, triggering the ship's destruction.

records.l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The Gloria Scott is a transport ship carrying prisoners that is captured during a violent mutiny. After the escape boat leaves, the ship's first mate threatens to blow it up using a powder barrel, and an explosion destroys the vessel and nearly everyone aboard. The Admiralty records it as lost at sea without learning its true fate.

records.l: the transport-ship mutiny and massacre, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The mutiny begins when the doctor discovers pistols hidden beneath a prisoner's bunk. The mutineers shoot the sentries, soldiers, and captain, then massacre many of the remaining prisoners and officers; the violence causes a dispute when Evans and seven others refuse to support further executions.

records.l: the escape from the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: Evans and seven others leave the Gloria Scott in a boat after refusing to participate in the planned executions. They receive sailors' clothing, provisions, a compass, and a false account describing them as shipwrecked mariners, then head toward Sierra Leone before seeing the Gloria Scott explode.

records.l: the destruction of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: The first mate escapes his bonds and hides beside an open powder barrel in the after-hold, threatening to blow up the ship if attacked. An explosion follows, possibly caused by a convict's misdirected bullet rather than the mate's match, destroying the Gloria Scott and killing the mutineers and remaining people aboard except for Hudson.

records.l: the threat and blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
records.s: Hudson tracks down Evans and Beddoes decades after the mutiny and threatens to expose their involvement in the Gloria Scott. Evans tries to keep the peace because of the danger, but a warning says that Hudson has told all; Hudson and Beddoes then disappear, with the narrator believing that Beddoes killed Hudson and fled.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. John Watson about the Musgrave Ritual case, an early investigation that helped establish his professional reputation. Reginald Musgrave asks Holmes to investigate the disappearance of his butler, Brunton, and the subsequent disappearance of Rachel Howells at Hurlstone. Brunton had been caught studying the family’s ritual document, while Rachel’s footprints led to the mere, where a linen bag containing rusted metal and dull pebbles was recovered. Holmes begins by asking to examine the ritual document.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Sherlock Holmes recounts the Musgrave Ritual case to Dr. John Watson. He is consulted by Reginald Musgrave after Brunton and Rachel Howells disappear, and he begins investigating by asking to see the ritual document.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Dr. John Watson listens as Sherlock Holmes describes the Musgrave Ritual case and its connection to Holmes’s early professional work. He had heard Holmes mention the case before but did not know its details.

records.l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The Musgrave Ritual is a private family observance performed by each Musgrave on coming of age. It is considered ancient and of possible archaeological interest, though Reginald Musgrave initially regards it as having no practical use.

records.l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Reginald Musgrave is a former college acquaintance of Sherlock Holmes and a member of an old family established at Hurlstone in western Sussex. He asks Holmes to investigate strange events at Hurlstone after Brunton and Rachel Howells disappear.

records.l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Brunton is the long-serving butler at Hurlstone, known for his intelligence, languages, musical ability, and womanizing. Reginald Musgrave catches him secretly studying a copy of the Musgrave Ritual and dismisses him, after which Brunton disappears from the house, leaving his clothes, watch, and money behind.

records.l: Rachel Howells, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Rachel Howells is the second housemaid at Hurlstone who had been engaged to Brunton before he abandoned her for Janet Tregellis. After Brunton’s disappearance she becomes ill and hysterical, then vanishes from her room; her footprints lead to the mere, but her body is not found.

records.l: Hurlstone, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Hurlstone is the Musgrave family estate in western Sussex. Strange events there include Brunton’s secret examination of the ritual document, his disappearance, and Rachel Howells’s disappearance.

records.l: the Musgrave Ritual case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The Musgrave Ritual case is one of Sherlock Holmes’s early investigations and is described as a singular chain of events with unusually large issues at stake. It concerns the ritual document, Brunton’s disappearance, Rachel Howells’s disappearance, and the objects recovered from the mere.

records.l: the ritual document, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The ritual document is a copy of the questions and answers used in the Musgrave family’s ancient observance. Brunton secretly removes it from a bureau and studies it in the library, prompting Reginald Musgrave to dismiss him; Holmes asks to examine it.

records.l: the library, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The library at Hurlstone is where Reginald Musgrave discovers Brunton late at night. Brunton is sitting there with a chart-like paper and secretly studies the ritual document by the light of a taper.

records.l: the mere, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The mere is the lake on the Hurlstone grounds, which is eight feet deep. Rachel Howells’s footprints lead to its edge, and a search there recovers a linen bag, though no body is found.

records.l: the linen bag, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The linen bag is recovered from the mere during the search for Rachel Howells. It contains rusted and discoloured metal along with several dull-coloured pieces of pebble or glass.

records.l: the rusted metal and dull pebbles, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The rusted metal and dull pebbles are found inside the linen bag recovered from the mere. Their nature is not explained in this unit.

records.l: the Hurlstone house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The Hurlstone house is a rambling old building with a labyrinthine original wing that is largely uninhabited. Brunton disappears from it despite its doors and windows being found fastened, and the house is searched without revealing his whereabouts.

records.l: the disappearance of Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: The disappearance of Brunton occurs after he is ordered to leave Hurlstone within a week for secretly examining the ritual document. He is last seen before retiring to his room, and afterward his clothes, watch, and money remain there while his black suit and slippers are missing.

records.l: Howells's disappearance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
records.s: Rachel Howells disappears from her room on the third night after Brunton’s disappearance while a nurse is watching over her. Her open window and footprints lead toward the mere, but neither she nor her body is found.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Musgrave shows Watson a paper containing the Musgrave catechism, a seventeenth-century family text of questions and answers. The catechism concerns ownership, succession, the positions of the sun and shadow, a sequence of steps, and a trust. Holmes believes the paper is practical and that Brunton had consulted it while comparing it with a map or chart. Holmes and Musgrave plan to travel to Sussex to investigate the mystery on the spot.

records.l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Musgrave gives Watson the paper containing the catechism and reads its questions and answers. He says the original has no date but uses the spelling of the middle of the seventeenth century, and he initially doubts that it can help solve the mystery.

records.l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Holmes believes Brunton had previously seen the Musgrave catechism and consulted it on the night Musgrave caught him. Brunton apparently compared it with some map or chart, which he put into his pocket when Musgrave appeared.

records.l: Musgrave family, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: The Musgrave family preserved the catechism, which each Musgrave had to answer when he came to man's estate. The original is written in spelling associated with the middle of the seventeenth century.

records.l: Sussex, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Holmes proposes that he and Musgrave take the first train to Sussex to investigate the matter more deeply at the location.

records.l: paper containing the Musgrave catechism, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Musgrave has the paper with him and shows it to Watson. It contains the catechism, has no date, and is written in the spelling of the middle of the seventeenth century.

records.l: Musgrave catechism, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: The catechism asks whose possession something belonged to, who will receive it, where the sun and shadow were, how it was stepped, what should be given for it, and why it should be given. Its answers refer to the person who is gone, the person who will come, the oak, the elm, a sequence of directional steps, all that is owned, and the sake of the trust.

records.l: map or chart, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: Brunton apparently had a map or chart that he compared with the Musgrave manuscript. He thrust it into his pocket when Musgrave appeared.

records.l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: The custom required each Musgrave to submit to the catechism when he came to man's estate. Musgrave says the paper was not hidden from others.

records.l: mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
records.s: The catechism gives Holmes another mystery, which he considers even more interesting than the first. Holmes suspects that solving one mystery may solve the other and plans to investigate further in Sussex.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Sherlock Holmes follows the Musgrave Ritual’s measurements from the oak and former elm at Hurlstone to the cellar beneath the old house. There he and Reginald Musgrave find Brunton’s muffler, a concealed chamber, a brass-bound box, and Brunton’s dead body. Holmes infers that Brunton and Howells opened the chamber, that Howells may have caused or concealed Brunton’s death, and that she took the box’s contents. The recovered objects are identified as the ancient crown of the Kings of England, a Royalist treasure hidden during the troubles after Charles I’s execution and intended for Charles II.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Sherlock Holmes interprets the Musgrave Ritual, uses the oak, the former elm, the sun, and the stated measurements to locate the concealed cellar chamber, and finds Brunton’s body there. He reconstructs Brunton’s investigation and probable death, identifies the recovered relic as the ancient crown of the Kings of England, and explains its historical significance to Reginald Musgrave.

records.l: Hurlstone, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Hurlstone is an old L-shaped building with an ancient nucleus dated by an inscription to 1607, though its beams and stonework are considered older. Its old section contains a cellar beneath a stone passage, and the estate includes the oak, the former elm, and a lake or mere.

records.l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The Musgrave Ritual gives directions involving an oak, an elm, measurements, cardinal directions, and a location under the old door and passage. Holmes uses it to find the cellar chamber and interprets its opening questions as referring to a crown belonging first to the dead Charles I and then to the returning Charles II.

records.l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Reginald Musgrave brings Holmes to Hurlstone and supplies information about the oak, the former elm, and the Ritual. He helps open the cellar, recognizes Brunton’s muffler and body, identifies the coins as belonging to Charles I, and learns from Holmes that the hidden relic is the ancient crown.

records.l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Brunton, the Musgrave butler, studied the Ritual, asked about the height of the former elm, located the concealed chamber, and apparently entered it with Howells. He was found dead inside the chamber beside the opened box, with no wound or bruise indicating how he died.

records.l: Howells, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Howells, a maid formerly devoted to Brunton, is believed by Holmes to have helped him raise the cellar flagstone and waited above while he entered the chamber. Holmes suspects that she either allowed the support to slip or deliberately removed it, leaving Brunton trapped, and that she took or disposed of the box’s contents before disappearing.

records.l: oak tree (Hurlstone), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The oak tree stands in front of Hurlstone on the left side of the drive and is described as an exceptionally old and magnificent tree. Its height and position provide one of the fixed points Holmes uses to calculate the location of the Ritual’s destination.

records.l: elm tree (Hurlstone), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The old elm at Hurlstone had been struck by lightning and cut down about ten years before Holmes’s investigation. Its former location, its remembered height of sixty-four feet, and the direction of its shadow allow Holmes to reconstruct Brunton’s measurements.

records.l: Hurlstone cellar, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The cellar beneath the old passage contains a concealed chamber about seven feet deep and four feet square. Holmes and the others find the chamber recently cleared of wood, with the flagstone raised, the box opened, and Brunton’s body beside it.

records.l: flagstone (Hurlstone cellar), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: A large, heavy flagstone with a rusted iron ring covers the concealed chamber in the cellar. Brunton and Howells apparently used pieces of wood to hold it open, but it later closed over Brunton and became his sepulchre.

records.l: Brunton's muffler, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Brunton’s thick shepherd’s-check muffler is attached to the iron ring of the cellar flagstone. Reginald Musgrave recognizes it as Brunton’s, showing that Brunton had been working at the concealed opening.

records.l: brass-bound wooden box (Hurlstone cellar), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The brass-bound wooden box lies in the concealed chamber with its hinged lid open and an old key projecting from the lock. It contains several old metal discs or coins, while Holmes infers that its more valuable contents had been removed.

records.l: crown of the Kings of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The crown of the Kings of England is identified by Holmes as the battered, twisted relic recovered from the mere and associated with the hidden box. It is said to have great intrinsic value and greater historical importance as a relic of the royal Stuarts.

records.l: Charles I of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Charles I of England is represented in the Ritual by the phrase “His who is gone,” which Holmes interprets as referring to the period after Charles’s execution. The coins found in the box are identified by Reginald Musgrave as coins of Charles I.

records.l: Charles II of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Charles II of England is represented in the Ritual by the phrase “He who will come,” referring to his anticipated return. Holmes says the crown was intended for Charles II, though Charles did not recover it after returning.

records.l: Brunton's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Brunton’s investigation involved mastering the Musgrave Ritual, asking about the former elm’s height, locating the Ritual’s destination, and opening the concealed chamber. He apparently entered the chamber to retrieve the hidden treasure and was trapped inside.

records.l: Brunton's death, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Brunton’s body is found crouched beside the opened box in the concealed chamber after he has been dead for several days. No wound or bruise is found, and Holmes concludes that the flagstone probably closed over him after Howells assisted or abandoned him.

records.l: Howells's disappearance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Howells disappears after the events in the cellar. Holmes believes she fled after taking the treasure and that she may have left England carrying the memory of Brunton’s death.

records.l: discovery of the crown, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The crown is discovered through Holmes’s interpretation of the Ritual, the cellar search, and the examination of the debris recovered from the mere. A dark, twisted double ring with a stone that shines after being rubbed is identified as part of the ancient crown.

records.l: historical identity of the crown, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: Holmes identifies the relic as the ancient crown of the Kings of England and connects it with the royal Stuarts. He infers that it was hidden by Royalists during the troubles after Charles I’s death and was meant to be recovered by Charles II.

records.l: Musgrave Ritual's riddle, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The Ritual’s riddle includes the questions “Whose was it?” and “Who shall have it?” with the answers “His who is gone” and “He who will come.” Holmes interprets these as references to Charles I after his execution and Charles II before his return.

records.l: Royalist treasure, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
records.s: The Royalist treasure consisted of precious possessions hidden during the period when the Royal party was defeated or in flight, with the hope of later recovery. The treasure at Hurlstone included the ancient crown and associated metalwork and stones.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, recovering from a severe illness after an international investigation, visits Reigate with Dr. Watson and stays at Colonel Hayter's house. They learn that the Acton burglary involved the theft of several unusual household items and that the Cunningham burglary has ended in the shooting death of William Kirwan. Inspector Forrester reports that the same burglar is suspected in both incidents and produces a fragment of paper found in William Kirwan's hand, bearing the hour of his death. Holmes investigates the Cunningham case, focuses on the fragment and William's letter, and asks to inspect Cunningham's house.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Reigate with Dr. Watson while recovering from the strain of a prolonged investigation. Although he initially agrees to rest, he becomes intensely interested in the Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder, examines the fragment of paper, visits the crime scene with Inspector Forrester, and develops theories about William Kirwan's letter and the missing portion of the note.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Dr. Watson goes to Lyons to care for Sherlock Holmes and then brings him to Colonel Hayter's house near Reigate for a restorative country visit. He recognizes that Holmes's interest in the Cunningham case makes it impossible for them to remain uninvolved and accompanies the investigation.

records.l: Colonel Hayter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Colonel Hayter hosts Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson at his bachelor house near Reigate. He tells them about the Acton burglary, discusses the Cunningham burglary and murder, and agrees to accompany Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Forrester to Cunningham's house.

records.l: Inspector Forrester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Inspector Forrester investigates the Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder. He tells Holmes that the burglar was seen fleeing after shooting William Kirwan, shows Holmes the fragment of paper found in Kirwan's hand, and joins Holmes in examining the crime scene and interviewing people connected with it.

records.l: Cunningham (Alec Cunningham's father), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Mr. Cunningham is a Justice of the Peace whose house was entered during the Cunningham burglary. He heard the alarm, saw the fleeing burglar from his bedroom window, and later showed Holmes and Inspector Forrester where the burglar crossed the garden hedge.

records.l: Alec Cunningham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Alec Cunningham was smoking in his dressing-gown when he heard William Kirwan calling for help. He ran downstairs, saw two men wrestling outside the open back door, and witnessed one of them shoot the other before fleeing.

records.l: William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: William Kirwan, the Cunninghams' coachman, was shot through the heart while confronting a burglar at the house. He died without speaking, and a fragment of a note was found between his finger and thumb; he had received a letter by the afternoon post on the day of his death.

records.l: the burglar, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: The burglar forced entry at Cunningham's house, struggled with William Kirwan, shot him, and escaped across the garden and over a hedge. He was described as a middle-sized man wearing dark clothing, and he is suspected of also committing the Acton burglary.

records.l: the burglars, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: The burglars who entered Acton's house ransacked the library, drawers, and presses before taking an odd volume of Pope's 'Homer,' two plated candlesticks, an ivory letter-weight, a small oak barometer, and a ball of twine. They remained at large, and the same party is suspected in the Cunningham incident.

records.l: the Acton burglary, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: The Acton burglary occurred on the Monday before Holmes and Watson arrived at Colonel Hayter's house. The house was extensively searched, but the burglars took only an unusual assortment of objects, and the police had found no clue.

records.l: the Cunningham burglary and murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: The Cunningham burglary occurred at about midnight after the burglar forced the back-door lock or entered through the pantry window. William Kirwan confronted the intruder and was shot, while Mr. Cunningham and Alec Cunningham saw the fleeing man; Inspector Forrester believes the incident was connected to the Acton burglary.

records.l: Reigate, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Reigate in Surrey is the area near which Colonel Hayter has a house. The Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder occur in this district.

records.l: Colonel Hayter's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Colonel Hayter's house near Reigate provides lodging for Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson during their country visit. From the house, they hear about the local crimes and meet Inspector Forrester.

records.l: Cunningham's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: Cunningham's house is entered by a burglar, and William Kirwan is shot outside its back door during the intrusion. Holmes and Inspector Forrester inspect the property, interview Mr. Cunningham and Alec Cunningham, and identify the hedge used by the fleeing burglar.

records.l: fragment of paper, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: The fragment of paper is found between William Kirwan's finger and thumb after his death. It bears the hour at which he was killed and appears to be part of an appointment note; Holmes believes the missing portion could help identify the person who wrote it.

records.l: William Kirwan's letter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
records.s: William Kirwan received a letter by the afternoon post on the day he was killed, but the envelope was destroyed. Holmes reasons that the letter may have contained the message bringing Kirwan out at the hour of his death and asks about the missing remainder of the sheet.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the murder of coachman William Kirwan and the attempted burglary at the Cunningham house with Dr. Watson and the Inspector. He questions Mr. Cunningham and Alec Cunningham, examines the house, and deliberately stages illness and confusion to obtain a reward notice and search the rooms. Holmes then provokes a confrontation, discovers the remainder of a sheet of paper, and accuses the Cunninghams of murdering William. The Inspector arrests them after Alec is found with a revolver and both men display apparent signs of guilt.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the Cunningham house and questions the family about the burglary, the house’s layout, and the events surrounding William Kirwan’s death. He pretends to suffer nervous attacks, deliberately knocks over a dish of oranges and water, and uses the confusion to search for evidence. After being attacked by the Cunninghams, he orders their arrest and produces the remainder of a sheet of paper as evidence.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes, the Inspector, and the Colonel to the Cunningham house. He helps Holmes maintain the appearance that Holmes is ill and takes the blame when Holmes knocks over the oranges, water, and dish. He rushes to Holmes’s aid when Holmes cries for help and witnesses the arrest of the Cunninghams.

records.l: Inspector Forrester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The Inspector assists Holmes in investigating William Kirwan’s murder and the attempted burglary. He questions the circumstances, helps search the house, and calls additional constables after Holmes accuses the Cunninghams. He arrests the men after Alec Cunningham’s revolver is knocked from his hand.

records.l: Cunningham (Alec Cunningham's father), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Mr. Cunningham, the older Cunningham and a J.P., explains where he was during the incident and shows Holmes through his house. He signs a reward notice after correcting the time of the attempted burglary from a quarter to one to a quarter to twelve. After Holmes accuses him and Alec of murdering William Kirwan, he is restrained and arrested.

records.l: Alec Cunningham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Alec Cunningham claims that there is no clue to the crime and argues against Holmes’s theory that the burglar entered the house before William Kirwan was attacked. He accompanies his father during the search and attacks Holmes when Holmes is discovered. After Holmes’s accusation, Alec displays apparent ferocity and attempts to cock a revolver before the Inspector disarms him.

records.l: William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: William Kirwan is identified as the Cunninghams’ coachman and the murdered man. He was found wounded after apparently tackling a burglar, and Holmes concludes that the Cunninghams murdered him.

records.l: the Cunninghams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The Cunninghams claim that a burglar forced the house door but did not enter, and they allow Holmes to inspect the house. They attack Holmes after he searches the rooms, and Holmes accuses them of murdering William Kirwan. Their expressions appear to the Inspector and Dr. Watson to show guilt, and they are arrested.

records.l: the Cunningham house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The Cunningham house is a Queen Anne house with a forced side door, an oak-lined avenue, and several rooms and stairways relevant to the investigation. Mr. Cunningham’s and Alec Cunningham’s rooms overlook the front, and both men say their lamps were lit during the incident. Holmes searches the house and finds the remainder of a sheet of paper.

records.l: the murder of William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The murder concerns William Kirwan, who was found wounded after an alleged struggle with a burglar near the Cunningham house. Holmes ultimately accuses Mr. Cunningham and Alec Cunningham of murdering him, and the Inspector arrests them.

records.l: the attempted burglary at the Cunningham house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The attempted burglary involved a door forced with a chisel or strong knife at about a quarter to twelve on Tuesday morning. The Cunninghams maintain that the burglar did not enter, while Holmes suggests that the burglar may have entered before William Kirwan confronted him.

records.l: the Cunningham burglary and murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The investigation examines the forced door, the positions of the witnesses, the lighting in the house, and the possibility that the burglar took unusual objects rather than valuables. Holmes uses a staged illness, a false mistake in the reward notice, and a staged accident to uncover evidence and expose the Cunninghams.

records.l: the burglar, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The burglar is described as an unusual and experienced criminal who allegedly forced the Cunningham house door. Holmes notes that such a burglar might have taken odd objects, as in the earlier burglary at Acton’s, and questions whether he entered the house before William Kirwan arrived.

records.l: the reward notice, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Holmes asks Mr. Cunningham to sign a reward notice offering fifty pounds, although Mr. Cunningham says he would willingly give five hundred. The notice initially gives the time as a quarter to one, but Mr. Cunningham corrects it to a quarter to twelve before signing it.

records.l: the revolver, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: Alec Cunningham produces and begins to cock a revolver after Holmes accuses the Cunninghams. The Inspector strikes it from his hand, and Holmes places his foot on it, saying it will be useful at the trial.

records.l: the evidence of guilt, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,
records.s: The evidence of guilt includes the remainder of a sheet of paper found by Holmes, Alec Cunningham’s revolver, and the Cunninghams’ attacks on Holmes. Their faces also appear to show a clear confession of guilt, with the father looking dazed and sullen and Alec appearing ferocious.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to the Colonel, Mr. Acton, and Watson how he solved the killing of William Kirwan and linked it to the original burglary at Mr. Acton's house. He concludes that Alec Cunningham and his father wrote the note together, staged the crime, and killed William after he blackmailed them. Holmes recovered the missing part of the note from Alec's dressing-gown after feigning a fit and provoking a distraction. Cunningham's confession confirms that William followed the pair during the burglary and threatened to expose them.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains his deductions about the note, the original burglary, and the killing of William Kirwan. He determines that the Cunninghams were responsible, recovers the missing part of the note, and obtains Cunningham's confession.

records.l: Colonel Hayter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The Colonel listens to Holmes's explanation and expresses admiration for his methods. He had told Holmes about the lawsuit between Mr. Acton and the Cunninghams.

records.l: Old Acton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Mr. Acton attends Holmes's explanation because his house was the scene of the original burglary. He explains that he had a claim to half of the Cunninghams' estate and that they sought a document that could have weakened his case.

records.l: Alec Cunningham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Alec Cunningham is identified as the younger writer of the note and the likely instigator of the burglary and killing. He lied about the shooting and the assailant's escape, tore the note from William Kirwan's hand, concealed it in his dressing-gown, and attacked Holmes when the paper was recovered.

records.l: Cunningham (Alec Cunningham's father), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Cunningham is identified as the older writer of the note and Alec's accomplice. After Holmes showed that the case against him was strong, he confessed that he and Alec had committed the burglary, lured and shot William Kirwan, and tried to conceal their involvement.

records.l: the Cunninghams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The Cunninghams are shown to have written the note together, with the older man and younger man alternating words. They lied about the shooting and escape, staged the appearance of an unknown burglar, and attacked Holmes to prevent him from exposing them.

records.l: William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: William Kirwan secretly followed the Cunninghams during their raid on Mr. Acton's house and threatened to expose them. He used this knowledge to levy blackmail, so Alec decoyed him and shot him.

records.l: Inspector Forrester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The Inspector submitted the scrap of paper to Holmes and overlooked the possibility that the Cunninghams were involved because he assumed the county magnates had no connection to the crime. He also nearly told the Cunninghams about the importance of the paper before Holmes's feigned fit interrupted him.

records.l: Mr. Acton's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Mr. Acton's house was the scene of the original burglary. The Cunninghams broke into its library seeking a document connected with their lawsuit against Mr. Acton.

records.l: the original burglary at Mr. Acton's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The original burglary was carried out by the Cunninghams to find a document that could have damaged Mr. Acton's claim to half of their estate. After finding nothing, they removed other items to make the incident look like an ordinary burglary.

records.l: the murder of William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The killing was staged to resemble a burglary-related attack by an unknown man. Holmes determines that William was shot from more than four yards away, that Alec lied about a struggle, and that no unknown assailant escaped across the ditch.

records.l: the investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The investigation follows the scrap of paper, the physical evidence at the scene, and the connection between the burglary and the lawsuit. Holmes's deductions establish the Cunninghams' involvement and lead to Cunningham's confession.

records.l: William Kirwan's letter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The letter was written by two people alternating words, with the stronger hand writing first and leaving spaces for the weaker hand. Holmes concludes that the two writers were the younger and older Cunninghams and that the stronger-handed writer planned the affair.

records.l: the scrap of paper, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The scrap of paper found in William Kirwan's hand is the key to Holmes's investigation. Its handwriting, wording, and missing portion lead Holmes to Alec Cunningham and eventually allow him to recover the rest of the note.

records.l: the complete note, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: The complete note asks William to come to the east gate at quarter to twelve and promises information useful to him and Annie Morrison. Holmes recognizes it as the bait used to lure William into the trap.

records.l: handwriting analysis, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Holmes's handwriting analysis identifies two alternating writers, one young and strong-handed and the other older with a broken-backed hand. He also detects family resemblances, including shared letter forms, and concludes that the writers were the Cunninghams.

records.l: the blackmail of William Kirwan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: William Kirwan blackmailed the Cunninghams after secretly following them during the raid on Mr. Acton's house. His threats gave Alec a motive to arrange William's killing.

records.l: Holmes's feigned fit, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he
records.s: Holmes pretends to collapse in a fit when the Inspector is about to tell the Cunninghams that the paper is important. The deception prevents them from destroying the evidence and gives Holmes an opportunity to obtain a handwriting sample from Cunningham.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Dr. John Watson late at night and asks him to accompany him to Aldershot to investigate the supposed murder of Colonel James Barclay. Holmes explains that Barclay, commander of the Royal Mallows, was found involved in a recent tragedy at his home, Lachine, though the facts are only two days old and have attracted little attention outside the locality. Colonel Barclay and his wife, Nancy Barclay, had appeared to have a happy marriage, despite his occasional violence, depression, superstition, and fear of being alone after dark. Holmes has several threads of the case but believes that Watson may help him reach a solution.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Watson at nearly midnight and deduces details about Watson's work and habits from his appearance and surroundings. He asks Watson to travel with him to Aldershot and outlines his investigation into the supposed murder of Colonel Barclay, saying that he is close to solving it but lacks one or two necessary facts.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Dr. John Watson receives Sherlock Holmes at his home and agrees to accompany him to Aldershot on the 11.10 train from Waterloo. He listens as Holmes describes the case of Colonel Barclay and offers to assist with the final step of the investigation.

records.l: Colonel James Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Colonel James Barclay commanded the Royal Mallows until the Monday night before Holmes's visit. He was a gallant veteran who rose from private to commissioned rank, married Nancy Devoy, and was generally regarded as devoted to his wife. His character included occasional violence and vindictiveness, periods of deep depression, superstition, and a dislike of being left alone, especially after dark.

records.l: Nancy Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Nancy Barclay, whose maiden name was Nancy Devoy, was the daughter of a former colour-sergeant of the Royal Mallows and married Colonel Barclay when he was still a sergeant. She was a beautiful and striking woman who remained popular with the regiment's ladies, and her marriage to Barclay was considered happy despite her being less demonstratively affectionate than he was.

records.l: Royal Mallows, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: The Royal Mallows is a famous Irish regiment, formerly the 117th, known for distinguished service in the Crimea, the Mutiny, and later military actions. Colonel James Barclay commanded its first battalion until the Monday night of the reported tragedy.

records.l: Aldershot, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Aldershot is the location of the first battalion of the Royal Mallows and of the recent events involving Colonel Barclay. Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. John Watson to travel there with him to continue the investigation.

records.l: Lachine, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Lachine is the villa near the north camp at Aldershot where Colonel and Nancy Barclay lived. It stood on its own grounds, about half a mile from the camp and within thirty yards of the high-road, and was occupied by the Barclays, their coachman, and two maids.

records.l: the supposed murder of Colonel Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: The supposed murder of Colonel Barclay occurred at Aldershot on the Monday night before Sherlock Holmes's visit. The facts were only two days old and had attracted little attention beyond the local area.

records.l: the case of Colonel Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: The case of Colonel Barclay concerns the unexplained tragedy at Lachine and is being investigated by Sherlock Holmes. Holmes has already examined the matter and believes he is within sight of a solution, but he still needs one or two missing facts.

records.l: Holmes's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. The Crooked Man
records.s: Sherlock Holmes's investigation focuses on the supposed murder of Colonel James Barclay at Lachine in Aldershot. He has gathered information from Major Murphy and other officers about the Barclays, their marriage, Colonel Barclay's character, and the regiment, and he recruits Dr. John Watson to help complete the inquiry.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Mrs. Barclay returns to Lachine after meeting Miss Morrison, quarrels with Colonel James Barclay in the morning-room, and is found insensible beside his dead body. Sherlock Holmes investigates the locked-room death, discovering that a man entered through the window with a strange, long-bodied animal and carried away the door key. Miss Morrison reveals that Mrs. Barclay encountered Henry Wood shortly before the quarrel, and Holmes traces Wood to lodgings in Aldershot. Holmes believes Henry Wood alone can explain what happened in the room and plans to question him with Dr. Watson present.

records.l: Nancy Devoy Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Mrs. Barclay, a Roman Catholic interested in the Guild of St. George, attends a meeting with Miss Morrison and returns to Lachine shortly after nine. She encounters Henry Wood in Hudson Street, becomes deeply distressed, and later angrily quarrels with her husband before being found insensible in the morning-room. She is suspected of attacking Colonel Barclay and is temporarily unable to explain events because of brain-fever.

records.l: Colonel James Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Colonel James Barclay joins his wife in the morning-room after her return and is heard arguing with her. He is found dead from a jagged cut at the back of his head, with his face contorted in fear and horror. His name is significant because Mrs. Barclay is heard referring to someone named David during the quarrel.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates Colonel Barclay’s death at Major Murphy’s request. He examines the room, lawn, footprints, missing key, and animal traces, then questions Miss Morrison and searches for Henry Wood. Holmes concludes that Wood followed the women, entered through the window with the strange animal, and may be able to explain the death.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Dr. Watson listens as Holmes explains the Barclay case and agrees to accompany him to Aldershot. Holmes intends for Dr. Watson to witness his questioning of Henry Wood.

records.l: Miss Morrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Miss Morrison accompanies Mrs. Barclay to the Guild meeting and witnesses her encounter with Henry Wood in Hudson Street. She initially withholds the information but later tells Holmes that Wood called Mrs. Barclay Nancy and that Mrs. Barclay identified him as Henry, whom she had believed dead for thirty years.

records.l: Henry Wood, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Henry Wood is a deformed conjurer and performer who has recently arrived in Aldershot. He encounters Mrs. Barclay in Hudson Street, carries a box containing an unusual creature, and is later traced by Holmes to lodgings there. Holmes believes Wood followed Mrs. Barclay and Miss Morrison, watched the Barclay quarrel, entered the morning-room, and removed the key.

records.l: Lachine, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Lachine is the Barclay residence. Its morning-room faces the road and opens onto a lawn through large glass folding-doors.

records.l: Aldershot, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Aldershot is where Colonel Barclay’s death occurs and where Holmes investigates the case. Henry Wood is found lodging there, and Holmes plans to return there with Dr. Watson.

records.l: Hudson Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Hudson Street is a quiet thoroughfare through which Mrs. Barclay and Miss Morrison pass on their way home. Under its single street lamp, Mrs. Barclay encounters Henry Wood and speaks with him privately.

records.l: the morning-room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The morning-room at Lachine faces the road, has an unshaded glass folding-door opening onto the lawn, and contains a canary cage. Mrs. Barclay and Colonel Barclay argue there, Colonel Barclay dies there, and a man and a strange animal enter through the window.

records.l: the strange animal, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The strange animal leaves small five-padded footprints with long nails and appears to have climbed the curtain toward a canary cage. Its prints indicate a long body, very short legs, and carnivorous behavior. It travels in Henry Wood’s box, but its species remains unknown.

records.l: key (Nancy Barclay's door), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The key to the morning-room door is missing after Colonel Barclay’s death. It is found neither on Mrs. Barclay, Colonel Barclay, nor anywhere in the room, leading Holmes to infer that a third person entered through the window and carried it away.

records.l: the supposed murder of Colonel Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The apparent murder of Colonel Barclay follows a violent quarrel with Mrs. Barclay in the locked morning-room. Colonel Barclay suffers a fatal head injury from a blunt weapon, possibly a carved wooden club, although Holmes considers that he may instead have fallen from fright and struck the fender.

records.l: the Barclay quarrel, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The Barclay quarrel begins after Mrs. Barclay returns from the meeting with Miss Morrison. Mrs. Barclay repeatedly calls her husband a coward and demands that he give her back her life, while the servants hear a cry, a crash, and her scream.

records.l: Holmes's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Holmes’s investigation identifies footprints leading from the road across the lawn and into the morning-room, as well as traces of an unfamiliar animal. He uses Miss Morrison’s account to connect the quarrel with Henry Wood and locates Wood in Aldershot.

records.l: the capital charge against Mrs. Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: Mrs. Barclay faces a capital charge because suspicion falls on her after Colonel Barclay is found dead beside her in the locked room. Holmes warns Miss Morrison that Mrs. Barclay may be placed in the dock unless the circumstances are clarified.

records.l: the creature's identity, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic
records.s: The creature’s identity is not established. Holmes thinks it may belong to the weasel or stoat tribe, but it is larger than any such animal he has seen and is unlike a dog, cat, monkey, or other familiar creature.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Watson visit Henry Wood in Aldershot to investigate Colonel James Barclay's death and the possible murder accusation against Nancy Barclay. Wood explains that James Barclay betrayed him during the Mutiny, leading to his capture, torture, and lifelong deformity, and that Barclay later died after seeing him confront him and Nancy. Wood also says that he accidentally took the door key and left his mongoose, Teddy, behind at the Barclay house. The inquest concludes that Barclay died of apoplexy, and Holmes realizes that Nancy's use of the name David referred to Barclay's betrayal involving Uriah and Bathsheba.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Henry Wood with Watson to investigate Colonel James Barclay's death and determine whether Nancy Barclay is in danger of being tried for murder. He learns Wood's account of James Barclay's betrayal and concludes that the inquest's finding of apoplexy makes further investigation unnecessary.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Henry Wood's house in Aldershot and listens to Wood's account. He asks about Teddy and later questions Holmes about the reference to David.

records.l: Henry Wood, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Henry Wood, formerly a corporal in the 117th Foot, tells Holmes that James Barclay betrayed him during the Mutiny, causing his capture, torture, and permanent deformity. He says he encountered Nancy Barclay again, followed her home, and witnessed Barclay die after seeing him; he then took the door key, dropped his stick, and fled.

records.l: Colonel James Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: James Barclay was a sergeant who loved Nancy Devoy and later married her. During the Mutiny, he secretly arranged for Henry Wood to be captured by the rebels, and years later he died after seeing Wood confront him during an argument with Nancy.

records.l: Nancy Devoy Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Nancy Devoy loved Henry Wood, although her father wanted her to marry James Barclay, and she eventually became Barclay's wife. After recognizing Wood years later, she argued with Barclay and fainted when Wood appeared; she was initially at risk of being tried for Barclay's murder, but the inquest found that his death was due to apoplexy.

records.l: Teddy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Teddy is Henry Wood's mongoose, which escaped from its box while Wood was at the Barclay house. Wood dropped his stick while chasing Teddy, and later explains that Teddy catches a fangless cobra to entertain people in the canteen.

records.l: mongoose, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: The mongoose is described as a thin, lithe, reddish-brown animal with stoat-like legs, a long nose, and red eyes. Henry Wood keeps one named Teddy, which catches cobras.

records.l: Bhurtee, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Bhurtee is the Indian cantonment where Henry Wood, James Barclay, and their regiment were stationed during the Mutiny. The settlement was surrounded by rebels, ran out of water, and was relieved by General Neill's forces after Wood set out to seek help.

records.l: Aldershot, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Aldershot is where Sherlock Holmes and Watson meet Henry Wood and later speak with Major Murphy. Holmes decides after the inquest that they are no longer needed there.

records.l: Indian rebels, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Indian rebels surrounded Bhurtee during the Mutiny and captured Henry Wood after James Barclay's betrayal. They took Wood with them during their retreat and subjected him to repeated torture.

records.l: the Mutiny, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: The Mutiny begins while Henry Wood and the regiment are shut up in Bhurtee. The crisis leaves the settlement surrounded and short of water, prompting Wood to volunteer to reach General Neill's column for help.

records.l: Colonel James Barclay's death, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Colonel James Barclay's death occurs after Henry Wood appears during an argument between Barclay and Nancy. Wood says Barclay was already dying and fell with his head on the fender, while the inquest determines that the cause was apoplexy.

records.l: the inquest, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: The inquest into James Barclay's death concludes that medical evidence showed conclusively that he died of apoplexy. Its finding brings the accusation against Nancy Barclay to nothing.

records.l: apoplexy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Apoplexy is identified by the medical evidence at the inquest as the cause of James Barclay's death.

records.l: the capital charge against Mrs. Barclay, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: Nancy Barclay faces the possibility of being tried for murder while the circumstances of James Barclay's death remain unclear. The accusation is dropped after the inquest determines that Barclay died of apoplexy.

records.l: James Barclay's betrayal of Henry Wood, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the
records.s: James Barclay betrayed Henry Wood during the Mutiny by arranging a route that led Wood into an ambush by rebels, using a native servant to facilitate his capture. Wood believes Barclay acted out of rivalry over Nancy Devoy and says Barclay's conscience reproached him for the deed for thirty years.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Dr. Percy Trevelyan visits Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson at Baker Street to report disturbances involving his resident patient, Blessington. Blessington has become fearful after a West End burglary and after two men posing as a Russian nobleman and his son apparently entered his rooms. Holmes and Watson accompany Trevelyan to 403 Brook Street, where Blessington threatens them with a pistol and shows them large footprints in his bedroom. Holmes refuses to advise Blessington because he believes Blessington is concealing the truth.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Holmes listens to Dr. Percy Trevelyan's account of Blessington's fears, the supposed Russian patients, and the footprints in Blessington's room. He accompanies Trevelyan and Watson to Brook Street, questions Blessington about the two men, and concludes that Blessington is not telling the truth.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Watson remains with Holmes during Dr. Trevelyan's visit and follows Holmes to 403 Brook Street. He observes Blessington's fear, the pistol, and the circumstances surrounding the alleged intrusion.

records.l: Dr. Percy Trevelyan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Dr. Trevelyan, a physician who specializes in nervous disease and has written on catalepsy and nervous lesions, seeks Holmes's advice about events at his house. He describes the visits by a supposed Russian nobleman and his son, the patient's disappearance during consultation, and the footprints found in Blessington's room.

records.l: Blessington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Blessington is Trevelyan's resident patient and financial partner, and he has become intensely fearful of unknown people entering his rooms. He keeps his money in a large black box, confronts Holmes and Watson with a pistol, and refuses or is unable to explain who the two intruders are. Holmes advises him to speak the truth.

records.l: the Russian nobleman, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: The Russian nobleman is introduced through an undated letter as a patient seeking Trevelyan's expertise in catalepsy. He arrives with his supposed son, experiences an apparent cataleptic attack during the consultation, disappears while Trevelyan retrieves medicine, and returns the next evening with an explanation that he had awakened in a strange room and left in a dazed state.

records.l: the young man (Blessington's assailants), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: The supposed son accompanies the Russian nobleman and presents himself as deeply concerned about his father's health. He leaves the consultation room, later claims that he mistook his father's departure for the end of the consultation, and is one of the two men suspected of entering Blessington's room.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Holmes and Watson share chambers in Baker Street and spend the evening walking through London before returning to find Trevelyan waiting for them. They accompany Trevelyan to his residence to investigate Blessington's alarm over the alleged intrusion.

records.l: Baker Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Baker Street is where Holmes and Watson share chambers. Trevelyan visits them there at about ten o'clock in the evening to request their advice and assistance.

records.l: 403 Brook Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: 403 Brook Street is the address where Dr. Percy Trevelyan lives and conducts his medical practice with Blessington. Holmes and Watson travel there with Trevelyan after hearing his account.

records.l: catalepsy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Catalepsy is the nervous disorder on which Trevelyan has conducted research and written a monograph. The supposed Russian nobleman claims to suffer from cataleptic attacks, and Trevelyan examines him during an apparent attack.

records.l: the burglary, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: A burglary in the West End causes Blessington considerable agitation. He responds by demanding stronger bolts for the house and temporarily abandoning his usual walk.

records.l: the consultation with the Russian nobleman, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: During the consultation, Trevelyan questions the elderly supposed Russian nobleman about his cataleptic condition. The man suddenly becomes rigid and unresponsive, but disappears while Trevelyan goes to fetch nitrite of amyl; he and his supposed son return the following evening and offer an explanation.

records.l: the intrusion into Blessington's room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: After the second visit by the supposed Russian patients, Blessington finds several fresh, unusually large footprints on the light carpet in his room. Nothing has been taken, but the footprints indicate that one of the visitors apparently went upstairs while Trevelyan was occupied.

records.l: the resident patient’s house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: The resident patient's house is Trevelyan's residence and medical practice at 403 Brook Street. Blessington lives there as a resident patient and becomes so alarmed about security that he carries a pistol and threatens approaching visitors.

records.l: the medical practice partnership, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Blessington finances Trevelyan's medical practice by taking the house, furnishing it, paying the servants, and providing Trevelyan with living expenses and a carriage. In return, Trevelyan keeps one quarter of his earnings and hands three quarters to Blessington, making Blessington wealthy.

records.l: the resident-patient arrangement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IX. The Resident Patient
records.s: Blessington lives with Trevelyan as a resident patient because he claims to have a weak heart and need constant medical supervision. He occupies the two best rooms on the first floor, rarely goes out, and checks the practice accounts each evening before taking his share of the earnings.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes concludes that Blessington was murdered by three men, including the young man who had previously posed as the son of a cataleptic Russian, rather than committing suicide. He identifies Blessington as Sutton, a former member of the Worthingdon bank gang who informed against his accomplices after the 1875 robbery, leading to Cartwright's execution and the others' imprisonment. The released gang members took revenge on Sutton, entering his room with help from the page, conducting a concealed judicial proceeding, and hanging him. The page disappears, while the three murderers are never found and are later suspected of having died aboard the steamer Norah Creina.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Holmes deduces that the catalepsy was a fraudulent imitation and that at least two men were pursuing Blessington. After examining the bedroom, cigar ends, footprints, lock, rope, and other traces, he determines that Blessington was murdered by three men and identifies Blessington as Sutton, a former member of the Worthingdon bank gang.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Watson accompanies Holmes to Dr. Trevelyan's house after receiving the urgent message about the Brook Street business. He observes the body, reports that Blessington had been dead for about three hours, and listens as Holmes reconstructs the murder.

records.l: Blessington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Blessington is found hanging in his bedroom after being attacked by three men. Holmes establishes that he was actually Sutton, the informer whose evidence helped secure Cartwright's execution and the imprisonment of Biddle, Hayward, and Moffat.

records.l: Dr. Percy Trevelyan, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Dr. Trevelyan reports Blessington's apparent suicide and admits that the event has shaken him. He explains that Blessington kept a coil of rope beside his bed because he feared fire, and later learns that his patient had concealed his identity as Sutton.

records.l: Sutton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Sutton is revealed to be the real identity of Blessington. He had been the worst member of the Worthingdon bank gang and turned informer, causing Cartwright to be hanged and the other three gang members to receive fifteen-year sentences.

records.l: the page (Dr. Trevelyan's house), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The page is identified by Holmes as the confederate who admitted the three assailants and barred the door after they left. He cannot be found after the murder, although proceedings against him later fail for lack of evidence.

records.l: the young man (Blessington's assailants), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The young man is one of the men who previously entered Blessington's room while his confederate distracted Dr. Trevelyan by pretending to suffer from catalepsy. Holmes identifies him as one of the three assailants who later entered Blessington's bedroom and took part in hanging him.

records.l: the Worthingdon bank gang, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The gang consisted of five men, including Sutton, Biddle, Hayward, Moffat, and Cartwright. After Sutton informed against them, Cartwright was hanged and the other three were imprisoned; upon their release, Biddle, Hayward, and Moffat pursued Sutton.

records.l: Brook Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Brook Street is the location of Dr. Trevelyan's house and the events involving Blessington. Holmes and Watson return there after receiving a note from the doctor reporting the subsequent tragedy.

records.l: the Worthingdon bank business, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The 1875 Worthingdon bank business involved five men who robbed seven thousand pounds and murdered Tobin, the caretaker. All five were arrested, but Sutton's evidence led to Cartwright's execution and the imprisonment of the other three.

records.l: Blessington's murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Blessington's murder is staged as a hanging but is shown by Holmes to be a planned, cold-blooded killing. Three men enter through the front door with help from the page, force the locked bedroom door, gag Blessington, conduct what appears to be a judicial proceeding, and hang him.

records.l: Blessington's supposed suicide, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Blessington's supposed suicide is initially supported by the appearance of his slept-in bed, the hanging body, and the early-morning timing. Holmes disproves it after finding that two cigar ends were smoked through a holder and two were not, with differing methods of cutting or biting the ends.

records.l: the Brook Street Mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The Brook Street Mystery concerns the attacks on Blessington, his concealed identity as Sutton, and his eventual murder. It is not fully dealt with in public print until the account given here.

records.l: the three assailants' revenge, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: Biddle, Hayward, and Moffat seek revenge against Sutton after being released from prison for their part in the Worthingdon bank business. They make two unsuccessful attempts to reach him and succeed on the third attempt by murdering him in his bedroom.

records.l: the rope (Blessington's bedroom), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had
records.s: The rope used to hang Blessington was cut from a large coil kept under his bed. Dr. Trevelyan says Blessington kept the coil nearby so he could escape through the window if the stairs caught fire, and Holmes infers that the murderers used it instead of assembling a separate gallows.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells John Watson about his older brother, Mycroft Holmes, whose powers of observation and deduction exceed Sherlock’s but who lacks the ambition and energy to investigate cases. At the Diogenes Club, Mycroft introduces the Greek interpreter Mr. Melas, who recounts being abducted and forced to interrogate the emaciated Kratides about signing documents. Kratides refuses to sign unless he sees Sophy married before a Greek priest, and Melas secretly learns that Kratides is from Athens and has been held for three weeks. The interrogation is interrupted when Sophy recognizes Kratides, but Harold and the older man separate them and threaten Melas into silence.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to John Watson that his older brother Mycroft Holmes has greater powers of observation and deduction than he does, although Mycroft lacks ambition and energy for practical detective work. He visits the Diogenes Club with John Watson and listens to Mr. Melas recount the abduction and interrogation of Kratides.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: John Watson learns for the first time about Sherlock Holmes’s family and accompanies him to the Diogenes Club. He listens as Mr. Melas describes being taken to an unknown house and forced to interpret an interrogation.

records.l: Mycroft Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Mycroft Holmes is Sherlock Holmes’s older brother and possesses even keener powers of observation and deduction, but he has little ambition or energy and prefers armchair reasoning. He belongs to and helped found the Diogenes Club, audits government department books, and brings Mr. Melas to describe the strange Greek case.

records.l: Mr. Melas, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Mr. Melas is a Greek-born interpreter who is chiefly associated with the Greek language and works in courts and hotels. Mr. Latimer abducts him by carriage and forces him to question Kratides, but he secretly inserts questions that reveal details about Kratides’s identity and captivity.

records.l: Harold Latimer, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Mr. Latimer, a fashionably dressed young man, takes Mr. Melas from his rooms under the pretext that an interpreter is needed for a Greek friend. He conceals the destination, carries a lead-loaded bludgeon, threatens Mr. Melas, and brings him to the house where Kratides is held.

records.l: Paul Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Kratides is a Greek-speaking man who is emaciated, weak, and restrained with sticking-plaster over his face and mouth. He refuses to sign papers unless he sees Sophy married before a Greek priest, and he reveals through Mr. Melas’s covert questions that he is from Athens and has been held for three weeks.

records.l: Sophy Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Sophy is a tall, graceful woman with black hair who enters the room during Kratides’s interrogation. She recognizes Kratides as Paul, and he tears away the plaster and rushes into her arms before Harold forcibly removes her.

records.l: Harold, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
