records.s: Harold is the younger man who helps control Kratides and assists with the interrogation. He brings Kratides into the room, seizes Sophy when she embraces him, and pushes her out.

records.l: the Diogenes Club, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: The Diogenes Club is a London club founded for unsociable men who want comfortable chairs and periodicals without conversation. No member may take notice of another outside the Stranger’s Room, and Mycroft Holmes is one of its founders and regular members.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: London is where Sherlock Holmes, John Watson, Mycroft Holmes, and Mr. Melas live or work, and where the Diogenes Club is located. Mr. Melas is known in London as a Greek interpreter, while Kratides is held at an unidentified house somewhere reached after a long carriage journey through the city and beyond.

records.l: Pall Mall, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Pall Mall contains Mycroft Holmes’s lodgings and the Diogenes Club, which stands opposite his rooms. Sherlock Holmes and John Watson walk there, and Mr. Melas is summoned from the club to tell his story.

records.l: the Greek interpreter case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: The Greek interpreter case concerns Mr. Melas’s forced involvement in an attempt to make Kratides sign documents. It includes Kratides’s confinement, his connection with Sophy, and the threatening men who prevent Mr. Melas from freely reporting what he witnessed.

records.l: Kratides's abduction and coercive interrogation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Kratides is confined in an unknown richly furnished house, weakened by starvation, and questioned about whether he will sign papers. The men use threats and his separation from Sophy to pressure him, but he repeatedly refuses and demands to see her married before a Greek priest.

records.l: observation and inference, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Mycroft Holmes demonstrate observation and deduction by identifying details about two men outside the Diogenes Club, including their military service, location of service, rank, family circumstances, and recent bereavement. Mycroft is described as superior to Sherlock in these abilities but unwilling to verify his conclusions through practical investigation.

records.l: the Greek language, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: The Greek language is central to Mr. Melas’s profession and to the coercive interrogation. Kratides writes his answers in Greek, while Mr. Melas uses Greek questions and covert additions to communicate with him without the captors understanding.

records.l: the plaster restraints, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, X. The Greek Interpreter
records.s: Kratides’s face is covered with strips of sticking-plaster, including a large pad over his mouth. He tears the plaster from his lips when Sophy appears and calls out to her.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Mr. Melas is abducted again and forced to interpret a second attempt by Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp to coerce Paul Kratides into surrendering his property. Sherlock Holmes, Mycroft Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Gregson trace the captives to The Myrtles in Beckenham, where they find Melas and Paul bound in a room filled with charcoal fumes; Paul is dead, but Melas survives. The conspirators have fled with Sophy Kratides, but a later report says that Latimer and Kemp died violently in Buda-Pesth, possibly through Sophy's vengeance.

records.l: Mr. Melas, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Mr. Melas is abducted for a second time by a small, bespectacled man who threatens him with a life-preserver. He is taken to The Myrtles, forced to interpret further threats against Paul Kratides, then struck unconscious and left bound in a room filled with charcoal fumes. Sherlock Holmes and the others rescue him, and he recovers with ammonia and brandy.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Sherlock Holmes concludes that Paul Kratides is in immediate danger and takes up the case. He telegraphs for information, brings Mycroft Holmes and Dr. Watson to Scotland Yard and Beckenham, deduces that a heavily loaded carriage has left The Myrtles, enters through an open window, and rescues Mr. Melas and Paul from the poisoned room. He later believes that Sophy Kratides may have avenged herself and her brother on Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp.

records.l: Mycroft Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Mycroft Holmes reports that his newspaper advertisement seeking information about Paul Kratides and Sophy has received an answer from J. Davenport, who says that Sophy is living at The Myrtles in Beckenham. He joins Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Gregson in going to the house and helps pull the poisoned captives into the hall.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Dr. Watson proposes that Sophy Kratides was carried off by Harold Latimer and that Paul Kratides was being held to force him to sign away property. He accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Mycroft Holmes, and Inspector Gregson to The Myrtles and helps remove the victims from the charcoal-filled room. He treats Mr. Melas with ammonia and brandy and observes that Paul has died.

records.l: Paul Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Paul Kratides, a Greek gentleman from Athens who cannot speak English, is held prisoner by Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp. They use cruelty, starvation, and threats to try to make him sign away his own and his sister's property, but he refuses. He is found bound and dead in a room filled with charcoal fumes.

records.l: Sophy Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Sophy Kratides is a wealthy Greek family's daughter who came to England to visit friends and was persuaded by Harold Latimer to flee with him. Latimer and Wilson Kemp keep her brother prisoner without her knowledge, but she recognizes him through the plaster disguise when she sees him during Mr. Melas's visit. She flees with the two men, and Sherlock Holmes suspects that she later avenged herself and Paul.

records.l: Harold Latimer, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Harold Latimer persuades Sophy Kratides to flee with him and later holds her brother Paul prisoner with Wilson Kemp. He attempts to force Paul to surrender his property and flees England with Sophy and Kemp when the conspiracy is exposed. A later newspaper report says that he died violently in Buda-Pesth.

records.l: Wilson Kemp, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Wilson Kemp is Harold Latimer's associate and is described as a man with foul antecedents. He helps imprison Paul Kratides, starve and threaten him, disguise his face with plaster, and abduct Mr. Melas. He later flees with Latimer and Sophy, and a newspaper report says that he died violently in Buda-Pesth.

records.l: the conspirators, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The conspirators are Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp, aided by the coachman and his wife, who serve as their tools. They imprison Paul Kratides, conceal his identity, abduct Mr. Melas to use as an interpreter, and flee with Sophy Kratides after their secret is discovered.

records.l: Beckenham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Beckenham is the place where The Myrtles is located. Sherlock Holmes, Mycroft Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Gregson travel there to investigate the house and find the captives.

records.l: The Myrtles, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The Myrtles is a large, dark house in Beckenham standing back from the road in its own grounds. It is the furnished house where Paul Kratides is imprisoned and where Mr. Melas is taken for the second interview. The investigators find it apparently deserted, then discover Paul and Melas in an upstairs room filled with charcoal fumes.

records.l: Athens, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Athens is Paul Kratides's home city and the place from which he comes to England after learning about Sophy's relationship with Harold Latimer. Mycroft Holmes considers sending a wire to the head of the Athens police.

records.l: the newspaper advertisement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The newspaper advertisement offers a reward for information about Paul Kratides, who cannot speak English, and about a Greek lady named Sophy. J. Davenport answers it and identifies The Myrtles in Beckenham as Sophy's current residence, but the advertisement also alerts the conspirators that Mr. Melas has betrayed them.

records.l: the carriage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The carriage takes Mr. Melas to and from the conspirators' house during his first abduction and leaves him at Wandsworth Common. Later, a carriage carrying heavy luggage leaves The Myrtles shortly before the investigators arrive, indicating that the conspirators and Sophy have fled.

records.l: the poisoned room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The poisoned room is an upstairs room at The Myrtles containing Paul Kratides and Mr. Melas, both bound and unconscious. A small brass tripod burning charcoal fills it with poisonous fumes; Paul dies there, while Melas is rescued alive.

records.l: charcoal poisoning, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Charcoal poisoning is used by the conspirators to kill or punish Paul Kratides and Mr. Melas after Paul refuses to comply and Melas is blamed for betraying them. Sherlock Holmes recognizes the danger, ventilates the room, removes the burning tripod, and helps rescue the victims.

records.l: Kratides's abduction and coercive interrogation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Paul Kratides comes to England from Athens after learning that Sophy has fled with Harold Latimer. Latimer and Wilson Kemp place him in their power, imprison him, disguise his face, and prevent him from communicating because he cannot speak English.

records.l: the attempted coercion of Paul Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp try to force Paul Kratides to sign away his own and Sophy Kratides's property. They rely on threats, cruelty, starvation, and repeated interpreted interviews, but Paul remains resistant and refuses to comply.

records.l: the murder of the two Englishmen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: Months later, a newspaper reports that two Englishmen traveling with a woman in Buda-Pesth were stabbed and fatally injured. The Hungarian police believe the men quarreled and killed each other, while Sherlock Holmes suspects that Sophy Kratides may have avenged the wrongs done to herself and Paul.

records.l: the inheritance and property dispute, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this
records.s: The dispute concerns Paul Kratides's own property and the property of his sister Sophy Kratides. Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp attempt to make Paul sign these assets over to them, but Paul refuses despite imprisonment, starvation, cruelty, and threats.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Dr. John Watson recalls how Sherlock Holmes became involved in the case of his former schoolmate Percy Phelps, a Foreign Office official whose career was ruined after the original Naval Treaty was stolen. Phelps describes receiving the treaty from his uncle, Lord Holdhurst, and copying it alone at the Foreign Office while waiting for coffee. When a bell rang from his room, he returned to find the original treaty missing, although the treaty copy remained. Holmes examines the circumstances, including the commissionnaire, his wife, the building layout, and the timing of the theft.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Sherlock Holmes agrees to accompany Dr. John Watson to Woking after reading Percy Phelps's letter. He observes that the letter was written by a woman of unusual character, questions Phelps closely about the treaty theft, and identifies several important details, including the quarter-to-ten time and the absence of muddy footprints.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Dr. John Watson receives Percy Phelps's appeal and brings it to Sherlock Holmes. He travels with Holmes to Briarbrae and records Phelps's account of the Naval Treaty theft.

records.l: Percy Phelps, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Percy Phelps is a former schoolmate of Dr. John Watson and a successful Foreign Office official whose career is ruined by the theft of the original Naval Treaty. After suffering nine weeks of brain-fever, he asks Watson to bring Holmes to Briarbrae, where he recounts how the treaty disappeared while he was copying it.

records.l: Lord Holdhurst, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Lord Holdhurst is Percy Phelps's maternal uncle and a prominent Conservative politician who becomes foreign minister. He gives Phelps the original secret treaty between England and Italy and instructs him to copy it securely at the Foreign Office.

records.l: Joseph Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Joseph Harrison is Annie Harrison's brother and is engaged to become Percy Phelps's relation by marriage. He is in Woking during Phelps's illness and is mentioned as someone Phelps hoped to meet after returning by the eleven o'clock train.

records.l: Annie Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Annie Harrison is Joseph Harrison's sister and Percy Phelps's fiancée. She has nursed Phelps at Briarbrae for two months and remains beside him when Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson arrive.

records.l: the Phelps family, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The Phelps family lives at Briarbrae and finds discussion of Percy Phelps's misfortune painful. Percy Phelps's father and mother ask Joseph Harrison to receive Holmes and Watson.

records.l: the Foreign Office, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The Foreign Office employs Percy Phelps in a position of trust and houses the secure room where he copies the Naval Treaty. The original treaty is stolen from a desk there while Phelps is away investigating a delay in receiving coffee.

records.l: Briarbrae, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Briarbrae is a large detached house in Woking where Percy Phelps recuperates after his brain-fever. Holmes and Watson visit it and hear Phelps's account from him while Annie Harrison cares for him.

records.l: Woking, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Woking is the location of Briarbrae, where Holmes and Watson travel by train to meet Percy Phelps. The area is described as having fir woods and heather near the station.

records.l: Charles Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Charles Street is reached through a side door and a short staircase from the Foreign Office. After the treaty theft, Percy Phelps and the commissionnaire rush into Charles Street, where a policeman reports seeing only one tall, elderly woman pass.

records.l: The Adventure of the Naval Treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The Adventure of the Naval Treaty is the second case in Dr. John Watson's list of notable cases from the July after his marriage. It concerns Percy Phelps, the theft of a secret naval treaty, and Sherlock Holmes's investigation.

records.l: brain-fever, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Percy Phelps's brain-fever lasts nine weeks and follows the misfortune that destroys his career. He has only recently recovered when he writes to Dr. John Watson and remains extremely weak at Briarbrae.

records.l: Foreign Office treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The Naval Treaty is a secret agreement between England and Italy concerning Britain's position toward the Triple Alliance and its policy if the French fleet gains naval superiority over Italy in the Mediterranean. It is written in French, contains twenty-six articles, and bears the signatures of high dignitaries.

records.l: the treaty copy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The treaty copy is the draft Percy Phelps makes at the Foreign Office after receiving the original from Lord Holdhurst. It remains on the desk after the theft, while the original treaty is taken.

records.l: Percy Phelps's letter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: Percy Phelps's letter asks Dr. John Watson to bring Sherlock Holmes to Briarbrae and explains that Phelps has recently recovered from brain-fever. Holmes studies the handwriting and determines that it was written by a woman of exceptional character, rather than by Phelps himself.

records.l: the theft of the naval treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The treaty theft occurs while Percy Phelps is copying the document at the Foreign Office. After a bell rings from his room, he returns to find the original missing; he concludes that the thief entered through the side door, while Holmes notes the importance of the timing and the lack of footprints.

records.l: Tangey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The commissionnaire keeps an overnight lodge at the foot of the Foreign Office stairs and ordinarily makes coffee for officials working late. During the theft he falls asleep beside a boiling kettle, hears the bell from Phelps's room, and follows Phelps in searching for the thief.

records.l: the commissionnaire's wife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XI. The Naval Treaty
records.s: The commissionnaire's wife is a large, elderly woman who works as a charwoman at the Foreign Office. She answers Phelps's summons and receives his order for coffee; a policeman later reports seeing a tall, elderly woman in a Paisley shawl leaving Charles Street, while the commissionnaire insists she is uninvolved.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Percy Phelps recounts to Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson how the Foreign Office treaty was stolen from a secured room and how subsequent searches failed to recover it. The investigation led to Mrs. Tangey being arrested and searched, but no papers were found, while young Gorot and the commissionnaire were also cleared of evidence. Phelps’s distress over the failure caused a severe illness lasting more than nine weeks. Holmes begins a renewed investigation with inquiries at Scotland Yard, a search for the cab that came to Charles Street, and questions about the unexplained ringing of the bell.

records.l: Percy Phelps, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Percy Phelps tells Holmes and Watson that the treaty was stolen from the Foreign Office after he found no possible secret door, trap-door, fireplace access, or other route into the room. He pursued Mrs. Tangey without recovering the papers, suffered a prolonged illness from the shock and disgrace, and now asks Holmes to restore his honour and position.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Phelps closely about who knew of the special task, the commissionnaire, and the circumstances of the theft. He identifies several possible clues, advertises for the number of a cab at the Foreign Office, and begins by consulting Mr. Forbes at Scotland Yard.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to hear Phelps’s account and assist in the investigation. Holmes also discusses the case and its possible suspects with him during their journey to London.

records.l: Miss Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Miss Harrison has nursed Percy Phelps during his illness and remains with him at his home. Holmes learns that she is engaged to Phelps and considers her a strong-charactered and apparently good woman.

records.l: Mrs. Tangey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Mrs. Tangey, the commissionnaire’s wife, hurried away from the Foreign Office and was suspected of taking the treaty. She was found at home, arrested, taken to Scotland Yard, and searched, but no papers were found; she gave explanations for her haste and conduct.

records.l: Forbes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Mr. Forbes is the detective who took charge of the case and questioned or shadowed the principal suspects. He tells Holmes that the commissionnaire, Mrs. Tangey, and Gorot have yielded no evidence connecting them to the theft.

records.l: the Foreign Office, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The Foreign Office is where Percy Phelps worked and where the important treaty was kept. The treaty disappeared from a room there under circumstances that appeared to rule out ordinary entrances and hiding places.

records.l: Scotland Yard, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Scotland Yard received the alarm, investigated the theft, and searched Mrs. Tangey after bringing her there. Holmes visits Scotland Yard to question Mr. Forbes about the unresolved case.

records.l: Charles Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Charles Street is the location of the Foreign Office entrance mentioned in Holmes’s investigation. Holmes advertises for the number of a cab that dropped a passenger at or near the Foreign Office there at about quarter to ten on May 23rd.

records.l: Foreign Office treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The Foreign Office treaty was the document stolen from Phelps’s room while he was carrying out a special task. It was not recovered from Mrs. Tangey, the kitchen fire, or any other examined location, and its loss threatened Phelps’s career and honour.

records.l: bell, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The bell beside Phelps’s desk was rung after the treaty disappeared, even though the person who rang it must have approached the desk. Holmes regards the ringing as the most distinctive feature of the case and considers whether it was deliberate, accidental, or intended to prevent the crime.

records.l: room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The room containing Phelps’s desk was examined for a secret door, windows, a trap-door, a fireplace, and other traces of an intruder. No physical clue was found, and Phelps maintained that the thief could only have entered through the door.

records.l: cab, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: Holmes suspects that the thief or another participant came to the Foreign Office in a cab because the night was wet but no damp trace was left inside. He places an advertisement seeking the number of the cab that arrived near the Foreign Office at the relevant time.

records.l: secret entrance investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The investigation examined the room, windows, ceiling, carpet, stove, corridors, and possible hidden entrances. No secret door, trap-door, or other concealed route was discovered, leaving Holmes to consider an outside approach.

records.l: the theft of the naval treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The theft occurred while Percy Phelps was working alone on a special Foreign Office task. The police investigated Mrs. Tangey, her husband, and Gorot but found no evidence, so the matter remained unsolved until Phelps appealed to Holmes.

records.l: bell-ringing mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: The unexplained ringing of the bell is central to the mystery because it required the intruder to come close to Phelps’s desk and seemed to serve no obvious purpose. Holmes considers several explanations and appears to recognize a new possibility while discussing it with Watson.

records.l: brain-fever, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret
records.s: After failing to recover the treaty, Percy Phelps became overwhelmed by shame and distress, suffered a fit at the station, and returned home practically a raving maniac. He remained unconscious and raving with brain-fever for more than nine weeks before his memory and reason gradually returned.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Lord Holdhurst in London about the missing naval treaty, then travels with Dr. John Watson to Woking to see Percy Phelps. Phelps reports that an armed intruder attempted to enter his bedroom during the night, increasing his fear that a political conspiracy threatens both his life and his reputation. Holmes examines the alleged entry points, separates Annie Harrison from the others, and sends Phelps and Watson to London while remaining in Woking to pursue the case. Phelps and Watson speculate about Holmes's reasons, while Holmes continues the investigation in secret.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Lord Holdhurst about the copying of the naval treaty and reasons that the thief may not have delivered it to a foreign government. In Woking, he examines the alleged intrusion, notices that the evidence is inconclusive, orders Annie Harrison to remain in Phelps's room and lock it from the outside, and sends Phelps and Dr. John Watson to London while he stays behind to investigate.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Lord Holdhurst's chambers and then travels with Holmes to Woking. He returns to London with Percy Phelps at Holmes's request and stays with him at Baker Street, while trying to reassure him about the investigation.

records.l: Percy Phelps, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Percy Phelps remains weak but is recovering under care at Woking. He reports that an armed man tried to enter his bedroom during the night and begins to suspect a conspiracy against his life as well as his honour. Holmes sends him to London with Dr. John Watson so that he will be away while the investigation continues.

records.l: Lord Holdhurst, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Lord Holdhurst receives Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson courteously in his Downing Street chambers. He confirms that he gave instructions there for the naval treaty to be copied, denies telling anyone about the plan, and says that the treaty becoming known could have very grave results. Holmes observes that Lord Holdhurst is not rich and that his boots have been resoled.

records.l: Annie Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Annie Harrison is present at Briarbrae and encourages Percy Phelps to keep his courage and patience. Sherlock Holmes insists that she remain in Phelps's room throughout the day and lock the room from the outside at night, and she agrees despite her surprise.

records.l: Joseph Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Joseph Harrison helps rouse the household after Percy Phelps reports the attempted night intrusion. He and the groom find marks on the bed outside the window and identify a cracked section of the fence, though the evidence does not establish when or how it was damaged.

records.l: Woking, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Woking is where Percy Phelps is recovering and where the reported attempted night intrusion occurs. Sherlock Holmes remains in Woking after sending Phelps and Dr. John Watson to London, intending to pursue further clues.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: London is where Sherlock Holmes interviews Lord Holdhurst and where Percy Phelps and Dr. John Watson return after leaving Woking. Holmes plans to resume the London investigation the following day.

records.l: Foreign Office treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: The naval treaty was entrusted to Percy Phelps for copying and then disappeared. Lord Holdhurst says its disclosure could have very grave consequences, but after nearly ten weeks no evidence indicates that it has reached the French or Russian Foreign Office. Its secrecy is expected to end within a few months.

records.l: the theft of the naval treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: The theft of the naval treaty remains unresolved. Sherlock Holmes considers that the thief may be waiting for a better price or may have been prevented from delivering the treaty, while Lord Holdhurst confirms that no one should have known in advance that it was to be copied.

records.l: the attempted night intrusion, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: The attempted night intrusion occurs at Percy Phelps's bedroom window in Woking. Phelps hears someone forcing the window catch, sees a cloaked man holding what appears to be a long knife, and raises the household; marks are found outside, but the trail cannot be followed.

records.l: the intruder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: The intruder is seen only briefly by Percy Phelps as a man crouching at the bedroom window. He is wrapped in a cloak covering the lower part of his face and appears to carry a long knife before fleeing across the grounds.

records.l: the political conspiracy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: Percy Phelps begins to believe that he is the unconscious centre of a political conspiracy aimed at both his life and his honour. Dr. John Watson suggests that, if the theory is correct, identifying the intruder could also reveal who stole the naval treaty, but the conspiracy remains unconfirmed.

records.l: the investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.
records.s: The investigation includes Sherlock Holmes's interview with Lord Holdhurst, inquiries concerning the missing naval treaty, and examination of the alleged intrusion at Woking. Holmes receives no answer to his advertisement, finds little useful evidence at the window and fence, and continues working in Woking while Phelps and Dr. John Watson return to London.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Sherlock Holmes returns to Percy Phelps with a bandaged hand and reveals that he has recovered the stolen State papers. Holmes explains that Joseph Harrison stole the papers, hid them beneath a floorboard in Phelps’s room at Briarbrae, and later returned to retrieve them. Holmes intercepted Joseph at the window, overcame him despite being cut by his knife, and obtained the papers. Phelps’s honour and the government’s interests are thereby protected, while Joseph may be apprehended by Forbes.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Sherlock Holmes spends the night watching Percy Phelps’s room at Briarbrae after arranging for Miss Harrison to lock the door and take its key. He intercepts Joseph Harrison as Joseph retrieves the stolen papers, overcomes him after suffering a cut to the hand, and returns the papers to Phelps. Holmes explains that Joseph’s actions and the earlier events form the solution to the case.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: John Watson visits Percy Phelps in the morning and observes Holmes’s arrival with a bandaged hand and a grim, pale face. He shares breakfast with Holmes and Phelps and listens as Holmes explains how the papers were recovered.

records.l: Percy Phelps, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Percy Phelps is initially depressed and fears that Holmes has failed, but he reacts with overwhelming joy when Holmes places the recovered papers before him. He thanks Holmes for saving his honour and learns that the papers had remained in his room at Briarbrae throughout his ten weeks of agony.

records.l: Joseph Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Joseph Harrison is revealed to be the thief who stole the State papers and hid them beneath a removable floorboard in Percy Phelps’s room. He returns at night to recover them, attacks Holmes with a knife, and gives up the papers after Holmes overpowers him. Holmes believes Joseph is selfish, financially desperate from stock speculation, and dangerous.

records.l: Miss Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Miss Harrison follows Holmes’s instructions by locking Percy Phelps’s bedroom door from the outside and taking the key when she retires. Her cooperation helps Holmes make Joseph believe that the room can be entered only by the window.

records.l: Foreign Office treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: The stolen State papers are hidden by Joseph Harrison beneath a removable board covering the gas-pipe T joint in Percy Phelps’s room. Holmes allows Joseph to retrieve them and then takes them from him, returning them to Phelps.

records.l: the knife (Joseph Harrison's knife), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Joseph Harrison uses the knife as a tool to force the window sash and raise the shutter bar. He then attacks Holmes with it, cutting Holmes over the knuckles before Holmes gains the upper hand.

records.l: the case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Holmes describes the case as one of the darkest and most remarkable he has investigated. He concludes that its principal difficulty was the abundance of evidence, which concealed the essential facts needed to reconstruct the events.

records.l: the theft of the naval treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Joseph Harrison stole the State papers from Percy Phelps’s office after entering through the Charles Street door and finding Phelps’s room empty. He recognized their value, concealed them at Briarbrae, and intended to retrieve and sell them, possibly to the French embassy.

records.l: the attempted recovery of the papers, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Joseph Harrison makes repeated efforts to recover the papers from Percy Phelps’s room, including a nighttime attempt when he believes the room is unguarded. Holmes prevents the final attempt by keeping watch outside the window and confronting Joseph as he leaves with the papers.

records.l: Briarbrae, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for
records.s: Briarbrae is the house where Joseph Harrison hides the stolen State papers beneath a removable floorboard in Percy Phelps’s room. Holmes secretly enters its grounds, watches the room from the rhododendrons, and intercepts Joseph outside its window.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. John Watson that Professor Moriarty is the organizing force behind much of London’s undetected crime and that Holmes has nearly completed an investigation against him. Moriarty visits Holmes and threatens him, warning that continued pursuit will lead to Holmes’s destruction. Holmes has already survived several attacks by Moriarty’s agents and asks Watson to accompany him on a carefully arranged journey to the Continent until the police can make arrests. Watson agrees to follow Holmes’s instructions and meet him at Victoria station.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. John Watson that he has spent years tracing the hidden organization behind numerous crimes and has identified Professor Moriarty as its leader. He has nearly completed his investigation and plans to withdraw temporarily so that the police can arrest Moriarty and the principal members of his gang. Holmes has survived several attacks, including an attempted vehicular assault, a falling brick, and an attack by a man with a bludgeon.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Dr. John Watson receives Sherlock Holmes at his consulting-room and learns about the danger posed by Professor Moriarty. He agrees to accompany Holmes to the Continent and follows Holmes’s detailed instructions for travelling safely to Victoria station.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Professor Moriarty is presented as a highly educated former mathematics professor and the hidden organizer of much of London’s serious crime. He visits Sherlock Holmes to demand that Holmes abandon his investigation, threatens him with destruction, and declares that he will never stand trial. Moriarty relies on agents to attack Holmes while keeping himself at a distance.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson's Continental journey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Sherlock Holmes proposes that Dr. John Watson accompany him on a temporary journey to the Continent while the police prepare to act against Professor Moriarty’s organization. Holmes gives Watson elaborate instructions involving luggage, separate cabs, the Lowther Arcade, a specially marked brougham, and a reserved first-class carriage at Victoria station.

records.l: the Moriarty criminal organization, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: The Moriarty criminal organization is described as a powerful, carefully protected network with numerous agents who carry out crimes planned by Professor Moriarty. It is linked to forgery, robbery, murder, theft, and other offenses, while Moriarty remains hidden behind the activities of his agents.

records.l: the police, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: The police are expected to arrest Professor Moriarty and the principal members of his gang on the following Monday, once Sherlock Holmes’s investigation is complete. They examine the site of the falling brick and take into custody the man who attacked Holmes with a bludgeon, but Holmes expects no connection to Moriarty to be provable in either case.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: London is described as the setting in which Professor Moriarty’s criminal influence extends throughout the city. Holmes regards Moriarty as responsible for organizing much of the city’s crime and for shielding wrongdoers from detection.

records.l: the Moriarty investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Sherlock Holmes’s investigation traces a hidden criminal power through many apparently unrelated crimes until it leads to Professor Moriarty. Holmes has spent months in an intellectual contest with Moriarty and believes that the evidence and arrests will expose more than forty mysteries.

records.l: the planned arrests, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: The planned arrests are to take place on the following Monday, when Professor Moriarty and the principal members of his gang are expected to be placed in police custody. Sherlock Holmes believes that the arrests can proceed without him, although his presence will be needed to secure a conviction.

records.l: the attacks on Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, XII. The Final Problem
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reports that Moriarty’s agents have tried to kill or injure him by driving a two-horse van at him, dropping a brick from a roof, and sending a man armed with a bludgeon to assault him. Holmes avoids the first two attacks and knocks down the assailant in the third, injuring his own knuckles in the struggle.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Watson follows Holmes’s instructions by using a hansom and then a brougham to reach Victoria Station without being easily followed. He boards the only carriage marked “Engaged,” but Holmes does not appear until the train is leaving, disguised as an aged Italian priest. Holmes reveals himself, warns that Moriarty and others are pursuing them, and says that further precautions are necessary. The train escapes the station while Moriarty tries unsuccessfully to stop it.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Holmes arranges Watson’s journey and reserves a carriage for him. He reaches the train disguised as an aged Italian priest, reveals himself just before departure, warns Watson that pursuit is continuing, and then removes and packs away his disguise.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Watson follows Holmes’s instructions, travels to Victoria Station, and boards the carriage Holmes indicated. He initially fears that Holmes’s absence means something has happened to him, but discovers that Holmes has been traveling beside him in disguise.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Moriarty is seen forcing his way through the crowd at the station and waving for the departing train to stop. He arrives too late to prevent Holmes and Watson from leaving.

records.l: Victoria, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Victoria Station is where Watson arrives, finds his luggage, and boards the train. Moriarty reaches the station as the train is already departing.

records.l: the Continental express, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: The train is preparing to leave Victoria Station when Holmes joins Watson in disguise. It gathers speed and clears the station before Moriarty can stop it.

records.l: carriage (Holmes's reserved carriage), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: The carriage reserved by Holmes is the only one marked “Engaged.” Watson boards it, but the porter mistakenly places the Italian priest in it as his traveling companion until Holmes reveals that the priest is himself.

records.l: Italian priest, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: An aged Italian priest is assisted by Watson and placed in Watson’s carriage by the porter. The apparent priest is actually Holmes in disguise.

records.l: Holmes's disguise, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Holmes’s disguise consists of the appearance and clothing of an aged Italian priest, including a black cassock and hat. He briefly drops the disguise to speak to Watson, then removes it and packs it into a hand-bag.

records.l: precautions against pursuit, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Watson uses a carefully selected hansom, travels through the Lowther Arcade, and takes a brougham to Victoria Station. Holmes also disguises himself and reserves a carriage, but says that every precaution is still necessary because pursuit remains close.

records.l: the pursuit of Holmes by Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A
records.s: Holmes says that pursuers are hot upon their trail. Moriarty reaches the station and attempts to stop the train, but Holmes and Watson escape as it gathers speed.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Holmes tells Watson that their rooms at Baker Street were set on fire during the night, though little damage was done. Holmes explains that Moriarty has followed Watson to Victoria and will likely pursue them by special train. Holmes and Watson leave the express at Canterbury, evade Moriarty's train, and plan to travel cross-country to Newhaven and then to Dieppe before continuing through Switzerland. Holmes says that arresting Moriarty would jeopardize their three-month investigation.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Holmes learns that the rooms at Baker Street were set on fire and concludes that Moriarty has been watching Watson. He arranges an evasive escape journey, predicts Moriarty's movements, and avoids him at Canterbury.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Watson tells Holmes that he followed the advised precautions and used a waiting brougham without recognizing the coachman, who was actually Mycroft Holmes. He travels with Holmes, learns that their rooms were burned, and helps evade Moriarty.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Moriarty is believed to have followed Watson to Victoria and to be pursuing Holmes and Watson. Holmes predicts that Moriarty will engage a special train, overtake them, attack Holmes, and then travel to Paris to watch their luggage.

records.l: Baker Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Baker Street is the location of Holmes and Watson's rooms, which were set on fire during the night.

records.l: Canterbury, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Canterbury is a stop on the express where Holmes and Watson get out. They find that they must wait an hour for a train to Newhaven, while Moriarty's special train passes through after them.

records.l: Newhaven, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Newhaven is the next destination in Holmes and Watson's planned escape journey. They intend to travel from there by boat to Dieppe.

records.l: Holmes and Watson’s rooms, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Holmes and Watson's rooms were set on fire during the night, but no great harm was done. Holmes believes the attackers thought he had returned there.

records.l: the fire at Holmes and Watson's rooms, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: The fire occurred during the night and caused no great harm. Holmes says it resulted from the attackers' mistaken belief that he had returned to the rooms.

records.l: Holmes and Watson's escape journey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Holmes and Watson leave the express at Canterbury to avoid Moriarty, then plan to travel across country to Newhaven, cross to Dieppe, and continue at leisure through Luxembourg and Basle into Switzerland. They also plan to replace their marked luggage with a couple of carpet-bags.

records.l: the Continental express, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: The express stops at Canterbury and runs in connection with the boat. Holmes and Watson leave it there, while Moriarty follows in another carriage and engine that rushes into the station.

records.l: Holmes and Watson's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”
records.s: Holmes says that arresting Moriarty would ruin the work of three months by allowing the smaller criminals to escape. He intends to avoid a premature arrest and secure the larger criminal network later.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson travel through Switzerland while Professor Moriarty, having escaped the London police, pursues Holmes. At Reichenbach Falls, a forged letter from Meiringen lures Watson away, leaving Holmes to face Moriarty on the narrow path above the falls. Watson returns to find evidence that Holmes and Moriarty struggled and fell into the chasm, and Holmes's farewell note explains that he accepted the encounter as the culmination of his career. The bodies are never recovered, while Holmes's evidence helps expose Moriarty's gang.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. John Watson through Switzerland while remaining alert to Professor Moriarty's pursuit. He confronts Moriarty at Reichenbach Falls and is presumed to have fallen into the chasm with him. In his farewell note, he states that he deliberately allowed Watson to leave and had arranged for evidence against Moriarty's gang to be found.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes through Switzerland but returns to Meiringen after receiving a forged request to attend a dying Englishwoman. He discovers that the request was a hoax, returns to Reichenbach Falls, and finds evidence of Holmes's struggle with Moriarty.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Professor Moriarty escapes after the London police secure his gang and follows Holmes to Switzerland. He confronts Holmes at Reichenbach Falls, where experts conclude that the two men fell together while locked in combat.

records.l: Moriarty's gang, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Moriarty's gang is captured by the London police except for Moriarty. Evidence accumulated by Holmes exposes the gang's organization, and the gang is heavily punished during the subsequent proceedings.

records.l: Meiringen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Meiringen is the Swiss village where Holmes and Watson stay at the Englischer Hof on May 3. A forged letter bearing the hotel's mark is used to draw Watson back there, and Holmes's farewell note directs Inspector Patterson to evidence stored in pigeonhole M.

records.l: Rosenlaui, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Rosenlaui is the hamlet where Holmes and Watson intend to spend the night after crossing the hills from Meiringen. Holmes tells Watson that he will walk there after remaining at Reichenbach Falls.

records.l: Reichenbach Falls, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Reichenbach Falls is a dangerous Swiss waterfall reached by a path cut halfway around the torrent. Holmes remains there after Watson leaves, and it becomes the site of Holmes's final confrontation with Moriarty.

records.l: the journey through Switzerland, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The journey through Switzerland takes Holmes and Watson from Geneva through the Valley of the Rhone, over the Gemmi Pass, and by way of Interlaken to Meiringen. Although the scenery is beautiful, Holmes remains watchful because he believes Moriarty is pursuing them.

records.l: Moriarty's escape, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Moriarty's escape occurs after the London police capture his entire gang except him. Holmes curses the news and believes Moriarty will devote himself to revenge.

records.l: the pursuit of Holmes by Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The pursuit of Holmes by Moriarty follows Holmes and Watson across Switzerland. Holmes watches faces and reacts to possible dangers, while a rapidly walking man seen on the path is later understood to have been Moriarty.

records.l: the confrontation at Reichenbach Falls, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The confrontation at Reichenbach Falls occurs after a forged letter separates Watson from Holmes. Footprints, disturbed mud, and damaged vegetation indicate that Holmes and Moriarty struggled near the edge before falling into the chasm.

records.l: the deaths of Holmes and Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The deaths of Holmes and Moriarty are inferred from an examination by experts, who conclude that the two men fell together while locked in each other's arms. Their bodies cannot be recovered and are believed to remain in the waterfall's chasm.

records.l: Holmes's career, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Holmes says that he has not lived wholly in vain, having used his powers on the right side in more than a thousand cases. He regards capturing or eliminating Moriarty as the culmination of his career and says that no conclusion could be more congenial to him.

records.l: the letter from Meiringen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The letter from Meiringen falsely claims that an Englishwoman suffering from consumption has arrived at the hotel and wishes to see Watson. Holmes later reveals that he suspected it was a hoax but allowed Watson to leave because he expected such a development.

records.l: Holmes's Alpine-stock, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Holmes's Alpine-stock remains leaning against the rock where Watson left Holmes at Reichenbach Falls. Its presence helps Watson realize that Holmes did not proceed to Rosenlaui.

records.l: Holmes's silver cigarette-case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Holmes's silver cigarette-case lies on top of a boulder near his Alpine-stock. Watson finds the case and discovers Holmes's farewell note beneath it.

records.l: Holmes's farewell note, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: Holmes's farewell note is addressed to Watson and written clearly in three pages torn from his notebook. It explains Holmes's final confrontation with Moriarty, directs Inspector Patterson to evidence against the gang, states that Holmes's property was given to Mycroft, and sends greetings to Mrs. Watson.

records.l: the Reichenbach waterfall, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,
records.s: The Reichenbach waterfall is described as a tremendous, spray-filled abyss with black rocks, a boiling pit, and a deep chasm. Its force and depth make recovery of Holmes's and Moriarty's bodies impossible.

records.l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: This document is a sequence of Sherlock Holmes cases narrated or framed by Dr. John Watson, moving from investigations of theft, murder, blackmail, and family secrets to Holmes’s apparent final confrontation with Professor Moriarty. Holmes’s methods, close observation, reconstruction of motives, and attention to overlooked clues, drive every case, while Watson accompanies him, records events, and sometimes supplies the personal connection that brings a client. The collection opens with the disappearance of the racehorse Silver Blaze and John Straker’s death: Holmes clears Fitzroy Simpson, finds the horse concealed by Silas Brown, and proves Straker drugged Ned Hunter and tried to lame the horse before Silver Blaze killed him in self-defence. Other cases reveal Jim Browner’s jealous murder of his wife and Alec Fairbairn; Effie Munro’s concealed daughter Lucy and Grant Munro’s acceptance of them; and a fraud in which the Pinner brothers use Hall Pycroft’s handwriting to infiltrate Mawson & Williams. Holmes then recounts formative earlier cases. In the Gloria Scott matter, Victor Trevor’s father is exposed as James Armitage, a transported convict whose past aboard the mutinied ship returns through Hudson’s blackmail. In the Musgrave Ritual, Holmes follows an ancestral catechism to a hidden chamber, Brunton’s body, and a crown concealed for Charles II. Later investigations identify the Cunninghams as burglars and William Kirwan’s murderers; explain Colonel Barclay’s death through Henry Wood’s history of betrayal; and uncover Blessington as Sutton, an informer killed by former bank-robbery accomplices. The remaining cases broaden Holmes’s circle and stakes. Mycroft Holmes introduces the kidnapped Greek interpreter Melas, leading to the death of Paul Kratides and the escape of Sophy with her captors. Holmes restores Percy Phelps’s stolen naval treaty by catching Joseph Harrison retrieving it from beneath a floorboard. Finally, Holmes identifies Moriarty as the force behind extensive crime in London. Pursued across England and Europe, Holmes and Watson reach Reichenbach Falls, where Moriarty lures Watson away. Watson returns to find signs that Holmes and Moriarty struggled and fell into the chasm; neither body is recovered, but Holmes’s evidence exposes Moriarty’s gang.

Other cases reveal Jim Browner’s jealous murder of his wife and Alec Fairbairn; Effie Munro’s concealed daughter Lucy and Grant Munro’s acceptance of them; and a fraud in which the Pinner brothers use Hall Pycroft’s handwriting to infiltrate Mawson & Williams. Holmes then recounts formative earlier cases. In the Gloria Scott matter, Victor Trevor’s father is exposed as James Armitage, a transported convict whose past aboard the mutinied ship returns through Hudson’s blackmail. In the Musgrave Ritual, Holmes follows an ancestral catechism to a hidden chamber, Brunton’s body, and a crown concealed for Charles II. Later investigations identify the Cunninghams as burglars and William Kirwan’s murderers; explain Colonel Barclay’s death through Henry Wood’s history of betrayal; and uncover Blessington as Sutton, an informer killed by former bank-robbery accomplices. The remaining cases broaden Holmes’s circle and stakes. Mycroft Holmes introduces the kidnapped Greek interpreter Melas, leading to the death of Paul Kratides and the escape of Sophy with her captors. Holmes restores Percy Phelps’s stolen naval treaty by catching Joseph Harrison retrieving it from beneath a floorboard. Finally, Holmes identifies Moriarty as the force behind extensive crime in London. Pursued across England and Europe, Holmes and Watson reach Reichenbach Falls, where Moriarty lures Watson away. Watson returns to find signs that Holmes and Moriarty struggled and fell into the chasm; neither body is recovered, but Holmes’s evidence exposes Moriarty’s gang.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is a London consulting detective, reasoner, and unofficial investigator who lives at Baker Street, works by observation, deduction, physical evidence, and analytical reasoning, and is chron­icled and frequently accompanied by his friend Dr. John Watson. He has remarkable detective gifts, medical knowledge of ears, expertise in chemical research, skill as a boxer, and habits marked by austere living, violin playing, occasional cocaine use when cases are scarce, and avoidance of unnecessary exertion. He loves London but has little attraction to nature, and he is generally disinclined to new friendships and averse to women. Across investigations in town and country, Holmes repeatedly separates fact from speculation and reconstructs crimes from small clues. At King’s Pyland, he recovers Silver Blaze and determines that John Straker died when the horse defended itself. He identifies Jim Browner as the killer connected to the packet of ears, investigates the cottage mystery and learns not to be overconfident, exposes the fraud involving Hall Pycroft’s handwriting, and recounts early cases involving the Gloria Scott cipher and the Musgrave Ritual’s concealed chamber. While recovering from exhaustion, he solves William Kirwan’s murder and exposes the Cunninghams. He investigates Colonel Barclay’s death, Blessington’s murder, the abduction of Paul Kratides, and the theft of Percy Phelps’s treaty, recovering the stolen State papers from Joseph Harrison. Holmes regards his methods as open to Watson and other interested observers, while Watson regards him as the best and wisest man he has known. Holmes says he has solved over a thousand cases and used his powers on the side of the law without known exception. The account culminates in his years-long effort against Professor Moriarty, his approximate intellectual equal and leader of a hidden criminal organization. Pursued and attacked by Moriarty’s agents, Holmes evades surveillance with Watson across Europe, ensures evidence against the gang will be found, and confronts Moriarty at Reichenbach Falls. After leaving Watson a farewell note, Holmes dies with Moriarty after their personal contest there.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dr. Watson is an English doctor, physician, former military doctor, and retired Army surgeon whose service in India left him with an old wound and whose health can be shaken by autumn weather. He is Sherlock Holmes’s longtime friend, fellow-lodger, companion, narrator, chronicler, and investigative associate. He shares chambers and rooms with Holmes at Baker Street, keeps notes on Holmes’s past cases, and writes Holmes’s memoirs, including A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four. Watson’s medical life runs alongside his partnership with Holmes. He has a medical practice, later takes over a practice in Paddington, makes long rounds by hansom, and after marriage lives at his London home with Mrs. Watson. He can also substitute for his doctor neighbour. His training repeatedly makes him useful: he identifies a cataract knife, examines injuries and deaths, aids Arthur Harry Pinner, treats Mr. Melas, and attends the apparent needs of others during investigations. Across the records, Watson travels with or accompanies Holmes through numerous cases, usually observing, questioning, proposing explanations, recording evidence, and witnessing revelations and arrests. He visits Devonshire for the Silver Blaze case; goes to Croydon, Birmingham, Reigate, Aldershot, Brook Street, the Diogenes Club, Woking, and other locations; and helps in moments of danger, including rescuing victims at The Myrtles and rushing to Holmes during the Cunningham investigation. He is also linked to Percy Phelps as a schoolfriend and to Colonel Hayter as an old friend. The account culminates when Holmes warns Watson about Professor Moriarty. Watson leaves his consulting-room, follows Holmes’s elaborate precautions, travels with him through Brussels and Switzerland, and helps evade pursuit. A forged call draws Watson back to Meiringen; when he returns to Reichenbach Falls, he finds evidence of Holmes’s struggle with Moriarty.

records.l: Colonel Ross, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Colonel Ross is a well-known sportsman, horse owner, and owner of the racehorse Silver Blaze and the King’s Pyland training-stable. When Silver Blaze disappears and John Straker is killed, he telegraphs Sherlock Holmes for help, seeking both the horse’s recovery and Straker’s murderer. He worries about Silver Blaze’s Cup entry, grows disappointed and doubtful when Holmes offers reassurance without producing the horse, and is distressed when the horse appears to run under his colours. Holmes reveals Silver Blaze’s identity and solves the murder, leading Ross to express gratitude and recognize Holmes’s achievement.

records.l: Inspector Gregory, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Inspector Gregory is an English detective and criminal-investigation inspector investigating the King’s Pyland case. Extremely competent but lacking imagination, he promptly finds and arrests Fitzroy Simpson, whom he considers probably responsible on circumstantial evidence. He thoroughly searches the moor, Tavistock, stables, and outbuildings and provides relevant effects and evidence to Holmes. By the end, Holmes directs him to investigate unusual lameness among the sheep, which Gregory recognizes as potentially important.

records.l: John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: John Straker, also called Derbyshire, was Colonel Ross’s servant, former jockey, and trainer of Ross’s horses at the Dartmoor stables. He had served Ross for twelve years, five as jockey and seven as trainer, and was married to Mrs. Straker. Secretly burdened by debts for his mistress’s expensive dresses, he drugged the stable-boy and led Silver Blaze onto the moor at night to lame the horse with a surgical cataract knife. Silver Blaze was frightened by Straker’s light and, acting in self-defence, kicked him in the forehead; Straker also cut his own thigh. He was found dead in a hollow near King’s Pyland, holding the bloodied knife and Fitzroy Simpson’s cravat.

records.l: Fitzroy Simpson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Fitzroy Simpson is a well-born bookmaker, living by sporting-club business after losing his fortune, who wagered five thousand pounds against Silver Blaze. He visited King’s Pyland seeking information about the horses and became the natural suspect in the disappearance of Silver Blaze and the murder of John Straker. Suspicion rested on his betting interest, presence in the storm, alleged poisoning of the stable-boy, heavy stick, and cravat, which he owned and which was found in Straker’s hand after Simpson dropped it while fleeing. Yet the case had weaknesses: Simpson had no wound despite Straker’s bloodied knife, and there was no clear means for him to hide the horse. The curried mutton and powdered opium show he could not have arranged the poisoning, so Holmes eliminates him as the murderer.

records.l: Silas Brown, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Silas Brown, trainer at the Mapleton stables, holds large Cup bets and has Silver Blaze concealed at Mapleton. After finding the horse wandering on the moor, he hides it; Holmes discovers this and compels him to keep it safe.

records.l: Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Silver Blaze is Colonel Ross’s five-year-old racehorse, descended from Isonomy stock, a celebrated and reliable favourite for the Wessex Cup. Known by his white forehead and mottled off-foreleg, he has won prizes for Colonel Ross and is favoured by the racing public. After John Straker’s murder, Silver Blaze disappears from King’s Pyland, having been seen near the place where Straker died. Sherlock Holmes follows his tracks to Mapleton stables, where Silas Brown conceals him and his white markings are disguised. Holmes ensures that Silver Blaze starts on Tuesday in Colonel Ross’s black cap and red jacket. Recognized despite the disguise, he wins the Wessex Plate by six lengths. He is then revealed to have killed Straker by kicking him in self-defence.

records.l: King’s Pyland, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: King’s Pyland is Colonel Ross’s small Devonshire training-stable and Silver Blaze’s home, containing four horses and guarded by stable lads. A stranger’s visit precedes Silver Blaze’s disappearance and John Straker’s murder on the surrounding moor. Holmes finds Silver Blaze is not there, then reconstructs that Straker drugged the stable-boy, removed the horse, and tried to injure it.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dartmoor is a sparsely inhabited moor and largely wilderness surrounding Tavistock, with open moorland, villas, gypsies, training establishments, hollows, ferns, and old mines. It contains King’s Pyland and becomes the setting for the search for Silver Blaze and investigation of John Straker’s murder, as Holmes follows tracks toward Mapleton.

records.l: Mapleton stables, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mapleton stables, near King’s Pyland across the moor, belong to competing trainer Silas Brown; horse tracks lead there, where Holmes determines Silver Blaze is concealed.

records.l: Tavistock, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a town [in Devonshire] Tavistock is the Devonshire town where Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, Colonel Ross, and Inspector Gregory arrive. Inspector Gregory searches its stables and outbuildings for Silver Blaze, and the party later prepares to return there.

records.l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: London is a city containing the Diogenes Club and Baker Street, Holmes’s address. It is a center of work, residence, crime, and investigation: Hall Pycroft receives Arthur Pinner’s offer there, while Mawson & Williams becomes the site of an attempted robbery, a watchman’s murder, and Beddington’s capture. Holmes, Watson, Mycroft Holmes, and Mr. Melas live or work there, and Holmes interviews Lord Holdhurst as he resumes an investigation. Across the city, Moriarty’s influence organizes much crime and shields wrongdoers from detection.

records.l: Wessex Cup, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Wessex Cup is a horse race in which Silver Blaze is the three-to-one first favourite, giving many people a financial interest in preventing his competition; four days later, Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Colonel Ross travel to Winchester to see it.

records.l: the disappearance of Silver Blaze, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The disappearance of Silver Blaze, favourite for the Wessex Cup, begins after a stranger appears at King’s Pyland and Ned Hunter is drugged with opium. Tracks lead from the hollow where John Straker died across Dartmoor to Mapleton, where Holmes concludes Silas Brown concealed the horse.

records.l: the murder of John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The murder of John Straker, Silver Blaze’s trainer, occurs at the Dartmoor training-stables on Monday night. After Straker fails to return from checking the horses, he is found in a hollow near the stables with a shattered head, a cut thigh, a bloodied knife, and a red-and-black cravat. Holmes initially leaves the killing unresolved after finding Silver Blaze, then concludes that Straker was accidentally killed in self-defence when Silver Blaze kicked him as he tried to lame the horse for race fraud.

records.l: the criminal investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The King’s Pyland criminal investigation concerns Silver Blaze’s disappearance, John Straker’s murder, and Ned Hunter’s drugging. Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory enlist Sherlock Holmes while Fitzroy Simpson is held as the principal suspect. Holmes finds the missing horse, postpononing further work on Straker’s murder.

records.l: the police theory, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The police theory attributes Silver Blaze's disappearance and John Straker's murder to Fitzroy Simpson: he drugged Ned Hunter, obtained a duplicate key, stole the horse, killed Straker with his weighted stick, then hid it or caused it to bolt.

records.l: Wessex Plate, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Wessex Plate is a one-mile-and-five-furlong horse race with six entries: The Negro, Pugilist, Desborough, Silver Blaze, Iris, and Rasper. Silver Blaze, owned by Colonel Ross, is the favourite, while Desborough is second in the betting. Colonel Ross considers withdrawing Silver Blaze, but Sherlock Holmes urges him to keep the horse entered and hopes it will start on Tuesday. Four days later, Silver Blaze wins by six lengths; Desborough finishes second and Iris third.

records.l: powdered opium, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Powdered opium, perceptible in ordinary food but disguised by curried mutton, was mixed into the stable-boy's meal to incapacitate him and helped Holmes identify the culprit's household.

records.l: curried mutton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains powdered opium [in the portion set aside for the stable-boy] Curried mutton was served to the stable-boy and provided a way to disguise the perceptible taste of powdered opium. Holmes reasons that only John Straker or his wife could have chosen and poisoned the portion set aside for the boy.

records.l: the circumstantial case against Fitzroy Simpson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a circumstantial case [considered strong but vulnerable to a clever counsel] The circumstantial case against Fitzroy Simpson includes his suspected motives, alleged poisoning attempt, presence during the storm, heavy stick, and cravat found in Straker’s hand. Sherlock Holmes argues that a clever counsel could undermine the case because key supporting details are missing or unexplained.

records.l: the horse tracks, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Horse tracks matched to Silver Blaze’s horseshoe are found away from the original crime scene, leading toward Mapleton, then alongside a man’s track and back to the gates of Mapleton stables.

records.l: Straker’s cataract knife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Straker’s cataract knife is a delicate, inflexible surgical instrument made by Weiss & Co., London. John Straker picked it up from his dressing-table, cork-protected its tip, and carried it on a rough expedition; it was later found bloodstained in his hand after his death. Though an unusual weapon, Holmes concludes Straker meant to use it to nick Silver Blaze’s tendons beneath the skin and lame the horse.

records.l: sheep, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A paddock group includes three recently lame sheep; a stable-lad reports this, and Sherlock Holmes considers it important.

records.l: dog, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_inactive_at night-time Sherlock Holmes calls attention to the curious incident of the dog in the night-time. The dog did nothing during the night.

records.l: murder of John Straker, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: has_victim John Straker [poor Straker] Sherlock Holmes says that there are grave difficulties in the way of arresting the murderer of John Straker. The investigation remains unresolved in this unit.

records.l: epidemic among the sheep, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: affects sheep [a singular epidemic of lameness] Sherlock Holmes describes the three lame sheep as a singular epidemic and recommends that Inspector Gregory investigate it. He considers the condition exceedingly important.

records.l: dog's inactivity at night, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a curious incident Sherlock Holmes identifies the dog's failure to do anything during the night as the curious incident. He draws Inspector Gregory’s attention to this fact.

records.l: Winchester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains racecourse [beyond the town] Winchester is the destination to which Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to see the race for the Wessex Cup.

records.l: Victoria, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains carriage (Holmes's reserved carriage) [at the time of departure] Victoria Station is where Watson arrives, finds his luggage, and boards the train. Moriarty reaches the station as the train is already departing.

records.l: horse-race fraud, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Horse-race fraud involved John Straker’s plan to secretly injure Silver Blaze’s tendons, preventing the horse from winning after bets were placed against it through agents.

records.l: thought reading, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
