records.l: the consultation with the Russian nobleman, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: takes_place_at the consulting-room [at Dr. Trevelyan’s practice] During the consultation, Trevelyan questions the elderly supposed Russian nobleman about his cataleptic condition. The man suddenly becomes rigid and unresponsive, but disappears while Trevelyan goes to fetch nitrite of amyl; he and his supposed son return the following evening and offer an explanation.

records.l: the intrusion into Blessington's room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_caused_by the Russian nobleman's son [according to the physical evidence] After the second visit by the supposed Russian patients, Blessington finds several fresh, unusually large footprints on the light carpet in his room. Nothing has been taken, but the footprints indicate that one of the visitors apparently went upstairs while Trevelyan was occupied.

records.l: the resident patient’s house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The resident patient's house is Trevelyan's residence and medical practice at 403 Brook Street. Blessington lives there as a resident patient and becomes so alarmed about security that he carries a pistol and threatens approaching visitors.

records.l: the medical practice partnership, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Blessington finances Trevelyan's medical practice by taking the house, furnishing it, paying the servants, and providing Trevelyan with living expenses and a carriage. In return, Trevelyan keeps one quarter of his earnings and hands three quarters to Blessington, making Blessington wealthy.

records.l: the resident-patient arrangement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Blessington becomes Trevelyan’s resident patient, claiming a weak heart and constant supervision; he takes the best rooms, seldom leaves, reviews evening accounts, and receives three quarters of earnings while Dr. Percy Trevelyan receives one quarter.

records.l: Sutton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sutton, later known as Blessington, is the worst Worthingdon bank gang member who becomes an informer, leading to Cartwright’s hanging and three accomplices’ fifteen-year sentences before his identity is revealed.

records.l: the Worthingdon bank gang, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Worthingdon bank gang was a five-man criminal gang that committed the Worthingdon bank business in 1875; Sutton informed on it, Cartwright was hanged, and released members pursued Sutton.

records.l: the Worthingdon bank business, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The 1875 Worthingdon bank business saw five men rob seven thousand pounds and murder Tobin; all were arrested, Sutton's evidence leading to Cartwright's execution and three imprisonments.

records.l: Blessington's murder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a cold-blooded murder [disguised as suicide by hanging] Blessington's murder is staged as a hanging but is shown by Holmes to be a planned, cold-blooded killing. Three men enter through the front door with help from the page, force the locked bedroom door, gag Blessington, conduct what appears to be a judicial proceeding, and hang him.

records.l: Blessington's supposed suicide, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a false suicide [actually murder] Blessington's supposed suicide is initially supported by the appearance of his slept-in bed, the hanging body, and the early-morning timing. Holmes disproves it after finding that two cigar ends were smoked through a holder and two were not, with differing methods of cutting or biting the ends.

records.l: the Brook Street Mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a unsolved public case [not fully dealt with in public print until this account] The Brook Street Mystery concerns the attacks on Blessington, his concealed identity as Sutton, and his eventual murder. It is not fully dealt with in public print until the account given here.

records.l: the three assailants' revenge, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: targets Blessington [to avenge Cartwright’s death] Biddle, Hayward, and Moffat seek revenge against Sutton after being released from prison for their part in the Worthingdon bank business. They make two unsuccessful attempts to reach him and succeed on the third attempt by murdering him in his bedroom.

records.l: the rope (Blessington's bedroom), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A large coil of escape rope kept under Blessington’s bed for fire emergencies. When Blessington was murdered, the killers cut rope from it and used it to hang him, avoiding the need to assemble separate gallows.

records.l: Mycroft Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mycroft Holmes is Sherlock Holmes’s older brother, seven years his senior, with even greater powers of observation and deduction. Despite this, he has little ambition or energy, treats deduction as a hobby, audits government department books, lives in Pall Mall, walks only between Whitehall, and spends much of his time at the Diogenes Club, which he helped found. He brings Mr. Melas’s Greek case to Sherlock, then advertises for information about Paul Kratides and Sophy. After J. Davenport identifies Sophy’s location, Mycroft joins Sherlock, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Gregson at The Myrtles and helps rescue the poisoned captives.

records.l: Mr. Melas, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mr. Melas is a Greek-born professional interpreter, long known as London’s chief Greek interpreter, working in law courts and guiding wealthy Orientals at Northumberland Avenue hotels; he lives above Mycroft Holmes. Mr. Latimer and other conspirators twice abduct him, forcing him to interpret questions and threats directed at Kratides and Paul Kratides. He secretly learns and reveals clues about captivity, then is threatened, struck unconscious, bound amid charcoal fumes at The Myrtles, rescued by Sherlock Holmes and others, and survives.

records.l: Harold Latimer, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Harold Latimer is a fashionably dressed young Englishman who, with Wilson Kemp, conspires against Sophy and Paul Kratides. He persuades Sophy to flee with him, holds Paul prisoner to force him to surrender property, and abducts and threatens Mr. Melas to interpret for Paul. After the conspiracy is exposed, Latimer flees England with Sophy and Kemp and is later reported to have died violently in Buda-Pesth.

records.l: Paul Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Paul Kratides is a Greek gentleman from Athens and Sophy Kratides’s brother. He is abducted and held prisoner in England by conspirators, restrained with plaster over his face and mouth, weakened by starvation and cruelty, and coercively questioned. They seek his signature in a dispute over his and Sophy’s property, but he refuses unless Sophy is married before him by a Greek priest. After three weeks of captivity, he is found bound at The Myrtles and dies from charcoal poisoning in a room filled with fumes.

records.l: Sophy Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sophy Kratides is a wealthy Greek lady, Paul Kratides’s sister, who speaks Greek and visits England as a young woman. There she becomes involved with Harold Latimer, who persuades her to flee with him. Unaware that Latimer and Wilson Kemp are holding Paul prisoner at The Myrtles, she sees him during an interrogation, recognizes him despite his plaster disguise, and embraces him after he tears it away. Harold removes her, and she later flees with the two men. Holmes suspects that she avenges the two Englishmen’s murder.

records.l: Harold, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: assists_in Kratides's abduction and coercive interrogation [under the direction of the older man] Harold is the younger man who helps control Kratides and assists with the interrogation. He brings Kratides into the room, seizes Sophy when she embraces him, and pushes her out.

records.l: the Diogenes Club, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Diogenes Club is a London club for unsociable and unclubable men, offering comfortable chairs and periodicals without conversation. Its rules forbid members from noticing one another outside the Stranger’s Room; Mycroft Holmes founded it and attends regularly.

records.l: Pall Mall, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains the Diogenes Club [near the Carlton] Pall Mall contains Mycroft Holmes’s lodgings and the Diogenes Club, which stands opposite his rooms. Sherlock Holmes and John Watson walk there, and Mr. Melas is summoned from the club to tell his story.

records.l: the Greek interpreter case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: concerns Kratides's abduction and coercive interrogation The Greek interpreter case concerns Mr. Melas’s forced involvement in an attempt to make Kratides sign documents. It includes Kratides’s confinement, his connection with Sophy, and the threatening men who prevent Mr. Melas from freely reporting what he witnessed.

records.l: Kratides's abduction and coercive interrogation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Paul Kratides comes from Athens after Sophy flees with Harold Latimer. Latimer and Wilson Kemp abduct, imprison, disguise, and isolate him because he cannot speak English. In an unknown furnished house, starvation, plaster restraints, threats, and separation from Sophy coerce written answers and a signature; he refuses unless he sees her married by a Greek priest.

records.l: the Greek language, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_spoken_by Mr. Melas [as his principal interpreting language] The Greek language is central to Mr. Melas’s profession and to the coercive interrogation. Kratides writes his answers in Greek, while Mr. Melas uses Greek questions and covert additions to communicate with him without the captors understanding.

records.l: the inheritance and property dispute, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_contested_by Kratides [he refuses to sign the papers] The dispute concerns Paul Kratides's own property and the property of his sister Sophy Kratides. Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp attempt to make Paul sign these assets over to them, but Paul refuses despite imprisonment, starvation, cruelty, and threats.

records.l: the plaster restraints, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Kratides’s face is covered with strips of sticking-plaster, including a large pad over his mouth. He tears the plaster from his lips when Sophy appears and calls out to her.

records.l: Wilson Kemp, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Wilson Kemp, Harold Latimer’s associate in the conspiracy against the Kratides siblings, helps imprison, starve, threaten, and disguise Paul Kratides and abduct Mr. Melas; after fleeing with Latimer and Sophy, he is reported to have died violently in Buda-Pesth.

records.l: the conspirators, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The conspirators, Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp aided by a coachman and his wife, imprison Paul Kratides and attempt to coerce him through cruelty and starvation, hold Sophy at The Myrtles, abduct Mr. Melas as interpreter, then flee with Sophy after exposure.

records.l: Beckenham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains The Myrtles Beckenham is the place where The Myrtles is located. Sherlock Holmes, Mycroft Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Gregson travel there to investigate the house and find the captives.

records.l: The Myrtles, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Myrtles is a large, dark furnished house in Beckenham, set back in its own grounds. Paul Kratides is imprisoned there and Mr. Melas is brought for a second interview. Investigators find it deserted, then rescue Paul and Melas from an upstairs room filled with charcoal fumes.

records.l: Athens, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Athens is Paul Kratides's home city and the place from which he comes to England after learning about Sophy's relationship with Harold Latimer. Mycroft Holmes considers sending a wire to the head of the Athens police.

records.l: the newspaper advertisement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: seeks_information_about Paul Kratides [and Sophy Kratides] The newspaper advertisement offers a reward for information about Paul Kratides, who cannot speak English, and about a Greek lady named Sophy. J. Davenport answers it and identifies The Myrtles in Beckenham as Sophy's current residence, but the advertisement also alerts the conspirators that Mr. Melas has betrayed them.

records.l: the carriage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: transports Mr. Melas [to Wandsworth Common] The carriage takes Mr. Melas to and from the conspirators' house during his first abduction and leaves him at Wandsworth Common. Later, a carriage carrying heavy luggage leaves The Myrtles shortly before the investigators arrive, indicating that the conspirators and Sophy have fled.

records.l: the poisoned room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains charcoal poisoning [from a burning brass tripod] The poisoned room is an upstairs room at The Myrtles containing Paul Kratides and Mr. Melas, both bound and unconscious. A small brass tripod burning charcoal fills it with poisonous fumes; Paul dies there, while Melas is rescued alive.

records.l: charcoal poisoning, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: causes the murder of the two Englishmen [at The Myrtles] Charcoal poisoning is used by the conspirators to kill or punish Paul Kratides and Mr. Melas after Paul refuses to comply and Melas is blamed for betraying them. Sherlock Holmes recognizes the danger, ventilates the room, removes the burning tripod, and helps rescue the victims.

records.l: the attempted coercion of Paul Kratides, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: concerns the inheritance and property dispute [over Paul and Sophy Kratides’s property] Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp try to force Paul Kratides to sign away his own and Sophy Kratides's property. They rely on threats, cruelty, starvation, and repeated interpreted interviews, but Paul remains resistant and refuses to comply.

records.l: the murder of the two Englishmen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occurs_in Buda-Pesth [after the men fled England] Months later, a newspaper reports that two Englishmen traveling with a woman in Buda-Pesth were stabbed and fatally injured. The Hungarian police believe the men quarreled and killed each other, while Sherlock Holmes suspects that Sophy Kratides may have avenged the wrongs done to herself and Paul.

records.l: Percy Phelps, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Percy Phelps is a young diplomatist and Foreign Office official, formerly a brilliant Cambridge scholar, Lord Holdhurst’s nephew, and the fiancé of Annie Harrison. Nervous and sensitive, he lives in Woking and is recovering from a long brain-fever after the original Naval Treaty vanishes while he is copying it at the Foreign Office. The loss ruins his career and puts his honour and position at stake. Unable to find any route by which the thief entered, he pursues Mrs. Tangey without recovering the papers, then falls ill for nine weeks. As Sherlock Holmes’s client, Phelps recounts the theft at Briarbrae, where an armed man later attempts to enter his bedroom, making him fear for his life as well as his reputation. Holmes sends the still-weak Phelps to London with Dr. John Watson while the inquiry continues. Phelps despairs that the effort has failed, but is overwhelmed with joy when Holmes returns the papers, which had remained in Phelps’s room at Briarbrae throughout his ten weeks of suffering, restoring his honour.

records.l: Lord Holdhurst, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lord Holdhurst is a prominent Conservative politician, statesman, nobleman, Cabinet member, and England’s foreign minister, regarded as a future premier despite limited means. Percy Phelps’s maternal uncle, he gives Phelps the original secret treaty between England and Italy and orders it copied securely at the Foreign Office. Later, in his Downing Street chambers, he courteously receives Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson, confirms the instructions, denies sharing the plan, and warns that disclosure could have grave consequences.

records.l: Joseph Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Joseph Harrison, Annie Harrison’s brother and Percy Phelps’s prospective brother-in-law, is present in Woking during Phelps’s illness and helps investigate signs of an attempted night intrusion. Beneath this helpful appearance, he is the thief of the stolen State papers. After heavy stock-speculation losses, he becomes willing to do anything to improve his fortunes, hides the papers beneath a removable board under the carpet in Phelps’s bedroom, and later returns at night to retrieve them. Armed with a knife, he attacks Holmes during the confrontation, but Holmes overpowers him and recovers the papers. He is characterized as selfish, financially desperate, and dangerous.

records.l: Annie Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Annie Harrison, Joseph Harrison’s sister and Percy Phelps’s fiancée, is Phelps’s devoted nurse during his illness at Briarbrae. She nurses him for two months, encourages his courage and patience, stays beside him during Holmes and Watson’s visit, and agrees to Holmes’s instructions to guard his room.

records.l: the Phelps family, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: owns Briarbrae The Phelps family lives at Briarbrae and finds discussion of Percy Phelps's misfortune painful. Percy Phelps's father and mother ask Joseph Harrison to receive Holmes and Watson.

records.l: the Foreign Office, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Foreign Office is an organization located on Charles Street, with a servants’ side door. It employs Percy Phelps in a trusted role and keeps the Naval Treaty in a secure room, from which the original disappears while he investigates delayed coffee; examination seems to exclude ordinary entry or concealment.

records.l: Briarbrae, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Briarbrae is a large detached house in Woking, near the station, where Percy Phelps recuperates after brain-fever while Annie Harrison cares for him and Holmes and Watson hear his account. It contains stolen State papers hidden beneath a removable floorboard in Phelps’s bedroom; Holmes watches from the grounds and intercepts Joseph Harrison outside the window.

records.l: Woking, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Woking is the place of Briarbrae, reached by train through fir woods and heather, where Percy Phelps recovers after an attempted night intrusion. Holmes and Watson meet him there; later Holmes stays to pursue clues while Phelps and Watson return to London.

records.l: Charles Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Charles Street is reached through a side door and a short staircase from the Foreign Office. After the treaty theft, Percy Phelps and the commissionnaire rush into Charles Street, where a policeman reports seeing only one tall, elderly woman pass. Charles Street is the location of the Foreign Office entrance mentioned in Holmes’s investigation. Holmes advertises for the number of a cab that dropped a passenger at or near the Foreign Office there at about quarter to ten on May 23rd.

records.l: The Adventure of the Naval Treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a case record The Adventure of the Naval Treaty is the second case in Dr. John Watson's list of notable cases from the July after his marriage. It concerns Percy Phelps, the theft of a secret naval treaty, and Sherlock Holmes's investigation.

records.l: brain-fever, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Brain-fever is a serious illness lasting more than nine weeks. It follows Percy Phelps’s failed recovery of the treaty and the misfortune that destroys his career. Overwhelmed by shame and distress, he suffers a fit, returns home unconscious and raving, then gradually regains memory and reason but remains extremely weak.

records.l: Foreign Office treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Foreign Office treaty, also called the Naval Treaty, is a secret French-language State document between England and Italy, consisting of twenty-six articles and signed by high dignitaries. It defines Great Britain’s position toward the Triple Alliance and its policy should the French fleet gain naval superiority over Italy in the Mediterranean. Lord Holdhurst assigns Percy Phelps to copy it, but it disappears from Phelps’s room, threatening his career and honour and raising fears of grave consequences if disclosed. For nearly ten weeks, there is no evidence that it has reached the French or Russian Foreign Office, though Joseph Harrison apparently plans to sell it to the French embassy. Harrison hides it beneath a removable floorboard over a gas-pipe joint in Phelps’s bedroom at Briarbrae. Holmes lets Harrison retrieve it, takes it from him, and returns it to Phelps before its secrecy ends in a few months.

records.l: the treaty copy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a copy of the Naval Treaty [made by Percy Phelps] The treaty copy is the draft Percy Phelps makes at the Foreign Office after receiving the original from Lord Holdhurst. It remains on the desk after the theft, while the original treaty is taken.

records.l: Percy Phelps's letter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Percy Phelps’s dictated letter asks Dr. John Watson to bring Sherlock Holmes to Briarbrae, explains Phelps’s recovery from brain-fever, and is identified by Holmes as written in an exceptional woman’s hand.

records.l: the theft of the naval treaty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The theft of the original Naval Treaty occurs at the Foreign Office while Percy Phelps is alone copying the document. A bell rings from his room; when he returns, the original is gone. Phelps concludes that the thief used the side door, while Sherlock Holmes stresses the timing and absence of footprints. Scotland Yard investigates Mrs. Tangey, her husband, and Gorot without finding evidence, leaving the case unresolved until Phelps appeals to Holmes. Although Lord Holdhurst says no one should have known the treaty would be copied, Holmes considers that the thief may be delaying delivery. Joseph Harrison entered through the Charles Street door, stole the papers from the empty room, hid them at Briarbrae, and planned to retrieve and sell them, possibly to the French embassy.

records.l: Tangey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Tangey, a Foreign Office employee, keeps an overnight lodge at the foot of the stairs and makes coffee for late workers; during a theft, he sleeps beside a boiling kettle, hears Phelps's bell, and joins the search.

records.l: the commissionnaire's wife, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The commissionnaire's wife is a large, coarse-faced elderly Foreign Office charwoman. Wearing slippers after removing her boots, she answers Phelps's summons and takes his coffee order; later a policeman reports a similar woman leaving Charles Street, though her husband denies involvement.

records.l: Miss Harrison, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Miss Harrison, Percy Phelps’s fiancée from Northumberland, nurses him through his illness and stays at his home. Holmes judges her a strong-charactered, apparently good woman. She cooperates in his recovery plan, occupying Phelps’s bedroom by day and, on Holmes’s instructions, locking it from outside at night so Joseph believes entry is possible only through the window.

records.l: Mrs. Tangey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mrs. Tangey, a commissionnaire’s wife with a bad reputation who drinks alcohol and has an eldest daughter, is suspected of taking a treaty, arrested and searched, but no papers are found.

records.l: Forbes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A Scotland Yard detective, Forbes takes charge of a theft case, questions and shadows key suspects, and reports that none yields evidence linking them to it.

records.l: bell, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_located_in room [on a wire just to the right of Percy Phelps’s desk] The bell beside Phelps’s desk was rung after the treaty disappeared, even though the person who rang it must have approached the desk. Holmes regards the ringing as the most distinctive feature of the case and considers whether it was deliberate, accidental, or intended to prevent the crime.

records.l: room, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A room containing Phelps’s desk has high, inside-fastened windows, carpet preventing a trap-door, and a whitewashed ceiling; examination found no secret door, intruder traces, or physical clue, leaving the door as the only possible entry.

records.l: cab, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_used_for advertised cab-number search [as the suspected means of arrival] Holmes suspects that the thief or another participant came to the Foreign Office in a cab because the night was wet but no damp trace was left inside. He places an advertisement seeking the number of the cab that arrived near the Foreign Office at the relevant time.

records.l: secret entrance investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: An investigation examines a room and its surroundings for hidden access, finds no secret door or concealed route, and leads Holmes to consider an outside approach.

records.l: bell-ringing mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: concerns bell [the reason for its ringing] The unexplained ringing of the bell is central to the mystery because it required the intruder to come close to Phelps’s desk and seemed to serve no obvious purpose. Holmes considers several explanations and appears to recognize a new possibility while discussing it with Watson.

records.l: the attempted night intrusion, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: An attempted break-in at Percy Phelps's bedroom window in Woking apparently threatens his life: Phelps hears the catch forced, sees a cloaked man with a long knife, raises the household, and marks outside yield no trail.

records.l: the intruder, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: carries the long knife [during the attempted night intrusion] The intruder is seen only briefly by Percy Phelps as a man crouching at the bedroom window. He is wrapped in a cloak covering the lower part of his face and appears to carry a long knife before fleeing across the grounds.

records.l: the political conspiracy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A suspected political conspiracy appears to target Percy Phelps’s life and honour. Phelps believes he is its unconscious centre after a naval treaty is stolen; Watson says identifying the intruder could expose both the thief and the conspiracy, which remains unconfirmed.

records.l: the knife (Joseph Harrison's knife), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Joseph Harrison's knife is a tool used to force a window sash and shutter bar, then a weapon against Sherlock Holmes, cutting his knuckles before Holmes gains the upper hand.

records.l: the investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes’s principal inquiry concerns the theft of the naval treaty and a related attempted night intrusion. After interviewing Lord Holdhurst, investigating the missing treaty, and examining the alleged Woking intrusion, he finds no reply to his advertisement and little evidence, remaining in Woking as Phelps and Watson return to London.

records.l: the case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes calls the case one of his darkest and most remarkable investigations; abundant evidence obscures vital facts, making reconstruction difficult from beginning to end.

records.l: the attempted recovery of the papers, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The attempted recovery of the papers is conducted by Sherlock Holmes, who lets Joseph Harrison make repeated efforts to take papers from Percy Phelps’s room, then watches outside and confronts him after the final nighttime attempt.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Moriarty is a phenomenally able mathematician, author of a Binomial Theorem treatise at twenty-one, and a former university mathematics professor who later became a mathematical coach. He is also the hidden central power and terrible chief of a criminal organization, employing numerous agents to plan and execute serious crimes; he is described as Europe’s most dangerous and capable criminal and as Holmes’s intellectual equal. As Holmes investigates him and planned arrests threaten his gang, Moriarty demands that Holmes stop, threatens destruction, and uses agents to attack while avoiding direct exposure and declaring he will never stand trial. After the police secure the gang, Moriarty escapes London, pursues Holmes and Watson through Victoria and beyond, and follows Holmes to Switzerland. At Reichenbach Falls, he confronts Holmes; experts conclude that the two fell together while locked in combat.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson's Continental journey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A planned Continental journey begins as Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. John Watson to accompany him while police prepare against Professor Moriarty’s organization, directing elaborate precautions before their reserved Continental express departs Victoria.

records.l: the Moriarty criminal organization, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A powerful, carefully protected criminal syndicate, it uses numerous organized agents to commit forgery, robbery, murder, theft, and other planned crimes while Moriarty remains hidden.

records.l: the police, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_planning the planned arrests [of Moriarty and his principal gang members] The police are expected to arrest Professor Moriarty and the principal members of his gang on the following Monday, once Sherlock Holmes’s investigation is complete. They examine the site of the falling brick and take into custody the man who attacked Holmes with a bludgeon, but Holmes expects no connection to Moriarty to be provable in either case.

records.l: the Moriarty investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes’s investigation traces a hidden criminal power through many apparently unrelated crimes until it leads to Professor Moriarty. Holmes has spent months in an intellectual contest with Moriarty and believes that the evidence and arrests will expose more than forty mysteries.

records.l: the planned arrests, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: precede the criminal trial [as the basis for prosecution] The planned arrests are to take place on the following Monday, when Professor Moriarty and the principal members of his gang are expected to be placed in police custody. Sherlock Holmes believes that the arrests can proceed without him, although his presence will be needed to secure a conviction.

records.l: the attacks on Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Moriarty’s agents mount indirect assaults on Sherlock Holmes: a two-horse van is driven at him, a brick is dropped from a roof, and a man with a bludgeon attacks. Holmes avoids the first two and knocks down the assailant, injuring his knuckles.

records.l: the Continental express, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Continental express prepares to leave Victoria Station, departs before Moriarty can stop it, then stops at Canterbury to connect with the boat to Dieppe. Holmes and Watson leave there as Moriarty arrives behind them in another carriage and engine.

records.l: carriage (Holmes's reserved carriage), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes’s reserved carriage, marked “Engaged,” is boarded by Watson and temporarily contains an Italian priest assigned by a porter, who is revealed to be Holmes.

records.l: Italian priest, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: An aged, venerable Italian priest who speaks broken English travels toward Paris with luggage, is assisted into Watson’s carriage, and is revealed to be Holmes in disguise.

records.l: Holmes's disguise, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes’s disguise is an aged Italian priest’s appearance and clothing, including a black cassock and hat; he briefly drops it to speak, then removes and packs it away.

records.l: precautions against pursuit, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: are_necessary continued vigilance [because pursuit is ongoing] Watson uses a carefully selected hansom, travels through the Lowther Arcade, and takes a brougham to Victoria Station. Holmes also disguises himself and reserves a carriage, but says that every precaution is still necessary because pursuit remains close.

records.l: the pursuit of Holmes by Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The ongoing pursuit of Holmes by Professor Moriarty follows Holmes and Watson through their Swiss journey. Warned that pursuers are close, Holmes watches for danger. Moriarty is seen approaching on a path, reaches a station, and tries to stop their train, but Holmes and Watson escape as it departs.

records.l: Canterbury, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: has_train_delay an hour [before a train to Newhaven] Canterbury is a stop on the express where Holmes and Watson get out. They find that they must wait an hour for a train to Newhaven, while Moriarty's special train passes through after them.

records.l: Newhaven, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Newhaven is the next destination in Holmes and Watson's planned escape journey. They intend to travel from there by boat to Dieppe.

records.l: the fire at Holmes and Watson's rooms, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occurs_at Holmes and Watson's rooms [last night] The fire occurred during the night and caused no great harm. Holmes says it resulted from the attackers' mistaken belief that he had returned to the rooms.

records.l: Holmes and Watson's escape journey, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes and Watson evade Moriarty by leaving the express at Canterbury, replacing marked luggage with carpet-bags, traveling cross-country through Newhaven and Dieppe, then via Luxembourg and Basle, and ending in Switzerland.

records.l: Holmes and Watson's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: targets criminals [with the aim of arresting the larger offender and the smaller offenders] Holmes says that arresting Moriarty would ruin the work of three months by allowing the smaller criminals to escape. He intends to avoid a premature arrest and secure the larger criminal network later.

records.l: Moriarty's gang, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Moriarty's gang is a criminal organization exposed by Holmes's evidence. London police capture all but Professor Moriarty; the evidence supports conviction and the gang is heavily punished in subsequent proceedings.

records.l: Meiringen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Meiringen is a village connected to Rosenlaui over hills, where Holmes and Watson stay at the Englischer Hof on May 3; a forged hotel-marked letter lures Watson back, and Holmes’s note directs Patterson to pigeonhole M evidence.

records.l: Rosenlaui, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a hamlet Rosenlaui is the hamlet where Holmes and Watson intend to spend the night after crossing the hills from Meiringen. Holmes tells Watson that he will walk there after remaining at Reichenbach Falls.

records.l: Reichenbach Falls, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A dangerous, fearful Swiss waterfall reached by a path beside the torrent, Reichenbach Falls becomes the site of Holmes's final confrontation with Moriarty after Watson leaves.

records.l: the journey through Switzerland, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The journey through Switzerland begins via Brussels and Strasburg, reaches Geneva, then continues for a week through the Valley of the Rhone, over the snowbound Gemmi Pass, and through Interlaken to Meiringen on 3 May. Holmes and Watson travel amid beautiful scenery while Holmes watches for Moriarty.

records.l: Moriarty's escape, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_from London police [after the gang is secured] Moriarty's escape occurs after the London police capture his entire gang except him. Holmes curses the news and believes Moriarty will devote himself to revenge.

records.l: the confrontation at Reichenbach Falls, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes and Professor Moriarty's final personal contest follows a forged letter separating Watson from Holmes; evidence shows them struggling near the falls' edge before falling into the chasm.

records.l: the deaths of Holmes and Moriarty, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occur_at Reichenbach Falls [following their locked personal contest] The deaths of Holmes and Moriarty are inferred from an examination by experts, who conclude that the two men fell together while locked in each other's arms. Their bodies cannot be recovered and are believed to remain in the waterfall's chasm.

records.l: Holmes's career, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Holmes says that he has not lived wholly in vain, having used his powers on the right side in more than a thousand cases. He regards capturing or eliminating Moriarty as the culmination of his career and says that no conclusion could be more congenial to him.

records.l: the letter from Meiringen, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a hoax [designed to separate Watson from Holmes] The letter from Meiringen falsely claims that an Englishwoman suffering from consumption has arrived at the hotel and wishes to see Watson. Holmes later reveals that he suspected it was a hoax but allowed Watson to leave because he expected such a development.

records.l: Holmes's Alpine-stock, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_left_at Reichenbach Falls [leaning against a rock] Holmes's Alpine-stock remains leaning against the rock where Watson left Holmes at Reichenbach Falls. Its presence helps Watson realize that Holmes did not proceed to Rosenlaui.

records.l: Holmes's silver cigarette-case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains Holmes's farewell note [the note lay beneath it] Holmes's silver cigarette-case lies on top of a boulder near his Alpine-stock. Watson finds the case and discovers Holmes's farewell note beneath it.

records.l: Holmes's farewell note, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A three-page note to Dr. John Watson, written at Reichenbach Falls, recounts Holmes’s final confrontation with Moriarty, identifies evidence to convict the gang, directs Inspector Patterson to it, gives property to Mycroft, and sends greetings to Mrs. Watson.

records.l: the Reichenbach waterfall, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Reichenbach waterfall is described as a tremendous, spray-filled abyss with black rocks, a boiling pit, and a deep chasm. Its force and depth make recovery of Holmes's and Moriarty's bodies impossible.

records.q: I drew aside my curtains before I went to bed and looked out from my window. It opened upon the grassy space which lay in front of the hall door. records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: This unit introduces *The Hound of the Baskervilles*, identified as another adventure of Sherlock Holmes by A. Conan Doyle. A. Conan Doyle dedicates the tale to Robinson, saying that Robinson’s account of a West-Country legend inspired it and that Robinson helped with its details. The contents list chapters concerning Sherlock Holmes, the Baskerville curse, Sir Henry Baskerville, Dr. Watson’s reports and diary, and events on the moor.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: The Hound of the Baskervilles is presented as another adventure of Sherlock Holmes. Its contents include chapters about the curse of the Baskervilles, Baskerville Hall, the moor, and the hound.

records.l: A. Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: A. Conan Doyle is identified as the author of The Hound of the Baskervilles. He writes to Robinson that Robinson’s account of a West-Country legend inspired the tale and that Robinson helped with its details.

records.l: Robinson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: Robinson receives A. Conan Doyle’s thanks for providing an account of a West-Country legend and helping with details used in the tale.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is identified as the central figure of this adventure. The contents name him in the opening chapter, "Mr. Sherlock Holmes."

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: Dr. Watson is associated with several sections listed in the contents, including his first report, second report, and diary.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
records.s: The Baskervilles are associated with a curse that is the subject of a listed chapter. The contents also refer to Sir Henry Baskerville and Baskerville Hall.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Mr. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson examine a stick left by Dr. James Mortimer and use it to infer details about its owner. Holmes corrects Watson’s assumptions, identifying the initials “C.C.H.” as Charing Cross Hospital and deducing that Mortimer is a young country practitioner with a dog. Dr. Mortimer returns for the stick and explains that it was presented to him by friends at Charing Cross Hospital on the occasion of his marriage. He then asks Holmes for help with a serious and extraordinary problem.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Mr. Sherlock Holmes examines Dr. James Mortimer’s presentation stick and uses its markings and wear to reconstruct details about its owner. He correctly infers that Mortimer is a country practitioner who walks a great deal, identifies “C.C.H.” as Charing Cross Hospital, and recognizes tooth marks from a curly-haired spaniel. He invites Mortimer to explain the serious problem that has brought him to seek assistance.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Dr. Watson examines Mortimer’s stick and infers that its owner is an elderly, successful country doctor associated with a local hunt. Holmes points out that most of these conclusions are erroneous, though Watson correctly identifies Mortimer as a country practitioner who walks extensively. Watson consults the Medical Directory and reads Mortimer’s professional record aloud.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Dr. James Mortimer is identified as a young M.R.C.S. and country practitioner serving Grimpen, Thorsley, and High Barrow. He returns to recover his presentation stick and explains that friends at Charing Cross Hospital gave it to him on the occasion of his marriage, which led him to leave the hospital and abandon hopes of a consulting practice. He describes himself as an unpractical scientific man and asks Mr. Sherlock Holmes for help with a serious and extraordinary problem.

records.l: Mortimer's presentation stick, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Mortimer’s presentation stick is a thick, bulbous-headed Penang lawyer with a silver band engraved “To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H.” and dated 1884. Its worn ferrule indicates extensive walking, while tooth marks show that a dog habitually carried it. Mortimer values the stick highly and returns to retrieve it.

records.l: Charing Cross Hospital, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Charing Cross Hospital is identified as the institution represented by the initials “C.C.H.” on Mortimer’s stick. Mortimer served there as a house-surgeon from 1882 to 1884, and friends at the hospital presented him with the stick when he married.

records.l: scientific deduction, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 1.
records.s: Scientific deduction is demonstrated through the examination of Mortimer’s stick, its inscription, its wear, and the marks left by a dog. Holmes uses these clues to revise Watson’s mistaken assumptions and infer Mortimer’s profession, history, age, personality, and ownership of a curly-haired spaniel.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Dr. James Mortimer brings Sherlock Holmes an 1742 Baskerville manuscript recounting the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles and its alleged origin with Hugo Baskerville. He also presents a Devon County Chronicle report on the recent death of Sir Charles Baskerville, whose body was found at the end of the yew alley after he apparently fled toward the moor. Mortimer explains that Sir Charles feared the family legend, suffered from heart disease and nervous distress, and died without visible physical injury. Mortimer finally reveals that he found fresh footprints near the body which he identifies as those of a gigantic hound.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Dr. James Mortimer, Sir Charles Baskerville's personal friend and medical attendant, brings Sherlock Holmes the Baskerville manuscript and a newspaper account of Sir Charles's death. He explains Sir Charles's fear of the family legend, describes the circumstances surrounding the death, and states that he found footprints resembling those of a gigantic hound near the body.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes dates the manuscript to the early eighteenth century by examining its script and reads the public account of Sir Charles Baskerville's death. After initially dismissing the legend as a fairy tale, he asks Dr. James Mortimer to provide the private facts of the case.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Dr. John Watson observes Sherlock Holmes examining the manuscript and listens as Dr. James Mortimer recounts the Baskerville legend and Sir Charles Baskerville's death.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville was a wealthy, generous, childless man who restored Baskerville Hall after making his fortune in South African speculation. He feared the Baskerville legend, suffered from heart disease and nervous distress, and was found dead at the end of the yew alley after appearing to flee toward the moor; Dr. James Mortimer later reported gigantic hound footprints near his body.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Henry Baskerville is identified as the likely heir to Sir Charles Baskerville because he is the son of Sir Charles's younger brother. He was last heard of in America, and inquiries were being made to inform him of his inheritance.

records.l: Hugo Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Hugo Baskerville is described in the manuscript as a wild, profane, godless, cruel man who abducted a yeoman's daughter. He pursued her across the moor with hounds and was found dead beside her, with a huge black hound tearing at his throat.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The Baskerville family is associated with a legend that a supernatural hound has plagued it since Hugo Baskerville's death. The manuscript states that many family members have suffered sudden, bloody, and mysterious deaths.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the ancestral residence of the Baskerville family and the home where Sir Charles Baskerville lived. It contains the yew alley from which Sir Charles took his final nightly walk, and its grim reputation could have made it difficult to find a tenant.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The moor surrounds the Baskerville estate and is the setting of the legend's pursuit and Hugo Baskerville's death. Sir Charles Baskerville stopped at a gate leading onto the moor before his death, and Dr. James Mortimer found no other footprints on the ground near the route except those of Barrymore and the alleged gigantic hound.

records.l: the Baskerville manuscript, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The Baskerville manuscript is a family paper dated 1742 and entrusted to Dr. James Mortimer by Sir Charles Baskerville. It records the origin of the Hound of the Baskervilles in the story of Hugo Baskerville and warns the family to avoid the moor during the hours when evil powers are exalted.

records.l: the Devon County Chronicle, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The Devon County Chronicle published an account of Sir Charles Baskerville's death on May 14th. It reported the evidence from the inquest, including his heart condition, his nightly walk through the yew alley, the absence of physical injury, and the coroner's verdict of natural death.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The Hound of the Baskervilles is described in the family narrative as a huge, black, hellish beast shaped like a hound. According to the manuscript, it killed Hugo Baskerville, and Dr. James Mortimer claims that footprints of a gigantic hound were found near Sir Charles Baskerville's body.

records.l: the Baskerville curse, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The Baskerville curse is presented as the belief that the family has been plagued by a hound since Hugo Baskerville's death. Sir Charles Baskerville took this supposed curse seriously and believed that a dreadful fate threatened his family.

records.l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles tells how Hugo Baskerville pursued an abducted maiden across the moor and was killed by a monstrous hound. It claims that the hound continued to bring sudden, bloody, and mysterious deaths to members of the Baskerville family.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death occurred after he went out for his customary nightly walk through the yew alley. His body was found at the far end of the alley with no physical injuries, but Dr. James Mortimer observed signs of terror and fresh footprints that he identified as those of a gigantic hound.

records.l: the yew alley, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 2.
records.s: The yew alley at Baskerville Hall was the route Sir Charles Baskerville habitually walked before bed. On the night of his death, his footprints led down the alley, changed after he passed the moor-gate as though he had walked on his toes, and ended where his body was found.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer tells Sherlock Holmes that Sir Charles Baskerville was found dead after apparently fleeing through the yew alley, and that enormous, unexplained footprints were discovered near the body. Mortimer reports sightings of a luminous, spectral creature resembling the Baskerville demon and fears that Sir Henry Baskerville, the heir, will meet the same fate if he goes to Baskerville Hall in Devonshire. Holmes agrees to meet Sir Henry at Waterloo Station through Mortimer but advises Mortimer to say nothing about the case until Holmes has considered it. After studying a map of Dartmoor, Holmes concludes that Sir Charles was likely waiting for someone near the moor-gate before running desperately from a source of terror.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Mortimer closely about the footprints, the yew alley, the moor-gate, and Sir Charles Baskerville's final movements. He studies a map of Dartmoor, considers natural explanations before supernatural ones, and concludes that Sir Charles was running for his life. Holmes advises Mortimer to meet Sir Henry Baskerville at Waterloo Station and to tell him nothing until Holmes has made up his mind.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Dr. Watson listens to Dr. Mortimer's account and Holmes's analysis, then spends the day at his club while Holmes studies the case. When he returns, he discusses the evidence with Holmes, including the change in Sir Charles's footprints.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer reports that he saw enormous marks near Sir Charles Baskerville's body and that several people had seen a luminous, spectral creature on the moor. Acting as trustee and executor of Sir Charles's will, he asks Holmes what to do with Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes instructs him to meet Sir Henry at Waterloo Station and bring him to Baker Street the next morning.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville was found dead about fifty yards from the summer-house at the end of the yew alley. He had apparently waited five or ten minutes near the moor-gate, then run down the alley in terror until he fell dead on his face.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville is the heir to Sir Charles Baskerville and the last of the Baskervilles. He has been farming in Canada and is due to arrive at Waterloo Station, after which Dr. Mortimer plans to take him to Holmes.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The Baskerville family is described as an old, masterful family whose members have suffered repeated evil fates when they went to Baskerville Hall. Sir Henry is the last surviving Baskerville, while Rodger Baskerville, the family's black sheep, died in Central America in 1876.

records.l: the Baskerville demon, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The Baskerville demon is described as a huge creature that several people saw upon the moor before Sir Charles Baskerville's death. Their accounts characterize it as luminous, ghastly, and spectral, and as unlike any animal known to science.

records.l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The hell-hound legend is known to Dr. Mortimer and influenced his interpretation of the marks near Sir Charles Baskerville's body. The witnesses' descriptions of the apparition correspond closely to the hell-hound of the legend.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The original hound in the legend is said to have been material enough to tear out a man's throat while also being regarded as diabolical.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Dartmoor is presented as a desolate, lifeless moor containing Baskerville Hall, Grimpen, scattered farms, and the prison at Princetown. Holmes studies a large-scale map of it while assessing where the tragedy occurred and whether danger remains there.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the home of the Baskerville family and lies beside the yew alley and the moor. Holmes says that Sir Henry might be expected to return to the home of his fathers, although Dr. Mortimer fears the place is deadly for a Baskerville.

records.l: the yew alley, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The yew alley has two impenetrable yew hedges about twelve feet high, with a central walk and strips of grass on either side. It contains a wicket-gate leading to the moor and an exit through a summer-house; Sir Charles was found on the walk after apparently running through it.

records.l: Waterloo Station, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Waterloo Station is where Dr. Mortimer is due to meet Sir Henry Baskerville after his arrival in England. Holmes directs Mortimer to go there and then bring Sir Henry to Baker Street the following morning.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: London is compared with Devonshire as a possible place of safety for Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes argues that if a supernatural force is responsible, it could harm Sir Henry in London as easily as in Devonshire.

records.l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Devonshire is the location of Baskerville Hall and the poor countryside whose prosperity depends on the Hall having a tenant. Dr. Mortimer fears that taking Sir Henry there will expose him to the fate associated with the Baskervilles.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death is surrounded by unexplained evidence, including enormous marks near his body, reports of a spectral creature, and signs that he waited at the moor-gate before fleeing. Holmes questions whether a crime occurred and how it was committed, while considering both ordinary and supernatural explanations.

records.l: the Baskerville curse, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The Baskerville curse is represented by the belief that every Baskerville who goes to Baskerville Hall meets an evil fate. Dr. Mortimer fears it will claim Sir Henry, while Holmes refuses to accept a supernatural explanation before other hypotheses have been exhausted.

records.l: the Baskerville mystery, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 3.
records.s: The investigation into Sir Charles's death has not yet formally begun, but Holmes identifies two initial questions: whether a crime was committed and what the crime was and how it occurred. He begins by analyzing the footprints, Sir Charles's movements, the moor-gate, and the possibility that someone or something frightened him into running.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Sir Henry Baskerville, who has received a warning letter telling him to keep away from the moor and has lost one of his newly purchased boots. Holmes determines that the warning message was assembled from words cut out of a Times leading article, with “moor” written in ink, and infers that its educated sender tried to disguise his writing. Dr. Mortimer then explains Sir Henry’s inheritance, his uncle’s death, and the family story of the hound. Despite the possible danger, Sir Henry insists that he will go to Baskerville Hall and invites Holmes and Dr. Watson to lunch at the Northumberland Hotel.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines Sir Henry Baskerville’s warning letter and identifies its words as having been cut from a Times leading article. He infers that the sender was educated, attempted to disguise his handwriting, used nail-scissors and gum, and probably composed the message in a hotel near Charing Cross. He discusses the possible danger of Sir Henry going to Baskerville Hall and agrees to meet him and Dr. Watson for lunch.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Dr. Watson is present during Holmes’s interview with Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville. He supplies Holmes with the Times and initially fails to see the connection between the newspaper article and the warning message. He agrees to lunch with Sir Henry and Holmes at the Northumberland Hotel.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer brings Sir Henry Baskerville to meet Sherlock Holmes and helps present the case concerning the Baskerville family. He argues that the warning letter may have come from someone convinced that the business was supernatural. He believes Sir Henry’s missing boot was merely mislaid and later tells Sir Henry the full account of his inheritance and his uncle’s death.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville meets Sherlock Holmes after receiving a warning telling him to keep away from the moor. He reports that one of a pair of new tan boots disappeared from outside his hotel room, and he insists that he will go to the home of his own people despite the possible danger. He asks for time to consider the information and invites Holmes and Dr. Watson to lunch.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The Baskerville family is associated with a long-standing story about a hound, which Sir Henry has heard since childhood. Sir Henry is the last representative of the family and has inherited its estate after his uncle’s death.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sir Henry has spent nearly all his time in the United States and Canada and is new to British life. He arrives in London, shops for clothing and boots, receives the warning letter, and plans to return to the Northumberland Hotel.

records.l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sir Henry is staying at the Northumberland Hotel when the warning letter addressed to him arrives. Holmes infers from the pen and ink that the address may have been written in a hotel and suggests that the sender might be found by examining hotel waste-paper baskets around Charing Cross.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the home of Sir Henry’s people and the destination under consideration after his inheritance. Although Holmes warns that there may be danger there, Sir Henry declares that no person or devil will prevent him from going.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The moor is the place from which the warning message tells Sir Henry to keep away. Holmes and Dr. Mortimer consider the warning evidence that someone knows more than they do about what happens there.

records.l: the warning letter, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The warning letter is a greyish envelope addressed in rough printed characters to Sir Henry Baskerville at the Northumberland Hotel. It contains a folded half-sheet of foolscap with a message assembled from pasted printed words, and it was posted from Charing Cross the previous evening.

records.l: the warning letter to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The warning message says, “As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.” All its words except “moor” are pasted onto the paper from printed material, and Holmes concludes that the sender took pains to hide identifying clues.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The hound is part of the Baskerville family’s traditional story and has been told as a pet story since Sir Henry was in the nursery. Sir Henry has not previously taken the story seriously, although it is considered in connection with his uncle’s death and the family’s affairs.

records.l: the inheritance, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Sir Henry has inherited the Baskerville family estate after his uncle’s death. He says that he has come into the inheritance “with a vengeance” and must decide whether to proceed to Baskerville Hall.

records.l: the Baskerville curse, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The unit discusses the family’s story of the hound and whether the events surrounding the inheritance and the uncle’s death are supernatural. Sir Henry refers to the possibility of a family fiend, while Holmes and Dr. Mortimer also consider danger from human beings.

records.l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: Holmes believes there may be danger connected with Sir Henry’s going to Baskerville Hall. The warning may have been intended to protect Sir Henry, or it may have been sent to frighten him away for someone else’s purposes.

records.l: the planned journey to Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The planned journey to Baskerville Hall is the main practical decision facing Sir Henry. Despite warnings of possible supernatural or human danger, he firmly decides that he will go and asks for time to think before giving Holmes and Dr. Watson his final view.

records.l: the newspaper clipping message, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
records.s: The newspaper clipping message was formed by cutting words from the Times’s leading article on free trade and pasting them onto a blank half-sheet of foolscap. Holmes identifies the source from the distinctive type, observes that “keep away” and “from the” were cut as single pieces, and concludes that “moor” was written in ink because it could not be found in print.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Holmes and Watson follow Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville from their lodgings in an attempt to identify the person shadowing Baskerville. The unknown pursuer, traveling in hansom cab No. 2704 and disguised with a bushy black beard, notices them and escapes down Regent Street. Holmes admits that his eagerness caused them to lose the man, though he had obtained the cab number. He then sends Cartwright to investigate the waste-paper of twenty-three nearby hotels for a cut-out center page of The Times and plans to identify the cabman by wire.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Holmes changes quickly from a languid dreamer into a man of action and follows Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville with Watson. He recognizes that a cab is following them, but his eagerness to pursue it betrays him and allows the unknown man to escape. Holmes records the cab number as 2704, sends Cartwright to search hotel waste-paper, and plans to identify the cabman by wire.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Watson follows Holmes in pursuit of Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville. He sees the pursuer's bushy black beard and piercing eyes but cannot swear to the man's face. Holmes asks Watson to record this failure alongside his successes.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Dr. Mortimer leaves with Baskerville and walks ahead of Holmes and Watson toward Oxford Street and Regent Street. He and Baskerville eventually vanish from Holmes and Watson's view.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Baskerville leaves with Dr. Mortimer and is followed through the streets by an unknown person. Holmes concludes that Baskerville has been closely shadowed since arriving in town, including after choosing the Northumberland Hotel.

records.l: unknown pursuer (Baskerville's shadow), The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: The unknown pursuer follows Baskerville in a hansom cab, apparently so that he can loiter behind or move ahead without being noticed. He has a bushy black beard that Holmes suspects was false and escapes after detecting Holmes and Watson.

records.l: Cartwright, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Cartwright, a fourteen-year-old district messenger with a bright, keen face, is assigned by Holmes to visit twenty-three nearby hotels. He is to search their waste-paper for a center page of The Times with holes cut in it and report by wire before evening.

records.l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: The Northumberland Hotel is the hotel Baskerville chose. Holmes reasons that the pursuer learned of this choice quickly, suggesting that Baskerville was being closely followed.

records.l: hansom cab No. 2704, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Hansom cab No. 2704 carries the unknown pursuer as he follows Baskerville. The pursuer escapes in it after seeing Holmes and Watson, and Holmes intends to discover the identity of its cabman by wire.

records.l: the twenty-three nearby hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: The twenty-three nearby hotels are listed in the Hotel Directory and are all in the immediate neighborhood of Charing Cross. Cartwright is instructed to visit each one and ask to inspect its waste-paper from the previous day.

records.l: The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Holmes gives Cartwright a copy of The Times and identifies the page he must search for in hotel waste-paper. The page is the center page, marked by holes cut with scissors.

records.l: cut-out center page of The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: The cut-out center page of The Times is the object Holmes wants Cartwright to find. Cartwright is told to recognize it by comparing it with the copy Holmes provides.

records.l: waste-paper from the hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: The waste-paper from the hotels may contain the cut-out center page of The Times. Holmes expects that in most hotels it will already have been burned or removed, while only three may still have heaps of paper available for searching.

records.l: Baskerville's shadowing, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Baskerville's shadowing is revealed by the pursuer's rapid knowledge of Baskerville's hotel and continued following through London. Holmes believes the pursuer used a cab to remain hidden, follow or pass Baskerville, and be ready to follow if Baskerville hired a cab.

records.l: Holmes and Watson's pursuit, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Holmes and Watson follow Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville while trying to identify Baskerville's invisible attendant. They approach the pursuer's cab, but the pursuer recognizes them and escapes before they can obtain more than the cab number.

records.l: Cartwright's hotel investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
records.s: Cartwright's hotel investigation requires visits to twenty-three hotels, payments to the outside and hall porters, and a search for the cut-out center page of The Times. Holmes gives him additional money for emergencies and requests a wire report at Baker Street before evening.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the surveillance and strange incidents surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville, including the theft and return of Sir Henry's boots and the black-bearded spy who followed him. Holmes learns that the suspected watchers are staying at other hotels rather than the Northumberland Hotel, while a telegram confirms that Barrymore is at Baskerville Hall. Sir Henry decides to go to Devonshire, and Dr. Watson agrees to accompany him because Holmes cannot leave London indefinitely. The cabman John Clayton reveals that the spy falsely identified himself as Sherlock Holmes, causing Holmes to lose his third investigative lead and worry about Watson's safety.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the Northumberland Hotel register, investigates the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, and questions the financial circumstances surrounding Sir Charles Baskerville's will and estate. He arranges telegrams to verify Barrymore's whereabouts, recruits Dr. Watson to accompany Sir Henry, and questions John Clayton about the black-bearded spy. Holmes concludes that three investigative leads have failed in London and becomes concerned about sending Watson to Devonshire.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Sir Henry Baskerville during the investigation. He agrees to go with Sir Henry to Baskerville Hall and report carefully to Holmes, despite Holmes's warning that the business is dangerous.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville is angered by the disappearance of one brown boot and one black boot, though the brown boot later reappears under a cabinet. He plans to go to Baskerville Hall at the end of the week and asks Dr. Watson to accompany him. He has not yet made a will and says that the money should remain with the title and estate.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer tells Holmes that Barrymore is a full-bearded man in charge of Baskerville Hall and that Barrymore and his wife each received five hundred pounds from Sir Charles Baskerville. He says that he received a thousand pounds and explains the succession of the Baskerville estate if Sir Henry dies.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville left five hundred pounds each to Barrymore and his wife, a thousand pounds to Dr. Mortimer, other smaller sums and charitable bequests, and the residue to Sir Henry Baskerville. His estate was worth close to a million, and his will becomes an important subject in assessing possible motives.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Barrymore is the son of the former caretaker and has served the Baskervilles for generations with his wife. Holmes suspects that his appearance could match the black-bearded spy, but a telegram confirms that Barrymore is at Baskerville Hall.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The Baskerville family is represented in the succession by Sir Henry Baskerville and, if he dies, by the distant Desmond cousins. The family title, house, land, and money are discussed as assets that Sir Henry believes should remain together.

records.l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The Northumberland Hotel is where Sir Henry Baskerville is staying and where Holmes examines the register. Holmes learns that the people interested in Sir Henry are staying elsewhere, apparently watching him without wanting to be seen.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the Devonshire residence to which Sir Henry Baskerville plans to return. Barrymore is reported to be present there and in charge of the Hall.

records.l: Baker Street, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Baker Street is Sherlock Holmes's residence and the place to which Holmes and Dr. Watson return after meeting Sir Henry. John Clayton comes there to answer Holmes's questions about the cab passenger who followed them.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: London is the setting for the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville and the investigation into the connected mysteries. Holmes decides that the city's size makes it difficult to identify the watchers, and he remains there because of his consulting practice and another important case.

records.l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Devonshire is the destination for Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson when they leave London. Holmes believes that the investigation may have better prospects there, although he warns Watson that the situation is dangerous.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Dartmoor is the region where Baskerville Hall is located and where Sir Henry Baskerville is expected to go. Holmes says he cannot be absent from London for an indefinite time to travel there.

records.l: Sir Henry's missing boots, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: One of Sir Henry Baskerville's new brown boots disappears, followed by one of his old black boots. The brown boot is later found under a cabinet, although no one explains how it got there, adding another unexplained incident to the investigation.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The black-bearded spy watches Sherlock Holmes's house and follows Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson in a cab. He hires John Clayton, falsely claims to be a detective named Sherlock Holmes, and escapes through Waterloo Station after anticipating that Holmes would trace the cab.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's will, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville's will provides five hundred pounds each to Barrymore and his wife, a thousand pounds to Dr. Mortimer, smaller sums to others, and the residue to Sir Henry Baskerville. It also raises questions about who would inherit if Sir Henry died and about whether the beneficiaries might have motives.

records.l: the Baskerville estate, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The Baskerville estate is worth close to a million, including a residue of seven hundred and forty thousand pounds after the other provisions described by Dr. Mortimer. The estate is entailed to the Desmonds if Sir Henry dies, while Sir Henry wants the money to remain with the title and property.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death remains the central background to the investigation. Holmes considers the death together with the surveillance, the boot incidents, and the other recent mysteries as part of an unusually complex case.

records.l: the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville continues in London through watchers who stay at hotels other than the Northumberland Hotel. A black-bearded man follows Sir Henry and Dr. Watson, but his identity and purpose remain unknown after he deceives Holmes through the cabman.

records.l: the investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
records.s: The investigation follows several leads: the hotel register, the missing boots, Barrymore's location, the financial interests in Sir Charles Baskerville's will, and the cabman who drove the spy. Holmes loses the leads concerning the hotel watchers, the newspaper clipping, and the cabman, leaving him to hope that the investigation will progress when Watson reaches Devonshire.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
