records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville, Dr. Watson, and Dr. Mortimer travel from London to Devonshire and arrive at Baskerville Hall, where Barrymore and his wife receive them. Sherlock Holmes instructs Dr. Watson to report facts, keep Sir Henry under close protection, and investigate the people surrounding him on the moor. During the journey, they learn that Selden, the Notting Hill murderer, has escaped from Princetown and is hiding somewhere nearby. That night, Dr. Watson hears a woman sobbing somewhere inside Baskerville Hall.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the ancient home of the Baskerville family, with ivy-covered granite walls, twin towers, a dark avenue, and a large, heavily timbered hall. Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson arrive there, and Barrymore and his wife receive them. During the night, Dr. Watson hears the sound of a woman crying somewhere in the house.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville travels with Dr. Watson and Dr. Mortimer to Devonshire to take possession of Baskerville Hall. He is delighted by the Devon scenery and eager to see the moor, but the atmosphere of Baskerville Hall makes him uneasy. He plans to install powerful electric lamps along the dark avenue.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Dr. Watson travels to Devonshire with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer at Sherlock Holmes’s direction. Holmes tells him to report all facts, especially information about Sir Henry’s neighbours and the death of Sir Charles Baskerville, and to keep his revolver close. At Baskerville Hall, Dr. Watson hears a woman sobbing during the night.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes accompanies Dr. Watson to the station and instructs him to report facts rather than theories. He says that James Desmond can probably be eliminated from consideration, but that the Barrymore couple and the other people around Sir Henry must remain under suspicion. Holmes also warns Sir Henry not to go about alone, to keep his revolver near him, and to avoid the moor at night.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer travels with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson to Devonshire. He says that he and Sir Henry have not been shadowed during the previous two days, although they separated for parts of the previous day. He leaves Baskerville Hall after bringing Sir Henry and Dr. Watson there because his wife is expecting him.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville formerly lived a very retired life at Baskerville Hall. Barrymore and his wife were strongly attached to him, and his death shocked them and made the house painful for them. The new building at the estate was begun with money from Sir Charles’s South African gold.

records.l: Barrymore couple, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The Barrymore couple have served the Baskerville family for several generations and looked after Sir Charles Baskerville. They remain on Sherlock Holmes’s list of suspects because Holmes does not want to dismiss them without determining whether they are innocent or guilty. They tell Sir Henry that they may eventually leave Baskerville Hall because of their painful memories of Sir Charles’s death.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Barrymore receives Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson at Baskerville Hall, helps with their luggage, and offers to serve dinner. He explains that he and his wife may leave when it is convenient because they were attached to Sir Charles Baskerville and find the house painful after his death. He shows Sir Henry and Dr. Watson to their rooms and the dining room.

records.l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Selden is identified as the Notting Hill murderer, whose conduct was marked by peculiar ferocity and wanton brutality. He has escaped from Princetown and has been at large for three days while warders watch the roads and stations. The driver says that Selden would stop at nothing and may be hiding somewhere on the moor.

records.l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville, Dr. Watson, and Dr. Mortimer travel to Devonshire by train. The countryside is described as greener, damper, and more rugged than the country they have left, with granite, wooded valleys, and moorland rising in the distance. Sir Henry recognizes its familiar features and expresses strong affection for the county.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The moor first appears to the travelers as a grey, melancholy hill with a jagged summit. As they approach Baskerville Hall, it becomes a vast, bleak, desolate landscape of tors, cairns, boulders, and cold wind. Sherlock Holmes warns Sir Henry to avoid it during the hours of darkness.

records.l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The Baskerville family has lived at Baskerville Hall for five hundred years and has left a deep mark on the area. Sir Henry Baskerville is described as a proud, strong, and fiery descendant of that line. The family’s ancestors are depicted in portraits and coats of arms throughout the hall.

records.l: the Baskerville legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The Baskerville legend is described as a queer old legend that Dr. Mortimer has read to Sherlock Holmes and the others. Holmes reminds Sir Henry of its warning to avoid the moor during the dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted.

records.l: the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes considers whether James Desmond, the next heir, could be responsible for the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville. He concludes that Desmond’s amiable disposition makes this unlikely and says that Desmond can be eliminated from consideration.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. Watson to seek fresh particulars concerning the death of Sir Charles Baskerville. Barrymore and his wife say that Sir Charles’s death shocked them and made their surroundings at Baskerville Hall painful.

records.l: Selden's prison escape, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: Selden has escaped from Princetown and has been at large for three days. Warders watch the roads and stations, while local farmers fear encountering him despite the five-pound reward for information.

records.l: the train journey to Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The train journey to Devonshire is swift and pleasant. Dr. Watson becomes better acquainted with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer, while Sir Henry watches the changing countryside and eagerly recognizes the Devon scenery. During the journey, Dr. Mortimer points out the first sight of the moor.

records.l: the Baskerville estate, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The Baskerville estate includes the lodge-gates, a long tree-lined avenue, the moorland surroundings, and Baskerville Hall itself. The lodge is partly ruined, while a new building begun with Sir Charles Baskerville’s South African gold stands nearby. The estate appears beautiful to Sir Henry but dark and melancholy to Dr. Watson.

records.l: the woman crying in Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
records.s: The woman crying in Baskerville Hall is heard by Dr. Watson in the middle of the night. He identifies the sound as a woman’s sob, a muffled and strangling gasp caused by uncontrollable sorrow. He believes the sound is inside the house and not far away, but hears nothing further for half an hour.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Dr. Watson investigates the Barrymores’ account of the telegram and suspects that Barrymore may have been in London when Sir Charles Baskerville died. On the moor, Watson meets Jack Stapleton, a naturalist from Merripit House, who discusses Sir Charles’s death, the Baskerville family legend, and the dangers of the Grimpen Mire. Stapleton brings Watson toward Merripit House, where Watson encounters Beryl Stapleton, who secretly warns him to return to London and leave the moor. During their walk, Watson and Stapleton hear a strange cry that Stapleton attributes possibly to a bittern, though local peasants call it the Baskerville hound.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Dr. Watson questions the Grimpen postmaster and his son about whether Barrymore personally received Holmes’s test telegram, but learns only that it was given to Mrs. Barrymore. He then meets Jack Stapleton, walks across the moor with him, hears the Hound’s cry, and is secretly warned by Beryl Stapleton to return to London.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville agrees that the gloomy impression of Baskerville Hall may have been caused partly by fatigue and the journey. He remains at the Hall after breakfast to examine papers while Dr. Watson investigates the neighborhood.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Jack Stapleton introduces himself to Dr. Watson as a naturalist living at Merripit House. He discusses the moor, the Grimpen Mire, the Baskerville family legend, and Sir Charles Baskerville’s death, and he claims to know safe paths through the mire. He pursues a rare insect, then returns and watches Beryl and Watson closely.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Beryl Stapleton approaches Dr. Watson on the moor and urgently warns him to return to London and never set foot on the moor again. When Jack Stapleton returns, she conceals the warning by pretending that she and Watson had been discussing the orchids.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has sent Dr. Watson to investigate the neighbors and has arranged a test telegram intended to determine whether Barrymore was in London. Watson hopes Holmes will soon be free to take responsibility for the case, but Holmes cannot leave town because of other cases.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Barrymore tells Sir Henry that the woman’s sob heard during the night could not have come from his wife, although Watson later sees that Mrs. Barrymore has clearly been crying. The postmaster confirms that the telegram was delivered to Mrs. Barrymore while Barrymore was supposedly in the loft, leaving no proof that Barrymore had not been in London.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Jack Stapleton says that he was fond of Sir Charles Baskerville and knew from Dr. Mortimer that Sir Charles had a weak heart. Stapleton believes Sir Charles may have seen a dog in the yew alley and died of fright.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: In the morning sunlight, Baskerville Hall seems much less gloomy to Dr. Watson and Sir Henry than it had the previous evening. The Hall remains associated with the unexplained sobbing heard during the night and with suspicions surrounding Barrymore.

records.l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Merripit House is the home of Jack and Beryl Stapleton, situated near the moor. Jack invites Dr. Watson to visit it and meet his sister, and Beryl approaches Watson from its direction.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: The moor is portrayed as vast, barren, mysterious, and filled with unusual natural and prehistoric features. Jack Stapleton says he has explored it extensively, while Beryl warns Dr. Watson to leave it.

records.l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: The Grimpen Mire is a dangerous bog in which a moor pony disappears and dies, with another pony apparently being swallowed while Watson and Jack watch. Jack claims that he can reach isolated areas within it by following complex landmarks, but warns Watson that entering it would almost certainly be fatal.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: London is the place to which Beryl Stapleton urgently tells Dr. Watson to return. Barrymore’s possible presence in London is also part of Watson’s investigation into the events surrounding Sir Charles Baskerville’s death.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: The Baskerville hound is described as a fiend dog believed by local peasants to haunt the family and the moor. Jack Stapleton says many peasants claim to have seen it, though he suggests that Sir Charles’s fear of such a creature may have contributed to his death.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: Dr. Watson continues to question the circumstances of Sir Charles Baskerville’s death, including Barrymore’s movements and the possibility that someone pursued Sir Charles. Jack Stapleton suggests that Sir Charles died of fright after seeing a dog because of his weak heart.

records.l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: The Baskerville family legend concerns a fiend dog said to haunt the family. Jack Stapleton calls the peasants credulous but admits that the legend strongly affected Sir Charles.

records.l: the Hound's cry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
records.s: A long, mournful cry rises over the moor while Dr. Watson and Jack Stapleton are walking. The peasants identify it as the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey, while Jack proposes that it may have been caused by bogs or the cry of a rare bittern.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Dr. Watson visits Stapleton and Beryl Stapleton at their bleak moorland house, where Stapleton explains their former life and present interests. Beryl initially warns Watson to take Sir Henry away from the moor, then follows him to withdraw the warning and attributes it to fears about the Baskerville curse. Watson remains troubled by the death of Sir Charles, the mysterious sound linked to the hound, and the danger surrounding Sir Henry. Beryl says she cannot provide any definite information and returns before her brother notices her absence.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Dr. Watson visits Stapleton and Beryl Stapleton at their moorland house and discusses their life there. He questions Beryl about her warning to Sir Henry and promises to convey it, but leaves without learning anything definite.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Stapleton lives with Beryl in a repaired former farm on the moor. He says that he formerly ran a school, which was devastated by an epidemic, and that he now devotes himself to botany and zoology. He plans to visit Sir Henry and make his acquaintance.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl Stapleton lives with her brother and says that she is devoted to Nature and is never dull. She first warns Dr. Watson to take Sir Henry away from the moor, then follows Watson to retract or qualify the warning, saying it arose from fears connected with the Baskerville curse. She says her brother would be angry if he knew she had tried to make Sir Henry leave.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Sir Henry is the new member of the Baskerville family living at Baskerville Hall. Beryl is distressed that he has come to the moor and believes he will face danger there, while Stapleton intends to visit him.

records.l: bleak moorland house, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: The bleak moorland house was once a prosperous grazier's farm but has been repaired and converted into a modern dwelling. Its stunted orchard and surrounding moor give it a mean and melancholy appearance, although the interior has large, elegant rooms.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: The moor is described as bleak, granite-flecked, and stretching unbroken to the horizon. Watson associates it with melancholy, vague fears, and the danger believed to threaten the Baskerville family.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl urges Dr. Watson to have Sir Henry return to London rather than remain at the place she considers dangerous.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the place where Sir Henry has come to live. Beryl says Stapleton wants the Hall inhabited because he believes this would benefit the poor people of the moor.

records.l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Dr. Watson compares his life on the moor to Grimpen Mire, with its deceptive green patches into which a person may sink and no guide to show the safe path.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl and Stapleton were deeply shocked by the death of Sir Charles, whom they knew intimately because he often walked across the moor to their house. Beryl says the tragedy strengthened her fear that the Baskerville family's curse had some basis.

records.l: warning to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl's warning tells Sir Henry to leave the moor and avoid the place that has supposedly been fatal to his family. She later tells Watson that she has done her duty but cannot give any definite information about the danger.

records.l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl says that Sir Charles was deeply impressed by the curse hanging over the Baskerville family. After his death, she felt there were grounds for fearing that the curse was connected with danger to Sir Henry.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl refers to the story of the hound and says that she believes in it, while Dr. Watson dismisses it as nonsense.

records.l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
records.s: Beryl believes Sir Henry will run a danger by living at a place that has always been fatal to his family. She cannot identify the danger or provide Dr. Watson with definite information about it.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Dr. John Watson writes a report to Mr. Sherlock Holmes from Baskerville Hall about Sir Henry Baskerville and the people and dangers surrounding him on the moor. He describes Sir Henry’s growing attraction to Miss Stapleton, Jack Stapleton’s apparent disapproval, and the continuing uncertainty surrounding the escaped convict. Watson also investigates Barrymore’s questionable behavior and observes him conducting a secret nighttime vigil at an upstairs window. Watson and Sir Henry have made a plan of campaign based on these observations, which Watson promises to explain in his next report.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Dr. John Watson reports from Baskerville Hall to Mr. Sherlock Holmes, describing the moor, the household, local residents, and his suspicions about Barrymore. He observes Barrymore’s nighttime movements and discusses the matter with Sir Henry Baskerville.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Mr. Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s letters and telegrams about events at Baskerville Hall. He had instructed Watson never to allow Sir Henry Baskerville to go out alone and asked him to provide factual reports about the people around them.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville becomes strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton and repeatedly refers to her after meeting her. He questions Jack Stapleton about supernatural interference in human affairs, confronts Barrymore about the test telegram, and works with Watson on a plan of campaign.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Jack Stapleton shows guarded interest in the legend of the wicked Hugo and appears to share the popular view that an evil influence may affect families. He repeatedly prevents Sir Henry Baskerville and Miss Stapleton from being alone and appears strongly disapproving of their growing intimacy.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Miss Stapleton is described as beautiful, fascinating, tropical, and exotic, in contrast to her cool and unemotional brother. She appears to return Sir Henry Baskerville’s attraction, while Jack Stapleton seems intent on preventing their intimacy from developing.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Barrymore confirms that he received the test telegram, though his wife brought it to him and wrote the reply after he instructed her what to say. Watson later sees him walking barefoot through Baskerville Hall at night, holding a candle to a window and staring expectantly across the moor before extinguishing the light.

records.l: Mrs. Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Mrs. Barrymore is described as heavy, solid, intensely respectable, and puritanical. Despite her unemotional appearance, she has repeatedly been seen with traces of tears, suggesting a deep sorrow or troubling secret.

records.l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: The escaped convict has not been seen or heard from for a fortnight, leading the local people to believe that he has left the moor. Watson considers it unlikely that he could have survived there so long without food, although the stone huts would provide hiding places.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the isolated household from which Watson sends his report and where he, Sir Henry Baskerville, and other residents live under concern about the escaped convict. Watson believes that secret business is occurring inside the house.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: The moor is portrayed as vast, grim, isolated, and filled with prehistoric huts, graves, and monoliths. It provides hiding places for the escaped convict and forms the dark landscape watched by Barrymore during his nighttime vigil.

records.l: the letters to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Watson’s letters to Mr. Sherlock Holmes record events and preserve his feelings and suspicions more accurately than memory. One page is missing, but the remaining letters are described as exactly written.

records.l: the reports to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Watson’s previous letters and telegrams have kept Mr. Sherlock Holmes informed about events at Baskerville Hall. Watson says that he had little important to report until the surprising events described in this unit and promises that his next report will explain the plan of campaign.

records.l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: The legend associated with the Baskerville family remains a subject of discussion at the place where the story of the wicked Hugo supposedly began. Jack Stapleton gives guarded answers about supernatural interference and leaves the impression that he shares the popular belief in an evil influence affecting families.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Watson revisits the yew alley and the moor-gate to reconstruct the fatal night of the old gentleman’s death. He imagines that the man saw something terrifying on the moor, fled down the alley, and died from horror and exhaustion, while still wondering whether a human agency was involved.

records.l: Barrymore's secret nighttime vigil, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Barrymore’s secret nighttime vigil begins when he quietly leaves his room carrying a candle and enters an otherwise empty room. He holds the candle against the window, watches the darkness of the moor with rigid expectation, groans, extinguishes the light, and later returns; Watson also hears a key turn in a lock.

records.l: the Stapleton–Sir Henry courtship, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville and Miss Stapleton appear mutually attracted after their first meeting. Jack Stapleton repeatedly prevents them from being alone and shows disapproval, despite the apparent advantages of their possible marriage.

records.l: the plan of campaign, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
records.s: Watson and Sir Henry Baskerville create a plan of campaign based on Watson’s observations of Barrymore’s nighttime behavior. Watson does not yet reveal its details, reserving them for a later report.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Dr. Watson reports that Barrymore appears to watch the moor from a particular western window at night, leading him and Sir Henry Baskerville to plan to observe Barrymore. Sir Henry goes onto the moor alone, but Watson follows and witnesses him meeting Miss Stapleton, whose brother Stapleton angrily interrupts their conversation. Sir Henry tells Watson that he proposed marriage to Miss Stapleton, but Stapleton opposed the relationship and demanded that the matter rest for three months. Stapleton later apologizes, and Sir Henry agrees to dine at Merripit House while limiting himself to Miss Stapleton’s friendship.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Dr. Watson examines Barrymore’s movements, reports them to Sir Henry Baskerville, and follows Sir Henry onto the moor despite Sherlock Holmes’s instructions not to leave him alone. He witnesses the meeting between Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton, then tells Sir Henry what he saw and records the events for Holmes.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes had instructed Dr. Watson not to leave Sir Henry Baskerville, especially not to let him go alone upon the moor. Watson tries to follow those instructions despite Sir Henry’s objections.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Sir Henry agrees with Dr. Watson to watch Barrymore at night, but later insists on going alone onto the moor. He meets Miss Stapleton, proposes marriage to her, quarrels with Stapleton over the relationship, and agrees to let the matter rest for three months while cultivating her friendship.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Barrymore is known to walk through the passages at night and is seen watching from the western window of Baskerville Hall. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson suspect that he is looking for someone or something on the moor.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Stapleton sees Sir Henry with Miss Stapleton on the moor and runs toward them in great anger, interrupting their conversation and taking his sister away. He later apologizes to Sir Henry, explaining that he feared losing his sister, and the breach between them is healed.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Miss Stapleton meets Sir Henry on the moor and speaks earnestly about the danger of the place, urging him to leave. She appears reluctant when Sir Henry embraces her and accepts Stapleton’s intervention without protest.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is being prepared for major renovation and refurnishing. Sir Henry has engaged an architect, a London contractor, decorators, and furnishers to restore the grandeur of his family home.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: The moor can be viewed most clearly from the western window of Baskerville Hall, and Barrymore appears to watch it at night. Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton meet there, where she warns that it is a place of danger.

records.l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Merripit House is associated with Miss Stapleton and Stapleton. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson are to dine there the following Friday as a sign that the quarrel between Sir Henry and Stapleton has ended.

records.l: Barrymore's secret nighttime vigil, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Barrymore’s nocturnal watch takes place from a western window of Baskerville Hall that overlooks the nearest part of the moor through an opening between two trees. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson plan to sit up and follow him to discover what he is watching.

records.l: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton's meeting, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton meet by appointment on the moor and engage in a serious conversation. Miss Stapleton warns him about the danger, while Stapleton observes them, interrupts angrily, and leads her away.

records.l: Sir Henry's proposal to Miss Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Sir Henry tells Miss Stapleton that he loves her and proposes that she marry him. Before she can answer, Stapleton arrives and objects angrily to Sir Henry’s attentions.

records.l: Stapleton's confrontation with Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Stapleton confronts Sir Henry after seeing him with Miss Stapleton and demands to know why he is paying her attentions. The confrontation becomes angry, but Stapleton later apologizes and withdraws his opposition temporarily.

records.l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Miss Stapleton repeatedly warns Sir Henry that the moor is a place of danger and says she will not be happy until he has left it. Sir Henry does not wish to leave after meeting her, offering instead to take her with him through marriage.

records.l: romantic love and marriage, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
records.s: Sir Henry is strongly infatuated with Miss Stapleton and believes that she returns his feelings. He proposes marriage, but Stapleton’s opposition and Miss Stapleton’s warnings prevent an immediate answer, and Sir Henry agrees to postpone the matter for three months.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Dr. Watson and Sir Henry Baskerville discover that John and Eliza Barrymore have been secretly signaling to and feeding Eliza’s escaped brother, Selden, on the moor. They pursue Selden but fail to capture him after he throws a rock and runs away. During the pursuit, they hear the cry on the moor, which Sir Henry believes is the cry of the Hound of the Baskervilles. Watson also sees a mysterious tall man standing on a tor, but the figure disappears before he and Sir Henry can investigate.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Dr. Watson works with Sir Henry Baskerville to uncover the Barrymores’ nighttime activities and reports the explanation to Sherlock Holmes. He helps pursue Selden across the moor, hears the strange cry, and sees a tall, unidentified man silhouetted on a tor.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is the intended recipient of Dr. Watson’s report and had sent Watson to investigate the case. Watson asks him to judge the progress of the investigation.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville helps Watson confront the Barrymores and learns that they have been assisting Selden. He joins Watson in trying to capture Selden, becomes frightened by the cry on the moor, and believes it may have been the Hound of the Baskervilles.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: John Barrymore is discovered holding a candle at a second-floor window as a signal. He admits that he has been helping his wife feed Selden, and Sir Henry allows him and Eliza to remain in service after hearing the explanation.

records.l: Mrs. Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Eliza Barrymore reveals that Selden is her younger brother and that the nighttime signal is used to communicate with him. She accepts responsibility for asking John Barrymore to help feed and protect Selden on the moor.

records.l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Selden is identified as Eliza Barrymore’s younger brother and an escaped convict hiding on the moor. Watson and Sir Henry find him by his signal light, but he escapes after throwing a rock and outrunning them.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the place from which the Barrymores send a candle signal to Selden. The signal tells him that food is ready and helps him identify where to collect it.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The moor is where Selden hides while the Barrymores secretly provide him with food. Watson and Sir Henry cross it during their pursuit, hear a frightening cry there, and observe a mysterious tall man on a tor.

records.l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The Great Grimpen Mire is identified as the direction from which Sir Henry believes the cry on the moor came. The cry had previously been heard on its borders.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The Hound of the Baskervilles is invoked when Sir Henry and Watson hear the strange cry on the moor. Sir Henry fears that the sound may confirm the stories of a supernatural hound connected with his family.

records.l: the Barrymores' nighttime signal, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The Barrymores’ nighttime signal consists of John Barrymore holding a candle at the window and waiting for a corresponding light from the moor. The two lights indicate that Selden is still present and show where food can be brought to him.

records.l: Selden's prison escape, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: Selden’s prison escape brought him to Baskerville Hall while warders were pursuing him. He then hid on the moor until the search had passed, relying on the Barrymores for help.

records.l: the Barrymores' secret assistance to Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The Barrymores secretly take Selden in, feed him, and care for him because Eliza cannot abandon her younger brother. They continue sending food while he hides on the moor, although they hope each day that he has moved on.

records.l: the cry on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The cry on the moor rises from a deep mutter into a howl and ends in a sad moan. Sir Henry identifies it as the cry of a hound, while Watson can only say that its source is uncertain.

records.l: the mysterious tall man on the tor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
records.s: The mysterious tall man on the tor appears as a thin figure standing against the moon with his arms folded and head bowed. Watson sees him clearly, but the figure disappears when Watson turns toward Sir Henry; Sir Henry suggests that he may have been a warder.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Dr. Watson records growing fears about the moor, the spectral hound, the unknown watcher, and the danger surrounding Sir Henry. Barrymore explains that Selden is still being secretly supplied and reveals that Sir Charles went to the gate to meet a woman whose initials were L. L., based on a partially burned letter. Dr. Mortimer identifies L. L. as Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey, prompting Watson to plan an interview with her. Barrymore also reports that another, non-convict man is hiding in the old stone huts on the moor and may be the stranger Watson has seen.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Dr. Watson uses his diary and recollections to investigate the dangers surrounding Baskerville Hall. He questions Barrymore, identifies Laura Lyons as a possible source of information about Sir Charles’s death, and resolves to investigate both her and the stranger hiding on the moor.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s reports from the moor, including the information about the woman identified by the initials L. L. Watson expects this new clue to renew Holmes’s interest and perhaps bring him to Devonshire.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Sir Henry is shaken by the sound on the moor and argues that Selden remains a danger to isolated houses. He agrees not to inform the police about Selden after Barrymore promises that the convict will soon be sent to South America, and he becomes interested in tracing the woman identified as L. L.

records.l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Barrymore asks Sir Henry not to report Selden because he believes Selden will leave for South America and fears that his capture would harm Barrymore’s wife. He reveals that Sir Charles received a letter from a woman with the initials L. L. and had gone to the gate to meet her, and he later tells Watson that another man is hiding on the moor.

records.l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Selden remains hidden on the moor and is being supplied with food and provisions by Barrymore. He told Barrymore that another, apparently non-convict man was also hiding there and had a boy bringing him supplies.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Sir Charles’s death is connected to a meeting he arranged at the gate with a woman whose initials were L. L. Barrymore learned this from a partially burned letter found in Sir Charles’s study after the inquest.

records.l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Dr. Mortimer gives Watson a lift from the moor and identifies Laura Lyons as the local woman whose initials are L. L. He explains that she is Frankland’s daughter, lives in Coombe Tracey, and was helped by several people, including Sir Charles, to establish a typewriting business.

records.l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Laura Lyons is identified as the woman whose initials match L. L. She lives in Coombe Tracey, is Frankland’s estranged daughter, and may possess information capable of clarifying an incident in the mystery surrounding Sir Charles’s death.

records.l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The stranger on the moor is a tall, thin figure whom Watson saw watching from a tor. Barrymore reports that Selden had seen another apparently gentlemanly man hiding among the old stone huts, suggesting that this stranger is still watching and waiting.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is surrounded by fog, rain, and the bleak moor, contributing to the atmosphere of danger. It is the home of Sir Henry and is repeatedly connected with the threats posed by Selden, the stranger, and the unexplained noises.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The moor is described as cold, rain-soaked, foggy, and increasingly dangerous, with the firm uplands becoming a morass. It conceals Selden and another unidentified man, and its noises and apparent watchers continue to trouble Watson and the household.

records.l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Coombe Tracey is the place from which the letter signed with the initials L. L. was sent. It is also where Laura Lyons lives and where the hidden stranger may obtain supplies.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The spectral hound remains an explanation considered for the reports of a strange creature and the repeated baying heard on the moor. Watson rejects the supernatural interpretation but admits that even the idea of a real large hound raises difficult questions.

records.l: diary (Dr. Watson's diary), The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Watson’s diary preserves his observations for October 16 and 17, including the weather, his fears, Barrymore’s revelations, and his conversation with Dr. Mortimer. He uses it to continue his narrative after abandoning his earlier method of quoting reports sent to Holmes.

records.l: the supernatural hound legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The family legend is cited as having been fulfilled by the death of the last occupant of Baskerville Hall. Its apparent connection with Sir Charles’s death contributes to Watson’s sense that a sinister influence surrounds the family.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: Sir Charles’s death becomes more mysterious when Barrymore reveals that he had gone to the gate to meet a woman. A burned letter bearing the initials L. L. suggests that locating this woman could provide important facts about the death.

records.l: the chase of Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The chase of Selden has ended without his capture, and Barrymore argues that pursuing him was unfair after the household learned his secret. Sir Henry ultimately agrees not to notify the police while Barrymore arranges for Selden to escape to South America.

records.l: the letter from Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The letter from Laura Lyons is not identified by a full name in the surviving fragment, but it was sent from Coombe Tracey in a woman’s hand and signed with the initials L. L. It asked Sir Charles to burn the letter and meet the writer at the gate by ten o’clock.

records.l: the warning letter to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
records.s: The warning letter to Sir Henry is cited as evidence of human agency in London. Watson notes that it may have been written by either a protecting friend or an enemy, and he wonders whether its writer is connected to the stranger on the moor.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: The narrator travels to Coombe Tracey to interrogate Mrs. Laura Lyons about her connection with Sir Charles Baskerville. Mrs. Lyons admits that she wrote to Sir Charles asking him to meet her at the garden gate at ten o’clock on the day he died, but insists that she never kept the appointment. She explains that she sought his financial help to regain her freedom from her husband, but received help from another source before the meeting. The narrator remains doubtful of her complete innocence and turns his attention to the clue concerning the lurking man among the stone huts on the moor.

records.l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Mrs. Laura Lyons is questioned about her relationship with Sir Charles Baskerville and initially denies writing to him on the day of his death. She later admits that she wrote asking him to meet her, explaining that she wanted financial help with expenses connected to regaining her freedom from her husband. She insists that she never went to the appointment because she received help from another source, though the narrator suspects that she is withholding part of the truth.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville had helped Mrs. Laura Lyons financially and was asked by her to meet her at the garden gate. He burned her letter, although part of it remained legible. He died at the place and hour at which Mrs. Lyons had arranged to meet him.

records.l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Coombe Tracey is where Mrs. Laura Lyons lives and where the narrator goes to question her. The narrator finds her rooms centrally located and well appointed.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: The moor contains the clue to the identity or whereabouts of the lurking man. After the inconclusive interview with Mrs. Laura Lyons, the narrator decides to return to that line of investigation.

records.l: the stone huts, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: The stone huts on the hillside are believed to be the place where the lurking man on the moor can be found. They become the narrator’s next focus after he is unable to resolve the questions surrounding Mrs. Laura Lyons.

records.l: the letter from Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Mrs. Laura Lyons's letter asked Sir Charles Baskerville to meet her at the gate by ten o’clock and urged him to burn it. She says that she wrote it to seek his help with expenses connected to her effort to regain her freedom from her husband. Sir Charles burned the letter, but part of it remained legible.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death occurred at the same place and hour at which Mrs. Laura Lyons had asked him to meet her. Mrs. Lyons says that she learned of his death in the newspaper the next morning.

records.l: the appointment between Mrs. Laura Lyons and Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: Mrs. Laura Lyons arranged to meet Sir Charles Baskerville at the garden gate at ten o’clock on the day he died. She acknowledges making the appointment but denies attending it, saying that something intervened and that she received help from another source.

records.l: the interrogation of Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: The narrator interrogates Mrs. Laura Lyons about her letters, meetings, and appointment with Sir Charles Baskerville. Under questioning, she changes from denying the letter to admitting that she wrote it, but she refuses to explain what prevented her from keeping the appointment. The interrogation leaves the narrator baffled and convinced that she may still be concealing information.

records.l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
records.s: The narrator has established that the lurking man on the moor is to be sought among the stone huts on the hillside. After questioning Mrs. Laura Lyons without reaching a conclusion, he turns back to investigating this man.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: Dr. Watson follows a boy across the moor after Mr. Frankland observes him carrying food toward a remote hill. Watson finds an occupied abandoned hut containing supplies and a written report that he has gone to Coombe Tracey. The message convinces Watson that the stranger has been monitoring him through an agent, possibly the boy. Watson waits in the hut, where the stranger eventually arrives and addresses him in a familiar voice.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: Dr. Watson learns from Mr. Frankland about the boy carrying food across the moor and follows him to an abandoned hut. He finds evidence that the stranger has been tracking him, then hides in the hut and waits for its tenant, who addresses him as Watson.

records.l: Mr. Frankland, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: Mr. Frankland tells Dr. Watson that he has seen a boy carrying a bundle toward a stony hill and believes the boy is taking food to the convict. He shows Watson the boy through his telescope but refuses to inform the police.

records.l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The stranger lives in an abandoned hut on the moor and receives food brought by the boy. He has apparently arranged for Watson's movements to be observed and reported, and he eventually comes to the hut and speaks to Watson.

records.l: Cartwright, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The boy repeatedly carries a bundle along the moor, apparently bringing food to the stranger. He is seen by Mr. Frankland through a telescope and may also be acting as the stranger's agent by reporting Watson's movements.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The moor contains many abandoned huts and is described as lonely, barren, and difficult to search. Watson crosses it to reach the hill and the hut where the stranger lives.

records.l: Black Tor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: Black Tor is the place where Watson previously saw the stranger standing. Watson treats it as the centre of his search, and Mr. Frankland points it out while identifying the stony hill beyond it.

records.l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: Coombe Tracey is named in the written report found in the hut: “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.”

records.l: the stone huts, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The moor contains many hundreds of abandoned huts. Watson finds one that has been used as a habitation, with blankets, a fire, cooking utensils, water, food tins, and spirits inside.

records.l: the inquiry into the stranger, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The inquiry has repeatedly been obstructed by bad luck, but Watson gains a promising lead through Mr. Frankland's observation of the boy. Watson discovers that the stranger's hiding place contains evidence of his identity or intentions only in the form of surveillance reports.

records.l: the stranger's surveillance, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The stranger's surveillance includes monitoring Watson's movements and recording that he has gone to Coombe Tracey. Watson suspects that the boy, or another agent, has reported nearly every step he has taken on the moor.

records.l: the written message, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
records.s: The written message is a roughly scrawled pencil note reading, “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.” Watson finds it beneath the boy's bundle in the stranger's hut and interprets it as a report on his movements.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Dr. John Watson discovers that Sherlock Holmes has been secretly living in a hut on the moor while investigating the danger surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes explains that he concealed his presence to avoid alerting their opponents and praises Watson’s reports and investigation of Mrs. Laura Lyons in Coombe Tracey. Holmes reveals that Miss Stapleton is actually Jack Stapleton’s wife and that Stapleton has deceived Mrs. Laura Lyons, who expected to marry him after divorcing her husband. Holmes concludes that the matter involves a deliberate murder plot against Sir Henry and warns Watson to guard him closely until the case is complete.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has been secretly living in a hut on the moor with assistance from Cartwright while investigating the case. He tells Dr. John Watson that Miss Stapleton is Jack Stapleton’s wife, identifies Stapleton as their enemy, and says that the murder plot is deliberate and directed against Sir Henry Baskerville.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Dr. John Watson finds Sherlock Holmes in the hut after tracking the investigation and initially mistaking him for a criminal. He reports his conversation with Mrs. Laura Lyons, learns Holmes’s reasons for concealing himself, and is instructed to guard Sir Henry Baskerville closely.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville is identified as the intended target of the murder plot. Sherlock Holmes warns Dr. John Watson that Stapleton may strike against him before the investigation is complete.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Jack Stapleton is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the enemy behind the danger to Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes learns that Stapleton is married to Miss Stapleton but presents her as his sister, and he suspects Stapleton of planning a cold-blooded murder.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Miss Stapleton is revealed by Sherlock Holmes to be Jack Stapleton’s wife rather than his sister. Stapleton has concealed the marriage because she would be more useful to him while appearing to be a free woman.

records.l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Mrs. Laura Lyons is questioned by Dr. John Watson in Coombe Tracey, and her conversation helps clarify the case. She has an intimate relationship with Jack Stapleton and, while expecting to become his wife after a projected divorce, does not know that he is already married.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: The moor is where Sherlock Holmes has maintained a secret retreat in a hut while investigating the case. It is also the setting in which Dr. John Watson searches for information and later meets Holmes at dusk.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is the place where Dr. John Watson is expected to remain with Sir Henry Baskerville. Sherlock Holmes reminds Watson that his duty requires him not to stay away from the Hall for too long.

records.l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: Coombe Tracey is where Dr. John Watson goes to interview Mrs. Laura Lyons. Sherlock Holmes says that she is the one person there who might assist them in the case.

records.l: the hut, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: The hut on the moor serves as Sherlock Holmes’s concealed retreat and base of investigation. Dr. John Watson enters it while waiting for its occupant and later shares the hut with Holmes while they discuss their findings.

records.l: the murder plot against Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: The murder plot is described by Sherlock Holmes as refined, cold-blooded, and deliberate. Holmes believes it is directed against Sir Henry Baskerville and fears that Jack Stapleton may act before the evidence is complete.

records.l: the blackmailing case, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: The case concerns the danger surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville and the activities of Jack Stapleton. Sherlock Holmes says that the investigation is nearly complete but requires another day or two and the continued protection of Sir Henry.

records.l: the intimate relationship between Stapleton and Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
records.s: The intimate relationship between Stapleton and Mrs. Laura Lyons involves meetings, letters, and a complete understanding between them. Mrs. Laura Lyons expected to marry Stapleton after a projected divorce, but Holmes believes she may help them once she learns that Stapleton is already married.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson hear a terrible scream and find a man apparently killed while fleeing the hound on the moor. They initially believe the victim is Sir Henry Baskerville, but discover that the body is Selden, who was wearing Sir Henry’s discarded clothing. Holmes concludes that the hound was attracted by an article of Sir Henry’s clothing, though he remains puzzled about how Selden knew the hound was pursuing him. Stapleton arrives, conceals his alarm, and accepts the explanation that Selden died in an accidental fall.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Sherlock Holmes runs across the moor with Dr. John Watson after hearing screams and initially believes Sir Henry Baskerville has been killed. He is relieved to discover that the victim is Selden, then reasons that the hound was drawn by Sir Henry’s clothing. Holmes conceals his suspicions from Stapleton and says that the investigation has not been satisfactory.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes across the moor after hearing the screams and helps examine the body. He initially believes that Sir Henry Baskerville is dead and blames himself for leaving him exposed to danger, but then recognizes that the victim is Selden wearing Sir Henry’s clothing. Watson explains to Holmes how the clothing reached Selden.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville is initially believed to be the man killed on the moor. It is learned that his discarded boots, shirt, cap, and other clothing had been passed to Selden, whose wearing of them apparently caused the hound to pursue him.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Stapleton approaches Holmes and Dr. John Watson after hearing the cries and seeing the body. He is visibly shocked and disappointed when he learns that the victim is Selden rather than Sir Henry Baskerville, but he conceals his reaction and supports the explanation that Selden died from exposure, madness, and a fall. He asks whether Holmes and Watson heard anything besides a cry, including evidence of the supposed phantom hound.

records.l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Selden, the escaped convict, is the victim found on the moor. He had been wearing clothing formerly belonging to Sir Henry Baskerville and was apparently pursued by the hound before falling over rocks and breaking his neck.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The hound is heard as a deep, menacing rumble accompanying Selden’s screams. Holmes concludes that it was released and attracted to an article of Sir Henry Baskerville’s clothing, probably the boot taken from the hotel, and that it pursued Selden to his death.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The moor is the dark, desolate setting where the screams are heard and Selden’s body is found. Its broken ground, rocks, cliffs, slopes, and gorse make the search difficult and contribute to the danger of the pursuit.

records.l: the death of the escaped convict, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Selden dies after fleeing across the moor while apparently pursued by the hound. He falls over rocks and breaks his neck, and his body is found with his skull crushed and blood pooling beneath it.

records.l: the hound's attack, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The hound's attack is heard through Selden’s terrified screams and the accompanying deep rumble. The pursuit drives Selden across the moor until he falls over a cliff or rocky slope, although the text does not establish that the hound physically reaches him.

records.l: the investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The investigation appears to have failed when Holmes and Dr. John Watson initially believe that Sir Henry Baskerville has been killed. After identifying Selden, Holmes recognizes that the clothing provides a connection between the hound and Sir Henry, but he continues to insist that the case requires proof rather than conjecture.

records.l: the supernatural hound legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The supernatural hound legend is discussed when Stapleton asks whether Holmes and Dr. John Watson heard evidence of a phantom hound. Holmes and Watson deny hearing anything beyond the cries, while the hound’s actual existence remains unproven in their stated evidence.

records.l: the old wardrobe (Sir Henry's), The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville’s old wardrobe had been given to Barrymore, who passed it on to Selden to help him escape. Selden was wearing Sir Henry’s boots, shirt, cap, and other clothing when he died, and Holmes believes the hound followed the scent of one of these items.

records.l: the body, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
records.s: The body is first mistaken for Sir Henry Baskerville because it wears Sir Henry’s distinctive ruddy tweed suit. Holmes and Dr. John Watson discover that it is Selden, lying face down in a grotesque position with a crushed skull, and leave it covered on the moor until morning.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. Watson that they are finally in close conflict with a highly capable criminal after the wrong man was killed by the criminal’s plot. Holmes says they cannot arrest the man because they lack evidence connecting him to the hound or to the deaths, and he hopes Mrs. Laura Lyons and his own plan will help establish a case. Holmes intends to conceal the hound from Sir Henry and asks Dr. Watson to avoid a dinner with Stapleton so that Sir Henry will face the ordeal alone.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Sherlock Holmes believes the criminal is an exceptionally worthy opponent and may respond to being discovered by becoming more cautious or taking desperate measures. He refuses to arrest him without proof and plans to use Mrs. Laura Lyons and his own investigation to establish a case. He tells Dr. Watson to conceal the hound from Sir Henry and to excuse himself from the planned dinner.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Dr. Watson urges Holmes to arrest the suspected criminal and argues that there is a case based on Sir Charles’s death. He reports that he is engaged to dine with the people the next day, but Holmes instructs him to excuse himself so Sir Henry will attend alone.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Stapleton has seen Sherlock Holmes, and Holmes believes this may alter his plans. Stapleton would have Sir Henry believe that Selden’s death had the explanation he provided.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: The hound is believed by Holmes and Dr. Watson to have frightened Sir Charles to death and to have been involved in the other man’s death, but they have never seen it. They heard it, yet cannot prove that it was following the dead man’s trail, and Holmes says there are no visible marks or other direct evidence connecting it to the deaths.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Sir Henry is expected to dine with Stapleton and the others the next day. Holmes wants him kept unaware of the hound so that he will have a better nerve for the ordeal and will attend the dinner alone.

records.l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Sherlock Holmes has great hopes that Mrs. Laura Lyons will help once the position of affairs is made clear to her.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Sir Charles was found dead without any mark upon him. Holmes and Dr. Watson believe that he died of sheer fright caused by the hound, but Holmes says they cannot prove this explanation to a jury.

records.l: the death of the escaped convict, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Selden’s death is described as another death with no direct connection yet proven between the hound and the victim’s death. Holmes tells Dr. Watson to let Sir Henry think that Selden’s death occurred as Stapleton would have him believe.

records.l: the trial case against Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
records.s: Holmes says there is currently no trial case against Stapleton, only surmise and conjecture. The evidence does not directly connect him to the hound or the deaths, so Holmes believes they must risk further investigation to establish a case.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies Mr. Stapleton as a Baskerville descendant by comparing his face with the portrait of Hugo Baskerville and plans to trap him. Holmes arranges for Sir Henry Baskerville to visit the Stapletons and walk home alone while Holmes and Dr. Watson secretly return with Inspector Lestrade. Mrs. Laura Lyons reveals that Stapleton dictated her letter to Sir Charles Baskerville, deceived her about his marriage, and persuaded her not to keep her appointment with Sir Charles. Holmes believes the evidence against Stapleton is nearing completion, though he intends to gather further proof before arresting him.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes recognizes a resemblance between Mr. Stapleton and the portrait of Hugo Baskerville, concluding that Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs upon the succession. He secretly arranges a trap involving Sir Henry, visits Mrs. Laura Lyons to obtain her testimony, and summons Inspector Lestrade with an unsigned warrant.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Dr. Watson reports on the recent events and accompanies Holmes to interview Mrs. Laura Lyons. Holmes instructs him to leave his belongings at Baskerville Hall as a pledge that he will return, while secretly planning to come back with Holmes and Lestrade.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville agrees to follow Holmes's instructions despite feeling deserted. He is to dine with the Stapletons, send back his trap, and walk home from Merripit House along the straight path to the Grimpen Road.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Mr. Stapleton is identified through the portrait of Hugo Baskerville as a Baskerville descendant who may be seeking the succession. Mrs. Laura Lyons states that he dictated her letter to Sir Charles, deceived her about his marriage, and frightened her into concealing her appointment with Sir Charles.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Mrs. Stapleton is revealed to be Mr. Stapleton's wife, although she has been presented as his sister. Holmes shows Mrs. Laura Lyons a photograph and descriptions identifying the couple as Mr. and Mrs. Vandeleur.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Inspector Lestrade responds to Holmes's message by traveling from London with an unsigned warrant. He joins Holmes and Dr. Watson at Coombe Tracey to assist with the investigation.

records.l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Mrs. Laura Lyons admits that Mr. Stapleton dictated her letter asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate and then persuaded her not to attend. She explains that Stapleton claimed the money was needed for her divorce, concealed his marriage, and threatened her into silence; she now agrees to hold nothing back.

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Sir Charles Baskerville was asked by Mrs. Laura Lyons to meet her at the gate at ten o'clock, the place and time of his death. Holmes treats her letter and the manipulated appointment as important evidence in the investigation of his murder.

records.l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Holmes tells Sir Henry that he and Dr. Watson must return to London, using the supposed journey to make the Stapletons believe they are absent. Holmes and Watson instead remain in the area after reaching Coombe Tracey, while Cartwright is sent onward to London.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Sir Henry recalls hearing the hound on the moor and insists that it is not merely superstition. Holmes says he intends to muzzle and chain it with Sir Henry's help.

records.l: the portrait of Hugo Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: The portrait shows Hugo Baskerville in Cavalier dress, identified by the family as the ancestor who started the Hound legend. When Holmes frames the face by covering the hat and hair, it strongly resembles Mr. Stapleton and supplies a missing link in Holmes's reasoning.

records.l: the nets, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Holmes describes his plan as a net already placed around the suspected criminal. He says the drag is beginning and hopes to catch the 'big, lean-jawed pike' before it escapes through the meshes.

records.l: the Baskerville mystery, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: The investigation advances through the discovery of Stapleton's connection to the Baskerville family and Mrs. Laura Lyons's testimony. Holmes says the case is becoming a connected narrative, but he still wants clearer evidence before proceeding against the 'very wily man.'

records.l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Holmes explicitly describes the death of Sir Charles Baskerville as a murder investigation. Mrs. Laura Lyons's appointment with Sir Charles, arranged and then canceled under Stapleton's influence, is presented as a significant connection to the crime.

records.l: the Vandeleur identity, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
records.s: Holmes produces a photograph labeled 'Mr. and Mrs. Vandeleur' and written descriptions from the time they ran St. Oliver's private school. The evidence is used to establish that Mr. Stapleton and the woman presented as his sister were actually married under the Vandeleur identity.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade ambush Stapleton near Merripit House while Sir Henry remains inside with him. A huge black hound attacks Sir Henry, but Holmes and Watson shoot it and discover that its fiery appearance was caused by phosphorus. They find Mrs. Stapleton bound and abused in a room at Merripit House, and she reveals that Stapleton may have fled to an old tin mine on an island in the Grimpen Mire. Stapleton is not found, while Sir Henry is taken back to Baskerville Hall and later becomes delirious with fever.

records.l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The family ghost is revealed to be a real but unusually large hound whose terrifying appearance was produced with phosphorus. Holmes and Watson kill it after it attacks Sir Henry.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes leads the ambush near Merripit House and keeps his plans secret until the action begins. He shoots the hound, rescues Sir Henry, finds Mrs. Stapleton, and learns that Stapleton may be hiding in the Grimpen Mire.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Dr. Watson observes Stapleton and Sir Henry through the dining-room window and reports what he sees to Holmes. He helps pursue the hound, fires at it, assists in rescuing Sir Henry and Mrs. Stapleton, and returns with Sir Henry to Baskerville Hall.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Inspector Lestrade joins Holmes and Watson in the ambush and carries a pistol. He helps rescue Sir Henry, gives him brandy, and remains at Merripit House while Holmes and Watson return to Baskerville Hall.

records.l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Sir Henry Baskerville is left in the dining-room with Stapleton and later walks onto the moor. The hound attacks him, but Holmes and the others rescue him before he is wounded; afterward, he is taken to Baskerville Hall and develops a high fever.

records.l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Stapleton entertains Sir Henry at Merripit House and secretly visits an out-house where the hound is kept. He follows the hound during the attack but is not found when Holmes, Watson, and Lestrade search the house; Mrs. Stapleton says he would likely flee to an old tin mine in the Grimpen Mire.

records.l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Mrs. Stapleton is found bound, gagged, and badly bruised in a room at Merripit House. She says Stapleton has tortured and deceived her, and she tells Holmes where he may have escaped.

records.l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Merripit House is the site of Holmes’s ambush and the hound attack on Sir Henry. Holmes, Watson, and Lestrade later search the house, where they find Mrs. Stapleton tied to a post.

records.l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Baskerville Hall is where Holmes and Watson take Sir Henry after the night’s events. Sir Henry later lies there delirious with a high fever under Dr. Mortimer’s care.

records.l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The Grimpen Mire is covered by a dense fog that threatens to disrupt Holmes’s plans and conceal the hound’s approach. Mrs. Stapleton says an old tin mine on an island in the mire may be Stapleton’s refuge, but the fog makes pursuit impossible.

records.l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The moor is the dark setting for the ambush, the hound’s attack, and the pursuit. The fog gradually covers much of it, making movement and visibility increasingly dangerous.

records.l: the fog, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The fog moves from the Grimpen Mire toward Merripit House and nearly prevents Holmes’s plan from succeeding. It limits visibility, masks the gunshots, and ultimately prevents immediate pursuit of Stapleton.

records.l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The hound is an enormous coal-black animal resembling a combination of a bloodhound and a mastiff. It attacks Sir Henry but is shot several times by Holmes and Watson and dies after Holmes empties five revolver barrels into it.

records.l: the pursuit of Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: Holmes, Watson, and Lestrade search Merripit House after the hound is killed, but Stapleton has disappeared. Mrs. Stapleton directs them toward an old tin mine in the Grimpen Mire, though the fog prevents them from following immediately.

records.l: the hound attack on Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The hound emerges from the fog and chases Sir Henry along the path. It knocks him down and worries at his throat, but Holmes kills it before it can wound him.

records.l: death of the hound, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 14.
records.s: The hound’s death proves that it is mortal and exposes the supernatural appearance as a trick. Its jaws and muzzle still seem to glow afterward, and Watson identifies phosphorus on the animal.
