records.l: photograph of the dead man, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
records.s: A snapshot found in the dead man's possession shows an alert, sharp-featured simian man with thick eyebrows and a pronounced lower face resembling a baboon's muzzle. Holmes studies the photograph and keeps it temporarily with Lestrade's permission for further investigation.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson trace the destroyed Napoleon busts from Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers to Gelder & Co., learning that Beppo worked at both establishments and had previously been imprisoned for knifing an Italian. Harding Brothers’ records identify the purchasers of their three busts, including Josiah Brown of Laburnum Villa in Chiswick, and Holmes predicts that Beppo will attack Brown’s bust. Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Lestrade ambush Beppo at Laburnum Villa as he breaks Brown’s bust, and Beppo is arrested with a bloodstained sheath knife. Holmes indicates that the connection between Beppo, the murder of Pietro Venucci, and the destruction of the busts has not yet been fully explained.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the source and destruction of the Napoleon busts, tracing them through Morse Hudson, Harding Brothers, and Gelder & Co. He uses the evening newspaper and a letter to Josiah Brown to lure Beppo into attacking the remaining bust at Laburnum Villa, where he helps arrest him. Holmes examines the broken bust and says that important details of the case remain unresolved.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes on the inquiries at Harding Brothers, Morse Hudson, and Gelder & Co. He helps watch Laburnum Villa, assists in seizing Beppo, and observes Holmes’s investigation of the broken bust.

records.l: Harding Brothers, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Harding Brothers of Kensington sold three Napoleon busts obtained from Gelder & Co. One was sold to Horace Harker, one to Josiah Brown of Laburnum Lodge, Laburnum Vale, Chiswick, and one to Mr. Sandeford of Lower Grove Road, Reading.

records.l: Morse Hudson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Morse Hudson told Holmes and Dr. Watson that he sold two of Dr. Barnicot’s busts and that a third was smashed on his counter. He identified the photograph of Beppo and said Beppo had worked for him as an Italian piece-work man before leaving the previous week.

records.l: Gelder & Co., The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Gelder & Co. of Stepney supplied Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers with the relevant Napoleon busts. Its manager said the six casts were half of a batch, made in two plaster moulds, and that there was no known reason for them to differ from other casts.

records.l: Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Beppo worked for Morse Hudson and had also worked at Gelder & Co., where he was considered a good worker. More than a year earlier he knifed another Italian, received a one-year sentence, and was later sought by Holmes as the person destroying the busts. He is caught breaking Josiah Brown’s bust at Laburnum Villa and is arrested with a long sheath knife bearing recent bloodstains.

records.l: Kensington, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Kensington is where Harding Brothers operated and where Horace Harker’s bust was destroyed. Holmes and Dr. Watson return there to question Harding Brothers about the busts.

records.l: Devine’s head of Napoleon, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Devine’s head of Napoleon was the marble original from which hundreds of plaster casts were made at Gelder & Co.

records.l: Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The Napoleon busts are plaster casts made from Devine’s head of Napoleon. Several are destroyed in a connected series of incidents, and Holmes expects Beppo to attack the remaining examples.

records.l: Morse Hudson’s three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Morse Hudson received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. two were sold to Dr. Barnicot, while the third was smashed on Hudson’s counter in broad daylight.

records.l: Harding Brothers’ three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Harding Brothers received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. They sold them to Horace Harker, Josiah Brown, and Mr. Sandeford; Brown’s bust is later broken by Beppo at Laburnum Villa.

records.l: photograph of Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The photograph is shown to Morse Hudson and the manager of Gelder & Co., who both identify the pictured man as Beppo. Holmes uses it to connect Beppo with the destroyed busts and with the man arrested at Laburnum Villa.

records.l: Mr. Horace Harker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Horace Harker bought one of the three Napoleon busts sold by Harding Brothers. His bust was destroyed, and his sensational newspaper account described the incident as a murder by a madman.

records.l: Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Josiah Brown bought one of Harding Brothers’ Napoleon busts and lived at Laburnum Villa in Chiswick. After receiving Holmes’s note, he locked the doors of his house and waited for developments while Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade watched outside.

records.l: Laburnum Villa, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Laburnum Villa was Josiah Brown’s house in Chiswick and contained one of Harding Brothers’ remaining Napoleon busts. Beppo entered the house and broke the bust outside, where Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade arrested him.

records.l: evening newspaper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The evening newspaper reported the Kensington incident under the headline “Kensington Outrage. Murder by a Madman.” It printed a sensational account and repeated the conclusion attributed to Inspector Lestrade and Sherlock Holmes that the events arose from lunacy rather than deliberate crime; Holmes also used it to plant a misleading clue for Beppo.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Inspector Lestrade identifies the dead man as Pietro Venucci and theorizes that the murder resulted from a Mafia pursuit. He accompanies Holmes and Dr. Watson to Laburnum Villa, helps arrest Beppo, and remains convinced that his Mafia theory will explain the case.

records.l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Pietro Venucci is identified as the dead man found in connection with the Kensington incident. Inspector Lestrade says he was from Naples, was a notorious cut-throat connected with the Mafia, and may have been pursuing the man in Beppo’s photograph.

records.l: Mafia, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The Mafia is described by Inspector Lestrade as a secret political society that enforces its decrees by murder. Lestrade believes Pietro Venucci was pursuing another Italian because that person had broken Mafia rules.

records.l: murder of Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The murder is attributed by Inspector Lestrade to a struggle involving Pietro Venucci and another Italian, whom he believes may be Beppo. Holmes captures Beppo but indicates that the full relationship between the murder and the destroyed busts still requires explanation.

records.l: destruction of the Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: The destruction affects busts sold through Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers, with Beppo connected to the incidents through his work at the relevant establishments. Holmes arranges surveillance at Laburnum Villa and catches Beppo breaking Josiah Brown’s bust, but his examination finds no visible peculiarity in the plaster fragments.

records.l: letter from Sherlock Holmes to Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
records.s: Sherlock Holmes sends Josiah Brown an urgent letter by express messenger. Brown follows its instructions by locking every door inside Laburnum Villa and awaiting the expected intruder, enabling Holmes and the others to catch Beppo.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Sherlock Holmes buys the last Devine’s Napoleon bust from Mr. Sandeford of Reading and breaks it open, finding the famous black pearl of the Borgias inside. Holmes explains that Beppo concealed the pearl in one of six wet plaster busts while fleeing the police, then later searched for it after his arrest. He connects the pearl’s disappearance with Lucretia Venucci, her brother Pietro, Pietro’s murder, and Beppo’s destruction of the other busts. Inspector Lestrade praises Holmes’s investigation, while Holmes returns immediately to another case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Sherlock Holmes purchases the Reading bust from Mr. Sandeford for ten pounds and has the seller transfer every possible right to it. He breaks the bust open and finds the famous black pearl of the Borgias, then explains how he traced it through the six busts and related crimes.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Dr. Watson observes Holmes’s uneasiness, excitement, and pleasure at the praise he receives after recovering the pearl. Holmes directs him to place the pearl in the safe and retrieve the papers concerning the Conk-Singleton forgery case.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Inspector Lestrade supplies Holmes with information about Beppo and witnesses Holmes recover the pearl. He praises the investigation and says that Scotland Yard is proud of Holmes.

records.l: Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Beppo is identified as an Italian former sculptor and known criminal who worked at Gelder & Co. He concealed the pearl in a wet Napoleon bust before his arrest, and later tracked the six busts through London, destroying them in search of the hidden jewel.

records.l: Mr. Sandeford, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Mr. Sandeford, of Reading, owns the last Napoleon bust and brings it to Holmes in an old-fashioned carpet-bag. He sells it for ten pounds after signing away every possible right he had in it.

records.l: Gelder & Co., The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Gelder & Co. manufactured the six plaster busts of Napoleon at its Stepney establishment. Beppo worked there, and the busts were drying in the passage when he concealed the pearl in one of them.

records.l: Lucretia Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Lucretia Venucci was the Italian maid of the Princess and the sister of Pietro. Holmes believes she was connected to the disappearance of the pearl through Pietro and possibly Beppo.

records.l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Pietro was Lucretia Venucci’s brother and was murdered two nights before this meeting. Holmes believes he was connected with Beppo and the pearl, though he cannot determine whether Beppo stole it from him, acted as his confederate, or served as a go-between.

records.l: Reading, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Reading is the location associated with Mr. Sandeford and the final surviving bust. Holmes determines that the Reading bust must contain the pearl after the other busts have been eliminated.

records.l: London, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: London is where the six busts were scattered after Beppo’s arrest and where he searched for them. One of the remaining busts was in London, and Holmes warned its occupants before Beppo could reach it.

records.l: Devine’s Napoleon bust, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Devine’s Napoleon bust is the type of plaster figure that Holmes seeks and that Gelder & Co. manufactured in a group of six. The last specimen, bought from Mr. Sandeford, contains the hidden pearl.

records.l: the famous black pearl of the Borgias, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: The famous black pearl of the Borgias is recovered from inside the Reading Napoleon bust. Holmes identifies it as the valuable jewel that disappeared from the Prince of Colonna’s bedroom at the Dacre Hotel.

records.l: the disappearance of the Borgia pearl, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: The disappearance of the Borgia pearl occurred two days before Beppo’s arrest and caused a sensation, but the London police initially failed to recover it. Holmes eventually traces the missing jewel to the interior of a Napoleon bust.

records.l: murder of Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Pietro’s murder occurred during Beppo’s search for the busts. Holmes says Beppo stabbed Pietro in a scuffle at Harker’s after Pietro, whom Holmes regarded as a confederate, followed him and held him responsible for the pearl’s loss.

records.l: Beppo’s arrest, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Beppo’s arrest followed a crime of violence at Gelder & Co. while the six busts were being made. He was sentenced to a year in prison, during which the busts were distributed across London and he lost track of which one held the pearl.

records.l: the bust investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: The bust investigation links Beppo’s criminal history, the six Napoleon busts, Pietro’s murder, and the missing Borgia pearl. Holmes tracks the busts from Harker’s through the London and Reading locations, ultimately recovering the pearl from the final bust.

records.l: Beppo’s concealment of the pearl, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
records.s: Beppo concealed the pearl by making a small hole in one of six soft, wet plaster busts, dropping the jewel inside, and covering the opening. Because the pearl adhered to the wet plaster, shaking the busts would not reveal which one contained it.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Hilton Soames asks Sherlock Holmes and John Watson to investigate the apparent theft and copying of a confidential Greek examination paper at the College of St. Luke’s. The paper had been disturbed, and the intruder left pencil shavings, a broken pencil tip, a cut in the desk, and black clay. Holmes examines the room, Bannister, and the three student rooms, developing clues but not yet identifying the intruder. He tells Soames to change nothing and promises to return before the examination.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Hilton Soames’s confidential examination-paper case. He infers that the intruder moved the pages to the window table, copied at least part of them, broke and resharpened a large soft-leaded pencil, and then hid in Soames’s bedroom before escaping. He examines Bannister and the three students’ rooms, takes the black clay and pencil cuttings, and postpones his conclusion until the following morning.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Hilton Soames’s rooms and records the investigation. He observes Holmes examining the evidence, Bannister, and the three student rooms.

records.l: Hilton Soames, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Hilton Soames, a tutor and Greek examiner at the College of St. Luke’s, asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate the tampering with his examination proofs. He explains that Bannister left a key in the door while Soames was away, and that the papers were found separated, with other traces of an intruder. He identifies Gilchrist, Daulat Ras, and Miles McLaren as the three students using the stair.

records.l: Bannister, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Bannister is Hilton Soames’s servant of ten years and is described as honest, though he left his key in Soames’s door after entering to ask whether tea was wanted. He becomes extremely upset when the papers are found disturbed and says he nearly fainted. Holmes questions him about his movements and learns that he sat near the corner after Soames returned, though he had first been near the door.

records.l: Daulat Ras, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Daulat Ras is an Indian student living on the same stair as Hilton Soames and had visited Soames to ask about the examination before the proofs were disturbed. He is described as quiet, inscrutable, steady, and methodical, with Greek as his weak subject. Holmes visits his room and sees him pacing restlessly behind his blind.

records.l: Gilchrist, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Gilchrist occupies the lower student room. He is described as a fine scholar and athlete who plays rugby and cricket, has earned his Blue for hurdling and the long jump, and works hard despite being poor after his father’s ruin. He welcomes Holmes and the others into his room.

records.l: Miles McLaren, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: Miles McLaren occupies the top student room. He is described as brilliant but wayward, dissipated, and unprincipled, with a prior card scandal and poor preparation for the examination. He refuses to open his door to Holmes and responds with abusive language, behavior that Soames considers suspicious.

records.l: the three students, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The three students using the stair are Gilchrist, Daulat Ras, and Miles McLaren, and all three are entered for the examination. Holmes considers their rooms and circumstances while investigating who could have entered Soames’s room.

records.l: College of St. Luke’s, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The College of St. Luke’s employs Hilton Soames as a tutor and lecturer and is preparing for the Fortescue Scholarship examination. Soames fears that the tampered paper could cause a scandal affecting the college and the university.

records.l: the Fortescue Scholarship, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The Fortescue Scholarship is the competition for which the confidential Greek examination is being prepared. It is described as valuable, creating a substantial incentive for an unscrupulous candidate to obtain the paper in advance.

records.l: the Greek examination, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The Greek examination begins the next day and includes a previously unseen passage from Thucydides for translation. Hilton Soames is one of the examiners, and the possibility that a candidate prepared the passage in advance threatens the examination’s fairness.

records.l: the examination paper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The examination paper consists of three proof slips containing half a chapter of Thucydides. While Hilton Soames was away, someone moved the slips, apparently copied from them, and left evidence including pencil shavings, a broken lead tip, a desk cut, and black clay.

records.l: the examination scandal, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The examination scandal concerns the apparent unauthorized access to and copying of the confidential Greek paper. Hilton Soames wants to avoid postponing the examination and exposing the College of St. Luke’s and the university to public disgrace.

records.l: the intruder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The intruder entered Hilton Soames’s room while the door was accessible through Bannister’s forgotten key. The person moved the papers to the window table, copied them in haste, broke and resharpened a large pencil, and apparently hid in Soames’s bedroom before escaping.

records.l: the key, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The key belonged to Bannister, who left it in Hilton Soames’s outer door after entering to ask whether tea was wanted. Because the outer door had no spring lock, the open door allowed someone to enter and leave the room.

records.l: the examination pencil, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The examination pencil was an unusually large pencil with a soft lead, dark blue exterior, and silver lettering. Holmes identifies the remaining piece as bearing the letters "NN" and estimates that the intruder had used and resharpened it while copying the paper.

records.l: the black clay, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS
records.s: The black clay is a small, roughly pyramidal, hollowed-out pellet containing specks resembling sawdust. Matching pieces are found on Hilton Soames’s study table and in his bedroom, supporting Holmes’s conclusion that the intruder passed through or concealed himself in the bedroom.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: Holmes and Watson discuss the three possible suspects after observing the Indian student pacing his room and the other students remaining unseen. Watson favors the foul-mouthed student, while Holmes is more puzzled by Bannister, the servant, despite considering him honest. Holmes visits the town’s four significant stationers with pencil chips, but none has the unusual pencil size in stock. He concludes that the pencil clue has failed, though he believes the investigation can proceed using other evidence.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: Holmes discusses the three students with Watson and considers the Indian student's pacing unimportant because he may have been memorizing material. He is particularly puzzled by Bannister's behavior and investigates the pencil by visiting the town's four significant stationers.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: Watson identifies the foul-mouthed student as his preferred suspect because of that student's poor record, though he also finds the Indian student suspicious. He accompanies Holmes to the stationers and discusses the possible suspects and the pencil clue.

records.l: Bannister, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: Bannister, the servant, is regarded by both Holmes and Watson as a perfectly honest man. Holmes nevertheless finds Bannister's apparent honesty puzzling and asks what his role is in the matter.

records.l: Daulat Ras, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The Indian student is observed pacing his room while the others are invisible. Watson thinks his behavior and his queer look may be suspicious, but Holmes explains that he could have been trying to learn something by heart.

records.l: foul-mouthed student, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The foul-mouthed student is Watson's preferred suspect because Watson considers him to have the worst record among the three students.

records.l: the three students, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The three students remain the central set of possible suspects, and Holmes describes the problem as requiring a choice among them. The Indian student is seen pacing his room, while the other two are invisible from the quadrangle.

records.l: nervous tutor, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The nervous tutor is mentioned by Holmes as one of the people involved in the problem that he and Watson intend to solve.

records.l: the examination pencil, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The pencil is described as an unusual size that is seldom kept in stock by stationers. Holmes attempts to find a duplicate by showing pencil chips to the town's four significant stationers.

records.l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The investigation considers the three students, Bannister, and the pencil evidence. Although the search for a duplicate pencil fails, Holmes believes the case can still be built from sufficient evidence.

records.l: pencil clue, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again
records.s: The pencil clue is tested when Holmes offers pencil chips to four stationers and bids high for a duplicate. Since none can immediately supply the unusual pencil, Holmes concludes that the clue has run to nothing.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes made no further allusion to the matter that day, though he
records.s: Sherlock Holmes identifies Gilchrist as the student who entered Soames’s room, took the examination proofs, and began copying them before hiding in the bedroom. Holmes traces black clay from the athletic grounds to Gilchrist’s jumping-shoes and uses the marks and clay samples as evidence. Bannister admits that he concealed Gilchrist and later urged him not to profit from his misconduct because Bannister had served Gilchrist’s father. Gilchrist confesses, says he will not sit the examination, and plans to leave for South Africa with a commission in the Rhodesian Police.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes made no further allusion to the matter that day, though he

Holmes learns that Staunton is the heir of the wealthy but miserly Lord Mount-James, then traces the telegram to an unnamed recipient and travels with Dr. John Watson toward Cambridge.

records.s: Godfrey Staunton is Cambridge’s leading three-quarter, a player for Cambridge, Blackheath, and England. He appears pale and troubled before leaving Bentley’s private hotel with a bearded stranger, leaving his belongings behind and missing the next day’s match.

records.l: Lord Mount-James, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Lord Mount-James is Godfrey Staunton’s nearest relative and presumed heir-giver, as well as one of the richest men in England. He initially refuses financial responsibility for finding Staunton, but becomes alarmed when Holmes suggests that criminals may have kidnapped Staunton to obtain information about his wealth.

records.l: the bearded stranger, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The bearded stranger is a grizzled, pale-faced man of about fifty who brings a note to Godfrey Staunton at Bentley’s private hotel. He appears agitated, speaks briefly with Staunton about “time,” and leaves with him in the direction of the Strand.

records.l: the hotel porter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The hotel porter receives and reports the bearded stranger’s visit, Staunton’s reaction to the note, and their departure. He also tells Holmes that Staunton received a telegram at about six o’clock and wrote a reply.

records.l: Cambridge University rugby team, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The Cambridge University rugby team is captained by Cyril Overton and is preparing to play Oxford. Its prospects are seriously damaged by the disappearance of Godfrey Staunton, whom Overton regards as the team’s essential three-quarter.

records.l: Oxford rugby team, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The Oxford rugby team is scheduled to play Cambridge University in the important match the day after Staunton disappears. Its players are mentioned as the opponents against whom Cambridge may be unable to compete effectively without Staunton.

records.l: Bentley’s private hotel, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Bentley’s private hotel is where the Cambridge University rugby team stays before the match. Godfrey Staunton receives the note there, leaves with the bearded stranger, and is found to have abandoned his room without sleeping in his bed.

records.l: Cambridge, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Cambridge is the home of the university rugby team and Godfrey Staunton’s expected destination if he returned by the late train. Holmes travels toward Cambridge because the available clues seem to point there.

records.l: telegram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: A telegram sent to Sherlock Holmes asks him to await Cyril Overton because the team’s right wing three-quarter is missing and indispensable the next day. Another telegram sent by Staunton contains an incomplete appeal for help.

records.l: Staunton's telegram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Staunton’s telegram was sent within hours of his disappearance and was addressed without a name. Its surviving words, “Stand by us for God’s sake!”, lead Holmes to infer that Staunton and another person faced a serious danger and sought protection.

records.l: the note for Godfrey Staunton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The note for Godfrey Staunton is delivered by the bearded stranger at Bentley’s private hotel. Reading it causes Staunton to collapse back in his chair, after which he leaves with the stranger.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's room, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Godfrey Staunton’s room at Bentley’s private hotel contains his untouched belongings and an unslept-in bed after his disappearance. Holmes searches the room, examines the papers, and finds an impression of Staunton’s telegram on the blotting-paper.

records.l: blotting-paper message, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The blotting-paper message preserves the reverse impression of part of Staunton’s telegram. Holmes reads the surviving words as “Stand by us for God’s sake!” and treats them as the principal clue in the investigation.

records.l: the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: The Cambridge–Oxford rugby match is scheduled for the day after Godfrey Staunton disappears. Holmes considers the timing significant because Staunton is the player whose presence appears essential to Cambridge’s success.

records.l: Rugby, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Rugby is presented as the amateur sport in which Cyril Overton and Godfrey Staunton are prominent. Overton describes Staunton’s abilities in passing, tackling, dribbling, kicking, and organizing the team.

records.l: kidnapping, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Kidnapping is considered by Holmes as one possible explanation for Staunton’s disappearance. He suggests to Lord Mount-James that criminals might hold Staunton to obtain information about the old man’s house, habits, and treasure.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's inheritance, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER
records.s: Godfrey Staunton is described as Lord Mount-James’s heir, although Lord Mount-James has never given him money. The inheritance provides a possible financial motive for Staunton’s disappearance, but no definite connection is established in this unit.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson travel to the old university city to question Dr. Leslie Armstrong about Godfrey Staunton's disappearance. Armstrong denies knowing Staunton's whereabouts, but Holmes confronts him with a receipted bill and an urgent telegram connected to Staunton. After Armstrong angrily expels them, Holmes investigates Armstrong's repeated carriage journeys and learns that he travels ten or twelve miles once or twice a day. Holmes fails to follow the carriage successfully but concludes that Armstrong knows where Staunton is and resolves to continue the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Leslie Armstrong about Godfrey Staunton and presents evidence linking Armstrong to Staunton. After being expelled, he investigates Armstrong's carriage journeys by questioning people and following the carriage by bicycle, but he loses track of it. He concludes that Armstrong knows where Staunton is and plans to continue investigating.

records.l: Dr. Leslie Armstrong, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Dr. Leslie Armstrong is a prominent medical lecturer, consultant, and thinker who strongly disapproves of Sherlock Holmes's profession. He denies knowing anything about Godfrey Staunton's disappearance, becomes furious when confronted with a receipted bill and an urgent telegram, and orders Holmes and Watson from his house. He makes long daily carriage journeys and detects Holmes following him.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Godfrey Staunton is an intimate friend of Dr. Leslie Armstrong who has disappeared after leaving his hotel. He paid Dr. Leslie Armstrong thirteen guineas the previous month and sent Armstrong an urgent telegram from London at six-fifteen the previous evening.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Dr. Leslie Armstrong's house and later stays with him at an inn. He helps discuss how Armstrong's carriage might be followed while Holmes investigates the doctor's journeys.

records.l: the old university city, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The old university city is reached after dark by Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson. Holmes describes it as an inhospitable town, and its flat surrounding countryside makes it difficult to follow or conceal oneself.

records.l: the police, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The official police are described by Sherlock Holmes as the regular forces of the country. Holmes says that once the case is in their hands, private matters would necessarily become publicly exposed.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's disappearance, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Godfrey Staunton's disappearance is investigated by Sherlock Holmes, who seeks information from Dr. Leslie Armstrong. Holmes believes Armstrong's unexplained journeys and his reaction to the evidence are connected with the disappearance.

records.l: Dr. Armstrong's daily journeys, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: Dr. Armstrong's daily journeys are made by carriage for ten or twelve miles, once or sometimes twice a day. Sherlock Holmes follows one journey but loses the carriage when Armstrong takes a side road, and Armstrong later returns to his house after detecting the pursuit.

records.l: the case, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The case concerns Godfrey Staunton's disappearance and Dr. Leslie Armstrong's possible knowledge of it. Holmes remains in the old university city because leaving would mean abandoning the case, and he refuses to leave the matter unresolved.

records.l: the receipted bill, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The receipted bill shows that Godfrey Staunton paid thirteen guineas to Dr. Leslie Armstrong the previous month. Sherlock Holmes finds it among Staunton's papers and uses it to challenge Armstrong, who refuses to explain it.

records.l: Staunton's telegram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The urgent telegram was sent by Godfrey Staunton from London to Dr. Leslie Armstrong at six-fifteen the previous evening. Holmes says it is undoubtedly associated with Staunton's disappearance, but Armstrong claims not to have received it.

records.l: the inn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, It was already dark when we reached the old university city.
records.s: The inn opposite Dr. Armstrong's house provides Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson with lodging while they investigate. Holmes returns there exhausted after his inquiries, and its proximity to a bicycle shop enables him to begin following Armstrong's carriage.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson follow Dr. Leslie Armstrong’s carriage from Cambridge by using aniseed and the draghound Pompey. They reach a lonely cottage and find Godfrey Staunton grieving beside his dying, or already dead, wife. Dr. Armstrong explains that Staunton secretly married his former London landlady’s daughter, whose illness prevented him from playing in the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match. After learning that Staunton’s wife has died, Holmes promises discretion about the marriage and leaves with Watson.
records.t: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson follow Dr. Leslie Armstrong’s carriage from Cambridge by using aniseed and the draghound Pompey. They reach a lonely cottage and find Godfrey Staunton grieving beside his dying—or already dead—wife. Dr. Armstrong explains that Staunton secretly married his former London landlady’s daughter, whose illness prevented him from playing in the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match. After learning that Staunton’s wife has died, Holmes promises discretion about the marriage and leaves with Watson.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Holmes investigates Dr. Armstrong’s movements and uses a syringe of aniseed on the doctor’s carriage wheel so that Pompey can follow the trail. He reaches the lonely cottage with Watson, discovers Godfrey Staunton and his dead wife, and promises Dr. Armstrong to keep the private matter out of the papers.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Watson accompanies Holmes during the investigation and reports the Cambridge–Oxford match’s result and the newspaper’s account of Staunton’s absence. He follows Holmes and Pompey to the cottage, where he witnesses Staunton’s grief and learns the circumstances of the secret marriage.

records.l: Dr. Leslie Armstrong, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Dr. Armstrong warns Holmes that following him is futile and tries to mislead him by taking a circuitous route through the countryside. He returns to the cottage, explains Staunton’s secret marriage and his wife’s illness, and is reassured by Holmes that the matter will be kept confidential.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Staunton is found at the lonely cottage kneeling beside his dead wife and overwhelmed by grief. He had secretly married his former London landlady’s daughter and had been unable to withdraw from the Cambridge–Oxford match without exposing the marriage.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's wife, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Staunton’s wife is described as beautiful, good, and intelligent. She suffers from virulent consumption and is found dead at the lonely cottage after Staunton returns from the rugby match.

records.l: Cambridge, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Holmes and Watson stay in Cambridge while investigating Staunton’s disappearance. Holmes searches villages around Cambridge and later follows Armstrong’s carriage from the town to the lonely cottage.

records.l: the lonely cottage, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: The lonely cottage is where Staunton has secretly lived with his wife and where Dr. Armstrong has helped conceal their marriage. Holmes and Watson find Staunton there grieving beside his wife’s body.

records.l: Pompey, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Pompey is a squat, white-and-tan draghound with a strong sense of smell. After Holmes scents Armstrong’s carriage with aniseed, Pompey follows the trail through a deceptive route and leads Holmes and Watson to the lonely cottage.

records.l: the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Oxford wins the match by a goal and two tries. The newspaper attributes Cambridge’s defeat partly to the absence of Godfrey Staunton, whose skill was greatly missed.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's secret marriage, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Staunton secretly married the daughter of his London landlady because public knowledge of the marriage would have threatened his inheritance from Lord Mount-James. The marriage was known only to Dr. Armstrong and one servant until the investigation reached the cottage.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's wife's illness, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Staunton’s wife develops consumption of the most virulent kind. Her dangerous illness causes Staunton to leave the rugby match and return to the cottage in a state bordering on frenzy.

records.l: Godfrey Staunton's wife's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the
records.s: Staunton’s wife dies at the lonely cottage, ending her suffering. Staunton remains beside her in overwhelming grief until Holmes and Watson arrive.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson travel to Abbey Grange after Inspector Stanley Hopkins summons Holmes to investigate the apparent murder of Sir Eustace Brackenstall. Lady Brackenstall says that three burglars from the Lewisham gang entered through the dining-room window, bound and assaulted her, and killed Sir Eustace with the blackthorn poker before escaping with some silver. Holmes examines the scene and notices details involving the bell-rope, the servants, the French window, and three wine glasses that may require further investigation.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. John Watson to Abbey Grange after receiving Inspector Stanley Hopkins’s urgent summons. He initially believes the case concerns a murder and examines Lady Brackenstall, the dining-room, the bindings, the French window, the poker, and the three wine glasses, noticing details that challenge the apparent simplicity of the burglary.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Abbey Grange and records the journey, the house, the people involved, and the apparent crime. He listens to Lady Brackenstall’s account and observes Holmes examining the evidence.

records.l: Stanley Hopkins, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Inspector Stanley Hopkins summons Sherlock Holmes to Abbey Grange after Sir Eustace Brackenstall is killed. He believes the crime was committed by the three members of the Lewisham gang and presents Lady Brackenstall’s account and the physical scene to Holmes.

records.l: Sir Eustace Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Sir Eustace Brackenstall is found dead on the dining-room hearthrug with his head horribly injured. According to Lady Brackenstall, he entered the room carrying his blackthorn cudgel and was struck with the poker by one of the burglars; Inspector Stanley Hopkins also describes him as a confirmed drunkard who could become violent.

records.l: Lady Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Lady Brackenstall tells Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Stanley Hopkins that three burglars attacked her, tied her to a chair with the bell-rope, gagged her, and killed Sir Eustace Brackenstall. She has a severe injury over one eye and two other red marks on her arm, and she says that the burglars took silver, drank wine, and escaped through the French window.

records.l: Theresa Wright, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Theresa Wright is Lady Brackenstall’s long-serving maid, who came with her from Australia and is devoted to her. She says that she saw three men near the lodge gate and later found Lady Brackenstall bound and Sir Eustace dead; Inspector Stanley Hopkins notes that Sir Eustace had previously thrown a decanter at her.

records.l: the Lewisham gang, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: The Lewisham gang consists of the father and two sons, known as the three Randalls. Inspector Stanley Hopkins believes they committed the burglary and the killing because they resemble Lady Brackenstall’s description of the three intruders and had recently committed another burglary at Sydenham.

records.l: Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: Abbey Grange is the Brackenstalls’ large country house in Kent, containing an older central block, a modern wing, and a dining-room with a French window opening onto the lawn. The apparent burglary and the killing of Sir Eustace Brackenstall take place there.

records.l: the murder of Lady Brackenstall's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: The murder of Sir Eustace Brackenstall is reported as a violent killing in the dining-room, where his head is struck with a poker. Lady Brackenstall attributes it to three burglars, while Holmes examines the scene for details that might confirm or undermine that account.

records.l: the burglary at Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: The burglary at Abbey Grange allegedly involves three men entering through the dining-room’s French window, binding Lady Brackenstall, killing Sir Eustace Brackenstall, taking several pieces of silver, and drinking wine. The apparent burglars close the window when they leave, and no clear tracks are found because the ground is frozen.

records.l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: The investigation is led locally by Inspector Stanley Hopkins, who asks Sherlock Holmes for assistance. Holmes questions the witnesses and studies the room, the bell-rope, the window, the servants’ circumstances, the body, the poker, and the wine glasses.

records.l: the poker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE
records.s: The blackthorn poker is found bent into a curve beside Sir Eustace Brackenstall’s body, and the damage to it is consistent with the force of the blow that injured his head. Lady Brackenstall says that an elderly burglar picked it from the grate and used it to strike Sir Eustace.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Sherlock Holmes reexamines the Abbey Grange crime and concludes that the three wine glasses and other physical evidence contradict Lady Brackenstall’s account of a burglary by three men. He determines that the burglary story was fabricated, that only one exceptionally strong man was involved, and that Lady Brackenstall was tied to the chair after her husband’s death. Holmes suspects the real criminal is Jack Crocker, a former officer connected with Lady Brackenstall’s voyage, but delays seeking a warrant because he does not want to act against his conscience. He also helps Inspector Stanley Hopkins recover stolen silver from the park pond, while the Randall gang’s arrest in New York undermines Hopkins’s original theory.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the cork, wine glasses, bell-rope, bracket, chair, window, curtains, carpet, and rope at the Abbey Grange. He concludes that Lady Brackenstall’s story is fabricated, that one unusually strong and agile man was involved, and that the evidence points toward someone connected with her past. He investigates Miss Fraser’s voyage and Jack Crocker’s record, sends a telegram, and delays seeking a warrant because he fears causing unjust harm.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Holmes during the investigation and observes his doubts, deductions, and detailed examination of the Abbey Grange. He discusses the unusual features of Lady Brackenstall’s story and the wine glasses with Holmes.

records.l: Stanley Hopkins, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Inspector Stanley Hopkins initially supports the theory that the Randall gang committed the murder and reports the evidence to Holmes. He later tells Holmes that the Randall gang has been arrested in New York and that the stolen silver was recovered from the park pond, leaving his investigation without a clear explanation.

records.l: Lady Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Lady Brackenstall maintains that three burglars entered the Abbey Grange, drank wine, murdered her husband, tied her to a chair, and escaped with silver. Holmes confronts her with his belief that the story is an absolute fabrication, but she refuses to change her account. He concludes that she was placed in the chair after her husband’s death and that she is protecting the real criminal.

records.l: Theresa Wright, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Theresa, the stern Australian nurse, describes Sir Eustace as abusive and says that he had mistreated Lady Brackenstall. She corroborates her mistress’s account but reacts angrily when Holmes says that Lady Brackenstall has lied.

records.l: the Lewisham gang, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The Randall gang had reportedly committed a substantial burglary at Sydenham and was initially suspected of the Abbey Grange crime. The gang is arrested in New York, making it impossible for its members to have committed the murder in Kent that night.

records.l: the three burglars, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The three burglars described by Lady Brackenstall are presented as having entered early, attacked her, murdered her husband, taken limited silver, drunk wine, and escaped. Holmes finds the behavior improbable and concludes that the three men were imaginary figures in a fabricated account.

records.l: the maid, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The maid supports Lady Brackenstall’s account of the three burglars and helps treat the bruise on her mistress’s brow. Holmes considers her corroboration part of the deliberate falsehood, and she refuses to provide any different information.

records.l: Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The Abbey Grange is the scene of the midnight murder and alleged burglary. Holmes returns there, locks himself in the dining-room, and conducts a detailed examination of the physical evidence.

records.l: the park pond, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The park pond, which is frozen except for a hole left for a swan, becomes the hiding place for the stolen silver. Holmes directs Hopkins to examine it, and the silver is recovered from the water.

records.l: the wine glasses, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The three wine glasses trouble Holmes because beeswing appears in only one of them, despite the claim that three men drank from them. He concludes that only two glasses were used and that their dregs were poured into a third to create the appearance of three drinkers.

records.l: the wine bottle, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The wine bottle was opened with a short pocket screw, probably from a knife, rather than the large corkscrew found in the drawer. Holmes observes that the screw was driven in three times and did not pass through the cork, allowing him to infer that the suspected man carried a multiplex knife.

records.l: the bell-rope, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The bell-rope was cut several inches from its attachment rather than torn down, and one end was frayed while the other was cut cleanly. Holmes concludes that a tall, strong man climbed onto the mantelpiece and cut the rope with a knife without ringing the bell.

records.l: the wooden bracket, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The wooden bracket bears an impression in the dust. Holmes determines that the suspected man placed his knee on it to reach the bell-rope and cut it.

records.l: the oaken chair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The oaken chair has a blood mark on its seat. Holmes uses this evidence to conclude that Lady Brackenstall was not sitting there during the killing but was placed in the chair afterward.

records.l: the stolen silver, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The stolen silver was taken as part of the supposed burglary and later found at the bottom of the park pond. Holmes suggests that it may have been used as a blind or hidden temporarily by people who did not actually want it.

records.l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The case initially appears clear to Hopkins but becomes doubtful when Holmes examines the wine glasses and physical evidence. Holmes ultimately regards it as one of the most remarkable cases in his collection, though he postpones decisive legal action while seeking more information.

records.l: the fabricated burglary story, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: Holmes concludes that the account of three burglars is an invented story supported by Lady Brackenstall and the maid. He believes it was created to conceal the identity of the real criminal and that both women have a strong reason to protect him.

records.l: the murder of Lady Brackenstall's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless
records.s: The murder is initially attributed to three burglars, but Holmes concludes that a single powerful and agile man committed it. The physical evidence indicates that Lady Brackenstall was tied to the chair after the killing and that the burglary was staged.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Sherlock Holmes summons Captain Crocker and obtains his full account of the killing at the Abbey Grange. Crocker says he killed Mary Fraser's husband after finding him assaulting Mary, then helped Mary and Theresa Wright stage the scene as a burglary. Holmes believes the account and offers Crocker a chance to flee, but Crocker refuses to abandon Mary. Holmes conducts an informal trial in which Dr. Watson finds Crocker not guilty, and Holmes acquits him while urging him to return to Mary in a year.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Sherlock Holmes summons Captain Crocker, demands a truthful account of the events at the Abbey Grange, and recognizes that Crocker is responsible for the killing. He concludes that Crocker's actions may have been legitimate self-defense, tests his willingness to protect Mary, and conducts an informal trial that results in Crocker's acquittal.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Dr. Watson listens to Captain Crocker's confession and acts as the jury in Holmes's informal trial. He finds Crocker not guilty.

records.l: Captain Crocker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Captain Crocker admits that he killed Mary Fraser's husband with a poker after the husband attacked Mary. He also admits helping Mary and Theresa Wright stage the scene as a burglary, refuses Holmes's offer to flee because he will not leave Mary to face the consequences, and is acquitted in Holmes's informal trial.

records.l: Lady Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Mary Fraser is described as having been mistreated by her husband and as loving Captain Crocker. After her husband attacks her, she helps Crocker and Theresa Wright make the killing appear to have been committed by burglars, and Holmes seeks to keep her out of court.

records.l: Mary Fraser's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: Mary Fraser's husband is described as a drunken and violent man who raises his hand to Mary and strikes her with a stick. He fights Captain Crocker and is killed when Crocker strikes him with a poker.

records.l: Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: The Abbey Grange is the location where Captain Crocker encounters Mary Fraser, kills her husband, and helps stage a false burglary. The staged scene includes a cut bell rope, Mary tied to a chair, and missing silver.

records.l: the murder of Mary Fraser's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to
records.s: The murder occurs when Captain Crocker intervenes after Mary Fraser's husband strikes her. Crocker says the fight was between the two men and that he killed the husband because it was his life or Crocker's, and because he could not leave Mary in the husband's power.

records.l: Captain Crocker's account of the murder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to

The letter, written by a foreign potentate, contains provocative remarks whose publication could cause Britain to enter a major European war. Holmes concludes that the document was probably taken between 7:30 and 11:30 the previous evening and may have been passed to an international agent. He identifies Oberstein, La Rothiere, and Eduardo Lucas as the likely agents, but learns from the narrator's newspaper that Eduardo Lucas was murdered the previous night.

records.l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: This document is a sequence of Sherlock Holmes cases narrated or accompanied by Dr. John Watson, following Holmes’s return after the Reichenbach Fall through investigations involving murder, fraud, abduction, blackmail, stolen property, and political danger. It begins with Holmes’s reappearance to Watson during the Park Lane Mystery: Holmes explains his escape from Professor Moriarty, uses a wax likeness as bait, and captures Colonel Sebastian Moran, who killed Ronald Adair with an air-gun. Holmes then clears John Hector McFarlane when Jonas Oldacre’s supposed murder proves a revenge scheme staged by Oldacre himself. The cases broaden across England and beyond London. Holmes deciphers threatening dancing-men messages, exposing Abe Slaney after Hilton Cubitt is killed and Elsie Cubitt wounded. He saves Violet Smith from Jack Woodley, Williamson, and a forced marriage plot connected to her inheritance, while recognizing Bob Carruthers’s partial effort to protect her. He finds Lord Saltire, exposes James Wilder and Reuben Hayes in the Duke of Holdernesse’s secret kidnapping scheme, and resolves Captain Peter Carey’s death by proving Patrick Cairns acted in self-defense, freeing John Hopley Neligan. Holmes and Watson also confront Charles Augustus Milverton, destroying his blackmail papers after an unnamed woman kills him; recover the black pearl of the Borgias from Napoleon busts smashed by Beppo; and uncover Gilchrist’s theft of examination papers, aided by Bannister’s loyalty to Gilchrist’s father. Holmes solves Willoughby Smith’s killing through Anna and Professor Coram’s hidden history, then finds Godfrey Staunton mourning his secretly married wife, promising discretion. The later cases stress Holmes’s judgment as much as detection. At Abbey Grange, he rejects a fabricated burglary narrative, accepts Captain Crocker’s account that he killed Sir Eustace Brackenstall while defending Mary Fraser, and informally acquits him. The document ends with its largest political threat: a stolen letter could provoke European war. Holmes links it to Eduardo Lucas’s murder and Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope’s blackmail, recovers the letter, secretly restores it to the despatch-box, and preserves both the state’s security and Lady Hilda’s secret.

records.l: The Adventure of the Empty House, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A story about Dr. John Watson investigating the murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair and Sherlock Holmes returning after being presumed dead. Holmes explains his survival after Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Fall, then Holmes and Watson lure Colonel Sebastian Moran into an ambush, ending in Moran’s arrest for the shooting.

records.l: London, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: London is a city and a capital in Europe, viewed in accounts of crime. Colonel Sebastian Moran acquired an evil name there and remained a serious threat to Sherlock Holmes, who calls him London’s second most dangerous man. The murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair interests the city and dismays its fashionable world as Holmes returns from abroad. After Professor Moriarty’s death, Holmes finds London uninteresting to a criminal expert, though John Hector McFarlane travels through it for help. The story culminates in Beppo’s search for scattered Napoleon busts across districts including Kennington Road, Lower Brixton Road, and Pitt Street, while Holmes warns occupants of a remaining bust.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is a living, six-foot-tall criminal investigator, detective, consulting detective, and criminal expert, based at and repeatedly returning to Baker Street, where he resides and works with his close friend, colleague, partner, and companion Dr. John Watson. He is famed for peculiar powers of deduction, uses deductive and inductive reasoning, studies physical traces, codes, maps, documents, and human conduct, and applies intense effort especially to strange, dramatic, or sympathetic cases rather than seeking large rewards or official position. After surviving the Reichenbach Fall and Professor Moriarty, Holmes spends nearly three years hidden, travelling in Tibet under the alias Sigerson, researching at Montpellier, visiting Khartoum, and concealing himself through disguises. He returns as an old book collector, learns an enemy remains in London, and uses a wax bust decoy to expose and secure the arrest of Colonel Sebastian Moran, whom he identifies as Ronald Adair’s murderer. With Moran removed, he is free to examine London again. His subsequent work unfolds through varied investigations with Watson and police contacts including Lestrade, Hopkins, and Martin. He exposes Jonas Oldacre’s staged death in the Norwood builder case; deciphers the dancing-men cipher, clears Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, and traps Abe Slaney; protects Violet Smith from an abduction and forced-marriage scheme; and resolves Lord Saltire’s disappearance by following bicycle tracks, recognizing a false cow-track trail, and confronting the Duke of Holdernesse. He also investigates Peter Carey’s death, attempts the recovery of blackmail letters from Charles Augustus Milverton, recovers the black pearl of the Borgias from a bust, identifies Gilchrist in the examination-paper theft, and investigates Willoughby Smith’s murder at Yoxley Old Place. Holmes’s methods include aliases such as Captain Basil and Escott, cultivated night vision, boxing, baritsu, revolvers when danger is expected, ciphers, and occasional burglary tools. He plays violin to soothe himself, smokes heavily, may forgo food during intense work, and keeps extensive biographical and other investigative materials. His work is marked by discretion, independence, readiness to confront danger, and a strong personal bond with Watson.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dr. John Watson is a doctor, medical practitioner, narrator, chronicler, and investigator closely bound to Sherlock Holmes as his friend, former companion, assistant, and professional partner. He keeps notes on unusual cases, writes investigations as stories rather than scientific exercises, and records events with admiration for Holmes while sometimes offering his own theories, doubts, or practical aid. He carries a revolver and check book, smokes tobacco, has irregular meals, and had helped wean Holmes from drug addiction. After selling his Kensington practice, Watson returns to share the Baker Street rooms with Holmes. Their renewed work begins after Watson investigates Ronald Adair’s murder, learns that Holmes is alive, and helps trap Colonel Sebastian Moran. Across subsequent cases, Watson accompanies Holmes to Norwood, Norfolk, Farnham, Mackleton, Sussex, Cambridge, Abbey Grange, Westminster, and elsewhere. He reads reports and messages, observes interviews and physical clues, assists surveillance and arrests, follows suspects, and records Holmes’s explanations. Watson also repeatedly contributes through his medical knowledge: reviving Thorneycroft Huxtable, examining injured people, reporting on Jack Woodley’s condition, and checking whether Violet Smith has recovered. His investigative efforts are not always praised, Holmes finds his position and methods in the cyclist inquiry inadequate, but Watson remains dependable in danger, helping stop a runaway dog-cart, restraining Patrick Cairns, holding Williamson at gunpoint, and assisting with the capture of Beppo. His loyalty sometimes leads him beyond ordinary legality. Though he disapproves of the planned burglary of Charles Augustus Milverton’s house, he prepares masks and rubber-soled shoes, stands guard, witnesses a woman’s revenge, helps burn documents, and escapes with Holmes. He safeguards the black pearl of the Borgias in a safe and is entrusted with confidential state information in the second-stain matter. At Abbey Grange, he serves as Holmes’s informal jury and finds Captain Crocker not guilty. By the end, he remains Holmes’s observant companion, sharing responsibility, secrecy, travel, and the continuing work of investigation.
records.t: Dr. John Watson is a doctor, medical practitioner, narrator, chronicler, and investigator closely bound to Sherlock Holmes as his friend, former companion, assistant, and professional partner. He keeps notes on unusual cases, writes investigations as stories rather than scientific exercises, and records events with admiration for Holmes while sometimes offering his own theories, doubts, or practical aid. He carries a revolver and check book, smokes tobacco, has irregular meals, and had helped wean Holmes from drug addiction. After selling his Kensington practice, Watson returns to share the Baker Street rooms with Holmes. Their renewed work begins after Watson investigates Ronald Adair’s murder, learns that Holmes is alive, and helps trap Colonel Sebastian Moran. Across subsequent cases, Watson accompanies Holmes to Norwood, Norfolk, Farnham, Mackleton, Sussex, Cambridge, Abbey Grange, Westminster, and elsewhere. He reads reports and messages, observes interviews and physical clues, assists surveillance and arrests, follows suspects, and records Holmes’s explanations. Watson also repeatedly contributes through his medical knowledge: reviving Thorneycroft Huxtable, examining injured people, reporting on Jack Woodley’s condition, and checking whether Violet Smith has recovered. His investigative efforts are not always praised—Holmes finds his position and methods in the cyclist inquiry inadequate—but Watson remains dependable in danger, helping stop a runaway dog-cart, restraining Patrick Cairns, holding Williamson at gunpoint, and assisting with the capture of Beppo. His loyalty sometimes leads him beyond ordinary legality. Though he disapproves of the planned burglary of Charles Augustus Milverton’s house, he prepares masks and rubber-soled shoes, stands guard, witnesses a woman’s revenge, helps burn documents, and escapes with Holmes. He safeguards the black pearl of the Borgias in a safe and is entrusted with confidential state information in the second-stain matter. At Abbey Grange, he serves as Holmes’s informal jury and finds Captain Crocker not guilty. By the end, he remains Holmes’s observant companion, sharing responsibility, secrecy, travel, and the continuing work of investigation.

records.l: the murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: In 1894 London, Ronald Adair was found shot dead in a locked room at 427 Park Lane; the unexplained crime led to a willful-murder verdict against unknown persons.

records.l: the Honourable Ronald Adair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Honourable Ronald Adair was a young aristocrat, the Earl of Maynooth’s second son, living with his mother and sister Hilda at 427 Park Lane. Formerly engaged to Miss Edith Woodley, he regularly and cautiously played card games at the Baldwin, Cavendish, and Bagatelle Clubs and was usually a winner. He played with Colonel Sebastian Moran and won considerable money; Holmes believed Adair discovered Moran cheating and threatened exposure. On March 30, 1894, Adair returned home at ten and was found fatally shot before 11:20 in his locked second-floor sitting-room. Moran killed him by firing an expanding bullet from an air-gun through the open front window.

records.l: No. 427, Park Lane, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: No. 427, Park Lane is a residence on Park Lane with the Honourable Ronald Adair’s second-floor front sitting-room. Adair was found dead there after being shot through its open window; the locked door and lack of visible entry or escape traces made the case remarkable. Holmes attributes the shooting to Colonel Sebastian Moran.

records.l: the Park Lane Mystery, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Park Lane Mystery is the unexplained shooting and death of the Honourable Ronald Adair, investigated after Sherlock Holmes returns to London; an inquest finds willful murder by unknown person or persons, with no known motive.

records.l: Park Lane, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Park Lane is a frequented thoroughfare in London with a nearby cab stand. It is associated with the shooting and murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair, who was shot from the open window of No. 427; no shot was heard and no ground disturbance was found.

records.l: the old book collector, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: An elderly, deformed book collector with a Church Street bookshop carries valuable books, then is revealed as Sherlock Holmes in disguise while hunted.

records.l: Kensington, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Kensington is where Harding Brothers operated and where Horace Harker’s bust was destroyed. Holmes and Dr. Watson return there to question Harding Brothers about the busts.

records.l: Professor James Moriarty, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor James Moriarty, a deceased criminal mastermind and leader of the Moriarty gang, was described as one of the great brains of the century and employed Colonel Sebastian Moran as chief of staff. Pursuing Sherlock Holmes in Switzerland, Moriarty confronted him at the Reichenbach Fall, tried to drag him over the brink, and fell to his death after Holmes escaped.

records.l: the Moriarty gang, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Moriarty gang, led by Professor Moriarty and including Colonel Sebastian Moran, was investigated after Moriarty's death; dangerous members remained free, forcing Sherlock Holmes to conceal his survival until only one enemy remained in London.

records.l: the Reichenbach Fall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Reichenbach Fall was the site where Professor Moriarty fell to his death and Sherlock Holmes appeared to die. Holmes secretly climbed to a ledge, evaded an accomplice who tried to kill him with rocks, and escaped over the mountains. The Reichenbach Fall is where Colonel Sebastian Moran previously attacked Holmes by dropping rocks over the cliff. Holmes refers to Moran’s attentions there when confronting him.

records.l: Baker Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Baker Street contains Sherlock Holmes’s rooms. After Holmes returns to London, Moran’s people watch the old rooms while Holmes uses a wax bust there as bait from Camden House. There Holmes and Dr. John Watson receive Stanley Hopkins, examine evidence, and prepare for Yoxley Old Place; later they discuss a missing letter with Lord Bellinger and Trelawney Hope.

records.l: Colonel Sebastian Moran, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Colonel Sebastian Moran, born in London in 1840, is the son of Sir Augustus Moran, educated at Eton and Oxford, and formerly served as a colonel in Her Majesty’s Indian Army and the 1st Bangalore Pioneers. A celebrated heavy-game shot, he served in several Indian campaigns, wrote two hunting books, and took part in a man-eating tiger hunt. After retiring, he developed a criminal career, became Professor James Moriarty’s chief of staff and bosom friend, and followed Moriarty in Switzerland. Holmes considers him London’s second most dangerous man. Moran is suspected, though never proved, to have caused Mrs. Stewart’s death; he shoots Ronald Adair after card cheating. At the Reichenbach Fall he attacks Holmes, then later fires an air-gun at Holmes’s apparent figure, is overpowered, and arrested.

records.l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Inspector Lestrade is an experienced plain-clothes detective, police inspector, and police official who works for Scotland Yard. He conducts official investigations, makes arrests, writes reports, and often works alongside Sherlock Holmes while retaining responsibility for police action. He arrives with officers when Holmes summons him and takes charge of Colonel Sebastian Moran’s arrest for the shooting of Ronald Adair; Holmes publicly credits Lestrade with the arrest, enhancing Lestrade’s reputation.
