records.s: The Trelawney Hope residence is where Holmes confronts Lady Hilda, obtains the political document, and replaces it in the despatch-box. Trelawney Hope and the Prime Minister later examine the box there and discover that the document has been restored.

records.l: Lady Hilda's indiscreet letter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope wrote the letter before her marriage about an impulsive, loving act; Eduardo Lucas obtained it and used it to force her to steal a political document, threatening Trelawney Hope’s trust.

records.l: letter's recovery, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_achieved_by Sherlock Holmes [without exposing Lady Hilda] Holmes secures the recovery of the political document by persuading Lady Hilda to hand it over and then placing it back in Trelawney Hope’s despatch-box. Trelawney Hope and the Prime Minister verify that it has been recovered and is intact.

records.t: His Last Bow has author Arthur Conan Doyle, 1908-04-17, His Last Bow

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: The preface to His Last Bow states that Sherlock Holmes is alive and well but occasionally suffers from rheumatism. He has retired to a small farm on the Downs near Eastbourne, where he divides his time between philosophy and agriculture. The approach of the German war leads him to offer his intellectual and practical abilities to the Government, producing historical results recounted in His Last Bow. John H. Watson explains that several earlier experiences from his portfolio have also been included in the volume.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: His Last Bow recounts the historical results of Sherlock Holmes's service to the Government during the German war. The volume also includes several previous experiences that John H. Watson had kept in his portfolio.

records.l: Arthur Conan Doyle, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: Arthur Conan Doyle is identified as the author of His Last Bow.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is described as alive and well, though occasionally crippled by attacks of rheumatism. He has lived for many years on a small farm on the Downs near Eastbourne, dividing his time between philosophy and agriculture, and had intended his retirement to be permanent until the German war led him to serve the Government.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: John H. Watson, M.D., writes the preface. He states that several previous experiences from his portfolio have been added to His Last Bow to complete the volume.

records.l: the German war, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: The approach of the German war causes Sherlock Holmes to end his permanent retirement and place his intellectual and practical abilities at the disposal of the Government.

records.l: the Government, His Last Bow, opening
records.s: The Government receives Sherlock Holmes's intellectual and practical service in response to the approach of the German war.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson hear John Scott Eccles describe his bizarre overnight stay at Wisteria Lodge, where Aloysius Garcia and his foreign household disappeared before morning. Inspectors Gregson and Baynes reveal that Garcia was murdered on Oxshott Common and that Eccles is connected to the case by a letter found in Garcia's pocket. Inspector Baynes produces a note addressed to Garcia containing coded instructions, while Holmes begins to examine the circumstances of the murder, the disappearance, and Eccles's claim that Garcia spoke to him during the night.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives and replies to the telegram from John Scott Eccles, then questions Eccles about his experience. He examines the note found by Inspector Baynes, adds observations about its seal and scissors, and agrees to collaborate with the investigation.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Dr. John Watson is present with Sherlock Holmes when the telegram arrives and records the events. Holmes refers to him as a man of letters and criticizes his habit of telling stories in the wrong order.

records.l: Scott Eccles, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: John Scott Eccles tells Sherlock Holmes and the inspectors that he stayed overnight at Wisteria Lodge with Aloysius Garcia, but awoke to find Garcia and the entire household gone. He denies knowing anything about Garcia's fate and asks Holmes to investigate, while agreeing to give the police a formal statement.

records.l: Garcia, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Aloysius Garcia is described by John Scott Eccles as a young, good-looking man of Spanish descent who was connected in some way with the embassy. He is found dead on Oxshott Common after being beaten to death, apparently without being robbed.

records.l: Inspector Gregson, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Inspector Gregson comes to Sherlock Holmes's rooms with Inspector Baynes while following John Scott Eccles. He informs Eccles that Aloysius Garcia was murdered and requests a formal statement, warning that it may be used against him.

records.l: Inspector Baynes, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Inspector Baynes traces John Scott Eccles from the telegram and examines Wisteria Lodge. He finds the partly burned note addressed to Aloysius Garcia, reports that Garcia had been dead before the rain, and invites Sherlock Holmes to inspect other remarkable findings at the house.

records.l: Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Wisteria Lodge is a run-down house between Esher and Oxshott where Aloysius Garcia lives with his foreign servant and cook. John Scott Eccles stays there overnight, but finds it deserted in the morning; the police later examine the house and discover the partly burned note.

records.l: Esher, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: John Scott Eccles travels to Esher to visit Wisteria Lodge. After finding the house deserted, he goes to Allan Brothers', the local house agents, who confirm that the rent for the property has been paid in advance.

records.l: Oxshott Common, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Oxshott Common is the lonely place, nearly a mile from Wisteria Lodge, where Aloysius Garcia's body is found. Garcia had been struck from behind and repeatedly beaten with a heavy instrument before the rain began.

records.l: the telegram (Eccles's telegram to Holmes), His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The telegram from John Scott Eccles tells Sherlock Holmes that Eccles has had an incredible and grotesque experience and asks whether he may consult him. Inspectors Gregson and Baynes use the telegram to trace Eccles from Charing Cross Post Office.

records.l: the note sent to Garcia, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The note addressed to Aloysius Garcia is written on quarter-sheet cream-laid paper, folded and sealed with purple wax. Inspector Baynes recovers it unburned from the back of the dog-grate after Garcia apparently threw it into the fire.

records.l: the mysterious message, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The note's message reads: "Our own colours, green and white. Green open, white shut. Main stair, first corridor, seventh right, green baize. Godspeed. D." It appears to contain coded instructions, and the note is identified as being in a woman's writing.

records.l: the letter (Eccles's letter found on Garcia), His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The letter from John Scott Eccles, found in Aloysius Garcia's pocket, said that Eccles would be with Garcia on the night of Garcia's death. Its envelope provides Garcia's name and address and causes the police to seek Eccles.

records.l: Garcia's household, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Garcia's household consists of a faithful foreign manservant who handles his needs and a skilled half-breed cook. Both disappear from Wisteria Lodge during the night along with Garcia.

records.l: the disappearance of Garcia's household, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: By morning, John Scott Eccles finds that Garcia, the foreign manservant, and the foreign cook have all vanished from Wisteria Lodge. The rooms are deserted, and Garcia's bed has not been slept in.

records.l: Garcia's death, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Garcia's murder occurs before the rain that began at about one o'clock. He is attacked from behind on Oxshott Common and beaten long after he is dead, with no apparent attempt at robbery and no clear clue to the criminals.

records.l: Garcia's body, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: Garcia's body is found on Oxshott Common with his head crushed by heavy blows from a sandbag or similar instrument. It is discovered after nine in the morning by the police.

records.l: the investigation, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The investigation begins after the police find Garcia dead and discover Eccles's letter in his pocket. Sherlock Holmes agrees to collaborate with Inspector Baynes and seeks further facts about the note, the house, the disappearance, and the timing of Garcia's death.

records.l: the police, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: The police trace John Scott Eccles through his telegram, examine Wisteria Lodge, and investigate Garcia's death. They find the note, identify Eccles through the letter in Garcia's pocket, and request Eccles's written statement.

records.l: Eccles's overnight stay at Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: John Scott Eccles arrives at Wisteria Lodge for an invited stay with Aloysius Garcia. The evening is tense and strange, and when Eccles wakes after sleeping through the night, Garcia and the household have disappeared.

records.l: the midnight encounter, His Last Bow, The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles
records.s: During the night, at nearly one o'clock, Garcia comes to John Scott Eccles's dark bedroom and asks whether Eccles rang for him. Eccles says that he did not, and Garcia apologizes for disturbing him before Eccles returns to sleep.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson analyze Scott Eccles's strange experience, the murder, the disappearance of Garcia's companions, and the mysterious message connected with Wisteria Lodge. Holmes hypothesizes that Garcia recruited Eccles as a respectable witness who could provide an alibi, while the message may have been an assignation at a large nearby house. A telegram supplies a list of possible houses and their occupants, narrowing the investigation to the area near Oxshott. Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Baynes travel to Esher and then set out for Wisteria Lodge.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the events surrounding Garcia, Scott Eccles, and Wisteria Lodge. He theorizes that Eccles was selected as a respectable witness who could establish an alibi for Garcia, interprets the mysterious message as a signal and assignation, and uses a list of nearby large houses to narrow the investigation.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Dr. Watson discusses the case with Sherlock Holmes and initially suggests that Garcia's missing servants were involved in the murder and fled from justice. He proposes that the message's initial 'D' might stand for Dolores, but Holmes rejects this because the writer was apparently English.

records.l: Scott Eccles, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Scott Eccles is described as a conventionally respectable Englishman whom Garcia quickly befriended and brought to Wisteria Lodge. Holmes believes Garcia intended Eccles to serve as an impressive witness and possible alibi.

records.l: Garcia, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Garcia is identified as the young Spaniard who cultivated Scott Eccles's friendship and brought him to Wisteria Lodge. Holmes suspects Garcia planned an action before one o'clock and relied on Eccles's testimony to show that he had remained at home.

records.l: Inspector Baynes, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Inspector Baynes is expected to return with further information and is later identified as Holmes and Watson's companion. He travels with them to Esher and joins their visit to Wisteria Lodge.

records.l: Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Wisteria Lodge is the house where Garcia's household, Scott Eccles, and the strange events were centered. Holmes infers that it lies within a mile or two of Oxshott and later travels there with Watson and Inspector Baynes.

records.l: Esher, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Esher is the Surrey village where Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Baynes arrive nearly at six o'clock. Holmes and Watson take rooms at the Bull before setting out for Wisteria Lodge.

records.l: Oxshott, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Oxshott is used as the geographical reference point for narrowing the search. Holmes reasons that the house named in the message must be a large house close to Oxshott.

records.l: the Oxshott murder, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The murder is treated as one of the grave events connected with Garcia and Wisteria Lodge. Holmes and Watson consider whether Garcia's companions were involved, but this unit does not establish who committed it.

records.l: the disappearance of Garcia's household, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The disappearance of Garcia's companions is one of the two major facts Holmes seeks to explain. He considers whether their flight resulted from their involvement in a conspiracy, while acknowledging that he does not yet have all the facts.

records.l: Eccles's overnight stay at Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Scott Eccles's experience at Wisteria Lodge is described as remarkable and mysterious. Holmes treats it as a major fact that must be explained together with the disappearance of Garcia's companions.

records.l: the hypothesis, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The hypothesis is that the household at Wisteria Lodge were confederates in a plan and recruited Scott Eccles to provide an apparently reliable alibi for Garcia. Holmes regards it as provisional and says it may become a solution if later facts fit it.

records.l: Garcia's alibi, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The alibi would have been supplied by Scott Eccles, who could testify that Garcia was at Wisteria Lodge during the relevant period. Holmes believes the plan may have depended on manipulating the clocks and having Garcia return by the stated hour.

records.l: the mysterious message, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The mysterious message contains the phrases 'Our own colours, green and white,' 'Green open, white shut,' and 'Main stair, first corridor, seventh right, green baize,' followed by 'Godspeed' and 'D.' Holmes interprets it as a signal and dangerous assignation written by an English person.

records.l: the appointment or assignation, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The appointment or assignation is inferred from the message's directions to use a main stair and find the seventh door in a corridor. Holmes concludes that it must have been at a large house near Oxshott.

records.l: the telegram, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The telegram received in response to Holmes's inquiry provides information used to narrow the investigation. Holmes reads it and passes it to Watson, explaining that it identifies possible large houses near Oxshott.

records.l: the list of names and addresses, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: The list of names and addresses includes Lord Harringby at The Dingle, Sir George Ffolliott at Oxshott Towers, Mr. Hynes Hynes at Purdley Place, Mr. James Baker Williams at Forton Old Hall, Mr. Henderson at High Gable, and Rev. Joshua Stone at Nether Walsling. Holmes regards it as a way of limiting the field of operations.

records.l: the journey to Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Baynes travel to Esher, take accommodation at the Bull, and then proceed toward Wisteria Lodge. Their journey takes place on a cold, dark March evening through rain and over a wild common.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson visit Wisteria Lodge with Inspector Baynes after Mr. Garcia is found dead and his servants flee. Constable Walters reports seeing a giant, terrifying face at the window, while the kitchen contains a strange mummified figure, a dismembered white cock, blood, and burned lamb or kid bones. Holmes and Baynes pursue separate theories, and Baynes later arrests a huge, savage man believed to be Garcia's cook. Holmes warns Baynes that he may be pursuing the wrong suspect, but Baynes insists on following his own methods.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the grounds and the kitchen at Wisteria Lodge, identifying a number twelve shoe print and judging the burned bones to be those of a lamb or kid. He becomes interested in the case but follows his own investigation while Inspector Baynes follows another line. After reading of the arrest of Garcia's alleged cook, Holmes warns Baynes that he may be on the wrong track.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Wisteria Lodge and observes the evidence and the developing investigation. He waits for Holmes to act and later reads the newspaper report announcing the arrest of a suspected assassin.

records.l: Inspector Baynes, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Inspector Baynes shows Holmes and Dr. Watson around Wisteria Lodge and points out the strange kitchen evidence. He insists on pursuing the case independently and later arranges an ambush that results in the arrest of a huge, savage man believed to be Garcia's cook. Baynes rejects Holmes's warning that he may be following the wrong line.

records.l: Constable Walters, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Constable Walters guards Wisteria Lodge and reports seeing a huge, unnatural-looking face at the window shortly before Holmes's arrival. He says the figure had enormous goggle eyes and large white teeth, and that it disappeared through the shrubbery. The newspaper later identifies him as the constable who pursued the suspected cook when the man revisited the lodge.

records.l: Garcia, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Mr. Garcia is identified as the deceased man connected with Wisteria Lodge. He was found dead on Oxshott Common, and the newspaper states that his body showed signs of extreme violence.

records.l: Garcia's cook, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Garcia's cook fled Wisteria Lodge after Mr. Garcia's death and was described by witnesses as a huge and hideous mulatto with yellowish, strongly negroid features. Inspector Baynes's ambush led to the capture of a man believed to be the cook; the prisoner was described as extremely strong, savage, nearly unintelligible in English, and capable of badly biting Constable Downing.

records.l: Wisteria Lodge, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Wisteria Lodge is a gloomy, largely furnished house where Mr. Garcia was killed and where his servants fled. Police find a strange mummified figure, the remains of a white cock, blood, and charred animal bones in its kitchen, while a giant visitor is reported at one of its windows.

records.l: Oxshott Common, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Oxshott Common is where Mr. Garcia's body was found after he was killed.

records.l: Oxshott, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: Oxshott is the district associated with Mr. Garcia's death and the investigation reported in the newspapers as the Oxshott Mystery.

records.l: the Oxshott murder, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The Oxshott murder concerns the violent death of Mr. Garcia, whose servant and cook fled from Wisteria Lodge on the same night. The police initially considered robbery as a possible motive and later arrested a man believed to be Garcia's cook.

records.l: the arrest of the suspected assassin, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The arrest of the suspected assassin is reported in the newspaper as a supposed solution to the Oxshott murder. Inspector Baynes's men capture a huge, savage man after an ambush near Wisteria Lodge, although Holmes doubts that the arrest identifies the true culprit.

records.l: the investigation, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The investigation involves the death of Mr. Garcia, the flight of his servant and cook, the unusual evidence in Wisteria Lodge, and the search for the giant visitor. Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Baynes work independently, with Baynes arresting a suspected cook while Holmes remains unconvinced by that theory.

records.l: the giant visitor, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The giant visitor appears at a window of Wisteria Lodge as a face with a strange clay-and-milk colouring, huge staring eyes, and large white teeth. A number twelve shoe print shows that the visitor had an exceptionally large foot, and the figure escaped through the shrubbery toward the road.

records.l: the mummified figure, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The mummified figure is a black, leathery, greatly shrunken object found on the kitchen dresser at Wisteria Lodge. It resembles either a dwarfish human figure or a twisted ancient monkey, and a double band of white shells is strung around its centre.

records.l: the white cock, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The white cock is found in the kitchen sink at Wisteria Lodge, torn savagely to pieces with its feathers still on. Sherlock Holmes identifies it from the wattles on its severed head and calls it a particularly curious and possibly unique feature of the case.

records.l: the lamb or kid bones, His Last Bow, 2. The Tiger of San Pedro
records.s: The lamb or kid bones are small pieces of charred bone found on a platter in the kitchen at Wisteria Lodge. They were raked from the fire, and a doctor determined that they were not human; Sherlock Holmes judges them to be from a lamb or a kid.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. Watson that Garcia was involved in a criminal enterprise and arranged Scott Eccles's presence to establish an alibi before Garcia's death. Holmes believes Garcia's household were confederates who fled after the failed attempt, while one servant returned for something valuable left behind. He identifies High Gable and its secretive occupants, especially Mr. Henderson, Mr. Lucas, and Miss Burnet, as the likely source of the note sent to Garcia. Since Miss Burnet has vanished, Sherlock Holmes and Watson decide to enter High Gable at night to investigate whether she is alive, imprisoned, or dead.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains his deductions about Garcia's criminal enterprise, Garcia's household, High Gable, and Miss Burnet's disappearance to Dr. Watson. He plans to enter High Gable at night through the roof of an outhouse with Watson to investigate the mystery.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Dr. Watson listens as Sherlock Holmes reconstructs the case and accepts Holmes's proposal to enter High Gable at night. He recognizes the danger but agrees that this may be the only way to find a solution.

records.l: Garcia, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Garcia arranged for Scott Eccles to be present in order to establish an alibi, indicating that he had a criminal enterprise planned for the night of his death. Holmes believes Garcia received a note from a confederate at High Gable and was killed by the person against whom his enterprise was directed.

records.l: Mr. Henderson, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Mr. Henderson is the wealthy, fierce, and secretive master of High Gable. He travels frequently, is accompanied by Mr. Lucas, is said to be afraid of something, and has violently threatened people with a dog-whip.

records.l: Mr. Lucas, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Mr. Lucas is Mr. Henderson's foreign friend and secretary. He is described as chocolate brown, wily, suave, catlike, and constantly with Henderson as his shadow.

records.l: Miss Burnet, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Miss Burnet is an English governess of about forty who looks after Mr. Henderson's two daughters. Holmes believes she wrote the note sent to Garcia and was his confederate, but she has not been seen since the night of the murder and may be dead, imprisoned, or otherwise in danger.

records.l: High Gable, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: High Gable is a large Jacobean grange less than half a mile from the scene of the tragedy. It is the home of Mr. Henderson and his unusual household, and Sherlock Holmes suspects that the note sent to Garcia originated there.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes and Watson, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Watson decide to enter High Gable at night through access from the top of an outhouse. They undertake this risk because the law provides no sufficient basis for a warrant and Miss Burnet may be in danger.

records.l: Garcia's household, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Garcia's household disappeared after Garcia failed to return from his planned enterprise. Holmes believes the servants were confederates who had arranged to flee to a prearranged place if Garcia's life was sacrificed, although one servant later returned for something precious left behind.

records.l: the High Gable household, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: The High Gable household centers on Mr. Henderson, Mr. Lucas, the two children, Miss Burnet, and a confidential manservant, with a larger staff of ordinary domestic servants. The family and servants occupy separate wings connected only by a door, and the household is secretive, violent, and difficult for outsiders to understand.

records.l: Garcia's criminal enterprise, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Garcia's criminal enterprise was planned for the night of his death, and his arrangement for Scott Eccles's presence appears to have been intended to provide an alibi. Holmes believes the enterprise was directed against someone at High Gable.

records.l: Garcia's death, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Garcia's death occurred during or after the criminal enterprise for which he had arranged an alibi. Holmes believes the person targeted by the enterprise was the most likely person to have caused his death.

records.l: the Oxshott murder, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: The murder refers to the killing of Garcia, after which Miss Burnet was never seen again. Holmes considers whether she met the same fate, was imprisoned, or remains alive and endangered.

records.l: the disappearance of Garcia's household, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Holmes explains the disappearance of Garcia's household as a planned escape by confederates after Garcia failed to return. Their flight was intended to avoid investigation and leave them able to renew the criminal attempt later.

records.l: the investigation, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: Holmes says the case is simple in its leading features but has serious difficulties, especially gaps preventing an arrest. He narrows the investigation to High Gable and plans a direct investigation because there is not enough evidence to obtain a warrant.

records.l: the note sent to Garcia, His Last Bow, “Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had
records.s: The note sent to Garcia at dinner indicates that he had a confederate at the other end. Holmes believes it came from the strange household at High Gable and was written by Miss Burnet as an invitation to carry out a previously planned attempt.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Baynes secure Miss Burnet, who escapes from the High Gable household after being drugged and taken toward a train. Miss Burnet reveals that Henderson is actually Don Murillo, the former dictator of San Pedro, and explains the revenge society's attempt to kill him, including Garcia's murder and her own imprisonment. Don Murillo and Lopez evade capture and later disappear from England, but they are reportedly murdered in Madrid six months later. Holmes concludes that the strange kitchen rituals belonged to the mulatto cook's voodoo practices and that the coded note concerned the planned attack on Murillo.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Sherlock Holmes arranges for the discharged gardener to watch the gate and recover Miss Burnet when she breaks away at the station. He learns from her statement that Henderson is Don Murillo and works with Inspector Baynes to connect the coded note, Garcia's murder, and the attempted murder of Miss Burnet. Later, he explains the mulatto cook's return and identifies the kitchen's sacrifices as voodoo ritual practices.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Dr. Watson witnesses Miss Burnet's drugged condition, listens to her account, and observes the discussion of the case's legal difficulties. He later asks Holmes about the mulatto cook's return and the strange objects in the kitchen, prompting Holmes's explanation of the voodoo rituals.

records.l: Inspector Baynes, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Inspector Baynes reveals that he had been investigating Henderson and deliberately arrested the wrong man to make Henderson believe that the police were no longer watching him. He confirms Henderson's identity as Don Murillo, explains that a plain-clothes officer had been tracking the High Gable household, and intends to prosecute its occupants when Miss Burnet gives evidence. He later recognizes the importance of the mulatto cook's return and leaves a trap that leads to the cook's capture.

records.l: Miss Burnet, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Miss Burnet escapes from Don Murillo's custody after being drugged and taken toward a train, with help from the discharged gardener. She identifies herself as Signora Victor Durando and explains that Murillo had her husband killed, after which she joined the revenge society and became governess in Murillo's household to monitor him. She describes Garcia's planned attack, her imprisonment and abuse, and the attempt to force her to reveal Garcia's address.

records.l: Signora Victor Durando, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Signora Victor Durando is Miss Burnet's real identity. She states that her husband, the San Pedro minister in London, was recalled and shot by Don Murillo, and that she entered Murillo's household as a governess to help the revenge society track him.

records.l: Mr. Henderson, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Don Murillo, who lived in England under the name Henderson, was formerly the tyrannical ruler of San Pedro known as the Tiger of San Pedro. He and Lopez discover Miss Burnet's betrayal, imprison and abuse her, and arrange for Garcia to be killed. Murillo escapes England with Lopez and is later believed to have been murdered with his secretary at the Hotel Escurial in Madrid.

records.l: Lopez, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Lopez, Don Murillo's secretary and former satellite, helps Murillo seize and imprison Miss Burnet. He addresses and sends the coded note that Miss Burnet wrote, remains to guard her while Garcia is killed, and later escapes England with Murillo.

records.l: Garcia, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Garcia is the son of a former highest dignitary in San Pedro and one of the revenge society's avengers. He waits near the High Gable house with two companions to attack Don Murillo, but Murillo's men discover the plan and Garcia is killed before the attempt can succeed.

records.l: the High Gable household, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: The High Gable household includes Don Murillo under the name Henderson, Lopez, the children, Miss Burnet as governess, and servants including the mulatto cook and José. Its members imprison and drug Miss Burnet, attempt to conceal Garcia's murder, and flee after the police investigation exposes their identities.

records.l: the revenge society, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: The revenge society is formed by people whose lives or families were ruined by Don Murillo. It is intended to remain active until Murillo is punished, and Miss Burnet serves it by joining his household and reporting his movements.

records.l: High Gable, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: The High Gable house is the English residence that Don Murillo took on his first arrival in England and later returned to. It contains the scene of Miss Burnet's confinement and the mysterious kitchen associated with the mulatto cook's ritual practices.

records.l: San Pedro, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: San Pedro was formerly ruled by Don Murillo, whose tyranny involved bloodshed, torture, executions, and the confiscation of property. Its green and white colors appear in the coded note, and its victims and their relatives organize the revenge society against Murillo.

records.l: the investigation, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: The investigation by Holmes and Inspector Baynes traces Henderson to Don Murillo, establishes Miss Burnet's connection to Garcia's death, and uncovers the attempted concealment of the crime. Although the police work advances, Holmes notes that legal difficulties remain because the evidence concerns a planned killing and the wider crimes occurred abroad.

records.l: the Oxshott murder, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Garcia is killed after Lopez and Don Murillo force Miss Burnet to disclose the address connected with the planned attack. Murillo is believed to have struck Garcia down among the gorse bushes, while Lopez remained behind to guard Miss Burnet.

records.l: the attempted murder of Miss Burnet, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Don Murillo and Lopez consider killing Miss Burnet after discovering her betrayal but decide that doing so would be too dangerous. Instead, they imprison, threaten, drug, and abuse her, and try to remove her from England before she can testify.

records.l: the escape of Don Murillo, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Don Murillo and Lopez evade their pursuers by entering a lodging-house in Edmonton Street and leaving through a back gate into Curzon Square. They are not seen again in England and are later believed to have been murdered in Madrid.

records.l: justice and vengeance, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: Miss Burnet maintains that the victims of Don Murillo must pursue vengeance because English law does not address the bloodshed and theft committed in San Pedro. Although Murillo initially escapes legal punishment, he and Lopez are later apparently murdered in Madrid, which the account presents as delayed justice.

records.l: the note sent to Garcia, His Last Bow, But it was not destined that our investigation should have so
records.s: The coded note contains Miss Burnet's final instructions to Garcia about the planned attack on Don Murillo. A green or white light in a window facing the drive was to signal whether it was safe to proceed, and the San Pedro colors were green and white. Lopez addresses and sends the note after forcing Miss Burnet to reveal the relevant address.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is asked by his brother Mycroft to investigate the death of Arthur Cadogan West, a Woolwich Arsenal clerk whose body was found beside the Underground at Aldgate Station. Seven of ten stolen Bruce-Partington plans were found in West’s possession, while three essential plans were missing. Mycroft explains the national and international importance of the Bruce-Partington submarine and urges Holmes to determine why West took the plans, how he died, and where the missing plans went. Holmes, accompanied by Dr. Watson and Lestrade, begins the investigation at Aldgate Station.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Sherlock Holmes learns from Mycroft that Arthur Cadogan West was found dead with seven of the ten stolen Bruce-Partington plans in his possession. He considers possible explanations for West’s actions and death, agrees to investigate the case, and sets out with Dr. Watson and Lestrade for Aldgate Station.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Dr. Watson reports the known facts about Arthur Cadogan West’s death and the evidence found on his body. He accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Lestrade to begin investigating the case at Aldgate Station.

records.l: Mycroft Holmes, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Mycroft Holmes, who serves as an indispensable information specialist under the British government, visits Sherlock Holmes with Lestrade because the theft of the Bruce-Partington plans has created a national crisis. He explains the importance of the submarine and asks Sherlock to recover the three missing plans and solve West’s death.

records.l: Cadogan West, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Arthur Cadogan West was a twenty-seven-year-old unmarried clerk at Woolwich Arsenal who had served for ten years and handled the Bruce-Partington plans in the course of his duties. He left Woolwich suddenly on Monday evening, disappeared from his fiancée in the fog, and was later found dead beside the Underground with seven stolen plans in his pocket.

records.l: Lestrade, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Lestrade accompanies Mycroft Holmes to Sherlock Holmes’s rooms and listens to the discussion of the case. He argues that West took the plans to sell them, was murdered by a foreign agent in a train, and had his body thrown onto the track.

records.l: London, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: London is covered by a dense yellow fog that obscures figures and buildings, making movement and crime difficult to observe. The city is where Arthur Cadogan West was last seen and where he was presumably carrying the stolen plans.

records.l: Woolwich Arsenal, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Woolwich Arsenal employed Arthur Cadogan West and housed the confidential office where the Bruce-Partington plans were secured. Ten plans were removed from the office, and seven were later found on West.

records.l: Aldgate Station, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Aldgate Station is near the place where Arthur Cadogan West’s body was found on the left side of the eastbound track. Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Lestrade plan to begin their investigation there.

records.l: the Underground railway, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The Underground carried the train from which Arthur Cadogan West apparently fell or was thrown. His body was discovered beside the track just outside Aldgate Station, and the absence of a ticket makes his journey difficult to trace.

records.l: the British government, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The British government employs Mycroft Holmes in a uniquely influential information-gathering role. It has also guarded the Bruce-Partington submarine’s technology as a major state secret.

records.l: the Bruce-Partington submarine, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The Bruce-Partington submarine is described as a revolutionary invention whose operation would make naval warfare impossible within its range. The British government spent a large sum to obtain a monopoly of the invention and has guarded it closely.

records.l: the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The Bruce-Partington plans consist of about thirty interdependent patents and were kept in a burglar-proof safe at a confidential Woolwich Arsenal office. Ten plans were stolen, seven were found in Arthur Cadogan West’s pocket, and the three most essential plans remain missing.

records.l: the fog, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: A dense yellow fog persists over London for several days, obscuring people and buildings. It may have helped conceal the movements surrounding Arthur Cadogan West’s disappearance and death.

records.l: Arthur Cadogan West's death, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: Arthur Cadogan West’s body was found at six on Tuesday morning beside the eastbound Underground track near Aldgate Station, with his head badly crushed. The circumstances suggest that he fell or was thrown from a train, but the exact cause of his death remains unresolved.

records.l: the theft of the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The theft occurred after the plans were confirmed to be in the Woolwich Arsenal office during working hours on Monday. Ten plans were taken, seven were recovered from Arthur Cadogan West, and three essential plans are still missing.

records.l: the secret of the Bruce-Partington submarine, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans
records.s: The secret of the Bruce-Partington submarine is treated as a vital international matter and one of the British government’s most closely guarded secrets. Mycroft Holmes fears that the missing plans may have been intended for sale to a foreign agent or may already have reached the Continent.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade investigate how Cadogan West's body came to rest near Aldgate Station and determine that it likely fell from the roof of a Metropolitan train at the railway points. Holmes and Watson visit Woolwich, where they learn of Sir James Walter's death, question Miss Violet Westbury and Mr. Sidney Johnson, and examine the government office from which the Bruce-Partington plans were stolen. Evidence suggests that Cadogan West may have pursued a foreign agent who took the original plans, but his actions and death remain unexplained. Holmes asks Mycroft Holmes for a list of foreign spies and international agents in England so that the investigation can pursue that possibility.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines the scene near Aldgate Station and infers that Cadogan West's body was probably carried on the roof of a train and fell off where the line curved over the points. He visits Woolwich, questions witnesses, inspects the government office, and develops the hypothesis that West may have pursued the thief of the Bruce-Partington plans. He asks Mycroft Holmes for a list of foreign spies and international agents in England.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Lestrade to Aldgate and then follows Holmes through the inquiries at Woolwich. He records Holmes's deductions about the body, the train, the stolen plans, and the possible involvement of a foreign agent.

records.l: Lestrade, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Inspector Lestrade accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson to the Underground scene and reports that a passenger heard a heavy thud near Aldgate at about 11:40 on Monday night. He says that the train carriages were carefully examined, though Holmes explains that he wanted to inspect the roof rather than the carriages.

records.l: Cadogan West, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Cadogan West is believed to have taken the 8:15 train from Woolwich to London Bridge, appearing nervous and excited. His fiancée says he had recently worried about official secrets and foreign spies, while Holmes considers that West may have followed a foreign agent who stole the plans before his own death.

records.l: Sir James Walter, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Sir James Walter, the dead scientist and senior official, dies on the morning Holmes and Watson visit his house. His brother says that the scandal concerning the stolen plans broke his heart, and Holmes wonders whether the death was natural or a suicide.

records.l: Miss Violet Westbury, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Miss Violet Westbury, Cadogan West's fiancée and the last person known to have seen him, says that he was patriotic, honest, and financially secure. She reports that he had become worried about official matters, mentioned the value of secrets to foreign spies, and suddenly left her in the fog near the office.

records.l: Mr. Sidney Johnson, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Mr. Sidney Johnson, the senior clerk, says that he closed the government office at five on Monday and placed the plans in the safe. He explains the office's key arrangements and confirms that the three missing drawings were considered the most important, while denying any involvement in the theft.

records.l: foreign spies and international agents, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Foreign spies and international agents are considered possible buyers or thieves of the Bruce-Partington plans. Sherlock Holmes asks Mycroft Holmes to provide a complete list of those known to be in England so he can investigate them.

records.l: the Underground railway, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The Underground railway is the setting where Cadogan West's body is found near the point at which the line emerges from the tunnel before Aldgate Station. The railway's curves and points lead Sherlock Holmes to conclude that the body may have fallen from a carriage roof.

records.l: Aldgate Station, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Aldgate Station is the location near which Cadogan West's body was discovered. A passenger reports hearing a heavy thud just before reaching the station, and the surrounding points and curve become central to Holmes's deduction.

records.l: Woolwich, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Woolwich is where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson investigate Sir James Walter's household, Cadogan West's fiancée, and the government office. They learn there that West took the 8:15 train to London and that the office had been entered or observed through a window.

records.l: the government office, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The government office is the place from which the Bruce-Partington plans were stolen. Holmes examines its safe, door, shutters, and a laurel bush outside the window, finding possible signs that someone approached or left through the window.

records.l: the body of Cadogan West, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The body of Cadogan West is found about three feet from the railway metals near Aldgate, with a crushed bone but little external bleeding. Holmes concludes that it may have fallen from the roof of a train after being carried there from another location.

records.l: the Metropolitan train, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The Metropolitan train is believed by Sherlock Holmes to have carried Cadogan West's body on its roof. The body may have fallen when the train pitched and swayed around the curve and points near Aldgate.

records.l: the railway points, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The railway points near Aldgate are significant because they create a place where an object on a train roof might be thrown or dislodged. Sherlock Holmes focuses on them as a possible explanation for where Cadogan West's body fell.

records.l: the Bruce-Partington submarine, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The Bruce-Partington submarine could not be constructed from the three missing drawings alone unless the foreigners independently solved the problem of the double valves with automatic self-adjusting slots. The returned drawings include that crucial feature.

records.l: the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The Bruce-Partington plans are government documents stolen from the office, with seven papers later found on Cadogan West and three still missing. The missing drawings are described as the most important, although the returned papers contain the design for the submarine's essential double valves.

records.l: Arthur Cadogan West's death, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Cadogan West's death remains unexplained after investigators find his body near Aldgate with the plans in his pocket. Holmes suspects that West died elsewhere and was placed on the roof of a train, possibly after confronting or pursuing the thief.

records.l: Sir James Walter's death, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: Sir James Walter's death occurs on the morning of Holmes and Watson's visit. His brother attributes it to the disgrace caused by the scandal, while Holmes considers whether it may have been suicide or a natural death.

records.l: the theft of the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The theft involves the removal of the original Bruce-Partington plans from a locked government office, with three vital drawings still missing. Holmes notes that taking originals was unnecessary for a clerk who could copy them, suggesting that an outsider may have been responsible.

records.l: the scandal, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The scandal concerns the stolen plans and the apparent implication of Cadogan West. It is said to have devastated Sir James Walter, who was proud of his department's efficiency and allegedly could not survive the disgrace.

records.l: the investigation, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The investigation follows the evidence from Aldgate to Woolwich and examines the train, the office, the witnesses, and the stolen plans. Each inquiry produces further contradictions, so Holmes plans to investigate foreign spies and international agents while continuing to reconstruct West's final movements.

records.l: the alleged treason of Cadogan West, His Last Bow, An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground
records.s: The alleged treason of Cadogan West is supported by the discovery of seven plans on his body and by his recent remarks about foreign spies and the value of secrets. His character, lack of financial need, sudden pursuit of someone in the fog, and the window evidence create serious objections to the accusation.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Sherlock Holmes traces the death of Cadogan West to Hugo Oberstein’s house in Caulfield Gardens, where a body could be placed on the roof of a stationary Underground train. Holmes, Dr. Watson, Mycroft Holmes, and Inspector Lestrade use advertisement-column messages to lure an apparent accomplice, but capture Colonel Valentine Walter instead. Walter confesses to stealing the Bruce-Partington plans and helping conceal Cadogan West’s death, while claiming that Hugo Oberstein delivered the fatal blow. Holmes then lures Oberstein to London, where he is arrested with the plans and imprisoned for fifteen years.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Sherlock Holmes deduces that Cadogan West’s body was placed on the roof of a train through a window overlooking the Underground railway at Caulfield Gardens. He burglarizes Hugo Oberstein’s house, discovers advertisement-column messages, and uses a false message to lure Oberstein. Holmes captures Colonel Valentine Walter, obtains his confession, and sends a letter designed to bring Oberstein to London, where he is arrested.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Oberstein’s house, carrying a jemmy, dark lantern, chisel, and revolver. He helps investigate the house and later joins Holmes, Mycroft Holmes, and Inspector Lestrade in waiting for the person responding to the advertisement.

records.l: Mycroft Holmes, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Mycroft Holmes informs Sherlock Holmes that the Cabinet awaits his report and that the force of the State is available to assist him. He later joins Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade at Oberstein’s house and urges Colonel Valentine Walter to make reparation by helping recover the plans.

records.l: Lestrade, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Inspector Lestrade joins the operation at Caulfield Gardens and waits with Holmes, Watson, and Mycroft for the person answering Pierrot’s message. He criticizes the confessed burglary as conduct that the police could not undertake, but recognizes that the advertisement may lead to the culprit.

records.l: Cadogan West, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Cadogan West followed Colonel Valentine Walter after suspecting him of taking the plans and confronted him and Hugo Oberstein at Oberstein’s house. Oberstein struck him with a life-preserver, causing his death, and his body was later placed on the roof of an Underground train.

records.l: Hugo Oberstein, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Hugo Oberstein lived at 13, Caulfield Gardens, whose back windows opened onto the Underground railway. He bought the stolen Bruce-Partington plans, helped conceal Cadogan West’s body, and fled to the Continent, but Holmes lured him back to London, where he was arrested and imprisoned for fifteen years.

records.l: Colonel Valentine Walter, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Colonel Valentine Walter, the younger brother of the late Sir James Walter, stole the Bruce-Partington plans because he needed money to pay a Stock Exchange debt. He confessed to helping Oberstein dispose of Cadogan West’s body while denying that he delivered the fatal blow. He was sentenced to prison and died there toward the end of his second year.

records.l: Pierrot, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Pierrot is the name used in the advertisement-column messages exchanged between Hugo Oberstein and the other party. Sherlock Holmes places a further message under this name to arrange a meeting and identify someone connected with the theft.

records.l: Caulfield Gardens, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Caulfield Gardens contained Hugo Oberstein’s house at number 13, whose back windows opened directly above the Underground railway. Holmes and his companions searched the house, found blood marks near the window, and waited there to intercept Oberstein’s correspondent.

records.l: London, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: London is the setting for the investigation, the theft of the plans, the concealment of Cadogan West’s body, and the attempt to recover the stolen material. Hugo Oberstein leaves London for the Continent but later returns to meet Holmes’s false correspondent.

records.l: the Cabinet, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The Cabinet awaits Sherlock Holmes’s final report with the utmost anxiety because of the national importance of the case. It is told that urgent representations have arrived from the highest quarter.

records.l: the Admiralty, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The Admiralty is among the institutions whose interests are endangered by the theft of the Bruce-Partington plans. Holmes invokes its importance when insisting that he and Watson must enter Oberstein’s house.

records.l: the British government, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The British state is presented as supporting Holmes’s investigation, with the whole force of the State said to be at his back if needed. The theft is treated as a matter of national security.

records.l: the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The Bruce-Partington plans are the naval documents stolen by Colonel Valentine Walter and sold to Hugo Oberstein. Oberstein takes three essential plans and later stores them in his trunk for auction in European naval centres; they are recovered when he is arrested.

records.l: the Underground railway, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The Underground railway passes beneath or beside the rear windows of Caulfield Gardens. Trains are sometimes held motionless there, allowing Cadogan West’s body to be lowered from the window onto a carriage roof.

records.l: the Metropolitan train, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The train carrying Cadogan West’s body stops beneath the window of Oberstein’s house after waiting for a suitable halt. Oberstein and Colonel Valentine Walter lower the body onto its roof so that it will appear that Cadogan West fell from the train.

records.l: the body of Cadogan West, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Cadogan West’s body is placed on the roof of an Underground train after he is killed inside Oberstein’s house. Holmes finds soot disturbed on the window-sill and blood marks on the window and stair, confirming how the body was handled.

records.l: the advertisement-column messages, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The advertisement-column messages in the Daily Telegraph record communications between Pierrot and an unnamed correspondent about terms, reports, payment, and a meeting at Oberstein’s house. Holmes arranges them in sequence and uses a new message to lure the correspondent back.

records.l: the theft of the Bruce-Partington plans, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The theft of the Bruce-Partington plans is committed by Colonel Valentine Walter, who takes an impression of his brother’s keys and removes the documents. He gives them to Hugo Oberstein in exchange for five thousand pounds, while Oberstein retains three essential plans.

records.l: the killing of Cadogan West, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The killing of Cadogan West occurs when he follows Colonel Valentine Walter and confronts him and Hugo Oberstein at Oberstein’s house. Oberstein strikes Cadogan West on the head with a short life-preserver, and the blow proves fatal.

records.l: the burglary of Oberstein’s house, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: The burglary of Oberstein’s house is carried out by Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson without a warrant because Holmes considers the national interests involved more important than legal formalities. They find evidence of the body’s placement and recover the advertisement-column messages.

records.l: Oberstein’s arrest and imprisonment, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Oberstein’s arrest and imprisonment follow Holmes’s false advertisement and letter, which persuade him to return to London for a payment. He is safely arrested and receives a fifteen-year British prison sentence, while the Bruce-Partington plans are found in his trunk.

records.l: treason, His Last Bow, Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government
records.s: Colonel Valentine Walter admits that he committed treason by stealing the Bruce-Partington plans for money. Sherlock Holmes tells him that he compounded treason with the more serious crime of murder, although Walter maintains that Oberstein caused Cadogan West’s death.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: In the spring of 1897, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson stay in a cottage near Poldhu Bay, Cornwall, while Holmes recovers from overwork. Mr. Roundhay and Mortimer Tregennis bring Holmes news of the Tredannick Wartha tragedy, in which Brenda Tregennis is found dead and Owen and George Tregennis are driven insane by apparent terror. Holmes visits Tredannick Wartha house, examines the sitting-room and surrounding garden, and finds no immediate explanation for the family’s mental affliction. The event becomes known as the Cornish Horror.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is ordered by Dr. Moore Agar to stop working and rest because his health is failing from constant hard work. He stays with Dr. John Watson in a cottage near Poldhu Bay, but investigates the Tredannick Wartha tragedy after Mr. Roundhay and Mortimer Tregennis appeal to him. He questions Mortimer, visits the house, examines the room and garden, and concludes that no new factor has yet appeared to explain the events.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Cornwall for Holmes’s rest and records the events. He observes the Tredannick Wartha tragedy, Holmes’s investigation, and the disturbing sight of Owen and George Tregennis being taken away.

records.l: The Cornish Horror, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The Cornish Horror is the name given to the events at Tredannick Wartha, where Brenda Tregennis dies and Owen and George Tregennis lose their senses while displaying extreme terror. The incident causes excitement throughout Cornwall and the west of England, though the London press receives only an imperfect account.

records.l: Mr. Roundhay, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Mr. Roundhay is the vicar of Tredannick Wollas and an amateur archaeologist acquainted with Sherlock Holmes. He brings Mortimer Tregennis to Holmes and describes the tragedy at Tredannick Wartha.

records.l: Mortimer Tregennis, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Mortimer Tregennis spends the evening with Owen, George, and Brenda at Tredannick Wartha and leaves them playing cards in good spirits shortly after ten o’clock. He discovers the family’s condition the next morning with Dr. Richards, reports the events to Sherlock Holmes, and recalls seeing or sensing something moving outside the sitting-room window.

records.l: Owen Tregennis, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Owen Tregennis is found seated at the table in Tredannick Wartha with George and Brenda after Mortimer leaves. He is alive but driven out of his senses, laughing, shouting, singing, and showing an expression of intense horror.

records.l: George Tregennis, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: George Tregennis plays cards with Owen, Brenda, and Mortimer at Tredannick Wartha. He is later found insane and displaying terror; during the evening he looks toward the closed window after apparently sharing Mortimer’s sense that something was moving outside.

records.l: Brenda Tregennis, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Brenda Tregennis plays cards with her brothers and Mortimer at Tredannick Wartha. She is found dead in her chair the next morning, with a horrifying expression still on her face and no sign of violence.

records.l: Mrs. Porter, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Mrs. Porter is the elderly cook and housekeeper at Tredannick Wartha. She says that she slept deeply and heard nothing during the night, discovers the family in the sitting-room in the morning, opens the window, sends for Dr. Richards, and decides to leave the house.

records.l: the Tregennis family, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The Tregennis family formerly worked as tin-miners at Redruth and later sold their venture to a company. Mortimer says that disagreements over the division of the money once caused tension, but that the family had become friendly again.

records.l: Tregennis siblings, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The Tregennis siblings at Tredannick Wartha are Brenda, Owen, and George. After Mortimer leaves them playing cards, Brenda dies and Owen and George become mentally deranged, all three retaining expressions of extreme horror.

records.l: Poldhu Bay, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Poldhu Bay is near the small cottage where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson stay. It lies at the further extremity of the Cornish peninsula and overlooks Mounts Bay.

records.l: Cornwall, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Cornwall is the setting for Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson’s stay and for the events called the Cornish Horror. Its landscape includes lonely moors, ancient monuments, coastal cliffs, and villages such as Tredannick Wollas.

records.l: Tredannick Wollas, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Tredannick Wollas is a hamlet of about two hundred inhabitants clustered around an ancient, moss-grown church. It is the parish of Mr. Roundhay and the nearest village to the cottage near Poldhu Bay.

records.l: Tredannick Wartha, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: Tredannick Wartha is the home of Owen, George, and Brenda Tregennis and the location of the tragedy. Mortimer visits it after leaving the siblings the previous night and finds Brenda dead and Owen and George mentally deranged.

records.l: Poldhu Cottage, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The cottage near Poldhu Bay is where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson stay while Holmes is ordered to rest. Mr. Roundhay and Mortimer Tregennis come there to ask Holmes to investigate the Tredannick Wartha tragedy.

records.l: the first Tregennis tragedy, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The Tredannick Wartha tragedy occurs after Mortimer Tregennis leaves his siblings playing cards in good spirits. Brenda Tregennis is found dead, while Owen and George are found alive but insane and terrified, with no apparent intruder or sign of violence.

records.l: the family’s mental affliction, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The family’s mental affliction affects Owen and George, who are driven out of their senses while retaining expressions of terror. Mortimer believes that something entered the room and destroyed their reason, but Sherlock Holmes finds no immediate natural explanation.

records.l: Tredannick Wartha house, His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The Tredannick Wartha house is a large, bright dwelling with a considerable garden. Mrs. Porter maintains that no one entered during the night, and Sherlock Holmes examines the house while investigating the tragedy.

records.l: the sitting-room (Tredannick Wartha house), His Last Bow, The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot
records.s: The sitting-room contains the table where the Tregennis siblings play cards, four burned-out candles, and the remains of a fire. Sherlock Holmes studies the chairs, window, garden view, floor, ceiling, and fireplace, but does not identify the cause of the tragedy.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: At Poldhu Cottage, Sherlock Holmes breaks his silence and walks with Dr. John Watson to reason through the unexplained case. Holmes concludes that three persons were grievously stricken by some conscious or unconscious human agency immediately after Mortimer Tregennis left the room. He examines Tregennis's movements, finding that footprints indicate he walked swiftly toward the vicarage. Holmes finds no convincing evidence or motive for an alleged outsider's frightening manifestation and sets the case aside until more facts become available.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Sherlock Holmes stops brooding at Poldhu Cottage and walks along the cliffs with Dr. John Watson while defining what is known about the case. He rules out diabolical intrusions, concludes that human agency was involved, examines Mortimer Tregennis's movements through his footprints, and postpones the case until more evidence appears.

records.l: Dr. Watson, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes on a walk along the cliffs and listens as Holmes analyzes the case. He agrees that the difficulties are clear and is reminded that his archives may contain similarly obscure cases.

records.l: Poldhu Cottage, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Poldhu Cottage is where Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson return before Holmes breaks his silence. Holmes later leaves it with Watson to walk along the cliffs.

records.l: Mortimer Tregennis, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Mortimer Tregennis left the room shortly before the card-players were stricken. His footprints were traced through the wet, sandy path and indicated that he walked swiftly toward the vicarage.

records.l: the card-players, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The card-players were grievously stricken immediately after Mortimer Tregennis left the room. Their cards and chairs had not changed position, although it was already past their usual hour for bed.

records.l: the three stricken persons, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The three stricken persons were affected by some conscious or unconscious human agency. The occurrence is placed immediately after Mortimer Tregennis's departure and no later than eleven o'clock.

records.l: Tredannick Wartha house, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The room contained the card-players, whose cards remained on the table and whose chairs had not been pushed back after the incident. Mortimer Tregennis had left this room shortly before the three persons were stricken.

records.l: the card-playing incident, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The card-playing incident involved three persons being grievously stricken immediately after Mortimer Tregennis left. Sherlock Holmes finds no sufficient explanation for how the effect was produced.

records.l: Mortimer Tregennis's departure, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Mortimer Tregennis's departure is treated as the key time marker for the incident. Sherlock Holmes estimates that the card-players were affected within a few minutes afterward, before eleven o'clock.

records.l: the unexplained case, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The unexplained case concerns the three stricken persons and the circumstances following Mortimer Tregennis's departure. Sherlock Holmes puts it aside until more accurate data are available.

records.l: human agency, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: Human agency is identified as the likely cause of the three persons being grievously stricken. Sherlock Holmes allows that the agency may have been conscious or unconscious.

records.l: the alleged outsider, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The alleged outsider is considered as a possible person who might have approached the garden window and affected the card-players. Sherlock Holmes finds no footmark in the flower-border, no convincing way for the outsider to produce such an effect, and no apparent motive.

records.l: the outsider's frightening manifestation, His Last Bow, It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes
records.s: The outsider's frightening manifestation is a proposed appearance at the garden window intended to alarm the card-players. The only related evidence is Mortimer Tregennis's statement that his brother noticed movement in the garden, but the dark, rainy conditions and lack of a footmark make the proposal difficult to accept.

records.l: His Last Bow, His Last Bow, I may have commented upon my friend’s power of mental detachment, but
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigate the death of Mortimer Tregennis, whose symptoms match those of the earlier tragedy involving the Tregennis family. Holmes discovers that a substance burned in a room can create a poisonous atmosphere producing terror, madness, or death, and he confirms this through a dangerous lamp experiment with Watson. Holmes concludes that Mortimer Tregennis probably caused the first tragedy, though the cause of his own death remains uncertain. Dr. Leon Sterndale returns from Plymouth after hearing of the family’s fate and arouses Holmes’s suspicion through his intense interest in the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, His Last Bow, I may have commented upon my friend’s power of mental detachment, but
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Leon Sterndale about his return from Plymouth and investigates Mortimer Tregennis’s death.
