Cecil James Barker discovers that Douglas has been murdered in the Manor House by a close-range blast from a sawed-off shotgun, while the raised drawbridge appears to make escape impossible. Sergeant Wilson, Dr. Wood, and Ames examine the scene and find evidence that someone hid in the room, escaped through the open window across the moat, left a card marked “V.V. 341,” and removed Douglas’s wedding ring. The unexplained brand on Douglas’s forearm and the other unusual evidence deepen the mystery.

records.l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The tragedy concerns the murder of John Douglas at the Manor House in Birlstone and the puzzling evidence surrounding the crime. The events bring Cecil James Barker, Sergeant Wilson, Dr. Wood, Ames, and the household servants into the investigation.

records.l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Birlstone is a small, ancient village on the northern border of Sussex, about ten or twelve miles west of Tunbridge Wells. Its picturesque setting and growing population have attracted well-to-do residents and led to the development of shops.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Birlstone Manor House is an ancient, many-gabled building surrounded by an inner moat and approached only by a drawbridge. John Douglas and Mrs. Douglas took possession of it after it had stood untenanted and begun to decay, and John Douglas was murdered there on the night of January 6th.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: John Douglas was about fifty, vigorous, genial, generous, and reputed to have made his money in the California gold fields. He was found dead on the floor of the Manor House in a pink dressing gown after receiving a shotgun blast in the face, and he bore a distinctive brand on his right forearm.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Mrs. Douglas was a tall, dark, slender Englishwoman about twenty years younger than John Douglas. She was retiring and devoted to her household, but had sometimes shown acute uneasiness when her husband was late returning; after the shot, she came downstairs and was taken away by Mrs. Allen before seeing the body.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Cecil James Barker was a wealthy English bachelor and an intimate friend of John Douglas from America. He heard the shot, reached the room within about thirty seconds, reported the murder, and told Sergeant Wilson that the open window and blood mark on the sill indicated that the killer escaped across the moat.

records.l: Sergeant Wilson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Sergeant Wilson was in charge of the small local police station and arrived at the Manor House shortly after midnight. He questioned Barker and Ames, examined the crime scene, and concluded that the case was too difficult for him alone and would likely require London assistance.

records.l: Dr. Wood, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Dr. Wood arrived with Sergeant Wilson and Cecil James Barker and immediately recognized that John Douglas was dead. He examined the shattered head and later drew attention to the unusual brand on Douglas’s forearm.

records.l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Ames was the prim, respectable, and capable butler of the Manor House. He stated that he had raised the drawbridge at nearly six o’clock, helped enter the room after the murder, identified the missing wedding ring, and confirmed that Douglas had long borne the brand on his forearm.

records.l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The drawbridge was the only approach to the Manor House and was raised every evening and lowered every morning. It was up from nearly six o’clock until Barker lowered it after the murder, making it appear difficult for an outsider to have entered or escaped.

records.l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The inner moat was about forty feet wide, surrounded the Manor House, and was fed by a small stream. The open window and a muddy, blood-like mark on its sill led Barker and Sergeant Wilson to believe that the murderer had waded across it.

records.l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The sawed-off shotgun lay across John Douglas’s chest after being fired at close range. Its barrel had been cut off about a foot in front of the triggers, and the triggers had been wired together so that the whole charge would discharge simultaneously.

records.l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: John Douglas’s murder occurred at about half-past eleven in the Manor House. He was found in a room with his head almost destroyed by a shotgun blast, while evidence suggested that a person had hidden behind the curtains, killed him, and escaped through the window.

records.l: the open window escape, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The long, diamond-paned window was open to its full extent, and a smudge resembling a bloody boot sole marked the wooden sill. Barker and Sergeant Wilson inferred that the murderer left through the window and waded across the moat, although the timing made the escape difficult to explain.

records.l: card marked V.V. 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: A card bearing the inked inscription “V.V.” and “341” was found beside John Douglas’s body. Sergeant Wilson could not interpret it, and Barker said he had not noticed it before and believed the murderer had left it.

records.l: the brand on John Douglas's forearm, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: A brown design consisting of a triangle inside a circle was visible halfway up John Douglas’s right forearm. Dr. Wood said it appeared to be a brand rather than a tattoo, while Barker and Ames stated that they had seen it many times before.

records.l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: John Douglas’s plain gold wedding ring was missing from the little finger of his left hand. Ames explained that it had been worn beneath a nugget ring, which had been removed and then replaced, indicating that someone had deliberately taken the wedding ring.

records.l: the mystery, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The mystery involves how a murderer entered the Manor House despite the raised drawbridge, killed John Douglas, and escaped through the open window. The hidden figure, the V.V. 341 card, the branded forearm, and the missing wedding ring leave the circumstances unexplained.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: White Mason meets Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector MacDonald at Birlstone and briefs them on the murder of Mr. Douglas. The investigators examine the Manor House, its moat, the window, the weapons, the footprints, the blood mark, the missing wedding ring, and the card marked V.V. 341. White Mason and MacDonald debate whether the killer came from inside or outside, while Holmes develops questions about a possible secret society and other unexplained clues. Cecil Barker then reports that the suspected killer’s bicycle has been found concealed near the Manor House.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Holmes travels with Dr. Watson to Birlstone and listens closely to White Mason’s account of the case. He examines the shotgun, moat, window, body, blood mark, card, ink, footprints, and dumb-bell, and suggests that the branded mark and card may point to a secret society. He finds White Mason’s outside-killer theory interesting but unconvincing and continues seeking further facts.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Holmes to Birlstone and the Manor House. White Mason notes that medical experts, including Dr. Watson, may have a role in interpreting the case.

records.l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: White Mason, the chief Sussex detective, briefs Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector MacDonald on the murder and leads them through the Manor House. He examines the hammer and shotgun, favors the theory that an outsider entered the house, and suggests that the card and branded mark may indicate a secret society.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Inspector MacDonald challenges the idea that an outsider entered the house, arguing that a deliberate killer would not choose a noisy shotgun when escape was difficult. He agrees that suicide is impossible and accepts that the evidence creates serious difficulties for both an inside and an outside killer.

records.l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Ames, the butler, is described as white and quivering from shock and is questioned about the house and Mr. Douglas. He confirms that Mr. Douglas often had the branded triangle mark, identifies the plaster on his jaw as a shaving cut, recalls that he seemed restless and excited, and says he has never seen the shotgun in the house.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Cecil Barker is present at the Manor House and is described as tall, sunburned, capable-looking, and masterful. He reports that the suspected killer’s bicycle has been found concealed within a hundred yards of the hall door.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Mr. Douglas has been murdered in the Manor House by a shot from a sawed-off shotgun. His wedding ring is missing, a card marked V.V. 341 lies near him, and he bears a branded triangle inside a circle on his forearm.

records.l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Birlstone is the Sussex location where the murder occurs and where Holmes, Dr. Watson, White Mason, and Inspector MacDonald meet. The village contains the Manor House and the Westville Arms.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Manor House is an old Jacobean house surrounded by a moat and approached by a drawbridge. Mr. Douglas is found murdered there, with clues including an open window, mud-stained footprints, a blood mark, a hammer, a shotgun, a card, and a missing wedding ring.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Holmes, White Mason, and Inspector MacDonald adopt the existence of a secret society as a working hypothesis based on the card marked V.V. 341 and the branded mark on Mr. Douglas’s forearm. They consider whether an agent of such a society entered the Manor House to carry out vengeance.

records.l: the police, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The police investigate the murder, examine the weapons and surrounding area, and search for a wet stranger who might have crossed the moat. By the time Holmes arrives, they have found no suspect but have located a bicycle near the Manor House.

records.l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The murder of Mr. Douglas is treated as a homicide rather than suicide. The circumstances include a close-range shotgun blast, a missing wedding ring, an open window, a blood mark, footprints, and a card marked V.V. 341, but the killer’s identity and escape remain unexplained.

records.l: suicide of Mr. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: White Mason and Inspector MacDonald reject the possibility of suicide. They conclude that suicide cannot account for the concealed wedding ring, the staged footprints, the opened window, the blood on the sill, and the other signs.

records.l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The investigation considers whether the killer was an insider or an outsider and examines the physical clues at the Manor House. Holmes insists on gathering complete evidence before presenting a final theory.

records.l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Manor House is surrounded by a broad moat that is about two feet deep at the sides and three feet in the middle. Holmes and White Mason find no clear signs on the far side that anyone climbed out, but agree that a person could cross it without drowning.

records.l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The drawbridge provides access to the Manor House and had been raised after dusk. White Mason reasons that an outsider could have entered between roughly four-thirty and six, before the bridge was raised.

records.l: window (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The window immediately to the right of the drawbridge is open as it was found after the murder. It is narrow but large enough for a person to squeeze through, and investigators consider it the suspected killer’s route of escape.

records.l: the hammer, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The hammer found on the mat is examined and shows no signs of violence or blood. White Mason suggests that Mr. Douglas may have gripped it during a struggle, but the evidence does not establish how it was used.

records.l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The shotgun is loaded with buckshot cartridges and has its triggers wired together so that pulling the rear trigger fires both barrels. It is less than two feet long, bears the partial name P-E-N, and is identified by Holmes as an American shotgun made by the Pennsylvania Small Arms Company.

records.l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Mr. Douglas’s wedding ring is missing from his finger. White Mason’s reconstruction supposes that the killer demanded the ring before shooting him, but the reason for its removal remains unknown.

records.l: card marked V.V. 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The rough cardboard card marked V.V. 341 is found beside the dead man. Holmes determines that it was not printed in the room and suggests that, along with the branded mark, it may be connected with a secret society.

records.l: the brand on John Douglas's forearm, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Mr. Douglas has a branded triangle inside a circle on his forearm, a mark Ames has often seen. Holmes identifies it as a burn that must have caused considerable pain and considers it potentially connected with the card marked V.V. 341.

records.l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: One dumb-bell is found under the side table in the room. Holmes asks where the other is, but Ames does not know whether there had ever been a pair.

records.l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: A well-used Rudge-Whitworth bicycle, splashed as if from a considerable journey, is found concealed in evergreens near the Manor House. It has a saddlebag containing a spanner and oilcan but provides no clue to its owner.

records.l: footprints (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Indistinct footprints appear in the mud-stained corner behind the curtain and are treated as evidence that someone waited there. The tread on the window sill appears remarkably broad and splay-footed, while the traceable sole in the corner seems more shapely.

records.l: blood mark (Manor House window sill), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The blood mark on the window sill is examined by Holmes with a lens. He identifies it as the tread of a shoe, though its broad shape does not clearly correspond with the other indistinct footprints.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Ames, Mrs. Allen, and Cecil Barker give evidence about the events surrounding the murder of Jack Douglas at Birlstone. Barker says Douglas feared an implacable secret society connected with his past in California, where threatening men sought him after he left. Inspector MacDonald questions Barker about Douglas's marriage, his friendship with Mrs. Douglas, the missing wedding ring, and the alleged connection between the marriage and the tragedy. Sherlock Holmes also questions Barker about the candle and lamp in the study, finding the change in lighting remarkable.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Cecil Barker about the candle and lamp in the study. He points out that Barker said the candle was lit when he entered, but that the candle was later out and the lamp was burning.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Inspector MacDonald questions Cecil Barker about Jack Douglas's past in California, the secret society, Douglas's first wife, his marriage to Mrs. Douglas, Barker's friendship with Mrs. Douglas, and the missing wedding ring. He presses Barker when Barker refuses to answer whether Douglas approved of his friendship with his wife.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack Douglas was a rich American-made gentleman who had lived at Birlstone for five years. He was described as fearless, kind, and considerate, but he had shown unusual restlessness and irritability on the day before his murder.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Mrs. Douglas came downstairs after the bell rang, but Cecil Barker stopped her and told her that Jack was dead. She returned to her bedroom with Mrs. Allen, where she remained trembling and greatly excited but made no outcry.

records.l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Ames had been Jack Douglas's butler for five years and considered his account of the night clear and sincere. He heard the bell, went to the front of the house with Mrs. Allen, later returned to the study with Barker, and lowered the drawbridge.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Cecil Barker says he believed the murderer escaped through the study window because of the bloodstain and the raised drawbridge. He describes Douglas's unexplained danger, his past in California, his habit of carrying a revolver, his jealousy, and his own loyalty to Douglas and Mrs. Douglas.

records.l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Birlstone is the quiet English place where Jack Douglas rented a house and lived with Mrs. Douglas. Barker believed Douglas's choice of such a secluded place was connected with the danger hanging over him.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The house has a pantry and kitchens at the back, servants' rooms at the extreme rear, and a study at the front. Its drawbridge was raised at night according to the old custom of the house.

records.l: California, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack Douglas lived and worked in California for about five years with Cecil Barker, becoming partners in a successful mining claim at Benito Canyon. Douglas suddenly left for England, and within a week several hard-looking American men came asking where he was.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Cecil Barker believes that an implacable secret society was pursuing Jack Douglas and would not rest until it killed him. Barker did not know the society's name or the reason Douglas had offended it, but thought the legend on the placard referred to it.

records.l: the police, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Ames and Barker found the study as the police had seen it after the alarm. Barker went to get the police, who arrived after the servants had been alerted.

records.l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The murder of Jack Douglas was discovered after the bell rang violently, although Ames and Mrs. Allen had not heard a shot. Barker believed the murderer escaped through the study window, but could not explain what became of the assassin.

records.l: Douglas's death, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Douglas's death occurred in the study while he was wearing a dressing gown and had left his revolver in the bedroom. Barker said Douglas might have believed he was safe once the drawbridge was raised.

records.l: Douglas's marriage to Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Douglas's marriage to Mrs. Douglas was questioned because his wedding ring was missing and because Barker acknowledged that Douglas had been jealous of his friendship with his wife. Barker insisted that Mrs. Douglas was loving and faithful.

records.l: the danger from Mr. Douglas's American past, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The feud against Douglas was believed by Barker to have begun at least eleven years earlier and to have continued with great persistence. Barker thought it had shadowed Douglas's whole life and was connected with the threatening men who sought him in California.

records.l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The drawbridge was raised at night as an old custom of the house. After Douglas was found, Ames lowered it, while Barker argued that its being raised left the study window as the only possible escape route.

records.l: the bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The bell rang violently after Douglas was killed, bringing Ames, Mrs. Allen, and eventually the others to the front of the house. Its ringing was heard even though the shot itself was not heard by the servants.

records.l: the study, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The study was where Barker found Douglas and where Ames and Barker later found everything as the police had seen it. The study had a candle on the table when Barker entered, but the candle was later out and the lamp was lit.

records.l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The moat was no more than three feet deep at any point. Barker therefore said that the assassin could not possibly have drowned in it.

records.l: window (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The study window was regarded by Barker as the route by which the murderer escaped. He based this belief on the bloodstain and the fact that the drawbridge was raised.

records.l: the candle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The candle in the study was lit when Barker entered after the crime. Barker said he blew it out because it gave poor light and then lit the lamp.

records.l: lamp (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The lamp in the study was burning when Ames and Barker returned to the room. Barker said he lit it to obtain better light after seeing what had happened.

records.l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack Douglas's wedding ring had been removed from his finger. Inspector MacDonald suggested that its absence could connect the marriage with the tragedy, while Barker said it did not reflect upon Mrs. Douglas's honour.

records.l: the bloodstain, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The bloodstain was considered by Barker to be conclusive evidence that the murderer escaped through the study window.

records.l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The assassin was believed by Barker to have escaped through the study window. Barker could not explain what became of him or why he had not taken the bicycle believed to be his.

records.l: Douglas's jealousy, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Douglas's jealousy concerned his friendship with Cecil Barker and Mrs. Douglas. Barker said Douglas could become angry when he saw sympathy between them, despite loving both his wife and his friend.

records.l: the alleged affair between Barker and Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The alleged affair between Barker and Mrs. Douglas was raised by Inspector MacDonald's questions about whether Douglas approved of their friendship. Barker refused to answer at first, then denied any implication against Mrs. Douglas's honour and declared that she was faithful.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mrs. Douglas tells Inspector MacDonald and Sherlock Holmes that Mr. Douglas feared a danger connected with his American past, though he refused to explain it. She recalls his repeated references to the “Valley of Fear” and his fevered mention of Bodymaster McGinty. The investigators also learn that Mr. Douglas's wedding ring was taken, and Holmes discovers that Cecil Barker's bloodstained carpet slipper matches the blood mark on the study window sill. This suggests that Barker himself made the apparent outside footprint, though Holmes and MacDonald do not yet understand why.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mrs. Douglas tells the investigators that she was stopped by Cecil Barker on the stairs after hearing the shot and never entered the room where the tragedy occurred. She says Mr. Douglas had powerful enemies connected with his American past and repeatedly referred to the Valley of Fear. She also recalls that Bodymaster McGinty was a name he spoke during a fever and that his wedding ring had been taken.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mr. Douglas regularly made a nighttime round of the house because he feared fire. His wife says he believed he was being pursued by powerful enemies from his American life and used the expression “the Valley of Fear” for the danger surrounding him.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Inspector MacDonald questions Mrs. Douglas about the shooting, Mr. Douglas's American past, his marriage, and the missing wedding ring. After Holmes matches Cecil Barker's slipper to the blood mark on the window sill, MacDonald concludes that Barker made the apparent window footprint.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mrs. Douglas about the words associated with Mr. Douglas's past and examines Cecil Barker's carpet slippers. He places one slipper on the blood mark on the study window sill and finds that it exactly corresponds, showing that Barker could have made the mark himself.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Cecil Barker stopped Mrs. Douglas from entering the room after the shooting and went to summon the police. His carpet slippers were stained with blood, and one of them exactly matched the blood mark on the study window sill, indicating that he made the apparent outside footprint.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Bodymaster McGinty is a name Mr. Douglas repeatedly spoke with anger and horror while delirious from fever. Mrs. Douglas believes there is a connection between him and the Valley of Fear.

records.l: America, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: America is identified as the place where Mr. Douglas had lived before his marriage. Mrs. Douglas believes that events there left him in danger from powerful enemies.

records.l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: The Valley of Fear is Mr. Douglas's expression for a dangerous period or place connected with his American life. He told Mrs. Douglas that he had been in its shadow and feared that they might never escape it.

records.l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: The tragedy occurred in a room that Mrs. Douglas did not enter after hearing the shot. Cecil Barker was present there and later summoned the police.

records.l: the gunshot, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: The shooting was heard by Mrs. Douglas, who came downstairs after putting on her dressing gown. Cecil Barker stopped her on the stairs a couple of minutes later and told her she could do nothing.

records.l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mr. Douglas's wedding ring was taken from him. Inspector MacDonald considers its removal extraordinary and questions what motive an enemy could have for taking it.

records.l: Mr. Barker's carpet slippers, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mr. Barker's carpet slippers were still under the chair in the hall and had bloodstained soles. One slipper exactly matched the blood mark on the study window sill, suggesting that Barker himself made the mark.

records.l: the danger from Mr. Douglas's American past, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: The danger from Mr. Douglas's American past was something he concealed from Mrs. Douglas to prevent her alarm. She inferred its existence from his precautions, his reactions to unexpected strangers, his references to the Valley of Fear, and his belief that powerful enemies were following him.

records.l: the enemies from America, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
records.s: Mr. Douglas's enemies were believed by Mrs. Douglas to be powerful and connected with his American life. She says he was always on guard against them and feared that they might eventually reach him.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Dr. Watson encounters Mrs. Douglas and Barker laughing together in the garden, then learns they are anxious about whether Sherlock Holmes would share confidential information with the police. At the village inn, Holmes argues that Barker and Mrs. Douglas are lying about the murder and conspiring to conceal the truth, though he is not certain they committed it. Holmes reasons that the gunshot was probably fired around a quarter to eleven, half an hour before the alarm, and considers the possibility that an outsider murdered Mr. Douglas and threatened the couple into silence. He plans to spend an evening alone in the study and borrows Dr. Watson’s umbrella while the investigation of the bicycle continues.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Dr. Watson returns alone to the village inn after the detectives continue their inquiries and walks in the garden. He encounters Mrs. Douglas and Barker together, reports the incident to Sherlock Holmes, and discusses Holmes’s theories about the murder. He lends Holmes his large umbrella.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes says he wants no confidential information from Mrs. Douglas or Barker because it could become awkward if they were arrested for conspiracy and murder. He identifies the missing dumb-bell as highly important and argues that Barker’s account is a lie corroborated by Mrs. Douglas. Holmes suspects they are conspiring to conceal the truth, but he remains uncertain whether they committed the murder and plans to spend an evening alone in the study.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Mrs. Douglas is seen laughing with Barker behind a hedge in the garden, apparently having put aside her show of grief. She asks Dr. Watson whether Sherlock Holmes must pass confidential information to the detectives and says that his answer could greatly affect her. Holmes believes that she and Barker are lying and concealing the truth about the murder.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Barker is seen sitting and laughing with Mrs. Douglas in the garden before assuming a solemn manner when Dr. Watson appears. He asks whether Sherlock Holmes acts independently of the police. Holmes says Barker’s account is a clumsy lie and claims that Barker deliberately placed the blood mark on the windowsill to mislead the police.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Mr. Douglas is the dead man whose body was found in the study. Holmes considers the possibility that he had a shameful secret in his past and that an outsider murdered him as an avenger.

records.l: the village inn, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The village inn is the modest lodging to which Dr. Watson returns after the detectives continue their inquiries. Sherlock Holmes returns there around five o’clock, eats a substantial tea, and discusses the case with Dr. Watson.

records.l: the garden, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The garden beside the village inn contains ancient yew trees, a lawn, and an old sundial. Behind a hedge, Dr. Watson finds Mrs. Douglas and Barker talking and laughing together within hours of Mr. Douglas’s death.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes spends the afternoon at the Manor House consulting with his two colleagues. The murder scene and the study are associated with the Manor House.

records.l: the study, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The study is where Mr. Douglas’s bloodstained body was found and where the gunshot was apparently fired. Holmes plans to spend an evening alone there, hoping that the room’s atmosphere or further observation will help him solve the case.

records.l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Holmes believes the reported sequence surrounding the murder is impossible, particularly the removal and replacement of the wedding ring and the placement of the card. He reasons that the gunshot probably occurred around a quarter to eleven, about half an hour before Barker and Mrs. Douglas raised the alarm.

records.l: the conspiracy, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Holmes believes Barker and Mrs. Douglas are involved in a conspiracy to conceal the truth about the murder. He also considers an alternative in which they are not the murderers but were threatened by an outsider and then delayed the alarm to protect themselves from suspicion.

records.l: the gunshot, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Holmes concludes that the gunshot was probably fired at a quarter to eleven, when Mrs. Allen heard what she thought was a door slamming. He notes that a shotgun fired at close range would be muffled but should still have been heard in the house.

records.l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Sherlock Holmes says that the case hangs upon the missing dumb-bell. He jokes about the danger of an athlete exercising with only one dumb-bell, while indicating that the other investigators have not grasped its importance.

records.l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The wedding ring was reportedly removed from Mr. Douglas’s finger and replaced beneath another ring, which Holmes considers an implausible part of the account. He also considers the possibility that an avenger took it because the vendetta might relate to Mr. Douglas’s first marriage.

records.l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: A bicycle was left concealed outside the Manor House and is treated as evidence of an outsider’s escape. Holmes finds it suspicious that a fugitive would leave behind the means of escape, while his colleagues travel to Tunbridge Wells to seek its likely owner.

records.l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The investigation examines the statements of Barker and Mrs. Douglas, the timing of the gunshot and alarm, the blood mark on the windowsill, the wedding ring, the bicycle, and the missing dumb-bell. Holmes conducts experiments about how sounds travel through the house and plans further examination of the study.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Inspector MacDonald and White Mason identify the bicycle as belonging to an American calling himself Hargrave, who stayed at the Eagle Commercial in Tunbridge Wells and is described as a roughly fifty-year-old, fierce-looking man carrying a concealed sawed-off shotgun. MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave cycled to the house, hid his bicycle, shot Mr. Douglas, and escaped through the moat or by another route. Sherlock Holmes maintains that the murder occurred earlier than reported and that Mrs. Douglas and Barker helped conceal what happened and fabricated evidence of an escape through the window. Holmes later makes a solitary investigation focused on Mr. Douglas's single dumb-bell and returns asking Dr. Watson whether he fears sleeping with a lunatic.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Inspector MacDonald returns with White Mason, reporting that the bicycle has been identified and that a description of the suspected outsider has been obtained. He traces the suspect from Tunbridge Wells to the house and theorizes that the man shot Mr. Douglas and escaped.

records.l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: White Mason accompanies Inspector MacDonald in identifying the bicycle and investigating the suspect's movements. He questions why the suspect did not return to the hotel and expresses difficulty explaining how Mrs. Douglas could be connected with an American assassin.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes listens to MacDonald's theory but argues that the murder occurred half an hour earlier than reported and that Mrs. Douglas and Barker helped conceal the truth. He undertakes a solitary investigation centered on why Mr. Douglas developed his athletic frame with a single dumb-bell, then returns appearing to question his own sanity.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Dr. Watson sleeps in a double-bedded room with Sherlock Holmes and is partly awakened when Holmes returns from his excursion. He tells Holmes that he would not be afraid to sleep in the same room with a lunatic.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Mr. Douglas had seemed disturbed after visiting Tunbridge Wells, which Holmes and MacDonald treat as evidence that he had become conscious of danger. MacDonald theorizes that he was shot during his usual nightly round, while Holmes argues that the crime happened earlier than reported.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes suspects that Mrs. Douglas was involved in a conspiracy to conceal something and helped the murderer escape, or at least reached the room before he escaped. He believes she participated in fabricating evidence of an escape through the window.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes suspects that Barker was involved with Mrs. Douglas in concealing something. Holmes believes Barker helped the murderer escape, or reached the room before the escape, and helped fabricate evidence involving the window.

records.l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Hargrave is identified as an American who stayed at the Eagle Commercial in Tunbridge Wells under that name, carrying only a bicycle and a small valise. He is described as about five foot nine, around fifty years old, slightly grizzled, gray-moustached, curved-nosed, and fierce-looking, and he disappears after leaving the hotel.

records.l: Tunbridge Wells, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Tunbridge Wells is where Mr. Douglas had been the day before he appeared disturbed and where Hargrave stayed two days before the murder. MacDonald concludes that a man arriving by bicycle might have come from there.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave approached the house at twilight, entered the first room he saw, and hid behind a curtain. Holmes instead argues that Mrs. Douglas and Barker reached the room before the murderer escaped and fabricated evidence that he had fled through the window.

records.l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: The bicycle is identified by the manager of the Eagle Commercial as belonging to Hargrave. MacDonald believes Hargrave left it concealed among the laurels near the house and abandoned it because it could identify him.

records.l: valise (Hargrave's valise), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Hargrave's small valise contained no papers or letters and had no identifying marks, but it was London made and held British contents. MacDonald believes the valise could have concealed the shotgun.

records.l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: The sawed-off shotgun was less than two feet long and could have been carried inside Hargrave's overcoat or concealed in his valise. MacDonald believes Hargrave brought it deliberately and used it to shoot Mr. Douglas.

records.l: single dumb-bell (Mr. Douglas's dumb-bell), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes repeatedly returns to the question of why an athletic man would develop his frame using the unnatural instrument of a single dumb-bell. He makes a private investigation of this matter during the night.

records.l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: MacDonald attributes the murder of Mr. Douglas to Hargrave, who allegedly waited near the house and shot him with a concealed shotgun. Holmes disputes the reported timing, saying that the crime was committed half an hour earlier than reported.

records.l: investigation into Mr. Douglas's murder, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: The investigation advances when MacDonald and White Mason identify Hargrave's bicycle and obtain a description of him. Holmes remains dissatisfied with their explanation and pursues a separate line of inquiry involving the timing of the murder, the suspected concealment, and the single dumb-bell.

records.l: the open window escape, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave escaped after shooting Mr. Douglas, possibly through the moat and then by another route toward London or a safe hiding place. Holmes argues that Mrs. Douglas and Barker may have helped him escape or reached the room before he did so.

records.l: conspiracy to conceal the crime, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes believes that Mrs. Douglas and Barker are in a conspiracy to conceal what happened. He says they aided the murderer's escape, or at least reached the room before his escape.

records.l: fabricated evidence of escape, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
records.s: Sherlock Holmes believes that Mrs. Douglas and Barker fabricated evidence suggesting that the murderer escaped through the window. He considers this part of their effort to conceal the crime.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Inspector MacDonald and White Mason to abandon their search for the mysterious cyclist because they do not understand what they are investigating. Holmes discovers that the missing dumb-bell had been used to weight a bundle containing American boots, a knife, clothing, and a yellow overcoat, and he traps Cecil Barker into retrieving it from the moat. Mrs. Douglas then reveals that John Douglas is alive and has been hiding in the Manor House. Douglas gives Dr. Watson his written account, identified as the story of the Valley of Fear.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Sherlock Holmes advises Inspector MacDonald and White Mason to abandon their search for the mysterious cyclist while he verifies his own theory. He finds the missing dumb-bell and uses it to test the moat, then announces that the moat-draining plan has caused the person who hid the bundle to retrieve it. Holmes identifies Cecil Barker as the retriever and concludes that John Douglas is alive and should tell the complete story.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Inspector MacDonald, and White Mason during the investigation and helps Holmes fish the bundle from the moat with his umbrella. Holmes refers to him as the historian of the group, and John Douglas gives him the written account of the Valley of Fear story.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Inspector MacDonald reports that supposed sightings of the mysterious cyclist have led to arrests in East Ham, Leicester, and Liverpool. He initially objects to abandoning the case and to the moat-draining plan, but agrees to follow Holmes’s instructions and witnesses Cecil Barker retrieve the sodden bundle.

records.l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: White Mason participates in the discussion with Inspector MacDonald and agrees to follow Sherlock Holmes’s advice. He accompanies the others during the vigil outside Birlstone Manor and witnesses the recovery of the sodden bundle.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Cecil Barker is found in the study retrieving a weighted bundle from the moat. He refuses to explain the secret and says it is not his to reveal, but Mrs. Douglas tells him he has done enough.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Mrs. Douglas listens to the confrontation in the study and tells Cecil Barker that he has done enough. She then embraces the man revealed to be John Douglas and says that it is best for him to tell his story.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: John Douglas is revealed to be alive and hiding in the Manor House rather than dead as previously believed. He has spent two days preparing a written account and gives it to Dr. Watson as the story of the Valley of Fear.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Birlstone Manor remains under observation while Sherlock Holmes and the others hide in a shrubbery opposite its main door and drawbridge. Holmes also studies an account of the ancient house and spends time alone in its study.

records.l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The Valley of Fear is associated by Sherlock Holmes with the Vermissa Valley, a coal and iron valley in the United States. He suggests that the initials V.V. on the card by the body may refer to Vermissa Valley.

records.l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The supposed murder of John Douglas is the investigation that Inspector MacDonald and White Mason believe they are conducting. The revelation that John Douglas is alive shows that the apparent murder has not been fully explained.

records.l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Sherlock Holmes tells Inspector MacDonald and White Mason that their case is hopeless because they have not understood what they are investigating. He believes the truth can still be found through a shorter course than tracing the mysterious cyclist.

records.l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The mysterious cyclist is reported from numerous places, producing conflicting descriptions and several arrests. Sherlock Holmes says that tracing him will not help solve the investigation and urges the detectives to abandon that line of inquiry.

records.l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The missing dumb-bell leads Sherlock Holmes to suspect that something has been sunk in the nearby water. He finds it attached to the sodden bundle and later removes it from the bundle.

records.l: the sodden bundle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The sodden bundle is weighted with a dumb-bell and hidden beneath the writing table in the study after being retrieved from the moat. It contains American boots, a deadly knife, underclothes, socks, a gray tweed suit, and a short yellow overcoat.

records.l: the yellow overcoat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The yellow overcoat in the sodden bundle has an inner pocket extended into the lining to hold a truncated fowling piece. Its tailor’s label reads “Neal, Outfitter, Vermissa, U.S.A.”

records.l: the study, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The study is watched from outside because it has a visible light and overlooks the moat. Cecil Barker is present there when the investigators enter, and the sodden bundle is found beneath its writing table.

records.l: the moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The moat is where Sherlock Holmes initially finds the weighted bundle and where Cecil Barker later retrieves it. Holmes uses the sound of disturbed water and Barker’s actions to identify who had hidden the bundle.

records.l: the moat-draining plan, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The moat-draining plan is announced to make the person who hid the bundle remove it before the water is diverted. The plan succeeds when Cecil Barker retrieves the bundle at night, giving Holmes and the others witnesses to his action.

records.l: the Valley of Fear story, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The Valley of Fear story is the written account that John Douglas prepares during his confinement and hands to Dr. Watson. Douglas says that Watson may tell it in his own way because the facts are contained in the papers.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: John Douglas explains that Ted Baldwin attacked him at Birlstone Manor, but Baldwin was accidentally killed when his own gun discharged during their struggle. Douglas, Barker, and Douglas's wife disguised Baldwin's body as Douglas's and hid Douglas in a secret hiding place, hoping to make his American enemies believe Baldwin had killed him. Sherlock Holmes had already inferred the deception after finding Douglas's clothes in the moat and discovering that the body was not Douglas's. Holmes warns that the mystery is not finished and that Douglas may face dangers beyond English law, leading the narrative back to the origins of the past conflict in America.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Holmes explains that the body found at Birlstone Manor could not be John Douglas because Douglas's suit of clothes had been found in the moat. He inferred that Douglas was concealed somewhere in the manor and warns that Douglas may face dangers from his American enemies as well as English law.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas reveals that he survived Ted Baldwin's attack and hid at Birlstone Manor while Baldwin's body was presented as his own. He says that enemies pursued him from Chicago to California and out of America, and he asks how he stands under English law.

records.l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Inspector MacDonald is astonished to discover that the man under investigation was not John Douglas and angrily questions Holmes about the concealed investigation. He hears Douglas's account and asks how long Holmes had known that the search was misguided.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Barker helped Douglas and Douglas's wife dress Ted Baldwin's body in Douglas's dressing gown and prepare the false murder scene. He also opened the window, made a mark on the sill, and rang the bell to suggest that the murderer had escaped.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas's wife initially knew little about his past but helped him and Barker conceal the truth after Baldwin's death. She learned the full story after the investigators had seen her, and Douglas says he hoped to reunite with her after escaping.

records.l: Ted Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Ted Baldwin, identified by Douglas as his worst enemy, secretly entered Birlstone Manor and attacked him with a knife and a buckshot gun. During their struggle, the gun discharged into Baldwin's face, killing him, after which his body was disguised as Douglas's.

records.l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Birlstone Manor contained a secret hiding place suitable for concealing Douglas and provided the setting for Baldwin's attack and death. Douglas, Barker, and Douglas's wife used the manor to stage Baldwin's body as Douglas's and to imply that a murderer had escaped.

records.l: Tunbridge Wells, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas saw Ted Baldwin in Tunbridge Wells before the attack and recognized him as a dangerous enemy. Holmes later concluded that the clothes found in the moat belonged to the bicyclist from Tunbridge Wells.

records.l: English law, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas asks how he stands under English law after concealing his survival and substituting Baldwin's body for his own. Holmes says that English law is generally just and that Douglas will receive no worse than his deserts.

records.l: the brand on John Douglas's forearm, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: The lodge's branded mark appeared as a brown triangle within a circle on Baldwin's forearm and also on Douglas's arm. Seeing the matching mark gave Douglas the idea of making Baldwin's body appear to be his own.

records.l: the dead bicyclist from Tunbridge Wells, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Holmes identifies the body found at Birlstone Manor as belonging not to Douglas but to the bicyclist from Tunbridge Wells, based on the suit of clothes discovered in the moat. Douglas's account identifies the dead man more specifically as Ted Baldwin.

records.l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: What appeared to be the murder of John Douglas at Birlstone Manor was actually Ted Baldwin's accidental death during his attack on Douglas. Douglas, Barker, and Douglas's wife staged the scene so that Baldwin's body would be mistaken for Douglas's.

records.l: Ted Baldwin's attack on John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Baldwin entered the study at Birlstone Manor and sprang at Douglas with a knife. Douglas struck at him with a hammer, seized Baldwin's gun, and struggled with him until the weapon discharged both barrels into Baldwin's face.

records.l: the hiding place at Birlstone Manor, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas used a known hiding place at Birlstone Manor after Baldwin's death. Holmes had suspected that Douglas was concealed somewhere in the house because it offered suitable shelter for a fugitive.

records.l: the buckshot gun, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Baldwin carried a buckshot gun, which Douglas believed could have killed him if Baldwin had confronted him outside. During their struggle inside the study, the gun discharged and killed Baldwin.

records.l: the suit of clothes, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas brought down his suit of clothes and put Baldwin's body in Douglas's dressing gown while sending Baldwin's own clothes through the window in a weighted bundle. Holmes found the suit in the moat and used it to determine that the body was not Douglas's.

records.l: the Valley of Fear story, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas's story recounts his long pursuit by enemies from America, Baldwin's attack, Baldwin's accidental death, and the plan to conceal Douglas while presenting Baldwin as the victim. He insists that he has done nothing of which he is ashamed and has told the truth.

records.l: the mystery of the past, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: The narrative postpones the origins of Douglas's conflict and moves back approximately twenty years and thousands of miles westward to recount them. The earlier events are presented as necessary to resolve the mystery of the past before the story returns to Baker Street.

records.l: the enemies from America, The Valley of Fear, “That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we
records.s: Douglas says that his enemies from America pursued him from Chicago to California and then drove him out of America. He hoped Baldwin's apparent success in killing him would persuade these enemies to stop hunting him, but Holmes warns that they may still pose a danger.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: On February 4, 1875, John McMurdo travels by evening train from Chicago to Vermissa, a grim coal- and iron-working settlement in Vermissa Valley. He reveals that he is armed, belongs to the Eminent Order of Freemen, and has fled Chicago because of serious trouble with the law. After befriending Brother Scanlan and provoking two policemen, McMurdo arrives in Vermissa and is warned about the violent Scowrers and their leader, Jack McGinty. He takes lodging at the Shafter boarding house, where he meets Jacob Shafter and his daughter Ettie.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: John McMurdo is a young Irishman traveling from Chicago to Vermissa. He carries a fully loaded navy revolver, belongs to the Eminent Order of Freemen, and admits he left Chicago because he was in deep trouble, possibly involving a penitentiary sentence or worse. He angrily confronts two policemen on the train, then takes a room at Jacob Shafter’s house and immediately attracts attention in Vermissa.

records.l: Jacob Shafter, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Jacob Shafter runs a boarding house on Sheridan Street in Vermissa. He accepts McMurdo as a boarder for seven dollars a week paid in advance.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Ettie Shafter is Jacob Shafter’s young, beautiful daughter, and she runs the household because her mother is dead. She answers the door when McMurdo arrives, speaks with him, and directs him to wait for her father.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Jack McGinty, also called Black Jack McGinty, is the Bodymaster of Vermissa Lodge and the boss of the Union House. McMurdo is told that nothing can happen in the area unless McGinty wants it and that he should seek McGinty if he is in trouble. A miner warns McMurdo not to mention McGinty in connection with the Scowrers.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The Scowrers are described as a gang associated with murder and terror in the Vermissa district. People are afraid to speak of them openly, and the miner who guides McMurdo warns that men have been beaten to death for less.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The Eminent Order of Freemen has lodges throughout the country, and McMurdo says that membership will provide him with friends wherever there is a lodge. He proves his membership to Brother Scanlan through a hand-grip and a secret gesture.

records.l: Vermissa Lodge, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Vermissa Lodge is a lodge of the Eminent Order of Freemen. Its Bodymaster is J. H. Scott according to McMurdo’s identification of his Chicago lodge, while Vermissa’s lodge is under the authority of Jack McGinty.

records.l: the evening train, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The evening train carries workers and other travelers up the railroad from Stagville toward Vermissa. During the journey, McMurdo speaks with Brother Scanlan, quarrels with two policemen, and becomes known to the miners before the train reaches Vermissa.

records.l: Shafter's boarding house, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The Shafter boarding house stands back from Sheridan Street in Vermissa and is run by Jacob Shafter with the help of Ettie. It becomes McMurdo’s new lodging after he agrees to pay seven dollars a week in advance.

records.l: Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Vermissa is the central township at the head of Vermissa Valley and the largest town on the railroad line. It is portrayed as a bleak, dirty settlement of wooden houses, stores, saloons, and gaming houses, dominated by fear of the Scowrers.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Vermissa Valley is a desolate industrial valley containing coal-mining and iron-working settlements. Its mountains, furnaces, slag heaps, mines, smoke, and crowded worker housing form the setting through which McMurdo travels.

records.l: Chicago, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Chicago is the place McMurdo says he last came from. He belongs to Lodge 29 there, and he left the city because of serious trouble that caused him to flee from justice.

records.l: Sheridan Street, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: Sheridan Street in Vermissa is the location of Jacob Shafter’s boarding house. McMurdo gives it as the address where he can be found.

records.l: the Union House, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The Union House is a saloon that nearly has the dignity of a hotel and is run by Jack McGinty. Brother Scanlan advises McMurdo to go there and see McGinty if he gets into trouble.

records.l: the Scowrers’ affairs, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: The Scowrers’ affairs are the notorious matters most often discussed in Vermissa, and they are associated with killings and intimidation. A miner refuses to speak openly about them and warns McMurdo that even mentioning McGinty in connection with them is dangerous.

records.l: McMurdo’s flight from justice, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: McMurdo’s flight from justice began in Chicago, where he says he had plenty of work but left because of trouble. He hints that the trouble may have involved imprisonment and possibly killing, but he refuses to explain further.

records.l: McMurdo’s arrival in Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, PART II / Chapter I
records.s: McMurdo arrives in Vermissa by train carrying a leather gripsack and a loaded revolver. He is escorted toward the Shafter house by a miner, meets Ettie and Jacob Shafter, and settles there as a boarder.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: McMurdo quickly becomes prominent at Shafter's boarding house, openly courts Ettie Shafter, and refuses to be intimidated by her existing connection to Teddy Baldwin. Mike Scanlan urges him to report to Boss McGinty, while Mr. Shafter reveals that the local Eminent Order of Freemen is also known as the murderous Scowrers and orders McMurdo to leave. Baldwin threatens McMurdo and Ettie, displaying a branded circle-and-triangle mark, but McMurdo declares that he is a Freeman and decides to visit McGinty immediately.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: McMurdo becomes the most important person among the boarders at Shafter's, gaining attention through his wit, singing, education, charm, and capacity for sudden anger. He falls in love with Ettie, refuses to leave the valley despite threats from Baldwin and the Scowrers, and reveals that he is himself a member of the Freemen. After Baldwin threatens him, McMurdo decides to go at once to see Boss McGinty.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Ettie is loved by McMurdo but has an existing understanding with Teddy Baldwin, whom she says she loathes and fears. She urges McMurdo to flee with her and her father because she believes Baldwin, McGinty, and the Scowrers will endanger his life, but McMurdo refuses to leave.

records.l: Scanlan, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Mike Scanlan visits McMurdo and urges him to report immediately to Boss McGinty. He warns that McMurdo must not encounter McGinty without doing so and suggests that McMurdo's hostility toward the police will please the Bodymaster.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Boss McGinty is the head of the local lodge and is called the Bodymaster. Scanlan warns McMurdo that McGinty will hate him if he does not report, and Ettie urges McMurdo to make McGinty his friend before the Scowrers act against him.

records.l: Ted Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Teddy Baldwin is described as a boss of the Scowrers and as the man to whom Ettie is attached. He confronts McMurdo, claims Ettie as his own, threatens to punish her and harm McMurdo, and displays a branded circle-and-triangle sign on his forearm.

records.l: Jacob Shafter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Mr. Shafter, McMurdo's German host and Ettie's father, tells McMurdo that the local Freemen are the Scowrers, a murder society. He gives McMurdo notice to leave the boarding house because he fears having a Freeman as a boarder, especially while Baldwin is courting Ettie.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: The Eminent Order of Freemen is presented by McMurdo as a society for charity and good fellowship, and he says that he has belonged to it for over two years. In the valley, however, Mr. Shafter says its bosses are also the bosses of the Scowrers and that offending it brings violent retaliation.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: The Scowrers are identified as the local form of the Eminent Order of Freemen and are feared throughout the valley. They are described as a murderous society whose members intimidate witnesses and escape prosecution through alibis and fear.

records.l: Shafter's boarding house, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Shafter's boarding house contains ten or a dozen boarders, among them McMurdo, who quickly becomes its most prominent resident. Mr. Shafter orders McMurdo to sleep there only one more night because he fears the consequences of housing a Freeman.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: The valley is a grim place of grime and snow where the Scowrers' power is widely feared. Its residents allegedly know the identities of those responsible for crimes, but witnesses are too afraid to testify against them.

records.l: the murders attributed to the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: Mr. Shafter cites the murders of Milman and Van Shorst, the Nicholson family, old Mr. Hyam, little Billy James, and others as proof that the Scowrers are a murder society. He says the crimes are common knowledge in the valley, while Ettie explains that witnesses are silenced and accused men are protected by false alibis.

records.l: McMurdo's membership in the Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: McMurdo says that he has been a member of the lodge for over two years and initially understands it as an innocent society found throughout the United States. He later tells Ettie that he is a Freeman himself and suggests that he may be no better than the other members.

records.l: McMurdo's proposed confrontation with McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
records.s: After Baldwin threatens him and Ettie urges him to seek protection, McMurdo decides to go immediately to Boss McGinty and make matters right. He intends to get his word in first and secure McGinty's friendship before the Scowrers move against him.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: Boss McGinty, the powerful Bodymaster of Lodge 341 and a feared official in the Vermissa Valley, questions McMurdo when he arrives at McGinty's saloon. McMurdo proves his lodge membership and admits that he formerly made counterfeit dollars and killed Jonas Pinto in Chicago. McGinty accepts him as a potentially useful brother after discovering McMurdo's nerve and ability to make counterfeit money. McMurdo and Ted Baldwin quarrel over a young lady, but McGinty forces them to settle the dispute under lodge discipline and instructs McMurdo to attend Lodge 341's Saturday meeting.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: Boss McGinty is the feared owner of McGinty's saloon, a municipal councillor, a commissioner of roads, and the Bodymaster of Lodge 341. He tests McMurdo at gunpoint, accepts his criminal past and counterfeit dollars as evidence of his usefulness, and prevents Ted Baldwin from continuing their quarrel. He orders McMurdo to attend Lodge 341's Saturday meeting and warns him that lodge discipline is severe.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: McMurdo visits Boss McGinty at McGinty's saloon after being directed there by Brother Scanlan of Lodge 341. He proves that he belongs to Lodge 29 in Chicago and admits that he made counterfeit dollars and killed Jonas Pinto before coming to the coal country. He reveals that he was covering McGinty with a cocked pistol during McGinty's test and later challenges Ted Baldwin over a young lady.

records.l: Ted Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: Ted Baldwin confronts McGinty and McMurdo over a young lady, claiming that McGinty has favored a newcomer over a man who has supported him for five years. McGinty overpowers and threatens him when he challenges the ruling, then compels him to reconcile with McMurdo through the lodge's quarrelling toast. Baldwin submits outwardly but remains visibly sullen.

records.l: Lodge 341, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: Lodge 341 is the lodge in Vermissa Valley whose Bodymaster is Boss McGinty. Its members use secret tests, ceremonies, and disciplinary authority, and McGinty says McMurdo must attend its Saturday meeting to become affiliated and be made free of the Vermissa Valley.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: The Vermissa Valley is a coal-country region in which Boss McGinty is feared throughout the township and the surrounding thirty-mile valley. McGinty says Lodge 341 can make McMurdo free of the Vermissa Valley after his affiliation.

records.l: McGinty's saloon, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: McGinty's saloon is the crowded, heavily patronized gathering place of the rougher elements of the town. McMurdo meets McGinty there, is questioned in a small room behind the bar, and witnesses the confrontation between McGinty and Ted Baldwin.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: The young lady is the subject of the dispute between McMurdo and Ted Baldwin. McMurdo and Baldwin are treated as having a choice to make because she is considered free to choose for herself, and McGinty says the matter lies outside a Bodymaster's jurisdiction.

records.l: counterfeit dollars, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: McMurdo says he made counterfeit dollars in Chicago and shows McGinty several examples. McGinty cannot see a difference between them and genuine money, and regards McMurdo's skill as potentially useful to the lodge.

records.l: the quarrel between McMurdo and Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, The bar of McGinty’s saloon was crowded as usual; for it was the
records.s: The quarrel between McMurdo and Baldwin concerns a young lady whom both men appear to claim. McMurdo offers to fight Baldwin, but McGinty rules that the lady is free to choose and forces the men to perform the lodge's reconciliation ceremony. McMurdo declares that he bears no grudge, while Baldwin complies reluctantly and remains sullen.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Jack McMurdo moves to the Widow MacNamara’s and lodges with Scanlan, while continuing his relationship with Ettie and showing the lodge members his counterfeit-money moulds. Captain Marvin recognizes McMurdo as a suspected Chicago criminal, but agrees to keep silent if he lives honestly, and this revelation makes McMurdo a hero among the local gang. McMurdo is initiated into Lodge 341, Vermissa, where he endures tests of courage and pain, accepts the Bodymaster’s authority, and receives a lodge brand on his forearm. The lodge is part of the Scowrers, a large and openly criminal organization whose members commit murders with little fear of conviction.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Jack McMurdo moves from old Jacob Shafter’s lodgings to the Widow MacNamara’s, where he lives with Scanlan. He becomes popular with the local gang because of his fearlessness, fighting ability, and reputation from Chicago, and he is initiated into Lodge 341 after enduring its tests. He accepts the lodge’s oath, secrecy, and the authority of the Bodymaster, and receives a brand on his forearm.

records.l: Scanlan, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Scanlan, McMurdo’s original acquaintance aboard the train, moves into Vermissa and lodges with him at the Widow MacNamara’s. He later leads McMurdo home after McMurdo becomes drunk while being celebrated by the bar crowd, and he is instructed to put liquor on the lodge table.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: McGinty runs the saloon where McMurdo becomes acquainted with the gang and serves as the Bodymaster of Lodge 341, Vermissa. He disputes Captain Marvin’s role as a representative of the mine owners and conducts McMurdo’s lodge initiation.

records.l: Lodge 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Lodge 341, Vermissa, meets at the Union House and has about sixty members, though it forms part of a wider network of lodges containing at least five hundred men across the coal district. Its initiation ceremony tests McMurdo’s courage and ability to endure pain, requires secrecy and fidelity, and marks him with a lodge symbol.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The Scowrers are a dangerous organization operating through several lodges in the coal district. Their older members give orders while younger agents carry them out, and their confidence comes from witnesses who will not testify, loyal supporters, and funds for strong legal representation.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Jack McMurdo is already a member of the Ancient Order of Freemen, belonging to Lodge No. 29 in Chicago. His sign and countersign establish his membership when he is questioned during the Vermissa lodge ceremony.

records.l: Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Vermissa contains the Widow MacNamara’s lodging house, McGinty’s saloon, and Lodge 341 at the Union House. The town is part of a coal district terrorized by organized criminal violence and has a lodge with about sixty assembled members.

records.l: Chicago, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: Chicago is Jack McMurdo’s former home and the place where Captain Marvin served as a police officer. McMurdo is associated there with the shooting of Jonas Pinto and with passing counterfeit money, though Marvin says that no clear case could be made against him and that Chicago is open to him.

records.l: the branding, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The branding is a painful lodge mark placed on McMurdo’s right forearm during his initiation. It consists of a circle with a triangle inside it, left deep and red by a branding iron; other lodge members show that they bear the same mark.

records.l: the Scowrers' terror and criminal rule, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
records.s: The Scowrers’ crimes include organized assaults and murders carried out against people who often have never harmed or even been seen by the attackers. Over ten years of outrage, there has been no conviction, and the members sometimes compete over who delivered the fatal blow while describing the victim’s suffering.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: At a Vermissa lodge meeting, McGinty assigns members to carry out violent acts, including an attack requested by Merton County Lodge and a warning against editor James Stanger. Brother Morris warns that the lodge's violence and extortion are driving out small businesses and provoking powerful companies and public opposition. McMurdo gains popularity by singing, volunteers for the attack on Stanger, and stops Ted Baldwin from continuing to beat the editor after the assault begins. The lodge members attack Stanger in the Vermissa Herald office and escape while maintaining an alibi at the Union Bar.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: McMurdo attends his first lodge meeting and openly approves of its violent methods. He volunteers to assist the lodge when needed, sings to win the members' approval, and joins Ted Baldwin's group in attacking James Stanger.
