During the attack, he draws his pistol and stops Baldwin from continuing to beat Stanger, arguing that the Bodymaster ordered that the editor not be killed.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: McGinty presides over the lodge meeting and assigns volunteers to carry out a violent job for Merton County Lodge. He defends the lodge's power, threatens Brother Morris, and orders Ted Baldwin to give James Stanger a severe warning rather than kill him. He also claims that the lodge can put two hundred men into the town and that the police and courts cannot effectively oppose it.

records.l: Vermissa Lodge, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The Vermissa lodge operates as a criminal organization that exchanges violent services with other lodges, extorts local firms, and supports members' families when they are killed carrying out lodge work. Its members discuss assassinations, arson, intimidation, and attacks while maintaining that their organization is beyond the reach of the law.

records.l: Ted Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: Ted Baldwin complains that workers and local employers are resisting the lodge and eagerly accepts McGinty's order to attack James Stanger. He leads the group into the Vermissa Herald office and repeatedly strikes Stanger after the editor has fallen. Baldwin tries to continue the beating until McMurdo pushes him back and threatens him with a pistol.

records.l: Brother Morris, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: Brother Morris warns that the lodge is driving small business owners from the district and replacing them with large companies that may have the resources to destroy the organization through the courts. He also argues against killing James Stanger because Stanger is respected and his death would provoke widespread demands for police and troops. After McGinty threatens him, Morris apologizes and promises not to speak against the lodge again.

records.l: Editor Stanger, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: James Stanger is an elderly editor of the Herald who has written against the lodge's violence in an article headed “Law and Order!”. McGinty orders the lodge to give him a severe warning. Baldwin and several members attack Stanger in his office, leaving him on the floor with blood on his white hair, but McMurdo prevents Baldwin from killing him.

records.l: Vermissa Herald, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The Vermissa Herald is the newspaper office where James Stanger works. Ted Baldwin and other lodge members enter the building at night and assault Stanger while the printing press is operating.

records.l: Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: Vermissa is the town in which the lodge operates and where the attack on the Herald takes place. The lodge's violence and extortion have made the district notorious, driven out small owners, and caused fear of eventual intervention by the authorities.

records.l: the lodge meeting, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The lodge meeting covers violent assignments, financial affairs, extortion payments, and the organization's response to criticism. McGinty presides over the proceedings, while Brother Morris's warnings about the lodge's growing danger are met with hostility and intimidation.

records.l: the attack on the Herald office, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The attack on James Stanger is organized by Ted Baldwin at McGinty's direction after the lodge discusses Stanger's criticism. The attackers beat Stanger in the Vermissa Herald office, and McMurdo intervenes when Baldwin appears likely to kill him. The group then escapes through the streets, relying on an alibi that places them in the Union Bar.

records.l: the murder campaign, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The murder campaign is described as a long-running series of assassinations and other violent acts carried out by the criminal organization. The lodge treats violence as reciprocal service between lodges and provides financial support to the families of members killed during its operations.

records.l: the lodge's extortion, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The lodge extorts money from local companies in exchange for leaving them alone. Max Linder & Co. pays five hundred dollars, Walker Brothers is pressed for five dollars after offering one hundred, and other companies make regular contributions; the lodge has also used arson and threats to force compliance.

records.l: the article “Law and Order!”, The Valley of Fear, When the drinks which followed the ceremony of initiation had all been
records.s: The article “Law and Order!” is written by James Stanger and condemns the region's murders, criminal organization, and reign of terror. McGinty reads from it at the meeting, rejects its criticism as “slush,” and uses it to justify ordering a violent warning against Stanger.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: McMurdo learns from Brother Morris that the lodge’s activities include murder and that members live under Boss McGinty’s control. McGinty warns McMurdo against associating with Morris, but police Captain Marvin arrests McMurdo for involvement in the attack on the Herald office. McGinty arranges a defense, and the court releases McMurdo and the other accused Scowrers because the evidence is inconclusive and citizens provide an alibi. The acquittal is applauded by lodge members but condemned by others who call the men murderers and threaten revenge.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: McMurdo suffers a headache and a swollen, branded arm after his lodge initiation, then meets Brother Morris on Miller Hill. He conceals the meeting from Boss McGinty, is arrested by Captain Marvin for the attack on the Herald office, and is released after the court finds the evidence insufficient.

records.l: Brother Morris, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Brother Morris tells McMurdo that the Freeman’s society has forced him into crime and threatens his life and family if he leaves. He describes taking part in a murder and warns McMurdo that the lodge’s violence has made Vermissa a valley of fear.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Boss McGinty visits McMurdo to question him about his meeting with Brother Morris and warns him not to associate with Morris, whom the lodge considers disloyal. He provides McMurdo with an alibi through six citizens, including himself, and promises to arrange his legal defense.

records.l: Captain Marvin, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Captain Marvin leads police into McMurdo’s house, disarms him, and arrests him for involvement in the beating of Editor Stanger. He searches the house for the concealed coining plant but apparently finds nothing.

records.l: Editor Stanger, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Editor Stanger is severely beaten during an attack at the Herald office but is reported to be in no immediate danger of death. He later testifies that he cannot identify the attackers beyond saying that the first man who struck him wore a moustache.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Freeman’s society is described as an organization that initially appears to be a benefit club and meeting place but has become a coercive criminal society in Vermissa. It controls its members through threats, punishment, and violence, and its local lodge is associated with the attack on the Herald office.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Scowrers are identified as the violent members of the Freeman’s society who terrorize Vermissa and are blamed for the attack on the Herald office. McMurdo and other accused men are called Scowrers by hostile townspeople after their release.

records.l: the police, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The police guard the Herald office with Winchester rifles and arrest McMurdo and other suspected participants in the attack. Their case fails in court because witnesses cannot reliably identify the attackers, and the bench implies that the police acted with excessive zeal.

records.l: Miller Hill, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Miller Hill is a winter-deserted public park in the center of Vermissa, overlooking the town, valley, mines, factories, and surrounding ranges. Brother Morris uses the place to meet McMurdo privately.

records.l: Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: Vermissa is a grimy mining town surrounded by mines and factories, where the Freeman’s society exercises powerful influence. Its residents live under fear of murder and retaliation, while the police struggle to secure convictions against the Scowrers.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Valley of Fear is Morris’s name for the valley around Vermissa, where the threat of murder hangs over the population. He describes terror as filling the hearts of the people from dusk until dawn.

records.l: the Herald office, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Herald office is attacked by members of the Freeman’s society because the Herald has opposed the society. Police guards armed with Winchester rifles are later assigned to defend the office.

records.l: the initiation ceremony, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The lodge initiation leaves McMurdo with a painful branded arm and the effects of heavy drinking. It binds him to the lodge through an oath of loyalty and introduces him to its violent discipline.

records.l: the attack on the Herald office, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The attack on the Herald office seriously injures Editor Stanger and leads to the arrest of McMurdo and several other suspected Scowrers. The prosecution cannot establish their identities because the witnesses were confused and the lighting was uncertain.

records.l: the arrest and acquittal of Jack McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: McMurdo is arrested at home by Captain Marvin while Boss McGinty is visiting him. He spends the night in a common cell with Baldwin and other accused men, but lodge members provide whisky and cards, and he is released after the next day’s hearing.

records.l: the court hearing, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: At the court hearing, witnesses for the prosecution admit that they cannot confidently identify the attackers, while six citizens testify that the accused men were at a card party during the attack. The magistrate dismisses the case and nearly apologizes to the defendants, while implicitly censuring Captain Marvin and the police.

records.l: the Scowrers' terror and criminal rule, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
records.s: The Scowrers’ terror and criminal rule force members to participate in violence and prevent them from leaving the society safely. Brother Morris recounts that a murder committed by the group left him excommunicated, morally condemned, and afraid that his wife and children would be killed.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack McMurdo’s arrest and acquittal increase his popularity among the Scowrers, while Ettie Shafter unsuccessfully urges him to abandon the criminal organization. Lawler and Andrews, assisted by other men, murder Crow Hill manager Josiah H. Dunn and engineer Menzies, and the lodge celebrates the killings along with Ted Baldwin’s murder of William Hales. Boss McGinty then assigns McMurdo to kill Chester Wilcox, the chief foreman of the Iron Dike Company, despite Wilcox’s wife, children, and hired help being in the house.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack McMurdo gains prestige among the Scowrers after his arrest and acquittal, and they regard him as capable of devising and carrying out violent schemes. He refuses Ettie Shafter’s request that he leave the lodge, but promises that within a year he will find an honourable way to leave the valley. After witnessing the Crow Hill murders, he accepts Boss McGinty’s assignment to attack Chester Wilcox.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Ettie Shafter remains deeply in love with Jack McMurdo but fears marrying a man regarded as a criminal. She begs him to abandon the lodge and proposes that they flee with her father to another city, the West, or Europe. McMurdo refuses to leave immediately but promises to depart the valley within a year, which gives her some hope.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Boss McGinty views McMurdo as an unusually capable instrument of the lodge and assigns him to important violent work. He celebrates the Crow Hill and Gilmerton killings with the lodge and then orders McMurdo to kill Chester Wilcox, chief foreman of the Iron Dike Company.

records.l: Ted Baldwin, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Ted Baldwin resents McMurdo’s rapid rise but avoids confronting him because McMurdo is ready to fight. Baldwin leads the party that murders William Hales of Stake Royal and is honored by the lodge for the deed.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The Scowrers are a violent secret society whose members carry out murders, intimidation, and blackmail against mine owners and others who oppose them. They celebrate the killings at Crow Hill and Stake Royal, causing the shadow over Vermissa to fall darker.

records.l: Lawler, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Lawler arrives in Vermissa with Andrews under orders from the County Delegate to carry out a secret operation. He is an experienced assassin who has completed fourteen such commissions, and he refuses to reveal the immediate target before the work is done.

records.l: Andrews, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Andrews arrives with Lawler as one of the men sent to perform a secret assassination. Though young, cheerful, and a total abstainer, he shoots Josiah H. Dunn in the stomach during the Crow Hill attack.

records.l: Chester Wilcox, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Chester Wilcox is the chief foreman of the Iron Dike Company and a scarred former colour sergeant who is armed and reputed to shoot quickly and accurately. The Scowrers have already made two unsuccessful attempts to kill him, and Boss McGinty orders Jack McMurdo to attack him at his isolated home.

records.l: the miners, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The miners gather at Crow Hill before the day’s work begins and witness the attack on the manager and engineer. They initially remain helpless, then some surge forward before gunfire scatters them; later, a few of the bravest return to the mine.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Vermissa is portrayed as a valley darkened by fear of the Scowrers. The organization operates there through the lodge and uses violence against mine owners and others who resist it.

records.l: Crow Hill, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Crow Hill is a large mine whose New England manager, Josiah H. Dunn, has maintained order and discipline despite the surrounding reign of terror. Lawler, Andrews, and several accomplices attack there and murder Dunn and the engineer Menzies.

records.l: Iron Dike Company, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The Iron Dike Company employs Chester Wilcox as its chief foreman. Its isolated crossroads house becomes the planned site of a Scowrer attack intended to kill Wilcox and everyone with him.

records.l: the arrest and acquittal of Jack McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Jack McMurdo’s arrest and acquittal, occurring on the very night he joined the lodge, make him more popular among his fellow Scowrers. The event gives him a reputation for boldness and strengthens their belief that he is suited for violent work.

records.l: the Crow Hill murders, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: The Crow Hill murders occur when Andrews shoots manager Josiah H. Dunn and another assassin shoots him again as he tries to escape. Engineer Menzies attacks the killers with an iron spanner and is shot twice in the face; the gang then escapes through the mist without being identified.

records.l: the planned attack on Chester Wilcox, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: Boss McGinty assigns Jack McMurdo, with Manders and Reilly, to kill Chester Wilcox at the isolated Iron Dike crossroads. McGinty suggests placing blasting powder at the front door, a plan that would also kill Wilcox’s wife, three children, and hired help.

records.l: the oath of secrecy and fidelity, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
records.s: McMurdo tells Ettie Shafter that he is under oath not to reveal the lodge’s business, even to her. He says that breaking the oath would mean breaking his word and deserting his comrades, and he argues that the lodge would not let a man leave with its secrets.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: McMurdo organized an attempt to kill Chester Wilcox with the help of Manders and Reilly by placing quarry powder against Wilcox's isolated house and blowing it up. Wilcox had moved his family and arranged police protection the day before, so the explosion destroyed an empty house. McMurdo vowed to continue pursuing Wilcox, and newspapers later reported that Wilcox had been shot at from an ambuscade. The unit describes the Society of Freemen and the Scowrers as responsible for numerous killings and acts of terror across the Valley of Fear.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: McMurdo planned and carried out an attempt to kill Chester Wilcox with Manders and Reilly. After learning that Wilcox had escaped, he vowed to continue pursuing him, and he was believed to be responsible for the later ambuscade in which Wilcox was shot at.

records.l: Chester Wilcox, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: Chester Wilcox was marked for destruction because of the Society of Freemen's campaign of violence. He moved himself and his family to safer quarters under police protection the day before McMurdo's attack, and he was later reported to have been shot at from an ambuscade.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The Society of Freemen used organized violence to spread fear over the district. Its members and associates carried out attacks, killings, mutilations, and explosions against victims who opposed or challenged them.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The Scowrers were responsible for deeds that spread a rule of fear across the great and rich district. Their crimes included shootings, murders, mutilation, and the blowing up of a family.

records.l: isolated house (Chester Wilcox's house), The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The isolated house where Chester Wilcox had lived was about five miles away in an adjacent valley. McMurdo and his companions destroyed it with quarry powder, but it was empty because Wilcox had moved his family the previous day.

records.l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The Valley of Fear lay under the shadow of the Scowrers' terror. Although spring brought running brooks and blossoming trees, the people living there had no hope under the continuing violence, and the situation was especially dark in early summer 1875.

records.l: the planned attack on Chester Wilcox, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: McMurdo organized the attempt with Manders and Reilly, approaching at night with pistols and a sack of quarry powder. They set the powder against Wilcox's house and detonated it, but the attempt failed because Wilcox and his family had already moved away.

records.l: destruction of Chester Wilcox's house, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: McMurdo, Manders, and Reilly blew up Chester Wilcox's house with quarry powder. The explosion tore down the building, but it accomplished nothing because the house was empty.

records.l: shooting of Chester Wilcox, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: Several weeks after the failed attack on his house, newspapers reported that Chester Wilcox had been shot at from an ambuscade. The text presents the shooting as connected to McMurdo's unfinished pursuit of him.

records.l: the Scowrers' terror and criminal rule, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The Scowrers imposed a rule of fear over the district and kept the men and women of the Valley of Fear under an oppressive yoke. Their terror was described as especially dark and hopeless in early summer 1875.

records.l: crimes of the Society of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, McMurdo thought long and deeply over the commission which had been so
records.s: The Society of Freemen's crimes included the planned shootings of Policemen Hunt and Evans, the shooting of Mrs. Larbey while she nursed her injured husband, the killings of the elder Jenkins and his brother, the mutilation of James Murdoch, the blowing up of the Staphouse family, and the murders of the Stendals.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: McMurdo learns from Morris’s letter that Pinkerton detective Birdy Edwards is investigating the Scowrers in the valley and warns the lodge. He identifies Edwards as the man using the name Steve Wilson and proposes luring him to Widow MacNamara’s house so the lodge can kill him. McMurdo also begins an escape plan with Ettie Shafter, promising to send for her if he must flee. The lodge accepts his plan and prepares to attack Edwards.

records.l: McMurdo, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: McMurdo has become Inner Deacon and an influential adviser to the Freemen. After learning of the Pinkerton investigation, he destroys incriminating papers, warns the lodge, identifies Birdy Edwards as Steve Wilson, and plans to lure him into an ambush. He also arranges an escape plan with Ettie Shafter.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: McGinty remains Bodymaster and dismisses reports that the Scowrers are threatened. At the lodge meeting, he accepts McMurdo’s warning about Birdy Edwards and agrees to the plan to bring Edwards to Widow MacNamara’s house.

records.l: Brother Morris, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Morris, a weaker and troubled member of the order, tells McMurdo that a Pinkerton detective is investigating the Scowrers. He gives McMurdo a letter from a friend and asks him to take responsibility for dealing with the threat.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Ettie Shafter meets McMurdo when he visits her secretly and recognizes that he is in danger. She agrees to leave the valley with him whenever he sends her a signal.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Birdy Edwards is described as Pinkerton’s best man and as the detective investigating the Scowrers for the corporations and railroads. He is operating under the name Steve Wilson and lodging at Hobson’s Patch. McMurdo and the lodge plan to lure and kill him.

records.l: Steve Wilson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Steve Wilson is the name under which Birdy Edwards is operating. He met McMurdo on the cars, claimed to be a newspaper reporter, questioned him about the Scowrers, paid him for information, and sent coded material through the telegraph bureau.

records.l: Pinkerton’s, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Pinkerton has taken charge of the investigation into the Scowrers on behalf of powerful corporations and railroads. Its best investigator, Birdy Edwards, is working in the valley.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The Scowrers are facing organized opposition from citizens, corporations, railroads, and the Pinkerton organization. Their lodge leaders respond to the investigation by planning to kill Birdy Edwards.

records.l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The Freemen regard McMurdo as an increasingly important adviser. Although they have terrorized Vermissa, citizens are beginning to organize against them and distribute firearms among law-abiding people.

records.l: Lodge 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The lodge is the Scowrers’ organized body and meets on Saturday evenings under strict guard and coded signs. It hears McMurdo’s warning about Birdy Edwards, appoints a committee to consider the matter, and approves the plan to ambush him.

records.l: the corporations, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Five large corporations and two railroads have joined forces to destroy the Scowrers. They have engaged Pinkerton to investigate and gather evidence against them.

records.l: Vermissa, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Vermissa is under the Scowrers’ reign of terror, though its citizens are beginning to band together against them. Rumors also circulate there about secret meetings and the distribution of firearms.

records.l: Vermissa Valley, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The valley is the area where the Scowrers operate and where Birdy Edwards is conducting his investigation. McMurdo believes events there will soon become dangerous and may force him and Ettie to leave.

records.l: Hobson’s Patch, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: Hobson’s Patch is where Birdy Edwards, under the name Steve Wilson, is lodging. McMurdo plans to go there to locate him through the telegraph operator.

records.l: the Scowrers' terror and criminal rule, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The reign of terror is at its height, with the Scowrers powerful, armed, and confident that their opponents cannot seriously challenge them. The threat of organized law and investigation begins to make their leaders fear retribution.

records.l: the lodge meeting, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: At the lodge meeting, McMurdo claims urgency and announces that Birdy Edwards is investigating the Scowrers. The members choose a committee, and the leaders agree to lure Edwards to McMurdo’s house and kill him.

records.l: the investigation of the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The investigation is being conducted by Pinkerton for five corporations and two railroads. Birdy Edwards is collecting evidence that could send members of the lodge to prison.

records.l: the Scowrers’ violence, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The Scowrers’ violence has been so constant that their members have treated it as part of ordinary life. The possibility of legal retribution now makes them confront the consequences of the violence they have inflicted on others.

records.l: the planned killing of Birdy Edwards, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: McMurdo proposes telling Birdy Edwards that he can sell him the lodge’s secrets and arranging a meeting at Widow MacNamara’s house. The lodge leaders plan to gather there, shut the door behind Edwards, and kill him.

records.l: the threat to the lodge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The threat to the lodge comes from Birdy Edwards’s investigation and from the financial and organizational support of the corporations and railroads. McMurdo warns that Edwards may already obtain the lodge’s secrets and that his evidence could send every man present to prison.

records.l: the letter from Morris’s friend, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The letter reports that five corporations and two railroads have organized against the Scowrers and that Pinkerton’s best investigator, Birdy Edwards, is operating in the valley. Its postscript says the information was written in a cipher handled daily in the telegraph service.

records.l: the secret investigation, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: The secret investigation is being carried out by Birdy Edwards under the false identity of Steve Wilson. He poses as a reporter, asks questions about the Scowrers, and transmits coded messages through the telegraph bureau.

records.l: the escape plan, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
records.s: McMurdo tells Ettie Shafter that he may need to flee the valley and instructs her to come to the depot waiting room whenever he sends word. He intends to take her to the place where he came from and leave her with a good woman until they can marry.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Birdy Edwards, posing as McMurdo, lures the Scowrers into a trap at his house and reveals that he is a Pinkerton’s detective. Captain Marvin and armed Mine Police surround the house, disarm the gang, and arrest its members. Edwards explains how he infiltrated the Scowrers and secretly prevented or limited several of their crimes. The Scowrers are later tried, with McGinty and eight chief followers executed, while Edwards eventually flees repeated vengeance attempts.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Birdy Edwards reveals that he has been posing as McMurdo while infiltrating the Scowrers for Pinkerton’s. He traps the gang at his house, helps Captain Marvin arrest them, and explains that he prevented or reduced several crimes while gathering evidence against the organization. After the trial, he is pursued by surviving Scowrers, changes his name several times, and eventually lives in England as John Douglas.

records.l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: John McGinty helps plan the capture and killing of the supposed detective, whom he believes is McMurdo’s informant. He is trapped with the other Scowrers, arrested by Captain Marvin, and later executed on the scaffold after the trial.

records.l: Captain Marvin, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Captain Marvin assists Birdy Edwards in the operation against the Scowrers. He leads the armed Mine Police surrounding Edwards’s house, prevents McGinty from escaping, disarms the gang, and takes them into custody.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The Scowrers gather at McMurdo’s house to capture and kill Birdy Edwards, believing him to be an informant. Edwards exposes himself as a Pinkerton’s detective, and the gang is surrounded, disarmed, arrested, tried, and broken up.

records.l: Pinkerton’s, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Pinkerton’s employs Birdy Edwards to infiltrate and destroy the Scowrers. Edwards operates in secret, with only Captain Marvin and his employers knowing his true identity.

records.l: Ettie Shafter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Ettie Shafter receives a sealed note from Scanlan and boards a special train with her much-muffled lover to leave the Valley of Fear. Ten days later, she marries Edwards in Chicago, with Jacob Shafter as a witness.

records.l: Chicago, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: Chicago is where Edwards was made a Freemen before traveling to the coal valleys, and where he later marries Ettie. After surviving two attempts on his life there, he leaves under a changed name for California.

records.l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The Valley of Fear is freed from the Scowrers after their organization is exposed, arrested, and prosecuted. Edwards’s work lifts the cloud of their control, though surviving members later pursue him for revenge.

records.l: the capture of the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The capture of the Scowrers takes place at McMurdo’s isolated house. Edwards admits his identity, while Captain Marvin and forty armed men surround the building, force the gang to surrender, and take its members into custody.

records.l: trial of the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
records.s: The trial of the Scowrers is held far from the Valley of Fear so their supporters cannot intimidate the guardians of the law. Edwards gives an unshaken account of their organization and crimes; McGinty and eight chief followers are executed, while more than fifty others receive prison sentences.

records.l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: John Douglas was acquitted at Quarter Sessions after being referred to a higher court, but Sherlock Holmes warned that he was unsafe in England. Two months later, Cecil Barker reported that Douglas had been lost overboard from the Palmyra near St. Helena, though Holmes concluded that the death had been staged and was murder. Holmes attributed the crime to Professor Moriarty, whose London-based organization had taken over the effort to eliminate Douglas. Holmes said that Moriarty could be defeated, but asked for time to act.

records.l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: John Douglas was acquitted at the Quarter Sessions on the ground that he had acted in self-defense. Holmes urged that he be taken out of England, but he was later reported lost overboard from the Palmyra near St. Helena.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Sherlock Holmes warned that John Douglas faced greater danger in England than the danger he had escaped. After receiving an enigmatic note and hearing of Douglas's death, Holmes concluded that the death was murder organized from London by Moriarty. He said Moriarty could be defeated but asked for time to plan a response.

records.l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Cecil Barker brought Sherlock Holmes the news of John Douglas's reported death and believed that the Scowrers had murdered him. He expressed anger and helplessness at the prospect of being unable to retaliate against Moriarty.

records.l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Ivy Douglas sent a cable reporting that Jack Douglas had been lost overboard in a gale off St. Helena and that no one knew how the accident had occurred.

records.l: Professor Moriarty, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Professor Moriarty is identified by Holmes as the criminal mastermind behind John Douglas's death. Holmes says that Moriarty first used his machinery to locate Douglas, then advised on the crime, and finally intervened personally after an agent failed.

records.l: the Scowrers, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The Scowrers are described by Cecil Barker as a vindictive nest of criminals who might have murdered John Douglas. Holmes rejects the idea that they acted alone, attributing the crime to a more powerful hand.

records.l: Moriarty's criminal organization, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The organization behind Moriarty is described as a huge criminal organization with machinery capable of locating and eliminating a victim. Its resources were used in an extravagant but effective effort to destroy John Douglas.

records.l: England, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: England is presented as unsafe for John Douglas after his acquittal. Holmes warns that forces in England may be more dangerous than those Douglas had escaped.

records.l: London, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: London is identified by Holmes as the source of the crime against John Douglas, rather than America.

records.l: Palmyra, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The Palmyra carried John Douglas and his companions toward South Africa. It reached Cape Town after Douglas was reported lost overboard in a gale off St. Helena.

records.l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The John Douglas case was referred to a higher court, and Douglas was acquitted at the Quarter Sessions for acting in self-defense. The later reported death of Douglas leads Holmes to conclude that the case involves a planned murder organized from London.

records.l: the enigmatic note, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The enigmatic note was slipped into Sherlock Holmes's letter box two months after the trial. It read, "Dear me, Mr. Holmes. Dear me!" and had neither a superscription nor a signature; Holmes treated it as evidence of deviltry.

records.l: the cable reporting John Douglas's death, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The cable reporting John Douglas's death was sent by Ivy Douglas to Cecil Barker. It stated that Jack had been lost overboard in a gale off St. Helena and that the circumstances were unknown, but Holmes believed the report concealed a staged murder.

records.l: John Douglas's disappearance at sea, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: John Douglas's disappearance at sea was reported as a fall overboard during a gale off St. Helena. Holmes insisted that it was not an accident and that Douglas had been murdered.

records.l: the planned murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The planned murder of John Douglas was carried out through a London-based criminal operation associated with Moriarty. Holmes describes it as an unusually elaborate use of a great brain and a large organization to ensure Douglas's destruction.

records.l: the danger to John Douglas in England, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: The danger to John Douglas in England was considered greater than the danger he had escaped. Holmes advised his wife to get him out of England at any cost because he believed there was no safety for him there.

records.l: Moriarty's criminal operation, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Moriarty's criminal operation involved locating John Douglas, advising on how to deal with him, and finally taking direct action when an agent failed. Holmes recognized the operation as the work of a master criminal rather than the Scowrers' crude violence.

records.l: Holmes's planned counteraction, The Valley of Fear, Epilogue
records.s: Holmes's planned counteraction is only foreshadowed in this unit. He tells Cecil Barker that Moriarty can be defeated, but asks for time while he considers how to respond.

records.l: The Valley of Fear
records.s: The document is a two-part Sherlock Holmes mystery linking the apparent murder of John Douglas at Birlstone Manor House to the violent history of the Vermissa Valley. In Part I, Holmes and Dr. Watson receive Fred Porlock’s cipher warning that Douglas is in danger, followed immediately by Inspector Alec MacDonald’s news that Douglas has been shot. At Birlstone, Holmes, MacDonald, White Mason, and Watson investigate a body apparently killed by a sawed-off shotgun in a house isolated by a moat and raised drawbridge. Clues include a card marked “V.V. 341,” a missing wedding ring, a forearm brand, a bicycle, and evidence suggesting escape through a window. Cecil James Barker and Mrs. Douglas offer incomplete accounts, and Holmes exposes their fabricated footprint and altered timing of the alarm. He finds clothing and other items weighted in the moat with a missing dumb-bell, then forces Barker to reveal that Douglas is alive. The dead man is Ted Baldwin, who attacked Douglas and was accidentally killed in a struggle. Douglas, Barker, and Mrs. Douglas disguised Baldwin as Douglas so that Douglas’s American enemies would believe him dead. Part II is Douglas’s account of the American past that produced the danger. Under the name Jack McMurdo, he arrives in Vermissa in 1875, enters the Eminent Order of Freemen, also called the Scowrers, and gains the confidence of their brutal leader, Bodymaster Jack McGinty of Lodge 341. McMurdo appears to be a criminal capable of counterfeiting and murder, is branded by the lodge, courts Ettie Shafter despite Baldwin’s hostility, and participates in or witnesses the Scowrers’ assaults, extortion, bombings, and murders. Yet he is really Birdy Edwards, a Pinkerton’s detective infiltrating the organization. He helps restrict its crimes where possible, lures McGinty and the leading Scowrers into a police trap, and secures their arrest; McGinty and eight chief followers are executed. The ending returns to England. Although Douglas is acquitted, Holmes warns that revenge still threatens him. Douglas is later reported lost overboard from the Palmyra near St. Helena, but Holmes concludes that the death was staged as murder by Professor Moriarty’s London organization. Holmes believes Moriarty can be defeated, but needs time to act.

In Part I, Holmes and Dr. Watson receive Fred Porlock’s cipher warning that Douglas is in danger, followed immediately by Inspector Alec MacDonald’s news that Douglas has been shot. Douglas, Barker, and Mrs. Douglas disguised Baldwin as Douglas so that Douglas’s American enemies would believe him dead. Part II is Douglas’s account of the American past that produced the danger. Under the name Jack McMurdo, he arrives in Vermissa in 1875, enters the Eminent Order of Freemen—also called the Scowrers—and gains the confidence of their brutal leader, Bodymaster Jack McGinty of Lodge 341. McMurdo appears to be a criminal capable of counterfeiting and murder, is branded by the lodge, courts Ettie Shafter despite Baldwin’s hostility, and participates in or witnesses the Scowrers’ assaults, extortion, bombings, and murders.
