records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, PREFACE
records.s: Arthur Conan Doyle bids farewell to Sherlock Holmes, expressing hope that Holmes and Watson may find a place in an imagined Valhalla. He recounts Holmes's career from his debut in A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four through the short stories published in The Strand Magazine and the collections that followed. Doyle explains that he once ended Holmes's career after The Memoirs but later revived him in response to public demand. He thanks readers for their loyalty and for the distraction and change of thought provided by the stories.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, PREFACE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is presented as a popular fictional detective whose adventures began in A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four. Arthur Conan Doyle says that Holmes was once brought to an end but was later revived, and he now bids Holmes farewell while acknowledging the public's continuing interest in him.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, PREFACE
records.s: Watson is mentioned alongside Sherlock Holmes as his companion in an imagined Valhalla for fictional characters. Doyle suggests that Holmes and Watson might remain there while another detective and companion take their place on the stage.

records.l: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, PREFACE
records.s: Arthur Conan Doyle explains that he created and wrote the Sherlock Holmes stories, initially intending to end Holmes after The Memoirs. He later responded to public demand by reviving Holmes and says that writing the lighter Holmes sketches did not prevent him from working in history, poetry, historical novels, psychic research, and drama.

records.l: Holmes's career, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, PREFACE
records.s: Holmes's career began with A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four, published between 1887 and 1889, followed by the first short story, A Scandal in Bohemia, in 1891. By this preface, the adventures comprise fifty-six stories in four collections, with twelve additional stories collected in The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes; the career spans the later Victorian Era, the reign of Edward, and the years afterward.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Baron Adelbert Gruner, an Austrian suspected of murdering his first wife and now planning to marry Violet de Merville. Sir James Damery explains that an unnamed client wants Holmes to prevent the marriage because Violet is completely devoted to Gruner despite his past. Holmes confronts Gruner, who threatens him indirectly and claims that Violet has been prepared to reject any warnings against him. Holmes recruits Shinwell Johnson to search the criminal underworld for information about Gruner.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Baron Gruner after hearing that Gruner intends to marry Violet de Merville. He visits Gruner, warns him to abandon the marriage, and receives veiled threats involving Le Brun. Holmes also calls on Shinwell Johnson to gather information about Gruner.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Dr. Watson reads Sir James Damery's request to Holmes and joins the interview at Baker Street. He suggests that Holmes speak directly with Violet and later discusses Gruner's danger with Holmes at Simpson's.

records.l: Sir James, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Sir James Damery approaches Sherlock Holmes on behalf of an unnamed client who wants Baron Gruner's proposed marriage to Violet de Merville prevented. He explains Violet's devotion to Gruner, describes Gruner's criminal history and interests, and gives Holmes Gruner's address and a private telephone contact.

records.l: Baron Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Baron Adelbert Gruner is described as a wealthy, handsome, persuasive, and highly dangerous Austrian suspected of murdering his wife. He intends to marry Violet de Merville and claims that she knows his past but accepts his explanations. When Holmes confronts him, Gruner warns Holmes to withdraw and refers to the violent fate of the French agent Le Brun.

records.l: Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Violet de Merville is described as young, wealthy, beautiful, accomplished, and strong-willed. She is completely in love with Baron Gruner, refuses to hear criticism of him, and plans to marry him despite his criminal past.

records.l: General de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: General de Merville is Violet's father and a former strong soldier who has become demoralized and unable to oppose Gruner effectively. He is not the unnamed client, although his distress over Violet's proposed marriage is central to the situation.

records.l: the illustrious client's unnamed principal, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: The unnamed principal is an old friend of General de Merville who has taken a paternal interest in Violet since childhood. He asks Sir James Damery to engage Holmes to prevent the marriage but insists on remaining personally uninvolved and anonymous.

records.l: Shinwell Johnson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Shinwell Johnson is a former dangerous villain who now works as Holmes's agent in London's criminal underworld. Holmes sends him to search for damaging information about Baron Gruner.

records.l: the death of Baron Gruner's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Baron Gruner's first wife died in what was called an accident in the Splügen Pass. Holmes believes Gruner murdered her, though a legal technicality and the suspicious death of a witness prevented his conviction.

records.l: the marriage between Baron Adelbert Gruner and Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: Baron Gruner plans to marry Violet de Merville the following month. Sir James Damery and his unnamed principal seek Holmes's help to prevent the marriage because Gruner is believed to be a murderer and Violet refuses to accept warnings against him.

records.l: the investigation and counterplot, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT
records.s: The investigation begins when Sir James Damery asks Holmes to stop Gruner's marriage to Violet. Holmes studies Gruner, confronts him at Vernon Lodge, and uses Shinwell Johnson to seek further evidence through London's criminal underworld.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes meets Shinwell Johnson and Kitty Winter to discuss stopping Adelbert Gruner's intended marriage. Kitty explains that Gruner abused and ruined her, may have committed other murders, and is pursuing another woman who dismisses evidence against him as slander. She describes Gruner's brown leather book containing photographs and details of women he has ruined, and identifies where he may keep it in his house. Holmes considers having Kitty confront the intended bride and asks Kitty to return the next evening.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Kitty Winter about Adelbert Gruner and learns that she may be able to help stop Gruner's marriage. He considers arranging for Kitty to meet Gruner's intended bride and is told where Gruner may keep his brown leather book.

records.l: Shinwell Johnson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Shinwell Johnson brings Kitty Winter to Sherlock Holmes within an hour of receiving Holmes's message. He has been telling Kitty about Gruner's pursuit of another woman and confirms that Gruner's fancy crockery would not interest burglars.

records.l: Kitty Winter, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Kitty Winter declares intense hatred for Adelbert Gruner, whom she says made her what she is, and offers to help put him where he belongs. She says Gruner used and ruined her, may have been responsible for other murders, and kept a book documenting the women he had ruined. She agrees to return to Holmes and to confront Gruner's intended bride if arranged.

records.l: Baron Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Adelbert Gruner is pursuing marriage with a woman who has been told about his murder but believes the accusations against him are slanders. Kitty says that Gruner collects and takes pride in women he has ruined, and that he hinted to her that other people had died within a month of his speaking about them. He is described as precise and tidy, with an inner study containing papers and possibly his brown leather book.

records.l: Adelbert Gruner's intended bride, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Adelbert Gruner's intended bride is described as madly in love with him despite being told about his murder. She dismisses the accusations as slanders and refuses to reopen the question after hearing Gruner's account and receiving his pardon.

records.l: Adelbert Gruner's brown leather book, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Adelbert Gruner's brown leather book has a lock and Gruner's arms in gold on its cover. Kitty says it contains snapshot photographs, names, and details of women Gruner has ruined, and that he may keep it in a pigeon-hole of the old bureau in the inner study.

records.l: the Prague murder case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: The murder of Adelbert Gruner's victim is known to Gruner's intended bride, but she treats the account as slander. Kitty also suggests that Gruner may have been connected with other murders when she recalls his remarks that certain people had died within a month.

records.l: the marriage between Baron Adelbert Gruner and Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Adelbert Gruner's marriage is the matter Holmes and his associates are trying to stop. Gruner is seeking to marry another woman, despite her knowing about his alleged murder and other wrongdoing.

records.l: evidence against Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Evidence against Adelbert Gruner may come from Kitty Winter's firsthand account of how he used and ruined her, her knowledge of his references to other deaths, and his brown leather book documenting ruined women. Holmes considers presenting Kitty personally to Gruner's intended bride.

records.l: Adelbert Gruner's ruined women, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,
records.s: Adelbert Gruner's ruined women are the subjects of the collection he kept in his brown leather book. The book reportedly contains their photographs, names, and details, and Kitty says Gruner took pride in collecting them.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Miss Winter visit Violet de Merville at 104 Berkeley Square to warn her against her fiancé, Baron Gruner. Violet remains unmoved, insisting that she loves Baron Gruner and believes his past wrongdoing is behind him. Miss Winter angrily reveals that she was one of Baron Gruner's former mistresses and warns Violet that he will destroy her. Holmes prevents Miss Winter from attacking Violet and concludes that he must devise another way to intervene.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I did not see Holmes again until the following evening, when we dined
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits Violet de Merville with Miss Winter and pleads with Violet to reconsider her engagement to Baron Gruner. When Violet rejects his warnings, he restrains Miss Winter from attacking her, then decides that a fresh approach is necessary.

records.s: Dr. Watson hears Holmes recount the unsuccessful interview at their Strand restaurant. Holmes tells him that he may have a part to play in the next stage of the case.

records.s: Miss Winter accompanies Holmes to warn Violet de Merville about Baron Gruner. records.l: Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I did not see Holmes again until the following evening, when we dined
records.s: Violet de Merville receives Holmes and Miss Winter but remains cold, self-contained, and unmoved by their warnings. She says that she loves Baron Gruner, believes he has repented of the evil he has done, and dismisses Miss Winter's testimony as ravings.

records.s: Baron Gruner has apparently learned of Holmes's visit and has influenced Violet against Holmes and his allies. He is described by Miss Winter as a man who has exploited and ruined many women, while Violet believes that he has sincerely repented.

records.s: Violet de Merville remains firmly committed to her engagement to Baron Gruner despite Holmes's warnings and Miss Winter's firsthand accusations. She believes that her influence can raise Baron Gruner to a better moral level.

records.s: Violet acknowledges that Baron Gruner has had a stormy life involving bitter hatred and what she regards as unjust accusations. She says that she knows of three episodes involving women and has been assured that he has sincerely repented.

Kitty Winter throws vitriol through the window, severely disfiguring Baron Gruner. Holmes and Dr. John Watson then return to Baker Street, having protected Kitty Winter and carried out their plan.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes is attacked by two men and suffers two lacerated scalp wounds and considerable bruising, though he deliberately exaggerates the seriousness of his condition. He sends Dr. John Watson to investigate Baron Adelbert Gruner and secretly joins the operation, appearing at Gruner's house in bloody bandages before escaping through a window.

records.s: The two attackers, respectably dressed and armed with sticks, assault Sherlock Holmes outside the Café Royal. They escape through the Café Royal and Glasshouse Street, and their escape appears to have been carefully prepared.

records.s: The vitriol attack on Baron Gruner is carried out by Kitty Winter through an open window. It burns his face, leaves one eye white and glazed and the other red and inflamed, and causes him agonizing pain.

records.s: The Ming saucer is a delicate deep-blue piece of genuine egg-shell pottery from the Ming dynasty. Sherlock Holmes uses it to support Dr. John Watson's false identity as a collector and to entice Baron Adelbert Gruner into receiving him.

records.s: The newspaper report announces that Sherlock Holmes has suffered a murderous assault by two men with sticks and is in a precarious condition. Later reports falsely maintain that Holmes is near death and has developed erysipelas, reinforcing his counterplot.

records.s: Vitriol is thrown through Baron Adelbert Gruner's window and eats into his face, ears, and chin. It blinds or severely damages his eyes and leaves his features badly discolored and deformed.

records.l: Baker Street, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, And it did. Their blow fell--or his blow rather, for never could I
records.s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes recovers while pretending to be near death and where Dr. John Watson receives his instructions. Dr. John Watson returns there after the operation at Baron Adelbert Gruner's house.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. Watson that he stole Baron Adelbert Gruner's incriminating book to prevent Gruner's marriage to Violet de Merville. Holmes believes the book will destroy Violet's idealized view of Gruner by exposing his moral corruption, whereas his physical injuries might make her love him as a martyr. Sir James takes the book and the blue saucer away, and the marriage is subsequently canceled. Kitty Winter faces prosecution for throwing vitriol, but receives the lowest possible sentence because of extenuating circumstances.

records.s: Sherlock Holmes, pale and exhausted after the evening's events, explains that he used Dr. Watson's distraction and the blue saucer to steal Baron Adelbert Gruner's incriminating book. He says the book is necessary to break Violet de Merville's attachment to Gruner and is later threatened with prosecution for burglary, though he has not stood trial.

records.s: Dr. Watson recounts the Baron's transformation to Sherlock Holmes and helps distract Gruner by discussing Chinese pottery and using a blue saucer. He later recognizes the armorial bearings on Sir James's carriage and realizes who their client is, but Holmes refuses to identify him.

records.s: Baron Adelbert Gruner possesses a compromising book recording his sexual or romantic conduct and takes precautions against burglary. He is distracted while Sherlock Holmes obtains the book, and his planned marriage to Violet de Merville is subsequently canceled.

records.s: Violet de Merville is expected to reject Baron Adelbert Gruner after learning the contents of his incriminating book. Holmes believes that Gruner's injuries alone would make her love him more as a disfigured martyr, but the book succeeds in bringing her back to reality.

records.s: Sir James comes to Sherlock Holmes after being summoned and listens to Holmes's account of the events. He carries away the incriminating book and the blue saucer, apparently to help ensure that the marriage is prevented; Dr. Watson infers from his carriage's armorial bearings that he is the client.

records.s: The incriminating book is a brown volume containing Baron Adelbert Gruner's own account of his sexual or romantic conduct. Sherlock Holmes steals it from Gruner's rooms and Sir James takes it away so that it can be used to prevent Gruner's marriage to Violet de Merville.

records.s: The marriage between Baron Adelbert Gruner and Violet de Merville is prevented after the incriminating book is used against Gruner. Three days later, The Morning Post reports that the marriage will not take place.

records.s: Kitty Winter's vitriol-throwing prosecution proceeds with a first police-court hearing on the grave charge. The trial reveals extenuating circumstances, and she receives the lowest sentence possible for the offense.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Sherlock Holmes recounts receiving a visit in January 1903 from James M. Dodd, who is trying to discover what happened to his missing friend Godfrey Emsworth. Dodd explains that Godfrey disappeared after being wounded in the Boer War, while Godfrey's father, Colonel Emsworth, claimed that he had gone on a voyage around the world. During a visit to Tuxbury Old Hall, Dodd is rebuffed by the Colonel and hears the butler Ralph say that he wishes Godfrey were dead. As Dodd reflects on the mystery in his bedroom, Godfrey Emsworth suddenly appears before him.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives James M. Dodd at his rooms and identifies Dodd's South African service and Imperial Yeomanry background through observation. He listens to Dodd's account of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance and begins investigating the matter through Dodd's testimony.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: John Watson is absent because he has married. Holmes says that Watson had not recorded this case and comments on Watson's value as a companion despite his tendency to write popularized accounts.

records.l: Mr. James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: James M. Dodd, a former Imperial Yeoman of the Middlesex Corps, visits Holmes to seek an explanation for Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance. He had served with Godfrey in South Africa, visited Tuxbury Old Hall, challenged Colonel Emsworth, and resolved to discover what had happened to his friend. While staying at the Hall, he hears Ralph imply that Godfrey is dead or worse, then sees Godfrey suddenly standing before him.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Godfrey Emsworth served with James M. Dodd in South Africa and was wounded by an elephant-gun bullet near Diamond Hill outside Pretoria. He later ceased communicating with Dodd, and his father said he had gone on a voyage around the world. At the end of the unit, Godfrey unexpectedly appears before Dodd in his bedroom at Tuxbury Old Hall.

records.l: Colonel Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Colonel Emsworth is Godfrey's father and a former Crimean V.C. known as a strict, intimidating man. He tells Dodd that Godfrey has gone on a voyage around the world for his health and refuses to provide the ship's name, line, or sailing date, ordering Dodd to stop asking questions.

records.l: Tuxbury Old Park, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Tuxbury Old Park is the Emsworth family property near Bedford, identified in Dodd's letter to Holmes. Dodd travels there to investigate Godfrey's disappearance and finds the estate remote and inaccessible, about five miles from the nearest station.

records.l: Tuxbury Old Hall, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Tuxbury Old Hall is a large, remote house in Tuxbury Old Park, containing features from several periods, including Elizabethan foundations, panelling, tapestry, and old pictures. Dodd stays there with Colonel Emsworth, Godfrey's mother, and the elderly servants Ralph and his wife, and Godfrey appears to him there at the end of the unit.

records.l: Godfrey's voyage around the world, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Godfrey's supposed voyage around the world is the explanation Colonel Emsworth gives for his absence. The Colonel says that Godfrey undertook the voyage because his health was poor after his experiences in Africa, but he refuses to identify the ship, shipping line, or date of departure.

records.l: the mystery of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: The mystery concerns Godfrey's silence after he was wounded in South Africa and the conflicting signs that his family is concealing what happened to him. Colonel Emsworth claims Godfrey is travelling, while Ralph says he wishes Godfrey were dead; the mystery deepens when Godfrey suddenly appears before Dodd.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth's fate, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: Godfrey's fate is initially uncertain because his father says he is travelling and Ralph reacts as if his condition is dreadful. Dodd suspects that Godfrey may have been involved in a criminal or disreputable matter, but the unit ends with Godfrey appearing alive before him.

records.l: the interview between Holmes and James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER
records.s: The interview takes place in Holmes's rooms after Dodd urgently seeks his help. Holmes identifies Dodd's background, listens to his account of Godfrey and Tuxbury Old Hall, and learns that Dodd encountered Godfrey immediately after concluding that his friend might be dead or disgraced.

records.s: The client tells Sherlock Holmes that Godfrey appeared outside his window at night and then fled into the darkness, shutting a door somewhere in the garden. The client searches the grounds and finds a detached lodge occupied by a small bearded man, who locks the building and watches him suspiciously. That night, the client sees the man inside with another figure he believes is Godfrey, but Colonel Emsworth catches him spying and orders him to leave. The client accuses Colonel Emsworth of concealing Godfrey and leaves for London, intending to seek Holmes's help.

records.l: Mr. James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The client recounts seeing Godfrey outside his window and pursuing him through the garden after Godfrey fled. He investigates a detached lodge, sees a figure he believes to be Godfrey inside, and then leaves for London to ask Sherlock Holmes for advice and assistance.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: Sherlock Holmes listens to the client's account and questions him about the newspaper being read by the little bearded man, treating that detail as essential.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: Godfrey appears pale and furtive outside the client's window before fleeing into the darkness and closing a door. The client later sees a seated man in the detached lodge whom he believes is Godfrey, although the man's face is turned away.

records.l: Colonel Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: Colonel Emsworth becomes aware that the client is watching the detached lodge and confronts him there at night. He orders the client to take an early train to London, condemns his intrusion into the family's privacy, and denies him any further welcome.

records.l: the little bearded man, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The little bearded man, dressed in a black coat and bowler hat, emerges from the detached building, locks it, and keeps its key. He watches the client from the garden and is later seen inside the building reading a small newspaper and smoking a pipe.

records.l: Tuxbury Old Hall, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The Emsworth house is large and rambling enough to conceal many people, but the client concludes that the door he heard closing was not in the house.

records.l: the garden, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The client pursues Godfrey through the garden after seeing him at the window and hears a door close somewhere ahead. He later explores the garden and locates the detached building at its far end.

records.l: the detached lodge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The detached lodge is a sizable building at the end of the garden, large enough to serve as a gardener's or gamekeeper's residence. Its windows are curtained and shuttered, but the client sees the little bearded man and another figure inside.

records.l: the mystery of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The family mystery concerns Godfrey's disappearance from public view and the Emsworth family's apparent efforts to conceal him. The client remains unable to determine the reason for the concealment.

records.l: Godfrey's concealment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: Godfrey appears to be hidden somewhere near the Emsworth house, possibly in the detached lodge. The client believes Colonel Emsworth is concealing him and insists that Godfrey may no longer be a free agent.

records.l: the client’s intrusion, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, My client had paused as one in deep emotion.
records.s: The client follows Godfrey, searches the garden, and spies through the shutter of the detached lodge. Colonel Emsworth calls this conduct a damnable intrusion into the family's privacy and says the client has become a spy rather than remaining a guest.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates why Godfrey Emsworth is secretly confined in a detached house at Tuxbury Old Park. Holmes infers that Godfrey may have leprosy from his pallid, bleached skin, the secrecy surrounding him, Ralph's disinfectant-smelling gloves, and other circumstances, and he confronts Colonel Emsworth with the conclusion. Godfrey explains that he was wounded in South Africa and exposed to leprosy after sleeping in a bed at a leper hospital. Sir James Saunders diagnoses the condition as non-infective pseudo-leprosy, or ichthyosis, rather than leprosy.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. James M. Dodd about the servants, food deliveries, local inquiries, Godfrey Emsworth's appearance, and the circumstances of his confinement. He infers that Godfrey may have leprosy, identifies the odour of disinfectant on Ralph's gloves, and writes "Leprosy" on a scrap of paper to force Colonel Emsworth to disclose the secret. Holmes brings Sir James Saunders to provide a medical opinion and explains how he eliminated criminality and insanity before adopting the leprosy theory.

records.l: Mr. James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Mr. James M. Dodd asks Holmes to investigate his old comrade Godfrey Emsworth, whom he saw looking pale and altered at a window. He accompanies Holmes to Tuxbury Old Park and insists that he must hear from Godfrey himself that he is under no restraint. Dodd learns that Godfrey's confinement was intended to conceal a serious-looking skin condition rather than a crime or imprisonment.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Godfrey Emsworth is secretly living in a detached house under the care of Mr. Kent after developing conspicuous whitish patches on his skin. He tells Mr. James M. Dodd that he was wounded in South Africa and later slept in a bed at a leper hospital, after which he feared he had contracted leprosy. Sir James Saunders determines that his condition is pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis, not infectious leprosy.

records.l: Colonel Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Colonel Emsworth angrily orders Mr. James M. Dodd and Holmes off his premises and threatens to call the police. When Holmes writes "Leprosy," Colonel Emsworth realizes that the secret has been discovered and permits them to see Godfrey. He explains that secrecy was intended to protect Godfrey from compulsory segregation.

records.l: Ralph, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Ralph, the elderly butler, is one of the few servants in the Emsworth household and carries food toward the detached house. He wears brown leather gloves, which he removes on admitting Holmes and Dodd. Holmes detects a tarry disinfectant odour coming from the gloves.

records.l: Mr. Kent, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Mr. Kent is the small bearded man who stays with Godfrey in the detached house and acts as his surgeon or attendant. He agrees that absolute secrecy is necessary and is present when Godfrey's condition is discussed. He is asked to remain with Godfrey's mother after she faints from the good news about the diagnosis.

records.l: Sir James Saunders, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Sir James Saunders accompanies Holmes to Tuxbury Old Park and waits in the carriage until called. He examines Godfrey's condition and announces that it is not leprosy but a well-marked case of pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis. He states that the condition is unsightly and obstinate but possibly curable and certainly non-infective.

records.l: Tuxbury Old Park, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Tuxbury Old Park is the Bedfordshire location to which Holmes travels with Mr. James M. Dodd to investigate Godfrey Emsworth's concealment. It contains the Emsworth mansion and the detached house where Godfrey is living.

records.l: Tuxbury Old Hall, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: The Emsworth mansion is Colonel Emsworth's house at Tuxbury Old Park. It contains Colonel Emsworth's study, where Holmes explains his reasoning, and is served by Ralph and his wife. Food is carried from the mansion toward the detached house.

records.l: the detached lodge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: The detached house at the end of the garden is where Godfrey Emsworth lives in secrecy with Mr. Kent. It is guarded by the arrangement of the household but is not a prison, since Godfrey can come out after dark. Holmes, Dodd, Colonel Emsworth, and Mr. Kent eventually enter it to speak with Godfrey.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth's wounding, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Godfrey Emsworth was hit by an elephant bullet through the shoulder during a fight at Buffelsspruit outside Pretoria. He remained on his horse until he fainted and later reached a nearby house, where his wound was still bleeding when he awoke.

records.l: Godfrey Emsworth's exposure to leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: After being wounded in South Africa, Godfrey reached what he believed was an ordinary house and slept in an unmade bed. He later learned that it was a leper hospital and that he had slept in a leper's bed, leading him to fear that he had contracted leprosy.

records.l: the mystery of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: The case concerns the secret confinement of Godfrey Emsworth in an outhouse or detached house on his family's property. Holmes considers three explanations, concealment after a crime, insanity, and disease, and concludes that the evidence most strongly supports leprosy before obtaining a medical review that identifies pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis.
records.t: The case concerns the secret confinement of Godfrey Emsworth in an outhouse or detached house on his family's property. Holmes considers three explanations—concealment after a crime, insanity, and disease—and concludes that the evidence most strongly supports leprosy before obtaining a medical review that identifies pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis.

records.l: leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Leprosy is Holmes's initial explanation for Godfrey's secrecy, altered appearance, and isolation. Godfrey feared it because he had slept in a leper's bed after being wounded in South Africa, but Sir James Saunders establishes that Godfrey does not have the disease.

records.l: pseudo-leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Pseudo-leprosy is the diagnosis Sir James Saunders gives for Godfrey's condition. He describes it as a scale-like, unsightly, obstinate, possibly curable, and certainly non-infective affection of the skin.

records.l: ichthyosis, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Ichthyosis is identified by Sir James Saunders as another name for Godfrey's condition, described as a scale-like skin affection that resembles leprosy. It is non-infective and may be curable.

records.l: insanity, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Insanity is one of the three explanations Holmes considers for Godfrey's confinement. Holmes finds it plausible because Mr. Kent appears to act as a keeper and the door is locked, but rejects it because the secrecy and other facts do not fit adequately.

records.l: segregation of leprosy patients, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Segregation for life among strangers is described as the feared consequence if Godfrey were recognized as having leprosy. Colonel Emsworth and Mr. Kent maintain secrecy to prevent authorities from taking Godfrey away, though the final diagnosis shows that such segregation is unnecessary.

records.l: the gloves, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Ralph's brown leather gloves smell strongly of a tarry disinfectant. Holmes notices the odour when Ralph removes the gloves and concludes that they have been impregnated with disinfectants, supporting his theory that the household is handling a contagious disease.

records.l: the scrap of paper, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: Holmes writes the single word "Leprosy" on a loose sheet and hands it to Colonel Emsworth. The word convinces Colonel Emsworth that Holmes has discovered the family's secret and leads him to permit the party to see Godfrey.

records.l: the leper hospital, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: The leper hospital is the South African institution Godfrey unknowingly entered after being wounded. He slept in one of its beds before learning from its medical superintendent that the building housed lepers and that his actions had exposed him to the disease.

records.l: the medical diagnosis, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as
records.s: The medical diagnosis is supplied by Sir James Saunders after Holmes brings him to examine Godfrey. It rules out leprosy and identifies pseudo-leprosy, or ichthyosis, a non-infective skin condition that is possibly curable.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Dr. John Watson visits Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street while Holmes investigates the burglary of the Crown diamond, also called the Mazarin Stone. Holmes explains that Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton are involved, and that Sylvius has come intending to kill him. Using a wax dummy, disguises, and evidence of the criminals' activities, Holmes confronts Sylvius and persuades him that surrendering the stone may secure his freedom. Holmes sends Watson to fetch the police and brings Merton into the discussion before giving the two criminals five minutes to decide whether to surrender the stone or face arrest.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Dr. John Watson visits Baker Street and finds Sherlock Holmes dangerously thin and engaged in a critical case. He agrees to help, is sent to Scotland Yard with Holmes's message, and plans to return with the police.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the missing Mazarin Stone and tracks Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton. He uses disguises, a wax dummy, and psychological pressure to confront Sylvius, learn the stone's location, and arrange for the criminals to choose between surrendering the stone and being arrested.

records.l: Billy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Billy serves Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street and explains the investigation to Dr. John Watson. He helps protect the wax dummy, admits visitors, and is sent to bring Sam Merton upstairs without using violence.

records.l: Count Negretto Sylvius, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Count Negretto Sylvius visits Baker Street intending to assault or kill Sherlock Holmes, but finds a wax dummy instead of Holmes. Holmes confronts him with evidence of his criminal history and involvement in the Crown diamond burglary, and offers him freedom if he surrenders the stone and behaves in the future.

records.l: Sam Merton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Sam Merton is identified as Count Negretto Sylvius's partner in the Crown diamond burglary. He waits outside Baker Street, is brought into the meeting by Billy, and is told that he may face imprisonment unless the stone is surrendered.

records.l: the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The Crown diamond is a missing jewel valued at one hundred thousand pounds. Sherlock Holmes has evidence connecting Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton to its theft but does not yet know where the diamond is.

records.l: the Mazarin Stone, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The Mazarin Stone is the great yellow Crown diamond that Sherlock Holmes is trying to recover. Holmes believes Count Negretto Sylvius knows its location and offers to overlook the criminals if they hand it over.

records.l: the burglary of the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The burglary of the Crown diamond has brought the Prime Minister and the Home Secretary to Baker Street to seek Sherlock Holmes's help. Holmes says he has identified witnesses and evidence involving Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton, including cabmen, a Commissionaire, and Ikey Sanders.

records.l: the attempted murder of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The attempted murder of Sherlock Holmes is anticipated when Count Negretto Sylvius comes to Baker Street with a loaded cane and a revolver. Holmes avoids the attack with the wax dummy and confronts Sylvius while keeping a weapon ready.

records.l: the investigation into the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The investigation into the Crown diamond leads Sherlock Holmes to follow Count Negretto Sylvius in disguises, observe his connection to the air-gun, and gather evidence against him and Sam Merton. The investigation has trapped both men, but the diamond's location remains unknown.

records.l: Baker Street, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: Baker Street is the setting for Sherlock Holmes's investigation and confrontation with Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton. Its bedroom provides Holmes with a second exit, while the window and wax dummy are used to watch and mislead the criminals.

records.l: the air-gun, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The air-gun was made by Straubenzee and is associated with Count Negretto Sylvius's plan against Sherlock Holmes. Holmes says he believes the weapon is in the opposite window and contrasts it with the noisy revolver.

records.l: the wax dummy of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE
records.s: The wax dummy of Sherlock Holmes is placed in the Baker Street window behind a curtain to make watchers believe Holmes is sitting there. Count Negretto Sylvius approaches it intending to strike Holmes, allowing the real Holmes to reveal himself and confront him.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: Holmes secretly leaves his bedroom through a second door and disguises himself as a dummy while Count Sylvius and Sam Merton discuss the Mazarin stone and their plans to deceive him. Holmes seizes the stone at the window, holds the criminals at gunpoint, and has the waiting police arrest them. Lord Cantlemere then visits, and Holmes secretly places the stone in his overcoat pocket to demonstrate how possession would establish a case against a receiver. Holmes retrieves the stone and sends Lord Cantlemere away, while arranging dinner with Watson.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: Holmes disguises himself as the dummy and listens from behind a curtain while Count Sylvius and Sam Merton discuss the stone. He suddenly seizes the Mazarin stone, threatens the criminals with a revolver, summons the police, and explains how he outwitted them. Later, he places the stone in Lord Cantlemere's pocket as a practical joke before recovering it.

records.l: Count Negretto Sylvius, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: Count Sylvius learns that Holmes may know about the Mazarin stone and plans to mislead him by claiming that it is in Liverpool. He intends to send Sam Merton to warn Van Seddar and arrange for the stone to be taken to Holland, but Holmes reveals himself, takes the stone, and leaves him to be arrested by the police.

records.l: Sam Merton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: Sam Merton agrees with Count Sylvius's plan to deceive Holmes and suggests killing him, though Count Sylvius rejects the idea. He is surprised when Holmes emerges from the dummy's chair and takes the stone, then acknowledges the arrest as a fair cop.

records.l: Lord Cantlemere, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: Lord Cantlemere visits Holmes to question the progress of the investigation and expresses skepticism about Holmes's abilities. Holmes places the Mazarin stone in his overcoat pocket and reveals it, demonstrating how possession could justify an arrest. Lord Cantlemere is bewildered but withdraws his criticism of Holmes's professional powers.

records.l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: The police wait below Holmes's rooms and enter after he summons them by pressing the electric bell. They handcuff Count Sylvius and Sam Merton and lead them away in a waiting cab.

records.l: the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: The Mazarin stone is kept by Count Sylvius in a secret pocket while he plans to send it out of England and have it cut into four pieces in Amsterdam. Holmes takes it from him during the confrontation and later uses it to demonstrate the significance of possession to Lord Cantlemere.

records.l: the wax dummy of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: The dummy is an effigy seated in the window and resembles Holmes so closely that Sam Merton mistakes it for a living figure. Holmes has occupied it secretly and springs from its chair to seize the stone.

records.l: arrest of the thieves, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A
records.s: The arrest of the thieves occurs after Holmes captures the Mazarin stone and summons the police. Count Sylvius and Sam Merton are handcuffed and taken away in a waiting cab.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the Harrow Weald case after Steve Dixie threatens him on behalf of an unknown employer. Mrs. Maberley explains that a supposed house agent offered an unusually generous price for The Three Gables and all its contents, but withdrew when she refused restrictive terms. Holmes suspects that something recently brought into the house, possibly among the luggage of Mrs. Maberley's dead son Douglas, is being sought. He questions Susan, warns Steve to stay away, and consults Langdale Pike for information about the people behind the scheme.
records.t: Sherlock Holmes investigates the Harrow Weald case after Steve Dixie threatens him on behalf of an unknown employer. Mrs. Maberley explains that a supposed house agent offered an unusually generous price for The Three Gables and all its contents, but withdrew when she refused restrictive terms. Holmes suspects that something recently brought into the house—possibly among the luggage of Mrs. Maberley's dead son Douglas—is being sought. He questions Susan, warns Steve to stay away, and consults Langdale Pike for information about the people behind the scheme.

records.l: The Adventure of the Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: This adventure concerns Sherlock Holmes's investigation of suspicious attempts to acquire The Three Gables and everything inside it. The case begins with intimidation by Steve Dixie and develops into a search for a hidden object connected with Douglas Maberley.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Holmes is threatened by Steve Dixie because he is investigating the Harrow Weald case. He identifies connections among Steve, Barney Stockdale, Susan, and an unknown wealthy woman, questions Mrs. Maberley and Susan, protects the house, and suspects that Douglas Maberley's recently arrived luggage contains the object sought by the conspirators.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Holmes to The Three Gables and records the investigation. He agrees with Holmes's conclusion that something recently brought into the house may be the object sought.

records.l: Steve Dixie, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Steve Dixie enters Holmes's rooms to warn him not to interfere in the Harrow Weald case, claiming that his friend and employer's associate has ordered the warning. Holmes identifies him as a bruiser connected with the Spencer John gang and frightens him by mentioning the killing of young Perkins. Steve later admits that Barney Stockdale gives him orders and is warned that Mrs. Maberley and everything in the house are under Holmes's protection.

records.l: Barney Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Barney Stockdale is Steve Dixie's immediate superior and is described as more astute than Steve. Susan is caught speaking to him, and Holmes infers that Barney carried information about Mrs. Maberley's letter to the unknown person behind the scheme.

records.l: Mrs. Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Mrs. Maberley asks Holmes to investigate strange incidents at The Three Gables. She explains the proposed sale of the house and its contents, identifies Douglas as her dead son, and agrees to have his recently arrived luggage examined.

records.l: Douglas Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Douglas Maberley was Mrs. Maberley's son, a former attaché at Rome whom Holmes remembered as exceptionally energetic and impressive. He died of pneumonia the previous month after becoming cynical and morose following a damaging love affair.

records.l: Susan Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Susan is Mrs. Maberley's servant who posted the letter to Holmes and was seen speaking over the hedge. Holmes exposes that she passed information to Barney Stockdale, and she leaves angrily after refusing to identify the person behind Barney.

records.l: The Three Gables house, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: The Three Gables is a poorly situated but well-furnished brick-and-timber villa at Harrow Weald. A suspicious buyer wants to acquire the house, its furniture, and apparently everything inside it, while the house is placed under Holmes's protection.

records.l: Harrow Weald, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Harrow Weald is the location of The Three Gables and the case that prompts threats against Holmes. Holmes travels there with Watson and investigates the people attempting to obtain the house.

records.l: the Harrow Weald case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: The Harrow Weald case concerns the unexplained effort to obtain The Three Gables and its contents. The effort is serious enough to involve intimidation, surveillance, Susan's betrayal, and the gang associated with Steve Dixie and Barney Stockdale.

records.l: the proposed sale of The Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: A supposed house agent offers Mrs. Maberley five hundred pounds more than she paid for The Three Gables and agrees to buy the furniture for an additional large sum. The buyer insists on acquiring everything and on checking anything removed from the house, causing Mrs. Maberley to reject the agreement.

records.l: the intimidation of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Steve Dixie warns Holmes that his life is unsafe if he goes to Harrow and tells him not to interfere in other people's affairs. Holmes links the threat to the gang's efforts on behalf of the unknown person behind the house scheme.

records.l: Douglas Maberley's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Douglas Maberley died in Rome of pneumonia the previous month. His death followed a period in which a love affair left him moody, morose, and cynical.

records.l: the house-agent scheme, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: A man calling himself Haines-Johnson, Auctioneer and Valuer, presents Mrs. Maberley with an agreement to sell The Three Gables and all its contents to a client. Holmes doubts that the man is a legitimate house agent and concludes that the scheme is designed to obtain something Mrs. Maberley does not know she possesses.

records.l: Douglas Maberley's luggage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Douglas Maberley's trunks and cases, labeled 'Milano' and 'Lucerne,' arrived at The Three Gables the previous week and remain unpacked. Holmes identifies their recent arrival as a possible explanation for the sudden interest in the house and orders Mrs. Maberley to examine them.

records.l: Mrs. Maberley's letter to Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Mrs. Maberley writes to Holmes about strange incidents connected with The Three Gables and asks for his advice. The letter bears a 10 p.m. postmark, yet Susan apparently informed Barney Stockdale about it quickly enough for Holmes to be threatened by the following morning.

records.l: the house's hidden valuable, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES
records.s: Holmes initially considers whether something valuable may have been buried or hidden in the house, but he rejects that explanation as insufficient because the conspirators also want the furniture. He later suspects that an unknown object, probably newly brought into the house, is valuable to someone but unknown to Mrs. Maberley.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: A telegram summons Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson to The Three Gables after Mrs. Maberley is chloroformed during a burglary, which the police attribute to Barney Stockdale's gang. Holmes recognizes that the burglars were searching for Douglas Maberley's manuscript and traces the crime to Isadora Klein, Douglas's former lover. Klein admits ordering the burglary and destroying the manuscript, claiming it threatened her impending marriage and social position. Holmes agrees not to expose her in exchange for a £5,000 cheque to fund Mrs. Maberley's travels, while warning Klein to be careful.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Sherlock Holmes goes with Dr. Watson to The Three Gables after receiving the telegram. He identifies the burglary as an attempt to recover Douglas Maberley's manuscript, confronts Isadora Klein, obtains her admission that she ordered the crime, and arranges for her to give £5,000 to Mrs. Maberley.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to The Three Gables and then to Isadora Klein's house. He observes the investigation, hears Klein's confession, and serves as a witness during Holmes's dealings with her.

records.l: Mrs. Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Mrs. Maberley is chloroformed and attacked during the burglary at The Three Gables after disregarding Holmes's advice to have someone stay in the house. She tries to seize one of the burglars but is knocked unconscious, and Holmes later secures £5,000 from Isadora Klein to send her around the world.

records.l: Douglas Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Douglas Maberley had been Isadora Klein's lover and wanted to marry her. After Klein rejected him and had him beaten, he wrote a manuscript describing their relationship under different names, intending it as a threat to her reputation.

records.l: Isadora Klein, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Isadora Klein is revealed as the employer behind the burglary. She admits that she hired Barney Stockdale and his gang to recover Douglas Maberley's manuscript, burns the manuscript when Holmes demands its return, and agrees to provide £5,000 for Mrs. Maberley's travels.

records.l: Susan Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Susan Stockdale is identified as Barney Stockdale's wife and one of the only people who knows that Isadora Klein employed the gang. Mrs. Maberley suspects that Susan arranged an entry into The Three Gables for the burglars.

records.l: Barney Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Barney Stockdale leads the gang that Isadora Klein hires to recover Douglas Maberley's manuscript. He and his wife Susan are said to know Klein's identity as the employer, and the police are pursuing him and his associates for the burglary.

records.l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: The police arrive at The Three Gables after the burglary, examine the property, question Mrs. Maberley, and take possession of the recovered manuscript fragment. They believe Barney Stockdale's gang committed the crime and begin pursuing the burglars.

records.l: Barney Stockdale's gang, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Barney Stockdale's gang burglarizes The Three Gables, chloroforms Mrs. Maberley, and searches Douglas Maberley's belongings for his manuscript. The gang escapes after Mrs. Maberley and the maid raise an alarm, while the police pursue its members.

records.l: The Three Gables house, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: The Three Gables is burgled during the night by men searching through Douglas Maberley's belongings. The house is examined by the police, and a manuscript fragment is found crumpled on the floor.

records.l: the telegram, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: The telegram from Sutro tells Sherlock Holmes to come out at once because his client's house has been burgled and the police are in possession. It brings Holmes and Dr. Watson back to The Three Gables.

records.l: Douglas Maberley's manuscript, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Douglas Maberley's manuscript recounts his relationship with Isadora Klein and portrays her conduct toward him under different names. Klein considers it a threat to her future marriage and hires burglars to find and destroy the remaining copy.

records.l: the recovered manuscript fragment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: The recovered manuscript fragment is a sheet in Douglas Maberley's handwriting, numbered 245, found after the burglary. It describes a man's humiliation, the death of his love, and his resulting desire for revenge; Isadora Klein later burns the manuscript, apparently destroying it.

records.l: the burglary at The Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: The burglary at The Three Gables is carried out to locate Douglas Maberley's manuscript. Mrs. Maberley is chloroformed and injured, the burglars search her son's baggage, and they escape with an unknown bundle while leaving behind the recovered manuscript fragment.

records.l: Douglas Maberley's beating, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Douglas Maberley was beaten and driven away by Barney Stockdale and his associates after Isadora Klein rejected his demands for marriage. Klein admits that she hired them and that they were somewhat rough in carrying out the beating.

records.l: Douglas Maberley's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious
records.s: Douglas Maberley's death occurs before the events of this unit. After his death, Isadora Klein fears that the manuscript describing their relationship will reach the public through his effects and therefore orders the burglary.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Holmes and Watson receive a referral concerning Robert Ferguson, who seeks help for an unnamed friend whose Peruvian wife allegedly attacks his children and drinks the baby's blood. The husband has confined his wife to her room while Mrs. Mason guards the baby, but he remains worried about Jack, whom the wife has assaulted twice. Ferguson visits Holmes and Watson, explains the family circumstances, and asks for advice. Holmes identifies inconsistencies in the accounts and agrees to investigate at Cheeseman's in Lamberley.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Holmes initially dismisses supernatural vampirism as lunacy but considers the possibility that the case involves a living person with vampiric habits. After questioning Robert Ferguson about the family, the wife, the baby, and Jack, he forms provisional theories and agrees to travel to Lamberley with Watson to investigate.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Watson reads the referral and Ferguson's letter, recognizes Robert Ferguson from their rugby days, and supplies information about Lamberley and its old houses. He accompanies Holmes in agreeing to investigate the case.

records.l: Robert Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Robert Ferguson, a former Richmond rugby player, asks Holmes to help a friend whose wife allegedly drinks their baby's blood and assaults Jack. He explains the household's circumstances, says the wife is confined to her room, and arranges for Holmes and Watson to visit Cheeseman's in Lamberley.

records.l: the unnamed husband, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The unnamed husband married the Peruvian wife after knowing her for only a few weeks and has a fifteen-year-old son from an earlier marriage. After seeing blood on the baby's neck and around his wife's lips, he confronted her, confined her to her room, and became so distressed that he sought Ferguson's help.

records.l: the Peruvian wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The Peruvian wife is described as beautiful, loving, devoted, and intensely jealous, but she has twice assaulted Jack and was twice seen apparently biting her own baby. She refuses to explain the alleged attacks or speak to her husband, and remains locked in her room with Dolores bringing her food.

records.l: Jacky Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Jack is the unnamed husband's fifteen-year-old son from his first marriage, described as affectionate, devoted, and physically disabled from a childhood accident. The Peruvian wife has assaulted him twice, once with a stick and once with her hands, while repeatedly saying that she hates him.

records.l: Ferguson's baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The baby is the Peruvian wife's child and is under one year old. A nurse and the unnamed husband each reportedly saw the wife beside the baby with blood on or near its neck, and Mrs. Mason now guards the child continuously.

records.l: Mrs. Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Mrs. Mason is the baby's nurse and claims to have seen the Peruvian wife apparently bite the child. She tells the husband about the incident and swears that she will not leave the baby, whom she considers herself responsible for protecting.

records.l: Lamberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Lamberley is identified as being in Sussex, south of Horsham. Holmes and Watson plan to travel there to investigate the case.

records.l: Cheeseman's, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Cheeseman's is the address in Lamberley from which Robert Ferguson writes and where the family lives. Holmes expects to learn more about the house and its occupants through a personal investigation.

records.l: Sussex, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Sussex is the county where Lamberley and Cheeseman's are located. The alleged vampiric events occur in this English setting rather than in the foreign places associated with traditional vampire stories.

records.l: the Adventure of the Sussex Vampire, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The adventure concerns Holmes and Watson's investigation of alleged vampirism, the Peruvian wife's attacks on the baby, and her assaults on Jack at the family house in Sussex.

records.l: vampirism, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: Holmes and Watson discuss traditional vampires as walking corpses held in their graves by stakes, as well as the belief that living people may drink blood. Holmes initially rejects the supernatural explanation but agrees to examine the reported case.

records.l: the alleged vampiric attack on the baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The alleged attack occurs when the Peruvian wife is reportedly seen leaning over the baby and apparently biting its neck, leaving a small wound and blood on the child, sheet, and her lips. The husband and Mrs. Mason treat the incident as evidence of vampirism, while Holmes considers the matter unresolved.

records.l: the assaults on Jack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The Peruvian wife has assaulted Jack twice without an apparent provocation, once striking him with a stick and once beating him with her hands. She has said that she hates him, but neither Jack nor the husband provides a clear explanation for the attacks.

records.l: the family house at Cheeseman's, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE
records.s: The family house at Cheeseman's contains the unnamed husband, his wife, Jack, the baby, Dolores, Mrs. Mason, and two recently hired servants, including Michael the stable-hand. The wife is confined to her room there, while Mrs. Mason guards the baby and Dolores brings food to the wife.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson visit Robert Ferguson's isolated farmhouse to investigate apparent vampirism involving Ferguson's wife and baby. Holmes determines that Ferguson's wife sucked poison from the baby's wound after Jacky Ferguson attacked the child with a poisoned arrow, likely dipped in curare or another drug. He also identifies Jacky's jealousy and hatred toward the baby and advises sending him to sea. Holmes's investigation resolves the Ferguson case and leads him to answer the original letter from Baker Street.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Sherlock Holmes visits the Ferguson farmhouse with Dr. John Watson and investigates the apparent vampirism. He deduces that Ferguson's wife saved the baby by sucking poison from the child's wound and that Jacky Ferguson was responsible for the attempted poisoning. He concludes that Jacky should spend a year at sea and later writes that the matter has been satisfactorily concluded.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to the Ferguson farmhouse and examines Ferguson's feverish wife. He observes that her condition appears to involve mental and nervous excitement rather than an actual seizure, and he helps Holmes bring her and Ferguson together.

records.l: Robert Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Robert Ferguson believes that his wife may be a would-be murderer after seeing her rise from beside the baby's cot with blood on her lips. Holmes reveals that she was saving the baby from poison and that Jacky Ferguson had attacked the child. Ferguson is devastated to learn of Jacky's jealousy and hatred.

records.l: Ferguson's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Ferguson's wife is found feverish, distressed, and unwilling to see her husband after he accused or suspected her. She had sucked poison from the baby's wound to save the child, but concealed the truth because she feared the effect on Ferguson. She confirms Holmes's explanation and is cleared of the apparent attempt to harm the baby.

records.l: Dolores, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Dolores, a tall, slim, brown-faced girl, cares for Ferguson's ill wife and fears being left alone with her without a doctor. She takes Dr. Watson to the wife's room, later admits Holmes and Ferguson, and remains present while Holmes explains the case.

records.l: Jacky Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Jacky Ferguson is Ferguson's pale, fair-haired older child, and he has a weak spine and a shambling gait. Holmes sees intense jealousy and cruel hatred on his face when Ferguson fondles the baby and concludes that Jacky attempted to poison the child out of distorted, possessive love. Holmes prescribes a year at sea for him.

records.l: Ferguson's baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Ferguson's baby is a beautiful, dark-eyed, golden-haired child whom Ferguson fondles protectively. The baby has a small puckered wound on the neck, caused by the poisoned arrow, but survives because the poison was sucked out.

records.l: Mrs. Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Mrs. Mason cares for Ferguson's baby while the child remains away from Ferguson's wife. Holmes learns that she knew about the danger and had been told to watch the child.

records.l: Carlo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Carlo is Ferguson's spaniel, which developed sudden paralysis in its hind legs about four months earlier. Holmes interprets the dog's illness as evidence that a poison had been tested on it before being used against the baby, and the dog is expected to recover.

records.l: Ferguson farmhouse, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The Ferguson farmhouse is an isolated, ancient building in Sussex with a large central room, old furnishings, and South American weapons and utensils on its walls. Holmes notices a small empty quiver beside a bird-bow there, which supports his theory about the poisoned arrow.

records.l: Baker Street, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: At Baker Street, before visiting the farmhouse, Holmes forms the theory that Ferguson's wife had sucked poison from the baby's wound. He later explains that the observations at the farmhouse confirmed the deductions he had already made there.

records.l: the Ferguson household, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The Ferguson household is divided by suspicion after Ferguson believes his wife harmed the baby, while she refuses to see him and asks only for her child. Holmes's explanation reveals that the danger came from Jacky's attempted poisoning and leaves Ferguson and his wife to settle the matter.

records.l: the poisoned arrow, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The poisoned arrow is inferred to have been fired from the small bird-bow kept among the South American weapons in the farmhouse. It pricked the baby's neck, and Holmes believes Jacky used it in an attempt to kill the child.

records.l: curare, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Curare is mentioned by Holmes as one possible poison with which the arrow may have been dipped. He explains that such venom could have caused the baby's death if Ferguson's wife had not sucked it from the wound.

records.l: the child's wound, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The child's wound is a small, puckered mark on the baby's neck. Ferguson's wife sucked the poison from it, preventing the attempted poisoning from killing the baby.

records.l: the letter to Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The letter to Sherlock Holmes, dated November 19, concerns Robert Ferguson's inquiry about the apparent vampire-related danger. Holmes's November 21 reply states that he investigated the matter and brought it to a satisfactory conclusion.

records.l: the Ferguson case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The Ferguson case concerns the apparent vampirism, the baby's wound, Ferguson's suspicion of his wife, and the danger within the household. Holmes resolves it by identifying the poison attack and Jacky's motive.

records.l: the attempted poisoning of Ferguson's baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: The attempted poisoning of Ferguson's baby was carried out with a poisoned arrow that pricked the child's neck. Ferguson's wife discovered the attack and removed the poison by sucking it from the wound, while Holmes attributes the attack to Jacky Ferguson.

records.l: vampirism, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Vampirism is initially suspected because Ferguson saw his wife rise from beside the baby's cot with blood on her lips. Holmes rejects the supernatural explanation and shows that she was sucking poison from the child's wound.

records.l: poisoning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags
records.s: Poisoning is the actual danger behind the apparent vampire attack. Holmes infers that the poison came from an arrow, may have been curare or a similar drug, and had previously been tested on Carlo.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: In June 1902, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson become involved in John Garrideb's search for two other men named Garrideb who can claim a fortune under Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will. John tells Holmes that the inheritance requires three adult Garridebs, while Holmes suspects that John's story contains numerous lies. Nathan Garrideb, a reclusive collector living in London, confirms John's account and eagerly hopes to obtain the money.
