John then produces an advertisement for Howard Garrideb in Birmingham and persuades Nathan to travel there to verify Howard's identity.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is approached by John Garrideb and Nathan Garrideb regarding the search for another Garrideb. He detects that John has lied about his background and the search, noting his worn English clothing, lack of newspaper advertisements, and false reference to Dr. Lysander Starr. Holmes visits Nathan, questions him about the inheritance and his collection, and agrees that Nathan should travel to Birmingham to meet Howard Garrideb.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: Dr. John Watson narrates the investigation and accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Nathan Garrideb's rooms. He records John's account of Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will, Nathan's collection, and the discovery of the Howard Garrideb advertisement.

records.l: John Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: John Garrideb, who presents himself as an American counsellor at law from Moorville, Kansas, tells Holmes that he must find two other adult Garridebs to obtain Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's inheritance. Holmes observes that John is wearing English clothing, has a smoothed London accent, and has lied about several details. John produces an advertisement for Howard Garrideb and persuades Nathan to travel to Birmingham to meet him.

records.l: Nathan Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: Nathan Garrideb is a reclusive collector who lives at 136 Little Ryder Street and rarely leaves his rooms. He confirms John's story and hopes to receive five million dollars, which he plans to spend on specimens for his collection. Nathan agrees to travel to Birmingham to obtain proof of Howard Garrideb's existence.

records.l: Howard Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: Howard Garrideb is identified through an advertisement as a constructor of agricultural machinery in Birmingham. John claims that Howard is the third adult Garrideb required by the inheritance, and Nathan is instructed to meet him at his office.

records.l: the Garrideb inheritance search, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: The search concerns finding three adult men named Garrideb who can satisfy the conditions of Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will. John says he has searched throughout the United States and then looked in England, while Holmes questions whether the search is genuine.

records.l: Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will divides his property into three parts and makes John Garrideb's share conditional on finding two other Garrideb men to share the remainder. The will requires three adult men named Garrideb to stand together before the inheritance can be claimed.

records.l: the Garrideb fortune, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: The fortune is described as approximately five million dollars for each of the three Garridebs. Nathan expects to use his share to buy valuable specimens and expand his collection, but the money cannot be claimed until the required Garridebs are found.

records.l: the Adventure of the Three Garridebs, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: The adventure concerns Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigating the unusual inheritance search involving John, Nathan, and the proposed Howard Garrideb. By the end of this unit, Holmes suspects deception and Nathan has agreed to travel to Birmingham.

records.l: the Howard Garrideb advertisement, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS
records.s: The Howard Garrideb advertisement identifies Howard as a constructor of agricultural machinery at Grosvenor Buildings, Aston, and lists machinery and estimates for artesian wells among his services. John presents it as proof that the third Garrideb has been found.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes discovers that John Garrideb, an American lawyer, is James Winter, alias Killer Evans, a dangerous criminal who murdered Rodger Prescott. Holmes and Dr. John Watson discover that Evans invented the three Garridebs deception to remove Nathan Garrideb from his apartment, where Prescott had hidden a counterfeiting operation. Evans opens a secret cellar, fires at Watson, and is subdued and arrested after Holmes finds Prescott's printing equipment and counterfeit banknotes. Nathan Garrideb is left devastated when his hopes of inheriting a fortune collapse.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the American's identity and learns from Scotland Yard that John Garrideb is James Winter, alias Killer Evans. He traces the connection between Rodger Prescott, the former tenant of Nathan Garrideb's apartment, and a hidden counterfeiting operation. Holmes and Dr. John Watson ambush Evans, disarm and subdue him, and arrange for the Yard to take him away.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes in investigating the apartment and hides with him near the cupboard. Killer Evans fires two shots at him, striking him superficially in the thigh, but Watson remains able to help Holmes and call the Yard.

records.l: Nathan Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Nathan Garrideb allows Sherlock Holmes to inspect his collection and gives permission for Holmes to enter the apartment. He is sent to Birmingham through the deception and later never recovers from the collapse of his hopes concerning the supposed inheritance; he is last heard of at a nursing-home in Brixton.

records.l: John Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: John Garrideb is presented as an American lawyer seeking another Garrideb, but Holmes identifies him as a criminal using a false identity. He is revealed to have used the three Garridebs invention to get Nathan Garrideb out of his apartment.

records.l: James Winter, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: James Winter is listed in Scotland Yard's records as an alias of Morecroft and Killer Evans. He is aged forty-four, a native of Chicago, and is known to have shot three men in the United States before coming to London.

records.l: Killer Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Killer Evans is identified as the American calling himself John Garrideb. He had shot Rodger Prescott, sought access to Prescott's hidden counterfeiting operation, fired at Watson, and was subdued by Holmes before being handed over to the authorities.

records.l: Rodger Prescott, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Rodger Prescott was a Chicago criminal known as a forger and coiner, and he had previously occupied Nathan Garrideb's apartment under the name Waldron. His hidden printing operation and counterfeit banknotes remained beneath the apartment until they were discovered.

records.l: Nathan Garrideb's apartment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Nathan Garrideb's apartment had previously been occupied by Rodger Prescott, who concealed a counterfeiting operation beneath its floor. Killer Evans used the three Garridebs deception to clear Nathan from the apartment so he could enter it and search for Prescott's equipment.

records.l: the Garrideb invention, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: The Garrideb invention was a scheme devised by Killer Evans to send Nathan Garrideb away from his apartment. Evans exploited the unusual name and arranged an apparent search for three men named Garrideb, including an advertisement designed to draw Nathan to Birmingham.

records.l: the secret cellar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: The secret cellar was hidden beneath a trapdoor under the central table in Nathan Garrideb's apartment. It contained rusted machinery, rolls of paper, bottles, and bundles of counterfeit banknotes.

records.l: Prescott's counterfeiting outfit, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Prescott's counterfeiting outfit was concealed in the cellar beneath Nathan Garrideb's apartment. It included a printing press and related materials, and its discovery pleased the Yard because the police had known the outfit existed but could not locate it after Prescott's death.

records.l: Prescott's counterfeit banknotes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Prescott's counterfeit banknotes were arranged in bundles on a table in the secret cellar. Killer Evans said there were two thousand notes worth one hundred each and claimed they were good enough to pass anywhere.

records.l: the shooting of Rodger Prescott, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Killer Evans shot Rodger Prescott in a London nightclub in January 1895. Prescott died, but Evans said Prescott had drawn on him and claimed that he had shot him to prevent him from flooding London with counterfeit banknotes.

records.l: Watson's wounding, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Watson's wounding occurred when Killer Evans fired two shots after emerging from the secret cellar. A bullet caused a superficial injury to Watson's thigh, and Holmes found that it was only a scratch.

records.l: Killer Evans's attempted murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Killer Evans's attempted murder consisted of firing two shots at Dr. John Watson after Holmes and Watson confronted him. Holmes said that, so far as he could see, the charge was attempted murder, and Evans was left for the authorities to deal with.

records.l: counterfeiting, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: Counterfeiting is the criminal activity associated with Rodger Prescott's hidden machinery and banknotes. The recovered operation was regarded by the Yard as a major public danger because the notes were difficult to distinguish from genuine Bank of England notes.

records.l: the three Garridebs deception, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the
records.s: The three Garridebs deception was Killer Evans's plan for removing Nathan Garrideb from his apartment without immediately harming him. It used the supposed inheritance connected with several men named Garrideb and sent Nathan on a false journey to Birmingham.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: John H. Watson recounts how Sherlock Holmes is asked to defend Miss Dunbar, a governess accused of killing Neil Gibson's wife at Thor Bridge. The victim was found near Thor Mere with a revolver bullet through her brain, while a matching revolver was discovered in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe and a note from her arranged the meeting. Estate manager Marlow Bates warns Holmes that Gibson was brutal to his wife, while Gibson insists that Miss Dunbar is innocent and eventually reveals the history of his marriage to Maria Pinto. Holmes suspects that Gibson has concealed the true nature of his relationship with Miss Dunbar and uses a bluff to make him disclose further facts.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: John H. Watson narrates this account from his own experience. He discusses the evidence with Sherlock Holmes and hears the statements of Marlow Bates and Neil Gibson concerning the case.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes agrees to examine the case against Miss Dunbar after receiving a letter from Neil Gibson. He questions Gibson about his relationship with Miss Dunbar, accuses him of giving false information, and bluffs him into revealing the history of his marriage to Maria Pinto.

records.l: Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Neil Gibson, an American senator and major gold-mining magnate, asks Holmes to prove that Miss Dunbar is innocent. He is described as powerful, harsh, and formidable, and Marlow Bates accuses him of treating his wife brutally. Gibson first denies having any personal relationship with Miss Dunbar, then admits that he had loved and married Maria Pinto before his feelings faded.

records.l: Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Miss Dunbar, an attractive governess employed to educate the Gibson children, is accused of murdering Gibson's wife. A revolver matching the fatal bullet was found in her wardrobe, a note signed by her arranged a meeting at the scene, and she admitted being near Thor Bridge at the relevant time, though Neil Gibson insists that she is innocent.

records.l: Maria Pinto, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Maria Pinto was Neil Gibson's Brazilian wife and the victim of the tragedy. Gibson says that she was once exceptionally beautiful, passionate, and devoted to him, even after his love for her had faded.

records.l: Marlow Bates, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Marlow Bates, manager of Gibson's estate, warns Holmes that Neil Gibson is a villain who treated his wife brutally. He says he has given Gibson notice and is leaving his employment, but states that he does not know how Gibson's wife died.

records.l: Thor Bridge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Thor Bridge is a broad stone bridge with balustrades carrying the drive over the narrowest part of Thor Mere. Maria Gibson's body was found at the mouth of the bridge, and Miss Dunbar was seen near it around the time of the shooting.

records.l: Thor Mere, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: Thor Mere is a long, deep, reed-girt sheet of water crossed by Thor Bridge. The tragedy occurred at the bridge over this mere.

records.l: Mrs. Gibson's killing, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The tragedy concerns the death of Neil Gibson's wife, who was found late at night in her dinner dress with a shawl over her shoulders and a bullet through her brain. No weapon was found near her body.

records.l: the murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The murder is attributed by the authorities to Miss Dunbar on the basis of the revolver in her wardrobe, the note arranging a meeting, her presence near Thor Bridge, and a possible motive involving Neil Gibson. Holmes considers the evidence serious but remains suspicious that important facts have been concealed.

records.l: the alleged attack on Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The case has been referred to the Assizes at Winchester after a coroner's jury and police-court proceedings found the evidence against Miss Dunbar persuasive. Neil Gibson hires Holmes to seek new facts that might establish her innocence.

records.l: the problem of Thor Bridge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The problem of Thor Bridge is presented as one of Sherlock Holmes's investigations into the apparent murder of Neil Gibson's wife. At this stage, the central questions concern the missing weapon, Miss Dunbar's connection with the scene, and the concealed relationships among Gibson, his wife, and the governess.

records.l: the letter from Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The letter from Neil Gibson asks Sherlock Holmes to save Miss Dunbar, whom Gibson declares innocent. Gibson offers all his resources and says that the injustice of her impending death has driven him to desperation.

records.l: the revolver, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: A revolver with one discharged chamber was found on the floor of Miss Dunbar's wardrobe. Its calibre corresponded with the bullet that killed Neil Gibson's wife.

records.l: the bullet, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The bullet passed through the brain of Neil Gibson's wife. Its calibre matched that of the revolver found in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe.

records.l: Miss Dunbar's note, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The note found on Neil Gibson's dead wife arranged an appointment at Thor Bridge and was signed by Miss Dunbar. It is treated as direct evidence against the governess.

records.l: the murder investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The murder investigation established that the victim was found near Thor Bridge late at night and that no weapon was beside her. It also gathered the revolver, the note, Miss Dunbar's presence near the bridge, and the possible motive involving Neil Gibson.

records.l: the fatal shooting of Maria Pinto, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The fatal shooting of Maria Pinto is identified with the death of Neil Gibson's wife, who was found with a revolver bullet through her brain. The text does not establish who fired the shot, although Miss Dunbar has been accused.

records.l: the love affair between Neil Gibson and Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE
records.s: The alleged love affair between Neil Gibson and Miss Dunbar is presented as a possible motive because Gibson was said to have shown the governess pressing attentions and she might benefit if his wife died. Gibson initially denies any relationship with her, while his emotional letter to Holmes leads Holmes to suspect that she is important to him.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: The millionaire tells Holmes that Miss Grace Dunbar became governess to his two children after answering an advertisement. He admits that he developed a passionate regard for Grace, told her he wanted to marry her, and offered to make her happy and comfortable despite being unable to marry her. Holmes criticizes the millionaire for trying to ruin a defenseless young woman under his protection and says that the millionaire's conduct may be no better than what Grace is accused of doing. The millionaire insists that he came to Holmes about evidence, not morality.

records.l: Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: Miss Grace Dunbar answered the millionaire's advertisement and became governess to his two children. The millionaire says that the whole world has proclaimed her a very beautiful woman and that she was under his protection.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: Holmes tells the millionaire that he does not blame him for feeling regard for Grace but would blame him for expressing it because she was under his protection. He criticizes the millionaire's conduct and says he is concerned with the case only for the young lady's sake.

records.l: Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: The millionaire admits that he developed a passionate regard for Grace and told her that he wanted her love and possession. He says he could not marry her but offered to do whatever money could accomplish to make her happy and comfortable, and he objects when Holmes criticizes his morals.

records.l: the millionaire's romantic desire for Grace Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: The millionaire says he could not live under the same roof as Grace and remain in daily contact with her without feeling passionate regard for her. He told her that he wanted to marry her and that he had never wanted anything more than her love and possession.

records.l: evidence, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: The millionaire says he came to Holmes with a question of evidence rather than a question of morals. The unit does not specify what the evidence is.

records.l: morality, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: Holmes distinguishes the question of morality from the question of evidence and criticizes the millionaire's admitted conduct. The millionaire says he is not pretending to be better than he is and objects to Holmes's moral criticism.

records.l: the millionaire's alleged offences against Grace Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, "Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and
records.s: Holmes says the millionaire has admitted trying to ruin a defenseless girl who was under his roof. Holmes suggests that this conduct may be no better than anything Grace is accused of doing.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.
records.s: The Gold King tells Mr. Holmes why his wife remained in the house and describes Miss Dunbar’s beneficial influence over his actions. He explains that his business dealings could ruin individuals, communities, cities, and nations, while Miss Dunbar believed his wealth should not be built on the ruin of others. The Gold King suspects that his jealous wife may have threatened Miss Dunbar with a revolver, causing an accidental shooting during a scuffle, but his wife denies this. Mr. Holmes plans to travel to Winchester to question Miss Dunbar.

records.l: Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.
records.s: The Gold King says he is grateful that his plans did not succeed as intended. He explains that Miss Dunbar influenced him for good and that his wife remained partly to use that influence, and he discusses the possibility that his wife attacked Miss Dunbar.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.
records.s: Mr. Holmes considers an accidental shooting during a struggle a possible alternative to deliberate murder. He plans to obtain the necessary permits and travel to Winchester to see Miss Dunbar.

records.l: the Gold King's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.
records.s: The Gold King's wife remained in the house after he swore that she would not be molested again, partly because others depended on her and partly because she wanted to influence him through Miss Dunbar's beneficial effect on him. She denies attacking Miss Dunbar.

records.l: Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.

It produces increased energy and vitality but also causes Presbury to display crawling, climbing, and other animal-like behavior, and Lowenstein warns that it is dangerous.

records.l: rejuvenescence, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
records.s: Rejuvenescence is associated with Lowenstein's reported scientific efforts to discover a means of restoring youth. Holmes concludes that Professor Presbury pursued the treatment because he wanted to become a younger man.

records.l: the wolf-hound attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
records.s: The wolf-hound attack occurs after Professor Presbury deliberately provokes Roy with pebbles, a stick, and gestures near the dog's mouth. Roy's collar slips, allowing him to seize Presbury by the throat and cause serious bleeding before Holmes, Dr. Watson, Bennett, and the coachman intervene.

records.l: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
records.s: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague precedes the beginning of his strange symptoms. Holmes connects the visit with Presbury's secret correspondence with a Bohemian dealer in London and with H. Lowenstein's serum treatment.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: After retiring to Sussex, Mr. Holmes investigates the death of Fitzroy McPherson, who is found dying near the beach after suffering terrible unexplained injuries. McPherson’s last words appear to identify the “Lion’s Mane,” while his body bears long, curved red weals resembling scourge marks. Suspicion falls partly on Ian Murdoch, who had visited The Haven, was dismissed by Harold Stackhurst, and may have had feelings for Maud Bellamy. Holmes and Stackhurst learn that McPherson and Maud were secretly engaged and begin examining the possible motives and circumstances surrounding the assault.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Mr. Holmes, living in retirement near the Sussex coast, discovers Fitzroy McPherson dying and takes charge of the initial investigation. He examines the beach, the footprints, McPherson’s belongings, and the correspondence connecting McPherson with Maud Bellamy.

records.l: Harold Stackhurst, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Harold Stackhurst encounters Mr. Holmes while going for a swim and helps him respond when Fitzroy McPherson collapses. He remains with McPherson’s body, reports on the relationships at The Gables, dismisses Ian Murdoch after their confrontation, and assists Holmes in questioning the Bellamy family.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson, the science master at The Gables, is found staggering up from the beach and dies after suffering severe unexplained pain. He had prepared to swim but apparently never entered the water, and he was secretly engaged to Maud Bellamy.

records.l: Ian Murdoch, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Ian Murdoch, the mathematical coach at The Gables, arrives after McPherson collapses and denies being with him on the beach. He had held the students back with an algebra demonstration, had visited The Haven, and is dismissed by Stackhurst after an angry exchange.

records.l: Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Maud Bellamy is the daughter of Tom Bellamy and is described as exceptionally beautiful and strong-minded. She confirms that she and McPherson were engaged, offers Holmes her help, and says that more than one person may have been needed to inflict his injuries.

records.l: Fulworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Fulworth is the nearby village around the bay, containing the police station and the Bellamy family’s home and boating business. Holmes and Stackhurst walk there to question the Bellamys.

records.l: The Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The Gables is Harold Stackhurst’s coaching establishment, where young men prepare for professions and where Stackhurst, McPherson, and Murdoch work. McPherson’s body is taken there, and Stackhurst later dismisses Murdoch from the establishment.

records.l: The Haven, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The Haven is the Bellamy family home in Fulworth. Ian Murdoch is seen leaving it when Holmes and Stackhurst arrive to speak with the Bellamys.

records.l: the beach, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The beach lies below the chalk cliffs and includes a lagoon, swimming-pools, caves, pebbles, and shingle. McPherson went there intending to bathe, but the beach appeared deserted apart from distant figures, and his footprints and towel were found there.

records.l: the chalk cliffs, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The coast near Holmes’s villa consists of chalk cliffs that can be descended by a single steep, slippery path. Small caves at their base are searched after McPherson’s death, but nothing is found.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson’s death occurs after he staggers up from the beach, cries out about the Lion’s Mane, and collapses. His death is treated as an extraordinary and apparently criminal event because his body shows signs of intense suffering and violent injury.

records.l: the assault on Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The assault leaves McPherson’s back covered with dark red, curved lines like marks from a thin wire scourge. He appears to have been tortured until he bit through his lower lip, then managed only to crawl away from the beach before dying.

records.l: the Lion's Mane mystery, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The Lion’s Mane mystery begins when McPherson’s final warning appears to be the words “the lion’s mane.” The phrase is initially unintelligible to Holmes and becomes the name of the unusual problem he begins investigating.

records.l: the investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The investigation examines McPherson’s movements, footprints, clothing, towel, body, personal papers, and relationships. Holmes and Stackhurst question the Bellamys and begin to focus on Ian Murdoch, Maud Bellamy, and the possibility of multiple attackers.

records.l: the McPherson–Bellamy engagement, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: McPherson and Maud Bellamy were secretly engaged to be married. They kept the engagement secret because McPherson’s elderly uncle might have disinherited him if he married against his uncle’s wishes.

records.l: the note from Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: A note in McPherson’s card-case, written in a feminine hand, reads, “I will be there, you may be sure.--Maudie.” The note suggests an assignation, and McPherson’s papers identify Maud Bellamy as its writer.

records.l: the scourge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: The apparent scourge is the suspected instrument that produced the long, flexible-looking weals on McPherson’s back. No actual scourge is found, and Holmes questions whether a human hand wielded it.

records.l: McPherson's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: McPherson’s body is found on the path above the beach, with his Burberry thrown around his shoulders, disordered clothing, blood on his chin, and severe red marks across his back. His pockets contain a handkerchief, a large knife, a folding card-case, and the note signed “Maudie.”

records.l: Murdoch's possible motive, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
records.s: Murdoch’s possible motive includes his former apparent interest in Maud Bellamy, his earlier hostility toward McPherson, and his visit to The Haven shortly after McPherson’s death. Holmes also notes that Murdoch had an angry temperament and appeared to be seeking a way to leave the scene.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes connects the deaths of Fitzroy McPherson and McPherson's dog, along with Ian Murdoch's sudden illness, to a deadly jellyfish in the bathing-pool. He identifies the creature as Cyanea capillata, whose radiating filaments produce the distinctive reticulated sting pattern and severe pain. The phrase “Lion's Mane,” spoken by McPherson before his death, is recognized as a warning describing the creature. Cyanea capillata is crushed beneath a boulder, McPherson's death is explained as an accidental envenomation, and Ian Murdoch is exonerated.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the unexplained death of Fitzroy McPherson and initially considers Ian Murdoch a possible suspect. After learning of the dog's death and recalling information from J. G. Wood's Out of Doors, he identifies Cyanea capillata in the bathing-pool and explains the deaths and attacks as jellyfish stings.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson died at the bathing-pool with strange injuries that initially suggested a violent assault. Sherlock Holmes concludes that he was killed by the stinging filaments of Cyanea capillata, and that his final words, “Lion's Mane,” warned of the creature.

records.l: Ian Murdoch, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Ian Murdoch is suspected of killing Fitzroy McPherson because of his temper, his past quarrel with McPherson, and his feelings for Miss Bellamy. He is attacked by Cyanea capillata at the same beach and survives after suffering severe pain, thereby clearing himself of suspicion.

records.l: Harold Stackhurst, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Stackhurst investigates the disappearance and death of Fitzroy McPherson and brings Ian Murdoch to Sherlock Holmes after finding him stricken on the beach. He helps Holmes crush Cyanea capillata beneath a boulder and later reconciles with Murdoch.

records.l: Inspector Bardie, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Inspector Bardie considers arresting Ian Murdoch because the evidence appears to point toward him, but Sherlock Holmes persuades him that the case is too weak. Bardie witnesses Murdoch's attack, the discovery of Cyanea capillata, and Holmes's explanation of the tragedy.

records.l: The Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The Gables is where Stackhurst's students Sudbury and Blount report finding McPherson's dog and where Stackhurst is initially found in his study. Stackhurst later leaves The Gables to bring the stricken Ian Murdoch to Sherlock Holmes.

records.l: the bathing-pool, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The bathing-pool is the site where Fitzroy McPherson died, his dog was later found dead, and Ian Murdoch was attacked. Sherlock Holmes discovers Cyanea capillata beneath the water in its deeper section and identifies it as the source of the danger.

records.l: the beach, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The beach is where Fitzroy McPherson met his end, where his dog's tracks were found, and where Ian Murdoch suffered his attack. Its secluded bathing-pool concealed the deadly jellyfish.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson's death is initially treated as a possible murder because of the severe, patterned injuries on his body. Sherlock Holmes determines that the injuries and his last words are consistent with an attack by Cyanea capillata rather than a human assault.

records.l: the dog's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The dog's death is first attributed to grief for its master after it refuses food for a week. Because it dies at the same place as Fitzroy McPherson, its death alerts Sherlock Holmes that the location itself is dangerous; its contorted body is later understood as another victim of Cyanea capillata.

records.l: Ian Murdoch's attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Ian Murdoch's attack occurs at the edge of the water where Fitzroy McPherson died. The attack produces severe pain, breathing difficulties, and a reticulated red pattern on his shoulder, matching McPherson's injuries and revealing the true cause of the earlier death.

records.l: the dog (McPherson's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: McPherson's dog, an Airedale terrier, follows the trail of its dead master to the bathing-pool and dies at the edge of it. Its rigid, contorted body and the location of its death provide Sherlock Holmes with an important clue to the danger in the water.

records.l: Cyanea capillata, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: Cyanea capillata is a jellyfish resembling a tangled mass of tawny and silver lion's mane. It radiates nearly invisible filaments over a wide area, causing red, dotted marks, extreme pain, cardiac distress, and potentially death; Sherlock Holmes and Stackhurst crush it beneath a boulder.

records.l: the murder investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The murder investigation initially focuses on Ian Murdoch because of his relationship with Miss Bellamy, his history with McPherson, and his apparent preparations to leave. The investigation is resolved when Sherlock Holmes proves that McPherson's death was caused by Cyanea capillata and that Murdoch was innocent.

records.l: the reticulated sting pattern, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The reticulated sting pattern consists of criss-crossed red, inflamed lines with uneven intensity and distinct dots of extravasated blood. Sherlock Holmes sees the same pattern on Fitzroy McPherson and Ian Murdoch and recognizes it as the mark left by the jellyfish's filaments.

records.l: the Lion's Mane warning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
records.s: The Lion's Mane warning is Fitzroy McPherson's final phrase before his death. Sherlock Holmes recalls that the phrase describes the appearance of Cyanea capillata and understands it as McPherson's attempt to identify the creature that attacked him.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigate the long-unresolved Abbas Parva tragedy after Mrs. Merrilow brings them to her veiled lodger, Eugenia Ronder. Eugenia explains that her husband, Ronder, abused her, and that she and Leonardo plotted to kill him with a spiked club and make the death appear to be a lion attack. Leonardo struck Ronder, but fled when Sahara King escaped from the lion's cage, leaving the lion to mutilate Eugenia's face. Eugenia concealed the truth to protect Leonardo and herself, and has since lived in isolation under a veil.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Sherlock Holmes is summoned by Mrs. Merrilow to hear the confession of her veiled lodger. He recalls investigating the Abbas Parva tragedy indirectly and having suspected that the coroner's verdict of death from misadventure did not explain all the evidence.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Mrs. Ronder's room and listens to Eugenia Ronder's account. He recalls the Abbas Parva case only after Holmes describes it and proposes an explanation for the positions of Ronder, Eugenia, and the lion.

records.l: Mrs. Merrilow, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Mrs. Merrilow has rented a private room to Eugenia Ronder for seven years and has seen her face only once. She tells Sherlock Holmes that Eugenia cries out about murder and asks him to come, while chiefly fearing that anything he does might cause her valuable lodger to leave.

records.l: Eugenia Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Eugenia Ronder, formerly Mrs. Ronder, has lived veiled and isolated for seven years because Sahara King tore apart her face. She confesses that she helped Leonardo plan Ronder's killing, but concealed the truth because Leonardo's fate and her own reputation depended on her silence.

records.l: Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Ronder was a famous but declining wild-beast showman who drank, bullied people, abused Eugenia, and treated animals cruelly. Leonardo killed him with a club designed to leave wounds resembling a lion's paw, after which the death was officially treated as misadventure.

records.l: Leonardo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Leonardo was the strongman in Ronder's show and Eugenia Ronder's lover. He devised the murder plan and struck Ronder with the spiked club, but lost his nerve and fled when Sahara King came out of the cage.

records.l: Sahara King, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Sahara King was a North African lion kept by Ronder's wild beast show. After Leonardo killed Ronder, Eugenia opened the lion's cage; the animal attacked and severely mutilated her before the circus men drove it away.

records.l: Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Abbas Parva is a small Berkshire village where Ronder's caravan stopped for the night while traveling toward Wimbledon. The killings and lion attack occurred there.

records.l: Ronder's wild beast show, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Ronder's wild beast show was once prominent but was declining because of Ronder's drinking and conduct. It included Sahara King and employed Leonardo, Griggs, and other circus workers who witnessed the aftermath of the attack.

records.l: Abbas Parva tragedy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The Abbas Parva tragedy involved Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's severe facial mutilation beside the open lion's cage. The inquest recorded the event as death from misadventure, although Sherlock Holmes and Edmunds found aspects of the evidence troubling.

records.l: the lion attack at Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The lion attack at Abbas Parva began when Eugenia opened Sahara King's cage after Leonardo struck Ronder. The lion attacked Eugenia, tore her face, and was driven away by Leonardo, Griggs, and other men.

records.l: Ronder's murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Ronder's murder was planned by Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder as a way to end Ronder's abuse. Leonardo used a club with five outward-pointing steel nails to crush Ronder's skull and imitate the marks of a lion's paw.

records.l: the case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The case concerns the unexplained circumstances surrounding Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's mutilation at Abbas Parva. Sherlock Holmes had once been unable to resolve it, but Eugenia's confession supplies the missing explanation.

records.l: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face was torn by Sahara King during the attack. She survived, hid it beneath a veil, and withdrew from society, later telling Sherlock Holmes that she wished the lion had killed her.

records.l: the lion's cage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The lion's cage held Sahara King and was normally used for performances by Ronder and Eugenia. Eugenia opened its door after Leonardo killed Ronder, allowing the lion to escape and attack her.

records.l: five-clawed club, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The spiked club was made by Leonardo with a leaden head and five long steel nails arranged to resemble a lion's paw. It was used to deliver the fatal blow to Ronder while concealing the murder's true cause.

records.l: domestic abuse, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Domestic abuse dominated Eugenia Ronder's marriage to Ronder. He tied her down, lashed her with a riding-whip, deserted her for other women, and became especially violent when drunk.

records.l: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's love affair, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's relationship grew from his pity and assistance to a deep, passionate love affair. Their intimacy led them to conclude that Ronder could not be allowed to continue living.

records.l: the murder plot, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
records.s: The murder plot called for Leonardo to kill Ronder with a spiked club and for Eugenia to release Sahara King so that the death would appear to have been caused by the lion. The plan failed to protect Eugenia when Leonardo fled and the lion attacked her instead.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and John Watson hear the unnamed woman's account of Leonardo's desertion and the five-clawed club. She says Leonardo was drowned while bathing near Margate and that she may have lost the club in a chalk-pit pool, so Holmes declares the case closed. When Holmes sees her disfigured face, he urges her not to take her own life. Two days later, Holmes receives a blue bottle of prussic acid and a message suggesting that the woman will follow his advice.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Sherlock Holmes expresses sympathy for the unnamed woman and asks about Leonardo and the five-clawed club. He tells her that her life is not her own and urges her to endure her suffering. Two days later, he shows John Watson a blue bottle of prussic acid sent to him by post.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: John Watson is present while Sherlock Holmes speaks with the unnamed woman. Two days later, he visits Holmes, examines the blue bottle, and identifies its almondy-smelling contents as prussic acid.

records.l: Eugenia Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: The unnamed woman says that Leonardo deserted her after the lion attacked her, though she could not bring herself to send him to the gallows. She reveals that the lion left her face horribly disfigured and says she may have lost the five-clawed club in a chalk-pit pool. After Holmes urges her not to take her own life, she sends him a bottle of prussic acid with a message indicating that she will follow his advice.

records.l: Leonardo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Leonardo deserted the unnamed woman after leaving her under the lion's claws, and she says she never saw or heard from him again. He was drowned last month while bathing near Margate.

records.l: five-clawed club, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: The five-clawed club is described as the most singular and ingenious part of the woman's story. She does not know what Leonardo did with it and suggests that it may lie in the deep green pool at the base of a chalk-pit.

records.l: Leonardo's drowning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Leonardo's drowning occurred last month while he was bathing near Margate. The unnamed woman learned of his death from a newspaper.

records.l: the case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Sherlock Holmes declares the case closed after hearing that Leonardo is dead and that the five-clawed club may have been lost in the chalk-pit pool. The unnamed woman repeats that the case is closed.

records.l: blue bottle, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: Two days after the woman's visit, Sherlock Holmes has a small blue bottle on his mantelpiece. It bears a red poison label and contains a substance with a pleasant almondy odour.

records.l: prussic acid, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: John Watson identifies the contents of the blue bottle as prussic acid. The substance was sent to Sherlock Holmes by post.

records.l: message, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
records.s: The message sent with the blue bottle says, "I send you my temptation. I will follow your advice." Sherlock Holmes and John Watson infer that it was sent by the brave unnamed woman.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson investigate troubling events at Shoscombe Old Place after John Mason reports that Sir Robert Norberton has become obsessed with winning the Derby, estranged from Lady Beatrice Falder, and visited a haunted crypt with an unknown man. Evidence includes Lady Beatrice's unexplained change in behavior, the removal of her beloved spaniel, mummy remains in the crypt, and a charred fragment of human bone from the central heating furnace. Holmes develops two possible lines of inquiry: a quarrel involving Lady Beatrice's maid, Carrie Evans, and the possibility that Sir Robert has killed Lady Beatrice and arranged for someone to impersonate her. Holmes and Watson travel to the Green Dragon near Shoscombe Old Place disguised as fishermen to investigate further.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Sherlock Holmes examines microscopic evidence in another case before hearing John Mason's concerns about Shoscombe Old Place. He theorizes that Sir Robert may have killed Lady Beatrice, concealed her body, and arranged for someone to impersonate her, then travels with Dr. Watson to investigate while posing as a fisherman.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Dr. Watson identifies the charred fragment as the upper condyle of a human femur and provides background about Sir Robert Norberton and Shoscombe Old Place. He accompanies Sherlock Holmes to the Green Dragon to investigate the situation.

records.l: Sir Robert Norberton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Sir Robert Norberton is described as a dangerous, reckless rider who has staked his finances on Shoscombe Prince winning the Derby. He has stopped visiting Lady Beatrice, given away her beloved spaniel, visited the haunted crypt at night with an unknown man, and allegedly may have killed his sister to protect his financial position.

records.l: Lady Beatrice Falder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Lady Beatrice Falder is Sir Robert's widowed sister and the owner of Shoscombe Old Place under a life interest. She has heart trouble and dropsy, has withdrawn from the horses, remains in her room, drinks heavily, and is described as brooding and sulky after the supposed quarrel with Sir Robert.

records.l: John Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: John Mason, the head trainer at Shoscombe, asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate what he believes is strange and possibly criminal conduct by Sir Robert. He reports the household changes, the nocturnal visits to the haunted crypt, the unknown man, the mummy remains, and the charred bone fragment.

records.l: Carrie Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Carrie Evans is Lady Beatrice's maid and has served her for five years. John Mason suggests that she is devoted, but leaves unclear whether her loyalty is to Lady Beatrice or to Sir Robert.

records.l: the unknown man in the crypt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The unknown man in the crypt meets Sir Robert there at night. When John Mason and Stephens approach him, he reacts with terror, has a yellow face, and runs away before they can identify him.

records.l: Shoscombe Old Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Shoscombe Old Place is the estate at the center of the investigation, containing the Shoscombe stud and training quarters, Lady Beatrice's rooms, a cellar furnace, and access to the park and old chapel. Its household has been disrupted by the apparent estrangement between Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice and by suspicious nighttime activity.

records.l: the Green Dragon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The Green Dragon is an inn at Crendall kept by Josiah Barnes, three miles from Shoscombe Old Place. Sir Robert gave Lady Beatrice's spaniel to Barnes, and Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson stay there while investigating.

records.l: the old ruined chapel, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The old ruined chapel stands in the park of Shoscombe Old Place and is of uncertain age. A crypt beneath it is associated with Sir Robert's nighttime meetings and the discovery of hidden remains.

records.l: the chapel crypt (Shoscombe Old Place), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The haunted crypt beneath the old ruined chapel is considered dark, damp, lonely, and frightening at night. Sir Robert visits it after midnight, an unknown man meets him there, and John Mason later finds a head and bones concealed in one corner.

records.l: Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Shoscombe Prince is described as the best colt in England and Sir Robert's principal hope for financial recovery. Sir Robert has secretly backed him heavily for the Derby and uses the colt's half-brother in public training spins to conceal his ability.

records.l: the Shoscombe spaniels, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The Shoscombe spaniels are described as an exclusive and famous breed, especially prized by Lady Beatrice. Sir Robert gives away her favorite spaniel after becoming angry with it, and the dog is later kept at the Green Dragon.

records.l: the central heating furnace, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The central heating furnace in the cellar beneath Lady Beatrice's room had been unused until Sir Robert had it restarted because he complained of the cold. A fragment of burned human bone is found among its cinders, and the furnace can be reached from outside or through a passage near Lady Beatrice's room.

records.l: the charred human bone fragment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The charred human bone fragment is found by Harvey while raking the central heating furnace's cinders. Dr. Watson identifies it as the upper condyle of a human femur, making it significant evidence of possible human remains being burned.

records.l: the ancient human remains (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The mummy remains consist of a human head and a few bones found hidden beneath a board in one corner of the haunted crypt. John Mason believes they may be a thousand years old and says they were not present there before.

records.l: the Derby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The Derby is the race on which Sir Robert has placed his last financial hope. He must win it with Shoscombe Prince to avoid being unable to satisfy his creditors and losing his racing stables.

records.l: the alleged murder of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The alleged murder of Lady Beatrice is Sherlock Holmes's hypothetical explanation for the crypt visits, the furnace evidence, and the changes in the household. Holmes suggests that Sir Robert may have disposed of her body and concealed the crime until he could realize his winnings from the Derby.

records.l: horse racing, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Horse racing dominates Sir Robert's life and finances, with Shoscombe Prince at the center of his plans. His obsession with the horses and the Derby is said to have affected his nerves and behavior.

records.l: gambling and debt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Sir Robert has staked everything he could raise or borrow on Shoscombe Prince and is deeply in debt to creditors. If the horse fails in the Derby, he expects to be financially ruined, with his racing stables liable to seizure.

records.l: the supposed quarrel between Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: The supposed quarrel is inferred from Sir Robert's sudden withdrawal from Lady Beatrice, his giving away of her favorite spaniel, and her refusal to engage with him or the horses. Holmes considers that the dispute may concern Carrie Evans, but also recognizes that the apparent quarrel could conceal a more serious crime.

records.l: the personation of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
records.s: Impersonation of Lady Beatrice is proposed by Holmes as part of a hypothetical scheme following her possible murder. He suggests that Carrie Evans could help arrange for another woman to appear in Lady Beatrice's place while Sir Robert remained at the estate until after the Derby.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson investigate the apparent personation of Lady Beatrice at Shoscombe Old Place. Holmes uses Lady Beatrice's black spaniel to establish that the carriage occupant is a stranger and later discovers Lady Beatrice's body hidden in an ancestral coffin in the chapel crypt. Sir Robert admits that Lady Beatrice died a week earlier and that Mr. Norlett had been personating her to delay his creditors until the Derby. Shoscombe Prince wins the Derby, allowing Sir Robert to pay his creditors, while the police and coroner treat the deception leniently.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the apparent illness and identity of Lady Beatrice at Shoscombe Old Place. He uses the black spaniel to show that the woman in the carriage is a stranger, finds Lady Beatrice's body in an ancestral coffin, and compels Sir Robert to explain the concealment and personation.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes in observing the carriage, questioning the coachman, searching the chapel crypt, and confronting Sir Robert. He recognizes that the voice from the carriage was that of a man and witnesses Holmes's discovery of the body.

records.l: Sir Robert Norberton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sir Robert owns Shoscombe Old Place and is financially dependent on Lady Beatrice while heavily indebted. After Holmes discovers Lady Beatrice's body, he admits arranging for Mr. Norlett to personate her and hiding her body in the chapel crypt until the Derby was decided.

records.l: Lady Beatrice Falder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Lady Beatrice was Sir Robert's sister and the source of his financial security, with an interest in the estate lasting for her lifetime. She died of what Sir Robert says was dropsy, and her body was concealed while another person appeared publicly as her.

records.l: Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Shoscombe Prince was Sir Robert's dark horse for the Derby, on whose success his financial recovery depended. The horse won the Derby, enabling Sir Robert to pay his creditors and retain enough money to re-establish himself.

records.l: John Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: John Mason, the trainer, meets Holmes and Watson at the park gates and leads them to the chapel crypt. He knows about bones found there but leaves before Holmes examines the ancestral coffins.

records.l: Mr. and Mrs. Norlett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Mr. and Mrs. Norlett are brought by Sir Robert to substantiate his account. Mr. Norlett is an actor who personated Lady Beatrice, while Mrs. Norlett had been Lady Beatrice's confidential maid under her maiden name of Evans.

records.l: Carrie Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Mrs. Norlett, formerly Evans, had served for years as Lady Beatrice's confidential maid. She was involved in the arrangement that allowed her husband to appear publicly as Lady Beatrice and protested when Sir Robert decided to explain the matter.

records.l: Shoscombe Old Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Shoscombe Old Place is Sir Robert's estate, where Lady Beatrice was publicly represented after her death and where the financial crisis surrounding Shoscombe Prince was centered. Its park gates and chapel crypt are the principal locations of Holmes's investigation.

records.l: the chapel crypt (Shoscombe Old Place), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: The chapel crypt is an old, dismal burial place containing the family's coffins. Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett used it to conceal Lady Beatrice's body after removing the remains from an ancestral coffin.

records.l: the Derby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: The Derby was the race on which Sir Robert's financial hopes depended. Shoscombe Prince won it, producing eighty thousand pounds in bets and allowing the creditors to be paid.

records.l: Lady Beatrice's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Lady Beatrice died about a week before Holmes confronted Sir Robert. Sir Robert attributed her death to dropsy, but he concealed it rather than registering it immediately because he feared financial ruin.

records.l: the personation of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: After Lady Beatrice's death, Mr. Norlett appeared as her for several weeks, mainly by riding daily in her carriage while Mrs. Norlett controlled access to her room. The black spaniel exposed the deception by reacting with fury when it encountered the disguised person.

records.l: the creditors, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sir Robert feared that his creditors would seize the estate, stables, and horses if Lady Beatrice's death became known. They held their action until after the Derby and were then paid in full from Sir Robert's winnings.

records.l: the black spaniel (Lady Beatrice's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: The black spaniel initially greeted the person in the carriage as though she were its mistress, but then recognized the stranger and attacked the black skirt. Sir Robert later said he had got rid of the dog after it followed him and Mr. Norlett while they were moving Lady Beatrice's body.

records.l: the ancestral coffin (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Holmes finds an ancestral coffin standing near the vault entrance and opens it with a jemmy. It contains Lady Beatrice's body after Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett removed the ancient remains and burned them in a furnace.

records.l: Lady Beatrice's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Lady Beatrice's body was first taken to an unused well-house and then moved to the chapel crypt. Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett placed it inside an ancestral coffin, where Holmes discovers it wrapped in a sheet.

records.l: the financial crisis surrounding Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sir Robert faced ruin because he depended on Lady Beatrice's estate and was deeply indebted. His financial crisis centered on the prospect that creditors would seize his horses and prevent Shoscombe Prince from running, but the horse's Derby victory resolved the danger.

records.l: Sir Robert's concealment of the death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
records.s: Sir Robert concealed Lady Beatrice's death for roughly three weeks so that Shoscombe Prince could run in the Derby and his bets could succeed. He arranged the public personation, hid the body in the chapel crypt, and delayed registering the death, receiving only mild censure afterward.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. John Watson to investigate Josiah Amberley's claim that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared together after taking money and securities from his strong-room. Watson visits The Haven in Lewisham, hears Amberley's account, and observes the neglected house, Amberley's artificial limb, and a tall, dark man who appears to follow him. Holmes identifies several overlooked details and obtains information confirming Amberley's reputation, his wealth, and Dr. Ernest's association with him and Mrs. Amberley. Although the case initially seems simple, Holmes concludes that it has developed serious complications.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Sherlock Holmes receives Josiah Amberley's case through the Yard but initially considers it commonplace. He sends Dr. John Watson to The Haven because he is occupied with the case of the two Coptic Patriarchs, then analyzes Watson's report and points out important details Watson missed.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Dr. John Watson visits The Haven in Lewisham as Sherlock Holmes's representative and interviews Josiah Amberley. He observes the house and its surroundings, records Amberley's account, notices a tall, dark man apparently following him, and reports his findings to Holmes.

records.l: Josiah Amberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Josiah Amberley, a retired junior partner of Brickfall and Amberley, lives at The Haven after retiring with a fortune and marrying a younger woman. He claims that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest left together with his deed-box and about seven thousand pounds' worth of cash and securities. He appears physically burdened and emotionally devastated, and is described as a miserly, harsh, and exacting husband.

records.l: Amberley's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Mrs. Amberley is Josiah Amberley's younger wife and is described as good-looking. Amberley claims that she had an intimacy with Dr. Ray Ernest, left with him, and took his deed-box containing money and securities.

records.l: Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Dr. Ray Ernest is a young, unmarried doctor who lives near Josiah Amberley and plays chess with him. He frequently visited The Haven and is suspected by Amberley of leaving with Mrs. Amberley.

records.l: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: This unit introduces Sherlock Holmes's investigation of Josiah Amberley's report that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared after a theft. It follows Dr. John Watson's visit to The Haven and Holmes's growing suspicion that the apparently simple case has a more complicated aspect.

records.l: The Haven, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: The Haven is Josiah Amberley's neglected house in Lewisham, surrounded by a high brick wall. It contains a strong-room with an iron door and shutter, as well as the rooms and passage Amberley has been painting.

records.l: Lewisham, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Lewisham is the London district where The Haven and Josiah Amberley's home are located. Dr. John Watson travels there to investigate Amberley's story.

records.l: the disappearance of Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Josiah Amberley reports that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest left together after she claimed to have a headache and remained at home while Amberley went alone to the Haymarket Theatre. Their destination is unknown, and neither has sent Amberley a letter or message.

records.l: the theft from the strong-room, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: Amberley reports that about seven thousand pounds' worth of cash and securities were taken from his burglar-proof strong-room. He says Mrs. Amberley had a duplicate key and that the door and window were open when he returned from the theatre.

records.l: the investigation of Amberley's case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
records.s: The investigation begins when the Yard sends Amberley to Sherlock Holmes after the police receive his report. Holmes delegates the initial visit to Dr. John Watson, gathers local information by telephone and through the Yard, and learns that Amberley was reputed to be a miser and harsh husband while Dr. Ernest had connections with both Amberley and his wife.

records.l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Sherlock Holmes investigates Josiah Amberley's claim that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared with securities, and tests Amberley by sending him to Little Purlington with Dr. John Watson. The telegram supposedly sent by the Vicar is revealed to be forged, allowing Holmes to search Amberley's house while he is away. Holmes, aided by Mr. Barker, Inspector MacKinnon, and the police, identifies the strong-room as the likely death-chamber and exposes Amberley's plot to murder the couple. Amberley is arrested after Holmes confronts him about the bodies and prevents him from swallowing a poison pellet.

records.l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Sherlock Holmes arranged for Josiah Amberley to follow the forged telegram to Little Purlington so that he could examine Amberley's house without interruption. He discovered the gas pipe leading into the sealed strong-room, identified the wall message, confronted Amberley about the bodies, and turned his findings over to Inspector MacKinnon and the police.

records.l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Dr. John Watson accompanied Josiah Amberley to Little Purlington and ensured that he actually made the journey. His observations of the smell of paint and the theatre seat number helped Holmes establish that Amberley's story and alibi were false.

records.l: Josiah Amberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Josiah Amberley was a miser, a jealous chess player, and the husband of the missing woman. Holmes concluded that Amberley had murdered his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest by trapping them in the strong-room and flooding it with gas; Amberley was arrested after trying to swallow a white pellet.

records.l: Amberley's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Amberley's wife was made wretched by his niggardly ways and became involved with Dr. Ray Ernest. Holmes concluded that Amberley murdered her in the strong-room.

records.l: Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Dr. Ray Ernest was a chess-playing doctor whom Holmes identified as Amberley's wife's companion. Holmes concluded that Amberley murdered him along with Amberley's wife.

records.l: Mr. Barker, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Mr. Barker was a private investigator engaged by Dr. Ray Ernest's family. He independently suspected foul play, confronted Holmes while Holmes was entering Amberley's house, then helped Holmes restrain Amberley and took charge of formalities at the station.

records.l: Inspector MacKinnon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Inspector MacKinnon represented the police and objected that Holmes's irregular methods had taken credit from the official investigation. He accepted Holmes's evidence, arranged a search, and was credited by the newspaper with deductions and discoveries that Holmes had actually made.

records.l: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest were the couple whose disappearance Holmes investigated. Holmes concluded that they had been murdered by Amberley in the strong-room, and their bodies were expected to be found in a disused well.

records.l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: The police had formed their own views of the case and were prepared to arrest Amberley. Three constables were sent to search the house, and the police took over the investigation after Holmes supplied his findings.

records.l: Little Purlington, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: Little Purlington was a remote village in Essex on a branch line, reached by a slow train and a two-mile drive. Holmes used it as the destination for the forged telegram so Amberley could not return promptly to his house.

records.l: the Vicarage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: The Vicarage at Little Purlington was the address named in the forged telegram. Its vicar, J. C. Elman, denied sending the telegram and said he had never heard of Amberley.

records.l: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: The case concerned the disappearance of Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest, along with securities that Amberley said had been taken. It culminated in Amberley's arrest and the discovery of evidence that the disappearances were murders rather than an elopement.

records.l: the murders, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
records.s: The murders were planned by Amberley out of jealousy and revenge. Holmes believed he lured the victims into the strong-room, sealed them inside, and killed them by releasing gas.

records.l: the forged telegram, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
