records.s: Sergeant Coventry, a tall, thin, secretive local police investigator, first examines the affair. Decent and honest though out of his depth, he guides Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson after an official delay and reports Mrs. Gibson's shooting, note, and Mr. Neil Gibson's summons.

records.l: Mrs. Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mrs. Gibson, who loved Neil Gibson vividly and physically and intensely hated Miss Dunbar, arranged a secret meeting at Thor Bridge. She planned her own death to implicate Miss Dunbar, using Miss Dunbar’s note, a concealed pistol, and a second pistol disposed of with a string and weight. She was found dead on her back near Thor Bridge, shot at close range behind the right temple, with the note clutched in her left hand.

records.l: the pistol hidden in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A pistol, one of Mr. Neil Gibson’s pair, is found beneath Miss Dunbar’s dresses during a police search. Though she denies ever seeing it, its conspicuous concealment and the missing matching weapon lead Holmes to conclude that Mrs. Gibson placed it in the wardrobe after firing one barrel, intending to incriminate Miss Dunbar.

records.l: the incrimination of Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: depends_on the revolver [found in her wardrobe] The discovery of a pistol in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe appears to incriminate her, but Holmes considers the placement inconsistent with a carefully planned crime. He concludes that someone wishing to incriminate her may have put the weapon there.

records.l: the investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The investigation advances when Holmes questions Miss Dunbar, examines the significance of the stonework chip, and tests his theory at Thor Bridge. The test confirms that a pistol could have been pulled from the fatal spot across the parapet and into the water.

records.l: the note from Mrs. Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mrs. Gibson’s note, left in the schoolroom, asks Miss Dunbar to meet at Thor Bridge and leave a reply on the garden sundial. Requested for destruction but retained, Miss Dunbar’s reply is used to make her appear connected to the crime.

records.l: Dr. Watson's revolver, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dr. Watson's revolver, short, handy, and serviceable, is used by Holmes to reproduce the crime pistol: altered with a cartridge removed, tied to a string and weighted stone, it strikes a bridge parapet and makes a matching chip.

records.l: the string, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: String tied to Dr. Watson's revolver and a stone; during Holmes's reconstruction, releasing it pulls the revolver across a bridge and over the parapet, demonstrating weapon disposal.

records.l: the stone, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a considerable stone [used as a weight] A considerable stone is tied to the far end of the string and hung over the bridge parapet. Its weight pulls the revolver from Holmes's hand, causing the impact that reproduces the stonework chip.

records.l: the stonework chip, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_evidence_of Mrs. Gibson's death [sign of violent impact] A fresh chip in the bridge stonework appears opposite Mrs. Gibson's body and initially seems unexplained. Holmes reproduces an identical chip with Dr. Watson's revolver, establishing that it was caused when the weapon was pulled against the parapet.

records.l: perverted love, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: causes Mrs. Gibson's death [as a motive for the plot] Holmes describes Mrs. Gibson's motive as an example of perverted love. In his account, her hatred of Miss Dunbar and her desire to punish her husband and rival led her to stage her suicide so that Miss Dunbar would face a fate worse than sudden death.

records.l: Professor Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury is a sixty-one-year-old, wealthy, widowed Camford physiologist, scientist, lecturer, and professor of European reputation. He is Edith Presbury’s only father, formerly known for an academic life, brilliant crowded lectures, a reliable memory, and a grave, portly appearance with unusually keen, cunning eyes. After a secret journey and secret correspondence with Dorak and, through a London agent, H. Lowenstein, his behavior changes: he becomes furtive, sly, intermittently fierce, and subject to queer fits and drug-related outbursts every nine days, though his intellect remains clear in ordinary periods. He secretly follows directions for a strong treatment supplied by a Bohemian intermediary, keeping its bottles and syringe in a locked box whose key hangs from his watch-chain. The treatment produces thick, horny knuckles and animal-like episodes in which he crouches, crawls, climbs ivy, and reverts to a black-faced Langur. When Holmes and Watson visit, he angrily denies calling them and blocks their exit. At the next crisis, Roy attacks him, tears his throat, and leaves him seriously wounded and unconscious; his box and letters reveal the Langur-based treatment from H. Lowenstein.

records.l: Mr. Bennett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mr. Bennett is Professor Presbury’s trusted professional assistant and secretary, living in the Professor’s household and engaged to Edith Presbury. He handles Presbury’s papers and correspondence, including correspondence with Dorak, and has a medical degree. As Presbury grows sinister despite seeming mentally clear, Bennett and Edith become alarmed. Bennett reports the secret correspondence, the Professor’s anger over a wooden box, Roy’s attacks, and Presbury crawling through a passage at night to Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson. He supplies Dorak’s address, helps observe and follow Presbury, rescues him after Roy’s attack, dresses his wound, and provides the box key.

records.l: Edith Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Edith Presbury, Professor Presbury’s only daughter and devoted to him, is engaged to Trevor Bennett. During a prolonged visit away from home, she reports her father seems an empty shell and saw him at her second-floor window. Bennett fears she is in danger; Holmes advises remaining away until it passes.

records.l: Roy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Roy is Professor Presbury's faithful wolf-hound, kept at the household stables. He repeatedly attacks only Presbury, reacting violently to Presbury's transformed behavior and special appearances. After Presbury torments him, Roy's collar slips and he bites deeply into Presbury's throat; he is then banished and chained near the stables, barking at Edith's window.

records.l: the Professor's case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury’s case is a curious mystery investigated by Holmes in Camford. It centers on Presbury’s transformation and unexplained behavior: secret communications, a guarded box, Roy’s attacks, nocturnal crawling, and Edith seeing him at her window. Holmes links incidents to particular dates, but ends unable to justify Presbury’s arrest or restraint because no crime or madness is proved.

records.l: Professor Presbury's transformation and strange behavior, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury's transformation begins after his Prague journey: though his lectures remain brilliant, he becomes furtive, sly, sinister, and forgetful on certain dates. His behavior escalates into crawling on hands and feet, fierce conduct toward Edith, and unexplained appearances at her second-floor window.

records.l: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury secretly leaves home, spends a fortnight away, and returns travel-worn without naming his destination. A fellow-student's letter reveals he was in Prague. The visit occurs before his strange symptoms and is connected by Holmes to secret correspondence with a Bohemian dealer and H. Lowenstein's serum treatment.

records.l: Roy's attacks on Professor Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occur_on July 2, July 11, and July 20 [before Roy was banished to the stables] Roy attacks Professor Presbury on July 2, July 11, and July 20. Since Roy attacks no one else, the incidents are treated as a significant part of the mystery, and Roy is later removed to the stables.

records.l: Professor Presbury's nocturnal crawling, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_performed_by Professor Presbury [in the passage at about two in the morning] On September 4, Trevor Bennett sees Professor Presbury crawling along the dark passage at about two in the morning. Presbury moves on his hands and feet, suddenly stands upright when Bennett speaks to him, spits out an atrocious word, and leaves the house until daylight.

records.l: Edith's sighting of her father's face at the window, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: depicts Professor Presbury [at Edith's second-floor window in bright moonlight] On the night before Edith comes to Baker Street, she sees Professor Presbury's face pressed against the window of her second-floor room. She sees no ladder or other possible means of access, and Presbury makes no reference to the incident the next morning.

records.l: the letters from London, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Letters from London, marked with a cross under the stamp and bearing the E.C. mark in illiterate handwriting, are reserved for Professor Presbury; his replies bypass Bennett and the household letter-basket.

records.l: the wooden box (Professor Presbury's box), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A small carved wooden box brought from Professor Presbury's Prague journey is kept in his instrument cupboard; when Trevor Bennett handles it while seeking a cannula, Presbury reacts with unusual anger and savagery.

records.l: Camford, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Camford is a famous, ancient university town where Professor Presbury lives, works, and lectures as a physiologist. Holmes and Dr. Watson travel there to investigate, stay at the Chequers, and plan to return the following Tuesday.

records.l: the Professor's engagement to Alice Morphy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury becomes engaged to Alice Morphy, the daughter of his colleague Professor Morphy, despite being sixty-one and much older than her. His family considers the relationship excessive, while Alice's father does not object, and Holmes notes that the engagement preceded Presbury's journey and later behavioral changes.

records.l: A. Dorak, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A. Dorak is an elderly, suave Bohemian London storekeeper on Commercial Road and H. Lowenstein’s agent in England, identified as the man to whom Professor Presbury writes.

records.l: the Professor's drug-related outbursts, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Professor Presbury's drug-related violent outbursts occur on July 2, August 26, and September 3; Holmes theorizes a poisonous drug intensifies them, with later episodes following a nine-day sequence.

records.l: the strong drug, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The strong drug causes Professor Presbury's outbursts, temporarily poisoning him and intensifying his violent nature. He learned it in Prague and receives it in London through a Bohemian intermediary.

records.l: the Professor's correspondence with Dorak, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_secret secret [the Professor writes to a man in London] Professor Presbury secretly corresponds with Dorak in London. Mr. Bennett obtains Dorak's address from Presbury's blotting-paper after seeing that Presbury appears to have written to him that morning.

records.l: the nine-day pattern, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: governs the Professor's drug-related outbursts [with one apparent exception] Holmes observes that trouble began on July 2 and then generally recurred at nine-day intervals, including August 26 and September 3. He considers the pattern too exact to be coincidence and expects new developments by the following Tuesday.

records.l: H. Lowenstein, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: H. Lowenstein is a Prague-based scientist developing the Serum of Anthropoid as a rejuvenation treatment. Using black-faced Langur because a specimen was accessible, he writes to Professor Presbury through his England agent, A. Dorak, warning that the treatment may be dangerous and that Serum of Anthropoid might have been better.

records.l: the Serum of Anthropoid, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Serum of Anthropoid is mentioned by H. Lowenstein as a possible treatment that might have been better suited to Professor Presbury's case. Lowenstein used black-faced Langur instead because that specimen was accessible.

records.l: black-faced Langur, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Black-faced Langur, a great black-faced monkey native to Himalayan slopes, is a crawler and climber; an available specimen supplied Lowenstein's source for Professor Presbury's serum.

records.l: the treatment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A dangerous treatment using black-faced Langur serum is injected on a regulated nine-day cycle to rejuvenate Professor Presbury. It boosts energy and vitality, but unfolds with alarming crawling, climbing, and other animal-like behavior.

records.l: rejuvenescence, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a secret sought by Lowenstein [described as an elixir of life] Rejuvenescence is associated with Lowenstein's reported scientific efforts to discover a means of restoring youth. Holmes concludes that Professor Presbury pursued the treatment because he wanted to become a younger man.

records.l: the wolf-hound attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a dangerous attack [by Roy against Professor Presbury] The wolf-hound attack occurs after Professor Presbury deliberately provokes Roy with pebbles, a stick, and gestures near the dog's mouth. Roy's collar slips, allowing him to seize Presbury by the throat and cause serious bleeding before Holmes, Dr. Watson, Bennett, and the coachman intervene.

records.l: Harold Stackhurst, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Harold Stackhurst is the headmaster of The Gables, a coaching establishment, and an excellent former rowing Blue. A neighbor and friend of Mr. Holmes, he employs Ian Murdoch as a mathematical coach. After Fitzroy McPherson collapses, Stackhurst aids Holmes, reports on The Gables, dismisses Murdoch after confronting him, investigates McPherson’s disappearance and death, helps destroy Cyanea capillata, and reconciles with Murdoch.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson is a science master at The Gables, an athlete and year-round swimmer despite heart trouble following rheumatic fever. Secretly engaged to Maud Bellamy, he is found staggering from the beach with severe injuries and dies at the bathing-pool after what appears to be an assault. The inquest initially fails to explain his death, but it is ultimately attributed to contact with the radiating, stinging filaments of Cyanea capillata.

records.l: Ian Murdoch, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Ian Murdoch is a tall, dark, thin, taciturn mathematical coach and teacher at The Gables, subordinate to Stackhurst. Though aloof and thought to have outlandish blood, he is McPherson’s friend and supports McPherson’s relationship with Miss Bellamy despite loving her himself, acting as their go-between. After McPherson collapses, Murdoch denies being with him on the beach and is dismissed after an angry exchange with Stackhurst. Suspected because of his temper, quarrel, and love for Miss Bellamy, he is later attacked by Cyanea capillata and survives, clearing him.

records.l: Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Maud Bellamy, Tom Bellamy’s beautiful, strong-minded daughter and William’s sister, was secretly engaged to Fitzroy McPherson before his death; afterward she helps Holmes and suggests multiple attackers.

records.l: the dog (McPherson's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: McPherson's dog, a faithful Airedale terrier belonging to Fitzroy McPherson, follows its dead master's trail to the bathing-pool and dies there from Cyanea capillata; its rigid, contorted body gives Sherlock Holmes an important clue to the water's danger.

records.l: Fulworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains The Haven [on the rising ground behind the hamlet] Fulworth is the nearby village around the bay, containing the police station and the Bellamy family’s home and boating business. Holmes and Stackhurst walk there to question the Bellamys.

records.l: The Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Gables is Harold Stackhurst’s coaching establishment, housing young men preparing for professions. Stackhurst, McPherson, and Murdoch work there. After McPherson’s body is brought there, students report finding his dog; Stackhurst is found in his study, then leaves to bring the stricken Murdoch to Sherlock Holmes and later dismisses him.

records.l: The Haven, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Haven begins as the Bellamy family home in Fulworth, where Ian Murdoch leaves as Holmes and Stackhurst arrive. It is also recorded as Tom Bellamy's poorly maintained Lewisham property and, finally, Josiah Amberley's neglected, walled house with a strong-room.

records.l: the beach, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The beach below the chalk cliffs contains a lagoon, swimming-pools, caves, pebbles, shingle, and a secluded bathing-pool. Though it seems deserted except for distant figures, it becomes the site of McPherson's death, his dog’s tracks and towel, and Ian Murdoch’s attack, caused by a deadly jellyfish concealed in the pool.

records.l: the chalk cliffs, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: border the beach [along the coast] The coast near Holmes’s villa consists of chalk cliffs that can be descended by a single steep, slippery path. Small caves at their base are searched after McPherson’s death, but nothing is found.

records.l: the bathing-pool, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_located_under the cliff [in a hollowed-out part of the beach] The bathing-pool is the site where Fitzroy McPherson died, his dog was later found dead, and Ian Murdoch was attacked. Sherlock Holmes discovers Cyanea capillata beneath the water in its deeper section and identifies it as the source of the danger.

records.l: Fitzroy McPherson's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Fitzroy McPherson’s death occurs at the beach and bathing-pool after he staggers up from the beach, cries out about the Lion’s Mane, and collapses. Severe, patterned injuries and intense suffering make it seem extraordinary and possibly criminal; after an inconclusive inquest, Sherlock Holmes identifies Cyanea capillata as the cause rather than human assault.

records.l: the assault on Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: An assault apparently using a scourge inflicts fatal injuries on McPherson, leaving curved red marks; tortured, he bites through his lip, crawls from the beach, and dies.

records.l: the Lion's Mane mystery, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Lion’s Mane mystery begins when McPherson’s final warning appears to be the words “the lion’s mane.” The phrase is initially unintelligible to Holmes and becomes the name of the unusual problem he begins investigating.

records.l: the investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: concerns Fitzroy McPherson's death [seeking the motive and criminal] The investigation examines McPherson’s movements, footprints, clothing, towel, body, personal papers, and relationships. Holmes and Stackhurst question the Bellamys and begin to focus on Ian Murdoch, Maud Bellamy, and the possibility of multiple attackers.

records.l: the McPherson–Bellamy engagement, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a secret engagement [between Fitzroy McPherson and Maud Bellamy] McPherson and Maud Bellamy were secretly engaged to be married. They kept the engagement secret because McPherson’s elderly uncle might have disinherited him if he married against his uncle’s wishes.

records.l: the note from Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_written_by Maud Bellamy [in a feminine hand] A note in McPherson’s card-case, written in a feminine hand, reads, “I will be there, you may be sure.--Maudie.” The note suggests an assignation, and McPherson’s papers identify Maud Bellamy as its writer.

records.l: the scourge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a flexible instrument [apparently used to inflict the injuries] The apparent scourge is the suspected instrument that produced the long, flexible-looking weals on McPherson’s back. No actual scourge is found, and Holmes questions whether a human hand wielded it.

records.l: McPherson's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_found_at the beach [after his fatal assault] McPherson’s body is found on the path above the beach, with his Burberry thrown around his shoulders, disordered clothing, blood on his chin, and severe red marks across his back. His pockets contain a handkerchief, a large knife, a folding card-case, and the note signed “Maudie.”

records.l: Murdoch's possible motive, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Murdoch’s possible motive includes his former apparent interest in Maud Bellamy, his earlier hostility toward McPherson, and his visit to The Haven shortly after McPherson’s death. Holmes also notes that Murdoch had an angry temperament and appeared to be seeking a way to leave the scene.

records.l: Inspector Bardie, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Inspector Bardie of the Sussex Constabulary considers arresting chief suspect Ian Murdoch, but Holmes judges the evidence too weak; Bardie then witnesses Murdoch's attack, Cyanea capillata's discovery, and Holmes's explanation.

records.l: the dog's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occurs_at the bathing-pool [at the edge of the pool] The dog's death is first attributed to grief for its master after it refuses food for a week. Because it dies at the same place as Fitzroy McPherson, its death alerts Sherlock Holmes that the location itself is dangerous; its contorted body is later understood as another victim of Cyanea capillata.

records.l: Ian Murdoch's attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_caused_by Cyanea capillata [at the bathing-pool] Ian Murdoch's attack occurs at the edge of the water where Fitzroy McPherson died. The attack produces severe pain, breathing difficulties, and a reticulated red pattern on his shoulder, matching McPherson's injuries and revealing the true cause of the earlier death.

records.l: Cyanea capillata, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Cyanea capillata is a fearful stinging jellyfish, a tawny-and-silver lion’s-mane-like mass in the deepest bathing-pool, possibly brought by the South-West gale. Its nearly invisible fifty-foot filaments leave reticulated red marks, causing extreme pain, cardiac distress, and possible death, until Holmes and Stackhurst crush it beneath a boulder.

records.l: the murder investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: includes Fitzroy McPherson's death The murder investigation initially focuses on Ian Murdoch because of his relationship with Miss Bellamy, his history with McPherson, and his apparent preparations to leave. The investigation is resolved when Sherlock Holmes proves that McPherson's death was caused by Cyanea capillata and that Murdoch was innocent.

records.l: the reticulated sting pattern, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a red inflamed lines [criss-crossed and reticulated] The reticulated sting pattern consists of criss-crossed red, inflamed lines with uneven intensity and distinct dots of extravasated blood. Sherlock Holmes sees the same pattern on Fitzroy McPherson and Ian Murdoch and recognizes it as the mark left by the jellyfish's filaments.

records.l: the Lion's Mane warning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: refers_to Cyanea capillata [McPherson's warning about the creature] The Lion's Mane warning is Fitzroy McPherson's final phrase before his death. Sherlock Holmes recalls that the phrase describes the appearance of Cyanea capillata and understands it as McPherson's attempt to identify the creature that attacked him.

records.l: Mrs. Merrilow, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mrs. Merrilow, a South Brixton landlady, owns a private house and lodges Eugenia Ronder for seven years. Having seen Eugenia’s face once and heard her cry about murder, she asks Sherlock Holmes to intervene while fearing the valuable lodger may leave.

records.l: Eugenia Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Eugenia Ronder, formerly Mrs. Ronder, is a former circus girl and lodger of Mrs. Merrilow who lives veiled and secluded in South Brixton after Sahara King permanently mutilated her face. Wasting away in poor health, she sends Sherlock Holmes a blue bottle and confesses her past. Abused by Ronder, she loved Leonardo and helped plan Ronder’s killing, but kept silent to protect Leonardo and her reputation. Leonardo deserted her after the attack, yet she could not condemn him. She considers suicide, then sends prussic acid while indicating she will follow Holmes’s advice.

records.l: Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Ronder is a famous but declining wild-beast showman, rival of Wombwell and Sanger, whose drunken violence, cruelty, and repeated abuse of Eugenia end when Leonardo kills him; his death is treated as misadventure.

records.l: Leonardo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Leonardo, a professional-acrobat strongman in Ronder's show and Eugenia Ronder's lover, devises a plot to murder Ronder and makes and uses a spiked club against him. When Sahara King emerges, he flees, abandoning Eugenia under the lion's claws. She never hears from him again; he later drowns while bathing near Margate.

records.l: Sahara King, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sahara King is a dangerous North African lion kept in Ronder's wild beast show; after Leonardo killed Ronder, Eugenia released it, and it severely mutilated her before circus men drove it away.

records.l: Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a village [in Berkshire] Abbas Parva is a small Berkshire village where Ronder's caravan stopped for the night while traveling toward Wimbledon. The killings and lion attack occurred there.

records.l: Ronder's wild beast show, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: travels_to Wimbledon [by road] Ronder's wild beast show was once prominent but was declining because of Ronder's drinking and conduct. It included Sahara King and employed Leonardo, Griggs, and other circus workers who witnessed the aftermath of the attack.

records.l: Abbas Parva tragedy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occurs_at Abbas Parva [during the show's overnight halt] The Abbas Parva tragedy involved Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's severe facial mutilation beside the open lion's cage. The inquest recorded the event as death from misadventure, although Sherlock Holmes and Edmunds found aspects of the evidence troubling.

records.l: the lion attack at Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The lion attack at Abbas Parva began when Eugenia opened Sahara King's cage after Leonardo struck Ronder. The lion attacked Eugenia, tore her face, and was driven away by Leonardo, Griggs, and other men.

records.l: Ronder's murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_committed_with the spiked club [disguised as a lion attack] Ronder's murder was planned by Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder as a way to end Ronder's abuse. Leonardo used a club with five outward-pointing steel nails to crush Ronder's skull and imitate the marks of a lion's paw.

records.l: the case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The case concerns Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's mutilation at Abbas Parva. Once unresolved by Sherlock Holmes, it is explained by Eugenia's confession; after Leonardo's death and the likely loss of the five-clawed club, Holmes declares it closed.

records.l: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face was torn by Sahara King during the attack. She survived, hid it beneath a veil, and withdrew from society, later telling Sherlock Holmes that she wished the lion had killed her.

records.l: the lion's cage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The lion's cage held Sahara King and was normally used for performances by Ronder and Eugenia. Eugenia opened its door after Leonardo killed Ronder, allowing the lion to escape and attack her.

records.l: five-clawed club, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A singular, ingenious spiked club made by Leonardo has a leaden head and five long steel nails arranged like a lion's paw. It delivers the fatal blow to Ronder while concealing the murder's true cause. Afterwards, its fate is unknown; the woman suggests it may lie in a deep green pool at a chalk-pit's base.

records.l: domestic abuse, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_inflicted_by Ronder [against Eugenia Ronder] Domestic abuse dominated Eugenia Ronder's marriage to Ronder. He tied her down, lashed her with a riding-whip, deserted her for other women, and became especially violent when drunk.

records.l: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's love affair, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's relationship grew from his pity and assistance to a deep, passionate love affair. Their intimacy led them to conclude that Ronder could not be allowed to continue living.

records.l: the murder plot, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: targets Ronder [planned by Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder] The murder plot called for Leonardo to kill Ronder with a spiked club and for Eugenia to release Sahara King so that the death would appear to have been caused by the lion. The plan failed to protect Eugenia when Leonardo fled and the lion attacked her instead.

records.l: Leonardo's drowning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: occurs_near Margate [while bathing] Leonardo's drowning occurred last month while he was bathing near Margate. The unnamed woman learned of his death from a newspaper.

records.l: blue bottle, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A small blue bottle, received by Sherlock Holmes by post two days after the woman’s visit, sits on his mantelpiece with a red poison label and prussic acid smelling pleasantly almondy.

records.l: prussic acid, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a poison John Watson identifies the contents of the blue bottle as prussic acid. The substance was sent to Sherlock Holmes by post.

records.l: message, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A message from an unnamed woman sends a blue bottle as her temptation and promises to follow Holmes's advice; Holmes and Watson infer she sent it after her troubling account.

records.l: Sir Robert Norberton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sir Robert Norberton is an unmarried baronet, prominent and daring horse racer, and owner of Shoscombe Prince. He lives with and depends financially on his widowed sister, Lady Beatrice Falder, while holding only a life interest in Shoscombe Old Place and facing deep gambling debts and creditors. His fortune is staked on Shoscombe Prince winning the Derby, and his obsession with the horse appears mentally destabilizing. As Lady Beatrice’s death would bring financial ruin and seizure of the estate, he stops visiting her, gives away her spaniel, and visits the crypt at night. Suspected of murdering her, he ultimately admits concealing her body in the chapel crypt and arranging Mr. Norlett’s personation of her until the Derby’s result.

records.l: Lady Beatrice Falder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lady Beatrice Falder is Sir Robert Norberton’s widowed sister, an invalid with weak heart trouble and long-standing dropsy. Through her late husband’s estate she holds a life interest in Shoscombe Old Place, making her the source of Sir Robert’s financial security. Devoted to him despite his difficult conduct, she lives with maid Carrie Evans, keeps prized Shoscombe spaniels, and withdraws to her room, drinking heavily and seeming brooding after a supposed quarrel. She dies, reportedly of dropsy, and her body is concealed while another person publicly impersonates her.

records.l: John Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: John Mason is head trainer at the Shoscombe training quarters, working for Sir Robert Norberton and training Shoscombe Prince. Concerned by Sir Robert’s strange, possibly criminal behavior, he asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate, reporting household changes, crypt visits, an unknown man, mummy remains, and charred bone. He later guides Holmes and Watson to the chapel crypt, then departs before their examination.

records.l: Carrie Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Carrie Evans is Lady Beatrice Falder’s longtime confidential maid, serving her for five years and described as devoted, though her loyalty may lie with Lady Beatrice or Sir Robert. Later, as Mrs. Norlett, formerly Evans, she helps arrange for her husband to appear publicly as Lady Beatrice and protests Sir Robert’s planned explanation.

records.l: the unknown man in the crypt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The unknown man in the crypt meets Sir Robert there at night. When John Mason and Stephens approach him, he reacts with terror, has a yellow face, and runs away before they can identify him.

records.l: Shoscombe Old Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Shoscombe Old Place is Sir Robert's estate at the centre of Shoscombe Park and of Holmes's investigation. It includes the Shoscombe stud and training quarters, Lady Beatrice's rooms, a cellar furnace, gates with heraldic griffins, and access to the old chapel and crypt. The household is troubled by Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice's apparent estrangement, suspicious nighttime activity, Lady Beatrice's public representation after death, and a financial crisis involving Shoscombe Prince.

records.l: the Green Dragon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_located_in Crendall [an inn kept by Josiah Barnes] The Green Dragon is an inn at Crendall kept by Josiah Barnes, three miles from Shoscombe Old Place. Sir Robert gave Lady Beatrice's spaniel to Barnes, and Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson stay there while investigating.

records.l: the old ruined chapel, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The old ruined chapel stands in the park of Shoscombe Old Place and is of uncertain age. A crypt beneath it is associated with Sir Robert's nighttime meetings and the discovery of hidden remains.

records.l: the chapel crypt (Shoscombe Old Place), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The chapel crypt is an ancient family burial place beneath the old ruined chapel, dark, damp, lonely, and feared at night. It contains family coffins, including an ancestral coffin, and newly found mummy remains concealed in a corner. Sir Robert visits after midnight and meets an unknown man; he and Mr. Norlett later use the crypt to conceal Lady Beatrice’s body after removing the ancestral remains.

records.l: Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Shoscombe Prince is a racehorse and leading Derby colt, Sir Robert Norberton's concealed decisive wager and principal hope for financial recovery. Faster than his half-brother, he is hidden behind that substitute in public training and entered as a dark horse. He wins the Derby, allowing Sir Robert to pay creditors and retain enough money to re-establish himself.

records.l: the Shoscombe spaniels, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Shoscombe spaniels are an exclusive, nationally exhibited breed prized by Lady Beatrice; after Sir Robert angrily gives away her favorite, it is kept at the Green Dragon.

records.l: the central heating furnace, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The central heating furnace, in the cellar beneath Lady Beatrice's room at Shoscombe Old Place, was restarted by Sir Robert after being unused. It contains a charred human bone fragment among its cinders and is accessible from outside or a nearby passage.

records.l: the charred human bone fragment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a human femur fragment [the upper condyle, burned black] The charred human bone fragment is found by Harvey while raking the central heating furnace's cinders. Dr. Watson identifies it as the upper condyle of a human femur, making it significant evidence of possible human remains being burned.

records.l: the ancient human remains (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Ancient human remains, a head and a few bones, were found hidden beneath a board in the haunted crypt after Sir Robert’s nocturnal visits; believed possibly a thousand years old, they were later burned in the chapel crypt furnace.
records.t: Ancient human remains—a head and a few bones—were found hidden beneath a board in the haunted crypt after Sir Robert’s nocturnal visits; believed possibly a thousand years old, they were later burned in the chapel crypt furnace.

records.l: the Derby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Derby is a horse race on which Sir Robert places his last financial hope. He must win it with Shoscombe Prince to pay creditors and keep his racing stables; Shoscombe Prince wins, bringing eighty thousand pounds in bets and allowing the creditors to be paid.

records.l: the alleged murder of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: involves impersonation of Lady Beatrice [Holmes's hypothetical reconstruction] The alleged murder of Lady Beatrice is Sherlock Holmes's hypothetical explanation for the crypt visits, the furnace evidence, and the changes in the household. Holmes suggests that Sir Robert may have disposed of her body and concealed the crime until he could realize his winnings from the Derby.

records.l: horse racing, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_practiced_at Shoscombe Old Place [through its stud and training quarters] Horse racing dominates Sir Robert's life and finances, with Shoscombe Prince at the center of his plans. His obsession with the horses and the Derby is said to have affected his nerves and behavior.

records.l: gambling and debt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: threatens Shoscombe Old Place [if Shoscombe Prince loses the Derby] Sir Robert has staked everything he could raise or borrow on Shoscombe Prince and is deeply in debt to creditors. If the horse fails in the Derby, he expects to be financially ruined, with his racing stables liable to seizure.

records.l: the supposed quarrel between Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The supposed quarrel is inferred from Sir Robert's sudden withdrawal from Lady Beatrice, his giving away of her favorite spaniel, and her refusal to engage with him or the horses. Holmes considers that the dispute may concern Carrie Evans, but also recognizes that the apparent quarrel could conceal a more serious crime.

records.l: the personation of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The personation of Lady Beatrice is a proposed and apparently enacted deception after her death: Holmes hypothesizes that Carrie Evans could arrange a substitute so Sir Robert could remain until after the Derby. Mr. Norlett then reportedly appeared as Lady Beatrice for weeks, until a black spaniel’s furious reaction exposed the disguise.

records.l: Mr. and Mrs. Norlett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: participate_in the personation of Lady Beatrice [as the two people who could substantiate Sir Robert's account] Mr. and Mrs. Norlett are brought by Sir Robert to substantiate his account. Mr. Norlett is an actor who personated Lady Beatrice, while Mrs. Norlett had been Lady Beatrice's confidential maid under her maiden name of Evans.

records.l: Lady Beatrice's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lady Beatrice died about a week before Holmes confronted Sir Robert, reportedly of dropsy; Sir Robert concealed the death and delayed registration, fearing financial ruin, until the Derby period ended.

records.l: the creditors, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Creditors delay their claims until the Derby can proceed, then are paid eighty thousand pounds in full from Sir Robert’s winnings after Lady Beatrice’s death.

records.l: the black spaniel (Lady Beatrice's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The black spaniel belongs to Lady Beatrice and recognizes her body. It mistakes a carriage passenger for its mistress, then attacks her skirt after recognizing a stranger; Sir Robert says he got rid of it after it followed him and Mr. Norlett moving Lady Beatrice's body.

records.l: the ancestral coffin (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains Lady Beatrice's body [formerly containing ancient human remains] Holmes finds an ancestral coffin standing near the vault entrance and opens it with a jemmy. It contains Lady Beatrice's body after Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett removed the ancient remains and burned them in a furnace.

records.l: Lady Beatrice's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lady Beatrice's body, a sheet-wrapped human corpse, is taken to an unused well-house, moved to chapel crypt, and temporarily placed by Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett in an ancestral coffin.

records.l: the financial crisis surrounding Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_caused_by the creditors [threatened seizure of Sir Robert's estate] Sir Robert faced ruin because he depended on Lady Beatrice's estate and was deeply indebted. His financial crisis centered on the prospect that creditors would seize his horses and prevent Shoscombe Prince from running, but the horse's Derby victory resolved the danger.

records.l: Sir Robert's concealment of the death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Sir Robert concealed Lady Beatrice's death for roughly three weeks so that Shoscombe Prince could run in the Derby and his bets could succeed. He arranged the public personation, hid the body in the chapel crypt, and delayed registering the death, receiving only mild censure afterward.

records.l: Josiah Amberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Josiah Amberley is a retired, old and miserly colourman, formerly junior partner of Brickfall and Amberley. At sixty-one he retires from business, owns and lives at The Haven in Lewisham, and marries Mrs. Amberley, twenty years his junior. Harsh, exacting, and regarded locally as a miser, he has chess as his only hobby and excels at it. After a financial loss, his jealousy of his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest becomes a frantic mania. He claims they fled together with his deed-box and about seven thousand pounds in cash and securities, but he has trapped and gassed them in his burglar-proof strong-room, hidden the securities, and later attempts suicide when questioned about the bodies.

records.l: Amberley's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Josiah Amberley’s younger, good-looking wife was made wretched by his niggardly ways and became involved with Dr. Ray Ernest. Amberley claimed she left with Ernest after taking his money and securities, but Holmes concluded Amberley murdered her in the strong-room.

records.l: Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Dr. Ray Ernest is a young, unmarried doctor living near Josiah Amberley who plays chess with him and visits The Haven. Suspected of leaving with Mrs. Amberley, he is identified as her companion; Holmes concludes Amberley murdered both Ernest and his wife.

records.l: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman concerns Sherlock Holmes's investigation of Josiah Amberley's claim that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared with stolen securities. Watson visits Amberley's home, The Haven, as Holmes suspects a hidden complication. The case ends with Amberley's arrest and evidence that the supposed elopement was murder.

records.l: Lewisham, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Lewisham is the London district where The Haven and Josiah Amberley's home are located. Dr. John Watson travels there to investigate Amberley's story.

records.l: the strong-room, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Before the theft, the strong-room contained stolen cash and securities. Its iron door and shutter could seal it almost hermetically, and an open gas pipe ended in the ceiling; Holmes identified it as a death-chamber.

records.l: green paint, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: conceals the gas [by masking its smell] The strong smell of paint was one of the first clues. Holmes inferred that Amberley was using it to conceal another smell, which he identified as the smell of gas connected with the murders.

records.l: the disappearance of Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: has_destination untraced Josiah Amberley reports that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest left together after she claimed to have a headache and remained at home while Amberley went alone to the Haymarket Theatre. Their destination is unknown, and neither has sent Amberley a letter or message.

records.l: the theft from the strong-room, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: involves the stolen cash and securities [approximately seven thousand pounds' worth] Amberley reports that about seven thousand pounds' worth of cash and securities were taken from his burglar-proof strong-room. He says Mrs. Amberley had a duplicate key and that the door and window were open when he returned from the theatre.

records.l: the investigation of Amberley's case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_referred_by Scotland Yard The investigation begins when the Yard sends Amberley to Sherlock Holmes after the police receive his report. Holmes delegates the initial visit to Dr. John Watson, gathers local information by telephone and through the Yard, and learns that Amberley was reputed to be a miser and harsh husband while Dr. Ernest had connections with both Amberley and his wife.

records.l: Mr. Barker, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: investigates the murders [independently and on behalf of Dr. Ray Ernest's family] Mr. Barker was a private investigator engaged by Dr. Ray Ernest's family. He independently suspected foul play, confronted Holmes while Holmes was entering Amberley's house, then helped Holmes restrain Amberley and took charge of formalities at the station.

records.l: Inspector MacKinnon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Inspector MacKinnon, a police inspector, investigates the murders, objects to Holmes’s irregular methods, accepts his evidence, orders a search, and receives newspaper credit for Holmes’s deductions.

records.l: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest were the couple whose disappearance Holmes investigated. Holmes concluded that they had been murdered by Amberley in the strong-room, and their bodies were expected to be found in a disused well.

records.l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: investigate the murders [through Inspector MacKinnon] The police had formed their own views of the case and were prepared to arrest Amberley. Three constables were sent to search the house, and the police took over the investigation after Holmes supplied his findings.

records.l: Little Purlington, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_in Essex [on a branch line] Little Purlington was a remote village in Essex on a branch line, reached by a slow train and a two-mile drive. Holmes used it as the destination for the forged telegram so Amberley could not return promptly to his house.

records.l: the Vicarage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_in Little Purlington The Vicarage at Little Purlington was the address named in the forged telegram. Its vicar, J. C. Elman, denied sending the telegram and said he had never heard of Amberley.

records.l: the murders, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The murders were planned by Amberley out of jealousy and revenge. Holmes believed he lured the victims into the strong-room, sealed them inside, and killed them by releasing gas.

records.l: the forged telegram, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: A forgery sent from Little Purlington, purporting to be from the Vicarage and signed Elman, summoned Amberley away so Holmes could search his house.

records.l: the gas pipe, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: delivers the gas [into the strong-room when the outside tap is turned] The gas pipe ran along the skirting, rose into the wall, and entered the strong-room. It ended openly in a ceiling rose, allowing the room to be flooded with gas from an outside tap.

records.l: the gas, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: Gas was released into the sealed strong-room, where Holmes said a person would have less than two minutes of conscious sensation. Its smell was partly concealed by the smell of paint.

records.l: the two bodies, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: are_found_in the disused well [concealed by a dog-kennel] The two bodies were those of Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest. Holmes directed the police to search the cellars and garden, especially for a disused well where the bodies could not be far away.

records.l: the disused well, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: contains the two bodies [concealed by a dog-kennel] The disused well was identified by Holmes as the likely place where the two bodies had been hidden. The newspaper later reported that the bodies were found there, concealed by a dog-kennel.

records.l: the wall message, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: The wall message, written in purple indelible pencil above the strong-room skirting, begins "We we----" and remains unfinished; Holmes interprets it as "We were murdered," recording the murders.

records.l: the suicide attempt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
records.s: is_a suicide attempt [made with a white pellet] The suicide attempt occurred when Amberley tried to swallow a white pellet after Holmes asked what he had done with the bodies. Holmes restrained him and forced the matter to proceed through the proper legal process.

In the year 1878 I took my degree of Doctor of Medicine of the University of London, and proceeded to Netley to go through the course prescribed for surgeons in the army. Having completed my studies there, I was duly attached to the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers as Assistant Surgeon. The regiment was stationed in India at the time, and before I could join it, the second Afghan war had broken out. On landing at Bombay, I learned that my corps had advanced through the passes, and was already deep in the enemy’s country. I followed, however, with many other officers who were in the same situation as myself, and succeeded in reaching Candahar in safety, where I found my regiment, and at once entered upon my new duties. CHAPTER I.
MR. SHERLOCK HOLMES.


In the year 1878 I took my degree of Doctor of Medicine of the
University of London, and proceeded to Netley to go through the course
prescribed for surgeons in the army. Having completed my studies there,
I was duly attached to the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers as Assistant
Surgeon. The regiment was stationed in India at the time, and before I
could join it, the second Afghan war had broken out. On landing at
Bombay, I learned that my corps had advanced through the passes, and
was already deep in the enemy’s country. I followed, however, with many
other officers who were in the same situation as myself, and succeeded
in reaching Candahar in safety, where I found my regiment, and at once
entered upon my new duties.

The campaign brought honours and promotion to many, but for me it had
nothing but misfortune and disaster. I was removed from my brigade and
attached to the Berkshires, with whom I served at the fatal battle of

I was dispatched, accordingly, in the troopship “Orontes,” and landed a month later on Portsmouth jetty, with my health irretrievably ruined, but with permission from a paternal government to spend the next nine months in attempting to improve it. I had neither kith nor kin in England, and was therefore as free as air—or as free as an income of eleven shillings and sixpence a day will permit a man to be. Under such circumstances, I naturally gravitated to London, that great cesspool into which all the loungers and idlers of the Empire are irresistibly drained. records.s: that I soon realized that I must either leave the metropolis and rusticate somewhere in the country, or that I must make a complete alteration in my style of living. Choosing the latter alternative, I began by making up my mind to leave the hotel, and to take up my quarters in some less pretentious and less expensive domicile. On the very day that I had come to this conclusion, I was standing at the Criterion Bar, when some one tapped me on the shoulder, and turning round I recognized young Stamford, who had been a dresser under me at Barts. So desirable in every way were the apartments, and so moderate did the terms seem when divided between us, that the bargain was concluded upon the spot, and we at once entered into possession. Like all other arts, the Science of Deduction and Analysis is one which can only be acquired by long and patient study nor, is life long enough to allow any mortal to attain the highest possible perfection in it. Before turning to those moral and mental aspects of the matter which present the greatest difficulties, let the enquirer begin by mastering more elementary problems. Let him, on meeting a fellow-mortal, learn at a glance to distinguish the history of the man, and the trade or profession to which he belongs. house-tops, looking like the reflection of the mud-coloured streets
beneath. My companion was in the best of spirits, and prattled away
about Cremona fiddles, and the difference between a Stradivarius and an
Amati. As for myself, I was silent, for the dull weather and the
melancholy business upon which we were engaged, depressed my spirits.

“You don’t seem to give much thought to the matter in hand,” I said at
last, interrupting Holmes’ musical disquisition.

“No data yet,” he answered. “It is a capital mistake to theorize before
you have all the evidence. It biases the judgment.”

“You will have your data soon,” I remarked, pointing with my finger;
“this is the Brixton Road, and that is the house, if I am not very much
mistaken.”

“So it is. Stop, driver, stop!” We were still a hundred yards or so
from it, but he insisted upon our alighting, and we finished our

His hands were clenched and his arms thrown abroad, while his lower limbs were interlocked as though his death struggle had been a grievous one. On his rigid face there stood an expression of horror, and as it seemed to me, of hatred, such as I have never seen upon human features. This malignant and terrible contortion, combined with the low forehead, blunt nose, and prognathous jaw gave the dead man a singularly simious and ape-like appearance, which was increased by his writhing, unnatural posture. CHAPTER IV.
WHAT JOHN RANCE HAD TO TELL.


It was one o’clock when we left No. 3, Lauriston Gardens. Sherlock
Holmes led me to the nearest telegraph office, whence he dispatched a
long telegram. He then hailed a cab, and ordered the driver to take us
to the address given us by Lestrade.

“There is nothing like first hand evidence,” he remarked; “as a matter
of fact, my mind is entirely made up upon the case, but still we may as
well learn all that is to be learned.”

“You amaze me, Holmes,” said I. “Surely you are not as sure as you
pretend to be of all those particulars which you gave.”

“There’s no room for a mistake,” he answered. “The very first thing
which I observed on arriving there was that a cab had made two ruts
with its wheels close to the curb. Now, up to last night, we have had
no rain for a week, so that those wheels which left such a deep
impression must have been there during the night. There were the marks
of the horse’s hoofs, too, the

records.s: wheels which left such a deep impression must have been there during the night. There were the marks of the horse’s hoofs, too, the outline of one of which was far more clearly cut than that of the other three, showing that that was a new shoe. Since the cab was there after the rain began, and was not there at any time during the morning—I have Gregson’s word for that—it follows that it must have been there during the night, and, therefore, that it brought those two individuals to the house.” “That seems simple enough,” said I; “but how about the other man’s height?” “Why, the height of a man, in nine cases out of ten, can be told from the length of his stride. CHAPTER V.
OUR ADVERTISEMENT BRINGS A VISITOR.


Our morning’s exertions had been too much for my weak health, and I was
tired out in the afternoon. After Holmes’ departure for the concert, I
lay down upon the sofa and endeavoured to get a couple of hours’ sleep.
It was a useless attempt. My mind had been too much excited by all that
had occurred, and the strangest fancies and surmises crowded into it.
Every time that I closed my eyes I saw before me the distorted
baboon-like countenance of the murdered man. So sinister was the
impression which that face had produced upon me that I found it
difficult to feel anything but gratitude for him who had removed its
owner from the world. If ever

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: that face had produced upon me that I found it difficult to feel anything but gratitude for him who had removed its owner from the world. If ever human features bespoke vice of the most malignant type, they were certainly those of Enoch J. Drebber, of Cleveland. Still I recognized that justice must be done, and that the depravity of the victim was no condonement in the eyes of the law. The more I thought of it the more extraordinary did my companion’s hypothesis, that the man had been poisoned, appear. I remembered how he had sniffed his lips, and had no doubt that he had detected something which had given rise to the idea. Then, again, if not poison, what had caused the man’s death, since there was neither wound nor marks of strangulation? But, on the other hand, whose blood was that which lay so thickly upon the floor? There were no signs of a struggle, nor had the victim any weapon with which he might have wounded an antagonist. As long as all these questions were unsolved, I felt that sleep would be no easy matter, either for Holmes or myself. His quiet self-conf

CHAPTER VI.
TOBIAS GREGSON SHOWS WHAT HE CAN DO.


The papers next day were full of the “Brixton Mystery,” as they termed
it. Each had a long account of the affair, and some had leaders upon it
in addition. There was some information in them which was new to me. I
still retain in my scrap-book numerous clippings and extracts bearing
upon the case. Here is a condensation of a few of them:—

The _Daily Telegraph_ remarked that in the history of crime there had
seldom been a tragedy which presented stranger features. The German
name of the victim, the absence of all other motive, and the sinister
inscription on the wall,

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: a tragedy which presented stranger features. The German name of the victim, the absence of all other motive, and the sinister inscription on the wall, all pointed to its perpetration by political refugees and revolutionists. The Socialists had many branches in America, and the deceased had, no doubt, infringed their unwritten laws, and been tracked down by them. After alluding airily to the Vehmgericht, aqua tofana, Carbonari, the Marchioness de Brinvilliers, the Darwinian theory, the principles of Malthus, and the Ratcliff Highway murders, the article concluded by admonishing the Government and advocating a closer watch over foreigners in England. The _Standard_ commented upon the fact that lawless outrages of the sort usually occurred under a Liberal Administration. PART II.
_The Country of the Saints._




CHAPTER I.
ON THE GREAT ALKALI PLAIN.


In the central portion of the great North American Continent there lies
an arid and repulsive desert, which for many a long year served as a
barrier against the advance of civilisation. From the Sierra Nevada to
Nebraska, and from the Yellowstone River in the north to the Colorado
upon the south, is a region of desolation and silence. Nor is Nature
always in one mood throughout this grim district. It comprises
snow-capped and lofty mountains, and dark and gloomy valleys. There are
swift-flowing rivers which dash through jagged cañons; and there are
enormous plains, which in winter are white with snow, and in summer are
grey with the saline alkali dust. They all preserve, however, the
common characteristics of barrenness, inhospitality, and misery.

There are no inhabitants of this land of despair. A band of Pawnees or
of Blackfeet may occasionally traverse it in order to reach other

records.s: misery. There are no inhabitants of this land of despair. A band of Pawnees or of Blackfeet may occasionally traverse it in order to reach other hunting-grounds, but the hardiest of the braves are glad to lose sight of those awesome plains, and to find themselves once more upon their prairies. The coyote skulks among the scrub, the buzzard flaps heavily through the air, and the clumsy grizzly bear lumbers through the dark ravines, and picks up such sustenance as it can amongst the rocks. These are the sole dwellers in the wilderness. In the whole world there can be no more dreary view than that from the northern slope of the Sierra Blanco. As far as the eye can reach stretches the great flat plain-land, all dusted over with patches of alkali, and intersected by clumps of the dwarfish chaparral bushes. On the extreme verge of the horizon lie a long chain of mountain peaks, with their rugged summits flecked with snow. In this great stretch of country there is no sign of life, nor of anything appertaining to life. There is no bird in the steel-blue heaven,

There is no bird in the steel-blue heaven, no movement upon the dull, grey earth—above all, there is absolute silence. Listen as one may, there is no shadow of a sound in all that mighty wilderness; nothing but silence—complete and heart-subduing silence. It has been said there is nothing appertaining to life upon the broad plain. That is hardly true. Looking down from the Sierra Blanco, one sees a pathway traced out across the desert, which winds away and is lost in the extreme distance. It is rutted with wheels and trodden down by the feet of many adventurers. Here and there there are scattered white objects which glisten in the sun, and stand out against the dull deposit of alkali. Approach, and examine them! They are bones: some large and coarse, others smaller and more delicate. The former have belonged to oxen, and the latter to men. For fifteen hundred miles one may trace this ghastly caravan route by these scattered remains of those who had fallen by the wayside. Looking down on this very scene

Looking down on this very scene, there stood upon the fourth of May, eighteen hundred and forty-seven, a solitary traveller. His appearance was such that he might have been the very genius or demon of the region. An observer would have found it difficult to say whether he was nearer to forty or to sixty. His face was lean and haggard, and the brown parchment-like skin was drawn tightly over the projecting bones; his long, brown hair and beard were all flecked and dashed with white; his eyes were sunken in his head, and burned with an unnatural lustre; while the hand which grasped his rifle was hardly more fleshy than that of a skeleton. As he stood, he leaned upon his weapon for support, and yet his tall figure and the massive framework of his bones suggested a wiry and vigorous constitution. Far away on the extreme verge of the alkali plain there rose up a little spray of dust, very slight at first, and hardly to be distinguished from the mists of the distance, but gradually growing higher and broader until it formed a solid, well-defined cloud. This cloud continued to increase in size until it became evident that it could only be raised by a great multitude of moving creatures. Right across the enormous plain stretched the straggling array, waggons and carts, men on horseback, and men on foot. On the little plateau which crowned the barren hill there stood a single giant boulder, and against this boulder there lay a tall man, long-bearded and hard-featured, but of an excessive thinness. His placid face and regular breathing showed that he was fast asleep. Beside him lay a little child, with her round white arms encircling his brown sinewy neck, and her golden haired head resting upon the breast of his velveteen tunic. Her plump little white legs terminating in white socks and neat shoes with shining buckles, offered a strange contrast to the long shrivelled members of her companion. Young speedily proved himself to be a skilful administrator as well as a resolute chief. Maps were drawn and charts prepared, in which the future city was sketched out. records.s: of John Ferrier. There was one way and only one in which he offended the susceptibilities of his co-religionists. No argument or persuasion could ever induce him to set up a female establishment after the manner of his companions. He never gave reasons for this persistent refusal, but contented himself by resolutely and inflexibly adhering to his determination. There were some who accused him of lukewarmness in his adopted religion, and others who put it down to greed of wealth and reluctance to incur expense. Others, again, spoke of some early love affair, and of a fair-haired girl who had pined away on the shores of the Atlantic. Whatever the reason, Ferrier remained strictly celibate. CHAPTER III.
JOHN FERRIER TALKS WITH THE PROPHET.


Three weeks had passed since Jefferson Hope and his comrades had
departed from Salt Lake City. John Ferrier’s heart was sore within him
when he thought of the young man’s return, and of the impending loss of
his adopted child. Yet her bright and happy face reconciled him to the
arrangement more than any argument could have done. He had always
determined, deep down in his resolute heart, that nothing would ever
induce him to allow his daughter to wed a Mormon.

records.s: He had always determined, deep down in his resolute heart, that nothing would ever induce him to allow his daughter to wed a Mormon. Such a marriage he regarded as no marriage at all, but as a shame and a disgrace. Whatever he might think of the Mormon doctrines, upon that one point he was inflexible. He had to seal his mouth on the subject, however, for to express an unorthodox opinion was a dangerous matter in those days in the Land of the Saints. Yes, a dangerous matter—so dangerous that even the most saintly dared only whisper their religious opinions with bated breath, lest something which fell from their lips might be misconstrued, and bring down a swift retribution upon them. The victims of persecution had now turned persecutors on their own account, and persecutors of the most terrible description. appeared in the harems of the Elders—women who pined and wept, and bore
upon their faces the traces of an unextinguishable horror. Belated
wanderers upon the mountains spoke of gangs of armed men, masked,
stealthy, and noiseless, who flitted by them in the darkness. These
tales and rumours took substance and shape, and were corroborated and
re-corroborated, until they resolved themselves into a definite name.
To this day, in the lonely ranches of the West, the name of the Danite
Band, or the Avenging Angels, is a sinister and an ill-omened one.

THE AVENGING ANGELS.

entirely

records.l: A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
records.s: to be suspended over their heads, and to need only a gust of wind to come hurtling down upon them. Nor was the fear entirely an illusion, for the barren valley was thickly strewn with trees and boulders which had fallen in a similar manner. Even as they passed, a great rock came thundering down with a hoarse rattle which woke the echoes in the silent gorges, and startled the weary horses into a gallop. As the sun rose slowly above the eastern horizon, the caps of the great mountains lit up one after the other, like lamps at a festival, until they were all ruddy and glowing. The magnificent spectacle cheered the hearts of the three fugitives and gave them fresh energy. For some months Jefferson Hope lingered among the mountains, leading a
strange wild life, and nursing in his heart the fierce desire for
vengeance which possessed him. Tales were told in the City of the weird
figure which was seen prowling about the suburbs, and which haunted the
lonely mountain gorges. Once a bullet whistled through Stangerson’s
window and flattened itself upon the wall within a foot of him. On
another occasion, as Drebber passed under a cliff a great b

records.s: erson’s window and flattened itself upon the wall within a foot of him. On another occasion, as Drebber passed under a cliff a great boulder crashed down on him, and he only escaped a terrible death by throwing himself upon his face. The two young Mormons were not long in discovering the reason of these attempts upon their lives, and led repeated expeditions into the mountains in the hope of capturing or killing their enemy, but always without success. Then they adopted the precaution of never going out alone or after nightfall, and of having their houses guarded. After a time they were able to relax these measures, for nothing was either heard or seen of their opponent, and they hoped that time had cooled his vindictiveness. Far from doing so, it had, if anything, augmented it. The hunter’s mind was of a hard, unyielding nature, and the predominant idea of revenge had taken such complete possession of it that there was no room for any other emotion. He was, however, above all things practical. He soon realized that even his iron constitution could not stand the incessant strain which he was putting upon it.

There was a hansom just in front of me, and he hailed it. I followed it so close that the nose of my horse was within a yard of his driver the whole way. records.s: he showed his students some alkaloid, as he called it, which he had extracted from some South American arrow poison, and which was so powerful that the least grain meant instant death. I spotted the bottle in which this preparation was kept, and when they were all gone, I helped myself to a little of it. I was a fairly good dispenser, so I worked this alkaloid into small, soluble pills, and each pill I put in a box with a similar pill made without the poison. I determined at the time that when I had my chance, my gentlemen should each have a draw out of one of these boxes, while I ate the pill that remained. It would be quite as deadly, and a good deal less noisy than firing across a handkerchief. He staggered back with a livid face, and I saw the perspiration break out upon his brow, while his teeth chattered in his head. At the sight, I leaned my back against the door and laughed loud and long. I had always known that vengeance would be sweet, but I had never hoped for the contentment of soul which now possessed me. “‘You dog!’ I said; ‘I have hunted you from Salt Lake City to St. Petersburg, and you have always escaped me. Now, at last your wanderings have come to an end, for either you or I shall never see to-morrow’s sun rise.’ He shrunk still further away as I spoke, and I could see on his face that he thought I was mad. So I was for the time. I soon found out which was the window of his bedroom, and early next morning I took advantage of some ladders which were lying in the lane behind the hotel, and so made my way into his room in the grey of the dawn. I woke him up and told him that the hour had come when he was to answer for the life he had taken so long before. I described Drebber’s death to him, and I gave him the same choice of the poisoned pills. Instead of grasping at the chance of safety which that offered him, he sprang from his bed and flew at my throat. In self-defence I stabbed him to the heart. It would have been the same in any case, for Providence would never have allowed his guilty hand to pick out anything but the poison. “I have little more to say, and it’s as well, for I am about done up. his hypodermic syringe from its neat morocco case. With his long,
white, nervous fingers he adjusted the delicate needle, and rolled back
his left shirt-cuff. For some little time his eyes rested thoughtfully
upon the sinewy forearm and wrist all dotted and scarred with
innumerable puncture-marks. Finally he thrust the sharp point home,
pressed down the tiny piston, and sank back into the velvet-lined
arm-chair with a long sigh of satisfaction.

Three times a day for many months I had witnessed this performance, but

Three times a day for many months I had witnessed this performance, but custom had not reconciled my mind to it. On the contrary, from day to day I had become more irritable at the sight, and my conscience swelled nightly within me at the thought that I had lacked the courage to protest. Inside, a gravel path wound through desolate grounds to a huge clump of
a house, square and prosaic, all plunged in shadow save where a
moonbeam struck one corner and glimmered in a garret window. The vast
size of the building, with its gloom and its deathly silence, struck a
chill to the heart. Even Thaddeus Sholto seemed ill at ease, and the
lantern quivered and rattled in his hand.

“I cannot understand it,” he said. “There must be some mistake. I
distinctly told Bartholomew that we should be here, and yet there is no
light in his window. I do not know what to make of it.”

“Does he always guard the premises in this way?” asked Holmes.

“Yes; he has followed my father’s custom. He was the favourite son, you
know, and I sometimes think that my father may have told him more than

records.s: , and in this I escorted Miss Morstan back to her home. After the angelic fashion of women, she had borne trouble with a calm face as long as there was some one weaker than herself to support, and I had found her bright and placid by the side of the frightened housekeeper. In the cab, however, she first turned faint, and then burst into a passion of weeping,—so sorely had she been tried by the adventures of the night. She has told me since that she thought me cold and distant upon that journey. She little guessed the struggle within my breast, or the effort of self-restraint which held me back. My sympathies and my love went out to her, even as my hand had in the garden. I felt that years of the conventionalities of life could not teach me to know her sweet, brave nature as had this one day of strange experiences. Yet there were two thoughts which sealed the words of affection upon my lips. She was weak and helpless, shaken in mind and nerve. It was to take her at a disadvantage to obtrude love upon her at such a time. Worse still, she was rich. If Hol

I explained, however, the importance of my errand, and promised faithfully to call and report any progress which we might make with the case. As we drove away I stole a glance back, and I still seem to see that little group on the step, the two graceful, clinging figures, the half-opened door, the hall-light shining through stained glass, the barometer, and the bright stair-rods. Chapter VIII The Baker Street Irregulars “What now?” I asked. “Toby has lost his character for infallibility.” “He acted according to his lights,” said Holmes, lifting him down from the barrel and walking him out of the timber-yard. “If you consider how much creasote is carted about London in one day, it is no great wonder that our trail should have been crossed. “By heaven, Holmes,” I said, half rising, “I believe that they are
really after us.”

“No, it’s not quite so bad as that. It is the unofficial force,—the
Baker Street irregulars.”

As he spoke, there came a swift pattering of naked feet upon the
stairs, a clatter of high voices, and in rushed a dozen dirty and
ragged little street-Arabs. There was some show of discipline among
them, despite their tumultuous entry, for they instantly drew up in
line and stood facing us with expectant faces. One of their number,
taller and older than the others, stood forward with an air of lounging
superiority which was very funny in such a disreputable little
scarecrow.

“Got your message, sir,” said he, “and brought ’em on sharp. Three bob
and a tanner for tickets.”

report to you, Wiggins, and you to me. I cannot have the house invaded

This, there could be no question, was the same that had contained the ill-omened treasure of the Sholtos. Chapter XII
The Strange Story of Jonathan Small


A very patient man was that inspector in the cab, for it was a weary
time before I rejoined him. His face clouded over when I showed him the
empty box.

“There goes the reward!” said he, gloomily. “Where there is no money
there is no pay. This night’s work would have been worth a tenner each
to Sam Brown and me if the treasure had been there.”

“Mr. Thaddeus Sholto is a rich man,” I said. “He will see that you are
rewarded, treasure or no.”

The inspector shook his head despondently, however. “It’s a bad job,”
he repeated; “and so Mr. Athelney Jones will think.”

His forecast proved to be correct, for the detective looked blank
enough when I got to Baker Street and showed him the empty box. They
had only just arrived, Holmes, the prisoner, and he, for they had
changed their plans so far as to report themselves at a station upon
the way. My companion lounged in his arm-chair with his usual listless
expression, while Small

My companion lounged in his arm-chair with his usual listless expression, while Small sat stolidly opposite to him with his wooden leg cocked over his sound one. As I exhibited the empty box he leaned back in his chair and laughed aloud. “This is your doing, Small,” said Athelney Jones, angrily. “Yes, I have put it away where you shall never lay hand upon it,” he cried, exultantly. “It is my treasure; and if I can’t have the loot I’ll take darned good care that no one else does.
